Example Reflection – Visualization

Challenge and Selection

Visualization is used in my daily work life to communicate and organize thought  in different ways. Using visual thinking enhances the way we see things. Since  working at a publishing company, I use this approach with workers and clients.

During a project at work a client wanted to rearrange his entire branding  strategy one week before his launch, a project we were working on for almost  five weeks. We delivered the first draft of the project which he approved and  then a few weeks after he was unhappy, so we were tasked in redoing the  entire project over in less than a week.

Application

I began the entire process by first doodling his new changes, then we  compared it with other successful designs from this and other clients, comparing  feedback and feedforwards. Then we put all our ideas together on the drawing  board.

With this strategy the client was ultimately thrilled with the new plan, including  the new ideas that were included.

Insight and Approach

I believe we became overconfident with our first ideas on the project at the  time, and that I did not check in with the client until almost the last week. I have  now learned to always check in with clients on a weekly basis.

Name: Bilal Sajid

Mind Mapping

Challenge:

Managing the starting up and opening of a restaurant business, all by myself.   (An appropriate title would be: ‘Project manager without a project team’)   Three years ago, I was hired as a project manager by a small businessman  to manage sales and inventory of a restaurant. Turns out, construction of the  restaurant has just begun. It was a long way from its first opening. Since, it was  a small business restaurant, I found it intriguing to see the whole process of the  start-up. So, I proposed to help manage the start-up by negotiating with the  business owner. The owner counted on me and handed over the entire project  for me handle. From exterior & interior designing to managing sales and  stocking kitchen & food supplies, I had to manage everything and time was  running out. I had been informed that only 8 months had been remaining in the  first opening. Knowing it was not a one-man job, I decided to take on the  challenge to gain experience.

Name: Bilal Sajid

Selection:   Given a vast variety of different tasks with dependencies related to restaurant  design and stocking inventory, I decided to use mind-mapping as a way to  organize all the work. The visualization aspect of mind-mapping helps to keep  track of tasks/activities and the order of completion for each of them.  (Mind mapping) I initiate by placing the main task in center and then divide it  into sub-tasks. Sub-tasks are ordered in hierarchically. I start working on the  lowest order activities and work my way up from there. Mind mapping is best  suited for me as it is a way to link key tasks using images, and lines to link them  according to their relations.    Moreover, mind mapping is a powerful apparatus for taking notes and for better  agreement and learning information. It is easy to utilize while examining or  consolidating any given task in life.       Application:   In the beginning, I assessed the work under construction to see which tasks are  being done and what is left. I separated the dependent and independent tasks  so I can manage them more efficiently. Given a time crunch of 8 months, I opted  to pursue a Scrum approach to the project. As, I did not have any particular  team to work with, I decided to push myself to the limits to see how much work I  can get done. I arranged 3 face-to-face meetings with the business owner each  week. Moreover, secondary conversation was done on phone and on  WhatsApp. I arranged plumbers, painters, safety regulators during construction.  I had the duty of arranging the required supplies for these jobs as well. So I  listed them all and linked them in a hierarchy using an online Mind Mapping  software tool. In the face-to-face meetings, the business owner would select  designs of materials and assign me to look for them and inform him. In doing so,  he would also advise me about the budget. So, I had to manage cost for the  purchases as well. I used Microsoft Excel to manage all numerical data.  A few months pass and the restaurant construction work gets finished. All this  time I enjoyed the knowledge and experience gain in surveying markets for  construction material and designing. BUT I knew that my work has just begun,  for which I was hired for, i.e. to manage sales and inventory of a restaurant.  The restaurant is finally open. In the beginning, the owner decided that it would  be better if I learn to make coffee and sandwiches as he was impressed by my  work ethics and learning capabilities. Having learned them quickly I was  unofficially a barista at the restaurant as well. Meanwhile, creating an inventory  for items, keeping track of weekly and daily purchased items, finances,  arranging and interviewing staff for hiring were some of the tasks that I had

Name: Bilal Sajid

coming. By using mind mapping, it allowed me to brainstorm faster task  completion with more efficiency. The more I used mind-mapping, the more the  business owner got impressed by my managing ability. In 2 years, the  restaurant turned into a successful business. Today, there are three branches of  the same restaurant and I am officially the manager of the first branch. Here’s a  small example of the mind map I had used.

Insight:   Mind mapping can be helped me in improving my memory and manage my  work with ease. This is because mind mapping helps visualize images and links  in our mind by drawing and adding pictures, lines and links.      Approach:   Provided that I was given plentiful tasks in hand that were co-related, choosing  mind-mapping was the appropriate decision. Basically, I had keywords and  ideas of tasks along with pictures, linked together, making the relation and order  or implementing the tasks, prominent.

Example Reflection – Learning Launch

Challenge

I am currently in the testing phase of my start-up Clean Team (http://mcneil.org/list/taghomepage.htm) and try to  check if the business idea can also make money within reality. The question, in  general, is if our business can create more interest online than average competitors  and if it is economically feasible to set-up this business and create/buy customers  through social media marketing. Next to it, I am still in the phase of showing a  business potential and telling an impactful story to inspire others to participate with  me and become co-founders.

Selection

I have already set-up hypotheses and assumptions about value and created a  prototype see here http://mcneil.org/list/taghomepage.htm. The target now is to test if this idea, with its  current underlying assumptions and hypothesis, can create enough engagement  through a social media marketing test to make money to productize it.

Application

For this learning launch, we focus on the possible engagement we can create  through social media marketing. This means we set-up a social media campaign.  People will see online some ads of our product and brand with its value propositions.  The big question is if we can create with X amount of euro enough engagement, that  the KPI of CPC (Cost per Click) and CTR (Click Through Rate) is better than the  competition, and it makes economic sense. Economically sense in this context  means we can create x more money from an engaged user through social media  than it costs.

The two main parameters which are interesting for us are

CPC – Cost per Click: How much does it cost that one user clicks on a social media  ad

CTR: CTR of people who click on our ad and get to our landing page. CTR of people  who leave their e-mail addresses.

Insight

We quickly identified that the CPC and CTR (landing page) was quite right, but not  many people left their e-mail addresses. Next to this, we identified that nearly all  mobile users left the website quickly. After an analysis, we identified that our mobile  landing page version had no excellent performance. In general, we learned from the  first test that there is a market interest, it seems economically feasible, but our  landing page has a bad performance. In the next learning launch, we want to check  again if the market interest exists and enough engagement with the more performant  landing page.

Approach

The next time it would do everything more systematically based on design thinking  and get some experts on board early to help with technical topics like the landing  page.

Kaur Rubio

Mind Mapping to identify Automation Opportunities

Design Thinking for Innovation by UVA Darden on Coursera

BY: Uwe Bas

21 Feb 2021

Challenge/Selection  I use the Mind Mapping often in defining a customer problem space when seeking to look at areas  where we can automate. Taking a customer centered approach to map out to the various stakeholders  and look at internal/external factors. Whenever presented with a customer problem I will build the  problem space. The challenges the team faces and mapping out how Automation can affect various  processes, value-chains and teams. It serves as a more engaging way than going through reports and  data. David Kelley, the founder of IDEO said, when I want to do something analytical, I make a list. When  I am trying to do something creative, I make a mind-map.

Application  I start the process by creating an overview of the value chain in the problem space and some select  focus areas based on understanding of the environment or other material. The understanding of the  environment is from a pre-work assessment and some interviews. Other material includes market  insights and our teams own automation expertise. The mind map is split into Above/Below the waterline  like a duck what the customer sees – Above the waterline vs what the customer does not see – Below  the waterline.

For the activity, we walk through the process at a high level and focus number of transactions and time  taken per transaction and high-level steps and applications used. After this initial walk-through, we do a  deeper dive on the key candidates looking at hand-off screens and data that is required to carry out the  activity. This allows us to exit the activity with a number of automation opportunity areas and some  candidates for automation.

Insights & Approach  What we have learned from these activities over the last 3 years is that people are engaged and they  openly share the challenges they see with the process. Also with the focus early on internal/external  factors, the team is able also identify areas of opportunity in other areas. We are always looking for  ways to improve how we carry out the exercises to drive better engagement. The team have built 100s  of automations and I have conducted 40 of these workshops. I approach this with a customer-centered  approach to reimagine tomorrow with automation.

Reflection – Stakeholder Mind Mapping

By Melvin Lu

Challenge

As a Senior Manager of a Shared Service Center(SSC) I work with multiple stakeholders for multiple  countries across Asia Pacific region for an FMCG company. Challenge on hand was the Quality of  operations that I run. Stakeholder including business in the country were really not happy with the  Finance Services delivered and constantly saw SSC as a task oriented team which really impacted the  morale of the employees who felt too disengaged with what they did. With the dissatisfaction of the  business it really impacted future projects which had a lot of dependency on upstream processes to  achieve the larger Finance Strategies. Missing deadlines on implementing/executing Finance Strategies  was not an option and we as a team were given 2 Quarters only to turn it around. Hence it was decided  to come up with a Design Thinking strategy which is scientific and can provide results too.

Selection

With several tools at our disposal, we as a team felt Mind Mapping for our stakeholders would be the  key tool to understand the AS IS situation and current minds of our stakeholders. We also understood it  was a ‘what is’ phase and not a ‘what if’. And since we had multiple stakeholders it was important for us  as a team to look for patterns through this tool.

Application

I invited all of my Direct Reports who are SSC country managers and managed these stakeholders  directly day in day out. Since we were 16 of us so we formed 4 groups of 4 each. I took my team through  the broad Design Thinking process for the first 1 hour and then discussed the tool we specifically chose  for the same. We assigned a white board to each group and gave 45 minutes for them to list out what  feedback we received from our stakeholders in terms of what they think, what they feel, what they say  and what they do. Another 15 minutes for the group to summarize and structure their exercise for a  teach back to the other 3 groups.

Once all groups had their white boards filled up with the sticky notes I asked the groups to walk around  and read what other groups had captured. Post the walkaround, I asked them to cluster the feedback  onto the 5th white board to look for patterns and most common ones and start bucketizing them into  themes such as People, Process, Data and Technology. Post this we worked as team to draft the  meaningful insight statement. While we didn’t had solution in mind but at least reached to a stage  where we felt where to start from. In our another session we firmed up the insight statement and  involved representatives from the country too who were in essence our business stakeholders and run it  pass through them to take their buy-in.

Insight

This exercise really made a huge difference in involving our teams together and looked at problems with  a wholistic view. It brought the sense of togetherness and the spirit of working as a team. We could  capture closure to reality feedback through the Mind Mapping exercise. This session was a stepping  stone for us to work on Idea Generation phase. Under each theme listed in Application stage garnered  ideas which were again bucketized under Process, People, Data and Technology. In collaboration with  our Management we started to assign timelines to these project ideas and started to prioritize them in  terms of efficiency and effective through feasibility study. Overall it was such a methodical process  which really helped teams looked at problem in a more strategic way.

Approach

I would like use Story telling and Visualization Tool in my day to day experience too. Would also like to  improvise my workshops in future. Reason why I want to work on Story telling tool is because I feel it  will also help me in my articulation of a problem better in sharing the purpose of the idea  implementation which basically is the cause. Visualization is also in a way connected to your story telling  and I am very certain if your visualization is strong your story telling will be very effective. Those were  my ideas overall.

Written by Rita Francois as final assessment of the course Design Thinking and Innovation   offered by the University of Virginia at the platform of Coursera.org

Reflection - Visualization

Challenge & Selection

At the beginning of my internship as an HR Assistant I noticed that the HR department  stored data at different places on their network. Sometimes it took them a while to find  certain information about their employees, which was time-consuming and very ineffective.  The existing file where they kept track of the attended trainings had become difficult to use  over the past few years. This was due to the fact that some data were manually entered,  which led to different ways of writing, typos and inconsistency. As my internship went on, I  discovered other administrative problems as well. I asked myself whether I could help them  solve their problems in an efficient way. I decided to focus on simplifying a part of the HR  department’s administrative process. I used design thinking to accomplish my goal. Since I  knew that the HR team was not used to work with a lot of technology I had to make  everything more tangible by creating a logical structure using a lot of images and making  everything as simple as I could. The main tool that I used was visualization.

Application

I had a conversation with my mentor to have a better idea of her expectations. I started  drawing some ideas and presented them to the team. After they gave me some feedback I  had an even better understanding of their needs. I started by filtering all the data, making a  distinction between the necessary data and the redundant data. After that I started creating  a database: a structure in which data only needs to be entered once.

To make the database easy to use and to visualize as much as possible, I created a  switchboard (a main interface) that gave access to all underlying forms and reports (in one  single click). The macros that I included were made of little drawings that made it very easy  to return to the switchboard.

I explained all the technicalities in a well-structured and visual manual so the HR team can  continue to simplify and automate their administrative processes.

When I finished the project and before I presented the manual to the team, I placed myself  in the minds of my colleagues. I knew and understood the tool that had created but they did  not. It was crucial to include more visual elements in the manual so the team would clearly  understand the functionalities of this new database. Therefore, I also created user stories.

With this in mind, I had the idea of re-building the old way of registration with Lego cubes  and the new database with Duplo cubes (to have a better idea of what I mean I included a  photo on the next page). Each cube in the front contains data from different categories. The  blue cube i.e. contains personal information (that comes from the green cubes in the back),  information on training courses (that comes from the yellow cubes) and information on  training courses (that comes from the red cubes). The database provides a link structure (if  you look closely at the picture you can see some wires). These categories can be linked to  each other. In addition, relationships with primary keys can be selected. Of course I was  using a lot of hand gestures while explaining this and as you can see from the blue cube at  the side of the panel, I was holding it during the presentation, so that I could show it more  visually.

Written by Rita Francois as final assessment of the course Design Thinking and Innovation   offered by the University of Virginia at the platform of Coursera.org

Insight & Approach

When I presented the manual and the cubes to the team I realized that it really depends on  the type of learner that I have in front of me because there are some profiles that are more  visual than others. I decided to adjust the strategy and to take visualization to the next level  by organizing 5 workshops that allowed me to conduct the team through the actual workings  of the database.

Later I also got to the idea to not only visualize how to use the tool but also why they should  continue using it. I tried to stimulate them in a different way. I made it very evident to the  leadership team that this database would represent savings to the company.

I cannot say that I would use this tool again in the future for this type of project seeing that  it depends on the public you are working with. In my case, I adjusted the strategy based on  the type of profile that I had in front of me as future users.

Peer-graded Assignment: Reflection

Jimena

30-12-20

The Challenge

During my current assignment as the Zonal Business Manager at my organization, I was presented with a  problem statement of designing the communication material around a new product, an entertainment  application, which was a supplement to our voice and data services based portfolio. It was launched in  lieu of creating differentiation and customer loyalty in the highly competitive and now consolidated  telecom sector.

The product of such a type was essential in the current scenario as pricing has been disrupted by a new  market entrant, and the products have been narrowed down to unlimited calls and data services, at a  fixed price. It was important to successfully use the newly launched product to attract new customers as  well as ensure stickiness of existing customers. There was a national campaign around the same, but  since in India, as per a famous saying, the language changes every 100 KM, so to cater to this diversity,  we decided to come up with a communication plan very specific to the geographic scope of my unit in  Punjab state.

Implementing the Tool – The process

The design thinking tool utilized here by me was visualization. Since we had a lot of verbal agreements  and disagreements on several ideas that came along, however, since we had to find a uniform design for  the communication material, we had to narrow down on only some ideas that could be effectively  implemented.

For this, I asked my team members (28 in total), to make 5 hand-made posters regarding the different  propositions of the product, which was a mobile entertainment application offering Live TV, and  streaming of shows and movies, as well as a music app used for online streaming as well as downloading  latest songs. They were given instructions to be creative with this and not stick to usual text only  communication we adopted. After this, the posters were displayed in a room, and put up on walls as  they would be across retail shops in the market. After the exhibition, I asked all team members to come  and take a walk inside the room, and later on exiting, write two most appealing propositions that came  to their mind and left a mark. Since they belonged to very different markets, and geographic regions, I  hoped we would be able to cover a fair bit of ‘WOW’ factors for different target segments.

The Result

On basis of the above exercise, we were able to finalize two major key insights, which appealed and  made a use case for the people who viewed it.

1. Live cricket, especially communication around upcoming tournament between India and

Australia, one of the most famous and sought after rivalry in the cricketing world

2. Communication around downloading latest Punjabi language songs, especially from the most

popular singers across the state.

It was also observed that a pictorial depiction of the same was much more impacting. On basis of  this feedback, we came up with the following communication to be put across ~10,000 retail shops  across my zone.

Modifications

In my opinion, and after understating and applying different processes of design thinking, the next time I  do this exercise I would make the following changes, and include ‘Learning launch’ tool:

1. I would ensure that the control group comprises of team members from varied backgrounds

such as finance or customer experience, to counter confirmation bias we might have

2. After deciding on the theme, I will design an experimental campaign in one of the markets,

capturing proper changes in app download numbers before and after communication, which will  be the key metric to define success failure of the theme of communication

The product in consideration is https://www.hart.com/posts/tagspost.htm

Reflection – Storytelling to draw the future

By Luz Marina Mora

Challenge & selection

Storytelling is a very useful tool when doing future studies and Foresight. I am a consultant and  researcher in strategic thinking and foresight, and in each exercise the main challenge is to empower  actors in a long-term vision and collective thinking about the future, be it a territory, an organization  or a productive sector. The main mission of foresight is to define a long-term future scenario, taking  into account some elements of the past, an analysis of trends and signs of the future, as well as  technological disruptors that can generate specific changes in the development of a specific  phenomenon, But the people involved have trouble having short-term thoughts, with anxiety to  solve current problems or “put out fires”.

Most of our leaders and decision makers think more about short-term planning than future  projection, therefore, the result of a foresight study should allow us to see the future in such a way  that it feels real, tangible and challenging, so that those involved are encouraged to work on its  construction, thus, the use of narration allows the prospective to create a logical, coherent message  that generates enough emotional and optimistic connection to influence strategies and actions in  the construction of that future.

Application

In 2018, a company dedicated to meliponiculture, that is, breeding and management of stingless  bees for the extraction of honey and other products, we requested to carry out a prospective study  for the sector of native bees or stingless bees in Colombia. Although it was a small and private  company, we wanted to promote a shared vision for all the producers in the country, that would  include the academy, government institutions and other producers, therefore, it was necessary to  sell the idea to all involved.

The participation of agricultural producers, the academy was achieved through researchers from  the country's leading universities, the state through the technical secretariat of the Ministry of  Agriculture and other professionals who were interested in the development of meliponiculture,  But there was a greater challenge than bringing them together, it was to generate a broader and  more complete vision of the breeding and management of stingless bees, in which all those actors  were interested in working.

Insight and approach

The best way was to build a history based on the importance of meliponiculture, its ancestral origins  and the great advantages it has in terms of ecosystem care, pollination, food security and, of course,  on the economic issue, in addition, this type of bees are part of our ecosystem.

We built history, which is also real, telling that since long before the arrival of honey bees from  Africa and Europe to the American territory, our continent had its own bees that were in charge of  doing the work of pollinating forests and the crops, which fed the native population and produced

Challenge   I have a business concept for a sustainability product that will help reduce single-use packaging.  The vision is to create a circular economy around a line of reusable cups, water bottles and  containers that can be borrowed on-demand, then returned for cleaning.  Similar to the  business model of car co-ops, e-scooters and bikes for transportation, I propose a membership- style system that would allow people to access these items at strategically placed vending  machines when they are on-the-go.     The challenge is that this idea has never been fully fleshed out and there are significant gaps in  terms of how the concept can be implemented in real life, both on the consumer side, as well  as the implementation side. Additionally, a big question looms as to whether this is a product or  service.    Ultimately, I need to better understand how this product/service might work so that I can move  forward research and development.    Selection   According to designer Angela Myer visualization helps unlock another part of our brain to  access parts of our creativity for complex problem solving.  These visual tools aid us with  imaginative thinking when more than just logic is needed; when extrapolation, inductive  reasoning and solving future problems is required.    Due to the complexity and type of thinking that’s required for my business challenge, the  design thinking tool I select to assist in this challenge is visualization. This is because there is an  immediate need to map out the experience from end-to-end. The purpose of mapping the  process out is both to help me create a more fulsome picture of the user experience myself, as  well as to communicate the business concept effectively to a group of collaborators.    Application  I participate in the Squamish Make-a-Thon, presented by the NATIONAL UNIVERSITY OF COLOMBIA and the District of Squamish, to put my design thinking skills to the test. With a  group of collaborators, I use storyboarding to draw out the user experience of my sustainable  solution from beginning to end.     We look at this from two angles: the user experience from an external perspective, and the  redemption process from an internal perspective. In this particular case, the fast and iterative  approach of storyboarding plays a critical role in developing the concept. Through this design  thinking tool, our group immediately identifies areas that may pose challenges to the  experience and exposes aspects of the concept that require more detailed thinking.

Anne Steiner  October 15, 2019

The storyboarding addresses both the front-end user experience, as well as the back-end  facilitation of the product. Through this, our group identifies several stages of the process that  we need to rethink.

For example, on the front-end, we realize that  when someone identifies their need for a  reusable container, they must have a mechanism  for locating the closest redemption point. To  solve for this, we integrate a location finder  mobile application into the process.    On the back-end, we realize that my original idea  of having a collection service to take dirty  containers away and clean them at a different  facility would be extremely complex,  cumbersome and not sustainable. We opt,  instead, to integrate self-cleaning technology

into the vending machine, enabling containers to be cleaned on site. This will speed up the  process and keep supplies stocked and reduce the overall carbon footprint of the solution.     Using the help of storyboarding throughout the process, our group continues to adjust the  concept until the flow makes sense to both the consumer and the business. The new  information gained from this visualization helps us hone in on what additional research is  required and what we need to include in our Design Criteria document.     Insight and Approach  After creating the storyboard, I have been able to address critical questions, better  communicate the concept, and create a more defined design road map.     Firstly, visualization helped me answer the most pressing question: is this more of a product or  is it a service? I have, in fact, established that this is more of a product (the self-cleaning  vending machine) and therefore, requires a different approach for research and development.    Additionally, through the help of visual tools, I was able to both better understand my concept  and to communicate it more clearly. Prior to drawing out the business idea, I was having  trouble explaining it because I did not have a foundational understanding of it myself.     Finally, with the help of iterative visual thinking, I have identified new questions to answer for  both the front-end and back-end of the product. This next round of questions will be the  foundation for further research and concept development.     I think storyboarding was the best tool for me at this until I had developed the idea stage of the  business concept because it helped me rapidly iterate more thoroughly.

Moving forward, however, I would like to fine-tune the consumer journey. In the future, I will  create more detailed storyboards with different versions of the user experience. Reflection

I choose one of the most powerful tools regarding the Design Thinking, the Mind Mapping. Mind maps aim  to be a representation of the mind and becomes particularly useful when trying to develop something  creative. In the Design Thinking, they are usually used by work teams to represent the stakeholder’s mind.  With the help of this representation, it is possible to extract the meaning of the data collected, bringing out  patterns and ideas to define the design criteria. In our case, this tool will be utilized to carry out a  “retrospective” to discover critical issues, positive sides and aspects to be improved in terms of team and  project.

Application  For our first Mind Mapping, we focused on the structure/execution of our activities in the project and how  we were facing them.

In particular, we wanted to see if we could structure our jobs, project and processes in order to optimize  them and improve the qualitative side, intended as the best quality of the work done, and how to improve  the gratification of the worker in performing that job. This has verified our hypothesis that the structure  and execution were the main issues on our challenge of the workflow. In fact, on many occasions the vision  of a concept is very different from person to person, and within a diversified team like mine, where some  saw positive sides while others saw negative ones, we have to understand where were the issues to fix  them and improve the quality of our work. So, we gathered in a room, took some post-it and a billboard:  from there our mind mapping started. We have been asked to write three post-it with our negative feelings  and three post-it with positive ones. After a first moment of reflection we were asked to put these post-it  on the board, dividing the negatives on one side and the positives on the other. Shortly thereafter, we  started identifying the common themes to these post-its and then grouping them together. Finally, we  were asked to highlight each team member the most relevant / important post-it note.

Insight & Approach

As I said, the mind map is over, however the mental mapping process of design thinking is still incomplete.  Now we need to turn these observations into intuitions, trying to find out what the observations could  imply. In the board, we created a new column entitled ''Actions to be taken'' where we discussed the  possible solutions of the post-it placed on the negative side of the board.

Once you have the design criteria in hand, you will be ready to move on to thinking about possible solutions  to your design challenge.

The design criteria are the basis of What-if?

We focused on possible solutions, testing them monthly and repeating mind mapping.

Since our team has already gone through several design activities/tools, Mind Mapping seems to be the  appropriate tool. As mentioned above, our team will have to review the information gained within our  firsts mind mappings. The future mind mappings should focus, in addition to the intuitions acquired (both

positive and negative), on the "actions to be taken" to understand if these have been undertaken and in  what modality, to see if the intuition has been corrected, etc.

And finally repeat the cycle.

This points out how fundamental mind mapping is for the design thinking process, and how it can trigger  creativity and intuition.

people who are nearby or possibly be inhaled into the lungs. Studies and evidence on

infection control report that these droplets usually travel around 6 feet.

Wear cloth face coverings in public settings where other social distancing measures

are difficult to maintain, such as grocery stores, pharmacies, and gas stations. Cloth face

coverings may slow the spread of the virus and help people who may have the virus and do

not know it from transmitting it to others. Furthermore, Cloth face coverings can be made

from household items.

who has aspiration to make a DIY face mask with air filter for people to cover their virus

spreading. It’s not only to protect people from the virus, but also boosting the income for

these lower-economy income.

This section, I chose mind mapping tools to organize the information. The reason

behind the selection is to look for and managing the information so I can find the proper

formula to create face mask with air filter.

Insight

The Mind mapping tool of Covid-19 condition makes face mask product high demand around

the world. This term will continue trough so-called “New Normal”.  The result of this mind

map are to create face mask with air filter with 5 excellences:

• Washable

• Reusable

• The filter can be refilled with material that easily obtained

• Soft cloth can be used everyone

• Substituting disposable mask

This DIY Cloth Face Mask With Air Filter use online delivery system to channelling with

commerce marketplace. Each delivery product comes with development feedback to be sent

INTRODUCTION

I work with a women oriented and welfare organisation. We organise and hold  out camps at different parts of the country, rural and urban both. Our first  objective is to – encourage the victims, survivors and the warriors of sexual  assault, physical abuse or of any other forms of oppression to come forward  and share their stories with us and also with other such victims, raise their  voice against their abusers, and we also try & help them to report those  wrongdoers to the women crime investigation cells, that is if they’re ready to.

Our second main objective is to educate those girls and women regarding the  human and women rights.

CHALLENGE

As much as I love getting to do the things that we do, I am afraid I don’t share  the same feeling when it comes to the challenges that we are hit with quite  frequently than not. They live in a perpetual fear of being judged  by the society for opening up about the unacceptable deeds that were or are  still being done to them. And also, they are oblivious or ignorant of the women  rights.

TOOLS

The tool that I selected for my challenge is the Storytelling tool. This tool is  used to put the human beings and their experiences front and centre. Take  listeners along on their journey. Create a more vivid image of what we are  trying to convey.

The reason that motivated me further to select this tool was :                                I had a first hand experience with how effective can sharing stories prove to  be. When I was 17, I was as unwilling as those women to recount my own  experience with physical abuse even privately, let alone publicly. Then one day  my aunt shared her own share of experience with the same and how she got  her abuser behind the bars. Her story encouraged me to speak up and report  my now ex-boyfriend, the guy who did wrong by me.

I applied this particular tool with many females, but I will just be sharing my  first attempt at this tool.

I  told her how I am no longer scared to admit that I have been in a physically  abusive relationship where I’d let him make me feel like it was all my fault. Even though he was locked up for  just a night, his parents, friends, and everyone he knew got to know the

monster he so carefully kept concealed behind the persona of ‘the perfect  boyfriend’.

Once I was done sharing my story and was almost done educating her and the  other women about their rights, this girl slowly stood up from her seat and  began sharing her story with us. Upon completing it, she said with a steel like  voice that she was going to tell that guy’s parents all about his inhumane deed  and also, report him to the village police station.                                                  This is how I applied the tool to tackle the challenge, by sharing my own story. I  used the tool to achieve the two major objectives of our organisation. With the  aid of this tool I empower those women and educate them to stand for  themselves and their rights because no matter how many times I scream my  truth at the top of my lungs, it will cease to free them. This also let the one using this tool to better perceive the  problems of the listeners and other related challenges.

Challenge

Problems are an inseparable aspect of our lives and business relations. If you want to start a business, you’ll inevitably run into several complex problems, such as: How do you found a profitable company, how do you make it stand out among the competition, how do you attract more customers, and how do you maintain and boost its reputation? In this article we’ll provide you with a step-by-step guide to problem solving with mind maps, a simple but powerful technique that’s already used by millions of entrepreneurs and other professionals across the globe.

Selection

Outline clear action items in your mind map Problem Solving with Mind Maps – a Step-by-Step Guide for Entrepreneurs Einstein nailed the definition of problem solving. He said, “The formulation of the problem is often more essential than its solution, which may be merely a matter of mathematical or experimental skill.”

A confident problem solver understands the problem, defines its various aspects, generates ideas and is able to turn those ideas into a solution. Mind mapping is a proven method that helps people surpass the initial chaos that occurs in the mind when the problem arises. Visualizing your goals, problems, ideas and potential action points in a mind map can help you see the bigger picture and make out connections between individual aspects that you might have missed otherwise. Seeing your whole business model mapped out like this also helps your brain form new ideas through association, and it is those ideas that path the way to the solution of your problem.

To illustrate the effectiveness of problem solving with mind maps, we’ll use a simple example of a young entrepreneur who wants to start their own dog walking business. Following this step-by- step guide, you’ll be able to visualize even complex problems and develop actionable solutions for them.

Approach

Start with the Goals, then Formulate the Problems Remember Einstein’s quote? We have to understand the problem before we can think of finding solutions. That’s the step you start with.

Step 1: Choose your preferred mind-mapping software and open a blank mind map. Write your business idea in the center of the map and create a branch for your business goals. Create a new topic for each individual goal.

Problem solving with mind maps: Start with the goals

The founder of our dog walking business has two main goals: staying in profit during all seasons while keeping dog walking rates low in order to stay competitive. Unfortunately, the distance between pick-up points and dog parks is so great that all dog walkers will need cars to get around. This in turn creates three major problems:

Some employees don’t have driving licenses; there are not enough vehicles for all employees; and having each dog walker drive back and forth between pick-ups and parks will lead to enormous gas expenses.

Step 2: Create a second branch for your problems and write them down individually.

Note down your problems

Brainstorming Ideas to Find Solutions Once you have the goals and problems visualized in your mind map, it will be easier for you to get ideas on possible solutions. Take each problem and simply write down whatever solution comes to your mind. Don’t worry if some of your ideas are far fetched or even impossible – the goal is to get your creative juices flowing. Ideas that turn out to be unfeasible can simply be deleted from the map when your brainstorming session is over.

Step 3: Take the first problem on your list and start brainstorming possible solutions. Don’t censor yourself at first, just write down what comes to mind. Focus on this particular problem only, if you try to solve all problems at once you’ll simply get overwhelmed.

Brainstorm solutions

For the problem “not enough vehicles for all employees”, our entrepreneur soon realizes that there is actually a very simple solution: dog walkers who work in the same area can share a car. He creates a third branch in the mind map for ‘Solutions’ and draws a line to connect the problem with its respective solution.

Suddenly, our entrepreneur sees that this idea will actually help with those big gas expenses too, so he connects it with this problem through another line. And what about the third problem? If employees share cars, only a few of them will need driving licenses, so this is another issue he can check off the list. Three birds, one stone.

Visualize the solutions

At this point, our entrepreneur realizes that letting dog walkers use regular cars will not work if multiple people and dogs have to be transported at the same time. To have enough space for everyone, he will need to purchase a few big vans for his business. This is big investment at first, but it’s one that will pay off in the long run. And with this, he has found his first action point.

Let’s revisit our goals: By having the dog walkers share vans the entrepreneur is able to keep costs low and thus offer similarly low rates to his customers. In order to build a large customer base and stay in business during all seasons, the entrepreneur can add additional action items such as “Create a strong marketing strategy” and related points such as ‘Create social media profiles’, ‘Learn how to maintain a successful blog‘ and so on.

Step 4: Outline clear action points based on the solutions you have developed.

Outline clear action items in your mind map

Just like the entrepreneur in this example, you can benefit greatly from creating a mind map to visualize your business and find solutions to whatever problems stand between you and your goals.

Extra Tips on Problem Solving with Mind Maps You can share your mind map with your business partners or team members to collaborate on it and brainstorm solutions together. Such virtual brainstorming sessions have been shown to be highly effective compared to traditional, in-person sessions. MindMeister allows you to add due dates to the action points in your mind map, or even turn them into full-fledged tasks. As soon as you’re finished mapping out your business plan, you can export those tasks to a project board and start getting productive. Don’t forget to update the mind map with new ideas, problems, and possible solutions as you make progress with the actions. The best aspect of online mind mapping is its flexibility; you can always add new points and get rid of the ones you no longer need.

Remember: every problem has a solution. Life would be so boring without the problem-solving challenges we face every single day. Thanks to mind maps, that aspect of our daily routine becomes much easier.

Reflection: Storytelling

Challenge:

The main challenge presented to me was that of a client of my company. As a client in the finance industry,  they wanted to learn how to reach new clients who would opt for his small and medium business services  program. The challenge is how to publicize the service, sell its good results and the advantages that people  or projects who decide to be part of this program can obtain. This challenge becomes more complicated  since the people who can opt for these services are not necessarily found through the internet or Social  Media, but they attend to carry out their procedures at offices.

Selection:

I selected Storytelling as it is a tool that offers versatility and possible creative outlets above a challenge.  In this case, I consider that the way to address success stories and cases is to make them known to our  potential consumers. According to Adan Stone (Global Leadership Development Director of Mars, Inc.)  more than solving a problem is about creating a cause. A cause that can unite and excite people. An  important aspect is that the most relevant thing is to know your audience. In this way, a good story can  be designed for that specific audience.

Application:

According to what Adan Stone (Global Leadership Development Director of Mars, Inc.) mentions, first  of all, when it comes to working with people, the ideal is to bring them to a state of mind where they want  to participate and make this challenge a cause in which to invest. In this way, my team created a series of  personalized invitations according to the characteristics. From this, a group of people was selected to  work in focus groups in which our different hypotheses were worked on. On the one hand, a first group  received information about services, channels and programs in a series of slides with related text and  images. On the other hand, a second group had access to testimonies from people who made use of the  support programs, recounting their personal experience with their small or medium-sized business.

As a result of these group sessions, a separation is built in which the most positively evaluated services  and channels are selected, as well as those that are below expectations. The last stage consists of  developing these testimonies and telling the story from an interactive perspective (with interactive  screens) and with availability for predefined consultations, which at the same time is designed to take to  the different branches and offices where this audience is located and continues to attend constantly. This  solves part of the first challenge, providing the information through the channels used by this group. It is  in this way that a seedbed of projects is born from this program for companies.

Insight:

Insight is usually difficult to identify, however in this case we worked on it little by little. The fact that  people can tell their own stories builds trust and hope. Telling stories as mentioned in the chapter of this  tool, allows you to create energy, passion and excitement about what is being presented. The creation of

a space that responds to a human truth such as empathy, is what allows us to reach this insight in which  people identify with their peers, with other people with similar characteristics to each other.

Approach:

Regarding the differences that would apply differently, it would be the application of interviews in the  initial stage, which allow to know more about the audience or, to know more about who is selected for  the focus group sessions. In this way, it is possible to know more in depth and take advantage of the  experience and testimony of each person and see the potential it has in attracting new interested  audiences. Being more specific and personalized, empathy can be built hand in hand with these  testimonials, in which people, rather than seeing a service, can feel support, support and an impulse that  allows them to meet new stories.

by gaining their attention over the main concept, i.e. HR policies or procedures of the Navy’s Child and Youth Program. I

Design Thinking for Innovation - Asignement

Challenge  I have been leading a digital accelerator project for NGO's working with youth entrepreneurship. Those  NGO's are part of a global network were wondering, where digital could create the most significant  impact for their young entrepreneurs. With a holistic approach, we are tackling external aspects, like  marketing and digital services, as also internal aspects, as such related to their business model and their  operating models. There was a considerable concern on the NGO's side that digital would distant them  from their entrepreneurs, and through that doubted that there could be a positive impact with digital. In  our "What is?" phase we conducted open interviews and shadowing with employees and with  entrepreneurs, through journaling and inspirational workshops we drew up personas and user journeys.  We wondered what to do with all the collected information.

Selection  We decided to do a massive mind map on a large wall, which we called "the mural". On a high level, we  followed similar steps like the ones presented in this course in week 3 ("Mind Mapping Steps"). Steps 1- 3 were the work described above in the challenge section.

Application  As a team, we did make some preliminary clustering mapping all findings within eight strategic themes  and a high-level grouping within the themes. We then performed a series of workshops together with  the different stakeholders from the NGO in order to review and adjust the clustering (step 4), and  worked in groups to set strategic priorities on which problems to solve and make sure that the right  problem and the right abstraction level of the problem is the one that we would be looking at (similar to  step 5). Those were then shared in the plenum and connections were identified (step 6). Separate  ideation sessions, internal and external, were performed bringing solution options for the key prioritized  problems to life (step 7 and on).

Insights   Using mind mapping technique at this step was crucial, as it helps to break down and simplify a vast  amount of information gathered limiting the level of overwhelming of the employees of the NGO. For  them, it was very insightful, as for them it was the first time they see all views in one view, and that with  a holistic perspective, their personal "large problem" might not be the biggest issue, or could be easily  solved in collaboration with the other team. An additional result was that the NGO's now understood,  that digital could help them to be closer to their Entrepreneurs and also by automating internal tasks  free up more time to add more value to them.

Approach  In my perspective, the mind mapping tool was beneficial to break down all that information and post it  in the plenum. I concluded that this exposure, even if pretty overwhelming for the employees, is the  right type of exposure for them to understand the change and transformation they require. We have  been thinking about what we could do to reduce the levels of overwhelming, and came to a conclusion,  that we provide them confidence through clarity in the process, and prepare them to be overwhelmed.

Reflection — Learning Launch  Guiding a Digital-First Mindset Shift in an  Online Enterprise SaaS Business

By Santosh Kumar

Challenge    Enterprise businesses offering digital SaaS (Software-as-a-Service) products often rely heavily  on traditional Sales workflows. This means, the selling process is entirely manually driven with  individuals, or even whole teams of Sales and Pre-Sales professionals being involved in  helping a customer make a purchase decision and closing a deal. While this has worked  traditionally because of such digital products usually being expensive, high dollar-value items;  it comes at a great cost to the scalability of a business, especially when entering and capturing  newer or larger markets.    As a member of my organization’s marketing leadership, my team of cross-functional experts  and I were faced with the challenge of proving the market demand for a scalable, fully digital,  “try-before-you-buy” business model to our Executive leadership who had grown accustomed  to the traditional methods of doing business and reflected a fixed mindset1, convinced that  the market, or the customers, didn’t voice such a need for change.

Selection    My team and I have decided to employ the Learning Launch tool as we have already gone  through several Design Thinking activities and tools such as co-creating a Journey Map2 of  “What Is” our customers’ current state of engagement with our product’s website to  understand what is or isn’t working in helping them express interest in buying our product  and starting a purchase-conversation with us.    We have also engaged in mind-mapping3 activities building alignment on the “What If”  scenario of our proposed solutions and we feel that a Learning Launch, being an  experimentation tool, will help us quickly gather valuable data4 in testing our hypotheses  and validating market-demand for a fully digital, instant “try-before-you-buy” experience of  our product as outlined in the “Challenge” section above.

Application    For our Learning Launch aimed at validating market demand, we focused on curating and  improving the information architecture5 of our product website. In particular, we wanted to  see if we could accelerate our customers’ journey, i.e., reduce the time they need on our  website to get them to understand the core value propositions of our product and sign-up for  a trial. For this we co-created an experiment, bringing together stakeholders6 from Design  and Engineering to prototype7 and implement a prominent call-to-action button that read  “Start your 30-day free trial” which led to a simple sign-up form that customers could fill up  to get on a priority waitlist for the product trial experience.    This would test our assumptions8 that (1) customers wanted to engage with us and try our  product before they bought it and (2) if given a fully digital route to try the said product, they  would express interest quicker by signing up on our website.

Insight    By applying the Learning Launch described in the “Application” section above, we found over  a 14-day period, that our customers were up to 6.2x more likely, on average, to engage with  us and sign-up for our product if a fully digital, “try-before-you-buy” experience were on offer.  We uncovered these insights by comparing the click-through rate on the new call-to-action  button against the number of e-mail Sales inquiries initiated by customers during similar 14- day periods at various points in the previous 12 months when the new call-to-action button  did not exist.    Upon further data analysis, this Learning Launch also helped us to definitively highlight  behaviors that led to the traditionally low interest from our customers, and therefore, our  Executive leadership’s misassumptions regarding market demand. It did so by confirming the  truth9 that our customers are fast-paced professionals and did not prefer their first  interaction with a business or a product to be a Sales call or an email thread, and therefore  avoided it unless necessary.

Approach    We found our experiments from our Learning Launch to be highly effective as they were fast  and inexpensive10 and helped us gather strong and definitive data points in setting the

direction for our next set of efforts. We plan to conduct more of such experiments and  incorporate the findings from these Learning Launches into a Storytelling format to  disseminate to an organization-wide audience in building a cohesive growth plan together.

Reflection – Visualization tool

Challenge and Selection

A friend of mine who is a businessman asked me for help to start the process of creating a  business idea: He wants to open a physiotherapy center. His hypothesis is that it will stand out  from the rest of physiotherapy centers of Lima-Perú due to its technological aspect. He wants it  to be full equipped with the highest technology and with equipments that other physiotherapy  centers don’t have. His hypothesis is not based on data, there are no research on this type of  business in the city. He has mapped the competition (that means, he called to ask which services  they offer and the prices), looked for technological devices on the internet that he thinks are  not used in Lima, and brainstormed to imagine his business. He also hasn’t done research to  know the clients´ point of view.

This is the “What is?” stage of his project. I want to help him to outline, expand or change the  definition of the opportunity he sees, starting by getting to know the customers’ reality from  their perspective, what they value the most and what needs aren’t covered. The tool I’ve chosen  is Visualization through drawing their customers’ experience as in a collage. I made sure that  this tool works well for this stage by listening to the video of Visualization of week 1. The speaker  says that “sketching can be a very important way of capturing that kind of information ". By  “information” she means: “not just people themselves, but the context in which they live". In  addition, in the “What is?” stage of the MeYouHealth case, they used collages of images that  symbolize the perception of potential users of well-being and their five-year projection of  themselves.

Application

I met with four people at different times and I gave them this task: “Reflect your current  experience as customer of the physiotherapy center you assist by drawing it. Draw yourself  going through that experience and all the stages you remember. Imagine the people, spaces,  the therapy itself, equipment, price, quality of the service, your feelings and anything else you  remember. After this step, choose a color and draw the aspects you don’t like and proposals to  improve your experience. Finally, choose another color to identify what you like about your  current experience. There are no ugly or beautiful drawings, neither bad nor good answers, this  is not an evaluation. Be as creative as you want! If you have questions, you can ask me at any  time.”. Before I started, I asked them their names, ages, occupations and the name of the center  where they assist. I gave each one a cardboard, markers of different colors, colored pencils,  colored glitter and pencils. There was an accident with the colored glitter, it was dry. I kept it  long time stored and it got dry, so the first participant couldn’t use it. I took it away immediately  and apologized myself for that incident. When they finished, I asked them to explain their  drawing to me. During the dialogue there were some new aspects that they remembered and  had not included. I wrote down all  the explanations on my computer while they told me their  experiences and went deeper with questions like: What exactly did you like about the massage?  And did some indirect questions to know if they value the technology used in the centers like:  What do you think of the equipment they use? Describe it please. Did it help you?

Insight

My friends hypotesis got a broader view. All of the participants mentioned that the aspect they  value the most is the quality of the massage, not depending on the technological devices, but  on the therapist’s skills and profile. They want a therapist who is: kind, skillfull, experienced,

quiet (that means he/she is not in a hurry to finish and transmits a peacefull feeling) and has an  enterprise culture. They said that in some cases, a less experienced therapist gave them a  massage and it was obvious that he/she had more to learn. One of the participants told me that  once an intern gave her a massage and told her that she had an irreversible disease (which  wasn’t true) and she got worried. So in this first finding, my friend’s hypotesis doesn’t match the  needs. However there were other points to observe. Every center has a main doctor who is the  expert and the rest of the staff seems less experienced. The participants value a lot when the  main doctor treats them, because he/she gives them a better massage and a detailed  explanaition of their case. This highlights another need to be covered: information. Besides the  doctor’s explanaition, they didn’t mention elements that provide information about health  problems, their health status (none of them have patients health histories) and most of them  complained about not having a modern system that helpes them to book an appoinment (in two  centers they can’t even call, the booking has to be on-site). This is an opportunity for my friend  to use technology to stand out from the competition.

The third most important aspect is the environment. All of them mentioned that all of the  centers had a bit dirty environments, with old furniture, some of them had old exercise  machines, not so comfortable stretchers and the centers were located in non-commercial areas,  but in households addapted to give the service. This is an aspect to improve and also an  opportunity for my friend.  One of the participants said that he liked a place where many patients  had to sit around the same table while they got therapy through electricity. This was nice  because the equipment was new to him (he had received electricity therapy with other  equipment before) and also because he got to know other people, share problems, sollutions  and socialize. This goes combined with the need for information. And finally, it is very important  for them that the center is located not so far from their homes. Two of them had to travel by  bus one hour to get to the physiotherapy centers and in terms of cost/benefit they ended losing  a lot of time and energy. My friend told me he had ideas to bring the service to peoples homes,  and to give them online service.

Approach

The first learning was that before starting any activity, I must check if the resources I will use  function correctly. This is because of the accident with the colored glitter. The second learning  is that some of the participants used the storyboard format to draw their experiences. This was  very useful to go more in detail and deeper in getting to know their reality, so I will suggest it  the next time I use this tool. Another finding is that the older ones didn’t use the colored markers  and pencils as the first resource to draw (and even during the process they didn’t use more tan  two colors). They prefered to start using a pencil. They said: “I prefer to start with the pencil to  be able to erase” and “The right way to start drawing is with a pencil”. For me, his shows the  results of their generation’s education, which teach them to avoid mistakes and not to risk from  start, not even a bit. Coincidentally they  used the same colors to show the things they like  (green) and dislike (red) (look at the pictures attached). Next time I will give them different  motivations such as images, to encourage them to get out of the traditional way to draw  “correctly” and explore their creativity.

Finally, I got valuable learnings and comments about the success of the tool for my goal. One of  the participants is a marketing university teacher. He recognized the benefits of this tool to do  a deeper research of customers’ experience tan with traditional research tolos (he uses themin  his lectures). Also, this tool was very useful to collect information about the different profiles,  because each participant used his/her profesional knowledges to plasm their experience: One

of the participants is a graphic designer and she used color codes to show her experience. The  teacher explained with a formula why non-monetary costs have often a higher value for the  customers than monetary costs and this lead to sumarize one of the principal findings.

Reflection – Storytelling

Prepared by Fatima Fatima

10JUL20

Challenge

I consider myself fortunate to work for the country’s largest membership-based organization, especially  as it presents the opportunity to take part in cross functional teams from multiple Lines of Business  (LOB). This blessing is also a curse as we frequently struggle with a core brand that eclipses all others  and as a result the other LOB’s, although expected to create big ideas and produce exceptional results, are  not afforded the proper budget and consideration as the core brand. One LOB, our travel division, is the  most overlooked, due to a Member Penetration Index (MPI) that is stagnant at 4% nation wide yet has the  potential to be considerably more profitable than at present state. To quote Ahmed, this is a truly  wicked problem.

Although multiple resources have been allocated to the promotion of this LOB, all projects are  underfunded and tend to be under prioritized, and as a result the department continues to struggle with  awareness not only within the executive team but with Members. I have identified that the largest  challenge with “moving the needle” on MPI is that not all associates/executives within the organization  understand and promote the department’s value proposition, and as mentioned previously, investment  requests are often reallocated to other LOB’s that appear to have a higher ROI.  What is most overlooked  is that the transactions within this LOB contribute to the overall satisfaction with Membership (core  business), and in fact that those Members using this department’s services have a 94% rate of  Membership renewal, significantly higher than any other LOB.

Selection – Storytelling

I am a natural storyteller. Born to an Irish family from the east coast of Canada, I did not learn to get to  the point right away. I was taught to paint a pretty picture, look for the moment of awe and bring people  into my world so they see things my way.  Limerick you say. Spinning a yarn maybe? Yes, this is what I  was born to do. Yet I seem to not have been able to summit the mountain of our core line of business’  priorities in order to shine light on an LOB that I truly believe will be the catalyst of success and  domination amongst our competitors.

The reason I chose storytelling is not only is it a business tool that seems more natural to me, but that the  product this LOB offers to Members is one that directly relates to the customers emotions; therefore,  storytelling appears to be the appropriate choice.  If I can deliver a clear and compelling story, relying on  the emotional connection of this department’s product with overall satisfaction of our Members, then  there is a greater chance of success in obtaining more focus and funding.  Unlike other reflections you  may be privileged to review, this one will be different as I have never purposefully implemented DT nor  storytelling as part of my process in the past. I shall not be sharing an anecdote of past presentations and  what I have learned from them. Not unlike other corporations, ours relies heavily on analytics,  PowerPoint presentations and Excel Spreadsheets. Traditional thinking is no longer working for this  LOB; therefore,  I chose the Design Thinking for Innovation course for a reason, which is the recognition  that we can no longer continue to follow the same processes and expect different results. Status quo is no  longer acceptable and must learn and adapt to succeed.

Application

In the week 2 video “Storytelling Tool”, Pedro Sanchez stated “Every great brand with longevity in the  retail space……has a story.”  As my company has been in business for over 115 years, with a core brand  with a well-known story, it now falls on my shoulders to uncover the story of this LOB to elevate the  awareness of the brand. What I have been able to take from the lessons of Design Thinking for  Innovation, is that storytelling for business requires the storyteller be able to convey a logical message by  understanding the following:

1. Who is my audience (what do they know about the value of this LOB and what is missing from

their current understanding – what do they need i.e./ data)?

2. When is the optimal time to tell this story (are they in the frame of mind to retain such

information)?

3. Can I communicate a clear sequence of events (does the story have an impactful beginning and

does it flow easily and compellingly to the end)? Can I present an intelligent argument for further  investment in this LOB using data from “What is” research?

4. This LOB represents the most emotional connection to our organization, can I describe this in a

way to elicit an emotional response from our executive team?

5. Do I allow for moments of reflection (I need to build in unanswered questions that will engage

the audience to be intrigued enough to look for answers)?

6. Am I prepared to present solutions or ideas to spark solutions so that no question remains

unanswered?

Insight & Approach

Using Mind Mapping Tool

By Vito Ivanov

May 2021

Challenge     I am the senior product manager of a mid-sized software company. We have a  business line in which we provide bulk messaging services to the market. It's  now a few years that this market is almost commoditized and all the  competition is mainly a price war. I have recently read the book "Reinventing  your Business Model" by Mark W. Johnson and I found many insights about  having an innovative business model in it.  So I asked my colleagues in the bulk messaging business unit to join me in an  endeavor to find a new way of offering value propositions to our customers  and differentiating our service from the competition.        Selection     Since I was familiar with design thinking methods and tools, I decided to use  the mind mapping tool for organizing the current state of our customer needs.  I like this tool because it assists a group of people to unite their diverse views  on the customer problems and attain a shared view about the current situation  of customers' needs. We have a team of about 20 colleagues in this business  unit and they have a good knowledge of what the customers need and what  job they want to get done.     Application     I invited most of our colleagues in different functions (marketing, sales,  operations, CRM, development) of the business to participate in the activity.  Based on what Mark Johnson proposes in his book, I asked every one to focus  on the "Job to be done" of the customers. First I made a presentation out of  the chapter 6 of the book "Designing for Growth" which is about mind  mapping tool and presented it to the team so that they became familiar with  the activity we were going to start.

I provided sticky notes in different colors and pens for the participants and  asked them to write down their perception of the job to be done of the  customers they know.   Then I gathered the notes and tried to delve into the real and deep needs of  the customers by asking every person "Five Whys" questions about what they  wrote on the notes. Therefore, after finishing this step I had a comprehensive  list of the needs of the customers written on the white board. This was what  we could rely on as the input to the What If phase.   We extracted the design criteria using this list and we were ready to start the  next step.     Insight & Approach     By using the mind mapping tool, we succeeded to attain a good picture of our  customers and their most important needs. My colleagues in different  functions had some implicit knowledge of the customer needs that through  this activity became explicit and shared among the team.   Now, we were ready to start brainstorming the solutions for those problems.  Moreover, my colleagues became familiar and so interested in using mind  mapping tool for their other activities in order to make a shared mindset on  their team issues.   In the next phases, we saw that how important is having a well-classified and  well-shared list of customer problems for finding a proper solution and a  robust value proposition.
