Deepak Das (Storytelling)

Storytelling is the process of using fact and narrative to communicate something to your

audience. Some stories are factual, and some are embellished or improvised in order to

better explain the core message. While this definition is pretty specific, stories actually

resemble a variety of things.

(1) Challenge:

When I work with seniors, we share stories for different reasons. Often they're lonely and

are so happy to share stories of their lives with me to connect and they find meaning in

sharing these experiences as a form of teaching and/or legacy, in a sense. With my

developmentally disabled clients I share stories of my life in order to help them visualize

a state of independence, I use their feedback against the context of my story to ascertain

their goals, and sometimes we use stories to better understand their interests and thought

processes. I use this information to develop different strategies to try and find a way that

works for them to gain more independence in the areas they find lacking in their lives.

(2) Selection:

Storytelling is a great tool that I use all the time. I work with vulnerable populations,

developmentally disabled individuals, senior citizens, and economically disadvantaged

people. Many of these people deal with oppression and dysfunction in every aspect of

their lives, they need to be empowered and inspiration is a path to empowerment. I spend

a lot of time “opening people up” and finding ways to inspire them to improve their

circumstances.

(3) Application:

In discussing policy changes with a social service agency, I was trying to explain to them

the benefits of taking a more client focused approach, among other things, and in

particular, of recognizing each person as a unique being, and addressing their individual

needs first and foremost. The agency was in the grip of a “compliance culture” and its

clients were failing in this non-empathetic, rigid structure. I was also explaining how

sometimes addressing the needs of one individual can impact everyone for the better,

even if it seems extreme or out of the ordinary. I told a story about when I ran an

emergency shelter after a natural disaster. Everyone was doing really well except for one

woman whose stress was making her very emotionally volatile. I could tell she needed

attention; in my mind I decided she would be “Princess for an hour.” I made her a cup of

coffee and sat down with her and let her talk. It turned out that her mother, who was with

her, had survived a brain aneurysm and she was terrified that she would fall or that some

other crisis would befall her during this disaster while in the shelter.

(4) Insight:

Well, wow, that was an eye-opener. Her mother was a calm presence and doing very

well. Clearly it was time for me to open up with my story. I told her how scary it was

when my father had his brain aneurysm in front of me and how I had to get him to the

hospital and how difficult and scary that all was. I shared how he recovered well, and

then tied us together, by noting how she and I both have parents who survived brain

aneurysms. This worked really well. She really needed individual attention for that brief

time, and she ended up with that and a true support. She calmed down, her mother, who

had become worried about her, calmed down, and everyone around them calmed down.

Peace reigned again in our little shelter.

(5) Approach:

This story I send to the agency, and I think it had a big impact on people there. The

policies are being reevaluated and the caseworkers are going through new training.

Sometimes a little story can do a lot of good. This course made me see this as a tool in a

new way. When I've done it before it was really "ad hoc," but now I can prepare ahead

and think of stories that will assist me in presenting my ideas and best illuminate them. I

have a design background, but I ended up as an entrepreneur in business. I had no idea

this would ever be considered an asset, but I am so very grateful that it is.

Reflection-Storytelling

Challenge    Storytelling is the process of using fact and narrative to communicate something to your  audience. Some stories are factual, and some are embellished or improvised in order to better  explain the core message.

Storytelling is an art form as old as time and has a place in every culture and society. Why?  Because stories are a universal language that everyone — regardless of dialect, hometown, or  heritage — can understand. Stories stimulate imagination and passion and create a sense of  community among listeners and tellers alike.

Telling a story is like painting a picture with words. While everyone can tell a story, certain people  fine-tune their storytelling skills and become a storyteller on behalf of their organization, brand, or  business. You might’ve heard of these folks — we typically refer to them as marketers, content  writers, or PR professionals.

I love to listen to stories. I get to learn a lot of things from them. Better storytelling can help in  better communicating with a person which would eventually help to understand someone in a  much more efficient way.

Selection

Every member of an organization can tell a story. But before we get into the how, let’s talk about  why we tell stories — as a society, culture, and economy. There are a variety of reasons to tell  stories — to sell, entertain, educate or brag.

Stories help solidify abstract concepts and simplify complex messages. Taking a lofty,  non-tangible concept and relating it using concrete ideas is one of the biggest strengths of  storytelling in business.

Take Apple, for example. Computers and smartphones are a pretty complicated topic to describe  to your typical consumer. Using real-life stories, they’ve been able to describe exactly how their  products benefit users … instead of relying on technical jargon that very few customers would  understand.

Stories make us human, and the same goes for brands. When brands get transparent and  authentic, it brings them down-to-earth and helps consumers connect with them and the people  behind them.

Application

I use the storytelling tool much often. I love UI/UX design. So whenever there a problem comes up  it’s very crucial to do the background research, take interviews of users, explain your insights to  stakeholders. So I use stories to make an impact, and help them understand things better. It also  helped me to create empathy and understand users’ emotions and frustrations so that I can  design a better product for them.

I also link filmmaking. Particularly I am interested in cinematography and scriptwriting. So as we  know and the great movie starts with a great script. So when a movie project is started, I start  brainstorming and as soon I come up with some good idea, it’s my job to explain my thoughts to  my team very clearly keeping in mind the budget constraints.

If you are interested too in music videos and filmmaking, please check out our youtube channel  Cinematic Section, IIT Roorkee​ or use the URL - https://www.jackson.com/list/explorehomepage.htm

Insight & Approach

It is really a great tool. It helped me explain myself and my thoughts to others in a much more  effective way. I got to learn that good stories are-

● Entertaining: Good stories keep the reader engaged and interested in what’s coming next.

● Educational: Good stories spark curiosity and add to the reader’s knowledge bank.

● Universal: Good stories are relatable to all readers and tap into emotions and experiences  that most people undergo.

● Organized: Good stories follow a succinct organization that helps convey the core message  and helps readers absorb it.

● Memorable: Whether through inspiration, scandal, or humour, good stories stick in the  reader’s mind.

Also, I learned that, for a better storytelling approach, carry out the following processes-

1. Know your audience

2. Define your core message

3. Decide what kind of story you’re telling

4. Establish your call-to-action

5. Choose your story medium

you selected or a different one -- and the reason(s) why.

Next time, I will apply the same tool, but I want to insert the innovation metrics. This can  avoid vanity metrics influence in the project development and bring a better management  along the testing.

Challenge

Since 2011 I lead a product team at a Peruvian bank. I have the role of Product Manager, which involves  leading and coaching a team of cross-functional people to develop and evolve a product. The product we  were in charge was called Manyar and it´s a mobile application to look for restaurant information and  menu and also to get dishes recommendations (we used machine learning for this one).

However, as COVID-19 stroke in Peru (we are already in day 60 and restaurants have been closed all this  time) we needed to change our business model in order to survive. We have a limited budget and couldn’t  afford to undertake a big bet and be mistaken. This is where Design Thinking enters.

Selection

We decided to use the Learning Launch since this would allow us to test small bets and measure the results  in order to get fast and cheap feedback from our users -as explained in the video about Learning Launch.  We would then use this feedback to learn if our ideas would serve to have a business model pivot towards  a new one.

Since conducting this pivot in the traditional way would involve time and money (and both were limited  resources to us), Learning Launch became a natural alternative to our challenge, since as the course  stated, it provides a better solution that is based on feedback instead of the traditional way based on  assumptions and tweaks.

Application

We decided to create small experiments. We had a Business Model Canvas from the previous business  model and we copied it 4 times in order to create 4 pivots we would like to test on the real market with  real customers.

Our principal criteria was the find product-market fit, which would allow the new business model to grow  and ideally become profitable. So, we select the 4 most voted ideas from our visual brainstorming session-  conducted with stakeholders and  early adopters from our business model. It was challenging since we  had to conduct this sessions remotely due to social isolation but we managed to get everybody  communicated using the tool Mural which also allows us to use visual tools to facilitate communication  among people. Once in Mural, we managed to rank the 4 most voted pivots: gastronomy social network,  take-away and delivery solution, restaurant to consumer marketplace and recipes/cook-it-yourself app.

We got the usability results from our previous user research and used it to design 4 prototypes using the  Marvel tool in order to have a testable high-fidelity version of the 4 new pivots, presented as mobile  applications. Marvel also allows you to install those prototypes on the phones so we had to distributed  these new versions according to a split test.

We selected 100 users who liked or loved us (had an NPS higher than 8) and also 100 users who hated us  (NPS lower than 3). We then created 4 random samples of 50 people (25 from each segment) to test the  pivots. We called and emailed the people and got down to 40 people per sample since some of them  never answered. After that, we sent the prototypes via WhatsApp so they could download it directly on

their smartphones/iPhones. After the test, we conducted some interviews to get qualitative and  quantitative feedback from users.

Insights

The learning launch was successful. We managed to get information about the prototypes and learned  our customers didn’t care about the delivery and take-away pivot since they were still fearing the COVID  and believed restaurants could potentially lie about or make mistakes about security measures to prevent  COVID. Even though they idea sounded good, most of the people learned to cook and were improving at  their cooking skills as quarantine continued. This insight was radical to the point only 1 person (which lived  in upper-class part of Lima city) mentioned they would consider using this application.

This applied to restaurant-user marketplace since it also involved restaurants. It seemed like customers  were really doubting about restaurants implementing and executing security measures correctly. They  also wanted to have more control about the food they and their families ate.

On the other side, the prototypes about cook-it-yourself and the gastronomy social network were the one  with better appreciation. Insights about having recipes and cook-it-yourself content inside the social  network were flowing in more than 80% of users (82.5%). For cook-it-yourself prototype, people told they  wanted to have a social usage, to share and get recipes and information with their families and friends,  who where locked away due to COVID. 67.5% of the users provided this feedback.

Overall, this allowed us to unify both prototypes into a food social network we could them take to a next  iteration of the prototype and also allowed us to create surveys which we would pass to all our users in  order to understand which features they would prefer to have implemented first.

Approach

The usage of Learning Launch was successful since it has allowed us to launch a business model pivot  which we just launched and got 1000 active users in the first weekend.

However, what I would do differently is to couple Mind Mapping as an alternative to traditional  brainstorming since this would avoid getting bias and too much confirmation bias about own ideas and  instead focus the development of ideas around design criteria. It would also allow us to consider the  number of design criteria met as a way to rank ideas instead of conducting a simple voting, which can lead  to some powerful ideas because we resist them for their novelty.

Visualization.

Challenge & Selection

The tool I selected is Visualization. I use this approach often with our students, who are still in the  initial learning stage. I have used many times the subcategory of visualization which are known as  charts, graphs, various tree diagrams to convert the textual form or the various geographical or  demographic and statistical aspects in visualized form. Sometimes there is hurry of conducting  meetings or the listener or the speaker has a less time to communicate or …the speaker or the  presenter sometimes gets short on his vocabulary …here the visuals a play a major role. Visualization  is there in work since the stone age man existed, rather I would say Visualization was the primary  language because visualization was primarily observed as the paintings carved in the caves of stone  age man, the stone age people used to communicate through those drawn paintings. They conveyed  their feelings; they conveyed the happened incidents etc and if you see in this 21st century we are  using pie charts, graphs, tree diagram, not only in education industry but also everywhere else.

The conditions we faced during covid pandemic situation…teachers, company meetings used this  visualization component on a large scale, we can say power point presentation is one of the tiny  components of visualization through those presentations the employees, students were able to  grasp the information and memorize it very quickly as well as the teachers and project managers  were quickly able to display or convey the thought process behind the lecture or sessions or  meetings.

Application

Charts- The main functions of a chart are to display data and invite further exploration of a topic.  Charts are used in situations where a simple table won't adequately demonstrate important  relationships or patterns between data points.

Graphs-Graphs are a common method to visually illustrate relationships in the data. The purpose of  a graph is to present data that are too numerous or complicated to be described adequately in the  text and in less space.

Tree Diagram-A tree diagram is a tool in the fields of general mathematics, probability, and statistics  that helps calculate the number of possible outcomes of an event or problem, and to cite those  potential outcomes in an organized way.

GIFs-GIFs lighten the tone of your presentation and are a useful tool for quickly engaging (or re- engaging) your viewers. They’re a great way to add humour in an otherwise mundane piece of  content, give instructions in a product or process, and so much more.

Animation-Animated videos, images, or words grab your viewer’s attention much more effectively  than a still or text-only image. Another power of animation is its capability to make complex ideas  simple and relatable to any viewer who comes across it.

Images-You’ve heard that a picture is worth a thousand words. If you can use one to visualize your  point, do it.

Infographics-Infographics offer complex information or statistics in an easy-to-digest, impactful way.  Charts and graphs help the viewer comprehend data quickly, in a way that’s much simpler than  explaining with words.

Insight & Approach

The lessons learned from this “Designed thinking for innovation “I would like to discuss here –

A visualization approach increase communication, increase critical thinking, and provides analytical  approach to various problems. ... The results also shows that the visualization motivates students to  learn, making them more cooperative and developing their skills for critical approach. Though the  approach is broad in nature, and it not only include education sector as well as it helps a lot in other  sectors also which are industries, pharma, politics, business strategies, it also simply helps to get  understood the upcoming financial policies. Visualization is a tool which makes things easy for the  less educated as well as educated people to understand the matter in a gist. And if we recollect the  facts or reviews from the people “The Visuals are remembered for long time …than a reading  comprehension”.

REFLECTION: MIND MAPPING

1. Challenge

I’m working on a redesign project of the exterior of an automatic cutting machine for  Ogilvy the Advertising and  Communication. Before starting the redesign, we had to better understand what were the  client’s needs, so we had a meeting before the briefing and the briefing itself.

2. Selection & Application

When designing, we need to gather a lot of information from research and also from  meetings with the clients, so we can design better products and achieve better  results. To overcome the challenge of being lost having too much information to deal  with at the same time, I always end up using mind maps. They’re a great tool if you  want better organized data in your project, like said in the course “Mind mapping is  one of the most powerful tools in the design thinker's toolbox.”     All the information gathered from a briefing with a client, like Ogilvy the Advertising and  Communication, can be better  organized utilizing sections, subsections and topics, for example, and you can also use  illustrations, drawings, images – everything that’ll make you visualize the information  in a better way. My team used Miro to create the mind map, an awesome site if  you’re a creative person that also likes practicality. There, we checked if all the data  gathered from the client’s meetings were organized in a simple way that everyone  could understand. Like David Kelley, the founder of IDEO said, “When I want to do  something analytical, I make a list. When I'm trying to do something creative, I make  a mind-map”.

3. Insight

A mind map is a great tool to look for patterns, insights, relations between  information, how they’re all connected in your project. All that leads to more creative  solutions to your designs. After using the tool, I realized how it’s important for a  design thinker to know how to use it, so he/she can take the next step in a project.  You can see the data way more clearly than if you were using a list and also can give  more creative solutions to your client.

4. Approach

Next time I use the tool, I’ll make sure to better summarize all the information using  shorter phrases and words to describe the client’s needs and information in general.  I’ll also use more images and references from the internet to visualize better what  I’m dealing with, the problems, the solutions and the opportunities.

Design Thinking for Innovation  June 12, 2020  Elizabeth Pedraza          Challenge    Our consulting team worked with a Planning and Scheduling Division of a family-owned pasta  company with inventory problems resulting in lost revenue. The company had times when they  had either too much inventory (food was going bad - obsolesence) or too little inventory (back- orders or shortages), both situations resulting in unhappy customer relationships and lost  profits. Our team was brought in to understand and find solutions to the company’s inventory  problems.    Selection      The team decided that a time-series visual view of the historical actions taken by the relevant  parties would illuminate opportunities for improving inventory-related decision-making.  Seeing  what happened, people could then discuss what happened and why.  This should lead to ideas  for process improvements to solve the shortage and oversupply issues.  We believed that doing  this would help reduce waste, increase margins, increase revenues and please customers.    What the team chose, after careful consideration, was the business intelligence visualization  tool Microsoft Power BI. Power BI allows the creation of interactive graphs, which a user can,  without any skill or training, manipulate or filter to show multiple scenarios or views of the  underlying data.  This was a simple, visual way for everyone to gain insight into the problems  and thereby trigger useful conversations leading to collaborative solutions.

Application   In addition to quantitative data gathering (and cleansing), particularly sales order, production,  shipment, and inventory status data, the team spent many hours interviewing officers and line  people.  They wanted to include multiple perspectives on what happened, hoping to reveal the  thinking that lead to poor decisions in the past and suggest better ways to handle similar  situations in the future.    The choice of Power BI and its graph of inventory data told a visual story. Because the graphs  were simple, easy to understand, and single-page, everyone could look at a chart and quite  easily see which weeks the company should have made more of a particular type of pasta and  which weeks they should have sold pasta from existing inventory.  They could also see order  patterns and production patterns, or lack thereof.  By seeing these patterns visually and  intuitively, it was easy for the stakeholders to offer improvement recommendations.    Insight

The visual tool was a nonverbal way using colors, symbols that could convey messages to all  stakeholders, create conversations leading to alignment and explaining patterns which lead to  ideation and prototypes of solving the problem as we learned from overall design thinking.    One of the biggest insights from the ideation sessions was how thirsty people are for more  information when asked to make decisions or improvements.  The most common questions  from the team usually began with “Can we …..?”.  They wanted more information to overlay  with what we presented.  Can we look at this by customer?  Can we look at this by region?  Can  we look at this by salesperson?  Etc.  In Power Bi, if the data exists, the answer is almost always  “yes”!  Curiosity was palpable in every session.  Easy visualization of complex data stimulates  creativity.      Approach  The clients (pasta company and customers) were very satisfied with the visual solutions our  team offered and demanded more. Our consulting team were satisfied with the platform we  used and created more graphs showing different pasta skus and applications of company  inventory data.   The clients have enhanced the tool themselves since the first workshops.      Next time our team will definitely use Power BI again, but we might spend more time up front,  collecting (and cleaning) more ancillary data, [e.g. forecast (past and future), raw materials  supply, or sales/marketing promotion calendars] and moving it into the Power Bi database so  that more “what if” scenarios could be run on the spot.  We under-estimated how curious the  team would be and how immediately thirsty they would be for more scenario modeling. Having  that instant response while the team is fully engaged seems to be much more productive than  re-convening at a later date to take the next steps.

Challenge

I live in a part of the word where residents are charged arbitrarily by service providers (government and  private organizations) for services rendered. We don’t get to know the basis and how much of such  services we enjoyed. All we see is bills at the end of the month and we get disconnected if not paid or  we are made to make payments in advance while deductions are made termed ‘pay as you use’.  Residents crave to know how they are billed so they can make plans in advance to match their income.

One of such services with arbitrary bills is water supply. The people in my community resisted these bills  and chased out the service providers. The wealthy ones in the community dug up bore holes to meet  their water needs while the poor ones move about in search of water. They use any available source  whether clean or not and in recent times, there has been outbreak of cholera in many homes with  children dying.

To address this, I formed an association of youths in the community. We planned on presenting a  proposal to one of the private owned organization and hope to partner with them in restoring portable  water supply in my community with a transparent billing system.

Selection

We selected a collaborative approach that will meet the needs of the residents without compromising  the profit objectives of the service provider. We adopted the co-creation approach. We hope to  collaborate with them and share ideas that will be beneficial to us all.

Application

The community representative had dialogues with the water service provider. Suggestions on billing  parameters, water needs and income level were shared by the youth representatives because they have  firsthand knowledge of the needs of the community and exchange of ideas were made. These meetings  were held between both parties until an agreement was made and water supply was restored in the  community.

Insight

This experience thought me that no man is an island. We need each other and we must consider what  the end user needs.

Approach

I would include us this method and maybe incorporate other tools next time am presented with a  challenge.

Design Thinking in Career Development and Counseling  Alessandra Farrag

Design Thinking in Career Development and Counseling      Introduction    With almost twenty years of experience in organizational and people development, I have  never knowingly applied design thinking methodologies or tools in order to solve business  problems or people issues. I was not even aware that design thinking exists.  Thus, it struck me by surprise when I discovered the similarities between the design thinking  approach (Malak, 2016) and the career coaching process based upon systems theory,  success strategy and cybernetics (Friedrich, Seiwert and Geffroy, 2003, p.23):

Design Thinking  Career Design

What is?  Looking inside: self assessment, analysis, synthesis

What if?  Looking outside: orientation, options, and evaluation  What wows?  What works?  Looking forward: career action plan design and implementation

Design thinking in general with its procedures and instruments appears to be useful in  dealing with career development issues. It may help finding answers to the question how to  effectively design and propose a unique portfolio of competencies in a world of work that has  become increasingly volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (Laurençon, 2014).      1. Challenge    A typical challenge in career counseling is to help the client discover and understand his or  her own work life story and its patterns without providing answers or even advice. Normally,  people are not used to analyzing their own history and development including a reflection of  their values, motivated skills, preferred work settings and satisfiers, barriers and constraints.  However, without a thorough self-assessment a client won’t be able to figure out what might  be suitable and sustainable career options. The ‘what is’ or ‘looking inside’ phase should not  be cut short or skipped – even if the client is itching to apply for a new job immediately.  ‘If you don’t know where you are going, you might end up somewhere else’ (C. Stengel) – but  if you don’t know where you are coming from, you might get stuck in the middle of nowhere  again and again. As career counselors we are supposed to put our clients back into the  driver’s seat from the very beginning in order not to waste time or talent or both.      2. Selection    In this initial stage of the career coaching process the instrument of choice is storytelling.  Storytelling is not just a design thinking tool (Malak, 2016, Module 2) but also the foundation  of narrative management and communications in a broad variety of contexts (Sammer, 2014,  p.36). Narrative management encompasses personal and corporate storytelling, narrative  knowledge management, leadership communications, and narrative change management  (Erlach & Müller, 2015/2016). ‘Stories or narratives are a unique derivative of systems theory  thinking and are key to constructivist approaches’ (Patton & McMahon, 1999, p.235).  Storytelling is very useful in human resources management in general, e.g. in recruitment  and selection. For instance, if you ask a candidate in a job interview to tell his or her story  rather than to take you through the stages of a polished résumé, the person will most likely  open up (and tell you much more than previously intended).  We all love stories. We love to use our episodic brain. We ‘think’ in stories and tend to forget  unrelated facts (Erlach & Müller, 2015, pp.3-4; Sammer, 2014, p.1). We all have a personal

Design Thinking in Career Development and Counseling  Alessandra Farrag

and professional story to tell with a myriad of twists and turns, touch and pain points. So,  administering standardized and primarily quantitative assessment tools (e.g., surveys or  psychological tests) in career counseling to gather data, to analyze types, and to pigeonhole  someone is definitely not enough and does not do justice to a person’s individuality and  character. These tools should be complemented by qualitative instruments like storytelling  (Patton & McMahon, 1999, p.236).  Consequently, I start the career counseling process with a seemingly simple question:  What’s your story?      3. Application    There are basically two reactions: a smile or a blank face. In our world of ‘hard facts’ many  people have forgotten how to tell stories, especially their own. Others get carried away as  soon as they are taken seriously and obtain ‘permission’ to talk about themselves.  In order to assist the client I ask guiding and probing questions (Guerriero & Allen, 1998,  pp.26-37 and own compilation), for example:

•  Tell me be about your career to date.

•  What were you trained for in school/college/university?

•  What career paths have you been following?

•  What do you regret/resent?

•  Which achievements are important to you and why?

•  What do all of your jobs/assignments have in common?

•  What have been the most rewarding/disappointing components of your jobs?

•  What are the highlights of your job history or career chronology?

•  Have you been repeating some of the same employment patterns that did not feel  right for you?

•  What is your current level of satisfaction at work?

•  Have you ever thought that you would be happier in a different work environment?

•  How do you define success and how will you know it when you have it?

•  When you are ninety-five years old, what will you want to say about your life?

•  What is it for you to have a full, rich life?

Telling one’s life and career story will assist the client with uncovering patterns and themes  and forgotten events, with making meaning of his or her own career, with understanding  experiences, and with re-constructing (Patton & McMahon, 1999, p.148, p.177 and p. 235).  The client will interpret his or her background and uncover the influence of significant others,  i.e. the roles in the career story: protagonist and antagonist (a person or a barrier), objectives  and helpers or mentors (Erlach & Müller, 2015, p.5). S/he will be able to deal with  (suppressed) emotions and focus on the WHY rather than the WHAT of his or her career  development to date (Sammer, 2014, p.56). This includes dealing with change, challenges,  and conflict as the key to and starting-point of any story (Sammer, 2014, p.117; Patton &  McMahon, 1999, p.177). Eventually, the client will find his or her unique strengths, motivated  skills, and a potential compelling offer (Friedrich, Seiwert and Geffroy, 2003, p.23) based  upon what constitutes individual success and failure.  For example, one of my clients, a gifted artist, realized throughout the process how much  pressure her parents had put on her in order to push her into a ‘real’ career. However, she  always wanted to be a painter and photographer. So, after getting a thorough understanding  of her own story, she worked hard to overcome the internalized parental voice, dominance,  and resistance and eventually became a famous artist. Another client, a frustrated bank  clerk, realized in an intensive (and painful) storytelling session, that his dream to go and work  on a farm in Iceland was not a stupid fantasy but his calling. He gathered plenty of  information, designed an action plan, and hopped on a plane.

Design Thinking in Career Development and Counseling  Alessandra Farrag

It does not have to be Iceland, though. One of my clients really loved her sales job, but  figured out whilst telling her story, that the performance-driven corporate world was not the  ideal environment for her to creatively find unconventional solutions for her customers. Today  she works for a medium-sized organization sharing her values.  The prerequisite for and key ingredient of an effective application of storytelling in career  design is listening with unconditional positive regard. The experience of not being assessed  or judged or discriminated against for one’s ideas and dreams, choices and decisions,   ‘mistakes’ and ‘failures’ will most likely enable the client to get unstuck, to find answers to  burning career issues, and to move forward or into a completely different direction.      4. Insight    Analyzing client stories helps me to understand work life values and stages, work adjustment  styles, the client’s degree of career maturity, self-concepts and learning strategies,  environmental conditions and events. These insights are the foundation of the career  counseling process and determine the direction the journey will take. By listening to the  client’s story and by observing emotional reactions, I am able to adjust the focus, intensity,  and speed of the entire consulting process and therefore to actively form and enrich the  coaching relationship.  For the customer, there is a ‘dual use effect’ and extra value deriving from storytelling:  knowing and understanding one’s own career story inward and outward will be of great help  to present the (essential parts of the) story combined with a unique selling proposition to a  potential employer or customer at a later stage. It’s always amazing to hear the exact same  career story in a myriad of truthful variations as soon as a positive attitude, self-confidence,  and courage come into play. For example, one of my clients used to constantly point out  negative issues of her career in an interview. As a consequence she gathered a depressingly  high number of rejections to her applications. Once she was able to re-frame her own story,  she came across much more self-confident and convincing and succeeded in obtaining a  position in a suitable work environment.  Career counseling is like working on a puzzle with a dizzying number of pieces. With the help  of storytelling the client will build and eventually see the bigger picture (Malak & Malak,  2011, pos.1028), i.e. his or her unique work life ‘painting’. It may sound contradictory, but  knowing and understanding the value of storytelling as a powerful instrument of design  thinking enables me to combine it more effectively with other selected and individualized  tools (e.g., card sorts, work diaries) in career counseling sessions.      5. Approach    As mentioned previously, I sometimes encounter clients whose approach to any kind of work  issue is driven by facts and figures (e.g., the stereotypical engineer or financial analyst).  Thus, I initially need to find out what kind of career assessment method the person may  prefer. If s/he is more of a straightforward, analytic, numbers, procedures (you name it) type,  other tools quickly providing structure (e.g., mind mapping, questionnaires, bullet point lists),  may be more appropriate to begin with.  However, storytelling should always be the key instrument. It does not have to be called  storytelling explicitly as this may put some people off. Apart from this, some may need more  or different probing questions than others. For example, one client told me right away that he  was not interested in telling stories but in producing results fast and furiously. He was  convinced that it was my job to provide the network, contacts, and leads he needed. With a  few WHY questions he could not escape, we broke the ice and got to the core of his career  issues. All of a sudden he talked about a number of poor work experiences he was ashamed  of and desperately tried to hide from others.

Design Thinking in Career Development and Counseling  Alessandra Farrag

Ultimately, when applying storytelling in a career counseling session I need to avoid jumping  to conclusions too fast or steering the client into a specific direction (in order to confirm my  own ideas or assumptions). As a skilled helper I am supposed to see, hear, and feel what the  client needs and select and apply the methodologies and instruments accordingly.      Conclusion    Discovering that a design thinking attitude has been part of my career counseling practice for  a long time (without my knowing that there’s actually a name to it), was demystifying,  liberating, and enriching. There must be a reason why I initially called my consulting services  ‘career design’.  It’s more or less a confirmation that analytic approaches only have never been effective  enough in this entirely human-centered, complex area of expertise (Malak, 2016, Module 1).  This is even more important when long-term career plans need to be complemented and  sometimes even replaced by constantly re-creating one’s career and re-designing one’s path  and place in our brave new world of work. Reflection – Mind Mapping – Johnny Bryant

Challenge

Being a  marketing professional in Telecommunications, I’m currently in charge of my company’s B2B  Customers’ Segment Marketing. My primary focus being the strategic management of mobile data  products, I aim to increase the market penetration, usage and revenue. Therefore I specified my  challenge as improving the digital data package buying experience of  B2B line users through our  mobile app, Digital Operator to accumulate incremental revenue and higher EBITDA. The Core  Project group consists of 16 stakeholders from different departments within the company, including  Sales, Marketing, Customer Experience, IT and Call Center.  In 20 business days we will expose the  main pain points preventing B2B users from buying online data packages to determine the optimum  digital buying experience as a result.

Selection

Mind Mapping is the most suitable approach to narrow down the pain points in our customers’  minds effectively with limited resources because our B2B customer database is very diversified  including 2,5 mio users with differing personas. Since our group has conducted etnographic  interviews and collected customer diaries to this specific database beforehand, mind mapping is the  appropriate design tool to explore “patterns and insights in this large quantity of data creatively” as  Josephine Aguero from  Darden explains.

Application

As mentioned before our group had massive data including etnographic interviews and customer  diaries. I divided the Project group into 4 groups of 4 stakeholders each. The first task was to write  down the most critical customer feedbacks mentioned in the interviews onto post-its. Then each  group put the post-its on the relevant stage of the B2B customer buying journey map, including the  outliers. After combining all of the feedbacks that seemed crucial to the stakeholders, we combined  the similar ones to simplify. Then the groups identified the insights related to each stage on the  customer journey map considering the clustered ideas. While forming the insights we included the  specific persona, what he/she needs & wants as a result and what his/her the current situation is and  what the main obstacle is. An insight statemet example is; The big company professional Andy want  to be able to use more mobile data for his personal causes via his corporate line but he should fit in  the package his company determined for him and he can not but additional packages on his  corporate line by his own decision. When we listed all the insights from the clusters the mind  mapping was complete.

Insight

The mind mapping approach worked very effectively because our “what is” question implied  understanding all of the current stages in the customer journey map of B2B customers digital  package buying experience. Since the stages and the customer personas differed dramatically, mind  mapping worked very well to organize the cluster of ideas, choose the most critical ones and form  the relevant insight sentences.

Approach

With the gathered mass of information of the diverse data base of customers I would use mind  mapping to narrow the pain points to the most crucial ones because it’s the most effective and  resource saving method. However, I would combine the method with visualization to better

comprehend the customer point of view, to see the customers mind more clearly. I believe Mind  mapping will be a more creative process with  imagery, color and visual expressions.

Eva Rivera  Design Thinking for Innovation  Simona Gamal  April 5th, 2021

Course Reflection

1) Challenge & Selection

At my current job, I was approached by a UX manager for whom I provided administrative support; he  had heard that I was passionate about the environment and asked if I would help him in standing up a  Green Team in our office. He and I connected with the Green Team leads in the Philadelphia office, and  we learned that the local office teams that already existed were the result of grassroots organizing. For  our office in Princeton, this meant that developing a team wouldn’t be as simple as getting buy-in from  our Office Manager and Office Managing Principal (OMP). The real challenge was understanding the  needs and priorities specific to the individuals in our office and figuring out how we could get maximum  engagement by catering our group’s sustainability efforts to suit those needs.

Our core team (me, the manager, and two other folks in the office) chose to use Mind Mapping for this  challenge. According to the guest video lecture from Eva Rivera, mind-mapping is a  strategy where you take the data you amassed during the “what is?” phase and look for patterns and  themes that emerge, as these patterns and themes can help inform the “what if?” phase. We chose  this tool because we wanted to see if any of the reasons people cited for wanting to participate in the  Green Team could be grouped into themes that could then inform how our core team planned events,  allocated time and resources, and recruited more team members moving forward.

2) Application

Our core team presented a slide deck for our office forum, introducing the idea of a Princeton Green  Team and asking people to help make it a reality. After the forum, we connected with several potential  participants and organized a brainstorming session/kick-off. During this meeting, we opened a MURAL  canvas (a web-based service similar to a virtual whiteboard), and asked people to add post-its to the  canvas to answer the question: “If we as a Green Team could accomplish one thing before the end of  2017, what would you like that thing to be?”

We wanted to understand why the people who joined the call cared about sustainability and what  made them want to be a part of the team. We tried to keep the question broad and hoped that we  could tap into folks’ unarticulated needs by establishing a concrete action that they wanted to pursue.  By including the end-of-year deadline, we could determine what the priority was for each respondent.

People began adding their post-its, and there were a variety of different reasons why everyone felt  passionate about the company getting involved in Green efforts. They ranged from “my daughter says  it’s important to care about climate change” to “I want to focus on the accessibility of sustainable living  practices for every socioeconomic status,” with several reasons in between. It was motivating to see so  many people sharing their Whys, but our core team knew that in order to make progress and develop a  game plan, we would need to assess the post-its we had gathered and tease out any patterns we could.

In another meeting, this time just with the core team, we all looked at the MURAL canvas and, one by  one, we started to move the post-its around when we noticed that they had things in common. Soon,  four distinct groups of post-its emerged, and we decided to label them as follows:

•  Community Involvement – Organize and participate in trail or park clean-ups, offer pro-bono  consulting, work on local government outreach, etc.

•  Awareness and Learning –  Conduct/find research on sustainability concepts and find engaging  ways to share this info with the office (lunch-and-learns, newsletters/email blasts, etc.)

•  Team Building – Engage in fun, social activities like sustainable facility tours or Green Bingo

•  Sustainable Practices –  Establish and reinforce Green habits at work and in our personal lives

These categories were all connected to each other but parsing them out helped tremendously when we  needed to figure out the best places to put our energy. Now that we had an idea of how others wanted  to spend their time engaging with the Green Team, and some concept of the ratio of people interested  in each area, we could begin to test events catered to each of these categories with the office.

3) Insight & Approach

It was actually through reflecting on this challenge after taking this course that I gained insight on how  we could have done things better. Applying the tools of design thinking more intentionally would have  saved us a lot of time and a lot of headaches during the process of standing up a Green Team.

In the beginning, both I and the manager came in with assumptions. Other offices within our company  had already started Green Teams, and I assumed that it would be easy to simply replicate what they had  done. Despite using design thinking tools for almost all his client work, I think this manager also  assumed that creating a local team would be a plug-and-play situation that wouldn’t require much in the  ways of time or effort. However, we discovered shortly after starting that we had underestimated the  scope of the problem by assuming “what is?” instead of being curious and finding out “what is?”.

Like in the story of the Good Kitchen, where the government assumed that the issue was as simple as a  menu change, we assumed that our office had no existing team because someone just hadn’t started  one. Once Hatch and Bloom did journey mapping and conducted ethnographic research of the seniors,  they discovered the problem was more complex, and required a more innovative solution.

If I were to do this again, I wouldn’t necessarily choose a different tool; I think that mind-mapping did  serve our team well once we arrived at that stage. What I would do differently is use the 4-question  framework (what is, what if, what wows, what works). I would do some ethnographic research of a  small sample of stakeholders in our office and use that research to inform the entire design process. It  would have been helpful to know more about the people we were trying to engage, to really take the  time to research the “what is?” for our office, before we put any time or effort into creating a slide deck  and trying to get buy-in from our Office Manager and OMP. I think our team jumped the gun, and in  doing so, limited ourselves from doing something innovative and made things harder on ourselves.

Visualization – Antonio Coppola

Challenge: Change Management on a proposed process change within the claims organization of a large  US based P&C insurer which will greatly modify how First Notice of Loss (FNOL) submissions are  processed. Change of process will introduce Robotic Process Automation (RPA) functionality and  significantly modify work content and responsibilities for Contact Center associates.

Selection: Selected Visualization, or visual thinking to create a shared understanding of the problem the  change of process was attempting to solve. The approach used leverages pictures to help visualize  painpoints and desired future state in a brainstorming format. The pictures are intended to evoke an  emotional response to real life issues, frustrations and ideals that the associates are feeling.

Application: I conducted several focus group sessions with customers to obtain Voice of the Customer  (VOC) and several focus groups with associates to obtain Voice of the Associate (VOA). The sessions  were held over several weeks to ensure we had a good representation of customers and associates. I  began the VOC sessions with a high-level process map to represent the customers experience as they  traveled along the process of filing an auto damage claim. I then asked the customers to select pictures  that best represented how they felt through the process. Pictures selected ranged from feelings of  frustration, fear, uncertainty, anger, etc.. which were not surprising. In most cases the claimant has just  been in a car accident, not saavy of the insurance process, and is flustered. The pictures that were  selected to describe their ideal state gave an indication that the wanted to be comforted, have  confidence that things were being handled (repairs, rental, etc.) and wanted to hear a human voice.  Shortly afterward I conducted Focus group sessions with the associates using a process map to show the  process they followed. As with the customer group, I had the associates select pictures to describe their  feelings through the process and to illustrate what their desired state would be.

Insight: After compiling the results from the two separate Focus Group experiments, I compiled the  themes from each of the groups using word clouds to visualize the results. The outcome was shocking!  The associates used similar words and selected similar pictures as the customers not only with the  painpoints and issues but also with the desired future state.

What I had learned from using this technique is that while you can often get participation from different  study groups through plain old brainstorming, putting the process in visual form and using pictures  absolutely energized the groups to share at a much more personal level.

Approach: After showing the similarities in response that the customers had, I revisited the change we  were proposing for the FNOL process and the use of automation. With a few minor changes to the  process as a result of the focus group feedback, we were able to implement the changes, realize a  positive impact on customer experience and provide more meaningful customer facing work to the  associate.

Cheese Startup - Learning Launch ​by Eladio Amaya

Challenge

We are a small company in Barcelona (Spain) that refines high-quality organic cheeses  from small producers in the Pyrenees. We also trade milk and yogurts from these  producers. We distribute our dairy products mainly to haute cuisine restaurants (60% of  our turnover) and to Delicatesens stores (35% of our turnover), the remaining 5% we  distribute to individuals, mainly family, friends and acquaintances.    Selection

I have chosen the "Learning Launch" because it is more adapted to my way of working  and the needs of the company.    Application

Due to the coronavirus crisis, all restaurants have closed and Delicatesen store sales  have dropped dramatically. therefore we have had to change our target niche and head  towards private individuals and common stores.    We have carried out a survey both in small stores and among individuals. In the survey  we asked what types of cheese are the most willing to consume, as well as milk and  yogurts, also the type of milk (goat, cow, sheep), the level of curing and the price they  would be willing to pay for our products. We have also proposed sending boxes with  different products on offer, in which the average price is significantly lower.    After the survey and the observations of individuals and small stores, we have focused  our offer on a certain type of product, we have distributed it and analyzed the result not  only with our customers but also with objective sales figures.    Insight

The result has been spectacular, our weekly turnover had fallen to 25% with a loss of  75% (60% of restaurants and 15% of delicatessen stores). The situation was dramatic  but nowadays sales to individuals have risen from 5% to 25% and common food stores  have gone from 0% to 15%.

Approach

Our situation is not good, but we hope that when the restaurants open and the economy  recovers. We will have a much broader portfolio of clients and a way of working based  on the client and transferred to the producer. Before, we used to transfer products from  small producers to customers. Now the flow has changed.

Reporting process

by Gilberto Gamboa

Challenge

I received a promotion of being the Regional Controller, along with my actual position of

Country CFO. The main responsibility of this new position was to weekly report the results

for the week and estimate the final results of the month of 4 countries and consolidated

those.

When I was receiving the position, I went to visit my colleague, former Regional Controller,

who was promoted to Country CEO and now had interest conflicts of being the controller.

The process to consolidate the information of the 4 countries was that the country controllers

sent him an email with the main figures for the week, he forwarded those to his country

accountant who consolidated it, the accountant sent him the consolidated report and he

finally reported to the headquarters. The whole process took almost a full business day to

complete.

Given that my responsibilities as Country CFO demanded more attention because my

country had more operations, I decided to change the process in order to reduce the

duration and to ensure standardization in the format, and actually, reduce the human

intervention, making that the country controllers work directly in the consolidation file.

Selection

Having in mind that there was a different kind of users of file, I select some of those to

determine what was the main important things to take into account in the moment of the

process of the information and the reading of the same. In that sense, we form a group of

the country controllers, country CEOs, IT guys, and people from the headquarters to find the

best solutions possible.

Application

For the first lunch, we focused on the consolidation process in order to avoid the copy-paste

processes and reducing the manual intervention so, we build an online application where all

the controllers fill the figure of their respective country, along with the comments. During the

first week of the first stage, we sent the new report along with the old one, and after the

meeting with the headquarters team, we ask for a post-meeting review of the new format, all

the assistants provided their comments and suggestions that were the input for the next

report.

For the second lunch, we focused on the feedback received from the assistants to the review

meeting, we adjust the report and we were able to eliminate the old one. The final report

included all the suggestions received but the best of all is that reduced the time investment

from about 36 men hours to around 8, without missing any valuable information and

including new data that the stakeholders appreciated so much.

Insight

With the application of the learning launch tool, the controller’s team along with the main

stakeholders identified different assumptions and designed tools to test these assumptions.

On the other hand, we found probable requirements from headquarters, expecting to find

that a more agile approach that improved the workflow, reduced the time investment of

everyone in the team and that both our team and the key stakeholders were very satisfied

with the results of the exercise and the new report.

The final report was slightly different from what we anticipated, but the differences were

more related to form and a few topics to be included in the report.

Approach

Despite that, the team was not used to design thinking tools, they were able to work with the

learning launch that was the appropriate tool. The team needs to review the insight gained

from our first two launches and continuously evaluate this insight and new ones into future

launch designs, especially taking into account that the full automation of the reports will take

at least 4 years more according to the ERP implementation plan of the headquarter.

Student: Maria Amin  Coursera: Design Thinking for Innovation, Maria Amin, UVA    Challenge:  The design thinking tool I chose from the Design Thinking course was storytelling.  This is a  skill I have wanted to improve as some of the most successful consultants I work with are great  storytellers.  Traditionally, the way we sell consulting within our service line is to identify the client's  current issues and demonstrate our group’s capabilities to address them.  We needed to change the way  we told our group's consulting story.  A story that moves from a capabilities to character-driven  approach that all team members could tell and customers wanted to hear.     Selection: Our consulting sales practice is based on developing relationships based on high value and  trust.  As a result, I chose storytelling as a tool to build on connecting with clients in the way Design  Thinking week 2 lecture described it “as a way to make a strategy relate-able, to give it color, life,  through character and plot." The lecture finally gave me a framework to build a story, develop suspense,  and create a seemingly simple answer.  I believe this simplicity is a key to building trust and developing  relationships with clients.       Application:  I began with white-boarding the steps of storytelling with a colleague in a two-hour design  thinking session. We sectioned off parts of the walls with the 5 areas:  main character, sell the challenge,  fellowship, tensions, and a path to move forward.  From a host of different characters, we started with  our main character as Valerie, a high level executive and a potential customer, tasked by her CEO with a  new annual goal to create a digital strategy to increase revenue for her business unit. We brainstormed  all the different ways Valerie could try to achieve this goal utilizing different colored sticky notes.   We  used the petal visualization tool as described in the week 3: Meandyouhealth story part 1 to map out  the fellowship step to fully understand the people associated with Valerie.  This visually connected the  tensions that each relationship created, their needs, and how we could overcome them through our  story.  We put an action item in our "parking lot" to mind map these relationships further to create new  solutions and offerings for these customers and channels.  We also planned to evaluate each  relationship as one that might need its own story crafted.  The path to move step was perhaps the  easiest as we aligned outcomes, activities, and outputs with Valerie's needs.  The alignment was  essential to create a simple solution and key to our story's purpose of building trust and rapport.         Insight: Our efficient minds hoped that this one session would create a story that would resonate,  however, we had to redo the white-boarding exercise again as we found we had an additional audience:  our consulting colleagues and leadership.  We had to add a layer to the story to engage our service line  leaders and to promote our new story internally.   After iterating on our final storyline, we tested with  select members of our audience through intentional practice sessions and in actual sales situations.   Feedback from these sessions was extremely beneficial and requires us to continue to iterate and adapt  the story.       Approach:  Our story, as technology consultants, needs to change as technology and our client's needs  change.  As a result, we will need to iterate our story continuously.  I will keep the framework of  storytelling as a tool to use again.  One of my challenges will be to create a few different characters and  plots for the different personas we work with and sell to.  As mentioned before, as a team we need to  revisit and build out the value and tensions for each of our fellowship members so we can create stories  that resonate with our different customers, internal and external.  In general, I was very pleased with  the process and results of our first story and I am looking forward to furthering my storytelling skills.

Reflection – Learning Launch  Leave Advisor

Ivan Tomac

Challenge

I am a senior UX designer for our organization and our challenge was to develop a decision  making application that helps employees pick the correct leave of absence (LOA) option which will  reduce the risk of taking an incorrect form of LOA and to help limit the time that a HR  representative would need walking an employee or manager through the decision making process.  This project would last two months and we would have an appropriate amount of budget to  support a 4 person design team with different backgrounds and skills. Our team will work to  develop the correct user experience and decision making guidance in the application so that the  overall experience would not last more than 5 minutes and the employee would be guaranteed in  taking the correct form of LOA.

Selection

We have already utilized journey mapping and empathy mapping so that we could best describe  our user personas. Based on our findings and understanding of the requirements and user needs,  we felt that a learning launch would be the method for us to test our design rapidly and give us the  opportunity to quickly refine our design.

Application

For our learning launch we set up a user experience test lab and relied on an agile design sprint  process. We conducted 2 test labs over a 3 day period. Each test had 20 users from our 3 primary  user group (Employees, Managers and HR Representatives).

As Thomas Koch stated in the training: “The key here is, is to do experiments that are  fast and cheap. Because you want to do lots of experiments. If they took a long  time you wouldn't ever get to a good idea. You would not ever get to a new  product that goes to market. If it was real expensive because you did lots of long  experiments, you'd run out of money before you found a new source of revenue.”

We tested our assumptions with each group and scored their experience with direct observations.  Using the feedback from our observations we made modifications to our prototype using rapid  prototyping. We looked for make or break assumptions. For example if the experience lasted more  than 5 minutes we considered it a fail. If the user quit and didn’t complete we considered it a fail. If

the user completed the task but had questions, we considered it a success, and used the feedback  to improve our experience.

We sorted our data by our key user group and looked for patterns and opportunities.

The prototype rapidly changed over the 3 day period and after our learning launch we were able  to demonstrate a working prototype with validation based on direct user feedback.

Insight

The learning launch gave us a number of insights and benefits. We were able to quickly adapt the  prototype with our observations. Our key stake-holders were also present and gained confidence in  the application by witnessing it firsthand. The rapid prototyping gave the team the opportunity to  see their assumptions play out right in front of them in a low risk environment.

By setting the tight parameters we were able to move the project forward quickly. Saving time and  money.

Our results changed from what we originally anticipated, but we were happy to see that our  assumed target was what we expected and that the benefits of the application would give us the  results that we wanted.

With the method we were also able to confidently hand over the application specifications to our  vendor that would be building out the production application. We were able to not only show them  the prototype, but also give them the necessary information that would validate our design  direction.

Approach

Our team had used agile methods in the past to quickly manage and refine a design, but the  learning launch gave the team the insights to move the project forward in confident manner.

Our stake holders were so pleased with the success of the learning launch that they have decided  to use this quick to win or fail approach on future projects. This will give us the opportunity to take  greater risks and have the ability to test or assumptions in a way that will show our stakeholders the  unforeseen gems in our work.

The next time with do a learning launch I think we will bring our Journey map into the test to  validate the map and to use as a tool to test out the assumptions of the journey map. We would  also want to bring in our previous insights into the next learning launch to confirm data from our  previous sample set.

Fernanda Moreira  School Head  Department of Education-Philippines

REFLECTION

ESSENTIALS IN OUR SCHOOL IMPROVEMENT PLAN:

VISUAL, MIND MAPPING, STORY TELLING, AND LEARNING LAUNCH TOOLS

Challenges & Selection

As a school team composed of school head, teachers and stakeholders, we make sure that in everything

we do is for the betterment of our learners. We are a learner-centered institution which main goal is to deliver  accessible and quality education for all. Our challenge is to identify the priority improvement areas which need  to be addressed for the attainment and improvement of learner’s performance:  We choose Visual, Mind  Mapping, Story Telling and Learning Launch tools in our school’s design and innovation because we believe a  combination of all these tools will give significant change in our school.    Application

When I started my new job as a business developer at e-Durable two months ago, I had a basic understanding of the cable industry, but no real customer experience. On Design Thinking: A Reflection On Reworking A Novel

A year ago I began working on a novel with the idea that all I needed was a cast of characters, a

world and a plot that went from A to B. I could not have been more wrong. Around three-fourths of

the way through the novel, I found myself writing without direction, caught in the nitty-gritties of

detail, worldbuilding and characters; unable to extract the story and push it in the direction that I

wanted it to go in. Towards the very end of the writing, the story had spiraled out of control, into

something that had too many motifs and themes to be truly thoughtful. It was directionless and

frequently contradictory – even incoherent, in places, with incomplete character arcs that ended in

the classic rookie writer’s problem: they simply disappeared off the map altogether.

This is, perhaps, an unorthodox example to pick for a design thinking project. But as I listened to the

lectures on design thinking, I was forcibly struck by the similarities between the description of the

process – what is, what if, what wows, what works – and the ways in which this process parallels the

creation of a novel. Early on in the lectures, Diaz picked apart the concept of the Moses

myth of creativity, i.e. that creativity resides purely in genius and is not something which can be

cultivated or organized. This was when I realized that all along I’d been treating the novel as a

mysterious entity which could only be produced through genius, rather than a project which could

be managed systematically – which, dare I say, could even be created by using design thinking

principles.

Selection & Application

So I went back to the drawing board and decided to treat the novel as a project, rather than a

mysterious entity which would spring fully formed from my mind. I selected the Visualization tool

we’d explored over the five weeks for this and began to rebuild my novel from the ground up. The

visualization tool felt like the appropriate choice in that it is a useful way in which to place ideas

which are not necessarily easily verbalized on paper – which gives it a tangible presence that makes

it easier to discern unconscious and latent patterns, needs and desires that would not have been

immediately evident otherwise. The intangible nature of themes and motifs were best matched to

the visualization tool which enables the formulation of the intangible in a way that makes it easier to

grasp and think about. It was also an excellent way of escaping from the tendency to return to

outlines and other collected material – words, in other words – and to force me to take a step back

and think outside the box – outside my preconceived notions and ideas – when examining what I

wanted to do with my novel.

Dawn James

29/10/2016

Rather than turn this process over to a group of people, however, I used the visualization tool in a

more personal and auto-ethnographical sense, to express the various concepts, themes and motifs –

occasionally even moments – I had been exploring in my novel. I did this by creating several collage-

cum-moodboard of images and fragments of thoughts, phrases and ideas that were both academic

and literary or poetical which I had been both unconsciously and consciously examining – which

struck a chord with me whenever I thought about my novel’s plot, various characters and themes. I

then laid it out and tried to trace the patterns and themes which emerged, to be more conscious of

what I had been working with and to see how they all fit together within the context of my novel.

Insights & Approach

By thinking conceptually, rather than falling back on the standard formats of novel outlining, I began

to notice certain themes and ideas which were connecting characters who had existed very

separately on the page before. Where they once crossed each other without ever interacting or even

appearing linked except for the bare necessities of plot, I noticed certain ideas which kept cropping

up and recurring, visually framed, across these different characters. They weren’t necessarily similar

themes so much as motifs; symbolic elements which I had failed to be conscious of while writing,

which had led to the characters meandering all over the page without necessarily going anywhere.

As a tool, the visualization tool forced me to quite literally build from scratch – to stay away from

falling back on ‘safe’ and ‘known’ things like the plot outline and the lists and sheets I’d built up over

the last year – and by doing so, it formed a new framework of thinking about the novel. I had a

‘thesis statement’, now, for the piece: one unifying theme and question I could come back to when I

worked on the various elements of the story. It was being able to reframe these verbal ideas I’d had

and transferring them into another medium, one which was more conceptual – like a Rorschach, as

it was called in one of the video lectures – that made it easier to trace the more subconscious

connections – or the possible subconscious connections at play – and to unify them in patterns and

ideas that could form a thesis statement for my novel.

I’d used this tool a few times before when writing stories, but doing it in light of thinking of it as a

design thinking tool helped me to be a lot more conscious of the process and to treat this less as a

fun or relaxing activity and more as a learning experience. These images and fragments of concepts

weren’t just images but tools which could yield insights into my own unconscious desires and needs

while writing this novel – a way of understanding what I’d wanted to explore and how to be

conscious about it, instead of going about it vaguely as I did before.

present to my beta-readers and writer friends along with my new ‘thesis’ question, as a means of

figuring out where to dig deeper into what suits my novel – what fits this project best.
