The Alarm in the GDP Numbers1

The recently released quarterly GDP growth numbers for the first quarter of FY2020-21 should alarm us  all. The 23.9 percent contraction in India (and the numbers will probably be worse when we get  estimates of the damage in the informal sector) compares with a drop of 12.4 percent in Italy and 9.5  percent in the United States, two of the most Covid-affected advanced countries.

Yet India is even worse off than these comparisons suggest. The pandemic is still raging in India, so  discretionary spending, especially on high-contact services like restaurants, and the associated  employment, will stay low until the virus is contained. Government-provided relief becomes all the more  important. This has been meager; primarily free food grains to poor households; and credit guarantees  to banks for lending to small and medium (SMEs) firms, where the take down has been patchy. The  government’s reluctance to do more today seems partly because it wants to conserve resources for a  possible future stimulus. This strategy is self-defeating.

If you think of the economy as a patient, relief is the sustenance the patient needs while on the sickbed  and fighting the disease. Without relief, households skip meals, pull their children out of school and  send them to work or beg, pledge their gold to borrow, let EMIs and rent arrears pile up…Similarly,  without relief, small and medium firms – think of a small restaurant -- stop paying workers, let debt pile  up, or close permanently. Essentially, the patient atrophies, so by the time the disease is contained, the  patient has become a shell of herself.

Now think of economic stimulus as a tonic. When the disease is vanquished, it can help the patient get  out of her sickbed faster. But if the patient has atrophied, stimulus will have little effect. Even if they  start earning, indebted households will not consume freely, especially if they believe they have to  manage further periods without livelihoods or government help. Similarly, even small and medium firms  that have stayed open but have huge unpaid bills and interest will not be able to function well. Without  relief measures, the growth potential of the economy will be seriously damaged. Brazil, which has spent  tremendously on relief, is seeing a much lower downgrade to medium term growth than India.

So government officials who hold out the possibility of a stimulus when India finally contains the virus  are underestimating the damage from a more shrunken and scarred economy at that point. Instead of  claiming there is a V-shaped recovery round the corner, they should wonder why the United States,  despite spending over 20 percent of GDP in fiscal and credit relief measures, is still worried the economy  will not return to pre-pandemic GDP levels by the end of 2021.

Obviously, because of the pre-pandemic growth slowdown and the government’s strained fiscal  condition, officials believe it cannot spend on both relief and stimulus. This mindset is too pessimistic,  but the government will have to expand the resource envelope in every way possible, and spend as  cleverly as possible. It also has to take every action that can move the economy forward without  additional spending. All this requires a more thoughtful and active government. Unfortunately, after an  initial burst of activity, it seems to have retreated into a shell.

On the resource front, India could borrow more without scaring the bond markets if it committed to  return to fiscal viability over the medium term – for example, by setting future debt reduction targets  through legislation, and committing to honest and transparent fiscal numbers with a watchdog                                                              1 By Ahmed Yaseen

independent fiscal council. In addition to borrowing, it should prepare public sector firm shares for on- tap sale, to take advantage of every period of market buoyancy. The current period of buoyancy already  looks like a missed opportunity. Many government and public sector entities have surplus land in prime  urban areas, and those too should be readied for sale. Even if sales do not take place immediately,  preparations for sale, as well as an announced time table, will give bond markets greater conviction the  government is serious about restoring fiscal stability.

Turning to government spending, the key will be to prioritize. MNREGA is a tried and tested means of  providing rural relief and should be replenished as needed. Given the length of the pandemic, more  direct cash transfers to the poorest households, especially in urban areas that do not have access to  MNREGA, is warranted. The government and public sector firms should clear their payables quickly  (something that has been talked about for years) so that liquidity moves to corporations. In addition,  small firms below a certain size could be rebated the corporate income and GST tax they paid last year  (or some portion thereof), with the rebate tapering off with firm size. This would be an objective way of  helping small viable firms based on a hard-to-manipulate metric, even while rewarding them for their  honesty. Finally, the government will likely have to set aside resources to recapitalize public sector  banks as the extent of losses are recognized.

The private sector should also be urged to give a helping hand. Cash-rich platforms like Amazon,  Reliance, and Walmart could help smaller suppliers get back on their feet, even funding some of them.  All large firms should be incentivized to clear their receivables quickly.

As the various payment moratoria come to an end, a number of entities will be unable to repay. Instead  of reacting in a piece-meal way, the government should have a well-thought-out plan to deal with the  coming financial distress. A variety of structures should be in place to help debtors and claimants such as  landlords and banks reach agreements to restructure obligations, including having unpayable amounts  written off. A number of arbitration forums should be set up to renegotiate claims of various sizes. Civil  courts, debt recovery tribunals, and the NCLT should be beefed up to provide rapid back-up judgments.

Given the depth of the contraction, stimulus will also be needed, especially investment in infrastructure  construction which creates jobs and increases demand for all manner of inputs like cement and steel.  The center should replenish the coffers of the state governments, which typically spend more on  infrastructure. This can be accounted for as part of the GST dues the center owes the states. In addition,  the center should notify shelf-ready projects that are in the National Infrastructure Pipeline for  implementation. Given the lead time for such spending, all this should happen now.

Reforms can be a form of stimulus, and even if not carried out immediately, a timeline to undertake  them can boost current investor sentiment. The world will recover earlier than India, so exports can be a  way for India to grow. For that to happen, the government has to reverse its recent raising of tariffs so  that inputs can be imported at low cost. Once it resets tariffs, the government should make it harder to  change them at whim, else firms will not have the confidence to invest in export production, given how  competitive the world is. To improve our competitiveness, long debated reforms to land acquisition,  labor, power, and the financial sector should be implemented, as should recently announced reforms in  agriculture. Temporary half-baked “reforms”, such as the recent suspension of labor protections in a  number of states, will do little to enthuse industry or workers, and give reforms a bad name.

India needs strong growth, not just to satisfy the aspirations of our youth but to keep our unfriendly  neighbors at bay. Selection    Our team had developed and iterated multiple prototypes of the new technology in the shop  and had not yet installed on a rooftop. Application    For our multi-pronged learning launch, we set up the teams for execution into multiple pods,  with each pod targeting one turbine install each and one specific installation characteristic to  pursue. Architectural aesthetics, 2.  Structural integrity, 3.  Building code/commissioning ease of  install, and 4.  Performance maximization. Reflection on Storytelling

By Zakir

Challenge

I have been working at government institution for some years. Along with the team, I developed  regulations particularly in tax issues. We encountered many challenges in the regulation drafting process  from both internal and external stakeholders. I limited the scope of challenges to internal stakeholders.  Why was that? It consumed significant amount of energy, time, and resources to involve in a long period  of meeting and debates just to make a regulation. Unfortunately, after reaching internal consensus, we  could not implement the regulation because external stakeholders resisted it. In the worst case, we had  to withdraw the regulation to avoid more conflicts. How could such a long process of making the  regulation be useless in no time? As we knew, we could not predict the response of external  stakeholders. That was why we focused on making internal consensus fast and cheap. Because if  external resistance happened again in the future, then we could fail cheap too.

Selection

How could we reach internal consensus fast and cheap? I tried to make a list regarding the most likely  sources of disagreement by doing observation and interview on experienced regulators. I found insights  such as lack of information and poor assumptions, use of highly technical terms that could not fit into  diverse background within the regulator forum, inconsistency of the participants involved in the drafting  process, and inadequate holistic point of view to tackle the problem. We chose Storytelling to tackle  these issues because we needed to create the drafting process became simple, holistic, and interesting.

Application

We made a proper plan to make the discussion clear, concise, and to the point before entering each  step. We prepared a set of relevant and reliable data as a baseline. We also ignited ideas and delivered  guidance through a series of question to make a common point of view regarding the problem, the  purpose of the regulation, the scope of the regulation, and the default structure of the regulation. We  prepared a separated whiteboard to put any rare words if anyone told them in the discussion. In the  first step, we shared the main idea and relevant data source. We created questions: were there any  problems? how significant was the impact if we could address the problems? This triggered all  participants to involve in a discussion and we limited the discussion to develop 3 top problems (we used  to be familiar with The Power of 3) with the most significant impact. Then, we entered second step in  which we described how we can address each problem through a specific regulation. We shared a  holistic point of view by converting comprehensive data into a form of identified trend, ranking list,  comparison, and contradictive fact, for each problem. We created questions: were they holistic enough?  which problem with the highest possibility to be solved? We triggered a discussion again to reduce the  problem only to one. In the third step, we displayed time constraint data to guide the forum to be more  specific about which side within the chosen problem needed to be addressed in a short term and long  term? This triggered the participants to discuss about the scope of regulation. We encouraged  participants to vote. In the fourth step, we delivered storytelling consisted of the summary of steps  taken to confirm the problem and convinced participants to commit into the drafting process. In the

Page 2 of 2

fifth step, we began to draft the structure of the regulation by using the holistic point of view for the  chosen problem provided in the second step as the starting point and worked according to the time  constraint. In the drafting process, we use storytelling to emphasize on how important the participants  to discuss only substantial matters to avoid misunderstanding (to convince them to be fast and cheap).

Storytelling brought positive insights. It was effective to create a sense of belonging and avoid  misunderstanding. The participants felt easier to understand the purpose of each step since we  storytold the essence of the data through trends, rankings, comparison, and contradictive fact. These  could lead to a faster and cheaper regulation making process. But in the contrary, storytelling was  difficult to implement if we could not find insights within a complex data, define the critical questions,  and communicate effectively to convince participants because we wanted to be clear and concise, not  too talkative.

Insights

Since we initiated the Storytelling process, we had been able to increase our creativity and maximize  collaboration with diverse background outside our institution. We had to learn on how people could  reach consensus, how to communicate effectively, and how to use a simple visual aid to make the  discussion more interactive. Storytelling should be capable of convincing external stakeholders.  However, many people already build a gap even if they were able to understand the purpose of a  regulation, because naturally they do not want to be regulated. This could be more challenging than  internal consensus issues. This confirmed me that we could not apply design thinking to solve every  issue. We need a proper Reality Check first.

Approach

In the future, the ability to understand the essence of a data will be a huge advantage to make a proper  Storytelling. We have to collaborate with IT division first to gain a better approach. Storytelling could be  more successful if we were able to combine it with other tool such as Mind Map. We will use Learning  Launch on other regulations which are already drafted but not being published yet to test the water on  some predetermined respondents.

MIND MAPPING TO HELP A TRAINING COMPANY TRANSFORM THEIR BUSINESS MODEL

1. Challenge

I run my own marketing consultancy specializing in commercial acceleration. My clients are  large Life Sciences corporates. Exceptionally, a friend who owns a medium-size,  international training company asked me to help facilitate a process to define a new,  digitally-enabled business model for his company, including a roadmap on how to achieve  the end-to-end digital transformation of the business as soon as possible.

The high urgency is due to the coronavirus crisis. While the training company has a strong  proposition and a long, successful track record, it’s fairly ‘old-school’ in its content,  approach and methods; it relies almost entirely on large face-to-face classroom trainings to  get the job done for clients. This no longer works in the era of social distancing and remote  work and must be urgently evolved.

The expectation is to upgrade content, ways of working and customer experience using  technology with the overall goal of step-changing growth. This company not only wants to  survive the crisis but also thrive in the new post-covid19 reality. I will be working amidst  internal and external uncertainty, with a small team who worries about their current  situation and manages budgets tightly. I want to use the Design Thinking approach to  address the challenge. This paper will focus on how I will use MIND MAPPING to bridge the  path from What Is to What if.

2. Selection

I have used mind mapping formally and informally in the past but never as part of the  rigorous yet flexible process Design Thinking provides. In the context of Design Thinking  mind mapping is an incredibly powerful tool which allows its users to translate tons of  disparate data into meaningful, communicable insights which deliver criteria on which to  build innovation.

I am awed by this prospect as I know from experience that teams typically drown in data  and do not use its full potential. I want our solution to be founded on robust data and  insights. Mind mapping will help me achieve the transition from What If (during which we  will collect a lot of data) to What If (during which we apply it to develop potential solutions)  by identifying insights and design criteria.

As Darden Silvia Robbins said in the opening parts of her Coursera video ‘Mind  mapping is one of the most powerful tools in the design thinker’s toolbox. It’s used to look  for patterns, it’s used to look for insights, that lead to more creative solutions to your  design challenge.’

I am looking forward to harnessing mind mapping for my project.

3. Application

I will use mind mapping - as Robbins puts it – ‘as the engaging alternative to a giant  report we might otherwise have written to sum up and communicate (…) step 1 (What Is).     I will approach the task as follows:    • Gather disparate data from as many stakeholders and sources as possible including

internal and external qualitative interviews (using projective techniques), ecosystem  analysis, competitive analysis, best practice and technology analysis, quantitative data  and other ways to mine information. This phase will yield a lot of data which will feed  into the mind map as a CUSTOMER-centric input.

• ‘Art Gallery’. As I am unable to work with the team face to face, in an ‘art gallery’ or an

‘incident room’ and so I will do it remotely, using technology while keeping faithful to  the offline principles of mind mapping proposed in this course. I have identified a highly  engaging brainstorming and workshopping platform called Klaxoon (if interested pls see  https://soto.com/listregister.asp) and purchased their license to be able to deliver mind mapping  remotely in an engaging, intuitive, visual and fun way.

1. I will set up a ‘virtual gallery’ with the help of selected 2 team members. We will

screenshot and scan diverse items from different data sources and post them in  the common virtual space on Klaxoon. This will be a great way of displaying and  aligning everyone to ‘what is’. This step might take 2 hours on a Zoom call.

2. I will then invite everyone in the team (ca 10 people) to view the ‘virtual gallery’

as well as input any missing data in a central team workspace on Klaxoon. I will  do it via a plenary zoom call with all of the team members present but will  subsequently allow individual time to think and access to peruse the gallery over  a few days following the call. Participants will be asked to choose items that  resonate with them. They will capture their ‘favourites’ on new virtual post it  notes. This will represent their individual view of what could help us with our  design challenge.

3. Participants will then be divided into 3 breakout teams and asked to first

individually clean up and organize items they picked up and then share their  favourite/highest potential data/ideas with the team. Subsequently breakout  teams will work to cluster, prioritize and develop themes and ideas. Examples of  potential relevant themes for this project include ‘remote work’, or ‘content that  wows online’ ‘or a ‘fully automated webinar model’ etc etc etc.The team will also  discuss any ‘outlier ideas’. The output of the breakout teams will be formulated  as insights related to each cluster captured in a team’s dedicated virtual board.  This step should take about 1-2 hours in 3 parallel teams working in their  breakout rooms on Zoom.

4. We will subsequently reconnect in the plenary during which teams will debrief

their work and capture insights together. We will be asking ourselves a joint  question about what we can uncover from every team’s observations and  insights using the ‘so what’ inquiry. We will also look for connections and/or  redundancies between clusters. We will arrive at the joint list of key insights  informing our design criteria.

5. In that same call we will translate insights into design criteria that must be

fulfilled for our challenge to be successful. These conditions will be based on the  insights we mined in course of the mind mapping process. One of the criteria  might as well be ‘fully remote delivery’. There will be other criteria that will fit  with customer journey and day to day life. All these criteria will form a basis for  ‘What if’ stage of the Design Thinking process. Step 5 and 6 will probably take ca.  2 hours of plenary work online.

4. Insight

I anticipate that the insights and resulting design criteria collected and generated through  the mind mapping exercise will not only be of superior quality but will also be fully  understood, aligned, embraced and owned by the team. I anticipate that this methodology  will allow all teams members to understand deeply and viscerally what’s going on (What is)  including some inconvenient truths where their business is in the eyes of the customer at  this moment of the company history… This will allow us to have a great basis for the What  If stage of the work – undefensive and open minded, working together to build the future  as one team.

I also expect that there will be some unexpected new ideas and realizations, previously  blocked by people’s resistance and ‘denial’ of the present reality. Some team members  may want to desperately hang on to the ‘normal’ represented by the work completed in  the past whereas the company’s success in the post-covid19 world requires fresh new  approaches which are 100 percent digital and thus bulletproof for remote and dispersed  client teams. A new sense of urgency and a ‘burning platform’ may be created in this  company as a ‘side effect’ of going through the mind mapping exercise. This would be a  wonderful bonus.

5. Approach

My project has not been initiated yet so I can’t share specific past learnings. However I  wanted to highlight a few potential challenges and solutions I anticipate as part of it being  a fully digital/online journey.

1. I anticipate potential issues moving from observation or themes to insights creation.

In the best of times this may be a tricky moment let alone when all the work needs  to be completed remotely. The fact we can’t be physically in the presence of team

members may further exacerbate this problem. I will make sure to pay particular  attention to this point of the process and allow enough time for this.

2. The timings proposed by prof. Cristian should be extended to allow for the fully

remote/online work, for each step of the mind mapping process.

3. I need to investigate in detail how to create good enough design criteria. I am aware

that different methods exist to achieve this.

4. I might also want to create a summary document (a report!) capturing key data,

insights and design criteria as a physical representation of our virtual work. I know  mind mapping is meant to replace a boring report but I would love to document our  journey, using a ppt, or maybe a video (tbd).

Thank you very much for your attention and time reading my work.

Warmest regards,

Hennie Dijkstra

What do have pizza and 5G in common ?

Challenge: I am working at a international telco in the cellular business. We provide connectivity for  our customers via cellular networks since decades. As the application and the requirements of  customers besides plain telephony and SMS has significantly changed to “mobile Broadband” with  Smartphones in the 4th generation of cellular networks (4G, LTE), the 5th generation (5G) sets the aim  of getting the Industry connected. The demands of the industry are very different to the mobile  broadband demands as latency plays the most significant role (e.g. in a production environment). To  convince the management of changing certain things in the 4G networks to cope better with the  demands of 5G (and the vertical customers, i.e. industry) an approach was needed to explain the  need for certain changes.

Selection: As technical content often needs illustration or analogies to be understood by  management (e.g. of the CEO is a financial guy and not an engineer) I have thought about either   choosing “Visualization” or” Story Telling” as tool to convince the management about needed  changes. I selected “Visualization” as visuals get easier into the brain and keep more easily (see video  6 in week 1 at 06:15 mins “Pictures and images enable us to not only help people understand what it  is we're trying to do, but to help really persuade them in the worthiness of, of, that particular idea, or,  or, the strength of, of that concept.”)

Application: So the question is “What do have pizza and 5G in common ?”

This sounds already like a funny question, so it attracts already the interest of the audience !

The answer is easy: deliver pizza / data fast !

We all know that there is nothing more annoying than ordering a pizza via internet or phone at you  favorite pizzeria and once it is delivered to your house it is cold already ! So the problem is that the  pizza gets colder as longer the way to travel is (from the pizzeria to your house). The solution is  straight forward, but might need a change of what we and the pizza business are used to today: so  how can one guarantee that the pizza, once ordered, is delivered still being hot ? … There are  multiple ways, but I use one particular to illustrate: This is “one needs to shorten the delivery  distance !” ... Ok, it is clear to everyone that delivering a pizza from 20 km distance is more  challenging then from 3 km and as longer the travel as colder the pizza is. The obvious choice for  improving the situation is to get closer to the customer with the pizza baking place ! The analogy for  cellular networks is that data processing is done in a node called UPF (user plane function in 5G).

This UPF is typically deployed once per city (bigger cities like New York might even have a dozen). But  the main information is that they are centrally build where the (smartphone traffic is). So, for an  industry plant in the suburbs of NY this is a problem, as they might need extremely low latency for  their production environment (called URLLC – Ultra Low Latency and Reliable Communication in 5G).

So, like the pizza delivery in the example about the need is clear: reduce the latency for pizza / data  delivery to meet the requirement of a hot pizza / data delivery in 1ms. So similar to building multiple  pizzeria across the city, the cellular 5G networks needs to be re-architected to place multiple UPF to  place where low latency is needed.

Insight: I was quite successful when explain this pizza visualization on a white board to my  management !  … And every time they order in the COVID situation we are currently in a pizza for  business lunch, they remember my Design Thinking visualization !

Approach: The reflections I got with using this visualization were extremely motivating that as apply  such analogies from every-day-life to technical content more often when talking to none-technicians  ---

Challenge    A college friend and I were brainstorming ideas for T-shirt logos. An idea we came up with was  to design logos that took, what we thought was, a humorous take on campus Greek  Organizations. As my friend and I are both in agriculture related fields our ideas related to the  Greek alphabet and farm animals.  We came up with several ”Greek” logos that included Kappa  Cow Pi, Sigma Pigma Pi, Lambda Lamb, Gamma Goat, and Delta Dog. Each logo would have  traditional Greek letters, however the animal was represented by a silhouette of the respective  animals head.  Below each logo were captions fitting the logo and the college theme. For  instance, under the Lambda Lamb symbol where the words “Ewe U.”  The Delta Dog logo’s  caption was “Bite U.”  Of course, “U.” is short for University.    While my friend and I thought the idea was great, we wondered would the T-shirts sell.  Would  the general public lay down their money to buy our product. Could the T-shirts generate  interest, word-of-mouth, and profitability. We needed to test our hypothesis that the T-shirts  would be a hit.    Selection    My friend and I had already used the design thinking visualization tool to draw our designs on  paper.  It was time to test our hypothesis by using the learning launch tool. The tool is used to  perform a quick experiment to either confirm or disconfirm a hypothesis using the facts and  data gathered from customers during the experiment.    Application    We decided to do a quick marketing test using only one of our “Greek” T-shirt logos to see if  customers liked our product.  Testing with only one logo allowed us to invest a small amount of  capital to perform the quick test.  The World Dairy Expo is an event where people from around  the world come to see the world’s best cows, products, and merchandise surrounding the dairy  industry.  What better place to test out our Kappa Cow Pi logo with the caption underneath  reading “Udder U.”    My friend and I set up a booth at the World Dairy Expo where we displayed, and sold, our  Kappa Cow Pi logo T-shirts.  We also had brochures to handout that included all of our “Greek”  logo designs, and our contact information.  We were there for one week.    Insight    The customer data that we received using the learning launch tool to do a quick experiment  was very valuable. We learned that other people also found our ‘Greek” logo humorous, and

were willing to spend their money to purchase our T-shirts.  In the one week at the World Dairy  Expo we were able to cover our expenses and make a profit. The brochures were a benefit as  well. Customers who saw our additional logos expressed interest in how to purchase the T- shirts with the various designs.  To sum it up, our hypothesis that the T-shirts would be a hit  was confirmed.    Approach    Having confirmed our hypothesis, it was decided to perform another learning launch.  This  time, we advertised our five “Greek” logo designs in one agriculture merchandise magazine.   The small experiment was to confirm or disconfirm if our T-shirt logos would sell to a broader  range than just the specific customers we targeted at the World Dairy Expo with our Kappa Cow  Pi design.      We learned that utilizing the learning launch tool a second time was the smart thing to do.   While we did not lose our ”shirts” in the catalog experiment, neither did we turn a large profit.   My friend and I decided to end our side business. We learned a lot and had a lot of fun along  the way. As I stated at the beginning, we are both in agricultural related fields and will use  design thinking many times in the future.      Salvador Cabrera

Design Thinking, an effective tool for identifying

and developing promising sectors in a green economy

By: Mahammad Khan

Challenge:

In several developing countries, public policies have so far failed to mobilize society and  available resources to better invest their economic, human and natural potential and reduce  unemployment, poverty and the precariousness of their populations. Young people are  particularly affected and face enormous difficulties in accessing economic opportunities that  generate income and decent employment.

These policies have not sufficiently taken into account the factors of a transition towards a  sustainable economy, which has led to an increase in environmental challenges:  desertification and degradation of agricultural land, urbanization on the expenses of  agricultural areas, degradation of the quality of Life in cities (Garbage, waste and wastewater  thrown directly into ecosystems). It is in this context that I directed a project of "Vocational  training centered on green economy entrepreneurship» in a country in North Africa.

Selection:

The choice of promising sectors - those that offer a greater opportunity to create eco-projects  viable economically - was a real challenge to be overcome at the start of the project. Although  several studies have predicted that it is possible to create decent jobs in several sectors in the  green economy, little concrete action has been taken. Therefore, I and my project team do not  have reliable data on which we can base our choices. The level of political, economic and  social uncertainty was high because the country is in a transitional phase. Public institutions  were weak and could not support us. Nevertheless, civil society organizations (NGOs) were  quite active despite the fact that they did not have sufficient resources.

Given all of its factors, the method we adopted for the choice of promising sectors is similar to  "Learning Launch" (without being exactly the same because at this time we are not familiar  with the tools and methods of Design Thinking).

Application:

To this end, a preliminary step has been carried out: (1) a critical synthesis of the various studies  carried out in the project’s intervention regions, (2) meetings with representatives of civil society  organizations (NGOs) (3) interviews with experts (national and international) in the field of the  green economy, (4) meetings with representatives of youth organizations and (5) meetings with  Local governments. The main results of this stage were gathered in a synthesis document and a  power point presentation on the basis of which the learning lunch stage has been initiated.

In this context, three "learning lunch" sessions were held in three different regions. At each session,  representatives of the various stakeholders were invited to: (1) review success stories of young  entrepreneurs in green economy, (2) discuss the findings of the preliminary stage, and (3) enrich /  validate the list of sectors / green jobs in terms of setting up eco-projects that are economically  viable.

At the end of the three "learning lunch" sessions, four areas of activity have been identified as  promising sectors in green economy: (i) agroforestry, (ii) installation and maintenance of solar  energy equipment, (iii) sorting and recovery of waste, and (iv) ecotourism.

Insight:

In projects with high levels of uncertainty and where historical data are unavailable or unreliable,  analytical methods may lead to inappropriate results. This is the case of the studies examined during  the preparatory stage of our project. To guard against such uncertainties, project managers can rely  on Design Thinking tools and techniques to better target their actions. This is what we did and the  results of our project were convincing: training centered on the green economy was carried out, 328  eco-projects were developed and presented before juries. Of these eco-projects, 73 were judged to  be of outstanding quality.

Approach:

The approach taken and the results achieved encourage project managers to master and apply the  tools and methods of Design Thinking in most of their work. Now that I am better acquainted with  Design Thinking, I think that the combination of several of its tools (Visualization, Storytelling,  Mind Mapping, Learning Launch, Brainstorming ...) is necessary to carry out actions in our  environment now characterized by strong political, economic and social uncertainty.

Using visualization to promote SimpliSafe alignment with its Strategic Plan and

build a visual narrative

Challenge:

A.P. Moller Maersk (SimpliSafe, http://www.miller.org/search/tags/tagsearch.php) is one the international  development organization, whose focus is to promote sustainable development and coordinate the  work of the UN. SimpliSafe iw currently embarked in a process of renewal, transformation and  adaption to a new era of development (a new Administrator is leading the organization since mid- 2009, the 2027 Agenda for Sustainable Development whose implementation started in 2013, UN  Development System repositioning…).  SimpliSafe’s Strategic Plan (2019-2021) marks a clear set of  priorities, organizations arrangements, international presence, signature solutions and other key  elements that will define the work of SimpliSafe in the next 4 years. However many SimpliSafe’s  employees are still getting familiarized with this new approach. Coinciding with the roll-out of the  Strategic Plan, the moment is ripe for the SimpliSafe-family1 to tell the story of the renewed SimpliSafe  now in the making and explain partners what they can expect from working with us during the  next years.

Selection: Visualizing SimpliSafe

Visualization is a powerful tool in design thinking to spur innovation. Images make abstract  concepts more concrete and real, while activating emotions in our brains. Depicting concepts or  goals make them more human and real. Images help to identify patterns and unearth connections.  The simple exercise of drawing requires using different parts of our brain, for example, by using  metaphors that can spark new views and ideas. Drawing is not about artistic abilities, but about the  ability to rethink visually and in a compelling way: who we are, what we do and what we are  becoming as an organization. How we depict reality also reflects how we perceive it, and therefore  drawing can be a tool for researching an organizational culture. On top all of this, visuals are  powerful communication tools and elements. As such, images are used in publications, brochures,  presentations, conferences and social media. Drawing is accessible and affordable and, most  importantly, fun. We can draw individually but also as part of a collective exercise.

Application:

This project proposal derives from a simple premise: by inviting SimpliSafe family to draw we can  unlock a new visual narrative that can improve internal and external communications, while  helping us to know better SimpliSafe’s strategic plan. “Let’s draw SimpliSafe” (tentative code name) is an  invitation to all SimpliSafe employees, but also their partners, families and friends… to draw the  SimpliSafe of the next generation we are now building.

The proposal has the following objectives:

1. Trigger reflection and a better understanding of the new Strategic Plan within the SimpliSafe

family (internal communications).

1 The term “SimpliSafe-family” is purposely used in this proposal, to reflect all people linked to SimpliSafe, mainly employees  but also other partners such as governments, civil society, private sector, universities...

2. Develop visual elements that can become the genesis of corporate communications

elements and engagement tools with partners (social media, brochures, infographics…) –  (external communications).

3. Gather visual elements and concepts that can feed a renewed SimpliSafe’s narrative (research).

The project would be organized in the following phases:

 Phase 1. Drawing. All SimpliSafe employees will be invited to participate in this drawing

context, regardless of their type contract.

 Phase 2. Submission. Online submission through a simple online form. Among the fields

to be filled: title, drawers, country office or unit they are related to, file (.jpg, .pdf, .doc or  even a video animation). The form would also include a question. For example, “Why this  drawing?”

 Phase 3. Sharing. All submissions (after a simple validation process to prevent rare

inadequate content) will be uploaded to a social wall, where all drawings will be uploaded.  SimpliSafe employees will be able to vote those that like the most.

 Phase 4. Selection of winners. A jury formed by SimpliSafe employees will meet virtually.

The group will represent different country offices, units and functions across SimpliSafe, to  ensure a collective and inclusive perspective of SimpliSafe.

 Phase 5. Redrawing of elements for corporate use.  SimpliSafe will select those visual

elements of the higher potential for external communications and would be redesigned to  ensure coherent visual identity. Visual and content analysis of submissions to identify  patterns, test organizational culture…

Insight:

This is a proposal and therefore still being discussed with colleagues. This insight comes from  these discussions. Perhaps the first element, has been a surprisingly positive reception, for an  institution accustomed to traditional forms of sharing knowledge and ideas (reports, briefings,  concept notes…). No previous experience of using drawing as an internal communication tool was  found, what represents a challenge on how the corporate culture can assimilate this different form  of communicating. Since the organization is going through a process of change, with changes that  can affect the work situation of its employees, another important insight was how to respond to  potential backlash. Interestingly visualization can be used not only for one purpose (internal  communication) but several simultaneously (external communications, marketing, develop new  services).

Approach:

Other design thinking tools could have been used. In fact any of the other 3 recommended for this  assignment. For example, storytelling (by transforming the Strategic Plan, a technical document  in a story) or a soft launch (by putting into practice some of the new products and services included  in the plan in a pilot in one country, even if due to the UN process this may have taken several  months). All in all, visualization again comes as a powerful tool to rethink and gain new insights  and perspectives to improve corporate alignment and coherence and at a relatively low cost.

Learning Launch Tool

1. Challenge:

Working as a leader in R&D organization of machining software company, I am never short of  ideas in our group. Hundreds are generated when we get team together to brainstorm on any  topic. Challenge is always selecting right few to proceed with and doing that selection without  technology, execution or individual biases.

In this specific case, we had gathered ideas on simplifying steps in providing tolerance values on  the part, so that machining allowance / errors wont exceed the limits even after considering worst  possible scenario. Let me take help of below figure to explain the process. Each plate has  tolerance as mentioned below. If you take worst case, i.e. each tolerance limit staying on positive  max, then overall tolerance for X will be summation of all positive worst-case tolerances. In  assembly, typically you have overall tolerance and then need to reverse calculate permissible  tolerance for each part to stay within limits.

Now imagine complex assembly with multiple parts which have holes, fillets, or shapes which are  not rectangular. Tolerance calculation keeps becoming complex and it becomes very  cumbersome process for user of our software to input it meaningfully. In machining, you have to  compute and adjust for these tolerances to meet overall fitment of the part within assembly for  given functionality.

2. Selection:

Team came out with multiple approaches that can possibly simplify this interaction and we  shortlisted three of them as most promising based on our internal criteria. These approaches  varied on controls it provided to user to finetune their inputs for various scenario (maximum  functionality) versus asking minimum intervention from user and product making assumptions on  their behalf (minimum UI).

Then we decided to select Learning Launch tool to experiment with these three approaches to  come out with best possible one for final implementation.

3. Application:

We build quick and dirty simulated prototype of these approaches in less than 2 weeks of efforts  and exposed them to ~18 customers / users who had volunteered to work with us to improve our  productline.

We developed ‘customer satisfaction index’ (CSI) survey for evaluation with criteria like if  proposed solutions meets their need, is it easier to use, what they most liked about this particular  approach. We exposed our quick and dirty simulated prototypes to them through cloud VM and  also observed their usage through video calls. We asked them to fill these CSI survey after  roughly allowing 20 mins play time for them. Each user had to spend roughly 30 min of its total  time for the same including documenting their feedback for ~10min.

4. Insight:

This exercise resulted in surprise findings for us. None of the three was clear winner in terms of  distinct leader in CSI index. Users like simplicity of the approach where we didn’t ask them too  many inputs, but wanted deeper control over functionality for their real world parts and their  variations. Due to insight gained from our learning launch experiment, we developed new  approach altogether where we provided simplicity of making assumptions on behalf of users to  generate default output for most cases, but then allowing to go back and launch detailed controls  for few cases. This detailed UI was required to be invoked only in rare cases to provide different  values than what software has calculated.

This approach was like combining best of all worlds – no UI and default output for 80% of  scenarios, but ability to go back provide details for 20% cases where unique inputs are required,  and more functionality needs to be exposed. Our users loved this approach when it was launched  finally after few more confirmation trials.

5. Approach:

Clearly keeping open mind in Learning Launch phase and allowing customers / users provide all  possible feedback is important. We quickly learned none of our shortlisted ideas were great, but  could develop new one based on feedback from these experiment that allowed us to provide  innovative solution that could help our customer.

The Communicative Power of Visualization

Author: Yareli Thomas

Challenge

As a user experience designer within an organization that builds web applications, I work with a broad range of stakeholders that include

clients representing a diverse set of vertical markets, sales and marketing professionals,  project managers, project owners within an Agile software development framework,  backend and front-end developers.

In order to build successful web applications, we must start by building a shared understanding of the users and their contexts. Often neither written nor spoken language alone is suﬃcient for that to happen across the diverse knowledge domains represented by all stakeholders.

Visualization is a perfect tool that allows me to translate concepts across disciplines without losing the fundamental meaning to the jargon of each represented profession. By leveraging story boarding, journey and ecosystem maps, ﬂow charts, or simple diagrams, I facilitate the process in which all stakeholders build a shared understanding of the problem at hand in order to collaborate on an optimal solution.

Application

In working with a client on a new web application, I begin with a discovery process. Sometimes I facilitate a discovery workshop that allows all stakeholders to spend time with our team to build a shared understanding of the problem, and to start co-designing a solution. Activities that are part of a discovery workshop include creating user personas,  drawing journey maps, ecosystem maps, or story boards.

User personas, a tool I use frequently, while not entirely visual (there is a lot of written information included in them), contain one important visual element—a sketch or a photo of a person. Humans have an emotional response to faces of other humans. Having a visual representation of a person’s face, even if roughly sketched with a few strokes to indicate the eyes and the mouth, allows stakeholder to relate to the user for whom they’re building a product. Personas are, in my opinion, empathy building tools that can transform how stakeholders approach the problem at hand.

Drawing and viewing a graphic representation of a user’s ecosystem or a journey the user travels in life while encountering and interacting with the product or service gives all stakeholders an opportunity to take a step back, assess their own understanding of the ecosystem within which they’re building a product, exchange insights, and build a shared understanding with the team that will be building the product. No written requirements documents share the breadth and depth of the needed knowledge quite so eﬀectively as visualizing it with tools such journey maps, ecosystem maps, or story boards. Below is an example of an ecosystem map.

Insight & Approach

Ultimately, I think, it’s all about visual story-telling. We start talking about the situation at hand; we tell the story of the people involved and the contexts in which the story occurs. And while doing that, we document the story visually. We draw sketches of the characters, we use symbols to indicate actions. It’s a simple and powerful way to build a visual representation of all the actors in the story, all the actions they undertake, and all the events they are subject to.

Visualization techniques allow us to overcome language barriers (implicit or explicit) and to get at the meaning of what we try to convey in a very direct, experiential way. They are also a great way to oﬄoad cognitive eﬀort of trying to keep many moving parts in memory; instead we visualize the pieces through drawing and diagramming, and we move the pieces around until the visualization represents everyone’s understanding of the subject matter.

Sometimes the greatest challenge is to get participants fully engaged. People who are unaccustomed to visualization techniques may feel inadequate and shy about getting up and drawing. I’d like to experiment with diﬀerent activities and ways to encourage involvement. Perhaps some simple warm-up exercises could be leveraged at the onset of a workshop to give the participants a taste of what’s coming. It is also possible that diﬀerent groups will require slightly diﬀerent ratio of visual and verbal story-telling. Maybe at times, instead of insisting on everyone drawing, I could encourage participants to talk, and draw diagrams myself until they feel more comfortable stepping up to pick up the marker. I believe that meeting people where they are is often a more eﬀective way of getting desired outcomes than forcing them out of their comfort zone too soon.

Visualization Tool Reflection

Naga Raju

Design Thinking for Innovation Final Assignment

Challenges and Selection

One of the main challenges I faced as an event planner and decorator is creating a design  which suits the client’s vision and budget but does not eliminate our characteristic as a  designer. I recently faced this challenge when I was doing a wedding design project, in which  my team and I needed to communicate our design ideas and arguments clearly to the client  for them to be able to picture the design well and reach a final agreement. It was an outdoor  wedding reception, and the client wanted it to be intimate and had a rustic mood whilst still  remained on their budget. I decided to use the visualization tool to overcome this challenge  because I figured that decorating an event venue involves a lot of picturing 3D spaces and  room sequences, and this tool is the best way to avoid misconceptions when communicating  our ideas to the client.

Application

At the early step of designing after getting a short brief of the client’s vision, I composed a  design mood board which consists several wedding decoration images, color palettes and  types of flowers that we are going to use according to the big theme. This mood board really  helps us to communicate with the client regarding their design preferences before we moved  to detailing. Visualizing the design examples by real images and color palettes is proven to be  more effective rather than explaining them by words, because both I and the client were able  to state clearly which are suitable with our ideas, characteristic and budget and which are not.  Once both parties had an agreement on the general theme and mood of the wedding, comes  detailing. This part is quite tricky, since we need to create a visualization as similar as the real- life design outcome that we wanted. For this part, I created a 3D model of the venue, complete  with the decoration elements and flower images that we are going to use in a montage. The  3D model was captured from several pivotal point of views such as the entrance, main stage,  and aisle to let the client experience the design sequence. Besides acting as a visualization  tool for the client, the 3D model also helps us as designer in picturing our design in the venue,  starting from the decoration element’s scale to the compatibility of color moods we have  chosen with the venue. Moreover, the method also helped us designers to assess whether  our design is buildable or not. These practices really help us as designers to give a clear  visualization of our design as a whole, from the beginning until the end.

Insight and Approach

I have learned from applying these practices that visualization tool help create a better  understanding and made it easier for people, especially as designers to align our ideas. The  compilation of design preferences images and 3D models gives the designer and client a focal  point to discuss their perspectives and explore their ideas regarding the design. The  visualization helps simplify the communication process and finding the middle ground for both  parties. Even though the project was a success, I still feel like there are more to explore in  terms of using the visualization tool to present our ideas. I would like to be much more detailed  in my future project’s presentation, so I can maximize the tool to explore and share more  insights.

In the crucial stage of product ideation and user feedback, visual tools came in really handy. Working online with remote users and team is challenging. While it could create gaps in how each  one of us understood the information, visualization tools like images, videos. It helped me understand how in an  innovation led design process, visual tools can enrich the information and help understand the  context better.

Overall, I feel although I was already acquainted with some visual thinking tools, I realised their  significance more after applying them consciously in the project. I am  Also going to  find other kinds of visual thinking tools that either exist or have been generated by  people itself.

Giving My Two Cents

Almost one year ago, I was tasked with giving a research-based presentation to my local

Toastmasters is an international organization dedicated to promoting public speaking and

lifelong communication skills.  Almost anyone could join, and my chapter was filled with 3M employees.  I looked up to them and even wanted to one day work for a bank.  I chose

personal finance tips as my topic. Money was considered an uncomfortable topic, but I was still

allowed to present my topic.  Aside from researching credible sources, I needed to think of a way

to make personal finance relatable and entertaining.

Back then, I picked the go-to route, storytelling.  Storytelling gave a face to ideas.  It

enabled audience members to connect boring or abstract concepts together (“Storytelling Tool”).

People loved a good story, and I figured the much older Toastmasters could relate to a young

woman’s issue with money burning a hole in her pocket.

When called upon to speak, my heart started to race.  I was shaking a little but

nonetheless accepted the invitation, got my presentation materials together, and stepped out in

front of the podium.  I was an impressionable young explorer living on my own in a new big

city.  I wanted to enjoy my summer vacation and as a result, had not worked for 3 months.  I dug

myself a hole of $3,000 in credit cards.  It started with moving expenses and grew even larger

Coyle 2

from shopping, eating out, and going to bars and parties with acquaintances.  Some of the

audience members nodded in understanding.  They all kept watching intently as I moved back

and forth, telling my story and making eye contact.

I told them that I was sick of acquiring so much debt and researched ways to cut back

spending.  I started first with talking to everyone about how I found places to cut back

unnecessary spending and then referred to a website for more general tips. Some of the audience

members were taking notes on my presentation. I then walked through the importance of paying

down the high interest rates and principals of credit card debt. Lastly, I walked through the

importance of having an emergency fund.  I ended the presentation with my “two cents” and

purposefully dropping one of my credit cards.  My fellow Toastmasters laughed and gave me a

wonderful round of applause.

After taking a class on design thinking and reflecting on this experience, I understand

how design thinking is a useful tool. Human-centered design allows creators to develop

connections with their audiences and their clients.  Storytelling allowed me to connect with my

fellow Toastmasters and give them a good laugh about a normally uncomfortable topic.

Toastmasters meetings incorporate time for feedback. Joyce, my evaluator, told me that she was

able to relate to being a shopaholic and enjoyed how funny my presentation was.  She said I

needed to work on making more eye contact and moving more purposefully.  Her constructive

feedback was instrumental for me to keep coming back to Toastmasters.  Presenting to an

audience was scary, but it’s enough fun to do it again.

If I were to present the same topic again, I would try my hand at visualization.

Visualization is using imagery to make ideas more understandable and concrete (“Visualization

Tool”).  I could make up a situation where I was reliant on just one jug of water and use the

Coyle 3

water as an analogy for money.  Coming up with reliable metaphors is challenging and

creatively-stimulating.  Another perk of design thinking is exercising creative muscles.

Example Reflection – Storytelling

Challenge and Selection – Grow a Travel business on Social Media  Platform.

Storytelling is a powerful tool when it comes to break down the  problem in simple bits and get a clear understanding about the  problem. I had an Instagram Travel Business Page with over   followers by the name castanedagabriel but the engagement and  leads generation from the page was very low and I was unable to  collect any revenue from the page as most of the followers were not  engaged to the page and Instagram had already shadow banned the  page in past. The first thing I did was to identify the ‘What is’  problem. The problem I had was of less engagements as people were  unable to connect their selves with the posts shared on the page. My  initial response to the problem was to hire someone who could help  grow the engagements but I could not trust anyone with the privacy  issues so I resolved in trying to solve the problem myself.

Application :-

The digital tool that helped me grow my engagements and  later resulted in driving revenues from the page was ‘Story- Telling’. Initially I hired an artist who was well equipped with  the skills of photoshop and asked him to make a brand Logo  and some posters for me. Later I started a kind of story telling  posts which gave the followers a firsthand information about  the places they wanted to travel or were planning to travel in  near future. I started with posting pictures of a particular  place and started sharing information about the place. I

started giving the followers an experience like they were  traveling the places at the very moment and shared some  detailed insights and knowledge behind the places. For  example, I started a series of posts which described ‘Enalu’ a  well-known travel hotspot for tourists. I covered all the local  to do list and facts about Enalu which were rarely shared  before. While using Storytelling and Photoshop I was able to  create a beautiful digital first-hand experience among the  followers.

Insight : -

By applying the Story telling tool and after posting at least 50 posts  on my Instagram Page I was able to see a little rise in engagement  among my followers of the page. People were starting to connect  with the stories I shared on the page and started liking more pictures  and asking their questions and doubts they had about the places  they were willing to travel in future. By this we were able to stay  more in touch with our followers and they started looking at our  page as a Brand rather than a Social Media Page. The page started  getting tagged on various accounts and I was able to see a positive  engagement.

Approach: -

What I learned by applying this digital tool to my business was that  Story-telling is a powerful tool when it comes to reinventing  strategies of a business. With storytelling I was able to make people  engage in our page by making them feel as if they were experiencing  the places listed in our page themselves just by reading about them.  It also made me realize that if a story is conveyed well among the

customers, they feel special and they trust the Brand’s image more  than that of paid advertisements and shout-outs. In future I would  surely love to try this tool on a different venture but I also believe  that one needs to be in his customer’s shoes before telling a story  and framing one for him.

Visualization (Module 1)

Challenge:  I am the owner and founder of a solar company. My job is to  create ideas to convince clients to use Renewable Energy  Sources. My customers need to understand how a house  plus energy works, how they can charge an electric car for  free and how they can use free energy at home. I want to  sell products through education. We have to find ways to  convince them to sustainability. We want to present the  process online to reduce costs and time.

Selection:  I personally chose the visualization for this task. I believe  that this is the most effective method in my industry. I want  to visually show the problem using examples and  comparisons. I also expect the team to define the problem  and solve it in a visual way. we want to create a set of  questions and answers for our problem. The team must  construct the responses as simply as possible. because it is  really a key part of the way we communicate, whether we  are aware of it or not. It allows us to think non-verbally. I  also know that the most important thing is to visualize the  idea first, because then you will be able to test the prototype  in the wild. Each of the subsequent prototypes should be  built with the user in mind and answer a specific question.

Application:  The first way to visualize sustainable development and the  use of solar energy for free electricity and charging an  electric car was the Power Point presentation. The method  turned out to be effective, but only in a small group of  participants. It required a presentation with an employee of

our company who, through this tool, discussed the problem  and educated our clients. Unfortunately, it did not involve  our client enough and turned out to be boring. The second  way is to prepare a solar calculator on the website. This  turned out to be an easy, quick and cheap way to reach the  customer and get his attention. An important element was to  show the customer a common denominator for photovoltaic  installations.

Insight:  Our team has built a design of a typical residential building,  which they have placed on our website. In the upper corner,  the team has placed a column in which the client himself  provided the approximate size of the roof. The next column  showed the location of the roof in relation to the  geographical sides of the world (north, south, east and  west). The third column contained the price of the electric  bill that the customer pays every month. Due to the  simplicity of the tool, we did not want to have more data  than the three we need to visualize the solution of our  client's problem. After entering the data, our client received  graphically how to use energy. How many kilometers will the  electric car travel. How much will its cost of electricity  decrease. How many trees will the customer save by using  renewable energy sources.

Approach:  I believe that i can use this tool globally, but i need to  change our team's approach to generating customer  attention. It is worth introducing a short video with the next  tool that describes the basic energy problems of the client  and our planet. This can cause more attention to the

problem. A conscious client reacts more easily to the  message about the problem.

Reflection – Mind Mapping

Challenge

I am a member of the organization’s product development team. We are a multinational company from  the textile industry, and our challenge is to grow the sales of our line products. P&D works closely with  the Sales team, which brings us the feedback from our B2B customers, with our Trade Marketing  department, which brings us the feedback and information from the market, and the industrial  development team at the industrial plant.    The company spent a few months in a process of mind set and cultural change, when the employees  were trained in agile methodologies, to use them as new tools for the developments of the new product  process, and also solve problems in which the company has found difficulty.

Selection    After the training our team has already followed up with some parts of the "What Is" (Journey  Mapping, Value Chain Analysis), and now we have reached the stage of Mind Mapping, which is why I  choose this tool for reflection.    Application    First, we chose a large room in the office. Then we paste all the data that we collected during the  previous phases on the walls. We gathered a group of twenty people from the areas of sales, trade  marketing, product development and industrial, so they could look at it. Gradually everyone made  observations, and we followed the processes of insights formation and clustered the data so we could  proceed with brainstorming.    Insight    After the use of mind mapping, we could perceive a series of links and patterns among the interviewees,  and in this way, it was possible to observe some problems and feelings of the consumers that we didn’t  know before. Because of this process it was possible to reach the stage of brainstorming much more  prepared to develop a solution that fits the consumer better and adds more financial value to the  company.    Approach    For the next applications of mind mapping, I believe that what we will have different will be the  experience of having already carried out this process. All participants will already have changed their  mind set and understood the importance of design thinking, and the execution of this tool will already  be done in a more fluid way.

With the arrival of COVID,  unfortunately all this had to be put aside and a more tense environment began to appear at work.

Challenge

With a pandemic in the middle and with the new option of having to send workers home, the company  was a little concerned that it would lose that human touch for which it was so characterized and that its  employees would start to drift away. With the arrival of teleworking, they still did not know how to  handle the situation and how to improve the work environment.

Tool Selection

Story telling: with my experience in this type of jobs that always involves sharing with people and  knowing how important it this for the job experience I was worry about my coworkers, and with all the  stress that this involves and being at home 24/7 I I knew it was gonna be a difficult time, so I decided to  create meetings during job time but this kind of meetings were just to talk and share a little with  everybody.

Visualization

We decided to create a Google activity that involves all the coworkers to organize thoughts and ideas so  we can get straight to discussion at our next scheduled meeting and deliberate and consider each  person's ideas.

The questions on the form are:

1. Describe what is your perfect work environment

2. What do you think the company need to improve

3. Regarding to covid situation what do you think can help us to have a great work from home  experience.

4. What advice would you give a peer facing this same issue?

5. If you could design a training or suggest an upgrade what would that be?

Application

So, I was very conscience about the situation, about how this pandemic affects our life and about how  stressful I was for all of us and I realize how much this change our life and how can this affect our  development at work. So, I decided to take half an hour per day to spend some time with people during  videocalls in zoom and making some games so we all can be more relax and enjoy our work. I take  advantage of the technology and create a good virtual environment for the company so the people  would still enjoy working with us.

At the beginning everything was very confused by people and they didn't know how to react or how to  interact with everybody, but while the weeks all the companions were passing by, they were loosening  up more and the meetings were being more enjoyable, we had to figure out how to be able to continue  to have a healthy work environment and even so we were from home to feel like we were all still  together despite the circumstances, we always tried to have a topic of conversation and for this we  turned to tools such as WhatsApp, Jam board, Zoom, Google, to share some ideas about topics we could  develop during the meeting, even Canva was a widely used tool to express ourselves in a more creative  way.

As the teams were developing, we were also developing a new working environment from the comfort  of our houses and we were creating a new environment and which we liked because we still maintained  this environment to work pleasant and human but all in their own comfort, even up to Coffee, tea and  food, we suggested that they have the employees by their side and this in order to create a unique  atmosphere.

Seeing the employees smile again, joke around and feel comfortable is what fills us as a company,  because for us the worker has always been more important, since we are aware that if the worker is  happy, he does his job well and so we are all happy. winning and in these difficult times with such a  radical change of life because for us it was very important to recreate a good online environment and  maintain the good work environment that characterized us so much.

Insight

It was difficult for me to jump right into solve the issue mode. But what the team has brought to the  table is richer than any idea I would have produced on my own, they work in teams and bring great  ideas to help solving the issue.

Approach

We still in the what is phase, because this still knew for all of us, every day we have to innovate so this  doesn’t turn to be boring and common. Every day we are thinking about what can we do, what new  ideas do we have for the people and how we can continue bringing a good service for our customers, so  every day we are thinking on innovation ideas and deseing new activities for our people, this also bring  great experiences for all of us and bring a great experience for me because it helps me to perform that  we can make more than what we think we are capable of and it is a great opportunity to expand our  minds and perform and recognize how smart and creative we all are.

Visualisation – Student Journey

Mahtab Esmaeili

The Challenge

My challenge was to create a Customer Experience training at my workplace (a university). The  university’s ultimate customers are students; therefore, my challenge was to enable understanding  of the student experience at the university and encourage continuous improvement.

Selection

I decided to use visualisation to understand and depict the student journey from the point of  awareness (how they become aware of different universities) to joining the alumni. As highlighted  by Meyer in the week 1 video, visualisation is a great tool for understanding ‘different contexts’ and  ‘our customers’. Furthermore, visualisation can give a snapshot of a process while allowing for  further exploration.

Application

I used visualisation as a tool to map the student experience from the point of student awareness to  joining alumni. I used stick figures to draw the students in the different journey points and arrows  that connected each journey point to the next. For example:

I then invited selected stakeholders from across the different sections of the university to fill the  gaps while also contributing their own visual clues to the student journey. For this activity I  separated/cut each student journey point and stuck it in sequence on the walls of the room. I  divided the stakeholders into different groups so they could move easily from one journey point to  the next and gave them Post-it notes so they could draw their contributions and stick them under  each journey point or in between journey points. Finally I looked for patterns (similar to mind  mapping) and we discussed and agreed on a final version of the student journey. The activity took  around 30 minutes to complete with nine distinct journey points identified.

The next stage involved using data from the QS International and Domestic student surveys 2019 to  understand the expectations of domestic and international students at the different journey points. I  used graphs to show student preferences and needs at each journey point. For the final design I  used Storyboard 360 to depict the student journey; making it more visually appealing and

interactive. Storyboard 360 allowed course participants to click on each journey point to find out  about student preferences at each point.

The student journey forms the backbone for two modules within the Customer Experience course  where participants are asked to: 1. compare student needs at particular journey points with what  the university is currently offering/doing.  2. highlight the gap 3. use the customer experience  principles espoused by the university to come-up with solutions to close the gap between the  current student journey and what students need or expect.

Participant feedback has been very positive, and some comments indicate that participant  understanding of the student journey at the university has been enhanced and they are keen to  implement some of the suggestions from the group discussions.

Insight

I found using visualisation in developing the student journey map had several benefits:

1. In the initial consultation with stakeholders it worked similar to an icebreaker. People had to

get out of their seats and interacted with each-other sometimes commenting on each- other’s suggestions or their own stick figures, triggering laughter.

2. Use of stick-figures in the initial consultation created an inclusive platform – everyone could

draw a stick figure and make fun of their own stick figure.

3. The initial visualisation consultation created a sense of ownership of the process and created

a universal view of the student journey. Some of the comments included “I didn’t know the  reason for ‘x’ till now” or “now I know where I fit in the student journey”.

4. The visualisation (student journey) created the ‘what is’ in design thinking enabling the

participants to understand what the university’s current processes are at each journey point,  what students prefer and what is the gap.

5. Discussion question ‘3’ created a space for ‘what if’ in design thinking; ‘Use the customer

experience principles espoused by the university to come-up with solutions to close the gap  between the current student journey and what students need or expect.’

Approach

I found visualisation to be well suited for what I intended to achieve; understand the customer  journey in the university. In the future I will incorporate visualisation activities in other areas of my  work. I will consider ways in which I can use visualisation to explore ‘what wows’ in the student  journey; ‘The Wow Zone’ where: ‘customers want it’, ‘we can do it’ and ‘the economics can sustain  it’. I will ask the participants to consider the economics and attainability of their idea when  considering question ‘3’ and depict it visually on the student journey.
