Reflection - Learning Launch

Challenge & Selection    The tool I chose to use was Learning Launch, due to the current stage of my client project. I  work with government clients in the technology space creating digital products. The digital  product my team is currently working on has already passed the Design Thinking steps 1-3. We  are in the “What works?” phase which is where the Learning Launch tool becomes important.  My team and I have gone through face-to-face user interviews with several stakeholder groups,  in addition to mind mapping exercises and persona creation based on our qualitative data from  interviews. Our goal for conducting the Learning Launch tool is to understand where our  current product fails and succeeds. We want to dive deep into user feedback and implement  changes to make our product the best it can be for our users.    Application    We want our testing to be iterative. Our Learning Launch will not be conducted in a silo.  Following in line with the Design Thinking timeline, we want to fail early to succeed sooner. We  will start the process by understanding the needs that our current product addresses. Then we  will craft a script made up of open-ended questions to ask users as they test our product. Users  will test our product via a digital prototype.    For the first Learning Launch, we wanted to test the main “happy path” through the product.  Our goal is to understand, “Can a user successfully get from point A to point B?”. This test will  be conducted with one of our several user groups. We conducted 30 user tests with a digital  prototype over the course of one week. Each test was 45 minutes, with 15 minutes to debrief  with our team afterwards. We also took notes during each session and used a voice recording.  We learned that users were able to successfully get from point A to point B, however a few key  visual elements threw our users off. Specifically, we realized there was a disconnect between  our product’s visual elements and the same visual elements used in the real world that provide  a different experience. After our first Learning Launch, we decided to circle back with the visual  team to rework some key elements that tripped our users up. The newly designed elements fell  in line with what users had expected to see in the “happy path”.    For the second Learning Launch, we decided to test a financial portion of the product. We  wanted to see if two different user groups could successfully navigate creating, submitting,  reviewing, and paying an invoice. We asked users to complete various tasks that led them  through different experiences within the prototype. Our initial assessments of the invoicing  flows were that they would require a decent amount of change. We used this second round of  testing purely as iterative and experimental. We wanted to understand specifically what data is  vital to our users to successfully complete the above tasks. This test was a great learning  experience for our entire team because our takeaways helped us to fully design the invoicing  process, utilizing the most important data.

Noa Cohen

Insight & Approach    As I learned from Ashley in the Design Thinking course, “True competitive advantage lies in  addressing people’s unarticulated needs.” Utilizing the Learning Launch tool, we were able to  uncover our users’ unarticulated needs. Observing users’ behaviors led us to get a sense of the  pain points and desires we need to address in our prototypes. Our results for both tests were  similarly in line to what we had anticipated. The first Learning Launch we successfully  understood the needs of our user group and only had to iterate on a few key visual elements.  The second Learning Launch we knew going into it that the prototype would not be successful  because we did not have a larger understanding of what the process should be. Our testing  from the second launch gave us the information we needed to design the best experience  possible for those user groups. The Learning Launch tool reaffirmed my trust in the design  thinking process because you will never create a successful product without asking your users  directly what they think. I learned that you need to ask question after question, to uncover your  users’ true desires and create a product that uniquely benefits your users.    As previously mentioned, given the stage our team is at for this product’s timeline, the Learning  Launch tool best suits our needs at the moment. However, our team would not be where we  are today without utilizing the earlier design thinking tools at the beginning of our process. We  have analyzed the feedback from our two Learning Launches and implemented the changes to  our prototypes. In the future, we intend to conduct additional Learning Launches in an effort to  continuously better our product. Even post-deployment of our product, I think it would create  value to continue testing because a product can always be improved with user feedback.

Challenge: Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.

Over the past decade, the financial industry in the United States has faced an unprecedented number of  transformative challenges including sweeping regulatory reforms with tougher compliance burdens.  This  regulatory scrutiny has forced a number of banking institutions, including my client, to begin a journey of  “defining and driving a culture of risk resiliency across the bank”.

This challenge is what can be easily described as a “wicked problem” where the stakeholders of the bank,  especially senior management, can't seem to agree on a definition of what resiliency or even culture is,  much less agree on a solution or a way of achieve a culture of resiliency.   In essence, as Rosangela Watkins  points out, “the only way to see if something works is to try it”.

So, our challenge of defining resiliency and developing a momentum plan to drive a culture of resiliency  by aligning a group of 50+ internal stakeholders from diverse backgrounds (business development,  technology, operations), is an ideal challenge for design thinking, in general and visualization, in  particular.

Selection: In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected

I specifically selected visualization because I needed a tool that could avoid endless debates amongst the  diverse stakeholder on how they might define risk, resiliency and culture, all concepts that are complex  and where no right or wrong answer truly exists.  As Rosangela Watkins writes, “when we´re talking and  we´re verbalizing things we see internally, we may all be understanding the words in a slightly different  way.”   So, the challenge requires a tool that is able to explore those different internal interpretations, find  common patterns or threads, and begin to think synthesize it.

The strength behind this tool is that the stakeholders can all “tap into a single picture”. This is critical  because people support what they help to create and visualization is the process of creating a picture of  something –like a culture of risk resiliency–that doesn´t yet exist in this particular organization.  “It´s  creating pictures of something that will soon be”.  Rosangela Watkins

Application: Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge

In order to apply this tool effectively during the actual half-day session whose objective was, in part, to  align around a common definition of risk resiliency and develop a momentum plan to drive a culture of  resiliency across the bank, I took the following steps:

1. Conducted numerous interviews with key stakeholders across three areas (business, technology,

and operations) to understand their definition of resiliency and consider an appropriate analogy

2. Eight different images where created for each of the most relevant analogies provided by the

interviewees, including: resiliency is the plumbing that Wall Street is built on, burying the electric  lines, or the foundation of a house.

3. As the senior leadership team arrived the day of the session, I asked them to reflect on all of the

analogies that they had shared with us and asked them to answer “what the analogies shared in  common”.  I wanted them to see that in spite of the fact that they were all different, there was a  common pattern that ran through all of them—the fact that these images all represented resiliency  as the “foundation” on which the bank was built on.

4. After conducting a number of introductory presentations and activities that helped clarify and

align the stakeholder on the rationale for why a culture of risk resiliency was so important now, I  developed a specific visualization activity that asked them to image a time in the future (say 3-5

years out) where, in this utopian ideal, they have been successful in evolving their culture to drive  and sustain resiliency at the bank.  They were then asked to write a headline to communicate their  vision forcefully and optimistically and draw an image that captures what good looks like.

5. After having crafted the headlines to the article, the groups began to converge on a number of

different images all of which, except for one, were distinctly different to the original eight  analogies. The groups were then asked to share their work to the rest of the group and focus, in  particular, on the discussions and thought process that went into the image.

6. As the groups began to share their pictures and thoughts, there was a general sense of excitement

among the senior leadership team as they began to rally around several of these visuals.  Perhaps it  was because they began to sense that alignment was possible?   That the future they were  visualizing was possible?  After approximately 10 minutes, one new image was proposed that  seems to catch on like wildfire—that of Atlas supporting the World.   After a few minor iterations,  it became clear that the message for this senior leadership team would be that risk resiliency was  “the power to prevail”.

Insight: Describe the insight you gained from applying the tool you selected to your challenge

I would highlight two new, key insights:

1. Visualization helps garner buy-in more easily.  While it is easy to pick apart a sentence by

focusing on the dislike or rejection of one word or focusing on the “interpretation” of another,  visualization seems to be a more universal language.  It allows us to first and foremost share in the  joy of “success” in aligning around a common picture.  This makes verbalization, or putting words  behind the image, become a much easier feat to accomplish.

2. Visualization also allows for an easier exchange of observations, ideas, and insights amongst the

stakeholders.  As the sense of alignment and consensus begins to grow as stakeholders discuss the  different images, it becomes easier to engage an even wider number of participants into the  discussion and deepen the conversation.  Since it is difficult to disagree with a drawing, the  conversation becomes lively and engaging, rather that confrontational.  As a result, it is much  easier to exploit the creativity amongst the group to generate a new and novel solution.

Approach: Describe what you might do differently next time -- applying the same tool you selected  or a different one -- and the reason(s) why.

One of the things I would do differently is use visualization jointly with storytelling.  While visualization  allowed the group of senior leaders to achieve alignment around the definition of resiliency and  eventually develop a momentum plan with a number of key initiatives geared to drive a culture of  resiliency, it is important to keep in mind what Rosangela Watkins highlighted when she stated that, “it´s not  about the list of things we have to do, it´s about the connection that we give to people about a piece of  information that we´re trying to share”.

In this case, I think using storytelling in developing the momentum plan would have allowed the senior  leadership team to create a powerful means of creating a “purpose” or a “cause” that could have ignited  and united all employees in the organization around the initiatives that they would be in charge of  implementing across the organization.  Rather than create a list of interesting initiatives to “solve” the  challenges of evolving a culture of resiliency as we did, storytelling would have allowed us to find a way  to ignite and untie people because stories are an agent of change…they change our hearts and minds.

Challenge

I work in a company that manufactures catalysts for the oil refining industry. A catalyst is a component that  increases the rate of reaction but does not take part in it. In the refining process, reactor is fed with heavy  hydrocarbons and, in the presence of the catalyst, valuable light products are obtained.

It is a very competitive market with few but very strong competitors. The market we serve has many state- owned refineries that buy the product by public procurement which includes catalytic test. Catalyst must  win the test to be selected.

My challenge was to develop a new product that could win the test and recover one of these customers in  particular, which we have not supplied for years.

Selection

We set out a series of experiments in the laboratory designed to impart the desired characteristics to the  product: activity (the ability to convert the heavy hydrocarbons into light ones) and selectivity (increase the  yield of one product relative to others).

Results were scaled to pilot plant and the product tested well in the lab and in a pilot reactor.

Some improvements were due, but we were running out of time to bid. So we decided to try the learning  launch tool.

After several sessions of ideation, brainstorming and visualization, we came up to a safe and effective  arrangement to perform a plant trial. Scale-up process raises several issues, such as different behavior of  fluid mixing, large amounts to be transferred and the need to install piping and instrumentation to run the  operation.

We modified our hardware and ran the production to get the minimum amount of product (a few tons) to  run a commercial trial in a small refinery with which we have an agreement.

Application

During scale-up, the usual protocol is to explore the operating window of process conditions, try different  formulations, and stress the boundaries of product physicals. But we decided not to go so deep in analysis  and testing, but go for the proof of concept: research basis was solid, product characterization and  performance test results were encouraging.

The product we obtained had no further improvements in formulation or cost saving activities in the plant,  but it carried the fundamentals of our research.

Catalyst was used in the small refinery and data were collected and analyzed, thus confirming our  expectations of higher activity and selectivity.

Insight

Using the learning launch tool has been a breakthrough in our organization. Mostly composed of chemical  engineers (as me), the approach to product development and launch has always had a conservative and  cautious bias. All causes of potential failure should be anticipated, massive and extensive product

characterization and performance were supposed to be run in each scale of  development before product  came into production. This protocol lengthens the time to market a great deal and hinders innovation.

The great insight was to show that we can have a consistent product and technology ready for market  launch even though we do not know all the answers and failure modes but based on solid fundamentals  and experimental work.

I believe we can use this tool more often to speed up our time to market and keep the innovation process  running smothly, but what I might do differently next time is to bring customer experience to the  development plan. Carry interviews and propose cooperation plans to test product at the customer’s lab in  between the tenders to have a deeper understanding of his protocols and decision making.

Reflection – Learning Launch

Challenge

In this reflection about learning launch and experimentation, I would like to tell an  incident when I influenced engineering to build a particular feature. In my current role,  I’m the monetization front-end designer for our free email product.

Two weeks ago, Irina, the engineering manager, gave me some bad news, "Leonardo,  I’m sorry, but we have to remove 140x500 skyscraper ad. My engineering VP told me  that the PM team wouldn’t mind."

I was thinking to myself: “Are you kidding me? Wouldn’t mind? This ad was only the 3rd  most valuable ad placement on the entire site. It delivered INR 45 million in revenue  per year. Who did Irina think was paying her salary?”

Selection

After I collected my emotions, I asked Irina, “When are you planning to remove it?”  She said, “Two code sprints from now. About 6 weeks.”

I told her, “Can you give me three days to pull some data? I’d like to understand the  impact of this decision.”

After she left, I thought: what could I do? I could have a hissy fit and complain loudly.  Or I could immediately escalate to the engineering VP.

While I was tempted to go with either or both solutions, I wouldn’t get what I want  unless I was armed with the facts. Before I figured my plan, I gave my boss Luca, a  heads-up. He wasn’t pleased with engineering’s unilateral response, but he agreed with  my plan.

Application

I logged into the data warehouse and pulled revenue numbers for the last 12 months.  Next I asked to sales team to gauge customer reaction if we no longer made the product  available. Lastly, I reached out to the VP Engineering’s Chief of Staff to better  understand why we wanted to remove the ad.

Insight

After I collected the data, I set up a meeting with Irina, Luca my boss, and  Luca the VP of Engineering. The VP of Engineering reiterated his decision to  remove the skyscraper ad. He maintained what I had heard earlier: the skyscraper ads  were the reason why the email product’s engagement and market share was down.

I asked him, “Why do you think the ads impact engagement?”

2 Leonardo Torres

He said, “They distract the user.”

I replied, “Are there times when you don’t find the ads distracting?”

He said, “Yes, when it’s relevant to the content. Let’s say I’m reading an email about  meeting with friends, and the ads suggest things new restaurants and bars.

So I summarized, “So, you don’t have a problem with ads. What you’re really concerned  about is the quality of the ads.”

Approach

I recommended that rather than remove the ads completely, we should revisit our ad  policy and make sure that we’re serving relevant ads. We can tighten up our ad editorial  processes so that low quality ads aren’t mindlessly approved by the system.

He was shocked when I told him that the ad placement generated $45 million in annual  revenue. And he also didn’t realize that by pulling the placement, customers would pull  advertising budget, primarily because it wasn’t worth continuing a relationship with us,  given the low ad volume and lack of attractive ad placements, relative to our  competitors.

Organisation

We minimized many of the low quality teeth whitening, weight loss ads that were  known for distracting tactics such as pop-ups, fake navigation, and blinking sections.

It required a lot more work on our editorial team and advertisers. Shortly after, we later  found that email user engagement did go up by 6.5%, and most importantly, we  preserved $45 million in revenue.

Imagine being inside of yourself, looking out through your eyes at the  ideal result.

Using Visualization techniques to focus on your goals and desires yields four very  important benefits.  1.) Reflection – The story of African rivers

Manuel Vazquez – Director Innovation and Transformation at Wollega

Challenge

With 2500 staff in Africa, Wollega is one of the largest engineering consultants on the continent and the

largest consultant in South Africa.  The company has completed its two year business plan which is

focussed on building a future ready Wollega. This future ready strategy is built on three platforms of

innovation, digital engineering and eminence. The innovation platform is defined in the Wollega

Business plan as follows: “Our innovation aspiration for our organisation is that our clients must see

benefits from that focus on innovation. Innovation will be focussed on clients and we need to

demonstrate the value of our ideas to both our clients and to the business. At the heart of our innovation

of the client experience will be the concept of design led thinking. Our innovation program is in place to

differentiate our offerings. We will encourage and nurture innovation and technical excellence from our

people.”

As Director Innovation and Transformation for Africa I am responsible for the implementation of the

innovation strategy and design thinking on the continent. The process of implementing an innovation

culture and systems thinking into an engineering consulting business is not easy in that engineers are

very analytical thinkers.

Selection

I have chosen storytelling as one of the tools to introduce design methodologies into the business.  We

all have our own stories and through using this approach we can hopefully get employees to understand

the power of using this tool.  By using storytelling we can get our engineers to have more empathy for

the end users of our projects.  Storytelling allows us to connect real people to our solutions.  If we can

get our engineers to reflect on the emotions and feelings of the end users it will allow us to approach

problems from a very different perspective.  Through storytelling we understand that there are much

larger group of stakeholders who we sometimes overlook or make assumptions about that are through

our world view. This requires us to spend more time asking questions relating to why.  As engineers we

tend to jump very quickly to the solution mode or what works?  Storytelling gives you a different

perspective that allows you to spend more time with what is?

Application

In applying the story telling tool we chose a project in Nairobi related to providing a solution for cleaning

up the urban rivers.  Instead of using a technical environmental approach we adopted a storytelling

methodology.  We looked at the relevance of rivers in African culture and the role it played in shaping

African culture.  We discovered a term: “By the rivers” which has its roots in African culture.  If you had

a special announcement to make you would go ‘down to the river’ to make the announcement.  The

term therefore has special significance in African culture and speaks to the history and legacy of the

area.  By adopting this approach we could tell a very rich African story of the impact that rivers play in

shaping culture and history.  We then speak about how local people can reclaim the rivers.  By

reclaiming the rivers they can reclaim their history and legacy as Africans.  After this story has been

told we introduce the environmental aspects and what innovation we can use for people to reclaim the

rivers.

Insights

Through using this approach we discovered that rivers play a significant role in shaping African history

and culture.  It is a special place linked to significant stories in the history of the continent.  Through

telling this story you can reignite pride and passion in people and their history.  By elevating this part of

their history and recognising the significance of rivers people start to have a renewed pride in being

African and they feel that their story has relevance.  A broad range of stakeholders were identified

through the storytelling process with most people being able to relate similar stories from their

forefathers.  The challenges that people experienced through the stories were very similar.  The idea

of cleaning up the rivers took on a new significance because it was much more than a “foreign”

environmental issue.  It became an opportunity to reclaim the history and legacy of whole communities.

It also became an opportunity to meet old and lost friends.  A rally point around celebrating what it

means to be African.  The environmental programmes and technology artefacts that were introduced

became tools to reclaim their history.  This is a significant different approach to the traditional way of

innovation and technology being brought into Africa.  The traditional way which says this is some great

technology that that will solve your problems.  “It works in the Western world and will therefore work in

Africa.”  We see numerous cases across Africa where inappropriate technology is implemented or when

solutions are provided that are not through the lenses of Africans. Storytelling allows us to place the

end user at the centre of what we are doing.  It allows us to have empathy and understanding of people’s

challenges, hopes and aspirations.

Approach

The storytelling approach worked very well with getting the local citizens on board and supporting a

river cleaning project in the locality.  The challenge is now to scale this up and include private sector

early on in the process for them to become an invested stakeholder.  This can be done by identifying

corporates that are located close to the river and getting them to “adopt” certain sections of the river in

the vicinity.  In order to do this corporates need to feel that they are also part of shaping the story and

in this way take joint ownership of a natural resource that can ultimately add value to the city and their

employees.

“My Learning, My Pride”

Challenge: As a Lecturer from Faculty of Business and Globalization from Vlisco,

since 2007 up to 2013 our students used to be so vibrant, so full of energy and always eager to

come to school. This created a very conducive environment for both students and staff

members. For the past three years (2014-2016) our Faculty has been experiencing a challenge

of students’ poor attendance (lectures and tutorials) and lack of interest in their learning.  This

has even affected lecturers’ performance in classes as well. As one of the experienced lecturers

in the faculty, I always reported this challenge in my weekly report. In one of the faculty

meeting I tabled the discussion about this challenge; it became evident that every lecturer was

facing the same problem. I therefore volunteered to lead a team that was to find solutions to

this challenge.

Selection: I chose the storytelling design thinking tool to address this challenge. Storytelling is

an “essential human activity” for sharing experiences, explaining values, and deciding on

solutions through vivid verbal and visual accounts. Stories take on a variety of forms :  visual

storytelling, storyboards, scenario generation, storytelling through videos, animation or talk. I

did use talk form of storytelling so as to be able to narrate the challenge as well as listen to the

students’ concerns. This will also give me the opportunity to discuss with the students the

negative impact of this current challenge on their academic work and why there is a need to

find solutions to resolve the challenge.  Listening engages people and empathy is an essential

and fundamental component in the process of solving the challenge.

Application: Through a series of consultative meetings, my team and I did collect the needs and

interests of students and lecturers. During these consultative meetings, we would use

questionnaires, sometimes interviewing the business students one on one or at times use the

assistance of class representatives to collect students’ views about their current state of

learning and what leads to their lack of interest in their learning. These consultative meetings

also aimed at imagining new solutions that could help the faculty of Business to be more

effective.  Collectively, we designed a learning approach called “My Learning, My Pride”, which

put emphasis on instilling pride in students towards their knowledge based learning not just

been receivers of information during lectures. The feedback we got while listening to the

students, their concerns were that: the teaching methods are the traditional boring writing on

the white board with a marker, there was lack of connection with the industry out there, they

are not able to practice what they are been taught while still learning and hence do not become

too eager to continue with the learning as well as not having sufficient facilities for extra

curriculum activities i.e. sports activities.

“My Learning, My Pride” approach came up with various solutions to meet the students’

needs and hence improved students’ interest in their learning as evident by more than 50%

improvement in the attendance and higher student achievement results in school within the

semester it was implemented(therefore February to May 2017 semester). The solutions we

came up with was: a) to encourage lecturers to make lecture delivery interesting by using

power point slides and projecting them in class instead of the traditional writing on the white

board using a marker (Projectors are already available in the IT department),  b) as part of

student assessment real life projects from the industry are given to students to work on ,

c)periodically organize seminars or workshops for both students and staff members  facilitated

by industry advisors, d) organize industry visits related to students courses for students to

appreciate  what they learn in class, e)Establishment of a Business club  and making club

activities to be more interesting, even involvement of more staff members in the club. The

faculty aims to share this “My Learning, My Pride” approach with every new lecturer during

their orientation. In realizing the success of this approach, other faculties have also developed

an interest in using this approach in the near future as they are also experiencing the same

challenge.

Insight: In applying this design thinking tool it helped me to understand elements that lead to

students’ lack of interest in their learning as well as poor attendance in class. Listening to and

empathizing with the students’ needs, I gained enormous insights into the types of lecture

delivery and different other ways to make their learning interesting and meaningful.

Innovativeness and creativeness are patterns of behavior I found among 21st century education

seeking students. This helped me a lot as before applying this design tool I was merely thinking

its students not been serious about their learning hence not attending lectures and lacking

interest in their learning.

Approach: Based mainly on students’ input, we were able to redesign their learning

environment to better meet their learning needs and desires. So next time, still using the same

storytelling design tool, we will also give more attention to member of staff  so as to get to

address their faculty academic needs and desires as per the faculty’s capability. This is because

lecturers play a very important part in motivating students while delivering lectures in class.

Unhappy lecturers will not be as effective and productive as they could be when they are happy

about their work environment.

Another obstacle was how to replicate the weekly interactions that built a strong student  community in the classroom with an online setting where students would interact in a relatively  isolating environment.

As an instructional designer, my focus has always been on creating a learner-focused  environment so the challenge was to take a complicated course structure and simplify it for  students as well as faculty.  Added to that challenge was the need to create an online structure  for a positive student experience to engage with the materials and activities as well as to  automate the students’ work in such a way that the TAs and professor need only to track it and  review it leaving a clear documentation trail and making grading easier.

Selection   (Terms in bold refer to the Learning Launch Design template as described by Douglas Wood in Week  4.)

I plan to discuss the Learning Launch Design Tool because I had the opportunity to develop a  prototype, 7-week course, and test it by offering it to a small group of 14 professionals (from  diverse backgrounds, all working full-time) with the same team — faculty, TA, and ID — who  would later implement the full 14-week version for full-time graduate students. Our key  assumption was that an online negotiation course could be successfully implemented by  developing an active student community, through relevant activities and course structure based  on user-centered design. As to who, we knew that working professionals often look for  training  in negotiation so the course would meet their ongoing needs. The how was implemented  through the existing communications and LMS systems. The costs to implement the learning  launch were minimal as it required staff time that was already allocated to the project and used  tools and processes that are part of the university system. The only real cost to anticipate would  be the program’s reputation (not a minor cost). We anticipated giving refunds if this were an  issue to maintain good relations. And the timeframe was short and completed a month prior to  the start of fall term, allowing us to make changes, where needed, to the prototype.

Application

A primary goal of the learning launch was to test the automation of assignments as well as the  structure of the course for ease of communication and engagement. Did the automation work  without being too complicated for the students? Were the students engaged? Did it free up time  for the professor and TA? A secondary goal was to evaluate the efﬁcacy of offering the course in  the online environment. Would the students not only remain engaged but would they achieve  the course outcomes and skill building? Did the structure of the course in the learning  management system (LMS) allow for clear communication and a positive user experience?

Design Thinking Prototyping an Online Course Monika Seifert

The course was structured and designed, applying user-experience effective practices. All  assignments were completed using online tools to aggregate responses in a spreadsheet. Pass/ fail quizzes were built into the LMS so that students could determine if they were absorbing the  material. Along with the automated grading system that was created, a survey was given to the  students at the end of the course to gauge their learning experience with questions focused on  their experience with the course structure, content, and assignments.

This was a surprisingly effective method for testing the course in the online environment. While  students did pay to take the course, we were using a curriculum that had been developed years  ago and improved upon in the subsequent years, so the quality was high. The professor is  highly regarded in his ﬁeld and enjoyed engaging with the students in web conferences. We  were focused on their engagement in the online environment and the use of new online tools,  but the students were focused on connecting with each other through the assignments and  absorbing the material.

Insight

Having been part of teams that had developed non-credit online courses for busy professionals,  I had warned the professor that he should be prepared for several to drop out of the course  sometime in the ﬁrst three weeks, even though I had recommended activities and materials that  would accommodate the schedule of someone working full-time. The results, however, were  astonishingly successful. Not one student dropped out, and all, but one student, completed all of  the activities required to receive a certiﬁcate of completion. I attribute this to the focus of using  the assignments to build community and having a weekly class meeting with the professor. The  professor and TA were thrilled with the automation of assignments and grading. They  determined to continue to use this model for the full 14-term course in the classroom.

That said, there were drawbacks which required correction to aspects of the course but even so  this new iteration will be a better and more effective course for the students as well as for the  faculty. What has been most effective, however, has been the experience of the faculty member  who has become a supporter of teaching online  through this experiment and now sees an  opportunity to meet the needs of non-traditional graduate students while maintaining the high- quality education expected at the university. One of the students also requested that he offer the  7-week course to her colleagues, so there are other potential markets for this course and others  that build on it.

Approach

In ID work, prototyping and testing courses is meant to be part of the process. However, it is  seldom implemented, in my experience, except on a very small scale, in large part due to tight  deadlines for launching a course. For this reason, there has been little innovation in the  structure of online courses. This opportunity for a learning launch was serendipitous and one for  which I had total control as the professor trusted my experience and insights as to what would  work for his students. The work that we did here can help promote differentiated courses that  meet the needs of both faculty and students and create a student-centered experience. I hope  to be able to continue to implement learning launches as the online learning environment grows.

Juana Taylor

Design Thinking for Innovation: June 7, 2020

Reflection: Visualization through Journey Mapping

Challenge

The design thinking tool that has been essential in driving innovation in my firm has been

Visualization though the use of Journey Mapping. Currently, I am supporting a Federal client within my  firm to assist with digitizing immigration benefits and improving the overall adjudication process for  those applying for citizenship. Currently, the adjudication process for citizenship has a multitude of  inefficiencies, from lengthy wait times ranging from 6 months to over a year to a large backlog of cases  for immigration service officers to parse through manually. Throughout the lifecycle of filing for  immigration benefits, there are opportunities to automate and modernize the existing adjudication  process.

Currently, I am spearheading an innovation initiative across my project in which I have tasked

team members to uncover a problem that our Federal client is facing, identify an opportunity that exists  for the team to provide value to the client, and prototype concepts yielding high value to the client.  Therefore, I recommended that all team members use journey mapping, a specific visualization tool, to  start this effort in order to understand the audience, outline the sequence of events, and uncover  unanswered needs. This will ultimately define the job to be done and areas of opportunities to  modernize the immigration process.

Selection

Using a journey map, we began with defining the “what is” for this innovation initiative to

improve the inefficient areas of the adjudication process for citizenship.  The end result was a  visualization that described step-by-step how a user interacts with the adjudication process. The process  is mapped from the user perspective, describing what happens at each stage of the interaction, what  touchpoints are involved, and what obstacles and barriers they may encounter while applying for  benefits. Overall, this journey mapping technique both visualized and identified differentiated value  propositions and opportunities for the adjudication innovation initiative.

Application

We started this exercise by reaching out to various stakeholders who have visibility into the

adjudication process for those applying for citizenship. We discussed the tensions that exist for  challenges within the adjudication process. This entire practice allowed us to not only explore the  current reality but also formulate an accurate assessment of what is happening today and identify the  unarticulated needs. Our interviews yielded a storytelling tool where we can put the applicant and  corresponding experience front and center, and can take the listener along the applicant’s journey to  attaining citizenship.

After gathering information on the adjudication process from these stakeholder interviews, we

summarized and visualized the lifecycle of the process into four categories: 1) arrival and sorting of  paper applications, 2) security and identity checks, 3) adjudicator reviews the application, 4)

Juana Taylor

Design Thinking for Innovation: June 7, 2020

adjudication team conducts final review before sending decision. Within these milestones, we further  defined and mapped the steps that occurs within each, noting systemic dependencies and lengthy steps  due to manual, repetitive, and time-consuming tasks. This action created an overall map from the entire  applicant’s journey to receiving immigration benefits that highlighted the overall challenges and  opportunities.

Insight

After mapping out the applicant’s journey, we parsed through the dependencies and

inefficiencies at each individual step. The major insight from this analysis exposed that applicants face a  lengthy and complex process where the reviewers need to make sense of data inconsistencies in  applications, redundant steps, and process dependencies resulting in downtime. There is a significant  opportunity to relieve taxed adjudicators through automating the highly manual and repetitive tasks.

For the first category, arrival and sorting of paper applications, we noted an opportunity to

tackle a highly manual and logistics-oriented process involving inputting data into system databases. For  the second stage of security and identity checks, there is value in finding an efficient method to  aggregate data while finding inaccurate information through the lens of security, fraud, and name  variation checks. For the third milestone where the adjudicator reviews the application, we noted the  challenge in which the adjudicator repeats multiple application check steps (e.g. security, fraud, and  name variation checks) and aggregates and synthesizes application data. In the last period when the  adjudication team conducts final reviews before sending the decision to the applicants, this task is  wholly redundant based on the previous milestones. By creating this journey map, we were able to gain  an understanding for the stakeholders' life, problems, and unarticulated needs and unravel the overall  adjudication process to identify challenges. The next step would include brainstorming possibilities to  address said challenges.

Approach

Aside from using the journey mapping exercise to outline the current reality, I would also

incorporate some projective techniques, such as open-ended ambiguous stimuli to attempt to uncover  hidden or deeper thoughts out of the stakeholders. Rather than guiding the conversation to understand  the overall steps that occur within the adjudication lifecycle, this additional technique would also have  provided an opportunity to take a step back and identify additional unarticulated needs within the  Federal agency. By employing both techniques, we would have had a thorough picture of the current  reality that can lead to concept development during the “what if” phase.

Reflection: Storytelling

Challenge: My client is one of the largest electronic payment company in the world. The client

was working to build a global merchant database product & while building the datasets the client faced  a lot of difficulty in identifying correct brands in different dispersed geographical locations.  The Problem  the Product team/Technology Development Team was having to create business rules which will  correctly identify the merchant. Like BP is a global oil giant, but does it mean all the Merchant which has  some sort of name variation close to BP globally (BP GAS, Harry BP GAS etc..) are all same brand or they  are diff entity.. The Product team needed to on board with different business cases & different scenarios  so that the Business Logic to build the Data Products can be modified & Fine Tuned.

Selection:    I used the process of storytelling to engage the product office/business

team/engineering leads & created several storytelling concepts for Brands to make the Product team  understand the crux of the issues. Storytelling helps user to visualize the problem makes them more  connected, makes them more aware of the scenarios & make them relate to the scenario.

The technique that I have used here is the FREYTAG’S PYRAMID method.

Application:

FREYTAG’S PYRAMID is a widely used Storytelling application that consists of five elements. Exposition,  rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution/revelation/catastrophe. I have used this  concepts to create an scenario replica of my client product managers to understand country  wise business dynamics/Business Policy Condition/Policy Condition & how all these conditions  should be used/Considered for the product development activity.to fine tune the Data Strategy.

I started with creating Exposition elements of the Business,, How the Business conditions are  diff in Different country, how is the corporate governance different in diff regions & created a  background for everyone for the Business Scenario.

Once the Product Strategy Teams are on boarded with the problem scenarios I raised the pitch  to have a rising action scenario, Like Wal-Mart when they wanted to expand its business to

Indian market how they faced political roadblock due to Political Roadblock how they almost  pulled out from the market. This helped me to evoke the Interest of the stakeholder through  creating internal tension of the Business Impact & what its obligation.

I then take the story to its climax by raising the curtain how the problem is resolved. Here Wal- Mart joined hands with a Leading Indian Conglomerate Bharti Enterprise then Launched a New  Brand & Business Model Bharti-Walmart in India in the Retail Segment & how they started &  continues its operation. This helped also to have the Falling action in the storytelling &  stakeholders are completely engrossed with the story.

What is the Resolution/Revelation of the Story: The Resolution/Revelation of the Story is that  The Business Rule Cannot be Same Everywhere. The Business Rules needs to be  changed/Changed in design as there is a need to understand geo Political Scenario/Business  Condition/Country policy for any global product development stage.

Insight & Approach

The Actual getaway of this story is that The Business Rule to identify all Transaction coming  from India where the Name Contains “Bharti” needs to be changed. A new Business rule has to  be implemented so that Retail category Business Volume That Begins with Bharti (ie Bhar- Walmart) are not actually the business volume Of Bharti Enterprise, but that is of a diff corporate  Entity, Bharti-Walmart Enterprise.

This Insight has changed the entire ballgame of making the Data Strategy of the Product. This  Insight gave Product Team Vision that There has to have Other Geo Political/Business  Regulation View of the product Design that needs to be incorporated & fine-tuned.

The Story Telling Concept here helped me to make the Product Team to look at the problem  into a completely different viewpoint, make them emphasize & understand the Global economic  condition & gave insight & roadmap of how these can be incorporated in the Product Strategy &  Innovation part.

Example – Process change – Storytelling

Challenge & Selection.   There is guy who works as a Talent acquisition professional in a multinational organization, his day to day  activity revolves around interacting with different level of professionals, He get involved into the process  of human resource starting from recruitment till separation. He regularly meets with different  stakeholders like hiring managers, head of departments, chief officers of my company also with the  representative of recruitment agencies.   But, why are we discussing about a day to day life of an employee, any clue?  Well, to answer your question this is the story of mine where I tried to show a glimpse of how my days  looks like any fine day. Meeting with various stakeholders require some data, bullets or facts to present  or to provide them update on day to day activities, SLA, projections, selections, forecasting and many  more data and figures. And here I use the method of Storytelling - Storytelling is an art as well as science  and it helps us presenting any data or facts in an interesting way.     Application:  I will tell you an incident of one fine day. There was a product presentation, which was related to my job  area mainly related to some automation. However, employees in my organization were very skeptical  about change in process and most of them were having fixed mindset.   Recently we been through the example or story of George and Geoff which was based on Fixed and  growth mindset. George was running a very successful product/project in one department since very long,  he was known for his performance and deliverables, however when he was transferred into another  department with pay raise and additional responsibilities, somehow, he was not able to show his charisma  because of his fixed mindset. On the other hand, Geoff came with Growth mindset, he developed  customer empathy, detected multiple hidden growth opportunities, managed risk, placed small bets and  ultimately, he succeeded in the new situation.     Similarly, I presented this story to the people of fixed mindset of my organization and tried helping them  in understanding about the benefit of automation tool at workplace. I was able to put my points in very  simple way with some of other example and hence most of the decision makers were convinced with my  idea and they decided to go for that product.     Insight & Approach:  Some of the key points I kept in mind about storytelling or I would say I divided my story in 5 steps which  are explained below.   1st part was exposition – exposition or (Purpose and origin of data) I was able to gather some key data to  represent on what we were missing by not having that product in our company. For example –  disadvantage of not having proper workflow to performance tracking tool, competitor’s analysis and  scope of improvements.

2nd part was Rising action – (Build excitement about finding, generate of introduce conflict) Rising action  is one of the most crucial part of storytelling, this the moment where we try to show the impact of not  having target product or services, in other word creating strong need or call for an action moment. Hence  as an action point I pitch about a product which might help in such scenario.

3rd Part was Climax – (Key finding to be remembered and acted on) This part always reminds me of a  movie trailer and trust me, movies are one of the finest ways of storytelling which has all mentioned points  here. Back to my product – here I bought some case studies of different tools and tried comparing them  with the example and some real time user stories and showed them importance and unique feature about  that product which was game changing or revolutionary as per that scenario.

4th part was Falling action – (more detail, context, interpretation) well here comes the pricing part of any  product or services, actuals, limitations, terms and conditions etc. Since I was able to cover above three  pointers very well, my audience were very convinced to go for that product and I was able to convince  FIXED mindset managers to for a product which was true value add to the organization.

5th & Final part was Resolution – (Key result, importance, action) here is the call for an action, every  story has it end and this is the moment where key findings/results, importance of my product was  considered as one of necessary tool to have and everyone in the room were convinced to with the idea  or product and the way of presenting it too.

Here comes to end of the story which started from a busy day which used to end-up late at hours, because  of manual data entry and reporting work, which is now changed to automation. Reflection: Visualization Tool by Veronica Giraldo

Challenge

During this hard times that the entire world is experiencing for the first time, the pandemic of COVID-19,  the way people are used to do business has change.  This including the automobile industry, where the  idea of visiting the dealer to buy a vehicle is no longer a choice (the traditional way) due to the  government lockdown.  The business as it is doesn’t work for us right now.  People are choosing to shop  online instead of visiting any facilities.  Right now, the way to start a sale is by these two options: an  online search or a phone call.  Looking for options in how I can help our dealer network I thought about  the online experience.  People now a days are used to buy online and they are looking forward to  complete their own vehicle transaction online.  The world is still moving thanks to the technology and  online retail sales and that is the way we should move in the automobile industry.  I visited their online  pages to see how they are moving and adapting to this new normal of online selling/shopping.  I noticed  that their web pages are not updated and is quite difficult for the customer to shop and navigate  through the site and the phone numbers announced have no answer due to the lockdown.  My  challenge was to think on how I can present all these finding to my team in an effective and easy way.

Selection

In order to help improve the web pages of the dealers and to communicate the finding to my team and  eventually to the dealers, I have chosen the visualization tool.  In the search of looking for a way to  explain the actual situation of the online sites to my team I found that this tool will let me explain myself  without even saying a word.  The pictures and online retail sales simulation will speak for themselves.   This way I can engage my team and they can have a better understanding of the current situation so we  can look for improvements and have a bigger impact.

Application & Insight

I started exploring the different online sites of our dealer network, going one by one and taking  screenshots of the pages, documenting in a Power Point the customers journey trying to shop online or  at least start the selling process in their pages.  I also took pictures of their social media pages.  I even  found out that, sometimes, the all 3 pages had different phone numbers and different messages, which  can confuse and frustrate the customers.  By documenting the process using pictures, I’m also  portraying how hard it is to navigate and shop and in most of the cases a dead end for the customer.

By using the visualization tool, in this case a Power Point presentation, I also created an ideal visual  process of what the online page must look like in order to start the sales process.  Demonstrated to my  team how, from the customer’s point of view, the online page should be configured in order to engage  the customer and satisfy their needs.

After presenting my findings to the team, all I received was good feedback and that it was an excellent  exercise.  I achieved a faster consensus and everyone in my team understood where the dealers online  page stands and the improvements that needed to be made. This was our first step in trying to resolve  the vehicle selling issue and move to the online retail experience.

Approach

For my next step which would be presenting the findings to the dealers I will like to complement the  visualization with the storytelling tool.  Using this tool, I can tell the customers journey, share findings  and engage our clients in trying to resolve the problem, but also, generate emotion and urgency to try to  resolve this issue.

Challenge

I am the executive sponsor of our Firm’s Ayoa Mind Maps, (“cotiza-partes”), a program intended to help our  employees improve as leaders for exponential growth, personally and professionally. cotiza-partes is a firm-wide  initiative that includes several programs that work synergistically to achieve desired outcomes. The  focus of this cotiza-partes program is “Connected to the World.” Hosted by our CEO and Founder, special guests,  Virginia Birra, Jeff Carrasco and Jeff Carrasco, will share their views on Politics & the Election; Social  Unrest; Role of Government and Coronavirus.  Successful leaders exhibit a growth mindset; grounded in  one’s beliefs and values, transformational leaders are open to new ideas and perspectives and are  continuously learning and growing. Our firm’s employees are encouraged to share insights and questions  throughout the program. The program is intentionally provocative.

The focus of this Challenge to enhance the employee experience at our September 2013 Live Event  given constraints due to the pandemic.  This live event is hosted from Las Vegas with a simultaneous  Firm-wide broadcast to 15+ live local venues.   Unlike past Live cotiza-partes events, our guest speakers are not  able to join us live at the host location; the interaction with our CEO host during the session and outside  of it is done in a virtual manner, and all presentations have been pre-recorded. Nor are we able to  convene our entire Firm in Las Vegas as initially planned; only 33% of employees are joining us at one of  the live venues with the balance joining one of three virtual make-up sessions.

The project scope includes the Ayoa Mind Maps project team (a cross functional team including Talent  Development, Marketing, National Events, Employee Engagement, Technology), the Facilitators  (selected local market leadership), our Professional Resources (~350+ attending local live venues), our  CEO and senior management.  The team is working within the approved budget for this program  (expenses and effort – CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION).

Selection

Our cotiza-partes project team has planned the September 2013 Live cotiza-partes Event, largely drawing upon its  experience from its many previous Live cotiza-partes Events, and more recent firm-wide guided Workshops held  in a virtual manner since March 2016 during pandemic times. We have opted to apply design thinking to  the Sept. 2010 Live Event give the unique challenges in order to achieve the desired outcome of a  meaningful, provocative program that builds one’s individual leadership.

Application

For our first cotiza-partes learning launch, we focused on employee engagement and inspiration for the Live  Event. We hypothesized that it was essential to select the right guest speakers, compelling yet within  the editorial direction of our CEO. A great deal of thought was applied to speaker selection with input  enlisted from key sources.  To avoid a series of pre-recorded, unrelated canned speeches, we would  engage each speaker in a meaningful dialogue prior to the event ensuring that they were grounded in  our mission and culture and inspired to customize their remarks. It was important for our CEO to build  rapport with each presenter and encourage them to bring their authentic self to the issues and give  them latitude re the amount of time and content in the areas of Politics & the Election; Social Unrest;  Role of Government and Coronavirus.  We enlisted our CEO to have one-on-one conversations with each  of the guest speakers.  Our program included a CEO-hosted panel that was Live from Las Vegas so the

run-through enabled the speakers to zoom live with our CEO in a walk-through, again building more  rapport and comfort.  Using a digital app platform, we encouraged all employees to continuously send in  insights and questions for the panel throughout the day.  Although we are in early stages of evaluating  the program’s impact and receptivity, we can observe that the guest speakers customized their  recorded presentations, and the rapport with our CEO host was very evident. Insights from the venues  and questions for the panel were plentiful (n=109 out of 354 attendees) indicating engagement. Many  of the insights shared live and questions posed of the panel were thoughtful and meaningful.   As with  all of our cotiza-partes Live event programs, we conduct a post-meeting survey to obtain a depth view on a wide  range of topics including “overall experience”, “value of pre-meeting communication and pre-work  exercises”, “specifics re the live venue”, “what we can do better”, and so forth.   Our cotiza-partes project team  also will add some questions unique to this program and look forward to the feedback for continuous  learning and improvements.

The second learning launch will be to ensure that our make-up program for the balance of our Firm  unable to attend a Live venue (~67%) is conducted 2-3 weeks post the live event.  We strive for the  make-up to be well-attended, engaging and achieve the meeting objectives.   The team plans to enlist a  pair of key leaders to guide the make-ups so as to enhance the programs’ value and importance; a  technology support leader will join each session, too.   Training will be provided to these facilitators to  help strengthen the engagement/interaction for attendees.

We have consistently conducted customer experience feedback surveys from all employee participants  as well as from leadership with the aim to keep learning and enhancing future programs.   The design  thinking tools continue to be very relevant to the current challenge. And the cotiza-partes Project team will  continue to iterate and enhance our programs into the future.

Insight

By applying the learning launch tools, our team identified a few key areas in which to experiment and  learn from.  We are in the early stage of distilling our learnings and collecting inputs from our employees  and local venue facilitators from our September 2013 Live cotiza-partes event.   The initial feedback suggests that  the CEO-hosted panel was well-received and that our employees felt energized to send in insights and  questions.  The additional care and effort to select the guest speakers and work with them as they  prepared their recordings appears to have been worth it.   Given the virtual nature of our program, we  believe it was possible to secure guest speakers renown in their field who are very active in national  news programming leading up to the November election.   Our next cotiza-partes Live Event will be held in March  2014; it is likely that we will have to plan for a Live Event orchestrated in a virtual manner with guest  speakers.   Also, that only a portion of our Firm will opt to attend a live venue, with a majority  participating via a make-up session.

Approach

The team very cognizant that we are now 7+ years in program design and execution for cotiza-partes.  Over the  years, our team has applied design thinking to the planning and execution of cotiza-partes and now with greater  knowledge of the tools can enhance its capabilities.  Putting design thinking to use in pandemic times in  the form of learning launches (a key tool), we believe that we were able to achieve a high quality  experience bar (awaiting customer survey results) as well as gain learnings that will help us design and  execute future programs. Had we neglected design thinking, and simply structured our program

similarly to all others, we would have missed the opportunity to enhance the program and take  advantage of the virtual design that allowed us to secure very distinguished, relevant television  personalities/political correspondents as guest speakers.  Going forward, design thinking principles can  help ensure our cotiza-partes program continues to meet its high expectation bar regardless of the cotiza-partes focus  area and/or whether portions of the program are executed in a virtual manner.

Design Thinking Tool Assignment: Learning Launch

Challenge

As a technology design consultancy, we were engaged by a large retail client with a request to “design  an app” for their store locations that would trigger an alert on a shopper’s phone when that shopper  was near clothing items the retailer wanted to promote. This retailer had good intentions and a clear  understanding of the ultimate business goals they sought to achieve; however, they had not fully  investigated other technology options that might prove less expensive, more effective, less risk to their  IT infrastructure, and faster to implement.  For this reason, we worked with them on further refining the  scope to establish the shared criteria of a great solution, and then used these criteria to design a suite of  five compelling concepts, including their beloved app. The problem, however, was that the concept  everyone loved the most was a ‘digital mannequin’, not the app that the SVP’s had tasked their teams  with delivering.

Selection

While we had the marketing and store-ops teams on board the new mannequin concept, we all  understood that it would take a fast test with compelling metrics and anecdotes to justify the change in  direction. This led us to the use of a tool called a ‘Learning Launch.’

A Learning Launch is a real-world experiment that is conducted quickly and inexpensively to challenge  our assumptions and to inform our final product design.  The purpose of this tool is not to evaluate the  project concept as a finished implementation, but to challenge our assumptions and learn any new  confirming or disconfirming data.  The launch needs to be constrained in time and sample size so  changes can be made quickly and inexpensively. It is also vital to track specific, measurable metrics and  behavioral data.

Application

The “Digital Mannequin” design called for double-stacked, flat panel TVs which could show video of a  life-size model wearing clothing items placed on tables and racks near the displays. We knew from prior  work with the retailer that traditional mannequins created a 10-15% increase in sales for the displayed  items and that 20-25% of passersby would glance at the mannequin.

The assumptions we wanted to question were:

1) The motion of a digital mannequin would increase attention given to the items on display.  2) The increase in attention would be significantly greater to that of a static traditional mannequin.  3) The expected increase in attention would lead to increased sales of the items on display.  4) The increase in sales would be significantly greater to that of a static traditional mannequin.

These assumptions would be proven or disproven with two metrics:

(1) Gaze Captures: A gaze measurement device from Intel would be mounted to a traditional mannequin  as well as to the digital mannequin. The technology notices every time a human looks at the device and  measures how long the visual engagement lasts.

(2) Unit of Sales: The sales numbers for the clothing items on display would be counted and compared to  each other.

The mannequins were installed, and the test was run for 7 days to accommodate the different shopper  patterns that occur throughout a week.  The gaze capture data and the sales receipts were plotted, and  our results were delivered.

Insight

While I am not allowed to reveal the exact results of the Learning Launch, I am able to say that the sales  increases were significantly greater with the digital mannequin than it was with the traditional  mannequin. The number of gaze captures was almost double for the digital mannequin and correlated  with the unit sales numbers through the week.  The client team was empowered to return to their  management armed with very persuasive numbers as well as positive customer intercept interviews  that we conducted as another aspect of the Learning Launch.

Alternative Approach

In retrospect, the tool was exactly what was needed for this project as we had limited time and budget  to unhook the team from their focus on a mobile application. While I would not change the Learning  Launch tool as described above, I would change the scoping process by immediately setting up an SVP- level meeting with the retailer to meet Jeanne Liedtka’s goals of aligning around a common definition of  the problem and the criteria of a great solution.  If the alignment had been done earlier, we could have  avoided a lot of tension and internal frustration in choosing the most appropriate answer to the  challenge.

Thank you for reviewing my assignment.

Example Reflection – Visualization    Challenge & Selection  As mechanical design engineers, we create drawings for the parts that we have designed. These  drawings then go through a release process where the tech reviewers check the drawing for quality in  terms of drawing correctness and if Corp standards have been followed. Most of the drawings are sent  back due to not following of the drawing standards properly, thereby affecting First time right (FTR) and  cycle time increase. I have used this Visualization tool for improving the quality of our drawings. As the  tool describes, this is a process of writing down different error areas with charts, presentation, etc and  discussing the presentation with other stakeholders. Through this process, we identified the different  areas for improvement on our drawings. We created a step by step process to achieve this goal.    Application  We started writing a procedure/check-list by discussing with our team about different areas (notes,  BOM, dimensions, etc.) of a drawing we need to review to avoid errors on our drawings. We first looked  at the major contributor of the errors and created the procedure/check-list on ways to minimize/reduce  them. We then looked at the next higher contributor of errors and so on and similarly created  procedures/check-list to reduce the errors. We also looked at an alternative approach in improving the  quality of drawing by automating certain drawing creation steps. Different sets of procedures/checklist  were created for different types of drawings - sheet metal, machined part, gas line tubing, assemblies,  etc. We also worked with different groups in the organization to identify their BKM’s and incorporate  those in the check-list.  We also looked to see if some of the steps in drawing creation is redundant (which increases the  chances of errors) and discussed ways to automate those details.    Insight & Approach  Once we had the procedure/check-list ready, we called a meeting with complete team and explained  them about the approach to be followed to improve the drawing quality. The team first looked at the  different areas for errors and the highest contributors and insight of the areas for improvement.  Finally, in a bigger forum, we discussed about the effect of incorporating this procedure/check-list and  have moved forward with this approach.  By implementing this procedure/check-list, we are making sure that we are reviewing all aspects of a  drawing and improving FTR thereby saving time where resources would have otherwise had to spend  time correcting a drawing on issues logged by tech reviewer. That time could well be used on other  productive work!  Our next step is to automate this process by incorporating this checklist into the drawing quality tool.

Learning Launch – Juan Velasquez

Challenge

I am currently the senior supervisor for the Resolutions department of a cruise vacation  company. The Resolutions department gives internal support to all customer service  and sales agents, helping with any questions or taking over escalation calls if  necessary. The Resolutions agents (agents that report to me) are both the most  capable and tenure agents on the Company, and that’s been mostly what’s given them  the opportunity to be in that position. As a senior supervisor for the department, my job  is to not only make sure the day-to-day tasks are met, but also make sure that we’re  aligned with the company’s policies and interests, as well as make sure that the  Resolutions agents deliver the best possible service. Unfortunately, the best service is  not always delivered by our Resolutions agents, and sometimes they miss key  empathetic communication factors, such as a good tone of voice, empathy, verbalize  willingness to assist, etc. Because of time and call volume, we’ve not been able to get  all the team together at once, to come together with action plans that will benefit all of  us. At the same time, we’ve gotten comments from the agents and customers we assist,  with areas of opportunity about the way interactions are handled. This time, we’ll focus  on first, identifying the critical areas of opportunity by reviewing the service expectations  of the agents that call us, and then uncover the reasons why we’re not being able to  deliver what needs to be delivered. In some cases, because of the service provided,  customer service and sales agents don’t contact us because of the service received,  and ultimately causes financial and loyalty impact to the company if wrong information is  given to our external customers.

Selection

All Resolutions agents already know what the expectations of the job are and have  already gone through training sessions in the past to be knowledgeable and deliver  reliable information. With this, we’re planning to show how both internal and external  customer satisfaction can be improved by following specific actions and how the overall  experience and perception of the department can be improved with these changes and  make it easier for everyone, making it a more open and collaborative environment. With  the learning launch, we’ll test our idea: customer satisfaction (both internal with agents  and external with customers) will be improved by focusing on improving the quality of  our interaction, by adding value to the brand of our department through personalization,  and ultimately reduce financial and loyalty impacts in the long run.

Application

First, we’ll start by meeting with diverse groups of customer service and sales agents,  and open discussion about the service expectations they had when contacting the  Resolutions department, and of course, any actions/attitudes they don’t like and have  experienced when contacting the Resolutions department. With this, we started to get  some of the feelings we anticipated and some of the behaviors we had anticipated too,  as customer service agents were feeling rejected and in some occasions preferred not  to call because of the service they received.

With this findings, we decided to gather some of our team members and started to get  their input to also detect the reasons why the best service was not being delivered. We  got some comments about not feeling supported enough on the agent’s end as they  were not willing to collaborate. With this, we decided to launch a WOW Service  program, in which we put specific guidelines for our interaction: focus on the branding of  the department, increase our tone of voice from a friendlier interaction, and personalize  our interactions by calling everyone by their name, inquiring about how their day’s  going, and genuinely generate interest and bonding. Applying this, we obtained a  significant improvement in the customer satisfaction scores, as well as in the way our  Resolutions agents and customer service agents felt about the interactions themselves  and the people they had to work with, as genuine interactions created a better work  atmosphere and a sincere want of doing things better. With this, we also got  recommendations from the team members that participated in the WOW program of  some other things that could be included, such as the use of specific phrases to  incentivize the use of a more “positive” vocabulary in all the interactions.

Insight & Approach

By applying the learning launch tool in this specific scenario, we were able to confirm  some of the assumptions we had and even got input from the different agents in both  departments, which confirmed once again the positive outcome this was having: more  positive interactions, greater bonding, proactiveness in finding ways to provide a better  service, etc. I’d say our results were actually even better than predicted, as we only put  it into place and it grew with time and input from the different stakeholders. With the  results obtained in this program, we’ll look into applying this to different departments  that work together or even for frontline agents with external customers.
