Submitted by Merna Ashry

Challenge:

In my role as an HR Business partner, one of the projects recently undertaken was to work directly with  my client groups on a People Strategy exercise with the intent of ensuring that we have the right  organizational structure manned with the right talent and capabilities, to achieve the company goals.  This approach required intensive scrutiny of the current organizational structure and a detailed thought  analysis of the workflow and activities being executed within the functional area.  Some of the other  imperatives we needed to address were:

•  How to prioritize the functional imperatives that face each leaders’ functional organization.    •  Identifying critical roles within the team   •  Highlighting talent that currently exists  •  Highlighting gaps in capabilities which are needed to support the business and determine how  to build talent in these areas to address these gaps  •  Identifying and selecting digitization opportunities within the function

Selection:

For this exercise I chose to use the mind mapping tool.  For me, this is the best way to break down a  complex situation. There was a large amount of data that we needed to review and synthesize, and as a  result we needed to break down the project into distinct areas to enable us to focus on each piece of  the strategy. We needed to outline each of the above-mentioned areas and establish the framework for  the strategy; and then work to generate the ideas to formulate the structure. This method is a creative  and visual way to capture the thoughts of the client and ensure we identify the appropriate information  in order to retrofit the data into the overall strategy. The example provided of the yard sale resonated  with me as you are going from a large and messy problem and categorizing the items into distinct areas  so they can be easily understood – or in the yard sales analogy – purchased.

Application:

From looking at the current reality of the situation, I chose to schedule an initial meeting of 30 minutes  with my clients to socialize the exercise.  This was to merely get them thinking about their organization  and what to expect when we delved into the actual exercise. After that, I scheduled a 2-hour block of  time with the Sr. Leadership team member and asked him to invite others to the meeting that would be  able to provide insight and add value to the process. During this meeting there was a great deal of  brainstorming that occurred and the questions ‘why’ and ‘why not’ were frequently used to force the  team to think out of the box and visualize utopia.  What would the department look like?  We asked  them to visualize a clean slate and inquired, “if you could restructure your department anyway you like,  what would it look like? If anything was possible, what would that look like?” This gave the team the  opportunity to unleash their creativity and intuition and come up with ideas that were perhaps a little  out there, but none the less, potentially brilliant. Lastly, we conducted a work-flow analysis and listed all  the activities executed and placed them into a 4-bucket prioritization matrix asking the questions, “What  are the must have/value added resources necessary?  What are the must have/nonvalue added  resources necessary?  Can these be automated or outsourced?”

There were many more sessions that occurred after that, and all in all the time spent with each client  group totaled approximately 10-12 hours.  This was an effective exercise and ultimately was presented  to the Sr. Leaders who were pleased with the outcome.

Insight:

Having to do this for 4 different client groups was a very burdensome task, but one that I am very glad I  undertook.  It was difficult at first for the leaders to look at a blank slate and fill it with ideas.  Equally  difficult was to constantly be asked the questions ‘why’ and ‘why not’. Eventually the difficulty subsided  and once they got the hang of it, the creatively juices started flowing.

Approach:

I don’t know if I would do this differently net time – the mind mapping worked very well for this  situation.  Visualization may also work well and it’s possible I will combine 2 of the tools the next time I  have a project of this magnitude. I really enjoyed the challenge of implementing this process in design  thinking and it helped to position me as a strategic business partner, but also one that was able to allow  the group to really become embedded in this design challenge.

Example Reflection : Storytelling

Challenge :  I’am the head actuarial department at NSIA Participations – holding of insurances companies based in  west africa. My Job consists in creating insurance products for all local market covered by my  organisation.  In my country – Cote d’Ivoire- only 10% of population had an insurance product and the  other 90% are uninsured and they  consider insurance product as a luxury.. However, to  realize the full  potential of insurance and particularly to increase our market share it was important for us to understand  why the large part of the population are not interested in insurance products or what kind of insurance  product could we propose them. So, the top management  charged me (as project leader) and some of  my colleagues to rethink our products and their distribution channels in line with the specific features  of local markets.  My colleagues was disappointed and thought that we would fail. The reason was all  our competitors failed by  trying to propose insurance product to people who work in informal sector  (the 90% who are not assured). My challenge was to motivate my colleague and lead the project to  success.    Selection  I have used storytelling tool to achieve my objective.  For me, storytelling is the art of producing an  existing story, or rather to master the art of creating. It is one othe the best way to connect us with our  audience and share feelings with him. Storytelling is also one the oldest way to deliver a message – or  to explain things or problems. Our parents used storytelling tool to give us advice even if we don’t call  it exactly that. For all these reasons I was sure that storytelling was the best tool which could help me to  motivate my colleagues and convince them to participate actively to the project.    Application

To lead the project, i decided to plane three meetings each week. At the first meeting, i told we all know  that  Insurance is a peculiar concept. Because it consists in paying a defined sum today to cover a risk  that may or may not materialize in the future, However, i think, insurance has always existed in some  form and today’s version is a product of tools developed by many traditional societies to create  “confidence” among people, private organizations etc. In this case, we must create confidence among  the other 90% of the population and we should also  know exactly what kind of product they need.    I used storytelling to share with them my feelings about the project. I told them a story that build my  confidence in the project. I told them that last year, i was in a village for vacation. I noticed that each  evening, a man named Leroy collected money from  the sellers, traders and farmers of the village.  The amount of the sum collected per person per day  was 1.5 $. Each person could pay his membership  fees daily weekly or monthly. When i discussed with Sullivan Leroy,  he explained me that each six month  he reimburse to each member 90% of his total membership fees and the other 10% is used to face  risks  that could occur in the village. For me, Leroy had create a micro insurance product even he didn’t  call it exactly that. So if Sullivan Leroy can create that kind of product for farmers or sellers, we can do the  same thing with rural population. I also told them the story of Muhammed Yunus who was awarded the  Nobel Peace Prize for founding the Grameen Bank and pioneering the concepts of microcredit and  microfinance. We looked some videos of what Yunus did.  Because a story with no surprise is sometimes  boring, at the end of my story  I presented them Sullivan Leroy whom I had invited.. All of my colleagues  really appreciated Sullivan Leroy participation to the meeting. He shared his experience with us and was  opened to assist us in this project.  At the end of the meeting, we had the feelings that nothing could stop  us.

Insight  Storytelling allowed me to motivate my colleague and to show them that our challenge was not  impossible. At the end of Sullivan Leroy’s speech, they all realised that we could create micro insurance  products for rural population. They also realised that our challenge was not so different from Muhammad  Yunus’s challenge who succeed. We were so motivated that we had  interview  two hundred persons  about micro insurance products. We also challenged  our traditional channel dstribution.  Broadly, techniques of design thinking were very useful during the different interviews. Design thinking  permitted us to have an insight into why 90% of the population were not interest in our insurance  products which were too expensive. We also noticed that 98% of rural population don’t have a bank  account. In addition, the fact that insurance premium shall be paid periodically (monthly- quartely –  annually etc.) was also an obstacle. Because they don’t have periodic income. They are not salary. In  conclusion we realised that we used to create products we wanted to sell them instead of create products  people really need.

Approach

Storytelling is a very useful tool to be connected to your audience. It can be used to movate, to explain  things and so one and forth. But in some cases, others design thinking tools seem more appropriate.  During our interview, i  used visualisation tool to explain to the interviewers the concept of insurance  and showed them an insurance policy. Visualisation permitted to reinforce their understanding of the  insurance. In conclusion, it is very important to master at least two design thinking tools for a better  communication with your audience.

Exercise: Visualization

Name: Maria Quispe.

Challenge & Selection

I work as a human management consultant and one of the main services we provide are  workshops and group coaching. In most of the workshops I do, there is a time when it is  necessary to use Visualization.

In this context personal and group activities are carried out. Most of the time we try to get  people to open up and internalize what is happening in that session so that they find things  that they may not have noticed or that are inspired to carry out the subsequent activities.

Many times, when a question is asked and asked to share opinions and share, not everyone  participates and express their opinions. That does not mean that they do not have something  to contribute, but sometimes they do not know how to express it or they feel insecure. At  other times, the activity requires that they bring about changes and they don’t know where to  start. That's where I pose a more tangible exercise like drawing.

Application

I have a specific anecdote in the use of the visualization tool. I was dictating a workshop about  positive psychology in the organization, the objective was for the group to identify how they  would like the company to be, presenting concrete actions that each could implement from its  role. For this, I told them to close their eyes and imagine that they get up one day and the  company they work in is perfect, everything is as they would like, anything at all.

I gave them a moment and then I told them to open their eyes, draw that company in which  they work that has everything they would like. To draw themselves and their team.

Each person performed the activity and let their imagination go. Then everyone shared their  picture and vision of this perfect company.

Insight & Approach

I notice how all people participated and commented on this vision they had. That was an  excellent starting point. After everyone had shared and were very motivated, I asked them to  draw together a shared vision.

It was interesting to see how a completely unreal idea with the contribution of all became an  idea that could be carried out in a creative way. One of these ideas started as having a spa,  then it became a place to rest from work, then in a place where they could learn, finally I

ended up being a library with a meditation space where employees could go and take a book  or look the garden at some point in their work day. Each one would participate and donate a  book.

The impact of using this tool, fist individually and then as a group, to make a change in  organization was great. They liked the workshop a lot. There were many things that everyone  could do from their role, for example the secretary of the area proposed to put together a  mural with the birthday of everyone in the area.

Whenever I did an exercise that way, it seemed like a useful tool. But learning the whole  process of design thinking and the key that is to visualize first has given me an idea of how to  include several tools in my work, starting with visualizing the change or the new reality and  combining it with other tools like storytelling and mind mapping, to return the ideas of the  participants in more concrete things and be a point of departure in my workshops.

4/27/2020

Visualization

Challenge

The challenge I have been tasked with is to convert a leader led class (installing fiber optic

cable), that is traditionally in a classroom setting, to a more virtual setting due to virus concerns as  well as for future classes that may not be able to be leader led. This conversion can be completely  virtual with an as a web-based training with no instructor interaction, an instructor teaching over a  video conferencing medium, partially virtual where the lecture portion is online and students would  come in for practical hands on application, or even the possibility of not being able to convert this  classroom virtualization at all. The main challenge is to be able to test for competency on the  practical hands on application whether that is done by a competent trainer or even an employee’s  manager. Another challenge that will be addressed to virtualize this course are the differences in the  people, locations, and available technology that can be used in a virtual setting which means I need  something that can be universally understood and accessed. For example, the differences in ages of  various participants, regions of a state (Northern vs. Central vs. Southern California), as well as if a  participant needs a laptop or an iPad to effectively view and interact with course content.

Selection

I selected the visualization tool in order to attack this virtualization challenge. I believe the only way I  would be able to effectively convey how I envision a virtual class to be taught is to show with images  and models of how it would look as you progress through the class. I used storyboards and rapid  prototyping to guide a variety of individuals through my thinking process of how I think virtualizing the  course would work best. I decided to use storyboards because the designers and trainers who are  working with me to virtualize this course need to understand the flow of the training and how it would  look from a student’s perspective. Rapid prototyping also will help me to take the feedback given by  my coworkers and change my idea for virtual interaction as well as hands on activities to better suit  the needs of the participant without spending countless hours trying to perfect my idea. As Mary Murillo explains in the video, “Visualization is anything from the things we write on a chalkboard or a  whiteboard. To the images that we create in a PowerPoint presentation, to photography, video. It's  basically anything that takes us beyond just using words or language alone.” Both the storyboards  and prototypes will be done as a simple PowerPoint presentation with slides from the original  training and with pictures (prototypes) that have been edited crudely with Paint. We will also observe  how this course would look on a laptop versus an iPad which has a smaller screen.

Application

I start the process by accessing the training materials we currently use that are already in a

virtual slide format for lecturing, listing out materials and tools that would also normally be used in  the classroom, and drawing from my own knowledge as a subject matter expert in delivering the  course. Next, I go through and figure out where a physical demonstration or hands on learning would  be occurring normally and start to think of many ways to complete these tasks virtually. Some of the  easiest ideas come to the forefront such as doing videos for demonstrations instead of being  surrounded by a group of people watching me. I can add a slide to the storyboard that would  illustrate when a video might be played. The video of the trainer could really be done in the  classrooms either as a recording or a live demonstration. This can be accomplished with the tools  and materials that would already be available in the classrooms at the training facilities.

The most challenging task was figuring out how to make what is traditionally a hands-on

practice into either a remote check for competency by a trainer, have a manager check for  competency if they have the knowledge, or just a virtual practice that would only be able to check for  the understanding of the processes and not the application. If we were only able to check for  understanding, then the legal verbiage of what they would be learning would also have to be  addressed. For example, we could not say “you will be able to demonstrate” and instead say “you  will gain the knowledge of…” if we can’t do a hands-on practice. Checking for competency remotely  or with a manager would not be too difficult if the correct tools and materials are available at the  technician’s workplace. I also came up with a storyboard that showed the switch from the virtual  lecture into working on a hands-on board that can be easily put together at a workplace.  Alternatively, this competency check could be done in the field with a manager on a real job.  However, this option might be too stressful for a technician who would be doing the practical  application for the first time at a customer’s house.

I decided to tackle the completely virtual option as well since this would be the most difficult

way to do “hands-on”. After coming up with as many ideas as possible, I decided to prototype a  “choose your own adventure” game in which you have pictures of the equipment you would be  working with and options for what you would want to do at any given point. I first used paper  prototypes to help me imagine what I wanted but also quickly realized I could not show my  coworkers my paper prototypes. Instead, I wanted to be able to add my prototypes were into a  PowerPoint. These prototypes were images that I quickly added text and “buttons” that you could  see what you would be doing by clicking through different options to get to the endpoint based on  the knowledge you gained by lecture and demonstration. Using PowerPoint allowed you to “click”  through the game (slides) to see how it would progress and how a user would be interacting with it.

After the completion of my storyboards and prototypes I need the review and feedback of my

coworkers so that I can alter my design if necessary. As Mary Murillo states, “Pictures and images  enable us to not only help people understand what it is we're trying to do, but to help really persuade  them in the worthiness of, of, that particular idea, or, or, the strength of, of that concept.” Thinking  about this statement, I created a 10-question survey with a scale of 1-10 along with a comment  section for each question. Questions include things like “Did the class design offer enough  theoretical and practical experience?”, “Were the storyboards and prototypes laid out in a  comprehensive manner?”, and “Did the hands-on prototype offer enough options to be able to  demonstrate proficiency?”

The scores, along with additional comments, help me to narrow down what will not need to

be changed as well as anything that I can quickly change on the storyboards or prototypes. I will do  this at least one more time with another round of reviews and surveys to show my coworkers the  changes and hopefully get consensus on whether anything else should be changed. Although I have  gotten some great feedback and made some adjustments so far, the project is still in the design  phase. However, I would say that the visualization tool has helped to design this virtual project very  effectively and has made it much easier to describe my concepts to the rest of the team.

Insight

Using visualization for this challenge really affected how I would design this class as well as

any future classes. At first, I just wanted to make a list of changes to the class and I would just  discuss them with my coworkers and leave it for others to put into practical application. However, I  realized that some of the things I wanted to list would not make sense to every individual or may get  misinterpreted from what my idea was. Once I started to put my ideas on storyboards and making  prototypes, I realized that I didn’t need to verbally explain anything. Instead, I left the interpretation  up to those who were reviewing it to get their input from what they see.

This has been my first time using my knowledge of design thinking to a challenge that I have

been presented. Other times I would only try to brainstorm and explain things to others verbally.  However, what I have learned is that it is much easier to convey your ideas to other individuals if you  can show them what you mean rather than trying to explain what you mean. Having storyboards and  prototypes ready for others to interact with, especially when changing from a traditional classroom  setting, has really helped get the appropriate feedback needed to narrow down what the class could  look like in a virtual setting for those who would be taking it. As Mary Murillo concludes, “The advice  I would give to business people who were interested in improving their visualization skills would be  shortly, just to practice.” I am looking forward for another opportunity to use my design thinking skills  and the visualization tool in my current and possibly future roles at work.

Approach

I would not change the visualization tool option that I chose for my challenge if I could do it

again. The benefits of using this tool for my challenge are that those who design the course or  deliver the course need to be able to comprehend the flow of the class since you only have so many  hours dedicated to this class (a 2-day class in this instance). I also needed to make sure that if we  were to have this class, including hands-on, as virtual, I would need to make sure that anybody who  looked at the storyboards or prototype hands-on exercises would be able to comprehend what to do  and how to do it. Additionally, the feedback gained from those who have seen the storyboards and  prototypes help to diversify input needed to get as universal of a course design as needed. We have  many different age groups, locations, and devices that we could view the content on and the  visualization tool with storyboards and rapid prototyping helps to quickly see what will and won’t  work pertaining to many different situations. If I would change one thing it would be to also include  technicians who will be learning this class, in the design. This would ensure proper feedback on user  experience of the practical application to those who would be learning the material for the first time  as well as those who already have experience with it.

Learning Launch: The Helpers Club  by Guadalupe Khan    Challenge  I am a journalist, working for a big publishing house. Because of the changing reading habits  through digitalization my company seeks for different ways of interaction with readers.  Therefore, it offered an innovation-competition. Together with four colleagues from  different fields (marketing, research, technical support) my team and I applied.    Selection  By using different techniques such as mind mapping and brainstorming (we also tried to  visualize readers) we asked ourselves the design-thinking questions: what is? and what if?  Then we came up with an idea: What if people could not only read stories (passive) but  could become active? We wanted to create a club for readers. But every club needs a  purpose for its members. Someone had the idea to set up a club for readers willing to  engage in social projects. Immediately we came up with a great name for our idea – the  “helpers club”. We were all enthusiastic but did not know if readers would like to become  members of this new kind of club. Therefore, we started a learning launch to test it.    Application  At first, we did research and selected data to come up with a hypothesis. According to  analysis from our department for reader research a lot of our readers are willing to spend  money if they read stories about hardship, bad fate, or catastrophes in our magazines. Other  social studies show that in general even more people are willing to help personally than to  give money. We thereby confirmed our hypothesis that our readers might be willing to help  others.  We then decided to start an ethnographic approach, we wanted to look for potential club  members, and ask them about their pains and needs. Therefore we started a call on the  homepage of one of our magazines. We asked readers if they would be willing to talk with us  about social engagement.  We did about 25 interviews with people from various age groups. We asked them what  social engagement means to them. If they have been engaged in social work before. What  they had expected. How their experience was, what was good and what was not so good.  And if they had stopped to be a social volunteer, why.   Searching for candidates, talking to them, and then clustering the answers took our team  about a week. Then we made up three personas.    Insight  By listening to our readers and potential members of the “helpers club”, we realized their  pains – and what gains we might offer. First of all a huge majority said, that they would really  like to help others. One man said:” This is better than just giving money for a social project.”  Another woman hoped that she might get something back like thankfulness. And a third  person said that it would be great if the magazine could identify social organizations and  write stories about them.   But we also realized that most of the people did not want to spend too much time (2-3 hours  per week at last), that the offerings had to be near their neighborhood and many of them  did not want a commitment on a regular basis. Most of the people only want to help when  they can afford to spent time, e.g. on weekends.

We clustered the outcome of the interviews by drawing 3 personas – potential members of  our new club: a young woman (around 25 years old), a mid-aged man (50 to 55 years old,  kids have moved out) and an elderly woman (65+ years old, retired, yet still very fit and  interested). We learned: Men and women in their thirties and forties cannot afford spending  much extra time, they are busy with family and job.    Approach  By doing ethnographic research we got a very good idea for the interests and needs of our  readers and potential club-members. While clustering and curating the outcomes, our team  appreciated the different approach of every team member.   And we also realized that we are just at the beginning of having an idea. We want to start a  second learning launch and identify organizations which might look for social volunteers. We  want to speak to experts (leaders of NGO´s) and then to professional helpers to learn about  their needs. We must look for competitors: Is there a market for social engagement? What  do social organizations offer already? What else could the “helpers club” offer to make it  attractive for readers?   The tools of design-thinking did not only help us to develop our idea so far – we also learned  a lot about ourselves by discussing what we think about helping others and social  entrepreneurship.

ASSIGNMENT-STORY TELLING (TO AVOID STUDENT DESERTION)

CHALLENGE  I work in a public university, where many of the teachers do not have formal training, this fact has  been tried to remedy with a continuous training program of short courses, which covers various  academic subjects, but it does not solve the problem entirety. One of the areas in which it impacts, in  addition to some problems in the classroom, is that corresponding to the detection and follow-up of  the cases of students who have some motivation problem, which is one of the main desertion factors.  My challenge is to support to the administrative department in the detection and monitoring of the  bachelor students who present a problem of this nature in my courses of electronics. The risk of not  attending to these cases is that, if the terminal efficiency rate decreases, not only the students who  drop out are affected, but the educational program can be closed, due to the financial problems of  our institution. This program started in 2009 but does not yet run a tutorships formal program.

SELECTION

For these situations, several tools showed in this course could be used, but I have no experience with  them. The tool I have used is like story telling, when I seek to motivate to the young students with  some academic problem. My familiar origin is very similar to most of them, and throughout my life I  have accumulated a series of very hard experiences, which fortunately I have solved. Empathy is  fundamental, and I think is easier, to understand and feel, when we have experienced similar  situations. My hypothesis is that story telling is very useful for motivating students facing academic  problems.

I have chosen story telling, because it is a design thinking tool that put the human being and their  experience front and center. Take the listener along their journey (video of course, week 2). In  addition, in accordance to some documents reviewed for this assignment, it also can be used in  different education ambits. “Storytelling, no matter in what form and created in whatever media is a  powerful  tool  to  transmit  knowledge,  culture,  perspectives  and  points  of  view”

(http://www.jackson.com/appcategory.html). Personal stories are one recognized category among educational tools,  which involve significant events in life and can be emotionally charged and personally meaningful to  both the author and the viewer (DOI: 10.1080/00405840802153916). Story Telling is one of the tools  that has impressed me most, because I have seen its impact as part of the pitch of some entrepreneurs  (https://youtu.be/1pM3sb7AMPs), as well as when it is used to motivate an audience  (https://glenn.org/postsindex.jsp), or to increment the product  value (https://youtu.be/Kb-hqNGr5lJ, video shared in the course forum). In the last video, I also  learned that each of us has a long list of stories to make the connection with people with whom it is  necessary to share information.

APPLICATION

With the support of the administrative staff, we identify those students, who face problems and an  individual talk with me is proposed. One of the students of the last semester who failed a course, also  suffered from negative attitudes of his teacher, making him feel that he did not have the ability to  approve and that no one would support him. His family gives him a limited economically support, but  its condition is that the student approves all his courses. The student felt into a state of susceptibility  and lack of self-confidence. He was determined to return to his village.

I told him a similar story that I had lived, in which I did abandon one course, because I suffered  harassment of my teacher. I showed him, that it was not the best decision, and that nobody, apart  from my classmates, knew about this situation, and that therefore I did not have orientation. I made  him see that this situation did not stop me but delayed one of my goals. I asked him to analyze my  case and think about some alternative solutions. He observed that there are always exits. I pointed  out to him that he could face his situation, that he had capacity and intelligence, and that regardless  of our humble origins we have as much value as other people, and that, in order to change our reality,  we need preparation. He began to study very hard and managed to get the best grade in his next  exam, his last chance to pass his course.

As it can be seen, the information provided was transformed into knowledge by the student and  allowed him to acquire security to face his own challenge, regaining self-confidence. Story telling was  successfully used.

INSIGHT

The results obtained in the last semester with the use of story telling have been satisfactory, three  students assigned to me continue their studies. Stories were different in each case. These results  increase the confidence in story telling for this kind of cases. In general, we take care about the results  of our courses, but we do not always attend, in depth, the problems that our students face. I learned  that empathy must be a daily exercise, because around us there are young people that constantly  need to be heard and oriented. Telling stories in which the overcoming and constant struggle are  fundamental, makes them see that it is worth falling, but that we must work hard to arise and get  ahead. We must support others, we can together make our work or study place flourish, being more  human.

In the course and in this assignment, I learned more aspects about story telling, and I understood its  potential in several areas. I had the opportunity to learn more design thinking tools that can support  my work, creating more appropriate environments and planning actions in a more structured way.

APPROACH

After the course, I know that there are several details of this tool, and that to improve its application  in my challenges, I must clearly identify them. I understand that is important to solve the problem but  also to create a cause. I must be careful with the story sequence, create suspense, ask and answer  questions, create moments of reflection and generate recommendations. For the next time I will try  to consider all these elements and other ones mentioned in the videos or suggested by other  trustworthy sources.

There are other design tools that could be employed to reduce the desertion and other problems in  my job place. Co-creation design tool could be used. The participation of stakeholders is very  important. Ethnography also would be great, as well as brain storming, applying them as they were  explained in the course. We need to front the competition with other institutions with similar  educative programs, using adequate design tools, for each specific situation. We also need to create  our wow zone.

Mind Mapping

By: Charlotte Jones

Challenge and Selection

At the National School of Arts and Crafts Casablanca, I am a member of the EAP Student Committee. The Student Advisory Board assists the Business School with improving the student  experience by providing a student perspective on issues facing academics, communication, and  career development opportunities. To better understand the student population’s wants and needs  we conducted a large in-depth interview at the Business School. All 15 board members,  including myself, each interviewed 10 business students with a range of grade levels and  degrees. We covered the main focuses of the admission process, academics, career preparation,  and overall communication.

Once we completed the interviews we were left with a massive amount of information.

Our challenge became decoding patterns in the data to discover where to focus our efforts. The  challenge promoted our selection of the Mind Mapping Tool. Mind Mapping is a term used for  the process of discovering patterns within the information you collected during the beginning of  exploration or the ‘What is?’ phase. As noted in the Mind Mapping Video, with Wendy Lopez,  mind mapping is a visual process of capturing the perspectives of customers, or students in this  scenario. The tool guides the team through a process of laying out all of your information,  observing trends, and noting clusters. The Mind Mapping process is a way for the student board  to narrow down issues for consideration.

Application

To start the mind mapping process, each student board member collected their data from

the interviews. On giant sticky notes, we all creatively wrote down the things that are working  and the things that are not working, based on conversations with students. What the likes and  dislikes were divided into two sides of the paper. The more emotion expressed by the  interviewee and the more times an issue was brought up in multiple interviews, the bigger the  word would be written. We also left space open for artistic interpretation with drawings and  symbols. When everyone was done, we stuck all our giant notes on the wall. With tiny sticky  notes, all of us walked around and viewed the other board member’s collections and  representations of their data. Topics, issues, and ideas began to emerge more distinctly. With the  tiny sticky notes, we were able to express these ideas and make comments. We took about 45  minutes to complete this process. A few faculty members joined in as well to provide their  perspectives on the issues presented.

After our “yard sale” or gallery walk, we all came together to discuss the unique themes

and strong issues that stuck out. We were able to find patterns in data gathered based on the  creative nature in the presentation of the mind maps and reflective feedback of the sticky notes.  We began arranging sticky notes into groups that seemed similar. We ended up creating 5 groups

of issues: academic, professional development, extracurricular, recruitment, and internship. Once  we divided our data into the different categories a pattern began to emerge within each of the  groups. Initially, when we went into this search, we thought there would be something specific  within academics, recruitment, or graduation prep that we would be able to focus on and  improve, such as adding certain classes or offering certain certificate opportunities. Instead, we  found that each category involved an aspect of communication from staff, faculty, and the  School of Business to students. Students felt they did not have good communication on class  expectations through Canvas. Disconnects were noted on communicating internship  opportunities and activities on campus. Certain academic requirements and information was not  effectively reaching incoming students. Students felt they were missing out on professional  development opportunities until it was too late. With this in mind, we are now in the process of  entering the ‘What if?’ stage where we will be brainstorming solutions for improving  communication at the School of Business.

Insight and Approach

The outcome of the mind mapping process shocked me. Many of the board members,

including myself, had no idea that the main issue we would be focusing on would be  communication. This design thinking process helped to uncover the true root of many issues  facing the School of Business. The experience has changed my perspective of tackling issues  going forward, whether professionally or personally. Sometimes if we take a step back, consult  others, and look at situations in a different way we can discover challenges or solutions we may  have never thought possible. I am pleasantly surprised of how well the process went for our  group. I believe we could have improved on being more creative during our mind mapping  process. As business students, we tend to think too analytically about issues. It is good to let go  and be creative. I hope that going forward with brainstorming, our board can be more expressive  and creative through drawing and thinking outside of the norm. Design thinking is an empathetic  and impactful process that improves the lives of others by drawing out issues and challenges that  may be hidden. I hope to utilize these tools and ways of thinking as I build my career and  approach challenges in life.

My challenge relates to advancing education in Mexico. In short, there is a big gap currently in the  Mexican education market when it comes to development of soft skills for people aged 17-22.  Research has shown that companies are looking for a great level of soft skills in graduates when  hiring them out of university. Thinking more deeply about the problem, and from speaking with  business owners, students and academics, the “what is” of the problem is clearly that universities  are not developing these soft skills. Instead, most universities still focus on academic skills  development. The kind of soft skills lacking are problem solving, innovation, creativity, negotiation  and initiative, amongst others. Thus, a gap exists to solve this soft-skills shortage in Mexico. How this  gap will be filled requires a mode of thinking that is outside of the current paradigm. Personally, I  think this is necessary to break from the traditional mode of thinking that proliferates the  educational system here and in many other countries.

My choice of tool to look at this problem is Storytelling. For me, it is a valuable tool because it will  aid in helping create a vision that differs from the current reality. The lecture in week 2 mentioned  how every great brand has a story that links it to an emotion. Moreover, another Coursera course  from the University of Colombia, relating to the future of education, states that traditional ways of  thinking about the future of education very limited. In other words, people largely have one-track  minds and are decided that the future of all education is technology. The result is that people  become narrow minded and are unlikely to shift their thinking and develop innovative ideas. This  lack of vision has inspired my choice of Storytelling. To solve my problem related to Mexican  education, it is necessary to use Storytelling’s ability to create a cause. Inspiring people and leading  people towards the possibility of breaking from the traditional mould is something that can help  solve the problem that exists. Breaking the status quo will be difficult, because I feel that the kind of  audience that the story will be told to (e.g. academics, teachers, business owners, and university  deans) are going to be rather reticent to hear something different. Therefore, how it will be applied  will be very important.

The application of this tool to the problem will rely on really highlighting what the core of this  problem is. The reality is that universities are not providing what they either claim they are. On the  flip side, some simply do not even claim to do work on soft skills. This message is central to the story,  however, simply going and telling someone a story of how they are wrong is likely to be met with  hostility. I believe it is therefore necessary to tell the story in a way that gets buy-in from these  stakeholders. In other words, the story needs to make these people part of the solution and to  empower them as design thinkers themselves. Building on the suggestion of the lecture, this is a  process of getting them into a mind-set that makes the cause worth fighting for. To give an example,  in Mexico there is quite a rigid social hierarchy in which in business it can be risky to question ones  superiors. The academic system is not very flexible and titles can bring with them great power, even  if the titleholder does not possess the knowledge, ideas or expertise to tackle everyday problems.  The consequence of this for applying design thinking, a concept that many academics would  consider radical, is that the story told would need to be told in such a way that it empowers these  people, rather than alienates them.

Until now, I have not been able to enter and tell the story at the highest level, i.e. to the businesses  and the academics.  However, on a different level I have already started building a vision amongst  peers to create the need for change. My work brings me into contact will all range of academics and  professionals in education. Two close contacts of mine are social entrepreneurs and already have

businesses established that work on generating change in Mexico’s education system. Just last week,  I met with both to tell them my story about ‘what is’ the current situation in Mexico. At the same  time, I got the opportunity to take on board their feedback and use this to adjust any of my potential  misconceptions. Moreover, I got them to connect with the vision of change I had, and used this to  generate more ideas about potential ways in which to focus the solution more on the people it is  trying to help. The storytelling tool was important here, because it resonated with feelings that they  had, and I realised how it aligns with their own stories. Thus, I think one of the real benefits of  applying this tool was the ability to find consensus and a common cause. However, as mentioned in  the course, a common cause will not be enough to generate the change. The real proof of the story  telling tool’s power will be when we use it to go to a higher level.

The application of the tool has taught me valuable lessons about bringing people together. It has  shown me there is a good way in which to shape a vision and connect to a process that can generate  change. I have no doubt that this will help in inspiring people to focus on the needs of the  community and to help make the new product something that really will add value to Mexican  students and academics.

If I could do something different, I guess it would be to think more about the story before asking /  telling others. While input from others is important, I believe there could be value in really  developing my own story first. By doing this, I feel more capable of leading from the front. More  than anything, I think next time I would like to actually try using some of the other tools. Mind  mapping would be a great supplemental tool that would allow me to work with others to device a  people-centred solution. Later on, I can also see a good opportunity to have a learning launch. The  ideas I have are early ideas and need development, thus trying out things and seeing what could be  learnt will be useful.

To conclude, this was a valuable learning experience. The tool is extremely powerful, and this is  obvious in the number of people using this today. Only the other day I saw the head of Starbucks  selling the power of storytelling.

By Hafiz Mat      Challenge & Selection    Faced with the problem of COVID-19, I have been thinking about how to provide  universities with quality virtual education options. In Colombia we have been in  quarantine for almost 3 months and we have realized that current platforms are  being used as a mediocre means of teaching, where teachers send PDFs, a good  teaching methodology is not implemented and there is no follow-up on student  requirements. To realize that this was a real problem and not rumors, we started  a process of identifying problems and solutions using techniques such as:    The tools required to identify the problem and detail it are:

● Map of actors: A review of each of the actors that are part of this  ecosystem was carried out to determine who influences our sales,  selection, usability and other processes.

● Covert observation: We requested permits from partner universities and  entered the current virtual classes to take notes of what was happening.

● Focus group: We called for groups of homologous characters that we  identified on the actor map.

The tools required to identify solutions and delve deeper are:

● 5 whys: we use this tool to be able to delve into the solutions identified.

● Selection by qualification: in the work team we began to qualify each of  the ideas, forming combos of them to strengthen the ideas and know  which one we would go for

● Competition analysis: According to the proposed ideas, we looked for  competitors who had similarities to determine points that are not being  addressed and add them to the ideas to be tested

● Interviews: We conducted interviews with actors who would use our idea  with a prototype version to identify more points that we should add or  remove.

Application & Insights:    As mentioned above, the following techniques were used:

1. Actor map: The actor map graphically reflects the connections between

the different users that make up a service. This helps to have a clear  image of the users involved in it, in order to identify the people to  investigate in the first phase of the process, or to structure the definition

of the functionalities of the final solution. An actor map is similar to the  following:

In our offices we sit down some of the team and professionals from allied  universities that would help us in the inquiry process. We discovered the  list of actors that would positively and negatively affect this project:

● User: teachers and students.

● Buyer: Academic direction of the universities. (Rector, vice-rector,  academic directors and researchers)

2. Covert observation: This activity consists of observing a user interacting

with a product, service or prototype, without them knowing that they are  being evaluated. It can be used in the initial phase of Empathy, to observe  the sincere reactions of the users.    We enter classes of our allies with the user of several students in different  classes and we participate as students in order to identify the  shortcomings of the teachers when giving the classes. We took note of  this and realized that teachers have not adapted to virtual education, they  only send readings and exams, without monitoring or controlling what  happens to students.

3. Focus group: Discussion groups or "Focus Groups" allow to deepen and

understand individual and collective perceptions, values ​and beliefs. It  brings us closer to the ways in which social subjects construct their

experiences and give meaning to their practices, based on their  sociocultural context and the relationship with the environment.    We use our offices to gather one person from each type of actor on our  map, we ask 5 questions with each of the 5 groups and we take note.    We realized the importance and relevance of doing a more advanced and  in-depth monitoring of the students than we had thought, this gave us the  basis to continue with our solution.

4. 5 whys: The technique of the 5 "why?" It is used when the interviewed

people respond with monosyllables or with short answers. To do this you  should ask again "Why?" for 5 consecutive times each time the person  interviewed gives us an answer. In this way, we will get to deep reasons  for the behavior or thought of that person.    With this technique we discover the way to determine how to do more  monitoring and establish better functionalities to our virtual education tool  to be more intuitive for users.

5. Selection by qualification: in this technique we proposed three ideas that

could work, Each of the group gave a value from 1 to 5, 5 being the  highest score, and thus determine the appropriate idea to solve the  problematic order of testing the prototypes.

6. Interviews: We conducted interviews with our prototype of around 20

people to see if it was a better or worse solution than that of the  competitors.

Approach:    All this gave us the opportunity to rethink our initial idea, modify the monitoring  and control strategies of the student, the user interface and move from  E-Learning to B-Learning. Therefore, we will describe the changes and  adaptations to be made to continue testing our innovation.

1. Monitoring and control strategies: in the digital tool we will implement

Watson's APIs for virtual education and thus be able to obtain detailed  advances in the training process of the students.

2. User interface: testing our ideas in interviews and with experts we realized

that we had processes that were repeated and others that were not  necessary.

3. From E-Learning to B-Learning: B-Learning presents an updated teaching

methodology that involves the presence and virtuality integrated to show  the student improvements in their training process.

Insight    Using learning launch tool really helped our design team as the assumptions that were made  during the requirements gathering phase were validated. There were couple of changes that  were suggested by the ICT team from the Client side and those were documented in their  feedback. The challenge that team faced was that, if the changes needed to be incorporated  in the newly developed alerting system, then the scope of the project would expand and also  the time line would get extended. So, the design team decided to hold a project extension  meeting with the client and presented a Phase 2 project proposal. This proposal is still under  approval status.     Approach    Learning Launch proved to be a very effective tool in order to know whether the assumptions  of our design team were accurate. At times, the design team had missed few requirements  that were identified and incorporated as the team followed agile iterative process. Combining  the usage of learning launch tool and agile methodology made our team successful in keeping  up with the project timelines that eventually made our client happy.

REFLECTION

Challenge

The bank’s financial reporting has been done by the MIS department for years. Any financial report

to any of the bank’s business lines/departments can only be requested from the MIS. A set of

monthly reports have been agreed upon, and they have been delivered to the business lines

unchanged for the past two decades. Each time any of the departments has a request besides

the monthly package, he contacts one of the business partners in the MIS department, he

evaluate the request, provide target date, implement the report and share it as an excel

workbook.

Waves of changes have happened, there is no MIS department anymore, the whole group has

been revamped to analytics and data management. Where the basic function is no longer

reporting, yet analytics and performance evaluation. The monthly reporting packages were kept

unchanged though.

This task has consumed many resources which we need to utilize for their main analysis jobs. And

we need to keep the monthly reports on going since this is the business lines only source of data.

Selection

I mixed the tools learning launch tool and ethnography in my solution for the challenge.

Ethnography is a study of the customer’s nature, needs and requirements done through a serious

of interviews and journey mappings. Learning launch tool on the other hand, is a tool where you

experiment suggested solutions to your challenge and test them in action before investing time,

effort and money in planning based on just assumptions. Based on the results of your experiment,

you either move forward with the solution, tweak it, or try another one.

Ethnography and learning launch have best suited my challenge, because we had too many

people involved, the reports requirements have been left unchanged for so long, the business

needs must have been changed ever since and we assumed the reports don’t meet these

requirements anymore. We needed to study our customers’ requirements and new needs. We also

needed to quickly engage with them to come up with a solution as fast as possible. We were not

sure if the suggested reporting automation through web tools would be acceptable to them. And

that is why learning launch is so special. You get to test your hypothesis and make sure they are

your quick fix before getting deeper into execution.

Video Reference: http://moore.com/explore/tagterms.php

Application

We started interviewing our customers in parallel to implementing a prototype of one of the old

reports. We replaced the excel workbooks with a report accessible through the web. Interviews

were scheduled with representatives from each business lines. They included intensive discussion of

what they need to report, their main performance KPIs, what they do with the data we provide

them and how satisfied they are with the current reporting packages and the report requesting

processes.

Once the prototype was ready, we started introducing the users to the new web tool, its main

features and illustrated the available data they could use to make their own basic reports. We also

collected opinions through feedback sheets and questionnaires.

Insights

Both the interviews and the learning launch turned out to be fruitful. The customers have rarely

used the sent reports by the MIS team, the data was insufficient and they don’t meet their

requirements anymore. They also didn’t like how dependable they were on other people for

producing their own reports. They said the process was time consuming and inflexible. The new

reporting tool has been faced with great welcome and acceptance. The new visualization tools

and dashboarding has eliminated the limitations in excel. And this opened the opportunity for a

new level of reporting.

Approach

If I get the chance to do it all again, I’ll follow the same approach and the tools used. They have

proven to be effective in my challenge. We were able to satisfy all the parties involved and we

managed to get out with a detailed plan of replacing the old process with a new automated one

in no time. It also made the customers feel engaged and involved.

Reflection – Mind Mapping Tool  By Tatsuya Kobayashi

Challenge

I work as a development manager in a multinational company and my challenge is to find  possibilities of reducing costs by implementing improvements in the development  processes chain. By doing that it is necessary to check with all the numerous developers  we have in our development teams the difficulties and possible chances we have to  improve the development process. Furthermore, the involvement of managers and  internal customers are as well necessary in order to guarantee that the changes in the  development process chain will not negatively affect the quality of our results. I have  researched and collected a large quantity of information and ideas about where to act  and what to improve in the development chain by interviewing stakeholders, customers,  developers and the management. As well the process operation has been reviewed and  analyzed in order to capture important data to consider in the data collection.

Selection

Mind Mapping is the term used for the process of looking for patterns in a large quantity  of data collected during the exploration of What is. I have chosen to work with mind  mapping tool as I have already collected a huge amount of data from different sources  and I needed to organize them in order to find patterns and insights about the current  situation around the problem of costs in the development process. Nevertheless, it was  also important to align among all the involved parties in advanced around the ideas  raised during the exploration step and reach a common understanding of design criteria  to be developed and discussed in brainstorming sessions.

Application

Due to the pandemic situation, it was not possible to reunite all the team and  stakeholders physically together in a room in order to present the data collected and  summarized for the project. However, an online group session was organized via  Microsoft Teams and with support of an online collaborative tool where was possible to  create material to present the results from the research too all invitees. The collaborative  tool used for the group sessions was MIRO. All materials for the presentation were  prepared in different formats: as infographics, graphics, personas and process/data flow.

The online session was organized and developed in the following way:

1. Initially all the invitees were online in the same session in order to have a big

overview about the material presented. This was a sort of an explanation tour  about the content.

2. Afterwards, the invitees were split in three groups of 5 people for analyzing

and discussing the material and collecting thoughts to be presented later on  by a team member who is going to be the representative person of the group.  As MIRO is a collaborative tool which permits work with dashboards and  create cards and virtual stickers (as post its), each group creates its own  virtual cards in order to bring them to be presented.

3. After the 30 minutes session in groups, all invitees accessed the big session

with all invitees together. Each team member representative of each group  brought and presented their thoughts about reality based on the material they  have analyzed. After all the 3 groups have presented all your insights, all the  cards were disposed in a big online dashboard.

4. As a next step, I worked as a moderator in order to help everybody to cluster

the thoughts reunited and create meaningful insights about the thoughts  clustering.

5. After all insights have been clustered, the connections between clusters in

order to show inputs and outputs have been identified by the team. This final  step has been the longest one considering all the discussions around the  connections among the clustering.

6. Finally, all insights have been translated into criteria with the posed question:

“Based on what we have learned, if anything were possible our design  would…” and then each insight in the dashboard was captured and transcript  into a list of design criteria.

As the design criteria list has been created, it was distributed to all invitees and a  common agreement and understanding has been delivered to go on for the next step of  the design. Based on all the criteria and insights collected, brainstorming sessions were  organized to discuss ideas for solving the target problem.

Insight

I have learnt that organizing such kind of exercise (mind mapping tool), in a pandemic  situation where is not possible to physically reunite teams, and everything needs to be  performed online, Is quite a challenge. The biggest challenge was to decide which online  tool would be the most appropriate one where it would be possible to organize material,  presentation, discussion and collaboration all in one. Besides, mind mapping is a very  difficult tool to conduct at first, but is the most helpful and enlightening for bring different  points of view to the topics and bring everybody who needs to be involved in the project  to the same baseline. However, it was quite difficult too to keep all the invitees a bit far  away from bringing direct solutions to the problems besides getting the insights and  thoughts about the reality that it was in discussion.

Approach

I believe that, for future the same approach of Mind Mapping tool needs to be  implemented. I don’t see any alternative approach which could support in the same way  of Mind Mapping tool. The main and most important aspect of this tool is to share and  build insights together in team in order to have a common understanding of the reality of  the problem for pursuing solutions based on what all the stakeholders understand.  Perhaps, the timeframe of the online session and the lack of experience with the tools  were a bit confusing and challenging. However, the engagement of all participants during  the session and the discussions were highly appreciated and energizing.

Reflection – Mind Mapping – Cesar Rivera

Challenge

I´m an innovation and design thinking consultant working with a Government State in México, one  of my objectives was to implement an Innovation Award to recognize all those brilliant ideas from  citizens about how to innovate government processes and services. A great challenge because you  need to make people think and understand what are those social problems, government programs  o services that could be redesign, innovated or changed but with a deep focus on proposing  innovative solutions and not only finger pointing what is wrong, a cultural change required.  In  Mexico when you talk about main social problems people tend to talk about their perception with  no facts or clarity about what the real problem is.

Selection

When you are designing a workshop and need to select the right tools  to develop new ideas to  solve government challenges, you will require to think about the different types or citizens that  will be participating on these events, you have students, non-government association,  professionals on different fields and universities, just to name some of them. You need to find an  easy tool that anyone can understand quickly and easy to use with pencil, paper sheets.

For the Innovation Award that I mentioned, I selected a tool that can help the participants to  explore real problems beyond the symptoms they see, most of the time what the citizens see as a  problem is the result of another problem not seen. There´s a need for a deep dive into what  exactly you are identifying as problem to propose the right solution.

The Design Thinking tool I selected to identify what are the potential sub problems is the mind  mapping tool, because it makes people think broader about what other problems can be seen  related to that.  Mind Mapping helps people and organization to be clear about a topic, any  related topics, called subtopic and ideas around subtopics as we see in the below picture

Application

For a workshop I present the main areas current government is focusing on, something called  “State Development Plan” that define the government priorities to align all the ideas around  government objectives and also to have budget assigned if a great idea comes from those  workshops that could be implemented

I organize the citizens by group of minimum three, maximum five, looking for diversity on age,  education, gender, etc., to have different perceptions and great discussions among the groups.  People take a flipchart sheet and stick it in the wall, start discussing what could be a problem that  needs faster and innovative solutions using the State Development Plan, write the problem  selected at the center of the flipchart sheet, the next step requires to identify from that selected  problem any other types of problems that could fall under this description, ask them to think and  write in post-it note all those problems related to the main one, one post-it note per idea, no  limits on number of ideas, usually the activity takes 20 minutes.

After that, you ask someone from each team to start reading all the post-it notes and start  grouping them if are related, looking for affinity groups among all or any connections, in this step  you have created different arms and secondary arms to the main problem, once you complete to  group them you can give a name of to each group with the most representative description,  connect with lines the main problem and the sub-problems. When this activity is completed you  have now defined multiple sub-problems, in most of the cases those are the ones that citizens see  as the ones to solve, problems specific to address.

Insight

Mind Mapping is a great starter when you need that everybody has the same understanding about  a concept; We at the government office expect that citizens can have a better understanding of  social problems and all the variation of those problems. We, as humans, tend to generalize our  perception about many things.  Mind Mapping helps us to have clear picture of what´s behind or  above the topic to analyze, and also helped citizens to think that social problems can´t be named  generically, they need to be clearly identified and the sum of all those problems solved will result  in a better perception of their reality. Design Thinking is a great problem-solving tool where  anyone can innovate

Approach

As an Innovation and Design Thinking Consultant I always make use of this type of tools that allows  teams to have a discussion, analysis, and agreements. I would applied the same tool but now with  engineering groups, mind mapping areas to do a research or trying to find different ways to solve a  problem, also with Human Resources teams I would use it identify employee needs listening to  their problems.

Gabriel Lara

Reflection – Storytelling

Design thinking for innovation Course

Challenge and Selection:

The tool chosen is storytelling. This tool was adopted by me when I had to present a HR Management  project to top management. The challenge was to present the creation of a tool that was useful and  effective for the purpose.

This tool was chosen because it allowed me to quickly and effectively represent the main phases  (problem; resolution; conclusions) of a complex project in an attractive and immediate way. In fact, with  storytelling it was possible to present the project in a figurative way and therefore to imprint it more easily  in the memory of the stakeholders. In this way, attention was more easily captured by simultaneously  stimulating their interaction, especially towards an audience diversified.

Images, music and effects are the best way to impress a memory. The challenge lies in adapting  everything harmoniously in order to produce a result that reflects reality in a coherent way.

Application:

The storytelling it was represented by a video animation with a fun scenographic content (cartoon style)  but consistent with real situation (both for the sequences and for the situations represented in it), using a  simple and precise script that it was able to describe the project in all its main phases. The storytelling in  video animation made it possible to represent the most articulated path of the project (made up of the  main project phases addressed) in a simple and attractive way and to lead the listener towards the final  product (the tool created for the purpose) which was presented in live and interactive mode after the  storytelling.

The storytelling in video animation was introduced by a standard presentation that technically exposed  the problem addressed through specific numbers and graphs (statistics data). The introductory

presentation however used a style adapted to the subsequent video animation, without ever creating a  clear and brutal detachment. The purpose of the initial introduction was to lead the auditors to a conscious  listening to the subsequent storytelling.

An emotional path was deliberately created, starting from an emotional state of alert (the numbers, the

problem that emerged from the statistics) without ever frightening and without ever losing the listener's  trust (use of fonts, scripts, gentle colors, references and timely statistics), to an emotional state of  expectation and curiosity through the vision of the storytelling in video animation without ever boring the  auditors until to the final solution of the product, leading towards an emotional state of relief.

The video animation was accompanied by room effects, managed in a pertinent way and in harmony with  the projected animation, in order to emphasize the messages conveyed in it. For example, when the  presentation switched from standard (statistics data presentation) mode to video animation, the lights in  the room were dimmed, changed in tone when the instrument was shown in live mode and raised when

it was time for questions and answers. During the whole presentation (slide, video animation and live  demonstration) attention was obtained, the contents were all dealt with and curiosity was stimulated.

Gabriel Lara

The compliments received at the end, mainly focused on the storytelling approached in video animation  mode (cartoon style).

Insight:

The tool I used was chosen by a main need, how to present something of which the others do not know  the details so as not to have constant and always stimulated their attention.

The intuition came from a fundamental principle: "If you cannot explain it in a simple way, you have not  understood it well enough" (Albert Einstein).

The criterion of simplicity has therefore led to an unusual and disruptive approach to the ordinary style  for which the top managers are subjected. The goal was to make something complex anyway simple and

fun. The complexity of the project was conveyed by the originality of its presentation and to do this its  necessary to have full mastery of the elements it contains. The desired and obtained effect was the wow  effect.

Approach:

At the end of the presentation, however, give useful references with which to interface for specific further  details and developments. In order to follow up on the project towards those interested in using it. The  storytelling, above all in cartoons-style video animation, tends to take up a lot of space in the listener's  memory, eroding a good part of the entire presentation of the project. The risk was that people remember  the cartoon more than the project itself, not considering what had to be done pragmatic for the project.  There is a risk of having fun replacing commitment.

Application

In our first learning launch, the web form was structured and the minimum data required by  the applicant was defined. We wanted to define the relevant data of the applicant, to speed  up the registration process to our roster of specialists / consultants and their subsequent  classification. For that, we carried out, within the first 10 days, 2 meetings of exchange of  opinions with those who interview, select and hire the applicants, experts in specific areas.

Validating through  mandatory fields that enter all the required data, consequently obtaining a more complete  database. Approach

After the complete implementation of the tool, it is visualized as progress from the manual  registration of the information of the applicants (received by mail in Word format and  organized in Excel spreadsheets) to its automation by recording relevant data, previously  discussed and defined, in a web form and the CV enclosed by mail.

We believe that our team adapted to this new way of working that tries to clarify procedures,  validate or quickly dismiss the assumptions based on the information obtained. It is the main  advantage of using a tool as a "learning launch" that is complemented with agile  methodologies, approving that in our meetings important results can be obtained in a brief  time.

We managed to comply with the project time, obtaining a functional prototype developed  with corporate tools, avoiding extra costs in our budget.

Based on this experience, we believe that future designs can be improved if this methodology  continues to be applied to obtain a definitive version that satisfies all the parties involved.
