Using Visualization to create lessons about educational platforms

by Brittany Jackson

Challenge

I am a high school Spanish teacher. The challenge I selected was how to create effective online

lessons for seventh graders. During the 2013-2011 school year, following emergency situations

in my country caused by earthquakes and COVID-19, online education became the teaching

method of the public system. I could see how parents and guardians of students complained

about the lack of time and mastery of skills, both technological and content, to help their

children. Similarly, the students claimed not to have achieved the desired academic

performance due to a lack of interest and knowledge in the use of educational tools. This

situation showed me the need to create online lessons on the use of different educational

technological tools, aimed at middle school students.

Selection and Application

I decided to use Visualization to create the lessons. First, I applied several projective techniques

since they use ambiguous stimuli to achieve a projection and delve into the user's thoughts

(Nahed, Design Thinking for Innovation Module 3, n.d.) Projective techniques would allow me

to know the needs of the students regarding the technology, as well as their skills and

preferences to create a course that is attractive and enjoyable. A group of twenty seventh

grade students was sampled. They were assigned to create a mind map in which they presented

personal data, technological skills, abilities, hobbies, future plans, among others. They were

also assigned existing digital presentations from different educational platforms with short

exercises and a journal in which they had to reflect on their experience using each platform,

identifying strengths and areas of opportunity. The data obtained from the mind map and the

journals would serve as the basis for creating technological lessons on the use of the different

platforms, according to the age, abilities and areas of opportunity of the students.

The next step was to apply the Visualization. According to the designer Brittany Jackson

(Visualization Tool, Design Thinking for Innovation, Module 1), visualization allows the user to

capture information, think about it and analyze it visually, achieving the development and

synthesis of the concept. Therefore, it was necessary to integrate the visualization so that the

student could understand the content of the lesson, obtaining meaningful and lasting learning.

Visualization was used in the creation of the lessons, presenting the information through

infographics and videos showing the use of each tool on the platforms. Visualization was also

used to present exercises and execution tasks in which the student had to respond by creating

diagrams, inserting photos or drawings. The lessons were administered to the students, who

demonstrated mastery of the educational platforms through a game in which they had to pass

different levels that simulated the use of the platform's tools. Students completed the lessons

in less time than stipulated, indicating that the visuals, topics and exercises were relevant,

attractive and easy to understand.

Insight

Using Visualization and projective techniques I was able to gain an in-depth of the specific

needs of students regarding their experience, knowledge and perception of educational

technology tools. I didn't know why a middle school student couldn't understand a tutorial

despite being from the tech age. Through the data obtained, I understood that the seventh

grade students of the public educational system in my country have not been exposed to the

different educational platforms, so they have very vague knowledge about them. Furthermore,

they do not fully understand the integration of technology into education because they

associate it with playful games. In addition, I could see that the existing tutorials on the market

are created for an adult user, without thinking about the learning capacity of a preteen and the

visual tools that they need. Using these tools, I was able to see the problem from the student's

point of view and understand that their success in an online class largely depends on their

mastery of the educational platform and how the content is presented to them. This allowed

me to create lessons aimed at meeting his need.

Approach

Due to the need to quickly solve the challenge, I was only able to sample seventh graders.

However, after knowing the need for students to successfully pass the online classes, I want to

repeat the exercise with students from fourth to eighth grade since they are the ones who

depend most on an adult as a study guide, especially if they do not know the educational

platforms. I will continue to use Visualization as a tool to create effective lessons, but I will

integrate the Learning Launch Tools to iterate and reinforce the lessons each year so that more

students can benefit and take their distance learning into their own hands.

Rob’s charisma

Learning Launch design tool

Lucas Medina

Design Thinking for Innovation

Challenge

Selection

Application

In my town there is a small shop of many years to which we want to lend a hand.  The owner is Rob, a friendly guy who knows the whole town and likes talking to the  neighbors very much and it seems that they do too. He and two other employees run  the store where they sell many types of products. However, in recent years his sales  have fallen because new companies have arrived and Rob does not know how to  adapt to the new competition. Rob is a tough nut to crack to deal with changes. It has  too many products, many of them sell poorly because they are not current, but Rob  does not want to get rid of them. He says “they are slow selling, but people like it.”

Another problem that Rob has and why sales have fallen is when it comes to charging  because he stays talking to customers for a long time and slows down work, and  some customers who want a quick purchase become desperate. Plus, it’s so chaotic  and disorganized that a new customer always has to call an employee to find the  product he’s looking for.

By establishing our key assumptions, after carrying out a preliminary study of the  market, we agree that the sector to which the store is exposed cannot vary much,  but the image, distribution, experience and scale of the store could be improved,  focusing on the products that most They sell and leave those who cannot compete  with other companies. In addition, Rob must be relocated, to speed up customer  charges.

Because we have strong competition and limited time, we selected the Learning  Launch design tool to do quick tests to verify that our hypotheses are on the right  track and convince Rob that the changes can be good.

To convince Rob that many of his products are not relevant, we put these at the  entrance of the store very striking, to see if customers are interested in them. Then we  made a reorganization of the shelves by type of product, ordering them and leaving  more space between them and with posters that indicate what type of product you  have. On the other hand, we placed Rob as stocker and specific manager to say  the deals of the day on the street, leaving the other workers in charge of charging  customers.

To differentiate ourselves from the competition, we developed test stands with four  types of new products, local food products, foreign food products, cleaning products  and pet products. At this stand Rob would be receiving feedback from customers  about what they would like to buy the most.

Insight

Approach

The elaboration of quick tests confirmed the hypotheses. The products placed at the  entrance did not interest either new or old customers. Proving to Rob that it’s not that  they sell slow, they just don’t sell.

Organizational improvement was frustrating for old customers, but improved  acceptance for new ones, who no longer had to alert workers to find products,  slowing down their other duties. On the other hand, the new tests revealed that many people in the town would like  organic and local products, something that helped us to improve the focus of the  store and make it competitive.

However, many of the customers after completing their purchase stay to talk to Rob,  because he has an amazing charisma. This is the best business value and its strong  point to enhance that the store has and that went unnoticed. For this reason we think  of adapting a chill-out area outside the store, to promote a lively atmosphere and  improve the recruitment of new customers. All this, opened the eyes to Rob accepting  that these changes can be productive and would not change their functionality in the  business.

This design process could have been improved using the storytelling design tool,  to get a better understanding of the store, the neighborhood and especially Rob,  who was the key. Making him understand the importance of adapting, which has its  difficulties, but a good reward.

Using Visualization to rethink the login process  Design Thinking for Innovation – Bas Klaas    Challenge   What is the point in providing great online banking tools, when the customer doesn’t log in?  In my company, a large bank, we encountered the problem that a large part of our  customers didn’t want to login online to use our banking tools.   Instead they went to our brick local branches, in far larger numbers than our competitors.  That was a big problem, because the costs of the physical banking activities at the local  branch are far greater than the costs of online banking activities, thus creating a large  competitive disadvantage.    In the past there had been efforts to optimize the login process. In the end this resulted in a  better technical login, but not an improvement in numbers of new customers that login. Our  challenge was described as: “improve the login process so customers who now go to the  local branch, use our online banking tools instead”.    Selection   How could we stay away from the trap of only marginally improving the login? We decided  to use Visualization. This would help us to get to the core problem and come up with more  creative ideas. We could then combine the insights and really leap forward.     Another major reason to use Visualization was to get all team members aligned: we wanted  to prevent that in an early stage ideas where shot down because they were deemed  technically too challenging. Visualization helps to create a shared starting point for idea  generation, and enforces the notion that we all are going to work together to create the best  possible solution.    Application  We used Visualization in two ways: in presenting the information that we gathered as a  starting point and to visualize possible solutions.    In gathering information, we asked team members for inspirational examples they knew of  login processes. We printed these examples and pinned them on the walls. We also  interviewed and made videos of customers who visited our local offices, and asked them  what they liked about their visit (we never mentioned our online channels). We showed  highlights of these video’s to the team and visualized key remarks. We also made prints of  the current login screens, to show what customers encounter when they login. We then  asked the team members to draw what our customer encounters both physically and  mentally when trying to login. That provided powerful insights in which areas we needed to  improve.    In a session with all team members, we went through all the input on the wall and let  everyone identify possible improvements and opportunities. These were written on post-its,  and grouped into key findings. We visualized the key findings to ensure that everyone had  the same understanding of the key finding and to make communication easier. Every team  member then identified the most important findings by placing stickers on them. That gave  everyone an insight in what the group thought was most important.

In visualizing the solution we split up our team members in small groups and asked them to  visualize their customer journey on paper. To help them, we prepared outlines of a  computer and mobile screen which they could use to fill in. When all groups had finished this  exercise, we pinned the papers on walls and focused our discussion on the unique elements.  That led for example to an interesting idea: add the local bank employees picture in the login  screen, because our customers value the familiarity of the local employee.  We then let the groups merge the different customer journeys into one, which we then  prototyped.    Insight  I discovered that process of sharing all information visually, and presenting the shared  insights visually is really effective to get everyone on  the same page and get everyone  involved in the process. It has the strong benefit that after the sessions, there really is a  shared understanding and drive to realize the solution together.   When I was just using words and group discussions without visualizations, often it appeared  that everyone was on the same page but after a few days I realized that was not the case.    Another insight I had was the importance of regularly summarizing visually, for instance  summarize the key findings. That really helped to ensure that everyone was still on board  and also eliminate any miscommunications that occurred when discussing together.     Approach  While the approach was successful, I believe that it would have been better to let  participants comment on their inspirational examples instead of just putting the examples  on a wall. Often it was one detail of the example that they found interesting, and that was  lost when we printed the example. Therefore the examples were barely used and referenced  in visualizing the solution.     I’ve also learned that it is really important not to focus too soon at the possible solution that  was presented by the visualizations, but also take note of the implications of the presented  solution. For instance, we should have broadened our visualization, and also interview the  already digital customers and visualize their needs. Then we would have taken the effects of  the change on our already online customers into account.    So, while visualization is a very useful and powerful tool to help achieve a shared outcome,  next time I will make sure that the scope of the project is clearly defined and includes all  relevant stakeholders (in this case including the existing digital customers). Then it becomes  much easier to define the right scope for the visualization.

Storytelling and Visualization in marketing for the bleach industry

Challenge & Selection

Working for the leading brand of bleach in México, we developed a case to build upon

brand values and product performance in order to maintain leadership considering we had a

90% of penetration in the Mexican households. Taking into account that bleach is considered a

commodity (a low price and poorly differentiated product), there was a challenge of keeping

white brands at bay while keeping our current consumers. The case would detail a deliverable

that would help us trigger further actions for this challenge. Even tough bleach is a product

commonly used in Mexican households due to its multi-purpose benefits such as: disinfecting

surfaces (bathrooms, toilets, counters and floors), disinfecting fruits and vegetables, purifying

water and whitening clothes. These benefits were widely known in the Baby Boomers

generation, but nowadays the millenials don’t fully know the many benefits of the product due to

the many alternatives in the market and many misconceptions around bleach (such as alleged

toxicity or it being highly damaging for clothes). The challenge was to find a way of

communicating with those consumers and deliver the benefits of bleach in their home.

The tool selected was Storytelling, in order to map all the brand’s touchpoints with their

consumers and define which of them would be the communication hub for all the brand’s

benefits. Besides, Storytelling allows us to discover underlying or unseen causes to the problem

that can really connect with an audience.      Application

Normally brands take upon themselves to communicate their benefits in the way that you

would tell in a TV commercial: fast and clear droplets of information that you can fit in 20 or 30

seconds. Sometimes they tell stories, sometimes they tell facts, but overall you don’t get much

space to share details. In order to apply the Storytelling tool we had to also use the Visualization

tool to map a consumer journey not as a purchase funnel that ends with them buying the

product, but as an information funnel where people (not consumers) make a research to

discover solutions to their problems. In this sense, we established that Millenials, being a highly

connected generation, use the internet as their principal source of information -besides TV isn’t

a hot medium for them as it was for older generations. We mapped platforms such as social

media (Facebook, Twitter, Instagram), video (YouTube) and search engines (Google, Bing) to

establish which roles they provide in their daily usage and define that search engines are the

primary platform when someone wants an answer to a specific issue. Having done this, we

partnered with Google for a deep dive on all search terms related to bleach in México to classify

and identify key drivers for the category and what aspects of the applications of bleach were

unclear. We discovered that a large number of queries weren’t properly about usage and doses,

Design Thinking for Innovation Alex Perez

but about the composition of bleach, how it's made, how it works and more technical features.

This made us rethink the way we would’ve conceived the campaign in order to address the

challenge. We would still communicate the benefits and ways the product could be used, but

had the start with basic information that people wanted to learn. There was no point of just

telling how many cups of bleach you need to disinfect a floor if people first want to know if

bleach is toxic or biodegradable in order to be sure they are willing to buy the product. With this

research we were able to take this journey into the official website to tell a story about bleach:

what is it, how does it work and the main uses that would connect with the different products.

We also added a myth-debunking section inspired by many queries found on Google such as “is

it true that bleach pollutes water?” or “is it true that bleach can dissolve clothes?”. Another

important section was derived from this investigation to tell the story of how bleach has been in

our households for the past hundred years helping us battle bacterias and viruses as the main

disinfectant in the world. Following the same Storytelling formula, we tried to steer away from

just providing fact sheets and plain benefits and created a visual section that included a grid

comparing the number of cases of popular diseases in México with the max occupation of

popular venues in the country such as the Chapultepec Park, the Zocalo or the pyramids of

Teotihuacán. This gave an introduction to talk about how bleach works at a molecular level

against bacteria and viruses and more technical aspects of how the formula works.      Insight

What we discovered with this process is that there is more than meets the eye when we

define a challenge or problem. If it wasn’t for the deep dive into what people were actually

searching, we never would’ve identified that newer generations didn’t understand the value for a

product as bleach given that neither us nor the competition was providing this kind of

information for our consumers. Due to the presence of bleach in many households for so many

years, we rarely questioned ourselves about what kind of concerns triggered an understanding

of the product.      Approach

Even though I’m confident that using a mix of Storytelling and Visualization were the

right tools to develop this proposal for the challenge, we could’ve reinforced the project with the

Mind Mapping Tool with real customers. At the company we have a lot of information and

studies about the category and consumers, but this project would have provided an opportunity

to incorporate new insights from consumers beyond the data available on our U&A studies.

Provided we had more time, a Launch Tool would’ve helped us make beta testing for the

website and launch various sections while checking the website data to understand which

sections were more interesting.

EXAMPLE REFLECTION - VISUALIZATION

Laura Poli

CHALLENGE  Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.  I advise people in their work transitions as they navigate from one job to the other.  In some  cases, people want to take advantage of the transition to think about doing something else,  something different, from what they´ve been doing in the past.  This is often not easy to pin  down, especially when people have many interests or there is fear or doubt.  My challenge was  to facilitate their thinking about career possibilities by using Design Thinking techniques.  In line  with what was taught in class, I tried reframing the challenge beyond career possibilities to  expand it and include what is that they really want in life.     SELECTION In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected (what it is and why you  selected it, including video references).    I selected the Visualization Tool, which is the representation of thoughts through images such  as photos, drawings, collages, etc.  I chose it because of its ability to “unlock different parts of  the brain and access parts we normally don´t use during conversation,” and enrich the  exploration phase, as discussed by Ana Meyer (designer), in the lecture video.     A second benefit I saw in utilizing the Visualization Tool is that it would allow me to take out the  guess work in the process, by helping me actually “see” what the subjects were envisioning.    And, because it would help keep me focused on exploring as well (vs. directing) as we worked  through the images and questions.       APPLICATION     I used a number of visualization tools which turned out to be effective.  I started out with the  Wheel of Life exercise, which is essentially a circle divided into categories important to one´s  life, such as family, work, etc., where the person has to rate their current level of satisfaction  (see image below).  I then asked them to do the same exercise in another wheel, but projecting  their ideal satisfaction levels in the same categories.  Once completed, we reviewed the results,  and left the tool aside for later reflection.

Wheel of Life

Source:  coactive.com

As homework, I asked them to do a mood board or collage, consisting of images, texts, etc.,  much in line with what we saw in class lectures, focused on today and 3-5 years from now.  This  exercise was a freer exercise, with a wider scope, as they could include interests, dreams,  success factors, inspiration, or any images that resonated with them as they thought where  they are now and where they wanted to be in the future.       We spent a lot of time understanding and discussing the ideas and inspirations.  We then put  the collage up, and looked at it from afar and try to see connections, mood, colors, and things  that resonated most.  We then tried to unify the canvass learnings or insights with the life  wheel ecercise.  For example, we tried to how some of the items in the collage would add  satisfaction to levels to the original Life Wheel by sticking Post-its with the activity or dream in  the respective category.  We then chose the categories where the “collage” post-its raised the  satisfaction levels to that sought in sought in the second, “Ideal”, life wheel.    INSIGHT    I found visualization very effective and powerful because it allowed us to play around, question  assumptions, and spark conversations that allowed us to actually feel the energy levels behind  certain activities or situations in the collage.  It was also easier to detect common themes and  powerful insights easier.  For example, we saw a lot of outdoor activities that generated  conversations around certain criteria in a new career that hadn´t been considered before.      Since it was the first time I was doing this, and playing with post-its, I was a little bit out of my  comfort zone, but it was interesting to see that the participants were not.  They were actually  enjoying the discovery exercise.  I also wasn´t sure if we had broadened the challenge correctly,  but I kept on thinking, “if it doesn´t work, you tweak”, and we ended up working our way  through.    APPROACH Describe what you might do differently next time, applying the same tool you  sleected or a different one, and the reasons why.     Next time, I would certainly use visualization.  What I would do differently is play around to try  different variants and see what works and flows better.  This will help me identify which specific  tools I should use for specific types of situations.  Secondly, I need to work more on  “broadening the problem” as I think is critical, but have a hard time knowing whether we are  reframing it correctly.  Keeping focus on the task is important as I found that I would go off on  tangents a lot, and needed to reel us in to keep focused and get the ideas flowing to finish the  task.

Daycare Electronic Notification Board by Abul Polidori.

Challenge and Selection  WICASA requested the creation of an Electronic Notification Board to  besides broadcast emails to a mail list also provide the same notifications on a web page accessible by  the parents and caretakers.

The team (One-man Team, in the case I) saw an opportunity to reframe the request and expand the  scope creating a new form of communication between parents and daycare staff, not only caretakers,  mainly focusing on children daily follow up. An ethnographic research was put in place and a series of  interviews were conducted to gather information from parents, caretakers, and staff about their  technologic savviness, how comfortable they would be to have information about their children on the  web, what kind of info they would like to have from the daycare.

In possession of these data a combination of Visualization (Week 1 - video 6) and Storytelling (Week 2-  video 4) were used to convey that it would be beneficial to broaden the scope. The combination was a  key aspect of the strategy adopted. Visualization was used to get an alignment among the stakeholders,  helping to convey to the different audiences (mainly the staff) all the aspects of the problem and the line  of experimentation that was adopted later in the process. Storytelling gave a seamless description of  what was the pain points and concerns of the key stakeholders and how the solution would be  experienced in a daily basis by parent caretakers, making the data more “digestible”, softening the  learning curve, allowing stakeholders learn from each other and creating empathy across the board.

Application  The team starts by creating a visualization of the original request’s problem domain and environment  just to understand what problem the Municipality wants to solve (because regardless of the solution  and approach taken that specific problem must be solved). It starts by drawing some stick figures of the  stakeholders and the environment they interact with then expand the visualization to include elements  of the request, the Electronic Notification Board, all these based only on information provided by the  requestors.

Then a workshop is booked to present the current understand to the stakeholders, walking through the  steps that the team went through to get to the current visualization and expand the conversation to  unarticulated needs that the team detected and that could be addressed on that engagement, get  feedback and permission to expand the scope, explaining the need for data and how it will support an  informed decision.

After the first workshop the team runs an ethnographic research, interviewing besides the stakeholders,  caretakers, staff, and parents (extended stakeholders group) from different boroughs with different  socio-economics profiles (since it was assumed that this would influence how the technology is  experienced), asking questions like How you experience smartphone in your daily life? How frequently  do you follow up your children’s daycare experience? What information you would like to exchange with  your children caretaker/daycare?

With the new data points the team runs a new workshop with the extended stakeholders group and to  create the visualization of the newly discovered problem domain, which encompassed besides the board

a 2-way communication platform, including a special channel to talk about a parent’s child. The team  covers different scenarios in the same visualization using different personas elicited from the data to  help understanding and give perspective. Each persona is used to tell a story associated to how they  experience/face the problem and 6 groups of 4 participants are assembled to discuss and enable  feedback collection.

In a next step the team and the extended stakeholders group focus on creating on extending the  visualization to describe the candidate solutions/experiments to the learn launch.

During the process 3 facilitators helped the groups to achieve collective agreement and avoid  polarization.

Insight and Approach  What the team learned is personas and storytelling help immensely the visualization tool, mainly to  convey why such persona would use a solution in a way not envisioned by the majority of the  stakeholders, giving meaningful context to a use case.  This is key to get a deeper alignment and once  that is reached unarticulated needs start to come to light seamlessly, enabling good feedback collection  and greater exchange of ideas and better insights. It allows not only the team but all the stakeholders to  understand what is to be in other person(a) shoes.

Having facilitators was also a successful approach that helped mainly the introverted ones to provided  good feedback and their own unarticulated needs (introverted parents are more comfortable using the  electronic means of communication instead of face to face). The facilitators also helped the stakeholders  to not drift away from the original problem and question.

REFLECTION - STORYTELLING

Challenge and selection

I teach at the Faculty of Engineering of the Pesto Pizza and one of the  challenges is to train future research students, as well as to develop the research skills of the students.  At the Beescoop a system of formative research was implemented  through three programs. The first program involves students from the first to the third cycle in which  research habits are developed. The second program involves from the 4th to the 7th cycle where  scientific thought is developed in the selected courses of the specialty. Finally, program III from the  8th to the 10th cycle in which contact and visibility of the research is achieved through the final  development of the research work and its publication in various congresses and academic events.

Storytelling or the creation of stories is a tool that connects from the beginning with the student and  inspires creativity and is one of the educational techniques that allows teachers and students to learn  and innovate. A story will impact differently on each student, as said in the previous paragraph at the  University we train student researchers through a system of formative research so that they through  creativity, research and the use of technologies can provide solutions to the problems of their  community. Many of these students to begin to develop their formative research work have to identify  a real problem and most of them begin with a question: what problem can I solve and investigate?  and this is where storytelling is applied to identify themselves and create meaning through a story,  inspire them to connect in the story, identify with the character, link the context by determining the  problems in their family or social environment and propose solutions using knowledge and applying  technologies.

Application

I have a story that I always use to connect and inspire young people to begin their formative research  work. It is the story of Jack Andraka, a young man who experienced firsthand the pain of watching a  family friend die, whom he loved as if he were his uncle in less than 3 months of pancreatic cancer.  But he decided that his death was not going to be in vain and at just 14 years old, he promised himself  that he would fight to change things.

He began his research by reading dozens of scientific articles about pancreatic cancer. Trying to find a  solution that would improve his diagnosis, he was lucky, because most of the studies he needed to  read had been posted online for free by the American medical authorities. After researching and  investigating the subject, he asked himself the following question.

- Why are we so bad at diagnosing pancreatic cancer?

- It was because "modern medicine" today uses "very old techniques" that are inaccurate and fail  many times and that each test costs $800.

He continued with more research using Google's search for nanotubes and cancer biochemistry, aided  by free online scientific journals (publicly accessible).

He then began thinking of ways to detect and prevent cancer growth before the cancer cells become  invasive.

199 scientists from various institutions rejected Jack because of his young age, only one of whom, Dr.  Anirban Maitra of the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, agreed to lend him some of his time in the  middle of an interview where he questioned him about cancer and his project.

The result of this project was a graduated-rod diagnostic test for pancreatic cancer using a new panel  sensor, similar to diabetes test strips.

Its protocol was 168 times faster, 26,000 times cheaper, and 400 times more accurate than the usual,  routine procedure for diagnosing pancreatic cancer. Jack Andraka's dream had become a reality.

Insight & Approach

This true story had a great impact and inspired many of the young students to start their research  work when they do not know where to start. This research work is very important because it is part  of the university's formative research system. One of the cases that became a reality was that of a  student in the Systems Engineering career who raised the problem of learning the native Quechua  language in children of 5 years old, she asked herself: how could the learning of this language be  improved by making use of the technologies?

She proposed the solution of her project using a mobile device, the use of RA augmented reality and  3D software so that mobile devices can both project an image of the animals and objects, as well as  the pronunciation of the native Quechua language so that the children can improve their learning in  the gardens of urban areas.

This worked very well and this technique was implemented in the course of scientific research  methodology that is part of program II of the formative research system, as part of the class sessions  to inspire more young people to develop and propose creative and innovative solutions to solve the  problems that afflict a community or society.

Another very important tool that should also be implemented in this system is visualization, because  in this way you have the concept and the clearest ideas about the problem and the possible solution  you want to implement. Sometimes it takes only a small story to inspire a whole new generation of  future researchers and great scientists who are going to give practical and viable solutions to the  problems of our society, using appropriate tools and methodologies such as Design Thinking, I feel  that we can all contribute and generate a little knowledge to change and improve the world we live  in.

Thank you.

Reflection – Story Telling Tool

Challenge

I would like to use the storytelling tool in the field of corporate training. Working in well-established  international companies provides chance to embrace opportunities, helps to learn from innovators  and also adds interpersonal skills, leadership skills and professional development.  However, in order  to withstand the tight deadlines and work pressure, each employee should be trained himself to  undergo attitudinal change and should be motivated to push their boundaries. Corporate training  helps each candidate to train himself to embrace every opportunity with positive attitude. Corporate  training usually involves training needs that are difficult to visualize. The training needs include  induction, professional skills, product training, application simulation and soft skills. For imparting  these skills in an efficient manner, powerful method like story telling is needed to create higher  retention and recall, leading to a memorable and sticky learning experience. It is the motivation and  inspiration contributes to more than ninety percent of the success. And the best way to motivate is  through success stories of experiences, hard work and positive attitude.

Selection

The selection of storytelling tool for corporate training is based on the fact that a story based  learning approach always helps to create desired outcome for the customers when the learners are  well equipped and quick learnt. Stories always help to simplify a complex subject. Story telling can be  used to convert an abstract concept into something that is relatable and easy to assimilate. Also, it  can help learners to understand the consequence of their choices and help them correct in future. In  addition, stories help the learners to connect emotionally to the content and can be used to drive  attitudinal change.

Application

The story based learning approach can be used to train during induction, product training etc. Here  we first go through the first example of induction. The story is based on a new-joiner character who  gets engaged in various tasks from the first day. The another character in the story, who acts as a  trainer or guide and guides him how to go through various situations inside the company,  procedures to be followed up and also describes the do’s and don’ts. The story line basically ends up  like a conversation between these two characters and describes how the new comer clears all his  doubts. The information regarding various facets of the company’s business, history, mission, vision,  values, products, policies, and procedures are clearly explained in the form of story. Another  example includes the product training for the sales agents on a new product line. The stories of  consumers who use this product will help the learners to understand which feature of the product  resonates with each consumer profile. This equips the learners to handle consumer queries and  position the product correctly to each profile.

Insight

The insight I had from this application of story-telling is that a good story and compelling narrative  can always trigger a change in learners. It can connect learners meaningfully to the content. It can be  used as a strategic learning tool in corporate training to meet specific learning outcomes. Also, for an  effective outcome it is needed to use the powers of two elements in story-telling. One is the

compelling narrative of story-telling and the other is creative instructional design principles. The  story should have a beginning to describe background and origin, a middle portion to build-up  through challenges and an end to provide a logical conclusion with take-aways or that triggers the  required reaction.

Approach

Apart from story telling a combination of story-telling and visualization tool can make a profound  impact on the learning outcome. When stories works by engaging the listening skills of learners,  visualization engages the imagination power of learners. Hence a combine effect can produce a  tremendous increase in the recall ability of learners.

Challenge

Currently, I work for the Arab Open University with the position of Welfare Coordinator for the  Faculty of Engineering, where I mainly develop strategies to maintaining the permanence of  students and leading them to timely graduation. Throughout investigations carried out with the  Student Welfare department, we realized the dropout rate of students is higher during the first 4  semesters, which is why we set ourselves as a challenge to be able to combat this issue. This tool was  chosen because we needed to experience the solution in a real environment to observe the results  and the students' experience with this new wellness strategy.      Application    After 3 months of construction of the new permanence strategy, we visualize a solution that we  called "Professional Laboratory", which consists of an experience fair where students can  experience the different Engineering careers and their work areas, in such a way that they identify  their career and know in early semesters the passion of being an engineering professional; This  approach based on the previous design phases, where we discovered that a large part of the  population of engineering careers was not really clear about the professional profile of their career  or was demotivated by the cycle of basic sciences, and this was due to their desertion. In building  suspense about the challenges of my family experience, I told the stories of dramatic exam  fees due and my father receiving his salary on the same date as the due date and avoiding  the calamity of not being able to make payment on time. I spark innovation for our team  processes I also reflected on my sister using my grandmother’s recipe to start a successful  milk shake business.

Insight Description: By challenging myself to tell a story which connected me to the team,  allowed me to first connect with my own emotions about change, to reflect on my  perspectives on my own experiences and how with strategy and with being open to new  opportunities created sometimes by negative events, one can change the course of a  business, an institution/organization and of lives. In telling my story, several team members  opened-up about their own stories and how it affected their inability to adjust quickly to  change. Sharing of  perspectives allowed us to all explore our roles in the team going forward and to identify  the new skills, partnerships and training needed to adjust and to excel in a changing  environment. The Application of Design Thinking Tool In Discovering Students’ Inability to Generate

and Develop Ideas in ESL Writing Class

Joy Cooper

Sabah, Malaysia

Introduction

The design thinking tool was applied in a classroom environment of a secondary school where  the focus was on teaching and learning. There are five aspects of this reflection: challenge,  selection, application, insight and approach.

Challenge

As a teacher in a secondary school of a rural area in Sabah, the least developed state of Malaysia,  teaching and learning are the core business of my job. Almost all of our students have difficulties  in generating ideas in writing tasks.  I am an English teacher and I always hear my students say  that they have no idea of what to write or they simply say “I don’t know” whenever I ask them a  question. There are many assumptions of how this could happen: lower English proficiency, lack  of confidence, lower grasp of thinking skills or poor level of motivation to learn. Therefore, it is  crucial for me to identify the root cause of this issue and help the students to generate and  develop ideas better. I therefore selected a class of 17 students where we intended to overcome  this problem by identifying what areas of our teaching and learning that should be improved.

Selection

I introduced the students with the design thinking tools I learned from this course and attempted  to make these techniques as relevant as possible to them with examples from everyday life,  school and teaching techniques. We decided that Learning Launch was the best tool for us to try.  The tool was discussed thoroughly in the Week 4 lectures which consisted of one particular  video on Learning Launch Tool. Learning Launch was selected because it was consistent with  the teaching stages that we do in schools that involve processes of learning and discovering via  testing and experimenting. Plus, this technique shows similarities with action research methods  that teachers usually conduct in their classroom. Since I always tell the students that trial and  error and discovery learning are essential in their development, we felt that this technique was  the most plausible one since it allowed us to test our ideas to seek confirmation or  disconfirmation.

Application

For the first learning launch, we attempted to focus on enhancing student-centered learning  where students were the ones who created their own questions instead of teachers based on Q- Matrix (Wiederhold, 1993).  I trained the students on how to construct questions using Q-Matrix  and how some higher order thinking questions could be designed based on the chart. We started  applying it in our class in which each individual student created their own higher order thinking  question based on a given literary text. We then selected one question for everyone to answer.  Their submitted their answers to me and I scored them using Structure of Observed Learning  Outcomes (SOLO) taxonomy (Hattie & Brown, 2004; Potter & Kustra, 2012). We conducted this

technique for four times in a row in our class. I then shared the results of the scoring to them and  discussed the feasibility of the technique.

For our second learning launch, we changed our focus on students’ development of creativity in  writing using the SCAMPER technique for students to generate and expand ideas creatively.  SCAMPER technique is an acronym for a set of operators or categories that are used to generate  ideas: (S) Substitute, (C) Combine, (A) Adapt, (M) Modify/Magnify/Minimize, (P) Put to other  uses, (E) Eliminate, and (R) Reverse/Rearrange ( Eberle, 1997).  I trained the students on how to  use this technique before applying in our class. The students were given a literary text that was  either a short story or a poem. The students were required to study the given text. They then  composed a short story or a poem using this technique where they applied at least one of the  operators of SCAMPER in creating their own version of the given text that could be short stories  or poems. In using this technique, the students were individually required to share their idea to  the entire class. Hence they orally spoke about their ideas as well as wrote them down. This  activity was conducted in four sessions. Their improvised short stories and poems were assessed  with SOLO rubric (Brabrand & Dahl, 2009) and Creativity Rating Scales (Dianaros et al., 2003;  Torrance, 1964, Sternberg, 1998;  Soh 1997)

Insight

The implementation of Learning Launch Tool in the first launch revealed that the students had  no difficulties in generating higher order thinking questions but their responses to such questions  in class remained poor, short, undeveloped and they exhibited lower motivation in doing the  tasks especially in generating and developing their ideas. We therefore discovered that students’  level of interest in the tasks highly influenced their commitment in generating and expanding  their ideas. They were able to generate several ideas but they did not elaborate these ideas in a  more developed manner. Thus, our assumption that the students could not generate ideas might  not be caused by their lower thinking skills or language proficiency but rather their interest in the  tasks that they were given.

Our second Learning Launch helped us to see that students were able to produce creative ideas  and expand them in details when they were given more freedom to be creative and they had the  opportunity to orally present their ideas to their classmates.  They demonstrated great level of  interest and commitment in the implementation of Second Learning Launch. Thus, these gained  insights will serve as fundamental information to the next steps in enhancing students’ ability to  be creative and critical thinkers.

Approach

Since the Learning Launch Tool appeared to be practical, consistent and effective in helping us  to gain more insights on the possible causes to the problem our students faced, this technique  will be used in our future thinking design processes especially if our focus is on the teaching and  learning that occurs in classroom. This tool allows students and teachers to work collaboratively  in a familiar and comfortable environment where students are more willing to contribute and  share their opinions in the class as well as to take part in the process. The nature of Learning  Launch which focuses on experimenting, discovering, learning and improving the next step are  more viable in helping us to identify the solution to our problem.

Conclusion

Thinking Design is a viable approach of facilitating the process of innovation and problem- solving in education. This technique should be promoted and expanded further in order to  enhance its application as an effective tool in identifying problems and solutions.

References

Peer-graded Assignment: Reflection – Visualization    Challenge and selection.    One of the tools I have used in problem solving/idea generation is the tool of visualization or visual  thinking, to understand a research problem and areas to work on before attempting to come up with  different solutions to the problem. In order to design the solution, first we must build a good  understanding of the problem that we are trying to solve. Visualization tool helps to build connections  between different findings and understand the bigger picture. I have used the technique of using a  research wall to display all the relevant research outputs, in one place. The visual aspect of the wall  triggers idea generation and enables project members to better understand research insights.    Application    I start the process by creating a graphic of the problem domain. To develop the graphic, I will draw from  any existing material available to understand the environment. The existing material may be existing  research data, manufacturing methods, market data and/or customer feedback.     For the activity, I will divide the researchers into groups of 2-3 participants each specialized in a different  area of study, such as chemistry, engineering and biology. Each group receives a copy of the graphic of  the problem domain that they can write on directly. They will get following questions to answer,

1. What are the customer pains and weaknesses of the existing problem?  2. What are the improvements you would make to eliminate existing pains and weaknesses?

Each group gets 30 minutes to discuss and answer the questions on the graphic. Then each group gets to  display their answers on a white board which helps to identify the commonalities of different solutions.  The research wall created at the end of the session is used to identify the most suitable solution to the  problem presented.    Insight and approach     What I have learned from conduction this exercise is that while the graphics with their feedback is  important in understanding the problem they are working to solve, more importantly this activity helps  to share insights of individuals from different disciplines among their groups and encourage learning and  using a multidisciplinary approach to solve the problem at hand. The graphic/research wall initiates  discussion and encourages individuals of different disciplines to come up with a much more informed  solution. During the final group discussion, they can clearly compare the different solutions suggested by  different groups and pick the most suitable solution to the problem.    The most valuable aspect of this activity is the shared insights and learning.

Storytelling tool  Brittany Robinson    Challenge and selection    The tool I’m going to be using to solve or understand better the problem I will present next is  storytelling, this to be able to achieve that all participants in the problem can give their opinions  and understand the problem by very simple stories and ways that can help to open the mind  and be able to be more creative to find a solution. This approach can be used with a negotiation  team in human resources area when negotiating with the labor union. Storytelling was chosen  because it gives humans, which, at the end of the story are the main actors in the problems to  solve, the ability to develop a deeper empathy, in this case needed to understand both, the  labor union’s petitions and requests and the negotiating team’s needs and responsibilities  during the process. The negotiation process begins with the labor union sending their petitions  fold and the negotiating team, reading them and analyzing what can be modified, what can’t  and what can be debatable with the union. The advantage of using the storytelling tool is that it  serves not just as an analysis tool, because in this situation analysis is needed but can’t be the  main focus, the negotiating team needs to prepare their minds for having a close observation of  the situation to be able to solve the negotiation in the shortest time and best terms possible.    Application    The storytelling tool starts being used during all times of the process of the negotiation: before  the petitions fold is sent to the negotiating team, the members begin to prepare by trying to  tell different stories understanding the reality in which they are negotiating, and, at the same  time, analyzing previous experiences they had when negotiating by establishing predictions,  rules and analysis that seem to work previously and could work in the present situation.       As the goal of the negotiation process is to succeed fast and find the better good for both parts,  ideas and steps during the process need to be taken slowly and one by one, you cannot  conclude the negotiation by having fights and difficult communication with the unions. By using  storytelling, the corporate culture of the organization is presented by the negotiating team for  both parts to understand the objectives of their meetings and have a way to see and  understand in very simple yet effective ways how the organization operates and how decisions  should be taken understanding this, not all organizations are the same, so creativity and a well  understanding of how the organization works is essential to the resolution of the problem.    When the petition from the labor union is sent to the negotiating team the next step is for the  negotiating team to use storytelling in all sorts of ways. First of all something that needs to be  understood is that this is an unstable environment where the steps towards the solution of the  problem aren’t written in any books, there are recommendations but every negotiation is  different where uncertainty can’t be limited or fear because it is going to be present in every  decision both parts will take and the role of storytelling here is to understand the labor union  not only as a number of workers trying to defend their labor rights but as objective employees

whose needs have to be understood and try to provide the best job environment the  organization is able to.    The negotiating team understands by storytelling that they need to have a growth mindset that  helps them develop empathy, empathy is a main actor in this process as it is needed for both  parts to understand what their “opponent” is doing, empathy helps the negotiating process to  be more effective and respectful of other’s point of view.     For the use of the storytelling tool, what will happen is that the negotiating team will divide into  groups and each of them will come up with stories that help obtain emotional connection and  understand the purpose of everything the labor union fights for. Next, the teams will  understand that what they’re doing is not only solving a problem, or doing a negotiation, but  the main focus and larger purpose is creating a cause, in this case trying to find the ways of  creating a better work environment, a better balance between life and work, and the wellbeing  of employees. By doing this stories, the negotiating team needs to first know well their union,  here the importance of empathy, understanding other’s needs and ways of acting. Also, to be  able to use the storytelling tool efficiently there must be moments to reflect what they’re  doing, understanding why the negotiation is going on, what is it that employees need, what is it  that the organization needs, what is the better good for both parts. Finally, by using storytelling  during the negotiation process everything gets concluded properly, nothing gets left behind or  forgotten and every aspect both parts are negotiating gets debated and finally a decision is  made.    Insight and approach    The storytelling tool was a good way of understanding the context and develop the necessary  empathy for the negotiating team to understand and comprehend the necessities of the labor  union, but, something I learned is that both the labor union and the negotiating team need to  understand the outside cause and bigger objective of what they’re doing, it can’t be just an  emotional process, other aspects get involved from outside of the two parts from the approach  I made, news, social pression, people that don’t want the negotiation to go well, politics, and  external situations that can have a negative effect on the negotiation process, so these need to  be analyzed and taken care of as well, maybe storytelling can’t always be the main focus, it can  be used as a way of preparing the negotiating team but can’t be the only approach made.    A final reflection I can make from conducting this experiment is that it can be helpful mainly on  the preparation process and the beginning of the negotiation process as it helps to understand  the needs of the employees and gives a clearer understanding of the reasons people ask what  they do, emphasizing in having empathy between leaders and employees.

Reflection on Visualisation

Sk Rana

Challenge    I work in a Fintech company and provide specialised services to the financial institutions. My stakeholders  are increasing facing challenges from their customers and increasing competition from their competitors.  On top, the increasing regulatory requirements are adding to their woes. The complexity of their problems  are overwhelming for me many times and bringing them together for a consensus is very challenging. I  work to provide an innovative solution to their complex problems. Many times I meet a diverse group of  stakeholders with a complex problem and a variety of wish lists and it becomes difficult to arrive at a  shared understanding of their problem and the possible solution. In my current problem I was challenged  to select only the functionalities which will enhance the user experience in using the financial tool while  increasing the operational efficiencies and meeting the key performance indicators.     Selection    In the kick-off meeting I user PowerPoint presentation and did not have a good experience in engaging  the participants. Many participants seemed to be un-interested with the bullet points. Incidentally I was  attending the course of Lobina and found the usage of the tool visualisation suitable for my kind of  problem to engage a large number of stakeholders. I followed the presentation of Angela Myer and came  to know the benefits of using the tool. As I use big room planning sessions with many stakeholders, I  selected visualisation tools to help my stakeholders define the scope and boundaries, the key elements  and their inter-relations and finally agree on the list of problems to solve. Visualisation is important in my  problem area to unlock the creative side of the brain of the stakeholders and to think in a nonverbal way  to visually understand the problems.     Therefore, I decided to use the visualisation tools more in my subsequent workshops to connect with my  customers and have a common understanding of the problem and eventually build consensus.      Application     For the next workshop my target was to decide on the list of functionalities to work on and set a priority to  them while getting consensus from the majority stakeholders. I started with gathering information  available with my company and gathered further information by conducting interviews with the pilot  stakeholders who intend to be the main users of the new service to be introduced to solve the problem.  Before the workshop, I used visualisation tool to create graphical representation of the problem with the  help of pictures and icons of real-life examples. I divided the participants into 4 groups with each group  having maximum 5 members with similar area of interests. For each such group, based on their problem  domain and interest area, I created big posters with the visual depiction of the problem. I had designated  work areas for each group. During the workshop I gave each of them their poster and I found out that they  were instantly connected with the posters and got engaged in discussing the problem. I challenged them  with key questions to identify the missing elements in the picture, identify the entities and their  relationships in the problem domain and encouraged them to directly update the picture and provide  comments with sticky notes.    While the groups were working and I was facilitating, I used the main common wall visible to all and  started drawing the big picture of the problem with more details and used the key elements of the  feedback from each group in the big picture. I also took photos, printed them and pasted them in the big  picture. In the next session with the stakeholders, I asked each of them to vote on prioritizing the list of

issues with the help of sticky notes and that way I built consensus on the list of issues to solve and their  priority.           Insight & Approach     With the highly encouraging results of using the visualisation tools in the workshop, I decided to use the  tool more often in the subsequent workshops. The visualisation tool helped my stakeholders listen to  each other, find patterns and make connections and build consensus. Once the problem space was  decided, I will organize additional workshops to engage the participants to visualize the future solution to  solve the problem and to create possibilities for them to create values for their end users.     Visualisation tools are rightly described as “the mother of all design tools” by Liedtka & Ogilvie as they are  used in every stage of a Design Thinking process. With my first workshops where visualisation were used,  I learnt that visualisation helped spark idea generation. I observed that the groups could build on top of  each other’s ideas by seeing what other groups are drawing, adding elements to their drawing or simply  discussing the sketches.  The revised graphic or the big picture I created on the common wall helped  them reinforcing the understanding of the problem. Each group could see their inputs in the big picture.  The usage of sketches and pictures helped unlocking their brain and helped them think in a non-verbal  way and be creative in sharing their perspectives and develop shared insights of the problem space. That  way with their shared insights I could build consensus.  The visualisation helped them listen to each other,  stimulate their thought process and encouraged them to draw their insights. The visualisation helped the  participants in applying the skills of listening, thinking and drawing to learn from each other and work  together in having shared insights in understanding the problem complexity, visualising the solution and  create new possibilities.    With the insights gained by using visualisation, I am now planning to use this important design thinking  tool in other areas of customer engagements like ideation, testing with pilots, sales and marketing  brainstorming sessions. I am strongly inclined to use the drawings created with the joint sessions with the  stakeholders to display them in my office areas to encourage other teams to apply visualisation in their  problem areas.

Final Assignment

Federico Ragni  Italy, 07/29/2016

The Challenge to Be Tackled    My daily work as project manager within an innovation centre is developing and implementing

projects aiming at devising innovative solutions for a wide range of techno­economic,

organizational and institutional issues, which involve various stakeholders with different (often

divergent) interests. Usually, in order to raise the financial resources necessary to realize the

interventions, we apply for financings to European public funding programmes.  When I started to attend this course on Design Thinking, I was finalizing a project proposal

dedicated to build a transnational incubator that should help to launch social innovation

initiatives answering both local and transnational territorial challenges. After having submitted

the application form to the funding programme, my colleagues and I were called to present the

devised solution to some of the stakeholders that should be involved in the project

implementation in the case we are granted the financings. In particular, we had to present the

project to a group of mayors administering some territories on which the incubator should have

some branches. In doing so, the tricky issue to be tackled was to translate a complex

international project written according to the bureaucratic rules of the funding programme in

something understandable for people not directly involved in defining it and looking for concrete

solutions to very contingent local problems. For this reason, our coordinator asked us to prepare

a presentation using a simple, clear and concrete language.    The Selected Tool    On the basis of what was presented during the Module 2 of this course (see the ‘Storytelling

Tool’ video), I decided to propose my colleagues to use the ‘storytelling tool’ in order to draft our

presentation. I thought about such a tool as it puts stakeholders and their priorities at the centre

stage of a product/service/initiative, it makes abstract concepts and models concrete, and

involve the audience through entertaining and emotional techniques. I was therefore convinced

that storytelling could have helped us to simplify the explanation of the project’s intervention

logic avoiding too technical details, to tune the incubator’s activities and contributions to the

contingent and concrete needs of the mayors, and to gain their attention through a fresh and

smart communication approach.    The Application of the Tool

My colleagues approved my proposal and we started to think how to draft the project

presentation through storytelling. That meant, first of all, to decide on two key aspects of our

presentation: a) the narrative to be implemented ­ that is, the story to be told and its structure; b)

the technical means to be used to tell the story. On the one hand, we decided to put at the

centre stage of our story the challenges these mayors and their local stakeholders had

highlighted as territorial priorities in a recent programmatic document (e.g. sustainable urban

development, labour market, healthcare), highlighting that all these problems shared a common

element that could be activated to solve them (= the people) and presenting the incubator as the

instrument to be used to activate such a factor. On the other, we were convinced that we should

have avoided to use Power Point (too analytical and too static) and then we opted for Prezi,

which enables to draft powerful presentation based on a canvas graphically representing a topic

and which can be navigated through. In our case, we decided to cartoonized the towns and the

surrounding territories administered by the mayors with whom we had to talk and to use the

graphic visualizations of the territories as a means to explain the meaning of the challenges. We

worked hard for some days on the presentation, more than usually as finalizing the graphic part

was time­consuming.  And finally the D­Day came. We launched our Prezi presentation in a meeting with all the

mayors sit around the same table and we started to tell the story prepared. And we failed. Our

audience was firstly captured and amused by the graphics implemented and followed with

attention and agreement our evocative presentation of their territorial problems. But when we

passed to talk about our solution to help them, they started to be confused up to get completely

lost during the presentation of the transnational partnership (although the organizations involved

are main players in the field of social innovation at European level). The boss and all the work

team were really disappointed and disheartened.    The Learnt Insights and the Approach To Be Adopted Next Time     In the following days, we started to think about what went wrong. Did that remain the first and

last time in which we used storytelling to present a project? At all! In fact, it was immediately

clear to all of us that such a tool allows us to translate the technical language we use in devising

the innovation solutions and in submitting them to the institutional financiers into a discourse

more accessible to all the other stakeholders. After all, our presentation of the mayors’ territorial

problems was well understood and enjoyed, and enabled us to connect a project taking into

account the prerogatives of very different actors to the specific needs of a specific stakeholder.

Yet, it was also clear that the presentation’s section dedicated to the more abstract aspects of

our innovation solution was the real problem: in this case, we failed to make our language

concrete and to present an intangible innovation (a service) as a tangible instrument to use in

the day­to­day work. In this regard, the use of examples of concrete social initiatives that can be

launched through the incubator could have helped to clarify how the incubator actually works

and which benefits can provide.   Such considerations convinced us that the logic behind the storytelling tool ­ that is, the very

logic of design thinking which suggests to start from real needs expressed by real people to

arrive to devise simple and concrete solutions easily understandable and usable by them ­ is to

be implemented not only for presenting the innovations but also and foremost for developing

them. Consequently, my work team decided to deepen the design thinking approach and to try

to adopt it, updating our work tools and models.

Design Thinking Tool: LEARNING LAUNCH

Challenge

One of the challenges of a company that is steadily growing is to be able to retain its employees  and contribute to their growth. Particularly for one where the program is at its early stages, and  especially in a remote work setting, engaging employees to take advantage of learning and  development (L&D) opportunities offered by the company can be rather futile. Employees tend  to be occupied by other priorities that L&D take a back seat in their careers. The L&D department  of Company BLD is now trying to find ways on how they can effectively address this challenge  and have decided to apply Learning Launches as their approach to design thinking.

Selection

For this challenge, the members of the L&D team have done brainstorming sessions and came  up with a list of possible ways to encourage learning in the company. The learning launch will  allow the team to conduct experiments quickly and inexpensively to gather data to determine  which of these possible solutions, if any, will most effectively promote L&D. If none of those  solutions will hold, this design thinking tool will allow them to pivot their approach through the  data gathered in the experiments.

Application

The first experiment is to gamify the learning process in the company. An efficient gamification  strategy has been found to have positive effects on motivation and engagement when  implemented in real-world situations. Learners tend to achieve learning outcomes more  effectively via an engaging journey rather than a traditional training approach. Adding that most  of the company’s employees are between the ages 23 and 40, this experiment is expected to  appeal to them.

The second learning launch is embedding the L&D aspect in each department’s OKRs. For  example, the technology solutions department came up with the objective to elevate their  delivery of quality solutions that will impact the whole company. One key result of this objective  is that the members take courses about the technology relevant to their skills, paid for by the  company, and obtain a certification. This could then translate into their acquired competence  and applied to the products they deliver. Another key result that another team came up is that  members are given immediate feedback regularly coached on their performance.

A third hypothesis that is tested is that employees are encouraged to take control of their  learning and development if they get recognized for it. As such, every month, during the monthly  “town hall”, active learners are recognized and rewarded for their efforts.

Insight

Through a set of metrics initially identified, the results of these experiments were gathered.  Compliance, efficiency, and quality were measured. By applying the learning launch tool, the  L&D team garnered insights on which programs were effective and which ones did not improve  traction. Results showed that having L&D as a team goal made it easier to incorporate the  practice in departments because they were concrete and done as a group. As such, this practice  has been rolled out to every department in the organization with a regular check up on their  achievements every quarter. Since the other hypotheses provided good numbers, but not as  much as the abovementioned, it was decided to incorporate them as well in smaller doses.

Approach

Since indirectly, the challenge is to create impact in an individual employee’s learning,  development, and career growth, learning about their personal and career goals before  conducting the experiments would have been beneficial beforehand. The L&D team could have  gained more understanding through listening to their stories.
