Design Thinking for Innovation: Reflection     Author:  Surya Mohamad ©      Title: The Power of Storytelling for a Start-up Pitch    Challenge:  My team and I are in the pre-start-up phase of incorporating our own BioTech Start-up company. We  are currently working on the first prove of concept on a new drug delivery system against a specific  cancer type. Already in this early phase of development, we are dependent on financial support as  BioTech require a lot of resources from a financial and people point of view. A huge challenge is to  bring business angles, private equity investors or venture capitalists on board at this very early stage  of high risk. How to convince them to support such innovation although “everything” remains  unclear at the beginning of this journey (Piero Vicari; module 1)? In a pitch the biggest challenge is  the limited time window (5-7 minutes) for convincing the right investors. Hence a short, simple and  compelling story has to attract them to invest into you and the team.    Selection:  I was choosing the Storytelling tool to address our challenge. According to Elroy Ford’s analysis  (Global Leadership Development Director @ Mars; Module 2) most business leaders are bored 90%  of the conversation. But he showed a great way to change that. In order to draw their attention  towards the prime goal of inspiring them!  In my view a very good example of storytelling is how Apple managers sell their new creations during  Apple’s Keynotes. They are able to connect emotions, characters and values of people that live that  product every day (see following video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tQSdE32O5KE). They  don’t only present a list of things but rather a connection of emotions and actions of what people can  do with their products.  Storytelling encompasses logics, emotional connection and a larger purpose. That’s why “The- Storytelling-Tool” is the ideal instrument to sell innovation in pitch and get the right people inspired.    Application:  First of all we started to put ourselves into the shoes of the investors and we analysed audience.  What is the background and what is the expertise of the individuals. It was clear at the beginning that  we need to simplify our scientific story in a way that everybody in the room understands what we  intent to achieve without losing the connection to a few hard scientific and financial facts. We  wanted to create emotions at the very beginning of the story. Over the course of the presentation  we targeted to create an arc of suspense by always referring back the initial feelings.  By telling a compelling story based on a logical path of how to realise our invention, my goal was to  visualise the bigger picture in a way that dry financial data come across juicy. Investors want to  understand the larger purpose. They want to know why they should invest into a creative team  knowing the high risk level. That’s a good way to inspire them to engage themselves personally by  supporting “their” winning team.    Insight:  Appling the Storytelling Tool from the “Design Thinking for Innovation” training was very  inspirational. The feedback rate from the audience was much better than we actually anticipated.  Nevertheless I realised that we have to do better next time.  Creating emotions is very important but the most powerful part of my message should have been  selling the larger purpose. More preparation time beforehand is needed. Explaining in a few  sentences that the challenge (how to treat the disease successfully) can effectively be solved at the  end and an investment seem to be logical.

One key approach to reduce the high risk of large investments would have been “prototyping”. I  need to spend more time on explaining what will happen in the “Wow-Phase” and why a money in  the beginning is needed to create prototypes for first tests before the pretended end solution is  developed (fail fast, fail cheap). That’s an important element of the story.  The “Design Thinking for Innovation” course opened my eyes towards successful innovation  management. It connects emotions with characters and as a consequence it creates a cause. In order  to tell a good story I also realised that most elements of the Design Thinking process can be unified in  the Storytelling Tool. Hence the story gets tangible and the audience starts to believe in you.      Approach:  Definitively I will use the Storytelling Tool again for the same purpose because it effectively addresses  the purpose of business leaders to be inspired. But I need to sharpen my skills by practicing it as  often as possible. Not only for pitches but also to sell an idea or products in general.  I also learnt once again that the preparation time is crucial and always takes a longer time as  planned. The more research and analysis you do on the audience and specific elements of your story,  the easier it gets to create a compelling story that people consequently will believe in you.

Overcoming the Known Unknowns by Applying “Learning Launch”                                    May 30, 2020

Yogi Yates

Challenge: Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.

The company I consult with has been trying to move toward the Agile methodology for project management,  initially through the software engineering group and slowly expanding to other parts of the business. The  main challenge that I encountered as a change management consultant is that, where software developers  have used Agile for most of their career, most of the engineering disciplines favor the waterfall approach. As  a result, project teams struggle with the notion of iterations and sprints when they are used to having the  entire project plan in place before starting. In order to adapt the change management planning approach, I  first had to get the project teams comfortable with the Agile methodology.

Selection: In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected (e.g., what it is and why you  selected it for your challenge -- including any appropriate video lecture references).

In my initial assessment of the problem, I identified two key issues: first, familiarity with Agile was not  consistent or uniform across the project teams, and in an engineering organization, that level of ambiguity  and open-ended planning creates more than a little bit of angst. Second, the adopted methodology for  change management across the corporation is heavily anchored in waterfall processes, and is, all by itself,  very rigid and bureaucratic. To bridge the knowledge gap and begin moving in the direction of a more Agile  approach, I selected the Learning Launch tool as a way to test some assumptions and possible approaches  without creating unwarranted disruption with the ongoing project efforts.

Application: Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., what you did and  how the tool was applied effectively or ineffectively).

In selecting the Learning Launch approach, I had to think of a quote from Donald Rumsfeld, former Secretary  of Defense, “… there are known knowns; there are things we know we know. We also know there are  known unknowns; that is to say we know there are some things we do not know. But there are also  unknown unknowns -- the ones we don't know we don't know.”

The uncertainty that is inherent in the Agile methodology is not comfortable for aerospace engineers,  but walking them through the process of identifying the "known knowns" and the "known unknowns" in  terms of current and future application of the work helped to temper this. By guiding the project team  through the discussion and answering the questions: "What do we know? What do we not know? What  do we need to know? How do we learn what we need to know?" I was able to get them to actively  reshape the project approach, and embrace the idea that what we were really working on was a product  that has customers internal to the organization, not a project that would be launched and checked off of  a list.

We knew why we had been tasked to create the in-house capability to support knowledge management  and to facilitate access to a repository of data. What we could not have anticipated, but where we  suddenly had a use case to test from start to finish, was how COVID-19 and the need for information  about its effect on our business would drive adoption of the capability we were building. It also forced  the project team to realize that there was much that was unknowable as an entire body of knowledge  was being created in real time. To see how this would inform our approach to the project, we launched  a pilot initiative specifically focused on COVID-19 response, and observed the level of interaction,  engagement and contribution to the knowledge base that was possible without any direction.

As a result of this testing and observation, the project team realized the need to continue with the  baseline project as originally specified, but with a built-in flexibility to adapt and rapidly create  communities of practice where the type of interaction and knowledge sharing that would happen  anyway could be harvested and captured for the future as well. And the project team acknowledged  that it was essential to adopt an Agile mindset to allow the product to evolve with the needs of the  business.

Insight: Describe the insight you gained from applying the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., how  an insight affected your thinking about the challenge and about design thinking more broadly).

I have worked in organizational development and change management for over a decade, and most of that  time has been spent with engineers and software developers. The most significant observation I've made  through these years of consulting and with this project in particular is that, with engineers, it is very difficult  to overcome the need for certainty. Acknowledging the inherent tension between the known and the  unknown, and helping the project team see this as a call to action to think differently about scoping the  project and testing different approaches, made it possible to guide the shift to a new mindset and an  iterative approach to the project.

By proving that the modified version of our project and change model was able to flex to the immediate and  unanticipated needs of the business, and in the process to become an incredibly valuable resource to the  organization, we were able to reach a level of comfort with the unknown, allowing for the possibility of co- creation of solutions based on the real-time needs of our internal customers.

Approach: Describe what you might do differently next time -- applying the same tool you selected or a  different one -- and the reason(s) why.

In a strange way, it was fortunate that the pandemic forced us to challenge our assumptions about the true  purpose and potential of the knowledge management capability we were developing. I feel that the Learning  Launch approach enabled the project team to grapple with the ambiguity of the situation and test tentative  solutions that they may not have been willing to experiment with in a normal "business as usual" situation.  Ultimately, it turned out that the emergent communities of practice needed a slightly different version of the  product we thought we were creating, and through the testing and observation process we were able to  achieve a "Yes, and" solution: the team stayed true to the original requirements while building adaptive  capability that could flex to the future.

The other tool I would have considered using for this project team is Journey Mapping earlier on in the  process, to better understand how the tools and capabilities would be used through the lens of our diverse  internal customer groups. Through our observation of the communities of practice that emerged during the  crisis, we were able to "reverse engineer" the journey of our users, but in our initial work on the scope and  capability design, we would have benefited from these additional perspectives much earlier in the planning  stage.

Example – Reflection – Mind Mapping Tool

On many occasions we are invaded by our thoughts and ideas, either as a result of our present  activities, as projects, objectives or goals we want to achieve. However, understanding and  projecting this information from our mind, for ourselves or for others, becomes in many cases, a  challenge, where we can fail in the attempt, if what we intend to communicate or capture a creative  idea.

The need to organize our ideas and the context of it is a challenge that all human beings have. In  particular, in the learning process, using a tool such as mind mapping, allows students or any other  group to be directed, to more easily appropriate the data and concepts that they want to offer. At  present, we know that the amount of information is not a problem, however, the challenge is how  we can sort and present, the entire amount of information, that many times we count when  performing an activity. And this situation is not exclusive to designers, as we mentioned, in our daily  life, we constantly have the challenge of drawing or designing schemes that allow us to understand  and learn in a better way.

Application

At the beginning of the "what if" process we are carrying out different exploration activities, where  the generation of ideas and verification of data and information is constant and we are looking for  progress in a pivoting that allows us to refine our innovation process. This tool leads us to go building  and defining the design criteria, in which we intend to move forward in this phase. The possibilities  of summarizing and communicating are virtues of this tool, when transmitting knowledge in focus  groups and work teams, given the intuitive and creative features it offers.

Currently we recognize that people learn more efficiently from images, videos, that is, all those tools  that encourage our capacity for visual learning. There is a fundamental characteristic in "Mind  Mapping" and it is the functionality of connecting ideas, this for the case of the design of business  models or processes, it is a function of great value, every time, that allows to clearly draw each one  of the components and how they integrate and relate

Today we find several apps and web solutions, which can support us to develop our mental maps or  diagrams, in short, I believe that this tool should become a common accessory in our design thinking  for all our activities.

Using storytelling to understand roadblocks towards equality

Fa Leclercq

Challenge

Because my organization wants to be a leader in how it cares for its talented employees, naturally the  issue of gender equality recently arose. More specifically, prior research had shown an inequality in the  amount of female leaders present in the company. Furthermore, one of the causes of this phenomenon  seemed to be a significant bottleneck at a certain level of management in the company, where some  women seemed to ‘get stuck’ in their career. Being assigned to conduct a project to discover the causes  of this bottleneck, I used the design thinking tool called storytelling as a guiding principle throughout the  project.

Tool description

Storytelling can be used as a tool to gain deep understanding into the journey your target population  goes through. It helps researchers go beyond spreadsheets, numbers, and graphs by putting the person  at the center of the conversation, getting to know him/her inside-out, and most importantly, going along  with them through their life and journey and gaining deep understanding in all the ups and downs they  go through. I used this technique at several stages of the project to gain understanding in the career  journey that employees, and more specifically female colleagues, in the company go through to get  insight in possible roadblocks and accelerators along this journey.

Tool application and approach

In a first phase of the project, we organized a handful of in-depth, meaningful interviews where we had a  one-on-one conversation with colleagues which we had localized as key figures in our target population,  i.e. women that seemed ‘stuck’ in their careers. In these hour-long conversations, we discovered the  ‘backstory’ of each of these women, their ambition, and their reflection on the company and the role  they play in it.  Although we found some overlapping subjects, we gained most insight from the  differences we heard in each story.

After getting a retrospective view on the journey, we decided in a second phase of the project to get to  know the story of the employees at different stages in their careers leading up to the bottleneck. Again,  we used storytelling as our main tool in our arsenal. By inviting a dozen colleagues, all at different stages  in their career, to a short coffee break, we got to know what was going on in the lives of these  colleagues. This gave us ‘contemporary’ input, which was very much complementary to the retrospective  insights we had gained from previous interviews. Although we heard that most colleagues were full of  ambition to grab their career with both hands, they also recognized some roadblocks along the way.

We combined our data to assemble a complete and comprehensive story of the career journey of our  female managers. This story was then brought into a simple lifeline, which was the basis of our third  storytelling phase.

We invited a dozen managers and upper management and divided them in two workshop groups. The  main purpose of these workshops was as following: to get the final input on the story of the career  journey they had gone through.

In the workshops, we discussed the scope of the project and explained briefly what we had already  gathered. However, the power of storytelling rapidly became clear. Because the story was now told in a  group setting, we noticed how participants could feed off each other’s input and chime in by adding  quotes and anecdotes they had completely forgotten about, but that had turned out to be of great  impact. Conversationally, the participants recalled and refined their story and found commonalities, as  well as unique aspects in their stories. We used the story of these colleagues as our guiding principle  when presenting our findings to the board of our company.

Insights

We quickly realized the strength of storytelling in this project. Although the quantitative research helped  us identify the main problem we wanted to solve and find our main population, it was the storytelling  that gave us the real insightful information. We did away with the numbers for a while to just focus on  what the actual people involved could teach us about the way things were going in the company and  how they had been perceiving their environment.

My first key take-away from this project is to not get stuck on finding similarities in the stories, but to try  and see the beauty in the uniqueness of each story. Although similarities can be useful to get a high-level  view of the situation, the unique details in each story can help you get to underlying root causes of the  problems you’re trying to solve.

My second key take-away would be to never be satisfied with the information you have. There are  always details, anecdotes or differences that can help you get a more holistic view of the story you’re  trying to grasp. In this case, even three angles on the same story in my opinion did not fully bring us to  our so-called saturation point.

My last take-away would be to not get lost in the stories when the saturation point is reached. Although  storytelling can bring us very rich data, Rome wasn’t built in a day. Keep the main problem you’re  investigating in mind throughout the process to not get lost in sidetracks. This might in turn help you in  identifying solutions to the very problem you are trying to solve.

Reflection – Visualization

1 CHALLENGE

I work in the marketing department of a multinational company that sells cameras and  printers. My work is mostly in the business to business (B2B) area, we partner with  retailers and ecommerce platforms to sell products.

As a result, there is a need to train external personnel in the use of our products so they  can deliver the best solutions and give good sales pitch to consumers.

Due to this need, we developed an e-learning platform to train salespeople from partners  in the correct use of our products, since in-person training is not always possible due to  large number of salespeople to train and the fact that they are spread throughout the  country.

However, initial implementation of the platform was rocky due to lack of resources and  when it finally took off the users didn’t use it steadily, they registered, did a few courses  and then never used it again.

We are currently looking for a way to make the platform more appealing and useful to  the users, since we hope to provide good resources and value to the users.

2 SELECTION

We are going to use Visualization. This is a technique that requires participants to  make use of graphics, photography, animation or any other visual medium to express  their feelings or ideas.

Since we are dealing with a website, we have a highly visual component that would  be better served by graphical techniques.

It also allows users to see themselves to see a physical representation of a website in  progress and to add any input in a way that is accessible to anyone, not just  programmers. It enables fluid communication.

Blanca Serrano  Peer review assignment

3 APPLICATION

First, we need to assemble a sample of users, to ensure diversity, we randomly pick a  group of 15 salespeople in each province of the country.

They are informed of the experiment and we request their consent and participation.

We go to each province to meet them at their workplace afterhours, with drawing  supplies on hand, both traditional and digital, for those who want to draw with things  like Illustrator.

We apply visualization in two different ways; the first, to have people do a sketch of  their learning journey, how the come to learning something new, what they enjoy  about it, what they don’t and so forth.

Those sketches might look something like this, or they might look entirely different  and that’s what we are looking for, for the difference in users’ perceptions.

Blanca Serrano  Peer review assignment

Second, we want users to draw their favorite website, regardless of what the website  is about. We don’t want to limit people’s imagination by putting strict rules in place.  Getting to know users’ tastes will let us apply favored designs to our page, even if the  content is very different.

We then analyze both sketches for common patterns and sum up those patterns in post it  notes.

We will then have a collective brainstorming session in which we will try to come up  with solutions to apply and implement in the platform. After that, we will retire, but  only after having created a group to stay in touch with the participants.

Blanca Serrano  Peer review assignment

Once we get back from this round of contacts, we will prototype solutions and poll our  users for opinions on ongoing progress, so we can course correct on time if something is  bad.

After we settle on the ideas we want to implement, we will make a schedule and we will  develop and apply them accordingly.

4 INSIGHT

The experiment proved to be a very empathic experience, we were able to see the way  people perceived their experiences and their preferences for design. It allowed us to  tailor design going forward in a way that was more user friendly, not only  aesthetically, but also functionally.

One of the things we learned was that the learning experience could not be a hurdle  for the learning materials themselves, it had to flow more easily, instead of having 3  different pages just to deal with registration and 4 clicks to get to a certain course.

It also proved the value of design thinking techniques in providing new ways to tackle  both routine and unexpected challenges, it provides a framework and resources that  were easy to understand for our users instead of complex flows or processes that would  have impeded the daily life of our users.

5 APPROACH

While we gained a lot of insight from this experiment, next time we might do better  using ethnographic research first, since a lot more people, specially salespeople, are  more comfortable with talking than with drawing.

Even if we did stress that artistic quality was not the point, some people felt more  inhibition that if it were simply a conversation.

Challenge

When I was working as the Banking Legal Manager of an Investment Bank one of  my responsibilities was to hire my staff with the support of HR Department.

And something I realized during the interviewing process of junior lawyers, was the  lack of preparation they had regarding banking and corporate law. It seemed that  the Universities only gave them an introduction and a few guidelines.  Also, I  noticed the lack of practical knowledge, analysis and drafting skills they had.  So,  after several interviews with no luck, I ended hiring the junior lawyers who  demonstrated a positive attitude, proactivity, great communication skills, resilient,  willingness to support the legal department, and most important: the one who was  eager to learn.

But the big problem, was that I had to spend a lot of time, training them, and as the  legal manager, with deadlines, working meetings in house and outside the office, I  had a very limited time to do so. But I remembered when I was beginning my  career, that I had to learn by practicing.

So, I decided to create a legal training program focused 100% in practice, to help  junior lawyers improve their day to day skills in banking law, so they could achieve  more job opportunities, and to support legal managers who wanted to train their  in-house junior lawyers.

Selection

I was convinced, that people learn more when they do things. Actually, there is a  pyramid of knowledge created by Cody Blair that says: 75% of knowledge after 24  hours comes from what we practiced.  So, It was time for a LEARNING LANCH. I  wanted to test my hypothesis, and I created a prototype course. The course will  contain 21 hours of 100% practical legal training, focused on corporate and banking

law, to give them a true idea of what meant to be a banking and corporate lawyer,  day by day.

Aplication

I reached 8 junior lawyers, who were passionate about banking law, and I offered  them the course for free. I rented a very nice conference room instead of a  traditional classroom, to make them feel like they were in an office working.

The first 2 sessions, where focused on the most simple topics, like creation of  corporations, and we had workshops where they learned how to draft and create  a corporation from scratch.

They had the opportunity of learn about banking products, and to draft credit  contracts. My method was based on “learning by doing”.

Insight

The group was composed by a 2nd year law school student, 2 junior lawyers working  on banks, 1 senior lawyer who never practiced banking law, and senior year law  school students, who wanted to become banking lawyers when they graduated.

It  was amazing to see them how they evolved in every class! I proved that practice in  legal industry is key.

Approach:

After we finished the course, I made some adjustments on the syllabus, and  included the use of TCs, to make classes more interactive.

After that learning launch, Beyond Law School was formally founded.

Castles in the Sky – Design Thinking through the Visualization Tool

Challenge

Today we face a challenge unlike another; with a magnitude so considerable that it’s made

countries literally quake. Forsooth, the pandemic known as COVID-19 has come to create a new segment  in history that generations after us will only be able to read about in their textbooks. Partially, this creates  an opportunity to take action; to do things right. In the other spectrum, our “What Is”, the context in which  we live in, also creates what could seem like an abysmal chasm from where we’re standing today and  where we want to be, our “What If,” if you will.  I believe it is important to put these things into concept  because like with all innovation, big or small, we must be able to understand what we’re dealing with so  that we can make informed choices. Change is inevitable, dear reader. It is a constant and perhaps the  only one that we’ll be able to distinguish in our lives. COVID-19 has brought this change and it’s up to us  deal with all the aftershocks that have ensued because of it. Now, forgive me if I’m being dramatic, but it’s  true. To elaborate on this, I take quote from Virgil’s Aeneid: “Through chances various, through all  vicissitudes, we make our way…” What this quote leaves us with is nothing more and nothing less than  the inspiration to do things right; to go out there and innovate and act as best we can.

With that said, I ask that you picture this: A very small class of young economists and the

respective lecturers for each course. These people form part of a slightly renowned university known as  Savitribai Phule Pune University in Guatemala City. The marginal issue for them that had arisen from the pandemic was  that the implementation social distancing measures created a disruption in the flow of face-to-face  classes, and everything, then, had to shift to a digital platform. This small group of young learners was  then tasked with adapting to this new methodology, as were the professors. However, proper organization  within the group turned out to be quite lethargic and most students no longer felt like they were learning  anything. As for some of the professors, they also felt quite helpless in this situation; some of them were  used to the “old methods” of teaching and couldn’t quite adjust their programs to the online tools that they  had to make use of. The “What Is” seems deplorable, and the biggest challenge faced was finding the  right model to consider and respect the needs of the parties involved. In this case I worked with a sample  of 6 students and 2 lecturers. All of which could not agree on an effective approach to a solution.

Selection

Since communication through video chats had become monotonous and everyone wanted to talk

over each other, it basically felt like we (the students and professors) were trying to build the Tower of  Babylon. There was no effective transmission and reception through voice conversation. Because of this,  I opted to use the Visualization Tool to transmit what we could not express as easily through speech. As  you will see in this work, my methodology required the participation of the people, who shared somewhat  similar ideas but didn’t quite know how to express them during class sessions. In retrospect, my role in  this was to provide the building blocks so that we could create our very own castle in the sky.

For this purpose, the definition I found in the book Designing for Growth by professor Maii and

Steven Cooper was quite helpful. If you want basic definition of Visualization, this book provides an amicable  way for beginners, much like me, to grasp that this tool involves the use of imagery to picture our What Ifs  and bring those to reality. Through Visualization it becomes much easier to identify trends, outliers and  patterns in information and yet, this can still be done in a simple and often attractive way so that everyone  can appreciate what’s being inputted onto the graphic. Finally, throughout the 8th video of the first week,  designer Isabel Patel explained something that had an effect on me; in her words: “Visualization is about  creating pictures of something that will soon be”. These words are what prompted me to adopt this tool to  approach the communication issue faced by the group. They inspired me to create a new reality.

Luis Gonzales  Savitribai Phule Pune University Student

Application

At first glance, the task of implementing the tool seemed discouraging. I didn’t know exactly

where to begin or how I’d go about compiling different ideas. After having completed most of the Design  Thinking course, I didn’t want to go about it in the usual way of creating a survey. I found it impersonal  and not as interactive. See, my goal here was to create a platform where people would be able to share  their ideas and opinions without being shot down by others or having the insecurity to express themselves  freely. The latter is what propelled me to make the process of gathering data anonymous; the former,  however, gave me the idea of using a digital bullet board. Here, students and lecturers alike would be  able to post little notes stating their opinion on questions like: how distance learning/teaching was  affecting their operative (academic) process (?); another question was if they could implement  anything to solve it, what would it be (?); and finally, I wanted to foment a positive perspective, so I  asked, do you believe anything has emerged from this methodology that has benefitted your  learning/ teaching process? Still, this seemed very wordy and I wanted to take a leap further but with  something simple so as to not lose the interest of the sample group.

Due to this predicament, I came up with the idea of having each person post one of three

emojis: a microphone (representing communication), a car (representing physical resources used) and  books (representing learning). They were to place one of these in their comment so as to state what was  most important to them; whether it was that they were irritated by the inefficient communication process or  that they were more concerned about the resources they needed to have for either in-person classes or  distance learning or that they simply wanted to learn despite all other frustrations. This helped me further  understand the perspectives of the different participants but also allowed them to be present while others  were typing in this bullet board canvas. I used a free online service called Padlet for all this. The website  essentially allowed me to give a description of the information I needed from them; moreover, it also gave  the benefit of people being able to add their comments through “sticky note” windows. With this, one  person was able to see what the other was typing in real time and yet, it provided the space necessary for  people to respectfully observe and disagree on the different questions I placed above without having any  real quarrel take place. I shared the invites to participate in the Padlet via link through social media; only  to the respective parties. As I said before, these people just required an outlet to express their opinion  without immediate backlash, which is why it also helped that this remained anonymous. Also, my  reasoning to keep the sample small was that qualitative data is much harder to interpret and I found that a  smaller proportion of the overall population provided better patterns to study and work with.

All in all, I was able to take these same principal components from each data sample to supply

myself and others with an idea of what our What Ifs looked like and how they somewhat correlated with  one another. From here, the What Wows factor came in as some saw specific ideas to be more viable  than others. This helped me create the “building blocks” of our castle in the sky (although it doesn’t look  as majestic as it sounds). Briefly, I want to elaborate on this last statement. Castles in the sky are referred  to as ideas, hopes and dreams that seem unrealistic or impossible. I learned from professor Maii that  there is no finished solution or magical answer to everyday problems. What’s important to remember is  that we’ll fail with a purpose; Always. The castle I made for this challenge, then, encompassed all that  these people wanted to achieve and expressed their need for that desire to be met. At the end of the  process, we were all able to relate to the little castle that was made. Despite previous disagreements, we  could look up from the chaos below and admire what our combined effort had created. There, we had  placed all that we valued as important as much for our learning process as for our emotional state. I have  no doubts of the Visualization Tool’s effectiveness. I know our work wasn’t lost by placing it all in the air  (like some would say); no, now we just have to build the foundation for our castle, our home- our dream,  for a better tomorrow.

Luis Gonzales  Savitribai Phule Pune University Student

Insight

This effort truly took a mental and emotional toll on me. I never understood the concept of

empathizing with others, but I think I learned quite a few about it through this method. What I found is that  we all have different ways of expressing ourselves, but also that we’re not so different. All many of us  want to do is be heard and understood. Many of us walk this life alone, so when we have the chance to  scream we do just that. We want to be noticed. Others have had the experience of being beseeched all  their lives by all kinds of questions, and in time, their voices become raspy and shy. These people fall into  the background and they’re no longer heard. What began as an investigation to see how we could reach  an agreement in our class sessions, became an outlet for people to express their feelings and opinions  without being ignored or muffled. I find that in trying times like the ones we live today, it’s important to feel  and to understand that life is rough but that we can get through if we make space for the things that  matter. We don’t want to fall in a cycle of insanity, and I use this word with all due respect. To me, and  many others, insanity is defined by repeating the same action and expecting different results. My peers  and I didn’t let ourselves be commandeered by stoicism or rigid postures; instead, what we created was a  movement based on understanding others and developing a love for progress through empathy. Approach

As you have seen, dear reader, this approach was many things, but not unsuccessful. Like many

structures, our castle has the potential to increase vertically in size; that is to say, we can always improve  on previous ideas to continuously adapt and innovate when the situation calls for it. If I had to use a  different method, then perhaps Storytelling would be another viable option. This tool would provide a similar platform for  people to share their opinions and ideas so that they can be considered and placed into focus in a shifting  context like the world we inhabit; we want to create holistic approaches. There’s no 100% solution. As  professor Maii said in the beginning: “we’re all expected to get lean- to do more with less.” And so I  reiterate, we can work smarter, not harder. the workflow (activities and projects) within the department in order to increase sales and ensure good

included several tests to arrive at a mutual decision, regular presentations of results to clients and

Selection

The learning launch was used for this project because it was indeed a test of capacity and stretch

threshold. It was the first time we would be embarking on a project with such short turnaround time and

we were willing to go through the test to determine if it was possible.

Application

For our first learning launch, we conducted a startup meeting with the client to discuss expectations and

how often they require feedbacks on the project  so as to be on the same page during each processing

steps to avoid mistakes and a re-run.  For our second launch, we focused on the structure/execution of

the tasks. In particular, to meet up with the deadline and possibly break and industry record within the

period we wanted to see if we could structure our tasks, projects, and processes to adapt the methods of

Scrum project management for our work (e.g., time boxed, daily, specific meetings, reviews, etc.) in an

effort to become more agile. This tested our assumption that the structure and execution were the main

causes of our workflow challenge. The team went through weekly meetings and reviews to structure our

tasks and processes in a more agile way. These two sessions occurred within in a three-week timeframe.

We expected to produce a document with a clear description of our new, more agile processes/workflow.

For our third learning launch, we focused on execution having clarified our tasks and priorities. This tested

our assumption that our prioritization of tasks was the main cause of our workflow challenge. At every

processing stage, we organized review meetings and sent out customer satisfaction forms to determine if

the project was being done to the client satisfaction and if not to review areas we were falling short. And

of course to make up the deadline, the team had to sacrifice extra hours and give up their movie times at

weekend sometimes to meet up with the turnaround time.

Insight

By applying the learning launch tool, we identified our assumptions and designed launches to test these

assumptions. Also, we thought through anticipated results, and of course expecting to find that a more

agile approach would improve our workflow, and that both our team and the key stakeholders would be

fairly open to the new prioritization of tasks and process.  For Our actual results, the extra hours put in

and dedication of the team made a huge success of the project and we were able to meet the project

deadline. But of course it wasn’t all together a smooth ride! There were bumps and hitches which all

together gave an insight on how not to do it a next time. The team decided to review this insight and

incorporate it into future launch designs, this incorporation of insight is particularly important and critical

for a next project as launches come before a full rollout in the design thinking timeline.

Approach

Given that it was the first time we were trying out such seemingly impossible task of completing a project

which ideally should span a period of 9months in 6months, the learning launch is the appropriate tool to

enable us plan a next project successfully as we can work on lessons learnt from execution of this one.

The team needs to review the insight gained from our launches and incorporate this insight into future

launch designs. Future launch designs should reflect insight gained, progress made, and come closer to a

compelling solution ready for full rollout.

A Reflection on the Use of Mind Mapping for Health Professions Education

Challenge

The delivery of healthcare education for nurses, physicians, dentists, physical therapists, social workers,  and pharmacists has historically taken a siloed approach. This approach is problematic because these  individuals are expected to work together in teams to provide quality patient care, yet they are not  trained to do so.  To address the “wicked” problem of how might we increase interprofessional  educational opportunities across healthcare disciplines, a national organization convened a group of  healthcare educators to participate in a design-thinking workshop.

Selection

The organizers selected a mind mapping exercise using sticky notes to get participants thinking  creatively about how we as educators might address the wicked problem.  As we learned in this course,  mind mapping is a visual method for helping others to understand how ideas relate to each other and is  one of the most universal ways to brainstorm. The unstructured setup allows individual ideas and  thoughts to flow freely. Similar concepts are grouped together, allowing ideas to jump around among  topics, rather than forcing them down a list.  I have personally used this technique in multiple  workshops and sessions to address difficult and challenging issues in medical education.

Application

In the most recent exercise using the mind mapping technique, we gathered together in one room 30  health professions educators and divided them into groups of six.  Everyone was given a pen and a set of  sticky notes and sent to their respective groups to begin brainstorming how we might increase  interprofessional educational opportunities across multiple healthcare disciplines. We had only one rule  which was that every idea offered up must in some way be “actionable.”  Each group was assigned a  staff person to manage the sticky notes, to group them on a wall according to concepts, and to refuse  any idea that was not actionable.  Each team was challenged to develop at least 50 different ideas over  20 minutes.  After the 20 minutes, each group reviewed their sticky notes and if necessary moved them  around for better concept grouping.  As you might expect, the exercise created a lot of noise and  excitement in the room as participants brainstormed and wrote down their ideas.  Once this activity was  completed, participants were paired with a participant from another group.  Each participant was asked  to share the ideas generated from their group session and to select one best idea for prototyping later  that afternoon.

Insight

Most of my previous experience with mind mapping exercises has been limited to 90-minute workshops,  and even in those sessions, the actual mind mapping part of the workshop lasted no more than 45  minutes.  The session I described above took place over a total of 4 hours.  I really appreciated having  another 2.5 hours to dig a little deeper and experience design-thinking methodology more fully.  Each  group generated at least 30 ideas, and several groups generated more than 50 ideas.  This process is  amazing for generating a lot of ideas in a very short time.  One downside was the small size of the room  in which the activity took place.  We worked in a small, windowless hotel conference room which was  not very conducive to creative thinking – although we did not let that stop us!  In the future, however, I

would want to make sure the room set up was appropriate for the size of the group and that the  surroundings encouraged creativity.

Approach

For this activity, mind mapping was a terrific design-thinking tool to use.  It rapidly engaged people and  moved them outside their comfort zone.  A lot of very good, actionable ideas were generated and are  available for continued discussion and thinking about this wicked problem.  I plan to use this  methodology more in future workshops.

With that said, there are other design-thinking tools that could have been used in this exercise.  I am a  fan of storytelling, or using narrative, to develop empathy around an issue or challenge.  This method  can really create a sense of urgency and move people to action quickly.  For example, we know that  patient care is improved when educational barriers are removed, and healthcare providers learn to work  cooperatively in teams.  In this workshop, the organizers could have used a story, perhaps a patient  story which described a poor patient outcome because of healthcare providers not working together as  a team.  This kind of story motivates, helps communicate the problem, and opens the door to  envisioning a different future.

Syed Aziz – Design Thinking for Innovation – September 5th, 2020

Example Reflection – Learning Launch

Context:

I am a Business Transformation Director at a major Oil & Gas company which has operations in 170  countries. My task was to develop a new Operating Model for Procurement and Supply Chain  Management (PSCM) Organization, to address feedback from business stakeholders. PSCM organization  has about 900 employees who are located across 14 regions in the world such as US, Canada, Trinidad,  UK, Azerbaijan, Angola, Egypt, Oman, Mauritania & Senegal & India. While the full scope of Operating  model project is outside the scope of this paper, I will describe the relevant elements here.

PSCM organization is responsible for Sourcing, Negotiating and Contracting for all Products and Services  that are utilized in the Exploration, Drilling and Production of Oil & Gas in the company, and they manage  all the resulting contracts as well as transactions (actual buying in the system).

Challenge:

What Is: In the existing model, each of the regions performed its own Sourcing & Contracting activities  based on the local demand. This process is not only inconsistent, but it does not allow for developing and  implementing best practices, scaling the business or for developing talent. This decentralized approach is  also not very efficient and effective. The feedback from business stakeholders was that the process of  sourcing & contracting is too long and has too process oriented, instead it should be fast, and business  focused.

What If/What Wows: After going through a complete design process over many months, reviewing many  concepts and options, our team created a new model that would centralize all Sourcing and Contracting  activities at two global hubs – Western Hemisphere Hub (Houston) and Eastern Hemisphere Hub  (London), this centralization will also be supported by the new Digital tool which will be used by the  Regional businesses to file Sourcing requests and track the progress.

The challenge here was that Sourcing & Contracting was majority of the job for some 900 people across  the globe, centralizing this activity will be hugely disruptive and will also result in the morale loss for the  staff. Secondly each of the regions have their own governmental requirements and governance steps that  have to be considered and can not be violated.

It is also important to recognize that by moving this activity from the regions to central hubs will also  require us to overcome human elements of fear, uncertainty and skepticism that it can be done centrally  without loss of quality and speed.

Selection & Application:

Our initial view was that once we have designed the operating model and the digital system is in place,  we can initiate the organizational change immediately. However, based on some preliminary reviews at  small focused settings it became clear that the wholesale change will not be accepted by the organization  and it will result in massive distraction for the business.

Syed Aziz – Design Thinking for Innovation – September 5th, 2020

It was then that we decided that to go fast, we will have to go slow and voila! We landed on the proof of  concept (MVP) approach or The Learning Launch as we call in this Design Thinking course.

What Works: But how do you do a proof of concept for an organization? we decided that there were  certain categories of Sourcing and contracting that were somewhat centralized and it will be relatively  easy to completely centralize that group (and transfer those people in the new central team at one of the  hubs). We also shortlisted a few ‘tricky’ categories where it will be challenging to centralize, we wanted  to do this to stretch the concept and see if it breaks.

Upon selecting a few categories, we announced the concept to the organization and solicited their  suggestions on how best to approach it as well. We confidentially spoke to the people who were going to  be moved to hubs and worked through the Human Resources nuances to carefully transition them to the  Hub team. Along with these individuals, we also moved their existing Sourcing & Contracting responsibility  to the Hub team, thus “seeding” the group with immediate responsibilities and an experienced team. This  team was then also tasked to develop the new processes to intake work (through the Digital workflow  system) and deliver the work most efficiently).

Insights:

Looking back this was the best decision we made, as expected as soon as the team was stood up, we had  naysayers all over the organization as to why and how it will fail. There was resistance in working through  the new process and transitioning work to this team. Since the team had brought their current  responsibilities with them, they were quickly able to gain credibility with the business stakeholders.

As expected, we did run into challenges related to work flow or better said flow of work – so the team  had to quickly step in and develop new agile processes to intake new demand, complete sourcing and  contracting while ensuring there is no gap in communication with the stakeholders and regional teams.  We also sorted out the quirks with the new digital system and improved the process even further.

During the same time, we unfortunately hit the COVID-19 crisis and that required us to adjust our  contracts and amend contracts with new safety clauses. This central team quickly stepped in and took on  that work, turning it around in record time demonstrating a 500% improvement in cycle time. This was a  huge credibility builder for the remainder of the organization.

Over a period of 6 months, this team meticulously absorbed the work from other teams, refined their  processes and delivered quality products.

Approach:

As mentioned earlier, the initial approach was a wholesale change without testing the new model, if we  had gone through our initial plan, we wouldn’t have been able to prove that the concept truly wows the  organization and that it works. I am fairly certain that it wouldn’t have, not because the concept wasn’t  sound or we didn’t have good team, the human factor and mental inertia from the organization would’ve  been too much to overcome.

What’s next:

We are gearing up for a full-scale launch and ramp up and by the end of this year the new team with  Eastern and Western Hubs will be fully in place.

Leveraging the learning launch tool to test innovation formats  Alexandra Beyer    Challenge:  Within my organization, I am working in the innovation lab and responsible for developing  innovation formats that will attract many clients, helping them to create innovative ideas for their  business. These innovation formats are supposed to serve as an initial inspiration phase, in  which we elaborate with them future business development opportunities that will help them  grow. Ideally, the clients will request future services from us such as the implementation of the  generated ideas or further workshops with a wider range of colleagues from their organization.  The challenge is to identify a set of innovation formats that suit to the potential client’s  requirements, budget and time frame and that provides the right environment and methods to  ignite the client’s ideas and future visions. Together with my team, we have developed several  innovation formats in theory, based on previous workshop experiences and innovation theory,  but we never tested these newly created innovation formats with potential client’s yet. It was  unclear to us, whether we could use the innovation formats within different industries and  whether the format would fit to the client’s way of working.    Selection:  Before starting a large marketing campaign for our new offerings, we need to test them with a  selected group of potential customers. After assessing different tools, it was clear to me that the  learning launch tool seems to be the perfect tool as it is a small experiment that tests my new  ideas in the real marketplace and allows me to reiterate it and refine it, based on the potential  client’s reaction. My decision was inspired by the IBM story, which leveraged the trade show  Sibos to validate their concepts in real life. Starting with a hypothesis and key assumptions, this  tool assesses the idea’s value creation, the way it is executed, its dependability and scalability  and designs the ideal experiment with the real target group. This would allow us to assess  whether our idea could be scaled to different client bases and industries and if it was suitable to  their way of working. By using the learning launch process structure and the learning launch  design table from Oliver Beyer, I could thoroughly detail out my ideas and prepare the experiment. I  defined the experiment as a ‘soft launch event’ of the new innovation lab on the topic of artificial  intelligence, which contained several breakout sessions, where the clients elaborated ideas  around the topic of AI and where I could test different innovation formats with real potential  customers.      Application:  To prepare the experiment thoroughly, I started with Oliver Beyer’s learning launch process  framework and stated the hypothesis that my innovation formats were better than the  alternatives out there and will enable my future potential customers to come up with new value- adding ideas that they can implement within their organization. I defined key assumptions such  as the applicability of the innovation formats to different industries and its scalability to different  company departments and countries. I prioritized the key assumptions and invited the target  groups that were selected based on the assumptions, international clients, from different  departments and industries.  Then, I filled the learning launch design template by Oliver Beyer and stated the key assumptions  together with the target group, the way I wanted to test them, the timeframe and the cost. This  resulted in the creation of my event, which I framed around a specific topic (artificial intelligence)  and offered them the added value of listening to keynote speakers and explore the latest  developments within these technologies. During the event, which was a real success as  numerous potential clients participated, I conducted the breakout sessions together with my  team and thus tested the innovation formats with the real marketplace. In the end, we included  feedback opportunities so that we did not only have our observations as a feedback, but also the  honest and direct feedback from our potential customers.     Insight:  The result of the soft launch event surprised me positively. First, we had full house and many  customers stayed until the very end, participating actively in all breakout sessions. Second, we  could observe this trend across the different industries that came, and we validated our  assumption, that the innovation formats would work successfully across industries. Third, we

generated creative and valuable ideas in almost every innovation format that we conducted,  which showed that the formats where well elaborated and suitable for the way of working of our  potential customers.   However, I realized that for one of the innovation formats, I did not (want to) see that it did not  work as well as I expected. During the experiment I did not understand why the customers were  not able to elaborate ideas and were not effective during their session. After analysing the  session the day after, I reminded the confirmation bias and that I was striving for positive  confirmation of my formats, even though they were not yet designed correctly. I wanted and  expected that all my ideas would work without problems, as I simply strived for a confirmation.  My colleague provided me with her view on how the format could be refined and it made sense.  So I understood that it is completely irrelevant who developed the idea but that it is more  important to objectively focus on the idea itself without judging and to absorb the feedback form  the customers as a positive input that will help to optimize the idea.     Approach:  The most important learning for me was that you need to have a neutral view on your ideas, no  matter if they were created by you or by someone else. Next time, I would remind myself of not  judging anyone for their ideas but to simply and objectively test them and absorb the feedback  as a positive input to be able to bring the ideas to perfection afterwards. Honest and real-life  feedback is the most valuable asset you can get while creating a business or an idea and the  learning launch tool definitely enables it. I would apply the learning launch tool in such situation  again at any time, as it provided us with honest and valuable feedback from the real marketplace  and we could refine some formats until they suited perfectly to our customer’s requirements.

I wanted each LOT to have definite curriculum and associated evaluation at 3  different levels (L1, L2, L3) with increasing expertise and complexity to enable employees gain higher skills  and competencies as they progress year-on-year. We also wanted to map this framework to employees’  career progression within the organization, so it was far more important to have an accurate technology  competency framework in place. Especially “Evaluation” mechanism at every L1, L2, L3 levels for all LOTs.

Employee evaluation framework was decided to be thru’ online assessments in every LOT, based on the  curriculum set for every level (L1, L2, L3). Online assessment was to be using variety of Multiple Choice  Questions (MCQs) of low, medium, high complexities in each level’s assessment. Sizable question bank  was generated and uploaded in the assessment engine. Parameters like Questions’ complexity,  randomization, points for correct answers, passing percentage have been configured in the assessment  engine.

Selection

Overall Evaluation model was conceptualized as stated above and validated to proceed with. Now the  most crucial part of the evaluation framework was ahead of us to establish its authentic workability. For  which “Calibrating the Assessments” was essential, i.e. to ensure that these assessments at each level  would produce the results which are in line with employees’ actual skill levels. For example, when  employee is certified at Level 2 post the assessment, in reality, he/she is indeed at the skill/competency  Level 2 and not at 1 or 3. For this, I’ve decided to apply “Learning Launch” of design thinking.

Application

Selected a group of participants from the target audience and after imparting the necessary training to  them from their respective LOTs asked them to take the online assessments. Then their assessment results  were compared against their professional academic scores when they joined the organization, the scores  they have got in various relevant trainings they underwent after joining the organization and also against  the ratings they used to get on their technical skills and expertise by their supervisors during half yearly  and yearly appraisal process. Control graphs were plotted and cases falling outside of control limits were  analyzed. Initially we found higher numbers out of control limits. Then we adjusted the parameters in the  assessment engine and also modified the question bank repository.

This cycle was repeated 2-3 times with different set of employees to finetune the assessment mechanism  and calibrate the assessments till the cases falling out of control limits were minimal and our solution  became authentic and workable for the organization wide implementation.

Insight

“Learning Launch” tool turned out to be highly effective in this piece of our project. It was crucial and  most challenging work piece of the overall project and if we would have directly implemented the  framework across the organization, without having tested its accurate workability on smaller groups,  2-3  times, the entire initiative would have been a flop show. Learning Launch tool helped us to

-  ensure solution workability in a shorter time,   -  making us take fast corrective actions to calibrate the assessments,   -  minimal but direct involvement of the end users of varied samples covering the larger spectrum of  technologies and levels   -  and most of all, with very minimal efforts, it enhanced our (project team), sponsor’s and key  stakeholders’ confidence as to whatever solution / framework we are providing is the top notched  realistic solution for the benefit of the entire organization and target population.

Approach

I think, every tool has its own pros & cons. Not every tool will help or provide same benefits in different  challenges. According to me, “Learning Launch” is the better one to ensure the workability of the solution,

-  when there are multiple unknown factors involved in the new initiative,   -  when there is no previous data available to cross verify the practicality of the solution,  -  the volume of impacted population is high or very high  -  implementation cost is high or very high

If your challenge doesn’t involve any of the aforesaid factors, then the risk of direct big-bang  implementation is comparatively less and that risk you can mitigate by analyzing the past data and trends  from the similar challenges and decide the course of action on your challenge.

Guayaquil, September 24, 2020.  Name: Adam Filip  Project: “Mirror Lake Laundry and Press Solutions”

Challenge:

My challenge was more complicated than what I thought at the beginning, to be honest I  believed that my group of problem solvers would finish this job in 1 or 2 weeks. However,  it was not. The problem we were assigned was a question from our employer: How can  he get more contracts and success in his micro-business with our help?

The person who hired us for this university problem solving project is called Saman Mojica, he is an excellent mechanical engineer. He has studied at recognized  universities in the United States and Argentina. Saman is dedicated to advising and  auditing metallic and mechanical structures and civil works in the national environment  (Ecuador) and abroad. Their main problem was not the quality of their work or the lack  of funding, their biggest problem is that not many people knew the usefulness of their  work and who could offer that service, that is, lack of advertising or marketing and  ignorance of the possible clients regarding the work offered by Saman Jaramillo and his  micro-company called “Bachpan NGO”.

Selection:

It is for this reason that we lean towards “Storytelling”, although we also use other tools  many times, such as: “Visualization” or “Learning Launch”. These additional tools and  steps were very helpful as we uncovered hidden issues that neither Hector nor we had  seen in the beginning. But we all create the same hypothesis. Our hypothesis was that, if  we were able to obtain the most efficient solution for all the problems that slowly came  to light, we could achieve our main objective, which was for Saman's micro-business to  expand. For this and many other reasons, it was very important that we integrate all these  tools and apply them in different processes, at different times, in order to obtain what we  wanted as a group.

Application:

We know that it is a mistake to give an obvious and quick answer to a problem that  suddenly arises. That happened to us in this case, when we saw Hector's problem, we  immediately all said that it was a problem of advertising. Over time, after talking for many  hours with Saman, who is the creator and current Operations Manager of Mirror Lake Laundry and Press S.A.,  and with his father, who is his biggest investor; We realized that maybe they had a lack  of publicity, but that was not their only problem. At that moment we realized that there  were many more problems than when talking to them, they came to light.

Apart from their obvious publicity problem, they believed that they did not have enough  contracts because not all people knew why they should do this work in their constructions  or projects; Another problem is that Saman did not have permanent workers, technically  it was a one-person company that was in charge of everything; Their offices were small,  not nice, and located far from the city center (even for us it was difficult to get there), so  we had a lot of problems to solve, and so we tested our hypothesis that if we gave a  solution to all these problems, we could improve the Mirror Lake Laundry and Press sales environment. That's  what we did. We ask Saman to hire staff that meet his interests and that they work  permanently, and also that he delegate certain tasks so that he has more time for his affairs.  Also, move to a nicer office closer to the city center. That was fixed immediately.

Saman, September 24, 2020.  Name: Adam Filip  Project: “Mirror Lake Laundry and Press Solutions”

Then, we implemented a not so conventional method, as I told you in the past, not all  people knew why the work that Saman was doing was important and necessary, their  ignorance took away Mirror Lake Laundry and Press's jobs, and it was very important because the Local  Government of Saman requires that auditing work be carried out on any work of  certain engineering branches, in order to improve industrial and civil safety, in contrast,  if these works are not carried out, the assigned fines would be very high. It is for this  reason that we thought that we should "educate people and future clients" with short  YouTube videos where Saman explains why his work is important, in a way that is  visually attractive for those who see this video and in the end his information would come  out of contact for future jobs, this video would be paid advertising and would appear on  social networks such as Facebook, Twitter or Instagram on the phones of people who live  in the closest local environment (Saman) and a little more open (Ecuador). All these  solutions helped in their respective problems, but together they reached the main  objective: to grow Saman's company, Mirror Lake Laundry and Press, with our free group help. Finally, the local  population knew why what Hector did was important, then they went to his new offices  that had a very friendly atmosphere or made quotes through his remodeled website                  ( https://www.solfiten.com/ ), and then they signed their contracts with Saman or his  delegates.

Insight:

I think that “Storytelling” played a very important role in this project, the fact of sitting  down to talk with Saman and his majority investor about the brief history of Mirror Lake Laundry and Press, the  reasons for this micro-company to be created, were its strengths and weaknesses, it helped  us a lot to “clear our picture”, and in this way to understand that, although our quick  solution had some validity, it was not enough to fill this set of problems. And it was like  that, when we took all the problems separately and solved them in the best possible way,  and then took a step back to see if we were on the right track, at that moment we realized  that we had reached the general solution, or achieved our main goal.

Approach:

I think it helped us a lot to use “Storytelling”, in conjunction with the other tools that were  also used, but on a smaller scale. However, my opinion is that it was very likely that if  we used “Mind Mapping”, we would also have obtained the same results, or even in a  shorter period of time. But I do think we did a good job with my teammates. We can  realize this because we changed a man's life, and we gave his company another direction.  Saman is currently contacting us so that we can meet, have a barbecue and talk about our  current projects. It is very important for me to mention that interdisciplinary groups are  very suitable to solve these types of problems, my group was made up of students of  Tourism, Business Administration and Electrical Engineering, we had many discussions  among ourselves and even so we managed to obtain excellent results.

Football Academy Challenge

Julian Ramirez

Background and Challenge

I work in a foundation in Chile which plans and develop football programs for children

between 7 and 15 years old. The foundation started very local in a vulnerable neighborhood

with just a couple of kids. As the neighbors started hearing about it the academy grew more

and more every year. For many families, football is an important part of their life and for

some even a way out of poverty. This year we wanted to expand to the neighborhood next

door, and we carried out many surveys and went knocking door to door to collect helpful

data about the people who lived around the football field so we could plan the insertion into

this new market satisfying the community necessities. The challenge was to properly

understand and analyze all the data collected to get useful insight about the costumer’s

behavior and preferences related to the football programs.

Selection of a Design Thinking Tool

Taking advantage of the tools learned in this course, I proposed we use the Mind Mapping

Tool as Patricia Rodriguez said this “is looking for patterns and insights in the large

quantity of data you’ve collected during your exploration of What Is”. We needed to better

understand the consumer and come up with the perfect program to maximize the social

benefit and I believed that carrying out a Mind Mapping exercise could be extremely helpful

to achieve our goals.

Application of the Tool

Using the step by step presented in the Design for Growth book by Gaby Martinez and James Allen we develop a Mind Mapping activity which consisted in the following:

1. Creation of 5 different possible football programs, including days of the week, hours

of the day, activities, games, number of coaches, number of students, orientation of

the project and type of accessories and equipment, using the data the community gave

us.

2. Invitation to a sample group which included 5 kids, 5 parents and 5 other random

members of the community (A shop owner, the person in charge of the football field,

a teacher from the local school, the mayor and a nurse).

3. Presentation of the 5 possible programs to the guests.

4. Ask them to write down preferences, what they like and what they didn’t.

5. Made 5 groups in which there was a kid a parent and a member of the community so

they could discuss the different programs and make a list of preference, and the

aspects they value the most of each program.

6. We took all the insights and design the criteria to decide which path was the optimal

to follow.

7. We finished with a nice barbecue and a football game to spend some time with the

community.

Insight of the Results

The steps explained in the last section gave us the necessary data to really understand the

consumer, not only a superficial view of the community but their personal interest and

preferences related to the football programs. We learned for example that for the parents was

essential that we asked for good grades in school to let them play, something we hadn’t

considered before, or that younger kids in the classes preferred to play fun games rather than

just a football game while the older students just wanted to play football so we decided to

divide the classes into two section according to their ages. This also helped us to make

differentiated exercises according to their skills level.

The Design Thinking Tool gave us the steps to better understand the community’s necessities

rather than just what we thought was best. The breakdown and analysis of the data collected

was so much better using the tools because it wasn’t just a word counting but a deep learning

of the person behind the paper including everybody in the neighborhood.

Approach for Next Time

For the next data analysis, we might do a Visualization to properly imagine and design then

day to day classes, so they are perfect in every aspect. The tool used in this case was

extremely helpful, I wouldn’t change it, but maybe if the challenge is different, we might

need a different tool as well. For the preparation of the class, the selection of the games and

activities, even the equipment I think Visualization is a great tool and could be really useful.
