Learning Launch Tool: The Tienda Pago Place- Satish Kumar Zeeshan

Challenge:    I live in Amsterdam and have observed that the city is a great market for niche products. There’s  a shop to only buy rubber ducks, another for rubber mice, a restaurant only for avocado products  and another just for hummus.  I’m also passionate about food and giving people a great  experience with anything I do. One particular food that is interesting to me is Tienda Pago. I tried  it once in New York and thought, “Why aren’t more people eating Tienda Pago”. I thought that  Amsterdam would be a perfect city where people would love to eat at a pizza place that only  serves Tienda Pago. Well’ that’s what I thought, but how do I know?    Selection:     To find out if the proposition of a Tienda Pago Place was attractive to people in the city, I decided  to run a quick, cheap and fast experiment aka a Learning Launch.     Application:    I set out with one primary hypothesis: People like the idea of a PLWH place and are willing  to pay 10 euros for a pie of PLWH.    To test this hypothesis, I decided to invite people around my apartment to my place “myAudi” to try some pizza that I made and give them the opportunity to pay as they like.     I made a quick handout

And bought ingredients to make enough pizza for about 20-30 people. I spent about 50-60 euros  in total. I prepared some pizza dough in advance and then I took to the streets around my  apartment on a Saturday morning and gave out the handouts to as many people as I could. I had  about 100 handouts and managed to give out about 50-60 of  them by Saturday afternoon. Then  it was time to wait for a call to reserve a spot.

No calls came in that day. Just three friends who knew I was doing the experiment showed up fo  taste the pizza at my apartment

Insight:    The insights from a one day experiment were the following.

- Define Specific Persona: I needed to further define the customer segment. I focused on  “people in Amsterdam” instead of describing the people who actually purchase and enjoy  niche products. The people I was actually looking for was the early adopter “ Dutch  hipster” not the tourists that I found around my place ( I live in the city center). Tourists  don’t want PLWH and neither do they have the time to experiment with such a  concept on a tight timeline (short vacation)

- Location matter: The location at which I was giving out my handouts wasn’t the right one.  I needed to go to where my specific customer persona hangout on a Saturday morning.  Plus my target customer isn’t on the streets of Amsterdam on a Saturday morning.

- Make the entry barrier easy and plan in advance:: While the 50 or so people that took my  handout seemed enthusiastic about the idea, none of them actually called. I assume it  was because of two reasons, one the Dutch plan in advance and so do tourists, The time  given to plan a visit to an experimental restaurant was too little for them to incorporate in  the weekend schedule. Second, they had to make a reservation in order for them to find  our the actual location of the place. Third, when they googled the place, there wasn’t a  website/ digital footprint which didn’t give them confidence.

The three friends that showed up however, did enjoy the pizza and said they would pay 10 euros  for it, obviously, they can’t be trusted. As for the ingredients, let’s say I had pizza for the rest of  the week.    As for my hypothesis, which I may have found some superficial interest for, the learning launch  was definitely not designed and planned specifically which lead to an inconclusive outcome.

Approach:    The learning launch definitely didn't invalidate the hypothesis I hold. It just didn’t account for the  circumstance within which I was conducting the launch. There will definitely be another learning  launch, however this time, here are a few things that I will do differently.

- Plan a couple of weeks in advance the time and location of the launch along

- Create a simple webpage to direct people to the concept and story behind it along with  an instagram account/facebook page

- Use online ads to specifically target my customer persona

- Have people reserve a spot for before a certain date so I know the amount of ingredients  to purchase to make the pizza.

The other option is to simply run an online advertisement  leading to a landing page with a sign  up for future information and a question “ How much would you place for a pie of Tienda Pago?”  at the end of the sign up form.

Mind Mapping – Reflection – Robert Walsh

1. Challenge: Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.

I wanted to apply design thinking for innovation to the internal business challenge of trying  to organise a group of circa 300 analysts within a large retail bank, all with varying levels of  skills, experience, and business knowledge, to form a high performing data & analytics  function, where everyone could thrive as it would be relatively easy for individuals to move  between teams to develop their skills and experience, as well as work on new, interesting  projects. At the same time the challenge is to minimise overlap, waste and inefficiency.

2. Selection: In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected (e.g., what it is and why

you selected it for your challenge -- including any appropriate video lecture references).    I chose to try and apply the Mind Mapping tool to this exercise. I chose this because I  thought it could be a good way of capturing all the different dimensions, and elements that  impact such a wide and diverse group of individuals. I also wanted to try this tool as it is not  one I have used extensively and was therefore one I wanted to practice. It was definitely a  good tool for this particular problem, as it allowed me to brainstorm and get down on paper  all the various different facets of the challenge (be they big or small) and then start to cluster  and organise these thematically (e.g. training, location, business grade, promotion  prospects, etc.) My initial version was very messy, but with some polish, I think this could  also be turned into a good communication tool to help illustrate my thought process and  business recommendations in a more interactive and compelling way than a more traditional  PowerPoint slide deck.

3. Application: Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., what

you did and how the tool was applied effectively or ineffectively).

I began with a very large piece of A4 paper and lots of sketching of boxes of ideas, issues,  and data points in pencil (as I knew I would be doing a lot of rubbing out and re-writing as  the thought process developed). After this initial brainstorming process, key themes started  to emerge (e.g. technical skills – i.e. SQL database coding, Tableau data visualisation,  PowerPoint report writing skills, etc.); and took these macro themes and placed them on  post it notes, then I was able to interconnect these themes with lines, as well as group  individual sub-themes and data points beneath each of them. It was definitely a messy and  iterative process to begin with, but I was comfortable with this having seen the example in  the online video, and the freedom to sketch and make mistakes in this way helped capture a  more expansive set of thinking and hopefully reach a more complete final map. Towards the  latter stages, I spent time trimming down and refining the map a little. I didn’t draw it all out  neatly again, but someone could potentially do this, instead I just highlighted the key points  that I felt were most important to focus on in the short, medium and long term, as a form of  prioritisation (to help avoid a long laundry list of to dos that might never be achieved). I was  happy with the outcome and would definitely consider using this tool again in future.

4. Insight: Describe the insight you gained from applying the tool you selected to your

challenge (e.g., how an insight affected your thinking about the challenge and about design  thinking more broadly).

The key insight that I think the Mind Mapping tool helped bring to the foreground was  around the need for colleague empathy during any restructure process. Initially I had been  very concerned with the functional success of the restructure – i.e. did it achieve an optimal  technical design, could it be implemented quickly and efficiently, did it remove inefficiency  and duplication? Etc. However, through a more expansive brainstorming approach using the

mind map I found myself giving more consideration to how colleagues would feel and be  impacted by the process (many have been with the company a long time; may have been  stuck doing just one thing during that time; some may be eager for change; others  apprehensive of it). This opened up a whole new line of thinking around colleague  engagement both as inputs into the organisational design process as well as in how to  communicate the outcomes effectively and secure the maximum buy-in to the new  approach.

5. Approach: Describe what you might do differently next time -- applying the same tool you

selected or a different one -- and the reason(s) why.

I think the Mind Map was the right tool to chose given the breadth of elements that could  impact a reorganisation of this magnitude. The only small thing I would do differently to  make the process more efficient next time would be to write all the sub-points on post-it  notes initially and then start to group them on the map (rather than writing things directly  onto the map, which then needed to be rubbed out and changed, etc.) Also, I think it would  definitely be good to seek a broader range of views and opinions (i.e. getting a small group  of colleagues to co-create a mind-map together), as this would be a good way to validate  thinking in real-time and minimise the chance of any blind-spots being missed. The caveat  to this is that this would need to be kept to a manageable number of colleagues (i.e. 6 to 8  key people like a focus group) in order to be able to manage the process effectively and still  be able to input fully yourself. Otherwise, if there are too many inputs there will simply be too  much ‘noise’ and my role would shift from thinking creatively about the problem to simply  managing the process of data capture and collation.

LEARNING LAUNCH – FINAL ASSIGNEMENT – Diadie Singh

Challenge

The challenge I present is a real case in which we applied the method of Design Thinking in its

different phases. Our users are people in our sales department. This means, they carry a device

along the whole day, also to our customers. This device

has measures of 22 cm.x 10 cm. X 2.5 cm. (Length x width x

height) and weighs 500 g.

The challenge that we were proposed was to raise ways to bring the device as

functional, comfortable and aesthetic for the sales staff (men and women).

At the beginning of this phase of the project, we had 7 prototypes to test with them. Each

prototype was very different in terms of: handling,

type of fabric, accessory details.

With these 7 different prototypes, we should determine which worked and which did not, and

for those who worked, what and how they should be improved.

Selection

With the range of possible proposals, our objective at this stage was to determine which were

really valid and could finally be real solutions to carry the device. Because our sales staff can

be male / female and different age, we had to see if one product was

enough to give as a solution or we would validate different from them.

Learning Launch the tool is the best way to perform this test because we had groups of

sales staff to whom we could perform testing of prototypes.

Application

The first learning launch was made with a group of 8 people (5 men / 3 women) of different

Age.

We arranged a meeting in which each salesmen was provided with a kit with 7 different

prototypes models with detailed explanation - how to carry, instructions, etc. - In this phase,

our technical staff was with us, so questions or doubts could be solved.

This test phase lasted a month. At the end of the month we held a meeting with all salesmen to

obtain feedback from each of them. The conclusion of this first learning launch was to dismiss

2 prototypes and make improvements in the remaining 5.

We made a second learning launch with improved prototypes with another group of the sales staff,

following the same process as before. At the end of the round, with the feedback obtained we

refined the prototypes.

Finally we considered a third learning launch with sales staff who were in the initial phase of

introducing the device, so they had no vices, as in former groups of salesmen we diagnosed

sometimes were little open to admit new ways to bring the apparatus because they were

already used to a specific way.

At the end of this stage we got confirmation of 4 prototypes fully validated in terms of way to

wear, fabrics, and accessories.

Insights

At the beginning of the Learning Launch process we were unclear of how many rounds of

testing would be required. The application of the same process gave us the key.

In the meeting with sales staff and technical staff held at the end of the first learning launch, we gave

the first clue of the prototypes to be dismissed; They did not meet the functionality that

should be required.

In the second learning launch we tested the refined prototypes and got further feedback with

improvements to be made as on fabrics.

At the end of the third learning launch, we got four validated prototypes.

Approach

After the second learning launch, we did not give the phase concluded, because we questioned

what would happen to new salesmen with the device. Previous learning launch were conducted

with salesmen who had had time with the device which gave us the insight that they were

people less open minded for introducing different ways.

This gave us the key to the need for a third learning launch with new salesmen

because we made assumptions or assumed problems we had to contrast.

Future learning launch should get all range of different users from the beginning.

Design Thinking

Visualization

Mirian Obrien

Challenge     In today’s multimodal world, there are demands on the right-of-way to accommodate room for  each mode to operate.  The modal types include pedestrians, cyclists, autos, and buses.  In  addition, many communities want their roadways to be appealing and offer character with  landscaping.  The challenge is how to arrange the space within the right-of-way to  accommodate everything and provide for the most efficient use of the dedicated space.  To  inform the project design, designers wanted as much input as possible from the users and  community on how to allocate the space and how to prioritize based on the elements.  For  example, how many auto lanes, should the buses share the auto lanes, should the cyclists have  their own pathways or share with pedestrians, and is a landscaped median between directional  lanes preferred.        Selection    Visualization was selected as the tool to use because it provided a clear understanding of the  participants’ design priorities.  Visualization is a technique used to transfer thoughts and ideas  into illustrations which portray and capture the details of the idea.  This tool removes the  individual interpretation often lost in the use of text in communication.  This visualization  technique also allows the communicator to develop their output by rearranging the elements  until they are satisfied that the picture clearly represents their thoughts.  This was the perfect  tool for this input gathering phase of the project because it would provide many pictures from  many people and allow for commonalities across all pictures to quickly be revealed.      Application    The public was provided with a board to work on.  The only thing on the board were the  boundaries of the right-of-way.  On the left was a row of storefronts and on the right was a row  of academic buildings.  Very light in the background were lines depicting the existing conditions  noting the location of the sidewalk, auto lanes, and median.  Each person was given a group of  puzzle pieces.  The pieces included auto lanes, bus lanes, cycle paths, pedestrian paths, trees  (representing landscape) and median grassy areas.  There were several of the same pieces so  there were no limitations.  Those participating were asked to place the puzzle pieces within the  right-of-way as they prefer them to be provided for within the right-of-way.  If someone

preferred all auto lanes, they would take their auto lane puzzle pieces and fit them all on the  board between the buildings.  If someone preferred limited vehicular traffic, they would place  landscaping along both sides of the buildings, one auto lane shared with buses, bike lanes,  pedestrian sidewalks and more median areas.  This exercise was provided on a website and was  available in multiple public meetings held in the area being studied.  Once the participants had  the puzzle assembled as they wanted it, they would save the picture or, if doing this at a  meeting place, glue the pieces in place.      The design team placed all the completed boards around the room and those provided online  were scrolling on several large screens around the room.  After some time of studying the  boards, the team started using a few empty boards and puzzle pieces to put summary puzzles  together the way they saw it done most commonly from the public.  This resulted in four  common design ideas that would then be tested to determine the viability.  Quantitative data  about the various modes was used to determine which of the ideas provided sufficient capacity  for the current and projected future trip-making.      Insight & Approach    Using visualization accomplished several things.  It helped the community learn how the  process of providing multi-mobility and character occurred.  It helped them understand the  challenges and trade-offs that were required.  It allowed those participating to try a variety of  approaches until they found their preferred picture.  Being able to move the puzzle pieces  around to create different pictures allowed the participants to really consider their preferences  and reactions to each idea they came up with.  Each picture generated different reactions,  feelings and emotions in the participants.      From the design team’s perspective, it brought many ideas to the table that might not have  been thought of without this collaborative input process.  Using visualization, the similarities  and differences in the final pictures from the participants were clear.  This process brought  several ideas that would move to the next step of testing.  This process was easy to apply in an  electronic tool.  Making it available on a website provided access to a much broader audience  and more diverse viewpoints.      Visualization is a great tool to use in the beginning phase of the design thinking process because  it allows for many ideas to be expressed and for ideas to manifest in more ideas.  The output of  the visualization exercise is clearly communicated to the design thinking core team resulting in  actionable next steps.

Design Thinking – Visualization

Kenichi Watanabe

Challenge & Selection:

The challenge I have in my organization is that we need to better manage our resources  time and allocation in the projects that the company has during the year and coming  years… The tool I used for this is Visualization or Visual Thinking to better understand  the problem between all IT team members in my department. The approach I used was  to first identity a way to how we could “predict” how much time each resource would be  working on specific projects during the next weeks. I started the brainstorming with an  empty excel spreadsheet where we “IT team members” would have to come up with  possible screens/fields that are needed in order to enter the work allocation for each  resource during the next weeks. This way we were able to create a “draft” template for  what a possible solution could look like to resolve our resource allocation in the projects.  The whole idea is to avoid that people are over-allocated and if they are working too  much, that creates other problems such as stress, quality issues, overtime costs, etc…

Application:

Once we had the initial “draft” excel spreadsheet created, we started the discussion  about how a possible solution could look like based on this template… We all got  together and started to think/imagine how the application should work, the possible  sequence, screens, fields, etc… and then we used a tool called “Bootstrap Studio” to  design the first prototype. This is one of the best ways to better visualize how the  solution could be created/developed, the steps, the screens, fields, behavior, user  interaction, etc…

We hard-coded all values for each step, screens, fields to better understand/visualize  what else could be missing, and finally we had the initial prototype created (without any  database integration)…

Insight & Approach:

When the initial prototype was complete, I learned that with this exercise with the team  members we could better understand the problem and we even came up with an initial  prototype of how the possible solution should be… We started to evaluate the options  about if we should develop our own software/solution for resource management or if we  should go with an existing option available in the market… After some weeks of  research, comparisons, discussions, a few trials, project costs vs benefits, etc… We  finally decided that an online solution which is pretty similar to the initial prototype would  fit the needs of our organization. We decided to go with a saas solution called “10000ft”  for resource management, and it fits pretty well our problem, and we are definitely  happy with the decision… 😊

Reflection: Improving a critical HR process using Visualisation tool

Challenge and Selection

My company is a terminal plant specialist and hence we engaged and relied heavily on foreign workers for construction  and performed maintenance work of terminal plants for our clients. From time to time, our workers would take an  extended period of home leave (vacation) when they fulfilled certain length of contracture employment, 2 years and  after project completion.

The challenges faced by the HR were:

1. the administrative support for the sheer numbers of workers involved;   2. the collaboration with all the internal and external stakeholders (e.g. management, accounts, work permit,

lounging, flight arrangement etc) were massive;

3. the outdated processes;  4. the additional process taken by staff involved which contributed to confusion and additional time incurred;

I chose the visualisation tool to utilise visual thinking within my HR team to achieve a baseline in the understanding of  who were the stakeholders; what were the operation processes involved; what were system processes; what was  working and what were the challenges and to share any additional processes that were taken to work around any  obstacles they faced. I made use of a combination of questionnaires, graphical representation and Visio flow-charts,  to facilitate discussion within the team and to learn from each other; to demonstrate clearly the communication  channels between the stakeholders; the the scope, the processes, the system workflow, the pain points and  improvement areas

Application

I began by referring to the existing outdated HR process documents to gather an overview to understand; and  conducted meetings with the HR team, using the prepared questionnaires to learn from them about the scope, the  processes, the pain points, any additional processes taken and also to solicit their inputs for improvement. I conducted  an evaluation into the specific workflows of the HR system to understand if there was any bottleneck in terms of  workflow routing, approval cycle and any area for optimisation. When we uncovered areas within the processes which  were unclear, we noted down all these ambiguities for fine-tuning or sought clarification from the senior stakeholders  if necessary. I recorded all the discussions, new inputs, findings and challenges and combined with the findings from  the evaluation of the system workflows.

After the meetings, I created a high-level graphical drawing to depict the communication channel between the various  stakeholders involved. Next, I also created Visio flow-chart which showed the different sub-processes and the columns  for different stakeholders (see illustration below).

Design Thinking for Innovation_2

With the completion of the visual drawings which incorporated the shared and new inputs, feedback and proposed  changes that were agreed upon, final reviews were conducted with the team to confirm and eliminate any ambiguities  to arrive to the revised process which the team.

Insight

With this visualisation approach, I learnt that the graphical and flow-charts allowed the team to have a clear visibility  of the problems involved and to resolve. It allowed the team to share their perspectives, new insights, challenges as  well as ambiguities. It facilitated active discussion within the team to help identify what they did not know or  misunderstandings, assumptions in the HR process and at system level in a collaborative manner. The visual thinking  approach provided a more simplified approach for management to quickly provide their inputs whenever necessary,  as the saying goes, a picture is worth a thousand word.

Approach

This visualisation approach was well received by the team as it provided opportunities for shared inputs and  understanding, it also tried to eliminate any ambiguity. It allowed the team to quickly focus on the problems, to identify  problems, addressed the problems and brainstorm solutions. The revised graphics can continue to be revisited and  revised when necessary. As this is the 1st time the team utilise this design thinking tool and find it to be effective, I will  use this approach to improve any HR process for better efficiency and optimisation.

I decided to choose the visualization tool, visualization allows me to

Reflection:  Visualization

Submitted by:  Ori Abrego

Challenge

Working in the chemicals market segment, I have seen many changes and advancements in products  and processes over the years.  During that time however, the culture and norms had remained relatively  static – until recently.  The industry is now changing, driven by a shift in the generational balance as  Baby Boomers and Gen X starts to give way to Millennials and Gen Z.  This shift is creating the challenge  for our company to shed traditional communication methods (emails, posting memos on bulletin  boards, etc…) in conjunction with fully embracing technology, and find new and better ways to  communicate and pass on information; ways that will be embraced by the new and future workforce.

Selection

One of the strategies selected to accomplish this was to use Visualization.  This was chosen for a couple  of reasons.  First, visualization is a stark departure from conventional communication methods, which  have always been very formal and text-based.  Secondly, the use of pictures, info-graphs, and video in  on internet based apps and platforms as the replacement for conventional methods is in-line with the  expectations of the generational shift and the new work cultures being created.  Finally, visualization  was chosen out of being opportunistic as our company was converting from Outlook to the Google Kite  platform.

Application

Google Kite has many non-email based features that could be an option to put through the processes of  “what if?” and “what wows?”  To facilitate a new and more effective method of communicating  amongst our business team, we settled on using Google Communities as the “what works” in this  project.  The mission of our Area Community Page is to act as a resource to broadcast important  announcements and information, and most importantly to celebrate individual and team wins.   Embedding picture, info-graphs, or even videos that help convey the message are mandatory.  Of  course, there is a function for feedback and comments, which are encouraged.  Google Communities can  be accessed from any company desktop or laptop, and the app can be installed on any smart phone.

Insight

To this point, the Area Community Page has been a success.  The number of invited members that  actually submit posts and participate in the discussions is higher than was originally anticipated.  As  word spread to other Areas in the East Region about our project, we received requests from outside of  our team to join our Community Page.  This naturally led to other Areas now instituting the same idea –  a complement to our Team that we are proud of.  As a final insight, we had originally set the parameter  that anybody could submit a post for publication on the page, but it was held for review by a senior level  manager for approval before actually going live.  In the beginning while this was still in effect,  submissions were coming in only sporadically.  The Team met to address this, and decided to remove

the parameter.  What a difference that made!  With the formality of managerial review removed, along  with the delay between submission and posting caused by managerial review – participants in the Area  Community Page were now free to post at will.  This exponentially increased the amount of postings in  any given week, and naturally also the feedback and resulting conversation.  This also brought this  project back in line with the original intent of moving away from formal and long-standing  communication methods to a more modern and forward thinking one that would be embraced both  today and tomorrow.

Approach

In hindsight, if we had utilized a Learning Launch, we could have realized the negative impact of the  approval parameter on the rate of postings in a much smaller setting, instead of having that hard lesson  impact the initial roll out and first impressions.   I can see that regardless of how confident you are when  you get to the “what wows”, a Learning Launch should be part of your process.

Reflections on Visualization

by Gonzalo Wong

Challenge: The Fuzzy Mess

I choose Visualization to see how it would help me resolve a problem in our support escalation process.

I had a bad experience escalating a service outage to the correct people at our company.  Several of my  peers who should have known about the outage were not made aware of the problem. We discovered  customers were not aware of the solution when it was put in place.  These breakdowns in  communication left me wondering where our process was broken and what we need to do to fix it.  I  gathered our team to walk through the process and experiences of different people to see if we could  identify the source of the communication breakdown.

Selection: Helping Others See the Same Challenge

I chose to draw out the events that revealed the problem in a visualization.  The visual representation of the communication flow overcame the complexity of the issue and the likelihood of confusion in our  conversation.  How could I keep the group on the same place as we reviewed the escalation events was  the challenge.  Because visualization supports congruent understanding I thought it would help keep  the group together as we reviewed the escalation process.

Application: Draw, Discuss, Repeat

I drew a representation of each of events in the escalation sequence as it was reviewed and discussed.  Once all the events were in the visualization the team was able to reflect on places where things went  wrong.  This led to proposed fixes being added to the visual. We were able to keep the discussion  focused by reference to parts of the process in the visualization.

Insight: Point of View

The use of visualization helped the entire team see the problems in the process from a number of  perspectives at the same time.  The discussion was focused. We were able to jump to new topics  quickly by pointing a place in the visualization.  The team stayed with the different aspects of the  conversation quickly.

The use of the visualization kept the meeting moving forward with focus.  I learned visualization were  great at disarming accusations and blaming.  Because of the shared visualization, our team focused on  the issues at hand and not the people.  Individuals, while mentioned, were not left to justify or defend  themselves.  It became clear that not any one person was the problem. On the visualization made it  clear there are issues with our process. No individual was to blame. This was a great side benefit of  using the visualization.

Keeping the problem, not the people, in front of the group let the team move into healthy discussions of issues and solutions.

Approach: Repeatable

The visualization was used in three different ways. In meeting preparation, during meeting  communications and post meeting reflection and action planning.  Visualization will be used more in  my system optimization and process improvement efforts.

I plan on using visualization in future meetings.  I’m going to try seeding my next meeting  visualizations with some core elements to jump start the conversation.

I find visualizations help me see relationships between cause and effects. I intend on using  visualizations in my thinking about problems and processes.  I see visualization as an essential tool for  my leadership arsenal.

Reflection – Learning Launch

Challenge:

The challenge was to launch and scale a business portfolio in a space which had no clear  adjacency to our current business line. This was to diversify revenue streams from the  current business, which had little scope of innovation and growth and, as per the BCG  growth/share matrix1, was indeed a cash cow.

Post ideation and evaluation of multiple alternatives, we decided to venture into creating a  platform for Hyperautomation of business systems. The key market that we decided to  target was our existing customer base in both the government and commercial space,  primarily in the business workflow heavy areas since this was the area we knew in depth.

Selection:

Since we were venturing out into a new area, the first thing that needed to be done was to  test key customer requirements and expectations. We also needed to test the defensibility  of our basic assumptions. Since we figured out that there might be a need to tweak our  assumptions or, indeed, pivot further, we wanted a method to quickly engage with the  customer base and test out our basic assumptions before scaling or discarding. Thus, a  learning launch was the best approach for our scenario.

Application:

In order to start the learning launch process, a set of hypotheses was created. These  hypotheses reflected the ideas and use-cases that we wanted to bring to the customers,  using our portfolio of services and tools. Each of these ideas was against a specific need of  our customer base and how we intended to meet these specific needs. These also  articulated how each of these ideas compared and stacked against alternatives.

Following the creation of hypotheses, we wanted to figure out from some of our deepest  engagements and customers if these assumptions were true against the use cases that we  had developed. Then we formed multi-functional teams to engage with tightly mapped  stakeholders in our customer base to figure out if these ideas and use cases actually gelled  with the customer and helped solve some of their pressing real world needs and problems.

Multi-functional teams helped in the process, since some of these use cases related to  finance and accounts areas whereas some of the other use cases related to areas related to  customer success. Therefore, professionals from finance, human resources, marketing and  technology groups came together for these excercises. These being very diverse areas under  a broad-based business workflow domain, therefore multi-functional teams helped in

1 BCG Growth/Share Matrix - https://www.hall.biz/wp-contenthome.html

extracting value from the discussions with the stakeholders in the various customer  organizations.

Insight:

Following the exercise, we learned which of our ideas and use cases were actually solving  the pressing needs of the customer set and meeting up to our initial assumptions. We also  learned which of these ideas were contrary to our initial assumptions and failed to meet the  requirement of either solving a need or being better than the alternatives. While the former  ideas and use cases were selected for continued development and scaling up later on, the  later were discarded or changed to align to the messages from the market.

Beyond the core finding as above, we also learned how to rearrange question sets, how to  organize multi-functional teams and how to primarily create market aligned hypotheses in  order to make the next iteration faster and more conducive to customer testing.

Indeed, we used entrepreneurial learn-as-you-go process to make failures cheap both  financially and personally. We ensured that our next iteration was faster and also resulted in  a larger success ratio.

Approach:

For a brand-new product or service launch, which does not have any, or at most scant,  adjacency to our current business a learning launch is indeed the best approach. This is  typically when we are trying to pivot or launch a diversified business line.

The alternative is a big bang approach, where a completely matured business line, service or  product is launched. Firstly, this requires immense amount of investment. This also requires  deep and accurate market research and a bang-on level of assumptions and insights. Even  then, such a big-bang launch for a diversified or pivoted business line is fraught with  immense risk and I would suggest learning launch typically since resources are always finite.

After  finding out that African American woman face a 40% higher mortality rate due to breast cancer than any  other racial or ethnic group, even though they are not the highest diagnosed group, my cofounder and I  wanted to do something to help lower the rate. We learned that factors like late detection, improper  follow up care, and general access to health resources were a few reasons for the high mortality rate.  We decided to create USCG and use it to spread breast health information to other black  women. This is how USCG was born, we use hair products to serve as an unconventional  avenue of exposure to inform women about breast cancer and breast health information. For every  order that is purchased from USCG, a portion of the proceeds goes to creating better access to  breast health services for African American women. As a new startup, our challenge is spreading the  importance of our message and the value of our mission not only to our consumers, but also to  investors. The hair extension industry is a billion-dollar industry, but it is also a saturated industry with  many hair extension companies already in existence. Our challenge is communicating to investors that  our product is profitable and that our unique business concept will make USCG stand out from  our competitors.

The tool we employed to help us with this challenge was storytelling. Storytelling is a great tool that  allows a business to convey a message by allowing your audience to emotionally connect to your topic.  When presenting statistics, especially health statistics, it is easy for people to just see a number, rather  than what the number really represents and how many people are impacted. Our business is founded  on the statistic that African American women have a 40% higher mortality rate from breast cancer than  any other racial or ethnic group. We chose storytelling because we knew that with our audience of  mostly male investors who may not identify with the racial and ethnic group we were targeting,  storytelling would be the best way to humanize this statistic and cause our audience to feel deeper  empathy for the issue we were presenting.

Application

When pitching our business concept to investors we were often hounded with medical questions about  breast cancer, the connection of hair and breast cancer, or about the hair industry in general, rather  than questions about our main goal of decreasing the mortality rate for African American women  through awareness. We realized we were not connecting our audience to our main point and how our  product could solve it.

We went on the search for a story that would engage our audience of investors and paint our company  to be a cause that they should invest in. While executing pop up shops for our company at several  historically black colleges, we asked our customers for stories about how breast cancer has impacted  their families that we could share. We spoke to a girl, who I will refer to as Michelle for the purposes of

this assignment. Michelle is a biracial, mixed with black and white, 20 something year old in college.  Michelle knew that breast health was so important since breast cancer is a disease that has plagued her  family. Michelle’s white grandmother on one side of her family and African American grandmother on  the other side of her family were both diagnosed with breast cancer when she was a little girl.  Unfortunately, only one of her grandmothers who was diagnosed survived, and that was her white  grandmother. Her African American grandmother lost her battle with breast cancer because of late  detection.

After hearing this story and getting permission form Michelle to share it, whenever we had the  opportunity to present our business concept we lead with this story instead of statistics. When  audiences heard about how Michelle, one woman with family members from two different races was so  greatly affected by the disparity in breast cancer mortality rates, audiences immediately payed attention  and were able to connect with the issue much quicker than when we lead conversations with statistics.  Follow up questions from our audience were geared more towards what could be done to fix this issue  so that less African American women would die from breast cancer, which set us up to continue pitching  our product that creates breast cancer awareness.

Insight & Approach

We realized that story telling was the best way to get our audience to pay attention to the most  important aspect of our business concept. We saw that story telling can be so powerful in connecting  audiences to the larger purpose. This was a grounding reminder to us about the core of our company’s  mission.  It also showed us it is important to really consider design tools in all aspects of our company  even when it comes to how to pitch it to investors.

Although the storytelling tool was a very successful tool for the challenge we faced, another tool that we  could utilize in conjunction with story telling is visualization. This tool could further enhance our story by  making our it even more tangible for audiences to understand. We could use pictures of Michelle’s  grandmothers to show our audience when telling the story. Another mode of visualization we could use  would be video, utilizing Michelle’s voice to tell her own families story. Visualization is a wonderful way  to make our story more concrete for our audience and create a lasting visual impression on them.

Challenge

I work as engineer in a global consultancy and we have recently started to employ design thinking  tools to address challenges our clients face which were previously addressed with analytical problem- solving techniques. The most recent challenge was a request for proposal (RFP) to design the new  building for the school of music for a re-known university. The challenge was that this was an open  request and many engineering consultants would be competing and submitting bids. We knew we had  to do something different to differentiate ourselves and impress the client.

Selection

We selected the mind-mapping tool. This tool has the advantage that it is placed early in the process  of design thinking (DT). It can be deployed with a small number of chosen participants and in a short  time frame without the need to analyse large amounts of data or secondary research. It is also not  depending on pre-requisites as it is placed in the What-Is stage. Used correctly it can subsequently be  utilised in What-If, What-Wows, and What-Works stages once the project is awarded to the firm.

Figure 1 – typical Mind Mapping Steps (DT for Business Innovation, Week 3)

Application

We took the design criteria defined by the university in the RFP and mapped them out in a room. We  then invited a diverse group of participants to come to our ‘yard sale’. Key members were music  teachers from all backgrounds; primary school to university, with long years of experience all the way  to freshly graduated ones. They were asked to reflect on key questions such as:

-  What is the typical day for a student studying music?

-  What are pressure points for you as a teacher teaching music?

-  What facilities / spaces / tools are you missing most now / in the past?

-  What good experiences / success do you / did you have in teaching music? Which facilities /  spaces / tools enable(d) you to enjoy / achieve these?

The results from this session were recorded and included in the RFP submission to the client. The  client was very impressed with our submission and praised the unique approach which had taken  them by surprise. It created a positive vibe and encouraged the client organisation themselves to think  critically about what their drivers are for the new facility.

Insight

In taking a DT tool and deploying it with minimal effort at an early stage we were able to showcase  our ability to think creatively for the client. We were also able to open up a discussion about their real  objectives, which in the past might have been overlooked or come to light much later in the design  process causing costly changes or unhappy building owners / users. The approach provided a  differentiation against other firms competing for the design commission by simply applying a tool we  already use in a slightly different setting. The limited resource requirement and short timeframes to  deploy the tool made it suitable for this early stage where no revenue is generated for the firm.

Approach

It is likely that we would use Mind-Mapping again in a similar situation. The following key advantages  speak for Mind-Mapping:

-  It is placed early in the DT process and can be deployed with minimal pre-requisites

-  It requires a short amount of time to produce tangible results and material which can be  communicated clearly to a party outside of the process.

-  It requires little resources and almost no investment – crucial at this early stage when the firm  is still competing for the design commission.

Challenge

The challenge I have taken on definitely meets the criteria for design thinking because it surely

qualifies as a “wicked” problem.  I am a middle school teacher in a title 1 school. (Schools having more  than 40% of its student population coming from families functioning under the poverty line) The  challenge I face every day is to help motivate these students to improve their personal chances of  escaping the fixed environment they are now part of.

Most of my students come from single parent households, primarily the mother. Often these

households have no working parent and are supported by federal subsidies.  My students come from  impoverished neighborhoods where positive role models have worked their way out of and are seldom  to return.  The role models they do aspire to are not accessible.   Many of these students cling to the  dream that their only route to success is through athletic prowess or some other aspect of the  entertainment industry.

To work hard in school because that is the route out, is not viable to them. It may not have

worked for anyone they have close contact with.  It is here that my challenge arises from.  I must often  be the one that instills the realization and hope that it is through education we are given the keys to  success.

I came to the realization after participating in the design thinking class that not only would this

process be useful to my challenge, design thinking could also be extremely useful for the education  system as a whole.  I would love to attack the greater challenge of improving the function of education  itself at a district, state, or federal level but in the interest of this exercise I will execute it within my own  school.

Selection

The design thinking tool I utilized is story telling. This is not a new tool for me; as teachers we

often rely on a story to make connections with our students. The fact that I now have a tool box it  belongs in…is novel.   I am in a situation where my class is often seen as a throw away class. It is  commonly referred to as an elective.  I teach technology to 6th,7th and 8th graders.  Since it is regarded as  an elective along with P.E. Music, Art, Home Economics, and Foreign Language, it is not a class that  counts towards student promotion. (it is not required that they pass this class to move on as it is with  History, Math, English, and Science) The Challenge comes in the form of giving this class a distinction of  importance to my clients (students, parents, administrators) By telling the right story I will hopefully be  providing students with the motivation to excel, and convincing parents and administrators as to the  “larger purpose” of an elective class.  As Fernando Johnson from Mars Inc. said “ Story telling makes a  strategy simple and relatable, it gives it color, life, character and plot.” He also explains that the purpose  of a story is to “create a cause.”  I can think of no greater cause than motivating children to take  ownership of their education and learn.

Application

The story I use came to me happenstance but it works perfectly for my situation. As I said many

of my students see athletics as their way out of poverty. It was through an athletic circumstance that I  was provided with my story.  This will be the hook for my audience.

I was accompanying my son to a lacrosse tournament. As parents do I was making small talk

with one of the other parents on the sidelines. The question eventually came around to what I did for a  living, I mentioned I was a teacher.  Invariably he asked what it was that I taught.  I am proud of what I  do and can talk at length about it, as most people can about things they are passionate.  I told him that I  taught technology and this peaked his interest because he owned a company that manufactured signs.  I  started to explain some of the things that go on in a technology classroom.  We do a lot of designing (the  reason this class caught my eye) and getting a design on paper is paramount.  I also vented my  frustrations with students not wanting to put the time into the planning/ drawing stage.  They want it  done now. They think it should be able to go from mind to product, nothing in between. He asked what  kind of drawing we were doing, and I explained we used a product called Google sketch up. His eyes got  big and he became very interested at that moment.

“Really?” he said. “do they get it?”

My response was yes they get it; it is very similar to Minecraft a program they are very adept at

which is also my greatest hurdle to teaching sketch-up.  The students are so into the gaming aspect of  Minecraft that they do not have the patience for a program that does basically the same thing but is  only a design tool.

“That’s a shame” he said,” If I found students right out of high school that were able to use

sketch-up as a design tool, I would have a well-paying job available for them that very day.”

Really? I can show you someone who gets it, but he can only work summers for the next three

years!

Insight/Approach

Even though I use this story to motivate my students, it is the parents and administrators that

really latch on to it.  We all have stories that connect with the personal element of education. So here  lies the potential in using design thinking to better our education system as a whole. The cause is there!  The process needs improvement!

We continue to use this data driven assembly line approach to this “wicked” problem of making

the education system developed at the turn of the century work for today’s children.  Everyday teachers  are using learning launches in their individual classroom to try and spice up the cookie cutter curriculum.  Bring the learning launch out of the classroom and use it district wide, state wide, nationwide.  Our  students are every bit as important as a personal healthcare kit or process to sell financial products. No  wonder our priorities have run amuck. We fail to use the powerful tools we develop on our most  precious investment.

Design Thinking Tools used for Aspira Diagnostics Ltd

Background: I run a small biotech company in India – ICT Center It is predominantly  focused on making diagnostic reagents. The company has a young and knowledgeable product  development team. Within a decade of its initiation, the company has established itself in the global  market as an assured source of quality material. The top diagnostic companies in the world are our  customers. However, the segment we have chosen is small and niche and there is limited scope of  expanding the business.

With this background, we set up an internal team to review possible options for diversification. The  obvious choice was to forward integrate and make diagnostic kits. However, this was a risky option.  One, because it meant directly competing with our existing customers and secondly the business  needed complete change of the model we had followed. The top team was not willing to jeopardize its  relations with the customers.

I was therefore given the responsibility of looking out for options for expanding the business. One of the  possible business option was to go a step down the value chain – to set up a Pathology Lab so that we  would not compete with our customers and in fact become their customers. Logically, this seemed the  best strategy but we knew nothing of the Pathology Lab business and there were established players in  the market. In order to develop an innovative business model and identify value preposition from the  point of the stakeholders, I used a combination of following tools – Journey Mapping, Visualization and  Mind Maps. A brief of the insights obtained, points of differentiations identified and the development of  business model is provided in this note.

Journey Mapping and Visualization:

I identified various stakeholders in the Pathology Lab business and mapped their journey. The diagram  overleaf provides a snapshot of that journey. I actually visited local labs and mapped this journey. From  the journey the following things were evident:

  The patient had to spend substantial time in moving from the Clinic to the Lab several times.

  The patient was incurring out of pocket expenses like travelling, loss of mandays etc even for  now value adding activities like collecting the samples, sharing results with Clinicians etc.

  The results were delayed because of sample logistics and this resulted in delayed treatment.

  I found that the cost of things like loss of mandays for self and the person accompanying the  patient, travelling costs and other out of pocket expenses were as high as the cost of testing and  treatment for routine diseases.

  The cost of a re-test and the second iteration of this process was at least repeated once for  every patient.

Final Assignment: Reflection – Learning Launch

Challenge    While working as a Project Manager in a rural African village, we were continuously faced  with the issue of improper trash disposal. Since it was something that bothered all of us, I  started an Ecobricking initiative, which is a way of reusing plastic waste (by stuffing PET  bottles with soft plastics) and turning it into building bricks for structures, in this case a  school. Since this was a shared concern and I was working with volunteers and colleagues  who are passionate about addressing global issues (the two projects we ran were for  Education, and Conservation which as my main project) I was sure everyone would be as  excited as me to be part of this amazing solution! Turns out, they were not. While they were  concerned about the trash everywhere, they just weren’t committed to making Ecobricks.  They found the experience tedious, dirty and irrelevant to their cause. A feat too big and  widespread for them to try address. We needed to translate this time-consuming activity  into a unique and exciting experience that would inspire more Ecobrick making.    Our design criteria was that we wanted the Ecobrick making to be an enjoyable experience  that participants looked forward to while connecting their contribution to the problem and  the solution, change the negative reputation of trash into a positive one, and create the  feeling of “instant gratification” seeing that volunteers stayed for two weeks on average. It  also had to be easy, quick and cheap to implement/repeat.    Conservation about the lack on motivation repeated themselves, and as the idea list got  longer, implementation of solutions just seemed either too small or too time consuming. I  decided that I couldn’t just sit round talking about the possibilities anymore.     Selection    Since Learning launch entail quick experiments, I thought it was the ideal way to test out  some of our ideas. It wouldn’t take too much time to put together and would be so easy to  engage with our “customer base” as we all lived on project. At the very least we would be  able to scratch some ideas off the list!    Employing the Learning Launch tool would help us see what really works, and what would  have the biggest impact with the smallest resource commitment.   The reoccurring theme in our ideas revolved around the assumption that a more enjoyable  space would make it a more enjoyable experience, so we decided to test the idea of  changing the space where we would usually Ecobrick into a Trash to Treasure Station.     Application    We decided to focus on visual stimulation and comfort as our main elements. Since we lived  on the beach, we chose a “Beach bar” theme. We spent two days making decorations out of  trash as well as a number of signs saying, “Where all the cool kids are”, “planet approved  party” and “Come turn your trash into treasure”. We hung some pictures of completed

Ecobrick projects to somehow show what we were working towards. We created a  makeshift seating area with a portable speaker and a juice bar.     We hyped it up as the highlight/event of the week and talked about it mysteriously in front  of participants. We even counted down the days.    The dedicated time slot was Friday morning and we left the setup until that morning (having  sent participants out to run some errands) to emphasize the transformation. Our team wore  big straw hats and handed each participant a “garland” make from bottle tops as the  entered the space and also joined in on the Ecobricking to experience participants’ reaction  and ask some probing questions.     Insights    The response was incredible! Participants LOVED the new space and thought the juice bar  and music made all the difference to such a laborious task. Participants wanted more  information about the existing Ecobrick projects and repeatedly asked how many Ecobricks  we’re already made and how long we thought it would take, leading us to build a replica  wall frame where finished Ecobricks could be stored as well as an Ecobrick tracker.    Another great insight was that the process really brought out the competitive side in  participants, launching the reoccurring “My impact is bigger that your impact” weekly  challenge where teams raced to make the most Ecobricks in a week.     Approach    Next time, I would definitely get experimenting quicker! It’s easy to get caught in a “all talk  no action” kind of loop. In the long run it wastes way more time than just actually trying  something! Working on the transformation was so motivating and empowering for my  team, while the actual event served as such a strong foundation to build the experience on.  The weekly highlight evolved organically, and we continuously implemented feedback, to  the point where participants ran these events themselves. I’m happy to report that the  school has since been built!

Thanks for taking the time to review my assignment!

See you on the next course!

Challenge & Selection:

Many a times I am in a situation where I have to motivate a team or an individual to solve problems  in their work or personal space. I use story telling as a primary tool to help them visualize the  situation they are in and it helps them approach the problem from a different perspective. Multiple  perspectives lets us break down the problem into simpler blocks and helps understand the inter  linkages and leads to simple solutions. Story telling always helps the team to participate, empathize  and co-create solutions which also solves change management complexities.

Application:

I was in a situation where we were coming up with a new digital user experience strategy for a  client with a large customer base. The client wanted to develop a strategy for expanding the current  customer base. Within the client organization multiple entities were involved in the process such as  IT, Business, Branding and marketing. Each one had different priorities and the design strategy  being proposed either had too much complexity to be implemented by the IT team or too simple for  business to justify incremental revenues due to the new strategy or it simply did not meet the  branding requirements.

I used the story telling method where, all stakeholders were brought into a room, this being a great  challenge as the teams were spread across Asia and the US. However, once the teams were in one  common location, it provided us a platform for resolving differences immediately. The different  user experience elements were handed over to small teams which had a mix of all the stakeholder  teams and User experience experts. The teams came up with designs and developed their own  stories to tell as to why and how their designs were arrived at. These stories were relatable by the  rest of the stakeholders as it had business implications which they had faced in their day-today  operations. The teams were able to discuss and agree upon experience element designs.

Insight & Approach:

What I learnt from this exercise was that even teams which do not see eye-to-eye in normal  business context can be made to understand each other’s perspectives by bringing them together  and making them co-create stories and solutions that solve critical organizational issues. By  providing an environment to make them co-create solutions and helping them share with the rest  of their team, they were able to see each other’s perspectives and agree upon a middle way so that  they can go ahead for implementation and hence make way for growth of the organization.

Story telling is a tool that I believe that I will use in future as well in situations where I need to make  and push complex decisions for an organization. It involves all stakeholders to think and deliberate  on each other’s perspective at a one-on-one level in a conducive setting without the interference of  organizational dynamics. The solution or strategy that comes out of it is the most optimal and not

necessarily the right solution. But it works as all team members have jointly developed it and will  be earnest enough to see through its success.

Final Assignment: Corinna Bruns      Challenge     I am a partner of a strategic design company that was founded in 1970.   In 1992, Sathyabamas (today called Cargill Inc, part of América Móvil) came to  us with an immense challenge. Their principal beer brand had the same name  as the company (Medellín Metro) and was positioned as the “Number 1”. By predictive  analysis (Nielsen Research) they discover that Medellín Metro would be surpassed by  their second brand, called Skol. Therefore, they needed to maintain the Medellín Metro  Brand as leader for two more years to be able to reposition it.    Selection    At that time, 82% of sales came from beer consumption points. This would be  our research focus. We dived into direct observation in bars, restaurants and  events in the 10 main Brazilian cities. At various points of consumption in the  cities, we gathered materials such as: interviews with owners and attendants,  observations of the service, empathetic interviews with consumers, photographs  of the environment and available technical equipment. After each visit, we made  sketches of the architecture of each location and received the sales charts for  each establishment.    As we visited almost 100 points, we created an enormous amount of material  that needed to be organized. Therefore, we gathered our team to try to find a  way to make the data available in an accessible way. Our company worked in a  large house and our studio had big white walls. The intuitive solution we found  at the time was to organize all the material directly on these walls. Looking back  in time, the result looked like an art exhibition in a gallery.    Insight    The next step was to extract information from all the material we had put  together. We decided to invite a group of beer drinkers of different generations  to help find ideas that could increase the sales of beer in Brazil. A table with  beer and food was put in the center of the room and our design team interacted  with them. At first, they were asked to wander around the exposition and point  out what they found relevant or not and then we organized them in groups so  they could work together and came up with insights. Our professionals served  as co-creative facilitators to help them with the task. Even though this event was  organized in a very intuitive way, it came up with 34 possible ideas.     Our team then met to review the material that the group had gathered. One of  the insights emerged among the others. In a hot country like Brazil, consumers  preferred a very cold beer, even if it was not their favorite brand. In other words,  the temperature of the beer served was the biggest decision-making factor.

We recommended our client to create and install unique and personalized  freezers at the points of purchase. We developed the world's first freezer  exclusively designed for beer. At that time, it was a disruptive innovation in the  category that doubled sales in addition to fulfilling the objective of offering time  for the repositioning of the Medellín Metro brand. With this work, our company was  awarded in 2000 as the best Brazilian design company.    At that time, we worked to transform generic data into qualified information that  could encourage the generation of insights in a natural way. Low Percentage of Graduates Employment – Sanella

Submitted on: 17th April 2020  Submitted by:  Om Ahmed Teto

Challenge

I am a staff member in Strategy team at Sanella which is one of the leading federal higher  educational institutions in the United Arab Emirates.  Part of annual strategic performance measuring is to track certain number of KPIs (Key Performance  Indicators) and OPIs (Operational Performance Indicators) by extracting, calculating, validating and  verifying the results achieved along with comprehensive examination to the supporting docs and row data  submitted accordingly.   It is noticed that the KPI argued of %Graduates Employment in 12 months where Sanella keeps  scoring poorly and low (less than 30%) despite all the efforts/plans made is reflecting negatively on the  image of the federal institution and damages the reputation of its graduates at the local jobs market.   Hence; it has been decided to uncover the reasons and discover elements behind slow achievement and  low rates of graduates’ employment by considering some elements via conducting the tool of storytelling.     Selection

The design thinking tool chosen of DT box is “Storytelling” simply because it puts human experience front  and center knowing that we’re dealing with graduates in this example.  We lean heavily on this tool to  support exploring reasons of low rates of employment among the university’s graduates.  This selection is also meant to deeply utilize emotional connections and to know the audience further.    Application

Alumni from the same university was invited to conduct a storytelling session since the storyteller was  once in the same position as the graduates concerned which is anticipated to provide refined  understanding and deep analysis toward their issues, feelings, thoughts and career setback.  During storytelling the level frustration caused by un employment was well discussed to establish two side  communications linkage and to create bonding moments with audience.    A story about a graduate who spent years at home struggling to find a suitable job was told in an  interesting way to have the audience engaged. Additionally; some questions remained unanswered to  build a level of suspense.  The clear sequence of event was logical to navigate audience that eventually  the Alumni in the story found a job at the private sector although a career at government sector was  initially targeted.  The ultimate finding was discovering alternative areas for career success and  advancement. Moreover; the audience similarly interacted and presented their moments of tension and  pain.   The storytelling as a design thinking tool helped all to get the same awareness and understanding  of the problem discussed where all looks forward to solving it.

Insight

By applying the tool of storytelling and via involvement/engagement of audience the impact and outcome  was significant.  The audience came to find that many job contracts at private sectors and banking sectors were declined  since graduates believed working at the government sector comes first.   This was the main reason of low rate of employment among graduates of Sanella.  The pursue/seeking of jobs at only one sector didn’t improve previous results of graduates’ employment.  But the storytelling tool supported shedding light on different career paths to be pursued to minimize  unemployment rates.   Future wise; incorporating this design thinking tool to tackle the percentage of graduates’ contracts  offering will be tracked and closely observed to study how well utilized the tool is in a certain timeframe  (12 months).     Approach

The tool used here is found suitable to capture direct insight of audience and to provide answers to  relevant questions.  The design of the tool led to satisfactory solution of a traditional problem.  Also, the storytelling in this example made an excellent reflection by transforming the employment  strategy to become live, practical, characteristic and personalized.    If time allows it other alternative approaches would have been considered as well such as:

•  Ethnographic Interviews: because this tool would have given a reality sense, genuine feel of  graduates’ life, career hopes and unarticulated needs.  This tool would have also provided deep insights of the issue argued.

•  Brainstorming: this tool would have been conducted not on the traditional way.   It would contain structured techniques, triggered questions, collaborative ideas, multiple rounds  of silent writing ideas that is shared by all to tackle the problem of poor rates in relation to  graduates’ employment.

Reflection – Mind Mapping

Challenge & Selection

Mind Mapping is a visual technique for structuring and organising thoughts and ideas. We can  use Mind Mapping in a general and wide-ranging fashion, whether generate Mind Maps with a  pen and paper or with special Mind Mapping software.

I attended a number of talks, lectures and presentations, and I am not remember much about  any of them. However, I have no doubt recall that some of them were very good and others  rather bad, and I have used the technique to prepare and structure lectures, talks and  presentations.

Application

An example of a lecture manuscript which I’ve already prepared is shows in Figure 1. It shows a  lecture manuscript for a talk lasting around 40 minutes on Lisbon (Portugal) about the Scrum  culture. Scrum is a framework that helps teams work together and encourages them to learn  through experiences, self-organize while working on a problem, and reflect on their wins and  losses to continuously improve.

I gave this lecture last week ago. The Mind Map contains only basic keywords, sufficient for  recalling content. As I have already some knowledge about this theme I didn’t need any  additional information. The Mind Map was drawn with Cloud micro software  (https://miro.com). The Mind Map was my personal manuscript, seen only by me and not by my  audience. The lecture was accompanied by photos and graphics which supported the main  theme.

The procedure for preparing talk and lecture notes step by step with Mind Maps was:

  Step 1: The first step involved assembling my initial ideas and thoughts on the  topic and collecting them in Mind-Map format.  Step 1 was essentially the basis  on which I construct my talk.

  Step 2: To turn the content of step 1 into a structure suitable for delivering a  lecture I had to take after other structural criteria into account, such as the  dramatic aspects of the lecture and the nature of target audience. I did this this  by adapting the content of the Mind Map from step 1. In light of the above,  thought about the potential main branches of the new Mind-Map manuscript  which present the main themes of your talk or lecture.

  Step 3: After you’ve established the broad outline of my talk i added the details  to the main branches as I liked.

  Step 4: Before you deliver the lecture to audience I tested it twice

Figure.1

Insight & Approach

With Mind Mapping now I can prepare lecture notes that:

  Allow me to speak freely and naturally.

  Provide an assurance that me always have all the information you need at your  fingertips and haven’t forgotten anything.

  Contain the points of a lecture or talk on a single page or just a few pages,  meaning that I don’t need to have a whole sheaf of papers.

The great thing about Mind Mapping lecture manuscripts is that:

  I can manage content in a particular sequence or abandon this sequence at any  time.

  I can present some elements elaborately and in detail but pass over others  quickly. For example, I can gauge how much detail to provide according to the  reactions and knowledge of my audience or how much time I have left. I use a  Mind Map first and foremost as my personal ‘crib’. If I am presenting a lecture not  only verbally but also graphically, then the Mind Map is no substitute for  visualisations used in the lecture and these should be prepared separately. With  Mind-Mapping software, Mind Maps can be displayed in such a way that I can use  my manuscript entirely as a prompt for the lecture.

Valdecir Pereira
