Storytelling: Using Empathy to Redesign Public Services

By Tarek Nady

Bangladesh is a small country with a very large population. More than 40% of the people are

engaged in agriculture and located in faraway rural locations. They are mostly wage earners or

smallholder farmers and for their livelihood they need to work every day. And like any other

developing country Bangladesh has quite slow and inefficient public services. These public

services are mostly distributed from the district cities. And transportation systems are expensive

and in most of the cases roads are also not in very good condition. So for rural population it is

very difficult to avail necessary public services. The opportunity costs are very high along with the

actual costs due to travel, corruption etc. Then again the bureaucratic processes and

administrative mechanisms were based on the system designed by the British back in the

nineteenth century. And the lack of empathy among the public officials and lack of understanding

about the challenges faced by the poor rural population to avail the basic public services are

clearly evident. From my project I was assigned to develop a pilot project involving the public

officials to deliver decentralized services for the rural population; a mechanism what would reduce

the number of visits required to a public office to avail a service. The first step was to make the

public service officials empathetic and agreeing in engaging in the pilot. The challenge was to

make the public service officials of the pilot project area to feel empathetic towards the service

recipients of rural areas, to understand the implications in the lives of the people who come to

take service. The lack of empathy among the public officials were the major challenge in

redesigning the service delivery processes.

The idea was to make the public officials feel the complications, costs and the difficulties of the

people of remote rural areas who sometimes needs to spend one full day of travel just to collect

a form. So in terms of tool selection I thought that storytelling would be the most suitable tool.

Because I felt that the challenge has certain elements of emotion and compassion because the

issues needed to touch the hearts of the people whose decisions could make a difference in the

lives of many. I did think of other tools, but I very strongly felt that storytelling would be appropriate

as I wanted to create a personal connection for the public officials.

I organized a workshop with the public service officials of the pilot area. Before the workshop I

collected some videos of interviews of the rural people who faced serious difficulties in availing

public services and did a survey to find out some statistical analysis on average total cost (actual

costs added with opportunity costs) of availing a service. Once all this information was ready I

Page 2 of 2

decided to develop a story taking bits and pieces from the information collected. I central character

of the story is a farmer, Rahim who is in his late forties, he needed to go to the district

administration office to collect a form to claim the irrigation subsidy. The challenge was he needed

to work in the field because the field needed clearing and at the same time he needed to pay the

examination fee for her daughter. He also needed to pay some bribe for the form along with the

costs of travelling to the district city, there were expenses for food also. Now the cost implication

for Rahim was huge as he needed to hire someone for clearing the field, he needed to travel to

the office and come back. To meet the expenses Rahim had to take money out of his savings.

This is not even the half of the challenge!! Because after filling up the form, getting the right

signatures he again needed to go back to the office to submit the form and finally a third time to

get the subsidy. Eventually he spent more than half of the subsidy amount he was supposed to

receive, in the process. This scenario keeps repeating every year and poor farmers like Rahim

keeps being underserved by the faulty system. They also become more and more vulnerable

because of almost no savings. I used some visuals for the storytelling and to portray the

helplessness of the rural population. The aim of the storytelling was to make the public officials

empathetic first, then engage them in discussing different aspects of the challenges for the service

recipients and the service providers.

The story followed by videos & survey findings were shared at the beginning of the workshop.

After that the public service officials were engaged to identify the reasons behind such a system.

At this point some interesting insights came up. To be more specific the policies, the service

delivery rules, documentations requirement, legal requirements for signatures, payment for

services, audit requirements, brokers and other many aspects that created the persisting scenario

of depriving the service seekers. It was identified that with the advancement of the technology

there were many possibilities opened up to make service processes simpler, to make access

easier, faster and cheaper. However due to many complex reasons such initiatives were not being

undertaken satisfactorily.

The workshop achieved its target of making the public service officials more empathetic, more

understanding of the challenges faced by the rural people and the prices they pay and engaging

the to identify the issues with the current service delivery model. The videos supported the story

and created the right environment for the discussion. Next time I would like to bring a real person

who faced the challenges in availing the public service. Because I feel interacting with someone

who faces such challenges on a regular basis, would be even more impactful for the public service

officials.

Sarah Calixto

Reflection – Mind Mapping

Challenge & Selection

There is currently a significant opportunity in the Oil and Gas industry for clear cost reduction driven by  innovative ideas.  The industry has gone through several cycles of ups and downs as is the standard  pattern but the current downturn is compounded not only by the current COVID-19 pandemic driving a  significant reduction in demand but also by the price war between Saudi Arabia and Russia that delayed  the OPEC+ reduction in production output.  Other methods for Continuous Improvement by themselves  will not drive deep enough understanding on any other untapped opportunities to drive this cost  reductions in an innovative way.  The scope includes a set of clients that are willing to be transparent in  the discussions to ensure we can define mutual value and implementation of solutions that will not only  create value for the company but maintain viability of both companies as we come out of the current  challenging business environment.  Initial exploration was done at the top levels of both companies to  define the guiding principles and focus areas for the collaboration by means of interviews.

After the interviews with the top leaders of the organizations and with a clear understanding of the  focus areas the approach was to hold a workshop with the identified stakeholders to discover all the  available information and establish areas of current activities and processes that are not working and  others that may have potential and can be further explored within the identified focus area.  This  workshop resulted in significant amount quantitative and qualitative data.  With such amount of data,  the next more obvious step was to establish some patterns and insights that would lead to creative  solutions.  Therefore, we selected the Mind Mapping tool.

Application

For our mind mapping workshop, we identified an additional set of stakeholders that hold key  knowledge of the various functions that might be impacted by any actions taken as part of the solutions  as well as key subject matter experts.  The workshop was done virtually using Mural and through zoom.   Participants from both the client and us were in attendance. The first step was to provide an overview of  the earlier activities that yielded the data that they will be reviewing and acting on and presentation of  the data. At this point we assigned 20 minutes to become familiar with the data and start exploring  whether they see any specific information that might be similar in nature that potentially have a similar  theme.  The data is spread in color coded post its that we asked the workshop participants to then start  moving into sets of data that could have a similar theme.  This resulted in seven buckets of similar  categories.  Next as a team we discussed and identified a main topic for each of the buckets of  information and assign a specific theme.  Upon further team discussion, we identified that two of the  data sets could then be merged and assigned a larger theme reducing the clusters to 6. At this point, we  took the opportunity to use the quantitative data associated with the specific themes and established  the top three priorities to further explore based on the highest potential impact if solutions are  implemented.

Using the top 3 categories we then did the exercise called “How might we….” Which is the last step of  mind mapping to define the design criteria statements.  The method of defining the how might we

Sarah Calixto

statements is aligned with the design criteria statements, in which if anything were possible what  criteria would our new design meet?  The first step was to assign each workshop participant to develop  individually in post-it’s a statement for each of the three categories identified.  Once everyone had  captured the “How might we” statements, the team was given the opportunity to review all the  statements developed.  Next we voted as a team on the main statement that more completely  establishes the intent of the insights obtained from the data.  These were then carried forward to  identify solutions.

Insight & Approach

What I have learned from conducting this activity is that collaboration is critical and having the  representatives from both client and us together with the clear understanding of transparency and  innovation allowed us to uncover great opportunities.  The discussions to define the real themes yield  areas of focus that we alone would not have even sought to investigate as an opportunity.  Looking at  the themes and insights resulting from the activity from both perspectives in collaboration allowed us to  identify areas where in some cases we were not fully aware of the collaborative opportunity.  With  regards to the statements, taking in consideration if anything was possible also allowed us to set higher  ambitions that could lead to breakthrough solutions.  The participants commented of how they enjoyed  the discussions and the statement starters was a new approach for them to use as well.

In the future, I think there is value of having the full set of stakeholders and subject matter experts  involved earlier in the process so that they can also contribute to the data with their specific experiences  and insights.  Also, with regards to the statement starters there is also an opportunity that instead of  selecting the best, we can also combine them into a more comprehensive if needed.

Jakeline Lunardi

DESIGN THINKING FOR INNOVATION

VISUALIZATION APPLICATION EXAMPLE

MAI 2017

CHALLENGE  (Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.)    The challenge was to think of an IT solution to a new business process that would allow to propose pricing  conditions for proposed products to potential clients. A potential client can not become a real client, if it  was not transparent which pricing conditions were proposed to him and got approved by the respective  approval body.   The basis to propose prices is the list of products that are proposed to the potential client.   The new process spreads across three different business units (client management, product management,  price management) and will have to integrate several underlying sub processes (currently executed  independently).   The change is pushed by the Pricing business and each business units have their own priorities/goals and  own roadmap/deadline towards achieving these goals.   A close collaboration, shared understanding of the importance of the change and implementation  alignment and agreement is a pre-requisite for the success of this initiative.     TOOL SELECTION  (In own words, brief description of the tool selected, e.g., what it is and why you selected it for your  challenge -- including any appropriate video lecture references)    The first tool used was visualization. Visualization was selected because the problem statement had to be  shared among three different teams and ‘a picture is worth thousands words’. So this way, we wanted to  ensure that everybody involved could get on the same page in a quick and easy way (seeing something is  better than having it described).   For the visualization itself, we selected a tool called MIRO.    MIRO is a visual collaborative whiteboard platform for team work.   This tool was chosen for several reasons:

1. It is a collaborative ‘white board’ platform, suitable for work to be shared across teams.    2. It is a powerful tool that enables to do various things like: meetings and workshops, ideation and

brainstorming, mapping and diagramming, etc. So it would possible to use the same tool for other  design thinking purposes/phases (brainstorming, mind mapping, etc.) and everything would is  available in one central place.

3. The tool allows to group elements, link different elements, etc. in a completely free way  4. It allows sharing and central access to artefacts/elements of the board.   5. It allows several people to work in the same time on the same board.   6. The tool is simple and intuitive. For someone who has not worked with it before, it was easy to

jump in and start using it, at least for a basic usage.

7. Changes can be ‘live’: changes are immediately visible to all to have access to the board. My

company is starting to use this tool in a broader way, so I want to use every opportunity to learn  the about tool as much as I can.

Link to MIRO: https://miro.com      APPLICATION

(How the tool was applied , e.g., what you did and how the tool was applied effectively or ineffectively)    The whole activity was planned as a set of four subsequent workshops (two more business-focussed and  two more IT focused workshops). The participants were not divided into different groups because there  was no need: the challenge topic was not to big and there were not too many participants (approx. 10).   With every workshop, the participants were diving deeper and deeper into solution finding and its  refinement.   For the first session, a basic picture of the new business flow was prepared and loaded into the MIRO  board. Access was granted to all participants and the link provided a couple of days before the workshop  in case the participants wanted to look and prepare themselves for the workshop.   The first draft of the new flow was generated based on information that was gathered from the end users  (the ones for whom the solution is targeted) but also by taking the relevant part of the company strategy  into consideration. This preparation work was executed by a smaller number of persons – let’s call them  ‘the core team’ (not all involved participants). The draft of the new flow did not contain too many details.  We also put a couple of boxes with ‘errors’ or wrong wording in order to trigger discussions.   In the first workshop, we started to discuss the draft of the new flow. After setting the scene and  explaining the goal of the first workshop, active discussion started immediately.   We started to ask questions like:

1) Do you understand why we put the picture exactly like this?   2) How does this fit into your goals and roadmap?   3) Is something missing?   4) What would you ‘draw’ differently? Why?   5) Did we forget something important?

Having a picture in front of people immediately starts the thinking process and triggers comments,  feedbacks, inputs, etc.   As questions arisen and answers were provided, we started to adapt the ‘picture’: change the wording of  the boxes, add missing boxes and move them around. Thanks to the tool capabilities, the persons that felt  ‘called to do the changes’ were able to this themselves, directly in the tool. The changes were live and  immediately visible to all.   After the workshop, the core team did the last updates to add the changes the changes that were not yet  reflected in the board. This was done based on notes recorded by the ‘core team’.   Participants got informed that the MIRO board is now finally updated with workshop #1 results and  further changes can be added.   The second workshop started based on the last version of the picture. Reflection – Visualization

Challenge & Selection       The first tool I used was the tool of Visualization, or Visual Thinking, to achieve a shared understanding  of a problem space among a diverse group of stakeholders before attempting to identify and define  possible solutions to the problem.  I use this approach often with our customers, who are government  agencies working to apply technology innovations to modernize their mission or the delivery of their  services to their customer, which may be Pakistani citizens, businesses, and non-citizens.  I have used  the technique of using a straw man visualization of a problem domain with a set of questions or  prompts for discussion to allow a diverse group of stakeholders to learn from each other in the process  of defining the scope, boundaries, key elements, and relationships between elements to consider when  identifying pain points and opportunities for improvements or solutions.      Application      I start the process by creating a straw man graphic of the problem domain.  To develop the straw man  graphic, I will draw from any existing material available to understand the environment.  The existing  material may be operational or procedural documents, training materials, marketing materials, GAO or  other auditing reports.  If materials are not available, then I conduct informal interviews with one-three  of the stakeholders who serve as my main points of contact on the initiative.      If appropriate to the situation, I will borrow the concept to “front-stage/back-stage” from previous  research, and discussed in David Gray’s book, “The Connected Company”.  The front-stage/back-stage  approach helps to reinforce the notion that every service – even an internal service – has customers  with whom the service provider interacts and internal processes that enable the organization to provide  the service.  The template I often start with also has a column on the left to identify Partners and Value  Chain Providers, and other entities that may add constraints to how the organization operates.  The  straw man graphic is simple, using simple shapes and icons available in Visio or on the Internet.  If the  front-stage/back-stage view doesn’t work, then I will create a different type of visual, either based on a  high-level process flow with swim lanes for different stakeholders, or another format.       For the activity, I will divide the stakeholders into groups of 5-6 participants each representing a  different organization or area of interest.  Each group receives a poster-size copy of the straw man  graphic that they can write on directly, or use sticky notes to make comments.  I give them two-three  questions to answer, such as: 1) What key elements are missing from the graphic?  2) What would you  change about the graphic to make it more accurately reflect your problem space?  3) What key insights  do you have about the relationships between the entities in your problem space?   I give them  approximately 20 minutes to discuss the questions and mark up the graphic.  Then I have each group  report out on their answers to those three questions while pointing to the mark-ups on their poster.  As  each group reports out, I record commonalities in the insights of each group, and then additional  insights that come from the group discussion on an additional copy of the graphic.  After the session, I  digitize each group’s poster as an artifact, create a view that combines the shared and new insights from  the group discussion, and then create a revised graphic that incorporates their feedback and proposed  changes that they agreed to as a group.

Insight & Approach      What I have learned from conducting this exercise with several groups is that while the graphic –  especially the revised graphic that incorporates their feedback – is important for reinforcing their  understanding of the problem they are working to solve, the more valuable aspect of the activity is the  shared insights and shared learning that occurs while they are working to define their problem space.   The graphic gives the diverse group of stakeholders a focal point for discussion that allows them to  share their perspectives and develop insights into potential root causes of their problems.  While they  could create the graphic from a blank slate in a collaborative manner, starting with a straw man jump  starts the conversation for them. They can quickly identify where they are in the graphic – or if they are  missing – and can more quickly gain new insights about relationships between key entities instead of  taking time to identify them.  They can also identify variables in the problem space – that is, it helps  them to identify what they don’t know, in what areas they need to obtain information or data to  provide the values for the variables.      Since I discovered that the most valuable aspect is the shared insights and learning, next time I would  use the visualization activity as a starting point for a series of design thinking activities. Then the revised  graphic that incorporates their combined feedback can serve as a reference tool throughout the  remainder of their work.

Opinion:  The Problem with Bottled Water   by Santiago Suarez

More than half of the people in the United States drink bottled water regularly. In general,

bottled water is considered convenient because it is portable. But that convenience comes with  problems and a high environmental cost. The problems include: pollution created during  production and transportation of bottled water; injuries to marine life from discarded bottles;  and ugly garbage dumps filled with empty bottles.

Plastic water bottles are typically made from crude oil. During their production, pollutants

such as nickel, benzene, and ethylene oxide are released. These harm the environment and  pollute the air we breathe. It takes 1.5 million barrels of oil to produce the plastic water bottles  we use each year. Additionally, trucks release more pollutants and use gasoline when they  transport bottled water to stores.

26 billion plastic bottles are made each year. That equals

30 million tons of plastic. Unfortunately, most end up in  garbage dumps rather than recycling centers. It takes hundreds  of years for a plastic bottle to decompose – to dissolve into the  soil. The bottles that are in the garbage dumps today will be  with us a long time.

Garbage dumps are often located near the ocean, and that is where many bottles wind up.

In the ocean, sea turtles and other animals can mistake plastic bottles for their main food source,  jellyfish. Eating plastic can injure or kill sea turtles as well as birds that feed in the ocean.

Across the United States, people can turn on sink faucets to get some of the cleanest,

healthiest tap water on Earth. Almost all chemicals and impurities have been removed to make  this drinking water clean and safe. It is also inexpensive. On average, a gallon of tap water costs a  small fraction of one cent. Considering these facts, the obvious question is, “Why do Americans  drink so much bottled water?”

Consumers in the United States feel bottled water is both safer and more convenient. The

fact is that tap water is just as safe and tap water carried in a reusable container is just as  convenient. Clearly, the advantages of bottled water are more imaginary than real.

It is time for major changes across the country. If every bottled water consumer in the U.S.

made the switch to drinking tap water from reusable containers, the environment would be  cleaner and safer for all living creatures. The percentage of plastic bottles that get recycled  needs to rise as well. Currently only about 30 percent of plastic bottles make it to a recycling  center. That means 70 percent wind up in garbage dumps!

It is important to communicate information about this environmental issue with others.

Many people are simply unaware of the harm caused by this problem and are willing to change  their behavior when they find out how the environment is being affected.

Reflection –  Visualization and Customer Experience

Challenge

I have worked for several years leading a global B2B1 Customer Experience department and my  challenge was to improve SME2 Customer satisfaction with the telecommunication services we  were providing. Our SME Customer satisfaction was much lower than that of our Corporate  customers and we were loosing market share. Through previous research analysis, we found out  that the main pain point for our SME customers was the excessive time that our technical  support was taking to solve their systems breakdowns. When looking at our internal KPIs3, you  could see that we were fulfilling all our SLAs4, so our challenge was to convince main decision  makers, within the organization, to set new SLAs that would fit our customers expectations. This  was not an easy task, as it involved investing and decreasing margins in the short run.

Selection

To tackle this challenge we decided to use the Visualization tool, as this is a good tool to make a  problem tangible and concrete. We thought this tool was the best one to ensure all people  involved understood our customer expectations. We had tried it before with reports and other  internal presentations of data, but without convincing of the urgency of the issue.

Application

In order to be able to applicate the Visualization tool, we decided to generate visual content that  we could share with main decision makers. We organized a two weeks workshop to meet and  interview our main types of SME customers, so that we could better understand their current  reality. We  picked up 15 SME customers, representing close to 80% of all SME different  subsectors in the country. The sample included many kinds of business models, from bar owners  to online service providers. We took pictures of them and recorded videos, making sure they  expressed the importance and impact in their business of early fast technical support. All of  them stated that early resolution of technical problems was vital for the survival of their  businesses.

We gathered all our Company decision makers in a room with one of its walls covered with the  pictures of the customers we interviewed, including below the main messages they came up  with. After all people in the room had reviewed the wall, we projected sketches of the three  most shocking videos. For example, having bandwidth/video properly working on the day of the  Champions league match was key for a barman’s monthly revenues, so if the break happened  on Friday and the match was on Saturday, he needed assistance in less than 12 hours. At that

moment we were offering more than 48 hours response at weekends for our SME customers,  while our Corporate Customers could benefit from 6 hours repair response.

It was clear for all attendees to the Visualization meeting that we could do it better if we aligned  everybody’s goals, including our customers’ view. So, at the end of that meeting main decision  makers agreed to reduce reparation time for SMEs to 12 hours and to launch a project to adjust  all our internal processes to achieve this goal.

Insight

By applying the Visualization tool, we reached a common understanding about our SME  customer priorities that hadn’t been possible before. My experience is that images and  testimonies clearly work much better than figures or reports when concerning customer  experience issues. The misunderstandings or prejudices disappear when is the customer itself  who explains his/her expectations, and all stakeholders are willing to work together to reach a  common goal. I did not call it Visualization tool before, but now I can tell I have used it  successfully and I am passionate about it!

Approach

Storytelling Problem Framing for Aviation

Shery Tavormina

Challenge  As a systems engineer, I am involved through the design, development, and deployment of new aviation  systems and services deployed. For the design process itself, I look for alternative, innovative ways to  address the problem faced by users in the aviation domain. Design Thinking adds value by providing new  techniques to extract operational shortfalls (issues) and needs (requirements) from the user community,  which includes air traffic controllers, safety and maintenance personnel, and pilots.

My current project is modernizing how information is shared and displayed to air traffic controllers.  Today, small pieces of paper capture a flight’s information, which includes destination and path taken to  get to the destination. The intent is to digitize this information, so electronic data can be easily displayed  and shared among air traffic controllers.

The challenge faced was to find innovative ways to solicit inputs on the problem space, gain consensus  on the problem, and identify possible solutions to address the problem with a very diverse group of  users. Traditionally, I would use surveys, interviews, loosely structured brainstorm sessions as a means  to quickly collect inputs regarding issues from the user community, who have different experiences, age,  and more. While these methods are valid ways to solicit user input, these traditional methods were  becoming very routine and we were having trouble soliciting diverse input and getting our users to fully  engage with us. I was concerned that my team was not going to be able to accurately articulate the  problem space, which we needed to be correct before having any discussions around the solution space.  I needed a more creative means to solicit user input, and Design Thinking afforded that opportunity.

Selection

Design Thinking provides a more methodological and objective way for problem solving. Storytelling is  one of the available tools within the Design Thinking toolkit, where a narrative (story) serves as a means  to communicate and share experiences in a very impactful way. This tool was selected to help facilitate a  discussion around the problem space. My team and I thought that Storytelling would be helpful in  framing the problem space and a strategy for solution, as described in Module 2. We wanted members  of our user community to tell about their experiences and problems that they faced.

This facilitation technique was helpful in that everyone was able to share their personal stories, events  they experienced, and lessons learned with the wider group. They shared what happened and who was  involved. These personal anecdotes were impactful and help build trust among the team. It helped my  team understand the operational shortfalls with how data is exchanged and displayed to air traffic  controllers.

Application  During the problem framing discussion, we wanted to explore the types of problems, the magnitude of  the problems, and the reason why the(se) issue(s) was unacceptable. We created a scenario that

sequentially laid out steps of what plane at an airport would be doing before departure. This scenario  served to guide our problem framing discussions and provide some context for our users, without trying  to limit the conversations too.

We asked our users to provide stories of the issues they faced (specifically any issues related to missing  data or getting data too late), in the context of how they would control the plane at their airport (the  scenario). The users shared stories about how information would be missed communicated during high  stressed situations. For example, large, popup, thunderstorms occur frequently in Chicago, Il, and one  controller from that area shared a story of how he had to write down on paper reminder notes to help  him keep track of which flights needed a reroute (to avoid the storm) or which ones wanted to depart  later after the storm had passed. They expressed how having information printed and written down was  very ineffective. And they shared how there could have been a big operational safety issue when his  papers accidently were shuffled and moved, because he had lost track of the flights he was working  with.

These personal stories included nuggets of the issues that the users faced, and we were able to capture  these issues. Others in the discussion were able to react to each other’s stories, empathize with one  another, and even coalesce around what they all felt were major issues that needed to be addressed.

Insight  The user community was a broad representation of air traffic controllers, with a range of experience.  Storytelling was a very valuable technique to use with my users because not all airports operate  similarly, so it was important for each member to listen and understand the experiences and pain points  that others face. It was very important that we had a pretty broad representation of the user  community to have a successful problem framing discussion. If we had a limited set of users, all with  similar experiences for the discussion, my team and I would have had had a very limited understanding  of the real issues, biasing any future discussions and limiting the solution space. Reflecting upon that  meeting, I also think trust is another key component to Design Thinking. It is necessary for everyone to  feel comfortable sharing their perspectives with one another. As stated in the videos for the course,  empathy is key, and it is important to listen, regardless if you are a user sharing your perspectives or an  engineer who is looking to develop a solution for the problem. In these discussions, I recognized that I  was not an expert on air traffic control, and that my role in these discussions was to recognize and  elevate the inputs to the problem space provided by everyone, only interjecting if I thought there was  an opportunity to dive further into the problem.

Storytelling is not a traditional systems engineering method for soliciting input on the problem or  solution space. Yet, it is critical for systems engineers to understand this from the intended users’  perspective. Design Thinking provides alternative methods for how to have these types of conversations.  Storytelling was a way to really engage with the user community, have a lively conversation, and  generate more meaningful feedback. In my job today, I am continuously looking for opportunities to  leverage these tools that will help with idea generation.

Approach  If I had to do this all over again, I may try Visualization or even mixing Storytelling with Visualization. We  had introduced a scenario in our Storytelling discussion as a means to provide some context (e.g., given

X scenario, what problems do you face). Visualization would be another way to express the problem  space, where our users could draw/map out their negative experiences in a storyboard. We could have  had a visual tool that outlined a journey map, and then collected inputs on what did not work. We did  not have any visual aids during the discussion, and only sticky notes to capture the issues gleaned from  the Storytelling exercises.

work. Tuesday I’ll go to work. Wednesday I’ll hear from my well meaning but risk averse friends and  family. By then, I’ll be right back where I started.” This story was consistent with my own story and  the story of countless people I know. We end up stuck living a life that is less than what we desire,

what we hope for and what we are capable of.

This may sound like a very major challenge. There are many reasons people are dissatisfied with life  and work. However, this is the beauty of design thinking. Problems like these are what motivated me  to learn about the discipline as the problems addressed by design thinking are often more interesting  than the ones addressed with linear thinking and analytics. Through my process, I was able to  determine what smaller piece of this issue I was able to impact.

I chose storytelling as my tool primarily because it is the tool that appeared the most clearly  connected with my initial motivation. Storytelling allows me to envision the very people I want to help  in order to discover the root of their problem. This video lecture describes how storytelling is  compatible with “having a cause”, and describes the power of selling a challenge through telling a  compelling story.

https://www.coursera.org/learn/uva-darden-design-thinking-innovation/lecture/PAXCd/storytelling- tool

I wanted some additional perspectives on storytelling and was inspired by the following blog post.

https://brown.info/posts/searchauthor.php

I wanted to tell a story through both data and human experience. The data was fairly easy to find.  Recent surveys had shown that 34% of employees are engaged at work.

http://owens-farley.com/blogprivacy.asp

This means that 66% are not engaged, in a bad place. During the pandemic, total U.S. employment  dropped below 150 million, but has since rebounded. We can assume that about half of these non- engaged employees are receptive to some form of inspirational message. There is additional

uncertainty in the final number as some disengaged employees may find life satisfaction elsewhere,  but some unemployed people may need to be included in this group. So, I say that 40-60 million  people in the U.S. alone are stuck in this limited mindset but looking for a way out.

that would be an ideal subject for a completely different write up.

Challenge & Selection:

I am a learning manager and I selected the storytelling tool to on-board our business  partners and learners to implement our L&D strategy and the new ways of learning.

In our company, employees are reluctant to use e-learning, they are much more  comfortable with face to face training. At the same time, change is accelerating; full  day(s) available for face to face training is shrinking and digital learning is spreading  offering much more opportunities than the classical e-learning.

The challenge is to modify the way we organize our learning model and to make sure  the trainings we deliver are more efficient, are more connected to the day to day  business, adaptable to the size and rhythm of our learners and are a direct leverage  in the upskilling.

Application:

I had to meet a business partner that was reluctant and refused to modify the existing  learning program (on technical expertise) that was built with her team and delivered  to other teams, especially new comers.

During the interview I had with the manager, I understood that his reluctance was  based on the believe that theoretical training was key to on-board new comers and to  make sure that everyone was aligned in terms of knowledge. It was more comfortable  for him to know that all the new comers had the same trainings even if at the end of  the training it meant that they didn’t learn anything, or not enough compared to the  amount of time spent in the training classroom.

On the other hand, the feedbacks we had on this training program were not very  good.

-  trainees complained about the content who was too theoretical for a part and  there was not enough time for practice,

-  their managers complained that the trainings were too long (2/3 days in a row)  and that trainees were not autonomous when they came back from their  training

-  and tutors (who trained the new comers on the job) were uncomfortable since  they sometimes needed to train the new comer on the job, the face to face  training not being delivered when needed (we need to have at least 6 new  comers to organize a training) so, they had to fill in the blanks on their own.

Insight and approach:

Clearly a presentation of the L&D strategy through the power point slides was not  going to do the job and I had to translate the concepts into a story that made sense  to the business partner I was meeting.

I shared the story of a technical quiz on theoretical knowledge that we launched  recently on two groups of people, new comers and seniors in the company. The  results were not what we expect for both groups.

The group of new comers (before training) had a similar or even a better score  compared to the seniors who were god performers in their job! When we analyzed  the results we realized that the knowledge on which the quiz was built by a few  experts was not really useful for the job and furthermore those new comers already  acquired this kind of knowledge during their studies.

I was able to convince him to try through a pilot a similar approach and also  convinced him to work closer with the tutors of his team to make sure of the efficiency  of the trainings delivered in terms of content, length and rhythm of upskilling.

This course was very useful to me, to on-board our business partners in changing the  ways of learning into more modern ways using also the visualization or the learning  launch tools.

Reflection – mind mapping for a new intranet  Design Thinking for Innovation | Assignment | Abdul Thomas

Challenge  I am the manager of online services for a government department. After several years without any  major changes to the intranet, we recently felt it was time for it to be redesigned, reinvigorated and  to become more of an engagement channel for staff. The challenge for us was to create an intranet  that met the needs of staff as well as senior management. In particular, to provide an intranet that  helped people do their job. To achieve this, we knew it was important for the new intranet to be co- designed, something that never happened previously.

To start our ‘what is’ investigation, we carried out a survey of staff to get their feelings about the  intranet. Analysing this data provided some useful insights. What we found was that most people  were generally happy with the intranet, though there were some common themes in the responses:  there were a number of common day-to-day tasks that needed to be made easier, the design was  tired and could be modernised, search could be improved, and the content could be reviewed for  currency.

Selection  While the survey provided some useful data and insights, I felt there was a need to re-affirm the  current reality and, as discussed by Cheryl Flores in the lecture material, ‘establish  criteria for the what-if idea generation phase’. The ideal design tool to use for this purpose was mind  mapping. Mind mapping is a method used to find common themes, patterns and insights from data  collected during the ‘what is’ phase, to help you to generate an idea or innovation that meets the  need of the customer. Mind mapping was important in this project because it allowed us to really  understand what staff wanted from their intranet, and notably what they didn’t want. It also was an  excellent tool to use to encourage engagement and ownership of the new intranet.

Application  In conducting the mind mapping, I organised for 15 participants to join in the session, and ran  several different activities. The participants were representatives from across the department and  were also at all levels, from senior management to more frontline staff.

I carried out five separate activities as part of the mind mapping session. Firstly, while together as a  full group at the beginning, each participant was asked to state what they felt was the main purpose  of the intranet, and these responses were recorded on a whiteboard. As responses were recorded,  there was open discussion from the group. This helped to clearly define the reason for the session  and unified the group with a common aim. Next, I had placed a number of examples of intranet  home pages on the wall around the room. The participants were asked to individually look at each  one, and using sticky notes, identify one thing they liked and one thing they didn’t like about each  example. Each of the notes were grouped together to create common themes. Then the participants  were divided into three groups. Each group was asked to design their ideal intranet using pens and  large sheets of paper provided. This started to bring together the ideas and help us to start defining  the criteria to use when moving to ‘what if’. The last two activities were online-based ones, firstly to  carry out some basic tasks using a rough wireframe my team had developed and secondly to  complete a top task analysis to help identify the most common activities carried out by staff. These  last two activities were carried out individually by the participants.

Insight  Using mind mapping as a tool in the design approach really helped us to be better prepared for the  ‘what if’ and ‘what wows’ phases of the project, which is where we are up to at the moment. It  allowed us to validate some assumptions, exclude some initial ideas and really understand what staff  wanted from the intranet. On a personal level, it helped me to ‘walk in the shoes’ of the staff (i.e.

our users) and appreciate some of their needs and frustrations. It also highlighted to me how critical  the intranet can be to allowing staff to do what they need to do.

Using this mind mapping approach has reiterated to me the power of design thinking in exploring  new possibilities for long-standing challenges. Intranets are not new, and are a source of frustration  in many organisations, but by using a design thinking approach I can see many opportunities to  create something that really works. In the past, the intranet team would have developed something  using their best understanding, which may have been an improvement but not ‘wowed’.

Approach  I have probably used aspects of mind mapping in many projects that I have undertaken before.  Working in the digital space, it is common practice for us to engage the user heavily in the process.  But the process had not been so clearly defined before. There were some practical learnings I had  which I would do differently next time, including the time allowed for the session (I felt a little  rushed—more time would be better), the rooms used and the process followed. I would probably do  the mind mapping a little earlier in the process too, as we had done some wireframing already.

The first tool I used was the tool of Visualization, or Visual Thinking, to achieve a shared

understanding of a problem space among a diverse group of stakeholders before attempting to  identify and define possible solutions to the problem. I use this approach often with our customers,  who are government agencies working to apply technology innovations to modernize their mission  or the delivery of their services to their customer, which may be U.S. citizens. I have used the  technique of using a straw man visualization of a problem domain with a set of questions or prompts  for discussion to allow a diverse group of stakeholders to learn from each other in the process of  defining the scope, and relationships between elements to consider when identifying pain points and  opportunities for improvements or solutions

I start the process by creating a straw man graphic of the problem domain. To develop the straw

man graphic, I will draw from any existing material available to understand the environment. The  existing material may be operational or procedural documents, training materials, marketing  materials, GAO or other auditing reports. If materials are not available, then I conduct informal  interviews with one-three of the stakeholders who serve as my main points of contact on the  initiative. If appropriate to the situation, I will borrow the concept to “front-stage/back-stage” from  previous research, and discussed in Victor Fernandez’s book, “The Connected Company”. The front- stage/back-stage approach helps to reinforce the notion that every service – even an internal service  – has customers with whom the service provider interacts and internal processes that enable the  organization to provide the service. The template I often start with also has a column on the left to  identify Partners and Value Chain Providers and a column on the right to identify Oversight  Organizations, such as Congress, GAO, labor unions, advocacy groups, and other entities that may  add constraints to how the organization operates. The straw man graphic is simple, using simple  shapes and icons available in Visio or on the Internet. If the front-stage/back-stage view doesn’t  work, then I will create a different type of visual, either based on a high-level process flow with swim  lanes for different stakeholders, or another format. For the activity, I will divide the stakeholders into  groups of 5-6 participants each representing a different organization or area of interest. Each group  receives a poster-size copy of the straw man graphic that they can write on directly, or use sticky  notes to make comments. I give them two-three questions to answer, such as: 1) What key elements  are missing from the graphic? 2) What would you change about the graphic to make it more  accurately reflect your problem space? 3) What key insights do you have about the relationships  between the entities in your problem space? I give them approximately 20 minutes to discuss the  questions and mark up the graphic. Then I have each group report out on their answers to those  three questions while pointing to the mark-ups on their poster. As each group reports out, I record  commonalities in the insights of each group, and then additional insights that come from the group  discussion on an additional copy of the graphic. After the session, I digitize each group’s poster as an

artifact, create a view that combines the shared and new insights from the group discussion, and  then create a revised graphic that incorporates their feedback and proposed changes that they  agreed to as a group.

What I have learned from conducting this exercise with several groups is that while the graphic –

especially the revised graphic that incorporates their feedback – is important for reinforcing their  understanding of the problem they are working to solve, the more valuable aspect of the activity is  the shared insights and shared learning that occurs while they are working to define their problem  space. The graphic gives the diverse group of stakeholders a focal point for discussion that allows  them to share their perspectives and develop insights into potential root causes of their problems.  While they could create the graphic from a blank slate in a collaborative manner, starting with a  straw man jump starts the conversation for them. They can quickly identify where they are in the  graphic and can more quickly gain new insights about relationships between key entities instead of  taking time to identify them.

In this course of Design Thinking I learned the basics about several design tools. One of those is storytelling. Storytelling is my favorite because it is so simple and easy to apply. It involves presenting your product or business in a story format that truly intrigues the potential customer or investor; while also creating a cause for a problem and making a list about different ways to solve it.

Application

Most likely, each and everyone of those reading this have gone for some shopping in some kind of clothing store and used a fitting room at least once in their lives. If you have used a fitting room several times, you must have felt that stress of not knowing when the employee might come knock on your door and open it because he couldn't hear you reply "taken" for some reason or another. Maybe the music inside the store was too loud, maybe you just panic and don't know what to do or say, or perhaps you happen to be deaf and/or mute. So, what happens next? The employee opens the door and there you are with barely any clothes on and some other customers catch a glimpse of you almost naked. If you go shopping regularly, then you must know the fear that I'm talking about.

While I was shopping myself I wondered: what if I were to design a device (either automatic or manual) that lets the employee know whether someone is currently using the fitting room or not?

Insight & Approach

My audience in this case, would be the customers that go shopping in clothing stores regularly, as well as investors and stores’ owners.

To apply this tool properly, it’s important to tell the story in the most intriguing way to the people that truly care about such things. After building a team for this presentation, we would need to be constantly asking relevant questions to our audience and then providing the answers to those questions. One of those questions could be: “How could this affect the overall customer’s experience apart from just using the fitting room?”. In that case, we can assure that the customer’s experience will be better, even if they don’t need to use the fitting room. Why? Because the employees’ workload will become less than usual, and that means they’ll be able to attend other tasks that are just as necessary, such as looking for a certain size for a customer, attending the cash register, welcoming customers into the store, and so on.

Visualization

Written by Saly, 5th Nov 2019

Challenge & Selection

I have been working for a telecommunication company as a designer. Now our

company is struggling to develop a new business model as a next-generation

growth power. We are testing a new service every day and frequently lose from it

and have to learn.

The most beneficial and convincing tool I have ever used as a service designer is

Visualization. Whenever I start a new project, there is countless further

technology information over tens of stakeholders I have to consider. It is

challenging to learn about brand new technological components, including AR,

VR, 5G, etc. for every upcoming project. It is the very first step and fundamental

procedure to define what is the goal of a new project and to be on the same

page with core stakeholders. Visualization could be a powerful engine for on-

going communication on how to explain new technology would be applied for a

new digital service. With the visualization tool, I could compare new tech into

daily life, such as a flying car or Japanese famous cartoon 'Dragon-ball' scout.

It is significant to share one's ideas with other project members, including every

little clue on their mind. If we discuss one's opinion dealing with "What is the key

problem we are struggling to solve together?", I frequently have experienced that

only a few members who have more experience in this filed or who have a higher

position might have a dominant position. Who are not familiar with the project

and who has different ideas would hesitate to raise one's opinion. I believe

visualization tools could prevent this kind of problem as a non-verbal way of

communication. Every member could imagine based on what the other's post-it

with a sketch or even doodling then develop it in positive ways. My role as a

service designer is to stimulate design thinking, not analysis what it is and why

this paint comes. In the first step, we need to elaborate on what we are facing to

figure out every element regarding the project.

Application

I usually apply this powerful tool with two contrasting images. It is essential to

get used to drawing because most of the project participants seldom have a

chance to bring. That's why I show my real painting with a straw man who looks

like kindergarten students made. To develop one's image, I utilize "Now" and

"New" moments, which are similar to "As-Is" and "To-Be" methodology. If we

could download a new Marvel Movie within 5 seconds on our existing

smartphone, what might happen to our daily life? (This question is closely related

to the latest technology 5G, AR, and VR.)

If appropriate to the project situation, I frequently adopt the tool 'Storytelling'

which display a synergy effect with 'Visualization.' People could imagine when

they recognize the virtual situation as their own real life. The strong story would

develop emotional connecting between participants and new conditions. The

facilitator should elaborate on compelling stories that every participant could get

immersed in their daily life. Then team members easily imagine what kinds of

new events are upcoming with a given situation with pros and cons. The more

powerful the story is, the more detail ideas might come with one's drawing. My

success point depends on could my narrative has an underlying need for

participants.

For this activity, I develop a persona representing their family members or friends,

even coworking employees. Imagination becomes powerful when stakeholders

shift their positions and then think outside the box. I show the famous actor or

actress image as a persona and suggest three questions to answer, such as; 1)

What kinds of activities are possible for the above persona? 2) What might be

still unmet needs for those personas? 3) With the new technology, how the

persona seems to feel? While they are imagining and developing one's idea, I set

a ground-rule "Do not talk with another participant." I give almost 5 minutes for

each question and then display each one's drawing on the wall. Then I give

another 5 minutes to look around the other's answer without talking to each

other. After this session, participants could redesign their ideas with different

color pens for 5 minutes. After 25 minutes, participants finally share own's

opinion and discuss one's draft and revision together.

Insight & Approach

What I have learned from conduction this exercise after starting this course work

is an emotional connection to the given situation is a crucial success factor to

utilize Visualization and storytelling. Even a participant who is not familiar with

drawing and persona methodology could be lost in a situational assignment and

build one's original story. Whenever I suggested ambiguous contrasting guide

images (As-Is vs. To-Be or A/B) at the first stage, participants rarely get immersed

into a persona. Furthermore, I have realized that imagination without

communication could be powerful than detail descriptions. Sometimes every little

detail might help participants develop their ideas more realistic; on the other

hand, it put a cap on the storyline. It is essential for imagination that there would

be room for creativity, story, and emotional engagement. As a service designer, I

try to find out the balance between appropriate enough instructions and

sufficient room.

I am still on my way to figure out how to apply design thinking methodology for

digital service innovation. I have to estimate which level of description is

appropriate for participants to get immersed in an imaginative story. The point

might be modified based on participants' experience with the new technology or

design thinking tools. As a service designer, I need to be conscious of the design

thinking methodology, including Visualization, Storytelling, and business case

studies from now on.

Challenge

It​ ​was​ ​then​ ​time​ ​to​ ​build​ ​a​ ​compelling​ ​story​ ​so​ ​I​ ​decided​ ​on​ ​the​ ​main​ ​building​ ​blocks​ ​of​ ​the  iDoctor​ ​patient​ ​story:    Setting:​ ​Introduce​ ​the​ ​main​ ​character,​ ​Sarah​ ​who​ ​is​ ​a​ ​busy​ ​mum​ ​with​ ​3​ ​kids​ ​under​ ​6.  Struggle:​ ​Sarah​ ​is​ ​unwell​ ​but​ ​it​ ​is​ ​always​ ​difficult​ ​to​ ​pack​ ​all​ ​the​ ​kids​ ​into​ ​the​ ​car​ ​and​ ​drag​ ​them  off​ ​to​ ​the​ ​doctors​ ​office.​ ​ ​There​ ​has​ ​to​ ​be​ ​another​ ​way! Resolution:​ ​Sarah​ ​successfully​ ​connects​ ​with​ ​a​ ​doctor,​ ​is​ ​easily​ ​diagnosed​ ​and​ ​prescribed  medication​ ​which​ ​is​ ​promptly​ ​delivered​ ​to​ ​her​ ​within​ ​the​ ​hour.​ ​ ​Sarah​ ​is​ ​absolutely​ ​thrilled​ ​and  recommends​ ​iDoctor​ ​to​ ​all​ ​of​ ​her​ ​friends.    Now​ ​that​ ​I​ ​had​ ​the​ ​bones​ ​of​ ​the​ ​storey,​ ​I​ ​fleshed​ ​out​ ​the​ ​detail​ ​and​ ​used​ ​visualisation​ ​to  enhance​ ​the​ ​story​ ​and​ ​show​ ​examples​ ​of​ ​every​ ​important​ ​touchpoint​ ​on​ ​Mary’s​ ​journey.

Insight

I​ ​found​ ​that​ ​using​ ​Storytelling​ ​in​ ​the​ ​final​ ​presentation​ ​to​ ​iDoctor​ ​was​ ​a​ ​very​ ​effective​ ​way​ ​for​ ​us  to​ ​convey​ ​the​ ​technology​ ​solution​ ​and​ ​vision​ ​for​ ​the​ ​business​ ​in​ ​a​ ​way​ ​that​ ​was​ ​easy​ ​for​ ​them​ ​to  absorb,​ ​understand​ ​and​ ​remember.    Using​ ​a​ ​design​ ​thinking​ ​approach​ ​to​ ​this​ ​problem​ ​and​ ​applying​ ​Storytelling​ ​allowed​ ​me​ ​to​ ​really  drill​ ​down​ ​on​ ​what​ ​was​ ​most​ ​important​ ​to​ ​iDoctor​ ​and​ ​that​ ​was​ ​their​ ​patient’s​ ​well​ ​being.​ ​ ​It  challenged​ ​me​ ​to​ ​look​ ​at​ ​it​ ​iDoctor’s​ ​offering​ ​from​ ​the​ ​point​ ​of​ ​view​ ​of​ ​a​ ​real​ ​patient​ ​and​ ​tell​ ​a  great​ ​story​ ​about​ ​how​ ​that​ ​patient​ ​was​ ​able​ ​to​ ​find​ ​and​ ​engage​ ​iDoctor​ ​and​ ​have​ ​a​ ​great,  frictionless​ ​experience.​ ​ ​Throughout​ ​the​ ​story​ ​I​ ​was​ ​able​ ​to​ ​dot​ ​in​ ​ways​ ​our​ ​technology​ ​could  help​ ​support​ ​the​ ​vision​ ​that​ ​I​ ​was​ ​presenting​ ​but​ ​only​ ​when​ ​it​ ​enhanced​ ​the​ ​patients’​ ​or​ ​the  doctors’​ ​experience.

Design Thinking for Innovation    Reflection Assignment - Design Thinking in the Broadcast and Media Industry    Richard Moseley  23 July 2021    Challenge & Selection    Part of my job in business development and sales requires telling a story to communicate a  compelling message to my customers to identify mutual new business opportunities, and ultimately  sell a product, solution, or service.    I work in the television broadcast and media industry, in which the technical landscape is constantly  evolving with new and interesting ways to deliver and consume video, audio, and data content.   Many of my customers can be overwhelmed by the broad-ranging new technologies available and  struggle to understand how they can adopt such technologies to create additional revenue streams  or generate greater profit margins.    I chose the Storytelling tool to help take my customers on an imaginative, learning, and interactive  journey to explore what their business model and consumer offering could look like embracing some  of these new technologies.  The aim is to ultimately generate interest in one or more of the products  or services I am tasked with selling and lead the way to produce a new technology design, agree on  commercial pricing and terms, and deployment of the new service.    Application    Since the successful deal closure with one of my customers’ a tier 1 UK broadcaster, using a state-of- the-art cloud-based technology solution, there have been no further immediate new business  opportunities emerging.  I, therefore, prepared two stories linked to new technologies that would  complement their cloud-based solution, which could ultimately once validated and refined, generate  additional revenue for my customer.    My first story relates to an enhanced consumer TV experience using personalised TV technology for  delivery of television channels through the Internet, providing a more immersive experience for the  end consumer, as the television programme content is specifically selected to match the individuals’  tastes.  The business proposition for my customer is (i) improved consumer retention as the TV  channels become more appealing to each individual and (ii) a greater commercial value of the  advertisement slots, as they too can be targeted and adapted to suite the individuals’ tastes.    I then told the story of another customer who also adopted a cloud-based technology solution and  how they capitalised on its attributes, such as flexibility, scalability, and speed to launch new TV  channels and services.  I explained all of these attributes enabled that customer to secure new  business over the competition, enabling new profitable revenue streams.  For example, (i) the  flexibility comes from a pure software solution enabling changes to take place with ease, such as  changing a standard definition channel to a high or ultra-high definition channel, (ii) the scalability  come from cloud solution expansion simplicity, enabling extra channels to be launched without the  need for significant investment, and (iii) the software and cloud solution facilitates the rapid launch  of new channels and feature, such as ‘ad-hoc’ PoP up thematic channels for special events such as  the Olympics and Christmas TV Shows.

Insight and Approach    With these first two stories my customer became fully engaged, not so much about what I was trying  to sell to them, but how they could now see the new business opportunities for them and how they  could succeed.  On reflection, perhaps the stories could have been enhanced with the aid of a  visualisation tool.    As for the next steps, I plan to deliver a broader version of the stories to a wider audience from  different departments within the customer’s organisation, this time with the aid of complementary  visualisation tools to help reinforce the message.  The visualisation tool will show (i) how the  technology will integrate within their new cloud solution, (ii) how the flow of the costs and revenue  streams will occur, and (iii) the human interactivity from my company, my customer, and the end  consumer.    Although telling a story about a new business idea seems to go hand-in-hand, I hadn’t fully  appreciated it as a ‘tool’ until this course.  I now feel story preparation and delivery complementary  to the product or service I am selling is a key item for success.

Reflection Assignment, submitted by Jose Lopez

Visualization Tool

Challenge

After more than 20 years working for large corporations, I have decided to take on the challenge  and the opportunity to reinvent myself as an entrepreneur. Luckily, a few weeks after I left my  previous job I met a college professor who was looking to build a startup but had not had the  time to develop it into a working business. I offered to help and we got started on our early stage  startup (code name: “The Box”).

It has been an exhilarating time, doing research on problems we both have encountered and  are eager to solve. We have very different backgrounds, so we needed to create common  ground so we could communicate effectively and efficiently in order to build trust and  commitment to our newly found mission together.

Selection

Previously, I understood visualization as a creative exercise that consists of creating a realistic  mental image of the future one desires in order to facilitate its realization. However, the  Visualization tool for Design Thinking is quite different as it consists of using visual artifacts to  express concepts, ideas and relationships in order to bring them forward in a way that words  cannot.

My cofounder and I quickly learned that we were having trouble understanding each other  because we would use terms that mean different things depending on the context. We soon  figured out that by making sketches and drawings we could reach mutual understanding much  faster whenever we got stuck. Thus, we intuitively adopted the Visualization tool and made good  use of it for our purposes.

Application

We started working on “The Box” as an ecommerce marketplace for subscription-based  shopping, as we both knew many young entrepreneurs who are having trouble retaining their  current customers and thought it would be a solution to their problem. We drew up many boxes  and circles to represent all of the kinds of sellers we were thinking about, and by collecting them  into a Venn Diagram we were able to make a preliminary segmentation in order to pick  customers for ethnographic interviews: we selected lifestyle products with high purchase  frequency.

Once we had a better grip of the pain points and jobs to be done that our customers are facing,  we used drawings to generate ideas of services, marketplaces and platforms that could help  solve the problem. At the moment, we are in conversations with a UX designer to build a

working model of our service (not yet a prototype), based on these hand-drawn figures that  describe the high-level steps for sellers and buyers:

We also got a bit ahead of ourselves and went ahead and drew lots of flywheels and virtuous  cycles to represent potential growth models we should consider in order to accelerate growth.  Visualization is our favorite innovation tool!

Insight

I learned that in many cases verbal communication (face to face speech or written messages)  falls short when one is trying to simplify a concept that is complex or based on intricate  relationships between basic ideas. On the other hand, using simple visualizations can help to  transmit and receive messages in a more direct and clear way, even if the drawings are of very  low quality from and aesthetic sense.

A key factor that makes visualization so helpful is that it makes metaphors like the “flywheel,”  “cycles” and “platforms” easier to process intellectually because the relationship is evident at a  glance. This may sound trivial but in the high-speed high-pressure world of startups it creates  great efficiency and focus.

Additionally, sharing drawings and sketches helps to build teamwork as it allows one to peek  into each other’s mind. It is fun to use it that way.

Approach

Next time I begin any kind of business project I will make sure to apply visualization as soon and  as often as possible. To improve the quality of my visual communication skills I plan to read Dan  Roam’s books on the subject.

student: Francesco Rizzi      Final Assignment

Challenge  Me and my team were contracted as design consultants for innovation by a Training Company  that offers courses for businessmen/women and entrepreneurs. These entrepreneurs have  various levels of knowledge and seek the most diverse types of courses, from basic courses to  more advanced courses in order to help them start a new business or improve their current  business. The Training Company has noticed a recurring decline in demand for its courses. So  we ran some design thinking activities and we mapped different customer profiles (personas)  and what was their main concerns which was causing the decreasing search for courses. The  main problem identified was that the lessons are being given just as 20 years ago - in a  “traditional” way, but the society has changed a lot since then. So, our challenge was to change  the dynamics and methodology of the classes, the tools used and the physical space that must  change to adapt the new reality of the students (access to technology, more information but less  time to learn).    Selection  As we have gone through other design thinking activities that allowed us identify the best  solution, we realised that we were ready to test the Learning Launch tool. This tool would allows  us to quickly test whether the new idea and concept of the classroom that we designed will meet  the students’ desires.    Application  The strategy for our learning launch was trying to test a new concept of classroom, class  dynamics and instructional design. Our assumption was that a new classroom layout would  engage students in a more dynamic class.     We reorganize the classroom with whiteboards around its wall, 3 lcd televisions in which the  students could group together and research topics together and also present their findings to  other classmates. We also asked the instructor to reorganize the class content, so the studends  would be engaged in trying to solve a problem (we called it a “mission”) without a previous  content/knowledge. This would test our assumption that students would be more engaged after  trying to accomplish a task - they would probably fail, but mainly they would understand “why”  they are learning.    Insight  After running the first learning launch test, we realized that our first assumptions seemed to be  right, but we are not able to compare with a more “traditional” classroom. So we ran a second

test, this time we created the same course with two different structures: one with a more “  traditional” approach and another one with the more innovative way. Doing this, was possible to  realize what worked better in the new classroom. We also tried to change some students during  the course to observe how they would react to different contexts of classroom, and we found  that the “traditional” students scored less than others in the final assignment.    Approach  When this training company contact us to solve their problem, we gone through several design  thinking activities but their staff (teachers and coordinators) were not confident if their ideas and  assumptions would work for real. So the best way to confirm if their idea would work was to  prototype and test in a real environment. So the best way to do this was using the leaning  launch tool.

REFLECTION

Introducing the Reflection Activity

•  During a study abroad experience, students worked on a collaborative

design project with international peers. The purpose of this design

project was to provide students with meaningful international experiences. At

three points in the project, students reflected on their experience working in a

cross-cultural team. The purpose of these reflection activities was for students

to look back on their experiences, learn from them, and be prepared for future

similar experiences.

•   Three times throughout the quarter, students were asked to reflect on their

experience working on a project in a cross-cultural team. In the first reflection,

students reflected on their interests and goals within their field of study and

how those connected to the course. The purpose of this reflection was to set

the stage for the course and students’ experiences in cross-cultural teams. In the

second reflection, students reflected on how they saw the project and the

intercultural collaboration, and how these related to their learning .

•    The purpose of this reflection was for students to pause a few weeks into their

work and see what they had learned and make any necessary adjustments for the

rest of the course. In the final reflection at the end of the quarter, students reflected on

their overall experience. The purpose of the final reflection was to support

students in looking back at their experience and thinking about what they had

accomplished and how it connected to their future.

•  After each reflection assignment was submitted, the teaching team read the

individual reflections of each of the teams they were mentoring and provided

feedback to that team. The reflection assignment was graded on whether the

student did the assignment and on the depth of the reflection using levels of

reflection by Neville Hatton and David Smith: Descriptive Writing, Descriptive

Reflection, Dialogic Reflection, and Critical Reflection1 students were asked to

write at the last two levels (and were given indicators for each level, so they

could judge for themselves). Additionally, the Rose-Hulman educator read all of

he Rose-Hulman students’ reflections because their reflections were a

component of their grade for the course.

•  In terms of outcomes, there was potential for students to better understand

Retroreflection

Working principle of a corner reflector

Main article: Retroreflector

•  Some surfaces exhibit retroreflection. The structure of these surfaces is such that light is  returned in the direction from which it came.

•  When flying over clouds illuminated by sunlight the region seen around the aircraft's shadow will  appear brighter, and a similar effect may be seen from dew on grass. This partial retro-reflection  is created by the refractive properties of the curved droplet's surface and reflective properties at  the backside of the droplet.

•  Some animals' retinas act as retroreflectors (see tapetum lucidum for more detail), as this  effectively improves the animals' night vision. Since the lenses of their eyes modify reciprocally  the paths of the incoming and outgoing light the effect is that the eyes act as a strong  retroreflector, sometimes seen at night when walking in wildlands with a flashlight.

•  A simple retroreflector can be made by placing three ordinary mirrors mutually perpendicular to  one another (a corner reflector). The image produced is the inverse of one produced by a single  mirror. A surface can be made partially retroreflective by depositing a layer of tiny refractive  spheres on it or by creating small pyramid like structures. In both cases internal reflection causes  the light to be reflected back to where it originated. This is used to make traffic signs and  automobile license plates reflect light mostly back in the direction from which it came. In this  application perfect retroreflection is not desired, since the light would then be directed back into  the headlights of an oncoming car rather than to the driver's eyes.

Multiple reflections

Multiple reflections in two plane mirrors at a 60° angle.

•  When light reflects off a mirror, one image appears. Two mirrors placed exactly face to face give  the appearance of an infinite number of images along a straight line. The multiple images seen  between two mirrors that sit at an angle to each other lie over a circle.[3] The center of that  circle is located at the imaginary intersection of the mirrors. A square of four mirrors placed face  to face give the appearance of an infinite number of images arranged in a plane. The multiple  images seen between four mirrors assembling a pyramid, in which each pair of mirrors sits an  angle to each other, lie over a sphere. If the base of the pyramid is rectangle shaped, the images  spread over a section of a torus.[4]

•  Note that these are theoretical ideals, requiring perfect alignment of perfectly smooth, perfectly  flat perfect reflectors that absorb none of the light. In practice, these situations can only be  approached but not achieved because the effects of any surface imperfections in the reflectors

propagate and magnify, absorption gradually extinguishes the image, and any observing  equipment (biological or technological) will interfere.
