Reflection - Learning Launch

Challenge

We are all living in a global world with millions of products but still we must deal with the scarcity of  time and budget. Especially in the design industry, the products are nearly same however there is  large scale of pricing. In addition, because of the limited time, we are likely to consume the best  option we come across between few alternatives. However, the marketplace is huge and there are  many other products that maximizes our satisfaction in terms of design, quality, and price but we  aren’t aware of them.

To solve this problem, me and my colleagues, had the idea of creating an application that the users  will take the picture of the product that they like and the application will provide the worldwide  similar alternatives according to the picture they uploaded. The main challenge for us is, there are  giant platforms like Amazon, Alibaba etc. that provides large scale of products. Therefore, the main  question is: “Are these platforms and filtering systems while searching for a product sufficient in  these platforms, or they are not? Is there need of a platform consists our idea, or not?”

Selection

The tool that I selected for this challenge is learning launch. Since we have limited budget and time,  we should do low-costed experiments that will give response quickly. In this tool, our main goal is to  “learn” if our idea will work or not, by getting feedbacks from the public. By using learning launch, we  will reduce the risk of experiencing big failures at the end. We will have the opportunity to test our  idea and be able to take accurate actions.

Application

For making rational experiments firstly, we determined our potential customers. Our main goal is to  attract the people who already uses online shopping. According to Eurostat’s data, the biggest share  of online shopping belongs to the population aged between 16 and 24. However while making our  surveys we considered that due to Covid-19 outbreak, the number of higher aged e-shoppers will  increase.

After determining our potential customers, we designed a survey for them. In the survey we asked  questions like “Before buying a product would you like to see other similar products? If yes, how  many products will be enough? Did you experienced regret, after buying a product because of you  missed another alternative? If yes, how frequent it happens?”. Lastly, we designed a small prototype  of our idea. We wanted from our participants to share the last cloth they bought with us. After, we  provide them 5 more similar alternatives and asked, “Do you want to replace your cloth with one of  our alternatives?”

Insight

After bringing the learning launch to life, we find out how consumption habits change according to  gender and age. In additions we had more accurate assumptions to the question of “Will our idea  work?”.

Firstly, while both men and women wanted to see the other alternatives, men were satisfied when  they saw less options than women. On the other hand, while most of the women who participated to  the survey felt regret after they bought a product and saw its better alternative, most of the men  declared that they didn’t felt any regret at all.

In addition, no matter the gender X generation wanted to see more alternatives than Z generation.  This result was not surprising for us however, it is significant. Even though the e-shoppers are mainly  members of Z generation, people who most wanted to see the alternative products were the  members of X generation. Therefore, our business model should include and prioritize generation X  as well. Most significantly, more than half of the people who tried our prototype, declared that “If  they had a chance, they would replace their product with one of the alternatives we provided.”

Approach

As a result, by using learning launch tool we gained many valuable information. Firstly, it helped us to  determine our potential customers correctly from the very beginning.  Secondly, it showed us that  our idea may work however some of our assumption were incorrect. For example, participants were  generally satisfied with seeing less alternatives than what we expected or generation X was our main  potential buyers, but we were about to miss it. Learning launch tool, allowed us to step in the shoes  of the customers. It taught us about their mindsets and their needs. It also lighted the path for  reaching to them. Finally, if we had a chance to change the tool that we used, probably we would  prefer to stay with learning launch. Since our idea is based on an idea in the future, for making it  clear in the minds of our potential customers, making prototypes and surveys are the most efficient  way of gaining information.

Reflection Visualization      Challenge    I work as a client partner in a data and insights company. One of my long time clients is a  manufacturer of products for the process industry and provider of related services and  solutions. Their customers are companies like dairies, oil firms, pharmaceuticals, chemicals  and the like. In a recent project we were assigned with the development of personas for the  typical functions within their customers’ organization. The overall objective was to make the  innovation process and communication activities more customer-focused. The personas  would help the organization get a better understanding of customers’ needs, requirements,  expectations and pain points in their everyday work.   The project sponsor understood the value of qualitative insights and had some experience in  design thinking. But most managers within my client had an engineering background and  had - as described in the course - a prevention mindset. They were obsessed with total  quality and lean management both in the area of production and product quality, as well as  in innovation. They dislike uncertainty and vagueness, and like hard facts and data, lots of  data, which they can analyze to the highest possible extent. So applying design thinking  elements to informing their future communication and innovation activities was somewhat  revolutionary to them.      Selection    In order to gain acceptance for the project outcome from all stakeholders involved, the  project team knew that a mix of tools and methods is required. In the What Is Phase we  applied In Depth Interviews with 40 customers from three countries and six different  functions, coming from several industries. I agree that a sample size of 25 - 40 is sufficient  for this kind of research, as mentioned in the course. In addition, the team condensed the  main insights from previous work we had done for that client.  When the team was almost done with the development of the personas, we decided to  apply the tool of visualization. To get a common understanding among the innovation and  communication managers and gain their buy-in, we wanted to transfer the key  characteristics of the personas, what is typical for each one and in how far they differ from  each other. And we wanted to do this using many media – not only the verbal description  and the key elements in words, but also sketches. This way we wanted to make the personas  more tangible, to give them an emotional dimension and a personality the managers can  relay to.      Application    We hired a professional graphic designer and briefed him by giving him the written  description of the five personas we had developed. One week later, the designer presented  us with drawings for each one of the personas. These included a full body sketch of the  persona itself, positioned within a number of smaller sketches, depicting typical situations  the person finds themselves in - either in their business life or in their private context. These

sketches were supposed to visually depict the expectations, values and the mottos in their  lives. So while a control-possessed persona might be depicted as a stamp collector, someone  who loves technical challenges would be shown repairing their old-timer car.       Insight    The visualization of the personas provided several insights, some of these on unexpected  domains. An example: The project team wanted to produce a diverse set of personas, so two  of the five personas bore female names and the designer sketched female persons for these  two. However, when the female managers saw the drawings, they protested that the female  personas were drawn as being too model-like, too attractive and too close to the  sexy/attractive young woman archetype as used in consumer goods advertising. This came  as a surprise to their male colleagues. But to me, this may have been a manifestation of the  male-dominated company culture. I think the female managers in this case found a way to  express their feelings about some superiors’ policy of underestimating or underpromoting  women in the workforce.   Another insight relates to the typical situations which the graphic designer used. Some of  these provoked discussions among the managers and with the project team, which we  otherwise would not have had. This helped us refine some core elements of the description  of the personas and clear some sources of misunderstanding. If we hadn't produced the  drawings, we would not have notice that the same wordings meant different things to  different people.      Approach    Visualization proved to be a very powerful and useful tool in this challenge. As an  improvement, the next time I would involve the stakeholders (the managers) into the  visualization. For example, in an activation workshop I would engage the managers and ask  them to brainstorm and describe what might be typical situations for each persona in their  business and private lives. Ideally, I would have the graphic designer also in the conference  room, catching the suggestions from the brainstorming and turning these into drawings.

Probably I had been very  practical and insensitive for which people could not  match the wavelength of ideas and my points were  not clear to them and they were bored. I was not  getting proper response and attention on the basis of  my scientific ideas encircled around logics and  numbers.      Selection of tool:   I choose the storytelling tool because it is more  captivating and interesting. Stories are more  interactive. It allows people to share knowledge and  emotions greater. Business Development requires  more than problem answer approach. More  convincing power is required one needs to link their  ideas and viewpoint with the audience or the  customers. It wins the hearts of the people and convinces their  minds ideas to invest in the ideas by creating a  connection emotionally. Both orator and audience can interact better and ideas  get clarity and emphasis.     Story telling tool is that vital push for any project or  innovation to reach the hearts and mind and make a  greater impact and earn success. Challenge and Selection

A key area of my job scope is to develop step-by-step digitalization guides for the  small and medium enterprises (SMEs) of various industries and sectors. The SMEs  are important to Singapore, collectively employing 70% of Singapore’s workforce and  account for almost half of Singapore’s GDP. Hence, digitalisation of SMEs can have  a profound impact on Singapore’s economy.

However, SMEs generally lack the technical know-how and find it difficult to divert  resources to digital transformation. Hence, it is important to develop a guide to make  going digital simple for the SMEs.

To develop a guide that is most suitable to the needs of the SMEs, I plan to conduct  a series of workshops with various SMEs, and use the Mind Mapping tool to  generate insights, collect information and create design criteria.

Application

In the first workshop that I conduct, I will gather information from the SMEs to  understand their experiences in digitalization. I will get each SME to fill up a form to  provide me with information regarding their digital transformation journey, such as:

-  Current mode business operations (manual vs digital)

-  Areas of improvement for business operations

-  Challenges that SMEs when digitalizing

-  Obstacles that are stopping them from digitalizing

In the second workshop, with the information consolidated, I will set up a room with  walls filled with the common problems faced by the SMEs in the industry and the  SMEs can go around the room to understand the problems and think about how  digitalization can come in to help solve the problems.

In the third workshop, SMEs will be put together in groups to share their experiences  and problems, and most importantly, how digitalization can help. The SMEs will then  work together, to discuss on how they want to digitally transform their businesses in  step-by-step manner.

Insight and Approach

We have vast amount of information and data regarding the SMEs, and we thought  we knew what SMEs need. So, we developed the guides for the SMEs without  gathering and consolidating in a structured manner. However, we noticed that SMEs  did not find the guides useful.

With the mind mapping tool, I believe that we can better organize the information  provided by the SMEs, draw insights from their businesses and scope the design

criteria to help generate better suited ideas to be included in the guides. Bringing the  SMEs together and getting them to map their needs and requirements together, will  provide SMEs with best-suited guidance in their digital journey.

It is important to view from the consumer perspective. In my case, SMEs are my  consumer. To provide them with a product, the step-by-step guide, that can benefit  them and help them digitalize, it is vital to hear from them on what they need and  want.

Storytelling solutions for stories that need telling

By Joe Hernandez

1. Challenge: Describe your challenge.

We define storytelling as the art of telling stories. Therefore, the first thing we must do is agree on what a story is.  A general definition may be a succession of events ordered in time, but, a very important element is missing… our  emotions. It is our emotions that create bonds between people. Our emotions link us with one another and create  relationships. Relationships will then allow us to sell our services. It does not matter whether you are a small  entrepreneur or a large company. If you do not know how to generate positive emotions in your potential clients,  you will not sell. And good stories can generate very positive emotions. It is important to remember that without  emotion, there is no story. My challenge is to be able to promote the island’s (in which I reside) project to convert  it into a SMART island , in order to reduce the damage that has already been done, and to improve the quality of  life of all of those that enjoy this beautiful island.

2.Selection: In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected

I chose the Storytelling tool. There are many ways of storytelling, especially when wanting to captivate a certain  audience.     I chose the “who are we?” type of story. This type of story is used to introduce ourselves, to have the public get to  know us and our mission. It is our own, personal story and, as in any good story, there must be a conflict. In other  words, a challenge that we have had to face and from which we have emerged. Becoming a more reinforced  company, which has helped us grow. People like to see that the speaker also has problems like them and can  overcome them, because that creates inspiration and help.

“Hard times” are one of the most powerful, empathy seeking and important stories to tell. Especially when you  explain how you felt and what you did to get out of the struggle. It’s all about transparency and showing that I am  afraid and doubtful about the future of our island. This in turn, makes me seem more human and links me better  with my audience. The key, I learned, is to always push to be authentic, and to not make things up or exaggerate. A  lack of honesty is easily detected, and authenticity has its reward: public loyalty.

3.Application: Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge

I studied who I was targeting, those who enjoy this beautiful island. The story has to do with the purpose, to  promote a better quality of tourism. I explained why we are transforming our island into a SMART island, why we  are focusing on efficiency and sustainability and how we strive to leave our island better than the way we found it.  I explained the island’s history, how it has evolved through the years and how tourism has affected everyone’s  lives here. The transformation has truly been astronomical, and even though it has brought many positive changes,  it also brought many consequences. Species of animals becoming endangered, ruining of landscapes,  contamination and pollution, corruption and economical inflation. The key was to use logic in explaining the story,  giving it meaning to create an emotional attachment, and offering solutions for a better future, for the benefit of  all of us who enjoy the island.

4.Insight: Describe the insight you gained from applying the tool you selected to your challenge

I learned, by applying the technique of storytelling, that every story has a structure that’s composed of:

A Body.

It is the presentation, the approach to the initial situation. It may be that the conflict has not yet appeared here, or  you are already beginning to intuit. The important thing is that, at some point, something happens that leads us to  the next part of the story.

A Knot.

Here the conflict is raised openly, and the protagonist looks for solutions to resolve it although he still cannot find  them (otherwise, the story would end here). The important thing about this phase is that learning, growth occurs  here. And this is what will allow the conflict to be resolved.

An Outcome.

After several attempts, the protagonist finds the solution and solves the problem. It is no longer the same from the  beginning. It is wiser. It has learned, it has evolved, it has grown. It has truly succeeded.

5.Approach: Describe what you might do differently next time

Next time I would concentrate more on the fact that we must know ourselves at a deeper level, the better you  know yourself, the better stories you will build. Let’s be ourselves, the public likes authenticity. It is also  fundamental to always get the audience involved in the story, and to get them involved. If the public does not feel  identified with the story, a bond will not be created. It is important to also project our ideas. To tell our audience  about our vision, our mission and our values. A laugh or a chuckle can go a long way, it is also crucial to use humor,  there is nothing better than humor to win the public over. Stories are a very powerful tool; we should always try to  avoid the temptation to manipulate and cheat with our storytelling because it can always turn against us.

This tested our assumption that the structure and  execution were the main causes of our sales and workflow challenge. Our whole team went through a one- week training programme on how to adapt to the consumers and what they expect from us instead of  what we are expecting to sell them, like in the case of IBM. Then they conducted a real-world test of who  sales the most and has the most customer satisfaction and that person received incentives and we  expected to produce a document with a clear description of our new, more agile processes and sales  strategies.

For our second learning launch, we focused on gaining clarity about our sales strategies, customer  expectations, tasks and priorities. This tested our assumptions about how our prioritisation differed from  customers priorities and what was the main cause of inefficiency in the sales of the product. Then our team  completed the survey. Then a meeting was held with our stakeholders about new marketing strategies and  ways to improve our product based on the customers suggestions. The surveys included questions about our  new, proposed process, understanding the process and the prioritization of tasks, and feelings about the  change, had to be conducted within a two-week timeframe.

Insight

By applying the learning launch tool, our team identified our assumptions, ways to improve our product,  decrease the sales cost and designed launched to test these assumptions. We were calculating our expected  results, getting used to a more agile and aggressive approach of marketing and meeting the expectations of  our customers. Both our team and the stakeholders would be open to these changes and the prioritisation of  our new tasks and processes. Our actual results were slightly higher than we anticipated, the whole team and  stakeholders were ecstatic. The stakeholders were satisfied and wanted to move forward, our team will  review the insight and incorporated more efficient designs into future launch designs. The ongoing  incorporation of insight is of utmost importance at this stage, as launches come before a full rollout in the  design thinking timeline.

Design Thinking Reflection

Tool: Mindmapping

Challenge

The company I work for is in the education technology business, and we are constantly

working to provide schools, teachers, students and their parents across the country with

solutions to support 21st century teaching and learning. Our challenge is that we tend to

create solutions for these user groups that end up being something we THINK they need or

want, but the end result shows that there are other solutions that they ﬁnd more helpful.

Selection

The tool that I have decided to use with our team is mind mapping, inspired by the

“Mind Mapping Tool” video in Week 3. This tool was selected because we believed it to be

the most important in identifying emerging patterns that we previously missed, from all of the

feedback, insight, and data that we previously gathered; mind mapping, we believed, was the

preferred tool for us to create a common mind and understand the “what is” of the

situation.

Application and Insight

To apply this tool, we gathered members from all teams (some were Marketing, some

were Operations, while others were from the Partnerships Team as well). We locked down in

that room for an hour and used post-its to write down all of the user feedback and insight that

we have heard/seen through previous interactions with our own stakeholders. For example,

the Partnerships Team noted down insights they had gathered about our end-users through

discussions with our corporate partners, whereas the Marketing Team provided insight

gathered through feedback they collected from their various marketing campaigns.

DESIGN THINKING REFLECTION �1

With all post-its stuck on a primary whiteboard, we took a quick break before returning

to the meeting room to start identifying connections and ideas that we have missed in the

past. Things that we did not consider before suddenly became crystal clear to all of us, which

meant that we found gaps we could ﬁll more accurately instead of adding features to our

solutions that we ASSUMED people wanted or needed.

Having said that, we also understood that our approach towards using this tool had one

ﬂaw: we were relying on secondary feedback. This feedback was not directly collected from

our end users, it was collected from our internal team member’s and our partners’

interactions with end users.

In order to generate more accurate insight, we realised there was one change we needed

to apply to our approach.

Approach

Using the same methods explained above, we have recently tried including actual end-

users in the process. It wasn’t always easy since we would have to identify and invite teachers,

parents and students to our ofﬁces but so far its been a very illuminating experience. These

end users would also go through the process with our team members, using post-its to put

down their thoughts and then stick it on a board where we could produce a mind map and

identify emerging patterns.

We are quite hopeful for the future in using these tools for our processes, so that we can

make our solutions much more user-centred than they’ve ever been before.

The challenge

I’m currently part of the IT Governance Team within my organisation and one of my projects over the year  has been to gather and report KPI information across the various IT departments. My challenge is to automate the whole process where possible and to get the senior management  meaningful reports out within 7-9 working days.

Selection

The tool I have selected is Mind Mapping.  I have gathered individual feedback and large amounts of data  around the problems faced by stakeholder and customers of the process.  My aim is to make sure they  are all involved along this journey and to help drive towards an automated solution where I have their  buy in.

Mind Mapping has been identified as an effective tool to help analyse ideas and identify pattern and  themes.

According to Vanessa Sanchez, “Design Thinking for Innovation, Week3, Mind Mapping”. Available at    https://www.coursera.org/learn/uva-darden-design-thinking innovation/lecture/lsFRa/mind-mapping- tool , a marketing professor at Darton:  “Mind mapping is one of the most powerful tools in the design  thinker's toolbox. Application

The first step I took was to arrange an offsite day away from the office for all the stakeholders. 40  stakeholders were invited across IT from those supplying the data to those receiving the reports. The aim  was to get a holistic view; I shared the current problems/ issues and feedback received.

The stakeholders were split in to small groups and  given sticky notes and asked to sort through the data and feedback received and to come up with recurring  themes.  Because of the visual nature of Mind maps the teams were encouraged to either write or draw  their thoughts on the sticky notes. Challenge  I work in a team whose leader loves helping people, organizations, and communities in achieving  their fullest potential. One day, he decided to tackle the problem of productivity, or the lack  thereof, and how we are losing so much potential from too much procrastinating. Thus, our  journey began in discovering ​why ​do​ ​people tend to procrastinate (or tend to be unproductive)  and ​what ​are the unproductive activities they engage themselves with in lieu of the productive  ones.    The challenge in this endeavour is that we do not have a lot of people in our team to do  participant observation nor do we have the resources to do a launch in an instant. And that we  want to know the reasons behind our audience’s actions and we need to get personal in order to  know them and understand their reasons.    Selection  Thus, we decided to employ storytelling as our tool to get to know our audience and to unearth  relevant information that will help us in determining how we would help them solve the infamous  problem of procrastination.    According to ​Storytelling Tool - Preparing Your Mind for Innovation​, a good story is designed for  the audience. It is about the audience. It connects the audience to the product, to the company,  to the ​cause​. This tool was chosen because we want to know the reasons behind people’s  unproductivity and how people perceive productivity and lack thereof. We want to understand if it  is human nature to become procrastinators or were there reasons behind them being one. I  believe that in using Storytelling, people will be more comfortable talking about a “negative” part  of themselves.    Application  We put up a form online which was shared through multiple channels. The form helped us in  determining the “subjects” of our storytelling. To our surprise, there were a lot of responses from  individuals willing to tell us their side of the coin.     In the end, we chose three respondents each team member (we are 5 in the team). The  respondents we chose varied from students, employed professionals, self-employed individuals,  freelancers, and housewives/house husbands.    It was up to the discretion of the team member if he/she would conduct an interview or a focused  group discussion. What we have agreed upon however was we would let our respondents do the  story telling, we would not be telling ​our ​story.    “​What do you do in a day?​” was our primary question that helped trigger the respondents to  share varying answers and stories about their everyday lives.  We learned about what each of our  respondents do everyday, from waking up to sleeping. We learned about how they structured

their day, what they feel when things do not go according to plan. They shared what they usually  do to fight off boredom or sleepiness. They also shared what makes certain tasks boring for  them. Different answers but they all have two common points: a) if it would be that easy, then  they wish to be productive everyday, and b) too many unorganized tasks/repetitive tasks is what  causes them to stray away from track.    Insight  What I learned from what happened is that people are not being unproductive because they want  to. They do not want to waste their time being distracted too. That there are several reasons (one  of them is that they have too many tasks to do that they do not know how to organize them) why  they seem to become unproductive. The whole process helped us in re-thinking about the  solution that we had first thought of (just constant reminders to do daily tasks). Because of our  findings, we are now trying to think of ways to help people be more organized    This also helped me in appreciating the Storytelling tool. We sometimes take our audience’s  opinions for granted, thinking that previous reviews and feedbacks about similar solutions were  already enough information. It served as a great reminder that our customers are human beings  with various, ever-changing experiences and needs that we need to take into consideration if we  want to address their problems.    Approach  Lastly, if we were ever to re-do this again, I think applying the Storytelling tool will still be the best  approach to take. It helped and will help us to gain insights to real-world problems from the  perspective of real human beings whose experiences and needs are communicated if only we let  them share their stories. We are creating solutions for them, not us, so we must hear them again  and again if needed.

Reflection - Mind Mapping (Sergio Dworak)

Challenge   A news organization needs to update a legacy editorial system that is used for editing and  publishing news items. The key components in a particular type of news organization (news  agency) are speed and accuracy. Both speed and accuracy need to be at a very high level, and one  without the other doesn’t work. The team is at the discovery stage. The project scope includes a  diverse team of participants, such us higher management, editors, reporters and member of the  development team. The team has approximately one week to gather insights for a next major  iteration of the system.

Selection   Mind mapping was selected because it’s a tool that allows people with different needs,  qualifications and user behavior to work together in groups on a problem that is company-wide  and thus transcends particular roles. The method also creates highly visual results that are more  easily digestible for people of different backgrounds who are not necessarily familiar with each  other’s professional terminology and methods.

Application and approach  Key to a right approach is the diversity of the team. Each of the participants is encouraged to  avoid professional jargon and explain a used functionality in a simple in simple terms as  possible. The team interviews approximately eight users who work in different roles and who use  the system a lot. An important insight that the team sees early in the process is that if you  interview people who use the system for many hours a day for a long period of time for relatively  simple tasks, they tend to be very experienced users who actually worked out some turnarounds  for the least usable aspects of the system. That doesn't necessarily mean that these aspects of the  system are usable. The people just get accustomed to it. And because they got accustomed to it,  they tend to say that everything's alright, even if they are forced to do many unnecessary steps or  go through a process that is not intuitive at all. So we need to focus on people who are actually  less experienced because they still haven't got accustomed to the system and thus see its  downsides more clearly.  The team interviews that participants, encouraging them to think aloud, and documents both  what they say and what they do, adding their emotions such as frustration or satisfaction.   The team documents their behavior because what people do and what people sell they do is are  actually different things in most contexts. Then the team has a large pool of sticky notes, which  work well if we have actual physical sticky notes and a physical wall but one could use Miro or  another tool like this. Then in smaller groups of five people which should be interdisciplinary the  team tries to group those sticky notes in order to have several groups that clearly show some pain  points, or decision points or emotions of the users. It's important not to discard outliers, because  some outlying notes could be useful later in the project. After most of the cars are grouped and  the outliers are clearly visible on the margins, the team tries to come up with insights that could  help formulate a solution for a particular problem on inflection point. Those insights are in turn  grouped onto a matrix which shows time and effort needed to implement such an insight and the

importance of this insight for the users, importance being measured in how many users actually  mentioned this or that problem. So this allows a complex view of how people actually think and  what people actually do and to have most important insights prioritized in terms of their  importance and cost.  Mind mapping in some forms is repeated in the usability study when the team has a prototype of  a new release. The tools used at that later stage are affinity / priority diagrams, traffic lights  diagrams and other prioritizing tools. In sum, such an approach allows for quite accurate  detection of design problems and for relatively quick solutions with short iterations.

Reflection – Storytelling (by Jan Fiala)

Challenge:

When I worked in Peru, my job was to implement a dual vocational education and training (VET) system, where  a company and a vocational school would train young people in co-managed programs, with structured training  plans and a common goal to educate specialists in the field of mechatronics for each company over a period of  3 years. For the duration of the program, students would receive full scholarships from their training company  (which was a huge economic benefit, as most students would have a middle-low socioeconomic background).

Once we finally finished the design and structure of the 3-year program (after a year of hard work with all  relevant stakeholders) we found out that besides all the advantages and opportunities, young Peruvians didn't  enroll/send applications for the program as we had foreseen – mainly because it was “too new” and they  wouldn't commit for 3 years.

Selection:

We needed to inspire potential students and show the advantages and opportunities this new program has to  offer them, while taking away their doubts. We wanted to win their engagement and that they feel they can be  part of a “new big thing” and the first ones to benefit. This is why I chose storytelling get the students on board  for our project, taking away their doubts along on a common journey, trying to connect to their emotions,  characters and values – or as Roberto Brown said in the video lecture: First, we had to sell the challenge.

As I started my carrier graduating from a VET program myself (Germany), I had a good starting point to share  my own story, in order to engage and visualize possible outcomes. This also helped them to open up, as I was in  a similar position, when I took a similar decision they are about to take.

Application

As I wanted to use storytelling, first I had to persuade the companies, vocational school and involved  institutions that our focus needs to be more human centered and we needed to address their individual needs  instead of only concentrating on hard facts. I wanted to visualize, where they can be if they participate and  which new paths open up. To start we invited all interested students for a workshop, in which I began as an  opener and then each company would present themselves to the students, to show them their commitment to  “be there for them” during all the program and that they´d had a common goal in an alliance of students,  companies and school.

I started by getting to know my audience, asking them why they came, where they come from, what are their  needs and most important their doubts “why wouldn't they apply to the program”? Then I tried to answer their  questions along with my story, why and how I decided for myself to start my career. Then I focused on the  unique chances and opportunities that opened up for them, if they participate in that program. I focused  strongly on soft-facts, as their mentioned doubts about the problem mainly came from this direction. Here I  could exploit the presence of the company representatives, showing and assuring that they really care about  them and their success within the VET program. They were even willing to give full scholarships during 3 years  as an investment for them, so there was a huge intrinsic interest of success from each firm. It was also  important to be honest, as of course there were some uncertainty, yet the program was new to all. But the  core message was to confirm, that the opportunities outweigh the risks by far and that nobody was to be left  behind in case of the unexpected: They would become part of a pact between school, institutions, companies  and students to guarantee each other support for success. And that all have the same goal: Ensure success of

the students in their companies and implement a new VET system with potential to solve the major issues in  the Peruvian economy – to be part of the future.

Insight

As most potential students had a middle-low socioeconomic background, we didn't expect that soft-facts were  the main issue to them. Later on they told us: The most important thing for them is to have a company that  cares for their needs and supports them (professional and personal) throughout the whole time. And that  every company trains with the interest for them to keep them after 3 years of training, which changed the  perspective of training for all participants. An additional and far deeper takeaway was, that companies started  to notice they need to be more attractive in the term of “soft-facts”: lifelong development, good atmosphere,  emphatic trainers, etc. to ensure the trained professionals stay with them after graduation. Companies in Peru  never invested in 3 year-VET-programs, now they had to rethink their strategy to retain the investment within  the company.

Approach

Even though the result was astonishing and a lot of the present students applied to the VET program,  application numbers wasn't portioned even between companies. Basically due to differences in  engaging/presenting techniques. The next time I´d like to prepare the firms representatives in a storytelling  workshop, to somehow level their approaches. I also want to mention, that this was a good example that  worked. But usually I just acted out of instinct and it didn't always work.

What I learnt in this course is that there is a lot of more structure and approach for storytelling that I was  aware of. This not only made me curious to learn more about storytelling as a tool, but also helps me to  prepare better for future presentations and asking the important questions. I like storytelling as a tool to get  people engaged and invested in a new project. I´d like to try it also as an opener for Design Thinking  workshops. Just like Roberto Brown said in the video lecture:  “First, we have to sell the challenge. You have to  help the audience understand how the current state is more dangerous than any other possibility out there. You  have to get them in the frame of mind that they want to take this on and make this challenge a cause that they  can invest in.”

Example Reflection – Learning Launch   Challenge   I am Luca Ciccone, Egyptian, Teaching Assistant at Teaching Assistant at  Macmillan and Innovation Ambassador at  Ho branch according to  Communication Ministry. Our problem in Egypt is the big gap between  scientific research and practical application in the labor market. Our team  is working to try to find a solution to this serious problem.     Selection   Our team has already gone through several design thinking activities/tools,  so we are ready to try the learning launch tool. Broadly speaking, the  learning launch is an experiment meant to quickly test an idea and  prototype.     Application   For our first learning launch, we focused on trying to find a way to link the  university parties and companies by obtaining a website to communicate.  For our second learning launch, we focused on the meeting between the  two parties where contact was made with the MLAND and the  J Gs Cupcake store company in Benha, as well as the Zurak Cancer  Foundation, and  thus our hypotheses were validated.    Insight   By applying the learning launch tool, our team identified our assumptions  and designed launches to test these assumptions. By practical experience,  we found the companies ’need for university research to develop their  products, but the company cannot fully finance the research or purchase  the basic equipment needed for development. Through this result, the  project was modified through the introduction of an intermediary  company to finance equipment from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab  Emirates. The ongoing incorporation of insight is particularly important at  this stage, as launches come before a full rollout in the design thinking  timeline.    Approach   Our team has already gone through several design thinking activities/tools,  the learning launch is the appropriate tool.

Applying the Design Thinking tool: Visualization

“I hate that lady!”

In a Workshop I coached a visualization process and participated an extraordinary turnaround.

Challenge and selection

First of all, I want you to gain a deeper insight of the setting and topic in which the visualization process  took place.

Last week I was a coach in a three-day-workshop about business model innovation. I coached a team of  four designers who worked in a design studio with a focus on branding and marketing in the B2B sector.  I call the design company I worked with DS, because I cannot share the real name for data protection  reasons. The DS-team contented the CEO, the CFO and two employees, one designer and one editor,  all of them were female.

Within three workshop days, we went through a process which was close to a real design thinking  process:

-  At first, we pointed out the DS-challenge regarding their business model.

-  Secondly, we defined the target group.

-  Thirdly we developed three questions and interviewed some people about how the marketing  process in their company was actually working, and which problems usually go along with  marketing.

-  Fourthly, we described the new customer experience and developed an approach for the new  business model.

Before the workshop took place, I thought about the challenge of applying a design thinking tool and  decided the visualization-tool would suit best for the definition of one special member the target  group. This was the second step of the process. I decided to do so, because also Anna Jones  constated that the visualization-tool is suited both for researching and for understanding the users  and customers (Anna Jones on Visualization, Design Thinking for Innovation, UVA,  min. 3:04).

Application

I gave the DS-team the assignment to think about one member of their typical target group for three  minutes alone and take some notes. Then they should share their thoughts.

It turned out, that all DS-members had in mind almost the same picture of one special type of person,  who was standing for their typical target group. The person was a female marketing leader of a medium  sized company with around 500 employers. Demographical attributes like age, gender, number of  children and income were very similar. This surprised me because I knew, that the DS-company had  more than this type of customers.

After that, they visualized the person on a flipchart. The CFO took a pencil and drew the person, referring  to the instructions, the other DS-members told her (see picture 1). They called her Tina.

Then we started thinking about problems which would occur in Tina’s daily work and which were the  jobs-to-be-done to make her happy. We hang up the flipchart and stood side by side to Tina. Within this  process, the DS-team talked a lot about their frustration and worries concerning Tina. The biggest  discussion topic was that Tina does not have the insights of strategic marketing knowledge which the  DS-team needs to do a good job. The frustration led to the following testimony: “I hate that lady”. When  the designer said that, her colleagues agreed.

Insights

I tried to handle the situation and asked them to visualize some positive aspects regarding Tina on the  flipchart as well (in picture 1 you see the red handwriting on the flipchart). But the frustration was  ongoing, and all of the positive aspects had a negative or unsympathetic touch. It turned out, that they  cannot do a good job for Tina, as a representative of their main target group.

We started thinking about alternatives for their business model because in step one they constated that  they both worked with medium sized and small companies. Then they visualized two representatives of  the other target groups in small companies (Marcel und Mia, as you see in picture 2). The DS-team was  much more creative, and they had many ideas within short time how to make Marcel and Mia satisfied  and do a better job.

In the end, the DS-team decided to change their main target group and, in the future, not to focus Tina,  standing for a marketing leader of a medium sized company with around 500 employees. The team  decided to change their business model and accompany smaller companies in their marketing  processes. Pivotal for the decision to make that holistic change were their strong emotions and the  frustration coming along with the visualized Tina and the barriers which hindered the DS-team on doing  a great creative marketing process for Tina.

Approach

The continuing non-verbal confrontation with the flipchart-tall visualized Tina was the key for the DS- team to verbalize the problems regarding the work with their main target group.

Looking back, I think about what would have turned out, if I would have had enriched the process with  even more elements of visualization. There would have been some possibilities to do so. For example:

If I - in the first place - had given them the assignment to draw a picture of their typical target group and  not just even to take notes, maybe their distinct problem with Tina would have become visible much  earlier. Also, I could have asked them to visualize the positive aspects regarding Tina on the flipchart,  rather than writing them down.

In addition to that, I really liked the fact that, in the end, we had two versions of Tina: On the one hand  we had one flipchart-tall visualized Tina with two catchy attributes like her bag and her plait. One the

hand we had a smaller version of Tina with the same catchy attributes on a post-it to work with and to  place her where ever she was needed within the creative process (as you see in picture 2). I didn’t plan  this before, but I will keep on drawing detailed pictures and small pictures which are easy to handle  within the moderation of a design thinking process.

All in all the DS-team could have also added more visualization-details to Tina, use more colors to go  more into the inductive reasoning process Anna Jones refers to, and to trigger the right side of the  teams’ brain more (Anna Jones on Visualization, Design Thinking for Innovation, University of Virginia,  min. 0:19). I didn’t tell them to do so. It was the team’s own decision to leave Tina uncomplete. I took  note that the visualized Tina had no eyes, no nose and no mouth. This was the first reflection within the  visualization process that made me think about the DS-teams relationship to her. My approach for the  next time will be to do an ongoing reflection of the visualizing-process within the process and to enable  the team to visualize more. When they hold back with visualizing (i.e. if they don’t visualize face- attributes), it will be a sign of some kind of barrier regarding the subject. For a coach it would be  recommendable to dive deeper into the subject then.

1. Challenge.

I was working with a big transportation enterprise, and they wanted to  redesign a core process related to the vehicles’ maintenance. They had a lot  of problems with the data, the flow of the vehicles in the process, and the  close of the process.

2. Selection.

I suggested using the design thinking frame because I was in the first weeks  of the course. We used the classic five steps: empathize, define, ideate,  prototype, and test. I used before in other exercises, the triz grid in the second  step but in this exercise, I didn’t consider it appropriate due to the audience  and the redundant ideas of improvement leaving the problem and its effects  aside. So, I preferred to use mind mapping.

3. Application.

I knew that they have a lot of information and histories around the process  development and performance. I needed a strong insight to continue with a  focus on the ideation step.

We started in an individual 10-minute session, in which the people organize all  the information about the complaints, misfunctions, pains, problems, and  knowledge lessons in his role in the process we were working about.

Then, I drew in a whiteboard my mind map, initially with three branches or  arms: pains, complaints, and misfunction. The people began to tell stories and  I painted the situation with a representative icon or sketch, when the map had  some graphics ideas, the magic occurred, we had in only shot of sight, years  of history.

4. Insight

The group realized as a whole shared comprehension not the cause of the  problem (we didn’t look for it), but the main insight related to the process and  his design. We found that people knew very good his functions at the routine,  that they communicate outputs to the next process in an appropriate way but  they didn’t work as a team, they didn’t know the goals and procedures of the  rest of the group, and the company as a whole. They want to help, participate,  or collaborate in the whole process flux.

I learned the great value of the graphics, the connections, and the one-page  representation of a situation, I learned how to put a lot of data in the same  place without too much work or boring analysis.

5. Approach.

First, I will use the frame I learned in this fantastic course. Second, I will  explain all the steps to construct the mind map and the result we are  expecting, there were people confused during the exercise and with some  kind of opposition.

Hi, during my internship I was given a task to design an app for the company named  “​Creativescapes,​” which in Sanskrit means unrestricted thinking knowing no boundaries, takes  its inspiration for boundary-less thinking from the free spirited birds. It is a flagship  workshop on Design Thinking that is conducted by Hari Sharma, Chairman & Managing  Director, Intelligent Designs Inc.

ABOUT ​Creativescapes,​ APP

‘​Creativescapes,​’ is one-of-a-kind platform that nurtures not only the Design minds, but also  reaches out to the common audiences to spread the uniqueness of application of  Design Thinking in all perspectives of everyday life.

The program covers the power of boundary-less thinking and how Design Thinking  helps in moving from mystery of business to heuristics and then to algorithm. It also  emphasizes the role of emotional elements in moving Design Thinking from ‘Just ideas’  to the ‘Implementation’ of ideas.

The aim of the app is to reach people with the ideology of ‘​Creativescapes,​’, thereby inspiring  them and unleashing their true potential. I choose Mind mapping as it is used to represent how ideas or other items are  linked to a central idea and to each other. Mind maps are used to generate,  visualize, structure and classify ideas to look for patterns and insights that provide  key design criteria. Storytelling Reflection

Challenge

I work at a Transnational huge company where Design Thinking is now part of the business  strategy; the company has managed to adapt Design Thinking to its own business so it can focus  in the users that really matter and in the type of business it offers. As this is a huge company  every center in each country had to start learning and applying Design Thinking and as change  is never easy but always good, in my country I was part of the leadership that was bringing Design  Thinking to everybody’s lives.

I started with education and it was naturally becoming known and used among my peers;  however, there was an important challenge in all the business processes when applying Design  Thinking as the framework it is; and the challenge was: How can we engage with our clients so  we can also design better experiences in the solutions we offer to them, including team  involvement, workshop management, projects and more.

Selection

I selected then Storytelling because I think telling a story is the best approach to get someone not  only to pay attention to something, but to understand and act with purpose and it was just what  was needed. This tool allowed every client real or potential and every person interested in  applying Design Thinking with their clients to actually had a guide on how to really engage.

Application

I got together with a group of other four Design Thinkers as passionate as me and with their  support a Playbook was created. This Playbook is a document that is now available for all of the  employees of the company I work for and intends to help any other team in the world that wants  to use Design Thinking to achieve a great engagement with their clients. In the playbook it is first  specified that a group of people working together is always necessary and that in our case we  received also guidance and strategic support from an Executive of the company. We also defined  the tasks of this team.

The playbook was also created in the format of Storytelling so there is this main Character that  will guide the reader through the playbook; she is the hypothetic user and she wants to implement  Design Thinking but she does not now how and explains a little bit of the background.Then, the  book shows how in our company there are different ways to make the first contact with the clients  and that having the final objective in mind is very important to know which one to choose.

In this storytelling playbook there is also visualization used; so our main character shows a simple  and visual depiction of how a Design Thinking engagement works to help the readers understand  that it is not just a workshop but a creative process. Then, the book shows step by step from the  planning with the problem statement or design prompt, going through gathering information and  research to creating a proposal, working on several tools in one or more workshops involving the  right stakeholders (being this moment where the creative work is on top), and then evaluating the  workshop or activities results. At the end it suggests some client playbacks to get the team aligned  and the way the implementation will work. All of this explanation is shown as a story that tells the

Stephanie Gonzalez

main character in the book, it is created with images, brief explanations and examples from real  business life and even maps so it can be better understood.

Insight

When every team in our company uses this guide and actually applies it, they know the case  study in a storytelling format will allow them and other people who read it to analyze the situation  including complexities, present results in a brief, accurate and creative way and at the end  learning from the challenges faced.

What did I gain? The learning that Design Thinking tools like storytelling are not only to tell a story  and solve a problem; but are a great learning tool as well. I this case I got to solve a problem (no  one new how to engage with commercial clients using Design Thinking) and also I got to share a  guide for learning a new framework and I think that is one of the most exciting experiences any  user could have.

Approach

Probably I would use more communication tools and strategies to make this playbook visible so  literally everyone knows about it’s existence. – Also maybe I would add the information in  animated videos and not just images and examples as it is right know. Just because learning  experiences are always into transformation.

Reflection – Storytelling

Challenge

I work as a Business Manager in the Sales & Strategy function of our organization. Our organization is in the  Telecom Infrastructure space. Currently, the telecom industry in our country is going through the cusp of a  revolution and consolidation owing to hyper competition from a new entrant in the telecom operator space.  Operation & Maintenance of telecom towers is the core business of our organization. However, to remain  competitive in our industry, our organization also needs to be moving forward in other related business  domains like Smart Cities, Optical Fiber business, etc.

Our organization aims to achieve its Mission and Vision through a set of BHAGs (Big Hairy Audacious Goals)  arrived through a series of Large Scale Interactive Process (LSIP) involving all employees at different locations in  the cities where its offices are based.

Last year we had a Strategy Meet with our Board of Directors where we proposed to them a list of finalized  business opportunities for their approval. The challenge was to prioritize these new business opportunities  based on the changing business environment.

Selection

Storytelling was one tool which we used for our entire Strategy exercise with an external consultant. As  described in the Design Thinking course, what I relate to storytelling is that it makes strategy accessible and  relate-able. Storytelling places the different stakeholders on focus and involve them on the journey – in this  case the strategy journey.

Application

A good story is required for any organization to link its vision with the strategies to achieve that vision. Our  organization’s mission (transforming lives by enabling communication) is connected to that of our country’s  government’s vision of a Digital country.

I was program managing the Strategy Exercise and used Storytelling as one of the key tools to arrive at our  strategy to achieve our BHAGs in a 5-year timeframe. We involved leaders of different departments of our  organization to articulate the pain points they faced in the business and elaborate on the changes which may  be required to address our future business needs. Basically, these are the Big Questions which they face when  going beyond Business As Usual. So, the stories which they described had to be in line with our vision and  business model. Hence storytelling bridges the gap between hard data and the recommendations for each new  business proposition.

Insight

Storytelling approach enabled me to understand how to put the stakeholders at the forefront by understanding  their interaction with the organization and how to derive a win-win situation for all. It enabled me to visualize  how to present data like a story and thereby derive actionable items for a data-driven organization based on a  human vision of putting everyone at the center of the communications revolution in the country. Assignment:  Visualization Reflection  Submitted by: Nadine Born  Course:  Design Thinking for Innovation    Trail Challenge: To Build or Not to Build    An environmental charity wanted to conduct a fundraising campaign to raise $4 million to build a  public path in a busy tourist area of a small town in British Columbia, Canada. They had been gifted a  large piece of land by a local landowner, which was a substantial gift and prevented them from  needing to purchase the land, however, they still needed to raise a large amount of money in order to  pay for the supplies and labor to build the trail.     Even though the local community appeared to be supportive of the trail, they could not provide  enough money from private donations to build it. If the summer vacation property owners did not  provide some funding, then there was a strong possibility that they would not raise enough money to  complete the trail. The charity did not know if the community as a whole would support the project  and needed to conduct testing with key influencers and potential donors to gauge their interest.  Building the trail without testing the support first was too risky because the charity did not have  enough money in reserve to cover the cost of the trail if the fundraising efforts were not successful.     Tool Selection: Visualization    Visualization is the process of “assembling scattered ideas into a compelling story that can generate  vivid mental images” (Designing for Growth, p49).  As the consultant for the study, I chose  visualization because the charity had a firm concept of why they needed the trail, how it would  benefit the town, and how much it would cost but needed a persuasive way to tie it all together. The  business case for the project was strong but without a tool to help them illustrate how the trail would  positively impact the residents, there was little chance people would donate enough to meet the  budget. We needed a tool that provided a “head and heart” message to convince people to support  the project. Visualization provided the perfect combination of key messaging, beautiful photography,  architectural renderings, safety data, and budget criteria to create the vision for the project in an  easy‐to‐read document that was only four pages in length. Visualization allowed us to describe the  urgent and compelling need for the trail in a succinct and tangible way.     Application    Once we drafted the vision document, we worked with the charity to identify a list of people whose  opinion would be important to the success (or failure) of the fundraising campaign. The list included  past and potential donors, key influencers in the community such as large landowners and business  owners, affluent summer‐only residents, and elected officials. We requested one‐hour meetings with  all of the people on the list. If people did not want to meet with us in person, which was often the

case with the part‐time residents, we offered to conduct the meetings by phone. When someone  agreed to meet with us, we emailed them the vision document so they could read it in advance and  prepare their questions. This created a good environment for an informed and candid dialogue.    While the scheduling of the interviews was in progress, we designed a questionnaire to guide our  discussions. Consistently using the questionnaire ensured that we covered the same questions with all  the interviewees. The goal was to speak with 20 – 25 key influencers in the community and gauge  their interest in, or opposition to, supporting the fundraising efforts for the trail as either donors or  campaign volunteers or both. We successfully met with 24 interviewees and compiled the feedback  into a summary report along with recommendations for the charity. The entire process took three  months.    Insight    Fundraising and design thinking both require a willingness to adapt and fail fast. Good fundraisers are  responsive to their donors and design thinking serves as the perfect platform to plan and launch new  fundraising initiatives; it is an ideal methodology for solving complex philanthropic issues. We are not  formally taught design thinking models in fundraising classes but they should be added to the  curriculum.     Although it is not explicitly stated in the course videos, it occurred to me that both fundraising and  design thinking are rooted in communication and relationships and both are iterative processes based  on testing and investigation. The elusive synergy between art and science is as beautifully illustrated  by design thinking as it is as inherent in daily fundraising practice.      Improvements for Next Time    Visualization was an effective tool in this circumstance and I would use it again in a similar situation.  However, it would also be enlightening to create a journey map with a wide spectrum of people from  the town because there were many assumptions made during the visualization process about how the  trail would be used and what benefits would be desired by the tourists, local public, and sponsors.  Journey mapping would have confirmed the validity of those assumptions and supplemented the data  gathered during the interviews.     The other tool that I would use next time in conjunction with visualization is storytelling. I would take  someone’s first hand account of the situation and create a short video to showcase the urgency of the  project or program from his/her perspective. A link to the video would be included in the email about  the interview along with a PDF of the vision document. I think this would provide a holistic micro and  macro perspective to the exercise and spark some interesting conversations in the interviews.

Mind Mapping (Module 3)

Challenge

I work as a Senior Business Analyst for a global corporation which has recently went through  restructuring. In short, the top management decided to spin-off part of the company as a separate  organization. The new company incorporates 3 business units and supporting functions (such as  Business Planning & Analysis - the function I work at) and has subsidiaries in over 50 countries. A key  change aspect for the functions is that the teams are not anymore responsible for the operations  only in their local country but have now regional responsibility – allocation of up to five countries.  This means that my team is now responsible for three big countries. Because of this change we faced  the challenge of coping with increased workload in a new environment with markets we were not  familiar with. However, as we work for a fast-growing organization, the work pace was too quick, and  we needed an efficient solution to stop the chaos around and re-design our processes. We wanted to  collaborate with teams from other regions to create unified processes within the division.

Selection

The key feature of the Mind mapping tool is looking for patterns and insights in large quantity of data  collected during the What Is stage, as Professor Marian Moor explains in a video from Week 3 of the  course. The goal is to create a mind map at the end of the What Is stage. The mind map typically  represents a drawing with short notes organized in clusters and shows graphically the connections  between them. I was standing between the What Is and What If phase and selected the tool because  it is an excellent approach to create an overview of the situation and set an impulse for going  forward in a creative and efficient way. On the one hand, the tool was very useful as it was not  supposed to represent only my mind, but what could be in the mind of our stakeholders – in our case  the business leaders of the regions. On the other hand, I was searching for an efficient way to draw  the attention of the people who work within the division and to facilitate the quick understanding of  concepts and the linkages between them.

Application

The Mind mapping tool was applied during a workshop of the EMEA Business Planning & Analysis  division. Around 40 division members representing 7 EMEA regions attended the workshop. The  communality between us was that because of the extended regional responsibility we were all facing  the same challenge. The Mind mapping workshop had the following structure:

1. What do we work on - All teams attending the workshop were required to write on yellow

sticky notes all the processes they are working at and on pink sticky notes all the  stakeholders they are working for. The teams were encouraged to have a discussion and to  pin the notes on a board.

2. How long does it take – The teams were asked to estimate the time for each process.  3. Where are the connections – The teams were required to link the yellow (processes) and

pink (stakeholders) notes to each other, multiple linkages were possible.

4. What are the priorities – The teams were asked to create a ranking of the stakeholders and a

ranking of activities required by each stakeholder. Discussion time was allocated to this  stage.

5. What are the communalities – At the end we combined the notes from all teams and

created a map which looked like the Solar System. Our division was representing the Sun,  and the stake holders were representing the planets. Thus, important stakeholders who  needed more attention from us represented planets closer to the Sun. Notes with a process

name and time estimation written on them were pinned to each planet. We used this map  for the final presentation and for the criteria establishment discussion.

Insight

This was a successful application of the tool as it allowed us to link the “What is” to “What if”. By  creating our Solar System and clustering the activities to stakeholders we gained a comprehensive  overview of the What Is situation. By allocating time to each process we were able to estimate the  time dedicated to each stake holder and to establish criteria for the What If phase. I realized that  having a mind map depicting the situation instead of creating a large list of related activities  facilitates understanding by providing an easy, visual access to the information. Further, involving  more people in the workshop enhanced the engagement of the teams and helped us gain insights  about the similarities between the regions. Applying creative solutions to people who are normally  occupied with analytical work created an atmosphere of experiencing something exotic and exclusive  and enhanced the attention and motivation of the teams.

Approach

In general, I would definitely continue applying design thinking tools to my audience – people who  are used to analytical approaches. The main reasons are that it creates exclusive atmosphere, leads  to good solutions and motivates people. As we used the Visualization tool for our next step, I dare to  say that a combination of Mind Mapping and Visualization is a strategy which proved its success in  our work. Thus, I do not consider the option of applying an alternative tool as this one works  excellently but consider a combination of two tools. However, if there is something which we can do  differently next time, it would be to hire a professional illustrator for our workshops who can give us  creative impulses and help us with the drawings. The reason is that many people stated after the  workshop that they could do better on the creative part and would like to improve. Limited drawing  skills should not be a reason to skip the workshop.

Joyce Ka

14 December 2015

Challenge  I work as an internal strategy consultant / project manager for an Operations division in an airline.     One of the departments recently got approval to spend USD 4 million on using virtual training technology for  training cabin crew (both new cabin crew and those being developed to move up to more senior roles on  board flights). The original business case for the project was admittedly quite flimsy and, having gotten  approved, there were varying views in the departments leadership team on which technology solutions would  benefit the most in terms of training engagement and effectiveness as well as drive operational efficiency.     My role as the project manager assigned to the project was to define a scope and requirements for the project  so that a tender could be floated for solution providers. That being said, the department head and her  leadership team were not aligned on what issues they were trying to solve and had a tendency to jump  straight into talking about technologies that should be brought in. The core team discussed the issue at hand  and agreed that, if we initiated a typical scope phase, we would struggle to get detailed and specific  requirements for the solution.     Selection  Given the two key issues of unaligned stakeholders and a focus on technology rather than  problems/opportunities, we decided that we needed to go through a mind mapping process i.e. a structured  process that would include a review of research conducted in order to jointly identify insights and patterns  that would be the basis of establishing criteria for the idea generation phase.      Application  We decided to hold a visioning session for the project where we could get the leadership team to collectively  identify the key challenges being faced within the training department today and establish a set of criteria  against which different virtual learning solutions would be assessed.     But before we held the visioning session, we reviewed the research done during the business case phase to  see if any additional areas needed to be explored or research revisited. Following was the research already  available:     Analysis of course volumes and resource utilization (facilities and trainers) for different types of course

  Aggregation of survey results from courses for the last year

  Interviews with full time and part time trainers to get their view on training effectiveness and engagement  for different channels and courses

  Identification of minimum training requirements from a regulatory and safety perspective

  Desktop research on virtual training technology trends

Having reviewed the above, the core team agreed that we needed to conduct one more activities before  planning the workshop:    Direct observation and interviews with cabin crew currently in training courses to understand their  perspective on the existing training process and course. This was later represented as a journey map of  cabin crew with key observations highlighted as crew went through their learning journey at the airline.

Having completed the research, we then planned the day long visioning workshop to include the following:    5 minutes presentation for each analysis/research to give participants background information on it.

  1 hour guided session for participants to walk through and synthesize all the research for themselves. A  table was setup for each of the top 5 courses with posters of all the research applicable to the course.  There was also an additional table to be setup where the trainer and leadership team interviews would be  made available with word clouds created from the interview script. Participants would be split into two  groups with a core team member assigned to guide the walk through. They would also be provided wit a  simple handout that let them note their key observations on what works well and what needs  improvement by course and overall.

  2 hour session to collectively identify insights relating to challenges from three perspectives - trainer,  cabin crew and internal department perspective

  1 hour session to use the insights to define criteria for identifying which virtual technologies would be  relevant for cabin crew training

The core team facilitated the visioning session based on the above plan and significant progress was made  towards aligning the training departments leadership team on what they believed they wanted to achieve  through introducing virtual learning technologies in their divisions. It was great to hear conversations during  the insights and criteria phase because, for the first time, we were focusing on issues and opportunities  instead of technologies. As we finished the day, we had a very clear set of needs that we believed the right  solutions should meet and the team was more aligned.

Approach  Having gone through the process and reflected on it, I believe we used the right process to get consensus on  the challenges being faced and establishing a set of design criteria. That being said, it would have been  beneficial to include a virtual learning partner as a collaborator during the visioning session especially to get a  different perspective when establishing design criteria. We do have a partner who has worked closely with the  organisation during the business case phase and it was a bit of a missed opportunity to not bring them into the  session.
