1. Challenge: Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.

In my role as Customer Experience manager, I consult and support new product launches in our organisation. My role is to be

the advocate for the customer and ensure solutions being delivered result in a positive experience for the customer. Recently I

was brought in to assess a seemingly simple project. It involved working with a partner and leveraging their state of the art

billing platform to provide a seamless and flexible wireless plan (I work for a Telecommunications company). One of those

projects that was labelled a needle mover! After a few meetings it became clear that there were a million concerns from

functions all over the organisation, from Customer Care to Finance to IT. Each person representing their own functional area

only knew one piece of the puzzle. Having worked in the organisation for over 10 years in a multitude of functions I felt that

there were a lot of employee and customer facing impacts that were being missed as most people on the project did not see

the interdependencies of their functions.

Everyone was focused on the “What If” phase of design, while I worried that the cross functional team needed to understand

and align on the current state- “What Is.” As mentioned in Week 2, the story of George and Geoff, my repertoire within the

organisation was allowing me to sense the need for developing customer empathy to drive insights, uncover opportunities and

identify risks.

2. Selection:

I had recently read about the Mind Mapping tool in “Creative Confidence” by Tom & David Kelley. I felt this would be a

great tool at this stage of the project since my goals was to bring about a common understanding of the customer needs,

stakeholder views, identify patterns of opportunity and risk and overall drive insights towards how best to execute this

project. (Week 2: The Me-You-Health Story.)

3. Application: Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., what you did and how the tool was

applied effectively or ineffectively).

Although I understood in principle what Mind Mapping was all about, and unconsciously used it many times in my personal

life while doodling and musing on tough problems, I had never used it at work. I decided to book a 3 hour meeting with all

the stakeholders. I made sure I booked a room with multiple white boards and brought with me an assortment of different

colored white board markers. After explaining to everyone the importance of looking at this project holistically, both from an

internal and external lens, I asked everyone to agree upon the goal of the project. This I wrote in the middle of the white

board with a rectangle around it. Afterwards I asked each stakeholder to introduce themselves and tell us what role they

performed within the context of this project, and what concerns they had.

As each person spoke I jotted down these items on the white board, connecting their roles as sub-nodes to the main goal, and

their concerns or ideas as sub-sub-nodes underneath their sub-nodes. Imagine a hub and spoke diagram growing outwards. In

between invariable other members of the group would think of an issue, opportunity or simply fact while they heard their

colleagues speak. I captured these in different colors and drew dotted lines between ideas to signify dependencies, putting

smiley faces next to wins and frowns () next to areas which required more work. As the map expanded there were several

aha moments, especially as people saw positive and negative feedback loops, concerns, etc. All the stakeholders finished the

meeting with a much more grounded understanding of the net new work streams that were required to be scoped and assessed

if we were to meet the objectives of the project.

Since this was my first time, I was improvising as I went along, however everyone appreciated as the complexity of the

situation developed visually for all to see.

4. Insight: Describe the insight you gained from applying the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., how an insight

affected your thinking about the challenge and about design thinking more broadly).

As the map expanded there were several aha moments, especially as people saw positive and negative feedback loops,

concerns, etc. All the stakeholders finished the meeting with a much more grounded understanding of the net new work

streams that were required to be scoped and assessed if we were to meet the objectives of the project. In a subsequent meeting

we reviewed these net new work streams, prioritized them by business impact and started testing/investigating these

scenarios. Half way through the exercise we realized that the cost to implement this project was under-estimated and would

be close to triple the amount originally presented. Ultimately the project was put on hold so the organisation could focus on

other priorities and saved everyone a lot of time, effort and money.

5. Approach: Describe what you might do differently next time -- applying the same tool you selected or a different one -

- and the reason(s) why.

Some key learnings for me after my first mind mapping attempt

  There will always be someone who cannot join in person and will be over the phone – ensure the white board can be

shared via web cam to ensure everyone can participate

  As more items were brought up, in hind-sight, there could have been better ways I could have captured this

information on the white board. For next time I will give some thought in advance to the types of information that

would be captured and plan ahead what that hierarchy would look like

  In this meeting, I was the one facilitating and writing on the board. In the future I would like to co-create better with

the stakeholders by finding creative ways for them to participate more than just giving their opinion e.g., pausing

mid-way and asking teams to go to the white board and put stick notes to provide more feedback, etc.

  Practice, practice, practice!

Storytelling

Challenge

I work for a non-profit organization that provides quality education to under-privileged children.  My company adopts under-performing public schools in low-income communities. After adopting  those schools, we implement reforms that lead to positive student learning outcomes and increased  student enrollment.

In order to raise funds for our initiatives, we organize fundraising dinners. Guests pay an entry fee  to attend a musical performance followed by dinner. During the event, my company’s Fundraising  department used to highlight important facts about the shortcomings in the public school system  by displaying shocking facts about the low student enrollment, high drop-out rate, and abysmal  student achievement. The Fundraising Department personnel would then distribute donation forms  among the guests and ask them to make donation commitments to address the problems that they  were highlighting. At the end of the event, we would collect these firms. Very few people would  make any commitments and those who did, would not follow though by actually sending a  donation check. We were unable to identify why our guests were not making any donation  commitments when they clearly cared enough about the cause to attend our event.

Selection and Application

Last year, we all sat down to discuss ways to collect more donor commitments during our  fundraising dinner scheduled for December. We decided to interview guests and tried to place  ourselves in the shoes of our donors. We realized from our discussions that our fundraising pitches  during the events did not draw any interest from the guests. They would mostly tune out or start  talking among themselves when our Fundraising Manager would come on stage. The Fundraising  Manager would list out a number of facts and figures about the abysmal state of public schools but  it did not resonate with the guests.

Therefore, we decided to come up with a different approach to our fundraising efforts. So we  decided that instead of presenting facts and figures, we will pick stories about our students who  had done well in our schools and gone on to attend University. We selected this approach because  people would be more interested to see the students, learn about their lives and see how our work  impacts them instead of viewing graphs.

This time, our CEO would tell the stories of these children and we would display photographs  from their time in school while playing sports or participating in one of our classes. At the end of  their story, we would invite the student to come on stage and narrate how he viewed our company  had impacted his life. After narrating our students’ stories, we would then ask the guests to commit  a donation that would sponsor a child’s education for a certain amount. We would then share  details about the sponsored student’s progress with the donor.

Insight and Approach

In previous fundraising dinners, we would receive donor commitments from 5 percent of the  invitees. But after using storytelling as a tool to inform the guests about our impact in the public  schools, we received commitments from 23 percent of the guests who attended the fundraising  dinner held in December last year.

We learnt that storytelling is a powerful tool to not only draw attention but to also drive donations  because people connected better to uplifting stories. What we have learned is that the stories we  pick should represent the diverse background of our students. We have students in our schools  who have overcome great odds to complete their education and start successful careers. These  stories can help highlight how our work helps these students accomplish their goals and overcome  hardships. We decided that we will highlight more of these stories on our website and on our social  media campaigns for fundraising purposes.

Reflection on Design Thinking

David Perez

June 7, 2020

The challenge:  In order to persuade prospects for a warehouse membership purchase, Sam’s Club uses  various incentives.  The company has found that many consumers will move from the consideration  state to the purchase state faster if incentives are offered.  While the purchase price would remain the  same at $45, additional incentives after purchase help hundreds of thousands of households annually  commit to an annual membership.  However, no incentives have universal appeal.  Equally important is  the fact that warehouse clubs sell products at a price that covers the overhead of club operations;  organizational profits are derived from membership fees.  Costly incentives essentially defer any  membership income to year two members up on renewal.  The challenge is to develop incentive  programs with a lower cost and in a new manner that do not require half a year to get measurements  on effectiveness.

The tool I have implemented is Learning Launch.  It’s important to note that this is not a hypothetical or  theoretical test.  An actual learning launch was launched a few weeks ago.  This tool was chosen  because it is an approach our team has not tried before.  In the past, we have executed large-scale  national campaigns making assumptions provided from our team.  The appeal is in the concept of “not  knowing what we don’t know.”

Instead of a large, national, multi-million dollar ad campaign, we have identified a test market and a  random audience and just launched a new program for the sake of learning.  We are testing five vastly  different offers with two different messaging themes.  For application, since we don’t know what would  be most appealing, we are pushing a variety of incentives and campaigns and starting off by giving each  of them equal funding in the test market.

The insights have thus far been fascinating, but we are still so early on in the findings that we don’t  know what we don’t know yet.  By launching multiple tiny programs with a very different incentive, we  are measuring real-time responses and social media shares.  Within the week, we will have enough data  to determine which ad messaging has been most effective in the test market, and will invest only in the  most productive 50% of the offers and messages.  We will repeat this process until we determine which  strategy or strategies are most effective.

We do not know what we will do different next time as we don’t have the data back to measure what is  a success this time.  The next iteration will just reflect what we learned as we are considering an  unsuccessful ad element as not a failure, but a learning toward optimizing what is more of a success.

Final assignment   Visualization

Challenge

Manchay is a poor place, located in Lima, Peru. The first time I arrived there I, immediately,  realized how many children were there and also how their parents let them spend almost all  the day on the street, without any worry (because they need to work hard to earn enough  money to maintain the family).

That was not only a risk for children, but also a waste of time, because they were full of  energy, ideas and skills that were not being developed or capitalized to do something in  favour of theirselfs, their families or, even, their community.

That is why some friends and I decided to start a project to generate a change, but we did  not want a project designed by us, we wanted to motivate people to design and manage their  own one.

Selection

Visualization is, I regard, the essential tool of Design Thinking, because is the one who let  us to realize the complexity of the situation we are facing and also the one who let us to  identify that details which can make the difference in our proposal. Visualization tools take  us to apprehending the challenge, transforming it we perceive into something that can be  seen, can be “touched” and, finally, improved.

I chose this for my challenge, because, as the designer Janine Ma says, visualization  also helps to make sure that all people has understood the same. And it is particularly  important on my challenge, because what I finally wanted is that people of Manchay assumed  the leadership of the solution we created together, so I needed that everybody can realized  the whole situation and its wealth, improvement opportunities and complexity.

Application

To start, I spent a week taking pictures of the place, of the kids, adults and also of the physical  space. Then, I also asked everybody to write or draw on a paper wall what they want for  theirselfs and for their community. And, finally, I asked them to say why they thought they  could not achieve their goals.

Some days after, I asked people to come and order all the material I have collected before,  making groups based on similiarity. Pictures showed how lonely children were and how they  spent many hours getting bored on the street. Other pictures showed how dirty the place was  and how it had a lot of spaces full of garbage. Also we, surprisingly, discovered that kids and

adults wanted exactly the same: a healthy place with happy people, working and having fun  together. And also they both did not know what to do to achieve their goals and felt they do  not have enough money to do anything.

At the end of the journal, the material was divided in three groups: Reality – Dreams –  Obstacles to overcome. On one side, the original situation and things to improve (public

cleaning, children loneliness, etc.). In the middle, all they want for their lifes. And on the last  side, a list of things to be changed.

I am totally sure it works, because this overview of the situation allowed everybody to know  what their peers want and, therefore, to realized that, as a community, exist a common goal.  And, specially, helped us to make connections and understand, deeply, the situation and be  able to propose solutions (that all the time was in front of us).

Insight

During the process, I have learnt that visualization contributes to share our ideas and  knowledge and to articulate it with others’. That is the reason why I think this process is not  only to “see” or understand something, it is also about creation, it is about creating a richer  common vision.

I also appreciate how useful this tool could be. Given that it is based on graphics and  schemes, it is suitable for everybody –kids, teenagers, adults, adults who cannot read or  write and others-.

Approach

The next time, for similar purposes, I am quite sure that I will select the same tool, because

it made people to touch their problems and also its solution, to take their problems, fears,

dreams and, over all, their opportunities for change down to the earth. But what I would

change is the way I used it. I would not ask people to write or draw their thinkings, I would

ask also to talk about them, so they can organize and recognize some topics better.

Challenge

I work as a Consulting Manager at an IT consulting firm in Mexico City. We specialize in the  implementation and support of ERP systems for clients of different industries. We started working  with a new client, a hospital. Another consulting firm had already implemented them an ERP  system for their financials and supply chain management. Although the new system is one of the  best in the market, the client had been facing many different problems with it: the nurses had to  wait a lot to place their medicine replenishment orders, clients had to wait a lot of time for invoices,  finance could not close their accounting periods on time, and so on.

As you can imagine, this situation had caused a big displeasure to the Board of Directors, and a  great dislike among end users (operations, IT, nurses, etc.), because the implementation of the  new system, instead of making their work easier, it was making it more difficult.

The managers of Operations and IT didn’t have a clear idea where the real problem was: if it was  the system configuration, the interfaces, deficient training about the system, etc. They had no  idea where to start, and they also didn’t know what to offer their end users to improve.

There were several challenges in this situation. In first place, to gather all the problems that the  client was facing in the different areas. Second, to make end users to get involved in the problem  and not only complaint all the time, so that they could provide their evaluation about the current  challenges and contribute with ideas on the improvements they believed could make each area  to provide more value to the company.

Tool Selected

We were clearly in the “what is” stage at this point. The tool we selected was mind mapping. As  the video lecture shows on week 3, this is a tool that can be used in the first phase of the design  thinking process, which allows us to look at the current reality. It could also help us to bring  together a large amount of data, because we would have to interview people from many areas  such as inventory, purchasing, accounts payable, IT, finance, etc. and finding possible patterns  would be more difficult in a traditional way. Finally, it could help to make all areas to empathize  about the problems that the whole hospital was facing and not just their own area.

Application

Example Reflection – Storytelling

Challenge

At the beginning of 2010, I was transferred to one of the bank’s branches in which I work as  the branch manager. After assuming my duties and acting my role as a branch manager from  the previous branch manager, I was surprised that some of the deposits belonging to the  branch’s customers would be broken and withdrawn during the first quarter of the year, which  negatively affects the total deposits in the branch and thus the branch’s profits decrease  compared to the previous year. From here, the challenge began to face this decline, with the  participation of all branch employees, whether employees of operations, sales, marketing and  customer service.

Selection

In facing such a challenge, I adopted one of the design thinking tools, namely Storytelling.  Storytelling is a powerful communication tool that enables us as a human being to understand  more about our emotional experiences. This makes it an efficient method to use during the  design process.

Storytelling helps explain the interconnections among people in situations and settings,  teaching broad lessons that engage real human beings. Listening engages people; and empathy  is an essential and fundamental component in the process.

Storytelling is a methodology for solving problems that focuses on asking questions and  listening, with empathy, to the needs of individuals and groups. Storytelling is an “essential  human activity” for sharing experiences, explaining the values, and deciding on solutions  through vivid verbal and visual accounts.

Application

I held several meetings with all the new branch employees, whether individual meetings or in  groups (meetings of teams and employees of each department in the branch), to find out the all  related issues to the challenge, and I began to tell many stories of many successes for me in  previous branches.

A story was presented to overcome one of the most difficult challenges as a branch manager.  The bank’s top management decided to make a full renovation of the branch, and then the  branch’s employees were transferred to work through nearby branches. How was the  coordination with all employees to focus on attracting the largest number of new customers  and then focus on the most profitable products for the branch with the lowest cost in order to  cover the fixed costs of full renovation of the branch during a period of seven continuous  months.

I also narrated one of the success stories when I took over the management of one of the newest  branches and how we cooperated in the branch to achieve a breakeven point within a time and  period less than expected from the bank top management to achieve such an achievement.

All this was done with the branch employees by listing and asking many questions during our  meetings, and listening to their opinions and comments on what we dealt with in terms of  stories and details of each step in the confrontations of each previous challenge, and taking into  consideration all their valuable suggestions, which are a roadmap for all of us in facing the  challenges.

Insight

Such stories and surviving experiences inspired the branch’s employees and seemed to feel that  they could overcome any difficulties or challenges they might face to achieve such a goal,  which is the ability to achieve and attract what is required from customers ’deposits and then  increase the branch’s profits/liabilities again. I saw the interest and enthusiasm of all the branch  employees to provide constructive ideas in achieving the branch's goal. Each employee has set  a target and is committed to the amount of deposits required to be achieved, and each of them  has increased this number according to the required value so that each employee has a share of  the required deposits value according to what he can achieve.

When collected the total of their promises, I found that they are higher than the required value,  after feeling a passion for success and achieving higher than required. Indeed, after the end of  the year, we achieved higher than the target required with the participation of all branch  employees, and we were able to add another success story and experience that they are proud  to tell later.

Approach

This Storytelling as a design thinking tool was used to increase the passion of the entire branch  staff to create a success story for another challenge like the previous examples. From my point  of view, I believe that in order to increase the results and the successes we have achieved in  this challenge, we can integrate another tool that can be relied upon to create a state of the most  effective participation of all parties associated with this challenge, namely Mind Mapping as a  design thinking tool.

This is in order to benefit from the advantages of each of them through the participation of  team members fully in presenting innovations and new ideas from their point of view, to be a  reliable roadmap with their capabilities because they are the ones who will implement and  apply to achieve the highest results and outcomes.

Reflection – Visualization

Challenge & Selection:

In order to design the solution, first we have to get a good understanding of the problem that we are  trying to solve. Interviews, observations, desk research and other research techniques that are applied  during this phase generate huge amount of data – data that has to be grouped and analyse. My  business is not in one place and my people work far from home and I have to keep tread on all these  activities?

Creating an activity wall is a great way to display insights, photos, and locations, all the relevant activity  outputs in one place. This approach helps us build connections between different findings and  understand the bigger picture. The visual aspect of the wall triggers idea generation and enables  project members to better understand activity insights. For this reason, design thinkers often use tools  such as persona which give a face to the customer/interviewee.

Visual tools that can be used for understanding the problem are for e.g. personas, mind map, customer  journey maps, mood board, photo safari.

Application:

In his book Change by Design, Tim Brown states that drawing for designers is a way to express their  ideas and only drawing “can simultaneously reveal both the functional characteristics of an idea and  its emotional content.” It is not necessary to poses good drawing skills, as the popular saying goes  “picture is worth a thousand words” and even a simple sketch can tell us more than a 10 minutes’  description of an idea. In a group setting, visualization helps to spark idea generation. Seeing what  other people are drawing, adding elements to their drawing or simply discussing the sketches helps  to build on top of each other’s ideas. Brainstorming sessions can be also enhanced by the use of visual  props such as nudge cards to stimulate idea creation.

Drawing can benefit our understanding of how the idea unfolds through different stages of the service,  particularly when generating ideas for a new service.

Insight and Approach:

Citing Katja Tschimmel “in the same way that sketching helps the designer to think and elaborate  ideas, early prototyping is another way of visualizing and testing new solutions, it is a visual  manifestation of concepts, the transformation of an idea in a testable model”. In another words, use  of prototyping transforms ideas from drawings on a paper to tangible solutions. This shift helps us  explore different possibilities, compare how the customers perceive prototypes, and improve  solutions without investing a lot of money. Prototypes tend to be “cheap and dirty”, which means that  they are not a polished solution but instead a working version of a service that is good enough to be  understood by the customer. For this reason, development of prototypes doesn’t require a lot of time  and money. Tim Brown summarizes it in a great way, “the faster we make our ideas tangible, the  sooner we will be able to evaluate them, refine them, and zero in on the best solution”.

Visual tools that can be used for prototyping are for e.g. desktop walkthrough, cardboard prototyping,  paper prototyping, role playing.

Reflection – Mind Mapping

Challenge & Selection

As I started this Design for Business Innovation course, I was immediately drawn to the messages in the  Physics of Innovation lecture.  As part of an applied innovation unit in my organisation that belongs to a  larger organisation, the challenges outlined in this lecture about the mindset for stability/execution  versus the mindset for innovation were something that really resonated with me.  It caused me to  question; Are we set up for success in our Innovation unit, how do other parts of the organisation see us  depending on their mind-set, and how is this impacting us?.   I felt it was essential to unpack/share with  leadership in my area – to allow an introspection of our current state and whether it caused us to  pivot/make any changes going forward.

Although this was not a project where I had planned to use design thinking – I felt that there were things  as an innovation group we perhaps “didn’t know what we didn’t know”.   I also felt there was a need to  really quantify insights/findings from the course learnings to take forward with leadership – therefore I  started using the data & learnings from the course as the input to challenge our current setup and really  look at how prepared we are for innovation, and ultimately allow this to drive introspection on our  What is, and then progress through the remaining stages.

As I progressed through the course I was conscious that I wanted to glean further insights, that could  also be considered by a wider group.  The course highlighted Mind Mapping as a very useful technique  used to consolidated results of the What is stage and allow findings/insights/themes to emerge.  As I  learned further on the Design for Innovation course - Mind mapping is an effective way of both  capturing and organising large and complex pieces of knowledge. It’s a powerful tool used to distil data  into information and insights that can be easily communicated and inform the What if stage of design  thinking.  Full details of using Mind Mapping for this purpose are described in the lecture:  https://www.coursera.org/learn/uva-darden-design-thinking-innovation/lecture/lsFRa/mind-mapping- tool and further information here: https://ideas.darden.virginia.edu/10-design-thinking-tools-turn- creativity-and-data-into-growth

I’d had some exposure to the use of Mind Mapping for other purposes like Impact Mapping and found it  to be very effective, therefore I chose the Mind Mapping technique outlined in this lecture to help frame  a picture of the learnings/key insights from this course to take forward in discovery with the wider  group.

Application

As I worked through the course I noted key learnings, knowledge, information from each week, and  insights that I knew would be useful to unpack later.

I used the xMind tool (see: http://www.johnson.com/categories/wp-content/tagabout.html) – a really good tool I’d had exposure to previously  – that allows you build up the Mind Map online.   Taking each part of the learnings, I grouped them into  the central topic, sub-topics, drawing out the insights, and sub-layers of information.  I flagged the areas  on the mind map (using ‘flag’ indicators) where there were real insights/findings relative to our  situation.  I also flagged areas where it was appropriate to disseminate a supporting visual, or reference  detailed supporting information.  Additionally, I flagged key findings by theme, to highlight some  recommendations.

Alongside the Mind Map, I created a summary view of the themed findings/insights – with associated  questions for introspection that would provide input to a sharing workshop session with leadership to  spark conversation into our real ‘What is’ and ultimately uncover more ‘What is’ information.

For the sharing workshop session, I setup the room with visuals including the Mind Map in large printed  view, and other key visuals that supported the findings/insights and used the space to disseminate the  information, allowing participants to interact with the visuals at key points in the story telling  walkthrough, to validate findings, co-create more findings and gain alignment on our ‘What is’.

I designed the session to step through the key themes in the Mind Map – telling the story, imparting  learning/knowledge, posing a question and answer, and allowing participants introspect on that  question and answer and co-create further – offering up more information to develop the current  picture relative to the insights/findings.  The workshop was designed to be interactive as we unpacked  the Mind Map insights together.

Insight & Approach

In terms of insights, it’s amazing to use a technique like Mind Mapping to distil a large volume of  information into something palatable that allows insights to emerge, but it’s also an extremely powerful  way of learning and staying “in the question” long enough to gain greater understanding.  The visual  aspect the Mind Map provided was an impactful way to theme and distil the information and allow  participants to interact with the map and the key messages - evidenced by their questions, and further  post-it notes on pain points/challenges.

My own question generated from that early lecture in Week 2 – the Physics of Innovation was: Are we  set up for success in our Innovation Unit, how do other parts of the organisation see us depending on  their mind-set, and how is this impacting us?  This allowed us to completely unpack the insights distilled  into the Mind Map additionally complimented by other techniques (discussed in the approach below).

I realised that in the full sense of design thinking I was largely working on my own for this initial stage.  However, I used this approach and the Mind Mapping technique with its resulting insights as the catalyst  to bring new knowledge and learning to leadership and springboard into a fuller design thinking ‘What  is’ stage.  What I was uncovering through this mechanism sparked the same thoughts in others in the  group and allowed learning and a recognition of mis-aligned mind-sets. Often, we are experiencing  symptoms of a problem we don’t yet have the knowledge to recognise or name!  In this case the  learning from the Physics of Innovation lecture was the knowledge that was needed alongside the  subsequent lectures on having a prepared mind.

As a result of the above, the insights & findings were further co-created by the group and others and this  ultimately allowed us to move to a ‘What if’ stage – applying the design thinking process to our  approach to innovation in our unit.  We settled on some early recommendations that would inform our  What if stage in terms of education, prepared minds, formalising our innovation practices, and clarifying  the difference in our work, to that of other parts of the organisation.

There will be more to come on this as we move through the remaining design thinking stages, but the  course, and the technique of Mind Mapping has greatly helped in distilling this knowledge and allowed  us ‘hold up a mirror’ to our ‘What is’ to recognise and address the challenges we face innovating in a  large organisation.

As a final insight, use several techniques to complement each other, validate your approach and cater  for diversity in the way people process information (further information below)

In terms of approach, I employed some other techniques alongside Mind Mapping as follows:

For example, traditional methods like writing notes, tables of information, prioritised items, key findings,  and recommendations, and generating a PowerPoint presentation.  I was aware I would have diversity in  the group in the way they took on information and processed it, therefore I wanted to cater for this, but  also to use the alternative approach as a validation for myself in preparation for the Sharing Workshop.

I wanted to keep this presentation very short – to really allow me “tell the story” in an impactful way –  bringing the attendees to different visual stations in the room as the story unfolded and allowing them  to interact with the material and give their feedback.  I took time in the story telling to ask questions,  and pose an answer, which I then invited the group to introspect upon.

I believe no one technique is going to suffice completely, the act of Mind Mapping was essential to  visualise the insights & themes emerging, but equally the distilling of the message into a short  PowerPoint – used alongside the visual stations in the room allowed the technique of “Story Telling” to  really have an impact on the participants.  It is vital to consider your audience and cater for how people  like to take on information, visual and otherwise.

Learning Launch

Challenge:

I’m Patrick, from Port Said, Egypt. I work with a charitable  foundation (Life Makers Foundation). Last year we had an annual  objective to empower 100 in need families with 100 micro  enterprises, to make them able to gain their own money rather  than keep getting money from people/donors.    To achieve this objective, our strategy was to raise money through  a one-month street/public fundraising campaign. The challenge  we’ve faced included both: 1) how to attract people to donate, 2)  where to locate our donations booths. In other words, as we had  some limited resources (volunteers, booths, budget, etc..), we  wanted to figure out how to raise money with the most effective  and efficient way.     Selection:

The selected tool is Learning Launch as we wanted to examine our  hypotheses in the real world and to get field data in which we can  rely on during our campaigns. Learning Launch is the tenth design  thinking tool, it allows us to make an affordable experiment to test  the impact of a new solution on the customers. The purpose of  Learning Launch is to get a truthful set of data and insights that  either confirm or disconfirm our assumptions, which lead to either  continue developing your idea or pivot/eliminate your idea.

Application:

Port Said city is divided into five districts, so we placed a donations  booth in the hottest spot of each district all day long, to test where  are the best places to raise money from, in addition to determining  what time of the day is better to talk to people at. The second thing  we did was collecting information and insights about the potential  donors’ behavior when we talk to them about our foundation and  its objectives and strategies    Insights:

Through our Learning Launch we’ve found out the following facts  and insights: (assumes the five districts are named K, L, M, N, O).

 Districts M and O generated 68% of the total donations.   District K generated only 4% of the total donations.   People show tendency to donate more when numbers/statistics

of achievements are mentioned (e.g. Past records).

 From 3pm to 6:30pm is the best time interval to raise money at.   People tend to donate more when they are given a brochure.   17% of people don’t prefer the idea of micro enterprises, they

prefer to give their donations to others in cash.

The insights gave us a realistic view of how could we tackle the  challenge we’re facing, and to design our fundraising campaign in  the most efficient and effective way.

Approach:

Learning Launch has been the perfect tool to test and examine our  hypotheses in order to eventually solve our challenge. We believe  that the whole experiment, insights and collected were crucial to  the success of our fundraising campaign.    Adding, the tool of Learning Launch wont probably works alone. As  I’ve learned from the course, design thinking is sequential process  with a number of tools and sub processes included. It’s preferable  that you integrate some tools and processes rather than picking a  single tools and ignore the rest.

Reflection – Mind Map

1. Challenge

I am part of the digital transformation team of a university in Monterrey NL. Mexico. The challenge  we had was to improve the student experience during their stay at the university, first at the  bachelor level. How to make the student's life less complicated? A university is like a mini-city, which  has many implications and simultaneous events. Many processes had to be improved, but which  ones, and of these, in what order to do it? How to ensure delivery of incremental value to the  student? We face this challenge with the Design Thinking methodology.

2. Selection

With the context expressed in the previous paragraph, we considered that we had to know and  understand what the student was currently experiencing from his experience in the university, so it  seemed appropriate to make a journey map as a first starting point for our understanding, then we  went to mind map.

3. Application

We selected a sample of 50 students from various disciplines to first generate a journey map and  then a mind map, thus achieving a better representation of what our students thought about their  experience in the university, making visible patterns of student needs that would improve their  experience. in college.

4. Insight

From the use of both tools, the student defined his experience at the university as a set of elements  among which were: communication, administrative processes, student life, academic needs,  infrastructure, physical and mental health, student support, and working life.

5. Approach

Of these elements we decided to start with "Student Accompaniment" as it is the highest priority  for the student. Again we made a journey map first and then a mind map to identify how it was that  the student needed to live a better experience, thus identifying the following elements of  accompaniment: Intellectual, Social, Emotional, Physical, Vocational and Spiritual. Of these  elements, we evaluated which was the most important for the students, identifying the Emotional  as the first to be addressed.

6. Conclusion

Through the use of tools such as Journey Map and Mind Map, we were able to identify the moments  that were a relevant part of delivering value for the student, "Accompaniment" being the most  important. Applying them again in a second stage, we identified which elements were part of the  accompaniment, the emotional being the most important. This allowed us to conclude that we had  to address emotional support as the first delivery to the student, and so on until we addressed each  element of the student's experience and then each sub-element.

Vinod Baker

Our Challenge

I work in an operational environment; the purpose of our business unit is to ensure the circulation  of money. Our staffs’ primary job is to handle the monies that is coming into the bank (deposits)  and the monies that is leaving the bank’s premises and transported to clients’ premises  (withdrawals). Dealing with clients’ money is an important job however quite stressful for our  staff. All our clients rely on our service offerings for them to continue with their business.

The staff morale and motivation is not at a desirable level for optimal productivity. Our challenge  is to change how our employees feel about working for this business unit. To create an  environment that employees find pleasant and a place that encourages growth and learning.  Furthermore, we want our staff to feel motivated and encouraged to improve how they work.  Having motivated and determined staff will have a positive implication on our productivity.  Therefore, as part of our People Program we need initiatives that assist in changing how our  people feel about their work. We also need initiatives that are cost efficient.

Our Selection

We started our design thinking journey by using multiple tools such as: interviews and personas  to understand why our employees came to work and how they felt at work. More importantly we  wanted to find out how we can make their lives better and what is important for them. Majority of  our people work an 8-hour shift, this means that they spend more time at work with colleagues  than they do with their families. Hence it is important that we improve this environment.

The team and I are now at a phase where we would like to test our hypothesis and assumption  by running small experiments and prototypes, learning launches. The objective is to see how  employees react and receive the new and different offerings made available to them. The  purpose of learning launches is to test a hypothesis and then to learn and improve on the  offerings and solutions.

Application

Firstly, we simultaneously interviewed our staff and had them complete a survey. The purpose  of this was to gather data to understand what matters for our employees and to answer the “what  is?” question in design thinking. Out of the data we were able to create personas and identified  themes by using mind maps.

One of the themes that derived from the data was that: our staff felt there was little opportunities  for growth and development.

For the Learning launch we introduced Learning Bytes, which is an online learning and tutoring  platform and is a form of virtual learning. From the data gathered there was other themes that  came out, which we thought would be great focus points and learning topics which we could  teach the staff through the virtual learning platform.

For example, employees had a concern with time management. Therefore, we scheduled a  learning session to cover this topic. Then we looked for a staff member in our business unit who  could build and deliver a course on time management. It was important to get the right individual  who had the qualification and the practice to facilitate the learning sessions. Therefore, we had  a senior project manager deliver the course as time management is a critical component of  project management.

Some of the other learning topics that we scheduled for the upcoming weeks came about merely  because of the environment. The environment we are working in is very complex and has many  changes, our team leaders often prepares the staff for these changes. Hence, we included a  change management learning session.

The flight plan for our learning launch:

1. We will schedule a learner bytes every second week for the next four months (that means

we will have approximately 7 learning sessions)

2. For every session we will take roll call of the staff attending these sessions. We will

monitor this as well, this will be a great indicator if staff find these Learner Byte  worthwhile.

3. After each session employees will provide feedback of the Learner bytes session. This

will help us to improve the interaction in these sessions.

4. After the four months we will conduct a survey again with staff. The reason for this is to

see how employees felt about these sessions and where we need to improve if we decide  to continue with these sessions.

Insight

It is funny how one thinks they know what is important to an employee. After all we, ourselves  are employees. It scary how one can miss the plot because we make decisions based on  assumptions. What design thinking allowed us to do was to build hypotheses from data and then  test these hypotheses before creating and implementing a solution. For example, what matters  for one person was career progression and for another was financial stability.

By answering the four basic questions through the design thinking process, we were  able to see  what the problem was, that majority of the staff felt like just a number and that there is no room  for growth and development. We were then able to brainstorm different solutions to make  employees feel like there is opportunities to learn and grow.

Approach

Some lessons learned from design thinking was not to build solutions based off assumptions. At  the bank we often have “great ideas” that is going to improve operations. As a result, we go off  a tangent; drafting business cases and jumping ahead to complete solution design. Then we  discover that we were boiling the ocean, by designing a solution that customer don’t really need  and will just complicate the lives of our staff.

In future we will complete Learning Launches, as this will allow us to test our assumptions and  hypotheses. Conducting Learning Launches help organisation to build appropriate solution and  doing so while saving organisation from waste money and time. The challenge is to find cost  efficient ways to complete Learning Launches.

Federation

By Sara Garcia

Challenge

With a history of working on multiple projects I (and assuming many others) have faced  a very peculiar conundrum throughout a project’s creation lifecycle.

Whenever a new project is executed, post an initial meeting, every team scatters and  starts ideating their own version of the project which ideally roots out and grows from

their areas of expertise. I.e a developer would ideate from a developer’s POV focusing

more on the technical aspects and a Business developer would do it from their POV

focusing on business goals etc.

The challenge here is to ensure that every team member involved in the project has a  common understanding of the project regardless of their involvement at any stage of

the project.

The solution to this challenge seems simple on the outside yet precarious when tackled.

Selection

The tool selected for this challenge is Mind mapping, due to its ability to visually  communicate large chunks of information in an organised manner. The tool would free

up useful time which would otherwise be wasted explaining all the information to bring

people up to speed.

Application

The approach was to create multiple mind maps at various stages which would  showcase the entire project journey and ensure any participant who would join midway

in the project would catch up with the least amount of time wasted, this would also

ensure that each member is in sync with the final goal of the project as well while being

able to see a broad view of the project to provide better ideas and spot potential issues.

Once a project was initiated, An empty room was selected and a ​client mind map​ was  created which contained all of the client’s insights. This helped the design team process

the information faster and proceed with the next steps of ideation. Post the ideation

session another mind map (​ideation mind map​) was created to showcase a refined

project idea which incorporated multiple missing facets that would otherwise impact

the success of the project. Post ideation was the research and design, we added in the

research information into the ‘ideation mind map’ and the result of the design team was

a set of wireframes organised as app flows which were placed beside the ideation mind

map and showcased the resulting output of the project.

At this stage the client, a few developers, and business development team were  brought in to look at the work in progress.

Rather than explaining the complete process and work done by the design team, we  asked the client, developers and business development team to spend a few minutes

looking at the Client mind map, then the ideation mind map and then the app flow.

This brought all the stakeholders of the project in sync with the current status of the  project, the direction and saved everyone a lot of time. We proceeded doing this at the

next few stages of the design and development cycles to ensure the complete project

journey is captured and each stakeholder is updated with the project status and

direction regardless of the time they joined the project.

Insight

During the complete process of this experiment I noticed increased efficiency, better  idea generation and a unified hive style thinking approach that is seen when

participants have spent close to 6-7 months working on the same project.

We were also able to generate ideas beyond our fields of expertise and also catch  issues that would have resulted in a lot of rework and significant loss for the client.

We had a few participants who had to keep shifting from project to project throughout  the process and they found it a lot easier to catch up with the progress and provide

useful insights during the time they spent.

Overall, I was able to open my mind and think from various other perspectives, in a way  following this process helped us to get out of our metaphorical boxes, work together

towards a common goal and this helped us provide better quality to our clients.

Approach

Next time, I would probably involve a few additional people from specific fields when  constructing and app of a particular user base. Ex - if I were to create an alternative to

facebook AD manager, I would do my research, but also include multiple digital

marketers to the team and create a custom mind map of their thoughts on an ideal

application and also involve them in ideation sessions to help refine the alternative

application even more to suit its end users.

Consistent positive onboarding experience across 7 offices in Central Eastern Europe, Middle East, Africa and Turkey

Challenge: In the summer of the year 2008, our company introduced a hiring program with the objective of increasing the number of sales people in the field sales organization by 20% of EMEA sales headcount. The intention was to extend offers to the selected candidates during the autumn 2008 in order to get the new hires to the company between November 2008 to February 2017. In absolute numbers, our company was about to hire approx. 400 new sales employees.

The growth of 20% of headcount was not evenly distributed across EMEA. For the emerging markets gathered under the region of Central Eastern Europe, Middle East, Africa and Turkey (abbrev. EXCOM), the allocated headcount was disproportionately higher as opposed to mature markets in the Western Europe (as EXCOM was expected to experience higher growth in demand and number of customers). EXCOM headcount in sales was expected to be on average 35%, with some of the offices growing as high as by 50%. The major number of new hires was expected to start in December 2008 and January 2017 (standard notice period in the region being 2 months, standard time to find, interview and hire a suitable candidate being 3 months, the hiring kicked off in early August 2008).

This steep headcount growth posed a particular challenge in EXCOM (as opposed to e.g. the Western Europe) due to the fact that the sales offices in EXCOM are small - on average around 25 employees - with no support functions (such as receptionist, office manager, internal IT, HR or finance) present on site locally. This means that any new hire that comes on board presents a tough load for the local team - who needs to help the new hire set up not just business-wise, but also from the perspective of setting up computers, email, entry cards etc.

Because the onboarding experience is of crucial importance for the first impressions and engagement of the new hires and their long-term retention in the company (as studies suggest1). Therefore, myself as the Human Resources Business Partner for the EXCOM region and the leadership team from EXCOM agreed that we must structure and scale our onboarding process in a way that will create a “Consistent Positive Onboarding Experience in the region”.

Selection: Because the onboarding process is a relatively complex issues consisting of multiple steps and multiple stakeholders acting as part of it and also because we had a lot of different qualitative and quantitative, but quite inconsistent and unstructured data, we decided that the best approach to sort all the information and engage all the relevant stakeholders would be Mind Mapping. We leveraged a combination of live whiteboard session with various virtual sessions (as the offices are quite far - spanning from South Africa to Moscow - so a workshop in one location would not be feasible). By leveraging mind mapping as opposed to a normal roundtable

1 http://www.chambers.com/wp-content/app/categorieshomepage.jsp

debate we were hoping to come up with some creative, out-of-the-box smart ideas as the participants will be building on each other's ideas.

Application: We had multiple mind-mapping sessions with various mixed groups of stakeholders. When inviting the stakeholders, we were paying attention to get together as diverse group as possible - for example managers and individual contributors, people from different offices, employees freshly hired to the company (less than 1 year in the company) and employees with more than 5 years in the company, men and women, different nationalities, different departments and different work experience (juniors, senior professionals, employees who came from start-ups as well as from industry giants…). During each session we started from the new hire and mind-mapped how this new hire experiences RH. I printed out results from historical onboarding surveys, comments from employee satisfaction surveys etc. While people were discussing, I was capturing the ideas into the mind-map (either on the wall, please see image below) or virtually in a drawing pad. With each group we had 2 sessions. The initial, when we drew the main mind map, and a follow up session, when we reviewed the mind-map and discussed actions/ideas that we may carry forward. There were on average 6 people in one group and we had 4 groups in total.

Insights: By applying the mind mapping and engaging a broad and diverse group of stakeholders in the activity, we were able to identify a lot of areas that were not covered by the corporate onboarding programs and at the same time were identified as very impactful for the onboarding experience. The visual map in front of us enabled us to see some not very obvious relationships between the various onboarding elements and based on these relations, we were able to identify 8 different small projects that we could do in order to improve the onboarding experience across the EXCOM offices without impacting negatively the workload of the employees in the offices (e.g. gathering new hires into virtual cohorts across the whole EXCOM and create for them virtual practical chats with e.g. operations or the EXCOM leadership etc.).

Thanks to the collaborative approach we were also able to get quite a few volunteers willing to assist with the identified projects - I consider this willingness to help as another positive outcome of the mind mapping activity. People were able to get their voice heard and this created an alignment and additional engagement. On the negative side, this whole exercise was obviously way more time consuming than the usual way (round table discussion, followed by management decision), but overall very rewarding. Also, as a by-product, we identified a couple of gaps and obsolete information in the global onboarding process - which we reported to the global talent team.

Approach: I think the mind mapping tool was the right one for this purpose. We were also considering mapping the customer journey (in this case simply following one of the new hires through his or her onboarding) - but, eventually, we leveraged the experience of the fresh new employees as part of the mind-mapping groups, which was more efficient. The activity was very bonding for the team and the element of visualisation helped to trigger a deep and detailed discussion about how are elements of onboarding related.

Design Thinking Tool: Story Telling

Challenge

My name is Alessio Putino and I am the Trainer-Training & Development for a group of  Engineering colleges in Andhra Pradesh, India. It is my responsibility to see that all  my Engineering students acquire a set of technical skills which are out of their  defined university curriculum. The main reason for this is because at the end of final  year of student course in Engineering, companies visit the colleges for placements  and recently these companies starting looking for additional technical skills in  students, apart from standard academic skills. Now, the challenge is to motivate  final year students to spend that extra hour of time in college for attending additional  technical training classes, as college time table for them is already hectic with their  regular academics and especially with final year project work. For the students, it is  very demotivating to stay in the college for an extra-hour regularly and then to go  home and practice those extra technical skills. It is even more difficult for those  students who commute college from different towns around, where the travel time  ranges from 40minutes to 90 minutes. The regular college hours are from 9am to  4pm and to accommodate this additional training session for one hour, we had to  extend the college timings till 5pm. As it turned out, the student attendance for these  training classes was lukewarm. So, we had a challenge to ensure healthy student  attendance for these classes and also to motivate them to go back home and spend  required time to practice these skills, which is in addition to their academic  homework.

Selection

I always use Story Telling to motivate students, to extract best out of them. Students  need inspiration to put those extra hours in their learning and practice. They need  inspiration from the role models. Especially, when students are in the final year and  successful completion of their degree is not the only parameter for them to measure  their success. Students take pride in earning that dream job along with their degree  completion certificate. I tell stories of most successful passed out students from my  college to motivate my students, and share what they have done/how they have  done extraordinarily to achieve, what they have achieved, which is excellent  campus placements. I also create safe environment for students by encouraging  them to open up and share their frank feedback against the context of my story to  ascertain their goals, and also see if they have anyone they know, in their family  and friends, who have achieved their dream job in the face of adversity.

Application

I wanted to share a story to my students. But I want them to be focused and relaxed  so that I can relate my story and make them feel the connection. So, I had arranged  a Movie to be played in college auditorium and I encouraged all the final year  Engineering students to watch the movie and have fun time with me and share their  feedback. I told them just that. They were not aware that I have a story to share  after the Movie or the whole event was related to their training or campus  placement. I even asked the students to come in their casuals so that they feel at  ease when interacting with me in the auditorium, so that they do not feel anything  formal about the whole event. The movie was scheduled at 10am. On a Sunday.The  Movie I played was ‘The Pursuit of Happiness’. Once it finished, I started asking  what they have experienced and what were their thoughts about the protagonist in  the story and how he came out of his troublesome life and how he pursued  happiness. Once I felt the students were opening up, I shared the story of a passed  out senior student, Kiran, who comes from a modest background, and whose father  was a farmer. Kiran had to travel 2 hours every day to college. In order to achieve  his goal of joining a Multinational Company-GOOGLE, Kiran had to acquire  technical skills in a particular programming language, which the college was not  offering at that time. Kiran was so determined that he joined a training institute in a  town far from his home. Which means, every day after  coming back from college,  he again had to travel one more hour to his training institute, where he will spend 2  hours and then come back home. He did this day-in and day-out for one whole year.

The result was- he got selected for GOOGLE that year. I found the auditorium fill  with silence, when I finished the story. Then, I asked the students present in the  auditorium to relate their training scenario to that of Kiran. Students now started  expressing how fortunate they were that they do not need to travel any further after  going home, for additional technical training. Infact, they started narrating the  stories they know of such students who took on adversities to achieve their goals

Insight

I was pleasantly surprised on how the students reacted as they started relating to  their current scenario with other successful stories that they know. They felt  immediately connected and obliged to put that extra hour of time both at college  and at home to land on their dream job.

Approach

Students really needed a story that they can relate to. They needed that Sunday to  enjoy a movie and perhaps to have complete grip of their scenario. I was confident  that I could make a difference but surprised to see almost all the students staying  back for extra hour of additional technical training class from there on. Yes, I had  few more success stories at the end of that year, when I saw good number of  students getting placed in the companies they dreamed to join. Story telling worked  for me and I tell my students stories regularly. But next time, I may have achievers  in the auditorium after my Movie!, to tell their story –First hand!

Defining the ‘Sony’ identity - Mind Mapping

Challenge

I am part of a nonprofit climbing organization, called Sony <a Quechua word meaning ‘misbehaved’.  In this case trying to symbolize the rebel and free spirit of the group>. Sony was created a year ago  by a group of mountain lovers and a group of specialized guides part of the oldest mountaineering  foundation in Ecuador. Their idea was just to get together and climb the Ecuadorian Andes. It all began  to take shape and the group has now 50 more members. A wide diversity of people from architects,  government officials, agronomists, young, old, men and women are part of it.

The challenge arises when the thought of formalizing the group and giving it a true structure is brought.  Due to the great diversity of members’ backgrounds and vocational trainings, the task seemed  impossible. There were too many ideas, all so disorganized and “floating around”, that nobody knew  even where to begin. The big idea, and mainly its execution, was starting to create chaos, more than a  real contribution to the group. The big question was how to capture everybody’s impressions, take  advantage of the group’s diversity and set a route for a possible solution or sets of solutions.

Selection

As Kenia Jj says, “mind mapping is looking for patterns and insights in a large quantity of data you  collected during your exploration of what is the current reality.” This was the main problem to be solved  at this stage. There as a vast variety of ideas and thoughts, which at this point didn´t say anything at all.  This huge amount of data needed to be somehow organized to stablish the current reality: the identity  of the group. After that its structure, formal organization, objectives and more could be defined. This  was to be done getting the members to feel involved so the best of their thoughts could be presented in  clear patterns and insights.

Application

A big challenge presented at this point was that all this happened during complete isolation, due to the  Covid-19 breakdown. An efficient mechanism was to be used in order to solve the problem with these  unique circumstances. I decided to use a direct communication channel: Ñarñaku’s WhatsApp group.

The first step was to find the right timing, and inform the group about the design challenge. Getting one  of the leaders to be the one informing the group about the objective, gave the activity acceptance,  importance and involvement. About 30 members of the group participated (which represents 60% of  the group). People were asked at first to communicate what did they feel the identity of the group was,  and what were its main goals and objectives. This led to a long group discussion that lasted almost a full  day. Most of the ideas were already known, although some very good and new insights were presented.  During this process my job was to capture all these insights and thoughts while they were presented in  an open discussion.

The tool had to be slightly modified due to the special circumstances, but the main idea of it was  preserved. Therefor the next step was to group these thoughts into clusters of ideas. A digital tool was  used to create the mind map. After the map was created it was presented to the group again to get the  members feedback. The response was more than favorable. Now the ideas were organized route was

clear in which to continue. Although the tool was not easy to implement, due to special circumstances,  the results where more than satisfactory.

Insights

One of the main insights obtained during the activity was to clearly land the group's identity. Sony is  a group of friends with a great love and passion for mountains (cluster 1), with a will for environmental  awareness (cluster 2) and social motivation (cluster 3). These ideas synthesize the identity of the group,  and lets us start thinking in possible “what ifs”. Once the ideas were clearly mapped, the conception of  the challenge, and specially its answers, suddenly became evident. It also made the members of the  group get more involved in it.

An important lesson I obtained from this activity is that when you aloud people to freely express  themselves, the ideas flow freely. A question was presented at the beginning weather to narrow down  the discussion topics, or to openly present them so people can freely talk. The second choice was  selected and what was only needed was a little guidance (someone to act as a moderator). In my  opinion the result was more effective when members felt free to express their ideas.

Approach

Next time, one thing that would definitely be different is the mechanism by which the tool was  presented. This time it was required to be an online activity. Results would have been immensely better  if the activity was taken place in person. Another aspect to be taken in account is to minimize the group  of participants. Even though the vast amount and diversity of insights presented by the group were very  helpful, sometimes it became an obstacle when trying to move forward. I think that these two aspects  contribute to making the process sometimes slow and not always helpful. It can definitely be improved.

Reflection – Mind Mapping with Visualization Embedded  Margarita Martinez    Challenge    I am a coaching psychologist who was tasked to identify the right people to form a military task  force at headquarters, design the team structure, help them design the best physical space for  them to operate in from a people perspective, do everything possible to nip systemic issues in  the bud to minimize burnout. As well, in our conversations, we discussed how we could  continuously improve on our design for future teams, allowing them to be flexible enough to  address their unique situations, level of intensity and immediacy.    What I had to address was the following: The team would be small. Having them located in the  same building as the rest of the staff at Headquarters was very distracting. The key decision- makers on the team had to be ‘present’, well-rested and well-supported. In past task force  teams, we realized the 15% of the team did 85% of the critical work; the rest of the team being  support systems and fact and information finders to support that core group. If any of the team  burned out, it would leave a gap in the information flow and seriously affect the work and short  time lines to move people on the field. We had to look at where they were physically located,  whether we have one team or multiple, smaller teams, keep in mind how resilient the team  members were (test for that) and how the information and decisions were disseminated.  Where the troops were located had a direct bearing on how quickly the decision had to be  made and implicated people’s lives. We had a very short time frame to get this team up and  running and make sure it was the best team design possible. Even though we had limited time,  didn’t mean we couldn’t constantly tweak how we did things and test approaches as the team  did their jobs.    Selection    The tool I decided to use was Mind Mapping (Video Week 3). I thought this would not only be  the best tool to capture all moving parts so to speak, but to create a common understanding of  the current reality, and address what was true in the moment as well as the multiple moving  parts that would change situationally. The Mind Mapping approach allowed for constant  tweaking and exploration. The basis of this tool that I used, also invited us to continuously live  in the questions. Embedded within this selection was a Visualization diagram (Video Week 1); a  tool I created (attached) to form a picture in their minds, one of movement and fluidity. We  wanted this to be an ongoing process. I call this the Dance of Change™ illustration.

Application    We identified a long hallway outside the team’s offices to create the map and covered it with  white board sheets. At intervals down the long hallway were white board markers where  people could stop, reflect on what was in front of them and add their insights and input. We  wanted the area to be a free flow area that wasn’t booked up with meetings and would be  available for addition and reflection. There was no right or wrong addition. Everyone’s input  (from the team, and their advisors) was invited.     What was critically important for us was to get everything possible out on that white board  wall, so we could see how complex this was and to have the ability to address certain situations  quickly and responsively. A great part of this was realizing we had to constantly ask the same  questions to tweak and strengthen the entire ‘system’. We started off with a map I created to  get the conversation and mapping started. We decided to meet a minimum of two to three  times a week for two weeks to discuss how the mapping process revealed priorities that had to  be addressed as well as ongoing team design that would benefit future task forces. By the end  of that period, the wall was covered with many moving parts to flush out the critical criteria of  what would make a strong, healthy and resilient team as well as their support systems. At that  point we convened to decide what priorities we would address to get moving and chose three  to test.    Insight    What occurred for me was that a linear approach would never work in this critical, fast-paced  environment. Using the Visualization illustration ensured that the What’s True piece (similar to  the What is) revealed what everyone knew to be true at that time. It was the status quo.

Looking at What’s Needed identified gaps and what we weren’t aware of or paying attention to.  The What’s Available determined what resources i.e. time, people, resources etc. were  available so we could act sooner than later which, in turn, changed the What’s True piece and  so on. Living in those questions and bouncing back and forth between them, allowed us all to  do more of the “’What If’ we approached things in ‘this way’ or ‘first?” conversation”. Keeping  us in the questions allowed for expansive conversation and be able to test various approaches  to find the best solution for this design criteria. It also eliminated the, “We can’t do this”  response and kept the conversation generative.    Approach    An alternate approach would be to condense the process into one day; booking a large space to  map out all moving parts, cluster the ones that were similar and look at what emerged in the  process. Once we would do this, identify the themes, look at what we could test in a team  design within a certain period. This would address immediacy and the short timeline we had  available to us. As it wasn’t a priority, we would address ongoing, future task forces separately.    With this option we would use Mind Mapping exclusively to shorten the process, the  consultation and reduce options so we could test earlier.    Insight 2    Using Design Thinking is a brilliant way to give everyone a voice. It also elevated levels of  engagement and accountability. In my opinion, one of the best parts of this approach is shifting  a solution-based conversation to one of curiosity and learning. Testing ideas helped other  emerge and so on.

Challenge in Projects, by Antonio Hanson    Page 1

Challenge in Projects - Identify Root cause and enable department to work on improvements.

1. Challenge

Not aligned working process and understanding of responsibilities in projects.  Project stakeholders have no common understanding of the working process and  responsibilities of the assigned role. This is causing massive delay and unwanted discussions /  confusion in projects.

2. Selection

I selected the tool VISUALIZATION (Module 1) to easily enable the workshop participants to  draft, draw / sketch their view of the process.

In week 1, the 7 minute video “Visualization Tool”, shows that it is great to enable thinking in  a nonverbal way.  Quote:” The visualization is a really core component of the way that we communicate,  whether we're aware of it or not. When we're dealing with very complex problems, we're  actually enacting a different kind of problem solving that has to bring in more than just logic.”

3. Scope

Identify Root cause and enable the department to work on improvements.

4. Application

My approach is conducting workshops with all project stakeholders to gather their  understanding of the process, including the good sides and the pain points.  To be efficient I invite all stakeholders in groups owning the same role in projects. Each group  size should be limited to 4-6 participants.
