CHALLENGE

Miriam’s Field Operations organization needs to reduce the number of technicians in trucks that it  sends out into the field to assist customers with troubleshooting their television and broadband  issues.  Customers call into customer care call centers and chat online about their service issues.   Those calls are handled but representatives who follow detailed troubleshooting process flows  that ultimately generate trouble tickets that in turn dispatch technicians out to a customer’s home  to help troubleshoot and solve a customer’s problem.

There is ample cost in operating the call centers and ample cost to roll a truck and a highly  skilled technician out to a customer’s home.  If Miriam could reduce the number of  technician/truck rolls by giving customer options to solve the problem themselves or proactively  solve a customer’s problem before (s)he must call in for assistance could save Miriam millions of  dollars in operating costs.   It could also give customers a much better experience that does not  involve the customer having to wait at home during a four-hour appointment window for a  technician’s visit.

SELECTION

Using a mind map could help identify better ways for Miriam to solve its customers’ problems  before having to roll a technician/truck.  As Marion Moore mentioned in Module 3 of this course  (https://www.coursera.org/learn/uva-darden-design-thinking-innovation/lecture/lsFRa/mind- mapping-tool, looking at the situation through a “what is” lens by using a mind map can be very  helpful to understanding existing challenges and roadblocks that create customer problems in the  first place.  Having this knowledge will be critical for the next step, the “what if” phase of the  design thinking process that helps to identify how to modify the current situation for the better.    Given the process nature of Miriam customers calling into a center, workflows being used, then  trouble tickets being recorded, and finally dispatching technicians to troubleshoot, the mind map  seems like a good approach to help solve its technician/truck roll challenge.

APPLICATION

When applying the mind map to Miriam’s processes, I found the challenge to be overwhelming  and decided that it might be best to focus on a specific type of reason for a technician/truck roll.   I opted for a scenario about a broadband customer self-install kit.  This kit is sent out to  customers who order internet service, who want to install the equipment themselves.  Quite  often, something in the process breaks down and the customer is unable to complete the self- install.  When that happens, the customer must call into a call center for help and this frequently  requires a technician/truck roll to solve the problem.

In looking at the volume of calls into a call center, related to the customer self-install kit, I used a  mind map to draw out the various process steps a customer goes through during the self-install.   While there are instructions in the self-install kit, it became clear that many technician/truck rolls  are related to issues outside of the equipment in the kit (e.g., modem/router, cables).  I mapped  out the entire customer process from call in to the call customer to place the order for a self- install kit, to receipt of it, opening the contents, reviewing the instructions through to install.  I

noted potential pain points for the customer along the way, such as potential areas of confusion  or instructions that relied heavily on technical “jargon” that were intended for a non-technical  audience.

INSIGHT

The insight I had from mapping out all the steps a customer must go through to do the self- install, was that the information about which port to plug which cable into could be  misconstrued.  If a non-tech savvy customer was unable to determine an input vs. an output port  on their own, the instructions provided would be of no help.  My mind map showed a clear gap  in the installation process.  There were just too many options for a customer to use the cables to  connect the router.  This insight was  likely the source of customer confusion and a failed self- install which would lead to a call to the call center and a potential technician/truck roll.  This  exercise also helped me to see why the “what is” phase of design thinking is crucial.  It now  seems obvious to me that this step demonstrates the problem in a clearer light so potential  solutions in the “what if” phase that comes next can be addressed.

APPROACH

If I were to do this mind mapping exercise differently next time, I think I’d look more closely at  the workflows used by customer care representatives.  My mind map showed gaps in the clarity  of the instructions.  I think a care representative should be able to walk a customer through  connecting a modem/router with the right cables and ports such that a technician/truck would not  have to be dispatched.  There may be more value (e.g., greater cost savings opportunities) in  using mind mapping on the customer care representative workflows as opposed to the customer  instructions.

Application    Working in an agency that has client fluidity has multiple creative challenges, you are faced with  numerous creative blocks having to steer from one client to another. Reflection – Mind Mapping

Challenge

In my spare time I help the coach of a local Rugby club to improve the game of their youngsters’ team.  The target group consists of 25 kids in an age between 12 and 14 years of age. During last season this  team won only 1 game in a tournament (out of 20 games played) and this clearly brought frustration  and dissatisfaction in the young players. The team coach was worried that many kids would drop out  from the team and look for a different sport. The local club isn’t a very wealthy one, and their success  is founded on building senior players from within the club. Losing young players today has a high  impact on the future of the club and their senior team. Our challenge was to design a new way of  training kids, aimed to improve their game and make them stay with our club for long time.

Selection

In the What is? phase, we looked at the current reality and collected some statistics around errors  occurred during games (like ball handling, missed tackles, missed catches etc.). We also focused on  the errors occurred during the training sessions, and collected interviews with different kids (across  different clusters, like as an example: by position, by maturity level, by fitness level, …). These  interviews were aimed to highlight problems of the kids with different fundamentals of the game.  Along with a colleague, we then selected Mind Mapping tool in order to explore the data we collected  and to identify common threads. Through Mind Mapping we were able to identify some common  patterns in how kids learn sports (observation, listening to, emulation, …) and translate them into  design criteria for the future training sessions.

Application

We began by using some visuals to display the common mistakes. We invited the kids (our customers)  to review these common mistakes and identify the fundamentals connected to those mistakes.  Individually then, they matched fundamentals with a specific training situations that they had  perceived as “good stuff” in past training sessions. We then brought all observations back together  and identified labels or clusters of observations. Once completed the labeling, we moved into  transforming insights into design criteria for the future training sessions. This wasn’t a trivial task but  we managed to identify what was important with a couple of sessions of work.

Insights

It became immediately apparent that kids learn fundamentals in different ways, there is no “one size  fits all” in sport practice. Some kids learn sport fundamentals better through emulation of a famous  player that they see on TV, some other kids must hear a clear explanation of the exercise before they  attempt it, some must try it for themselves in a safe environment, before they can display it correctly.  Above all, we learned that the practice sessions must have fun elements (like challenges with rewards  and fees, …). In a nutshell, “training diversification” and “fun elements” were the 2 biggest takeaways.

Approach

Next time I would definitely select the same tool, as it is easy to review the findings as in a “art gallery”  (as portrayed by Rodriguez). One mistake that we initially made was to present common  mistakes done by specific kids in real situations. This put them on the spotlight and triggered a  defensive behavior. We had to correct this immediately and selected instead a generic representation  of common mistakes, to avoid making them too personal.

Ali Zarei Reflection – Learning launch

Challenge & Selection

I was appointed to assist the Management to get an IT project back to the track. The project aims to  deliver an IT tool to support financing activity for several business lines in many regions involving 43  countries. The project has been started 3 years ago, and by now, is entering a crisis mode as the team is  struggling to deliver and finalise the project. The costs are steadily growing, and the end date is  uncertain. The project partially delivered some functionalities. The end-users are not satisfied and are  reluctant to adopt the new tool, they keep using manual processes or existing tools that are supposed to  be decommissioned. My role is to identify and implement a solution to get out of this situation.

Based on the preliminary discussions with various stakeholders, it was obvious that the project suffers  from "tunnel effects" and end-users un-satisfaction, I decide to use the learning launch as it will bring  visibility to the users. They can see quickly what the tool looks like and they interact with IT team.

Application

The starting point was to identify the roots of the crisis, what is behind the "tunnel effect" and the un- satisfaction of users. Based on "what is" technics: first, I gathered all data available on the project  documentation. Second, I prepared 3 types of interviews forms, one for the project team, one for the  end-users (clients) and one for the management.

The "what is" phase allowed to find out the following root causes:

1- The requirements have been amended several times, the project team adjusted the roadmap

involving costs increase and planning extensions

2- The end users (clients) are not appropriately represented in the project governance, some

business lines are absent, so their needs are not captured

3- The tool reached a degree of complexity that any change requires significant time and money

Then, we organised an offsite (1 day) involving project team managers and end-user's representatives.  It was the first time in 3 years that all stakeholders are gathered. We discussed the main findings of the  previous phase and asked each stakeholder to envisage what will be the ideal tool for him. The main  outcomes:

(a) the end-users want visibility (no tunnel effect) and simplicity (break complexity)  (b) the project team wants stable requirements committed by all business lines

The decision was made to build a learning launch initiative in 2 months' time. The initiative was  conducted by a core representative team including IT, end users and operations. A set of common  requirements was established and committed. The objective was to implement a tool for financing files  validated at local level. To break complexity factors, the tool will serve 2 main functionalities:  documents storage and files status management.

The IT platform was replaced by an "on the shelf IT tool" to minimise customisation. The working mode  was also changed to involve Agile interactions and strong governance.

A business line present in 2 countries was chosen to use the new tool for their financing activity. They  were satisfied by the new tool. The users find the tool user friendly, they divide their file processing  time by 2 and they are able to know the financing file status with one click.

Insight & approach

Two elements are key in this approach, (1) gathering all stakeholders and making them discuss and share  the problems and the solutions, (2) adopting the learning launch showing concrete results reinsuring the  end-users and bringing confidence to IT team.

All these elements were used to build a case for change and propose the abandon of the old project and  start a new project with a roadmap of 12 months and a reasonable budget. The roadmap was based on  the scale up of the 2 main functionalities built in the learning launch, split in 2 waves and 2 deliveries  each 6 months. A pragmatic approach was introduced to manage perimeter changes: any add on should  be coupled with a take off a lower priority feature. So, the waves weight will remain stable to keep the  budget and planning on the track.

The case for change was validated by the high-level management and the new project was started by  scaling up the learning launch tool.

Reflection Assignment- Mind Mapping                                                                         By Margarita Bonilla      Challenge and Selection    The design tool, Mind Mapping, refers to extracting patterns and insights from all the data that we gather  during the ‘What-Is’ phase. This tool facilitates the journey from ‘What-is’ to ‘What-if’. I use this tool all  the time while working with data analytics projects like poverty prediction and examining customer  shopping preferences. It may seem counter-productive to try and make a mind map to extract meaning  from such large datasets, but it is actually very efficient.     Recently, I used this tool while working on a project for designing improvements to the healthcare offered  at local hospitals, as part of a summer course I completed at Francisco de Paula Santander University. The challenge was to conduct an  exhaustive study on the current scenario(What-is) and using this to suggest possible solutions and  strategies(What-if) to improve patient satisfaction and the overall quality of healthcare provided.     Application    Based on the data collected, we found that a greater number of patients were moving towards private  hospitals, despite the free healthcare offered at local clinics and hospitals. We decided to use design  thinking to solve this problem, so the first step was to dig deeper, narrowing down our vast amount of  data, to tailor our research in an ethnographic manner with a comparatively smaller sample set. A field  visit was organized to one of these local hospitals, where we interacted with around 25 patients. These  interactions were personalized and took place over the course of five days.     A common, unarticulated need that was showing up indirectly yet conspicuously through all these  conversations was the subconscious human need for trust and connection. In the local hospital we were  surveying, although the service was free, the patients had no control over which doctor would treat them.  Every time they went to the hospital, a different doctor would randomly be assigned to them. The  interactions would be too professional and dry, lacking the human touch. This is something we could not  figure out from the analytical method used to study our initial, vast dataset. There were other factors too  such as lack of automation and efficiency in the process of booking an appointment, patient waiting time  and bureaucracy that came up. Gathering all these advancements in our project made using design  thinking, we created a mind map to further examine the links between these factors, their relative  importance and to work on idea generation.     Insight and Approach    From the mind map created, we could clearly see that the lack of human connection and personalization  was the underlying cause of all the other drawbacks. We also added bubbles of possible solutions to the  mind map and traced these solutions to the problem they attempted to address. One such solution was  the introduction of a mobile application that would offer interactive features apart from automating  appointment bookings. However, the insights we derived from our ethnographic research using a small  sample set of people suggested that such a mobile application would only address the symptom without  solving the root cause of the problem. Moreover, further expanding the mind map to incorporate a cost- benefit analysis of a potential mobile application hinted that this solution was not economically

sustainable. Also, the charts that we generated from the original dataset showed that senior citizens made  up a considerable portion of the people in need of medical care. They would not be comfortable with such  a mobile application. Even if we assumed for a second that senior citizens would be well-versed with such  an app, it does not address the lack of connection and personalization, in fact, it makes the process even  more impersonal and dry.     We successfully concluded from our mind map that the entire healthcare scenario needs to be  restructured. We then came up with constructive solutions which were economically sustainable and  incremental yet effective. Assigning two doctors to a certain set of patients, which would encourage  greater familiarity and bonding in the doctor-patient relationship, for instance. Specialists could be  recommended, as required, but every patient must have a specific general practitioner(GP) assigned to  him or her. Receptionists and help-desk assistants must ease the appointment booking process by not  only setting up an appointment for the patients at the desired time but by placing a reminder call on the  day of the appointment, which further adds a personal touch.     Notice how we have used the design tool of journey mapping as well, apart from mind mapping, to  improve the quality of local healthcare in Cambridge, UK. Journey mapping, which refers to uncovering  unarticulated needs on the emotional side in order to create better value for people, coupled with the  potent tool of mind mapping, helped us to innovate for the benefit of patients. Leveraging my experience  with innovation and design thinking, coupled with the skills acquired from this course, I hope to work on  more such projects that enhance customer experience and create value.

Final Assignment – Design Thinking of Innovation- Maria Panagiotopoulou – Visualization

Challenge & selection

I  am a member of my organization’s  customer experience department. The company  defined a challenge: to significantly improve the experience of the new customer (the  customer who visits for the first time a branch of the organization's network) in order to  increase the market share and customer loyalty. In order to meet this challenge, a team of  12 members  was set up, involving executives from the Process Improvement Division, IT, HR  and other business departments. Since the challenge was wide, the team decided to apply  many of the principles and tools of design thinking for empathizing , such as observation in  branches, interviewing new customers & branch managers,  identification & observation of  extreme/ analogous users-industries   & form insights (discover what is).

The next step was to form and describe the insights, to conceptualize solutions  and ideate,  to explore  IT solutions that can improve customer experience, optimize current procedures   and of course to create and test our prototypes(describe what if)  . The visualization tool  that we used in order to create and then test our prototypes was the storyboards .This tool  was very helpful to achieve a shared understanding of our ideas, to agree to the core  assumptions that we wanted to test with our customers-users and to have something  concrete to show to the customers when we would addressing to them in order to test the  prototype . I will describe in detail the procedure we followed using the visualization tool in  the application section below.

Application

We decided to do the prototyping actions related to the three of the ten insights we have  identified.  For the activity, the group divided into smaller groups of four participants each representing  an idea for prototyping action   In order to make concrete our ideas we decided that each group  to use a poster size  white  paper  to design  a storyboard in which the members could simply draw a high level story,   which consisted of 4 to 6 pictures in order to describe the idea and the customer journey  related to that. The activity had to be completed within 10 minutes.  When the storyboards were ready each team presented the story to the members of the  other teams .Every member of the other team had to say 2 things that he liked in this story  and one that makes him wonder about something else, to write them  down in 3 post – it    and stick them to the relative picture.   For example in a storyboard of one team which described the story of  a new customer who  applied digitally through website for a financial service offered by the company, one  member of the other team said and wrote in post – it:  I like that the customer has the possibility for digital application anytime he prefers,  I like  that he could avoid the queues in the branches in order to be serviced by an officer for his  application (something that usually degrades the customer experience), I wonder if the  customer is not using digital ways in order to be serviced and prefers the human touch with  an employee.  Then every team had to take into consideration and maintain the feature which the other  teams liked and to find ways to redesign / clarify the features they have make some

members to wonder and in a new poster size white paper to design  the new, refined  storyboard. This process had to be repeated two more times before we go with the final  storyboard to the customer/user to test our prototype.   When the final storyboard was ready, each team had first to decide to the core assumption  related to the prototype that was necessary to be tested.  Then every team needed to find a user and make an appointment with him to show him the  storyboard (prototype) and experiment-test it - get feedback from the  customer-user by  making him open questions in order not to direct his answers , to give him the chance by this  way to express himself about what he  thinks, feels, says, does about the story, what he  likes, dislikes or suggests  in order to improve about the idea.  After this procedure, every team had to take into account all the things that emerged  through this experiment and to design a new even more refined storyboard, which had to  test it with another user.    We agreed to repeat this test 5 times trying to evolve our ideas and then the team had a  workshop in order to discuss, present  the final storyboards of each team and decided which  ideas considered viable  & feasible to deal with in order to significantly improve the new  customer’s experience. We managed to define what wows to the customer & what works.     Insight & Approach  What I have learned from conducting this exercise is  that the usage of a storyboard  – especially the final-refined storyboard that incorporates the feedback of the members of the  team & the customers feedback – is very significant for reinforcing the understanding of the  problem the group trying to solve.  But the aspect of the activity that has significant value is that the team during this process  shares insights and learning that emerge while they are trying to define the space of their  problem.  The storyboard gives the diverse group of members,   a focal point for discussion which gives  them the opportunity to share their perspectives and develop insights into potential root  causes of their problems.  While the team could use a narrative to describe their ideas ,and then after discussion to  rewrite and refine the narrative to describe the idea,  by using visualization tools such as  storyboards, managed to engage the logical & the creative side of their brains (and the  customers brain during the experiment). Unlike the narrative that can in each one's mind  create different images, the usage of simple sketch can help make our ideas more  understandable to someone else, and allows ideas to be heart and built upon.  By using simple storyboards to design prototypes we have proven to the company that it is  not necessary to invest a lot of time and resources in order to design and run an experiment  in order to learn about aspects of our   ideas. We understood that by using simple  visualization tools like storyboards,   we could conduct low risk experiments, at a minimal  cost with a safe audience, which are easy, quick to design & run and most important to be  generative and help the  teams to learn and grow the ideas. It think that it would be a good  idea next time to combine the storyboard with a simple role-play with the customer, in  order to have a more interactive and more vibrant experience during the experimentation.

Mind mapping is one of the most powerful tools in the design thinker's toolbox. Before moving to the  next phase, what if, we need to distill all that data into information and insights that can be easily  communicated. Mind Map is a graphical and pictorial illustration of the interrelated ideas for a common  goal or objective. It truly makes its mark for empowering imagination to produce new theme of ideas.  Mind Mapping drives people, with a multi-dimensional approach, to generate a consolidated and  concentric solution to the problem. We chose to create a training course for the design engineering(DE) personnel. We chose the Learning  Launch tool for this project. We used surveys and focus groups to determine the most appropriate  delivery method for the training. The data showed a preference for on online video training course  which could be viewed at the end users’ convenience.

The best way to provide this training is a one on one session where the Subject Matter Expert(SME) can  answer the individual design engineer’s question. This is not always convenient as the SME is not always  available to address the question to meet the individual’s need. The challenge was to present experience  based  knowledge  to  them  in  a  format  where  they  can  consume  the  training  using  the  latest  media  capabilities. We are in the online video generation, so a similar format was selected to ensure success.

ASSIGNMENT ON REFLECTION – LEARNING LAUNCH

As I advanced through this course, I came across many design thinking tools. But  the one that created a vital impact on my mindset was – Learning Launch.  Learning Launch is a carefully designed experiment designed to test the key  underlying value-generating assumptions of a potential new-growth initiative. The  attitude of learning overcomes the stigma associated with success or failure that  limits innovation and growth in many businesses.  As this particular tool is  specifically based on continuous improvement, it is able to identify the customer’s  unarticulated needs and cater to emotional sensations of the product experience.  It captures the emotional highs and lows in relation to the customer’s perception  of a new idea/product. Unlike the pilot study, used to evaluate the feasibility of  new methods and implementation of novel intervention, learning launch focuses  on continuous improvement through iterations.

Challenges that led to the selection of the tool

I am an academician and basically my workplace consists of my engineering  college campus. I work in the capacity of an HOD in the department of mechanical  engineering. The challenge was to detect the reason for absenteeism of students  from the college after the lunch breaks.

Now the reflection according to my perspective is that we, being an engineering  college are service providers of our students. In other words, it can be said that  we are offering a product of learning/knowledge to a fixed set of customers, i.e.   our students. Hence, in this particular context, our students are essentially our  customers.

It was sure that there was some dissatisfaction among the students, because of  which they were motivated to behave in a particular way. We and our team  members consistently observed that the students were not available for the  lecture and practical sessions arranged after recess time. We tried counseling the  students with positive and negative reinforcement techniques as well but this did  not work. Ultimately, we came to the conclusion that the problem was more

deep-rooted and we had to tackle the young impressionable minds  EMPATHETICALLY.

Inorder to accomplish this task, we formed a group of interested faculty  members, something that we call quality circles in “Total quality Management”  and tried to resolve our challenge with a very human-centric approach.

Our college timings are from 8:45 am to 3 pm. We extended our search beyond  the college campus. We started keeping tracks of groups of students from the  nearby centres of commute like bus stops and railway stations. Going beyond the  campus and making observations led us to the conclusion that there was a lot of  students, almost 1/4th of the entire college strength belonging to all semesters  who willingly chose not to enter the college campus at all. We formed a special  team of faculty members to first observe and understand what were their  activities are. We also tried to understand the influences of peer behavior on the  student groups.

For our target audience, we had to figure out the behavior trends exhibited by  each one of them. Through careful analysis and observation, we followed first a  few most notorious ones, representative of the entire sample and then the whole  lot. By being friends with them and through ethnographic surveys and open- ended questions, we inferred that the students were not interested to attend the  practical sessions of the otherwise dull, boring and uninspiring faculty members.  Also more than 50% lot was under the influence of their peers.

We also concluded that the intrinsic motivation not to learn and the extrinsic  motivation to escape from the college campus had led many students to take up  substance abuse like smoking and tobacco consumption. We had to involve the  parents of such students in the counseling process and be cognizant with the  deeper psychologies of the teenagers.

So basically, we had to make changes in the system itself to make it more  acceptable to our set of target customers, in this case our students.

Sneha Santu

Example Reflection – Learning Launch

Challenge    I am the CEO of a local newspaper in a small city and want to increase the listing advertisement revenue  of the newspaper. This task is a challenging task because local consumers in a small city nowadays are  putting up their ads or listings in a bigger online listing websites such as https://hernandez.com/exploremain.html or  https://www.roman.info/list/appindex.html (these are just fake names to illustrate concept) and generate far more responses or get  attention. So, my team and I have to develop a new advertising product for our newspaper to increase  advertising revenue. We made a design thinking workshop and come up with the following ideas with  “What if questions”:

-  What if we make partnerships with those digital advertising websites like https://hernandez.com/exploremain.html or  https://www.roman.info/list/appindex.html, to extend our newspaper’s reach?

-  What if we utilize our newspaper’s ad salesforce or relationships with our local consumers to  bring more advertisers to those websites and ask for a revenue/value share from those websites  in return?

-  What if we find ways to reach out to less tech savvy consumers of our newspaper who are not  able to put their advertisements to those websites themselves?

-  What if we offer a new ad service, with these partnerships, to local consumers that, if they place  their advertisement to my newspaper, we will also publish the same ad on those websites with a  seamless and convenient way?

Selection  Since as it is described in the lecture by Kevin Dietrich “lots of ideas: what is next?”, we have lots of  ideas too and we need to do a learning launch to test these ideas to find out which ones are worth  putting into action. Again, as described in that lecture, we will quickly engage with stakeholders and test  these questions, assumptions.    Application    As the first step, we need to create hypotheses. Our hypotheses would be:

Storytelling for adult education

Paola Romano

Challenge & Selection I

I work as leader of an information technology team, training adults. I have a team of young instructors who are very technologically skilled. On many occasions, I have used storytelling as a way of bringing technology to be used during the day-to-day life of our students, who must use it in their daily professional work.

Many of our students are employees in large companies with middle and senior management positions, who are dealing with the way they work through new technological platforms.

When it is working with young teachers and students are sometimes twice their ages, students feel fear of learning new technologies, the use of storytelling facilitates the creation of bonds of trust and empathy.

Application

With groups of older students, small groups, usually they do not want to participate or ask questions about the use of Google Workspace applications, for example, I tell the story of a manager of a company in which we carry out a training plan for the use of these technological tools.

The manager was an older man from middle management who in the class on using Workspace showed a negative position regarding the use of these ofﬁce applications, did not perform the exercises and was always on the defensive.

After the group training, he approached the trainers' room and he asked for help to explain the basic concepts of using Workspace. I spoke to him and noticed that his fear was being vulnerable to other managers if he asked questions. In his words, being the oldest in the company, he was a benchmark for others and because he was the oldest, technology was not his strong point.

In order to achieve empathy and the adults decrease his fears about learning, the use of a new technology, I told him my own story: A person with whom for 20 years I had handled different ofﬁce automation applications and 4 years ago when he entered the start up where he worked They gave me a couple of hours of training and told me "well for tomorrow we need you to build a presentation but it can't be in powerpoint, you must use Google slides, if you have any questions look for the answers on the internet or ask your colleagues". At ﬁrst I had a lot of fears about whether I would be able to learn as fast as the rest of the people in the ofﬁce (largely millennials). Over time I have discovered that it is worth making a

mistake at the beginning, asking others and using self-learning resources to adapt to the use of new technologies.

Being open minded to learn keeps us encouraged in organizations and a leader who is capable of learning and accompanying the learning of the people in his charge is highly appreciated by his work team.

With this story I managed to calm down this manager and agree that one of the young coaches will explain the basics of using Workspace to answer his questions.

As time went by, this manager became enthusiastic about collaborative work with Workspace and even took his colleagues to the teachers' lounge and encouraged them to seek the answers to their questions about the technology platform.

Insight & Approach

With the use of stories like these, my team's coaches and I have made several advances in training on the utilization of information technology in organizations, including:

● Breaking down the resistance to change produced by the use of

technology among old people.

● Establish a climate of openness and empathy for the questions of those attending the training sessions.

● Show with examples how we can all work on our self-learning.

● Change the perspective of error in learning as an opportunity to advance knowledge.

In summary, the use of a tool such as Storytelling has facilitated the work of trainers and has allowed an easier approach to technology by our students.

Reflection: Learning Launch

Challenge:

How do we drive the adoption and use of self-service on digital channels like Apps and Bots to reduce  calls to our contact centre and still ensure that customer satisfaction measured by a high NPS (Net  Promoter Score) is attained?

My team and I faced that question as we looked to increase the penetration and usage of digital  channels to self-serve to reduce the number of inbound calls to the call centre.

As a team, we have been introducing new channels over the past few years and despite the growth in  these channels, we needed to increase the usage and ability of the customers to resolve their issues by  themselves without having to call or contact a live agent by introducing a chat bot.

The use of chat bots within our market was not that common and very few corporates had adopted this  as a means to serve customers. We therefore needed to do something different to get customers  engaged and to use the chat bot to resolve the issues especially for simple and repetitive queries.

The current penetration stood at 40%, we needed to get this to 60% within a period of one year. We felt  this was a high target but we knew we could do it- if we asked the right questions and got the right  solution together with our customers.

Selection:

Having reviewed the different tools, we chose to go with the Learning Launch, as the purpose was to  learn and then improve through running experiments and gathering insights and feedback from real  customers.  The learning launch gave us an opportunity to test, learn and improve on the chat bot  service so we could scale it up to drive engagement and usage with the customers.

Application:

We started the process by first developing a working prototype accessible to customers on an  application they already use to minimize any barriers to them testing the chat bot service.

As the team was already working in agile, we were able to develop this within a couple of sprints and  ensured the integrations to internal systems were working well.

For the first phase of the learning launch, we engaged a number of customers using our online platforms  and informed them we were testing the chat bot service and needed them to give us feedback and  suggestions on services and features they wanted. We ran this for a period of 3 weeks and collected the  feedback both online and within the bot.

After reviewing the feedback from the users and suggestions on what we could do to improve the  service, we spent some more time in development and worked on the quick wins we identified from the  insights and road mapped the items that were more complex and required more time to integrate.

We then took an updated prototype to the customers and observed usage of some of the new features  as well as received additional feedback and this helped firm up the preferred customer journey and  method to engage with the customers using the chat bot before the full launch with a more aggressive  Go to Market campaign.

Insight:

From the learning launch model, we learnt the need to let go of some of the things we thought would  work and was relevant to us but was not that relevant to the customer. We also got additional insights  on the importance of personalization where the customers want the bot to greet them using their own  names and to have additional features that are not necessarily linked to self-service. This insight helped  us introduce brainteasers and riddles to the bot and increased the relatability with especially the  younger users who are the majority of the customers using digital platforms.

These insights together with the others picked during the learning launch phases really helped us launch  a chat bot that stood out from the other corporates and enabled us to achieve the desired growth in  penetration.

Reviewing the suggestions and feedback continuously from the customers and acting on it is necessary  for the long-term success of any product.

Approach:

From the experience we had as a team and a better understanding of Design Thinking through  additional training, we would still use the Learning Launch tool as this enables us to test a hypothesis,  experiment and pick learnings that will create more value.

We would however refine the questions we were asking to get deeper and better insights that would  enable us develop more innovative features that will drive repeat use by the customers and higher  engagement as we meet the business objective to increase self-service usage.

1.  Challenge

Story telling is a very powerful tool which I use all the time.  As a professional I work in a  highly complex and challenging environment, being responsible for sales teams, engineering  teams, support teams as well as administratively functional teams providing our customer  base with solutions in the engineering space, through Industrial Digital Transformation.

I have found that when my management team has decided and agreed on a new strategy  (for example X) with a end-goal to increase customer satisfaction (where every single person  in the organisation can contribute either positively or negatively towards customer  satisfaction ratings, the best way to get a point over to all, irrelevant to where you fit into the  organisation, is through story telling.  Story telling provides the means to an end.

2.  Selection

One of the recent interactions which was spurred by story telling, was the required to  become ISO (quality certified) as a company.  On a managerial level we have decided that in  order to become more qualified for specific projects, we would require an ISO certification  and would need to make such investment.  However, there were some internal personnel  who did not share the same positivity around ISO (negative mindset).

I have decided to utilise a story telling method to deal with individuals and groups internally  to resolve the issue.

3.  Application

It was clear which internal “clicks”, groups and individuals were against the ISO certification  initiative.  Having been through an ISO initiative as part of another organization in a previous  role, I have understood the requirements and the importance of change management.

Individual sessions with groups and specific individuals were scheduled, where the “story”  was presented, based on hard data (from previous experience and market analysis), had  facts as well as recommendations – all gelled into a story of future vision for the organisation.

4.  Insight

Once the story telling was in place, the most common kick-back and element opposed from  all was the fact that ISO certification was seen as a “paperwork” exercise, and most people  was against paperwork.  Once the story has highlighted this fact, it was clear that if one could  find a way to eliminate the implementation of any paper-trails as part of implementation, the  complete buy in would be achieved by everyone.

Our management team has gone back to the drawing board and agreed that a no-paper  certification methodology will be implemented.  Story telling spurred design thinking for  business innovation in this case, to understand the “What Is” and “What If” stages, and  based on the what-if (i.e. no paper) we have successfully implemented a no-paper (system  based) ISO/quality management system.

5.  Approach

I believe that story telling creates the framework and basis for communicating a desired end- state to staff (and clients), but also provides the platform for interaction and trust for internal  staff to provide valuable insight on “what is” and “what if” questions, as part of the design  thinking methodology.

I will use story telling as a toolset/skill again and again.

Reflection – Learning Launch

Challenge      My name is Karen Gonzalez. I am ICT Director of a school in South Africa. Some fifteen years ago I co- wrote some software to manage the internal venue bookings at our school. Being a software  developer was and is still not part of my role at the school, but integrating technology into the  curriculum and empowering staff and children to become responsible and capable adults in a  technology rich world, certainly is. We developed the software because there was nothing  commercially available at that stage that suited our needs and pocket. Another reason was that, in  those early years, when we were trying to get staff to use technology to improve the learning and  teaching experience, we reasoned that giving teachers (and administrators) tools to do their daily jobs  would improve literacy and have positive educational spin offs. The software has lived on and is used  extensively by an increasing number of people and for more than the original, quite simplistic,  purpose. The software in function and form is very much end of life but the tool(s) is so interwoven in  the fabric of how we manage events, sports practices, and classroom activities that we simply can’t  manage without it for any time at all. The software is buggy and is written in a language that is no  longer supported. Our challenge is to seamlessly replace the software with something that will meet  the new needs of the school, without disrupting daily activities, on a very tight budget and at the  same time win the buy in of the various managers who will very likely need to change their process.    The project scope includes the marketing departments and admin, grounds and teaching staff across  our three campuses, each of whom are responsible for different and varying components within the  current booking system model; it particularly includes the academic staff who quickly and easily want  to book venues (including equipment and resources) for sport and teaching, with minimal fuss and  effort.     The project is limited to internal resources (i.e. budget and employee time) and there is no official  development team available. There is some in-house expertise with database and HTML knowledge  but the constraints of time and the competing needs of other educational demands is a challenge.     All systems in the school synchronise with active directory (which means resources, venues and  groups of people are seamlessly available for selection / contact) and a challenge is to offer a similar  feature in a replacement system. Not doing so would present overhead issues in terms of  management.     The IT team consists of the ICT Director, an ICT integrator, an ICT admin support person and the  Computer Studies teacher. The IT team is tasked with rolling out a replacement solution virtually  immediately as the current solution is causing frustrations. The school prioritises budget for  educational endeavours and simply doesn’t have budget to spend on an expensive commercial  solution. The budget is very much capped (non profit school)  and creativity is needed to deploy the  most effective tools within the proportional amount available for software.    Because of the urgency there is pressure to simply replace the current solution without a full  investigation into what is actually needed and why.

Selection    We decided to use the learning launch tool to deliver NOT a final product but a solution in the  making.    The design thinking process helped us understand expectations and needs. We chatted to staff and  students and used forms to gain further insights. We observed how staff were using the current  system and tried to journey map a wide variety of situations. We agreed as a team to put aside  discussions about solutions in the early stages and simply gathered as much information as we could.     What followed thereafter were some brainstorming sessions. The team invited a diverse range of  staff to join in and dream about what would be ideal in terms of managing bookings and the  brainstorming included, not only the booking itself but the event and after event activities too. We  sorted and organized our findings and from that came up with some design criteria, basic  functionality without which the staff would not be able to function. We also came up with a variety of  other needs/wants/wow factors that our staff had not really spoken of but that we surmised were  causing problems or frustrations or would perhaps add value. For example, when booking during an  exam time, the squash courts should only be available after teaching hours from a noise perspective;  another insight was that the teaching day doesn’t necessarily operate in typical calendar type time  slots and staff may want a view of their timetable when trying to book a teaching venue, which they  would think of for example as period 3, rather 10.05 am.     Another insight / assumption that emerged was that the different types of bookings could be  differentiated. The ‘booking type’ was identified as one of a possible three types

1. Teaching venue  2. Sporting venue  3. Pavilion, hall, theatre, chapel

The team then looked at free / inexpensive technology tools or solutions that could be adapted in  creative ways to meet the criteria and decided to prototype solutions for each of the three types.  We had closely observed the students and staff to uncover their unmet needs and used the  learning launch tool to work as a team through iterative cycles of live experimentation;  prototyping to test our assumptions, discovering and learning from feedback, refining and  relaunching the new prototype.     We began experimenting with existing software – Wordpress; Office 365 Cloud calendars and  HTML as well as free web software (and some paid demo software). We launched a number of  different prototypes to quickly test whether what we thought the staff wanted would make a  positive difference to how they worked.     Application      Our staff had a specific need; they wanted to be able to book venues. Several design ideas met that  need better than the current alternative because the process involved in booking one sort of venue  was very different from the process involved in booking another sort. All sorts of ‘Cloud’ features  offering anytime, anywhere access were also possible. Furthermore, existing controls were frustrating

for the staff and students; lack of control in management for more ‘public’ venues was also an issue.    Initially we focused on frustrations around booking the group venues in our resource centre. Students  traditionally made the bookings via their teacher but had no way of seeing which rooms were  available via the resource centre website, a place they would regularly visit to find research and other  material. We wanted to test our assumption (quickly and cheaply) that students wanted to be able to  book directly, in their current work space and that they would respect each others’ access to a venue  and not pre-book all venues in a way that excluded others from having a fair chance. Our resource  director who was frustrated by the current system agreed to give this a ‘go’.     We committed as a team to six things

1. Roll out a prototype within one week   2. Choose a particularly difficult student year group as they would push the boundaries and be

hard task masters

3. Focus on the assumptions of needs/wants   4. Question our own bias  5. Listen to feedback  6. Adapt, refine and redeploy as we worked

We met every day as a team for an hour to share our progress and review where we were at. We built  a web interface that made use of existing Office 365 calendars that we could overlay with the school  timetable and other features. There were buttons on the page that didn’t yet do what was ultimately  intended but gave the students and staff sufficient feedback. Feedback was immediate (a comment  button on the page), coupled with lots of interaction with the students and staff. Our first few  iterations of the prototype were very much work in progress but felt real.    Then team observed how the staff and students engaged with the software and were easily and  quickly able to test the assumptions about where responsibility could lie, where to host the solution  and how the features and screen should be arranged to best accommodate the requirements. The  team also spoke to boys and staff to find out if

1. Their needs had been met  2. They were ‘wowed’  3. What problems they could anticipate i.e. what could the pitfalls be (and boy did the students

come up with some curved balls!)

In this way, the team were able to quickly and iteratively roll out and test alternative suggestions /  improvements and adapt the solution on the fly. The outcome has exceeded expectations and work  will follow on tackling the other booking types in a similar way.    Insights    Involving the staff and students in the design of a new system had three positive spin offs.  Staff and students

1. were accommodating of mistakes and less frustrated with the current booking issues   2. made good (and bad) suggestions and those not accommodated are recorded for future

releases

3. have taken ownership of the process and collaborate to make it work

The IT team had felt responsible for the existing software issues but had been powerless to resolve  them. Through the design process they better understood the staff and students’ needs and were  more patient with human errors in the existing system, which will continues to operate in parallel  until all the features have been met in the new solution.     The team used data from feedback to resolve conflicts and get buy in a democratic way. There  certainly were challenges and frustrations. Real effort needed to go in to make sure that people felt  that they had been heard.    The speed of deployment was positive. Immediate feedback was hugely rewarding and in a ‘live’ test  even criticism felt constructive and was well received. The team were unanimous in preferring to  know virtually immediately whether they were going down the right road in terms of meeting needs.    The diversity of the group, who don’t normally collaborate in this sort of way, added huge value. The  management overhead on staff was reduced and the students were given a new responsibility within  a safe space.     Approach    Having identified our assumptions the iterative learning launch cycle tested these assumptions in a far  more satisfactory way than the traditional approach of delivering a solution that may/may not meet  expectations.  The below illustration attempts to describe the somewhat linear and limited approach  to a problem versus the more chaotic but yet more effective design thinking approach. We are  presently modelling design thinking principles in our planning for other component to resource  management and other projects.        An illustration of old approach      vs    New Approach

Mind Mapping

Piotr Czarnecka

Challenge

At the Institute of Cardiology at my University Hospital we are challenge to provide the best care for  patients that undergone Percutaneous Coronary Interventions (e.g., stent implementation). To  accomplish our task we need to have a deep understanding of patients’ lifestyle choices, biochemistry  processes, genetic profiles, and other determinants of disease-free survival. Much is already known on  the factors influencing survival however to establish better treatment schemes further hypotheses  must be generated and tested in clinical research. The process of generating hypotheses on relation  between survival and other seemingly uncorrelated actors from different research fields (e.g.,  behavioural studies, work activity)  is particularly challenging.

Selection

A Mind Mapping technique was chosen as a tool to organise the knowledge across various science  disciplines and to show existing relationships between different aspects of patients’ wellbeing and  health. A Mind Mapping tool was chosen because it is one of the most effective way of organising  knowledge that inspires creativity. It is constructed as a diagram of relationships leading from one main  concept to another – potentially providing indirect connections between seemingly unrelated ideas.  The concepts in our applications are the health aspects with the potential of being analysed as factors  indirectly influencing survival. The Mind Mapping technique was discussed in Week 3 of the class. it is  important to recognize, that the “mind” is associated with the patient who can be interpreted as a  customer in traditional design thinking approach.

Application

A highly interdisciplinary team of scientists, researchers and clinicians was put together to provide  insights from different disciplines. During on-site meeting, those experts discussed different aspects of  patient health and wellbeing in the context of treatment after Percutaneous Coronary Interventions.  The Mind Maps were created by the meeting moderator. Big white board with markers was used as  well as pieces of paper and magnets with construct mind maps during the meeting.

Insight

This process continued over several meetings produced number of mind maps of different ideas  connected by few other concepts. We have discovered few factors that could have hypothetical  influence on survival that have not been studied before. Those insights are planned to be tested during  clinical research.

We have learned that quality of sleep can affect blood coagulation and levels of inflammation. Also  both coagulation and inflammation can affect patients’ outcome after Percutaneous Coronary  Interventions. However direct influence of quality of sleep on survival of patients after the intervention  and the potential mechanism of such an influence have not yet been studies and have a potential for  development of further treatment and guidelines.

Approach

The use of Ming Mapping to our challenge was very successful, however using a white board with  markers was difficult due to huge number of concepts and great level of details. Documentation of  created Mind Maps was done using photos which made difficult to work with them in the future.

Next time we will implement software to create Mind Maps which will eliminate need for other  documentation methods. Good solution could be to use online applications like www.mindmup.com  to enhance collaboration.

1. Challenge and selection: Describe your challenge, including all relevant

information.

I work for a municipality in the Netherlands. Like many cities in the world, the  municipality is trying to develop to a smart city (we prefer to call it smart  society because it is all about the people and businesses and not about  techniques)). A few years ago, I was working on a project called “smart  lighting”. Basically, this project was about upgrading our public lighting system  to a smart and interconnected lighting grid which serves as a carrier for  innovative services. At a certain stage of the project we came across questions  on ownership of data processed by the sensors of the public smart light grid.  Should we treat it as open data that belongs to the public or as proprietary data  that only belongs to the private company? The private company we talked with  experienced a lot of uncertainty when data should be treated as open data. They  thought that this would have a negative impact on their business model, which  was based on selling of data. At some stage of the project we had endless  discussions on legal aspects of ownership of data. This led to a serious deadlock  of the project. We decided to take a step back and look at the vision on open  data and open innovation. We decided to “re-scope” (test) this vision: which  beliefs did we have to be tested? Where are our blind spots? I choose the method  of storytelling for this re-scoping of the project.

2. Application: Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge

(e.g., what you did and how the tool was applied effectively or ineffectively).

We decided not only to involve people who were directly involved in the  project. We also invited outsiders. The audience I had to speak to was very  broad: there were business developers, light architects, lawyers, policymakers  and financial experts. I decided that if I wanted to create an impact I should  present a real-life case which really impressed me. I started by putting the next  question to the table “Who owns the data?” Then I presented some hard facts  on the growth of data. I asked the audience, how many times you should fold a  piece of paper with a thickness of 2 cm’s to bridge the distance to the moon? I  did this to express that tremendous growth of data with figures you can’t  imagine. There is an abundance of data and it is ubiquitous like air (and nobody  asks the question: “who owns the air?”). Then I presented this real-life story. It  is about a girl who, at the age of 17, was confronted with breast cancer in her  family. The diagnosis of breast cancer can be very painful and sometimes even  inaccurate. This 17-year-old girl just finished classes on coding (writing  computer algorithms). She decided to write an algorithm that could detect  breast cancer. She used data on cellular characteristics from the internet and  research institutions (open data). She managed to write a prototype that was  really powerful and promising. It turned out that her algorithm was pretty

accurate when it came to predicting breast cancer. She now studies at a  university where she is perfecting this algorithm. I then asked the audience  what they think would have happened if the data feeding her algorithm was  monopolized by a few research institutions or companies. And I asked the  audience the question on what level the real value was added: at the level of  data or at the level of the intellectual capital of this 17-years old girl? I then I  answered the question on ownership of data: this question is not relevant: the  value of data is in the flow not in the source!”

3. Insight: Describe the insight you gained from applying the tool you selected to

your challenge (e.g., how an insight affected your thinking about the challenge  and about design thinking more broadly).

The most important insight was that storytelling led to a meaningful discussion  on possible business cases on open data. We decided not to ask the “boring”  legal question on ownership of data anymore. Another insight I got is that, like  Einstein said, a problem can’t be solved in the context in which it arose. We  therefore took the problem out of its context and asked outsiders to help us  unlocking the deadlock, by re-scoping (testing) our vision on data (using the  story).

4. Approach: Describe what you might do differently next time -- applying the

same tool you selected or a different one -- and the reason(s) why.

The first thing I would do different is obvious: focus on aligning mutual  interests. Telling a meaningful story can be helpful by defining problem field  (extensive legal discussions on ownership of data) and solution field (finding  new business cases). In our case we came in the end to the conclusion that  problem and solution were actually interconnected. We could have saved  ourselves time if we recognized this at an earlier stage of the project.

Yu Wang

Challenge

In the payments industry, one of the challenges is how we can help our merchants increase their  sales through higher conversion rates and basket sizes. This could be via various ways to generate  demand such as promotions, marketing, etc.

Selection

As mentioned in the lectures, ideas are many and usually not good. Hence, I needed a way to be able  to sieve out the good ideas from the bad. In my organization, there are many stakeholders with  varying priorities and needs and allowing a diverse group of stakeholders to discuss and be non- biased is very important to prevent group think. As a result, I have decided to select the learning  launch tool from module 4.

Application

I start the process by gathering all stakeholders into a large Zoom meeting (this would be a large  meeting room during pre-Covid days) to brainstorm. After brainstorming, everyone will write their  ideas on a Google Sheet and we will try to cluster the ideas into certain categories (or business  concepts).

Once we have identified these business concepts, the next step is to identify the hypothesis of the  concept. For example, providing promotions will help increase traffic and basket sizes. Next, we will  need to identify the key assumptions that will make this hypothesis work. In this case, it could be  that brands must be willing to fund or co-fund the amount.

Once we have identified the key assumptions, it is time to create an experiment to test it. I will first  need to find the key stakeholders who will be involved, for example, sales to reach out to the  brands, marketing, and operations to configure the promotions, and analytics to track the  performance before and after the test. Ideally, this experiment should be carried out on about 5 to  10 merchants during a non-sales period to prevent any skewing of sales data.

After the experiments are completed and collated. the team can decide if they are satisfactory and if  we should go ahead or pivot to another solution.

Insight

What I have learned from this tool is that it helps reduce confirmation bias and group think. This  allows ideas from less senior and vocal individuals to be surfaced to the rest of the team. Often, in  most organizations, when ideas are suggested by a more senior person, people are less likely to  disagree and tend to agree and this can be dangerous.

Through this tool, we can better brainstorm and select ideas on a more pragmatic and non-biased  approach. Through experimentation, it also allows the organization to test and fail fast before  spending too much time on development.

Approach

If I do it again, I will try to incorporate the other tools discussed in the course such as visualisation,  storytelling and mind mapping to better enhance the design thinking process. For example,  visualisation of the problem will help the team better identify the issue and could lead to better  brainstorming of ideas.

cables, and waited for sound. None came. As he headed back to work from lunch, I set to work

on conquering my system. I did not want to experience the failure I did three years ago, and I

was determined to be successful. Before immediately jumping to frustration, I decided to try the

design thinking approach because I needed a creative, systematic approach to a challenging

problem that I was facing.

Selection

After I decided to try applying the tools of design thinking to this problem, I had to

choose where I would start. Clearly you start at the beginning, but that goes without saying. I

decided to start my process with the visualization tool. Being able to see the problem would

allow me to explore the solutions. As Katia Rania presents, visualization is a design tool

Design Thinking: Final Assignment    Rhiannon Karim

that is used throughout the entire process; from start to finish. The visualization tool forced me to

think differently, as I was using the right side of my brain (instead of the left). Not only was it

important that I define my problem, but it was also important that, as I moved through the design

thinking process, I continued to utilize the visualization tool. The visualization tool can be

applied to the other design tools discussed in this course, thus carrying me throughout the entire

process. Visualization also allows the problem-solver to think in a nonverbal way. Too often I

think in a linear, verbal manner; however, by using visualization, I could think in a more global,

creative manner. I selected visualization because it suggests I make a map or draw a picture of

my problem. I wanted to be able to utilize this map in the future if I needed it, so I felt like I was

killing two birds with one stone. The visualization tool suggested that I move through stages of

exploration, pattern finding, ideation, prototyping, and scaling. Visualizing was much easier to

begin with than physically changing the set-up of my stereo system because that required me to

move my equipment, as well as reconnect cables, potentially cut new cables, and even buy new

cables. I started with visualization because, without this process, I was looking at increasing my

time and cost with a high probability of failure.

Application

By using the right side of my brain, I was not focused on the step-by-step approach an

individual generally focuses on while installing equipment. Rather, the visualization tool helped

me explore the challenge of my stereo system, which enabled me to find a pattern. The pattern I

found was mostly that my boyfriend and I had used the same approach at least three times to no

avail. I believe there is a saying that goes, “repeating the same actions and expecting a different

outcome is the definition of insanity”. I was getting close to insanity before I consciously

decided to visualize. Once I had discovered this pattern, I was able make my problem tangible

and concrete. I drew a photo of the back of my receiver, television, and speakers. I was working

with the what is. I wanted to know exactly what is working, what is not working, and what could

be changed. I turned the receiver on to an FM radio, pulled off the front of my speakers, and

checked to see if my handmade copper wiring was still working. To my great triumph, it was

working. That meant that either the optical cord was not working or else it was an issue with the

receiver. I had another optical cord, so why not try it? Well, this cord was too short. So, I

unplugged my speakers, moved my receiver to a place I thought the cord could reach, and I re-

connected everything. The cord still did not reach. Even though I had made a conscious effort to

Design Thinking: Final Assignment    Rhiannon Karim

work in terms of design thinking, I slipped back into linear thinking immediately after I had

success with visualization. I found out the answer to the what is, and immediately went to what

works. Needless to say, it did not work. I returned to the drawing, or should I say visualization,

board.

My old optical cord has a red light indicating it worked, so why was I so fixated on the

cord not working? I had narrowed my problem too much. It was time to think of the what if. I

began to develop some concepts of the problem while looking at my maps. I knew the cords

were working, as well as the receiver, because I had tested them. I also knew my television

worked. Then it hit me, as I broadened my problem to the television, which I had dismissed

earlier because I knew it was a separate entity that was only connected to the stereo, I realized

the problem could be my television, not my stereo. I was not keen on moving shelves and heavy

speakers again nor purchase a new system to test a theory, so you could say I skipped the

prototyping step (aka what wows) and went straight to scaling (aka what works). I went into my

television menu and changed my sound settings. It worked! I cannot say that I was even

surprised because I had calculated the outcome during my concept development in the what if

stage.

Insight

I like to think of this as a thought experiment turned prototype to the use of design

thinking in my life. I was hesitant to try an approach I had never used before when I was alone

and out of my area of expertise, but I was comforted knowing that my potential failure would not

affect others because I was in a controlled space and I was alone. Thinking back to the course, I

started this thought experiment with the mindset of George, under the belief I was of the mindset

of Geoff. After I started applying what I learned, I was able to achieve the mindset of Geoff, but

it took me some time. I even slipped into the mindset of George a few times during the process. I

am so accustomed to working with a narrow mindset that it is easy to fall into the habit. My

boyfriend can attest to when I was slipping into a narrow mindset because he bore the brunt of

my attitude when my successes depreciated and my frustration multiplied. Without using design

thinking, I can easily say that I would have either re-wired my speakers unnecessarily or paid an

expert to discover my problem. Had I taken that route, I would have lost time, money, and

valuable knowledge about problem-solving and my speakers. Using visualization made my

problem coherent and concrete. Before I created a map, I was flying blind and trying various

Design Thinking: Final Assignment    Rhiannon Karim

methods of the same strategy. The problem felt as if it were beyond my scope of knowledge and

skills. Ironically, by broadening the problem, I was able to identify specific, targeted solutions

that were within my realm of knowledge. Ultimately, by broadening my thinking of the problem,

I not only found a simple solution, but I was also able to discover my competencies.

Approach

One thing I have ensured I did, was to keep my maps in order to help me in the future should

Design Thinking for Innovation  Learning Launch Reflection  Ravneet Williams  May 5, 2018

Challenge

I have worked as a Senior Project Manager in the engineering and construction industry for over fifteen  years. Most recently, my work has been managing large scale façade projects for skyscrapers and large- scale medical or commercial campuses. A typical project budget would average around $40M with a  project duration of roughly eighteen months. The three key phases of a project would, in order, include  1) design engineering (where our engineers would turn the architect’s vision into hundreds of detail  drawings), 2) production (where the detail drawings would be converted so the product could be  fabricated and assembled at one of our production facilities), and 3) field installation (where the  assembled product would be installed onto the building). A near constant that occurs once a project team  has been assembled is that many of the team members across departments have not worked together  before. Also, the mindset of individuals from each department is different simply because their job duties  are vastly diverse. The monetary scale of a given project, the risk that comes with such a long project  duration, and the possible issues within the project team makes, among many other things, the challenge  of fostering and constantly improving efficient communication of the utmost importance. For this  assignment, I am going to reflect on such a design thinking challenge I encountered while managing a 4- building biotech campus south of San Francisco, California.

Selection

After taking this course, I realized that I was using the “learning launch” tool on a regular basis. For the  reflection I am going to describe a situation where I encountered an appreciable communication challenge  at the forefront of a project. As conveyed in Week 4, particularly in Ed Hesse’s “Learning Launch Tool”  video, a learning launch is essentially a quick-fire experiment performed when trying to flesh out “What  Works?”.

Application

I held a series of weekly meetings that included a check-in meeting with key stakeholders from each of  the three key departments. In this meeting we would attempt to identify and analyze the structure of the  project and brainstorm solutions to further improve its process, as well as returns on team member  commitments. After taking this course, I realized this was essentially an ongoing general analysis of “What  Is?” and What If?” At one of the first of these meetings for the San Francisco project, I encountered a  significant disconnect between project team members from each of the different key departments. I met  with team members in private in order to figure out how to right the ship. It came to light that the  disconnect was derived from the fact that the majority of project team members lacked knowledge about  the other departments and how they operated.  For example, the structural engineers had been working  in their field for several years but had never visited a production facility or live construction site.

I organized a quick experiment (what I now identify as a learning launch) in the form of a field trip for a  group of the team’s engineers to visit a production facility as well as a live construction site the following  week. I took great measures to carefully craft the event in a way I thought would be the most efficient  and beneficial learning experience for all attendees. In particular, I made it a comprehensive “tour” with  key staff from the department giving brief presentations on the ground followed by Q/A. Also, and  perhaps most important, I organized dinner and social interaction so that the team members could  become better acquainted. The response was overwhelmingly positive. I then crafted and organized a  program of field trips where key players from each of the major sectors visited each other in rounds over  a 3-month period.

Insight

In just three months, managers noticed an appreciable increase in efficiency of the project process, as  well as an increase in the overall morale and empathy between departments. Empathy increased because  team members from each department now better understood the mindset of the other (having seen their  job duties in real-time) as well as the implications of their actions on the other. Morale spiked due to  newly fashioned comradery amongst the project team after getting a chance to engage socially. This  program of field trips was thereafter attempted on other projects with success. Minor difficulties  encountered included (as is common in the business world): time and money. It is difficult to remove  employees from their busy schedules. Also, there was no line item in the budget for these events and  Corporate was unwilling to absorb the costs as overhead expenses – forcing me to draw from the sparse  contingency line. However, I felt strongly that the new value brought to the project well out-weighed such  difficulties.

Approach

Thinking back on this experience, some of tools learned in this course might have brought greater success  to the program. The full adoption of the program at a company-wide level did not pan out as I would have  liked. I wish I had more a formal recording of people’s experience to provide something tangible to  corporate to further sell the program; perhaps something similar to what Marion Moore conveyed in the  Week Three “Mind Mapping Tool” video, where people’s thoughts and reactions were well drawn out. In  summary, I feel I determined “What Is?” and “What Wows?” in the bi-weekly meeting with “What  Wows?” being determined in the first field trip experiment. “What Works?” ultimately did not pan out as  the program was not determined scalable on a company-wide basis.
