Learning Launch Tools Find Effective Fuel Surcharge Methodology

By

Sachin Cordova

Challenge

I am a consultant for a Last Mile Delivery/Less-than-Truckload (LTL or small freight) logistics company in  Ohio. The challenge I have been tasked with is to find an appropriate fuel surcharge methodology that  will not alienate any existing customers, nor be an impediment to attracting new business. The project is  limited to internal resources, with the project team consisting of myself, and members of both the sales  and marketing departments. Other key stakeholders include company senior management and  members of the accounting department. We are focusing on trying to discover what customers will  accept best and respond to most positively. The fuel surcharge will be a new line item, going live as a  new company revenue stream and appearing on all customer invoices beginning January 2.

Selection

After detailed usage of other Design Process activities, including spending time with several Accounts  Payable personnel to understand how current invoices were received and processed, we have been  utilizing Learning Launch Tools. We have been placing “small bets” in hopes of discovering what  invoicing methodology will be most effective now and in the future with clients.

The IBM trade show booth section of the course materials was particularly helpful in this stage of our  process, as the stakes to my client are as high or higher than a trade show attendee not entering a booth  or leaving quickly. The wrong billing approach could lead to the ending of the business relationship. Just  as the course explained, gaining “Greater Comfort” is crucial to adoption.

Application

The Learning Launch has been two-fold: first, testing multiple billing formats, and gauging reaction from  a group of Client Contacts on the receipt of an invoice containing a new line item, breaking out Fuel  Surcharges for the previous month. Would they contact our company and question the need for it?  Would they not contact the company, but instead silently have a measure of resentment? Would it  affect their view of the company and impact future business opportunities?

Second, the multiple billing formats have been reviewed by a group of Accounts Payable personnel.  Would the new formats create questions? Would it cause their internal management to need to review  the new invoices? Would any of them create an impediment or any other kind of delay in getting the  invoice processed?

These were some of the questions we asked, in the hopes of finding out where there would be a “Big  Fail”, to use the Corning example from the course materials. Would, and if so under what conditions,  would customers reject this new billing methodology?

Insight

What we have found is generally good news … customers understand and accept the need for a  separate line team for a Fuel Surcharge in their monthly invoices. Many customers are familiar with the  methodology, having done extensive business with global logistics chains such as FEDEX and DHL.  Additionally, the Learning Launch Tools and process uncovered that customers understand that the Fuel  Surcharge is linked to national market rates for fuel and can increase as market conditions change.

One surprise we discovered, however, is that customers have little to no tolerance for any “Black Box”  formula on how the surcharge is calculated each month. A simple formula, easy to understand by all  client personnel, accounting and non-accounting alike, is expected as a baseline for instituting any new  methodology.

Approach

The Learning Launch Tool has been appropriate, and has given us the proper range of testable solutions  needed to uncover a commonality in client acceptance: Feel free to add the Fuel Surcharge line item  next year, but with complete transparency on its calculation. As such, I feel confident that my client will  go live on January 2 with a new Fuel Surcharge line item on its invoices. It will utilize a simple formula  with $2 per gallon as a reference point, that any Client Contact can calculate easily after passing by a gas  station and seeing the day’s prices.

While our process appears to have proven to be sound, and we gave a wide variance of billing formats  for clients to review, we came away with a usable takeaway for similar processes in the future. As an  alternative, it would have been better to limit the sample billing formats to a maximum of 5-6. We used  8-10 different concepts in this process, and the surplus of choices likely took away from the overall  curation to a small degree.

Reflection: Storytelling

Helena Cavaco

Challenge & Selection

As a community outreach fellow working for the SOCAMIRAL through the Banco Santander Río de

Argentina, I have been tasked with supporting the expansion of bilingual communications  and programming in English and Spanish aimed at reaching the Latino community. Ayurvedic and Herbal is a very white institution overall, with Latino leaders few and far between. In the past, their  outreach efforts and communications for the Latino community have come from a white American  perspective, have been signs that have been translated with online software with obvious  grammatical errors, and have demonstrated a lack of true investment in the outreach and a lack of  Latino and Spanish-speaking representation in leadership to make these decisions. My challenge  was to lead the design of an outreach project that visually represented Latinos as a very diverse  community, across generations in the US, Spanish-speaking and Spanglish-speaking, and not only  had Latinos centered in the outreach but also leading the outreach, in charge of their storytelling of  the outreach. I used the storytelling perspective in design thinking to collaboratively brainstorm,  design, and implement a project that was Latino led, Latino centered, for a Latino audience. Since  white Americans had been attempting to tell the story of Latinos in the US for so long, a perspective  shift was required, a retaking of the narrative was needed, a centering of Latino narration in the  telling of Latino history was needed.

Application

Storytelling is key to any marketing, community outreach efforts. The design thinking

principle of storytelling was needed because there has been a historical disconnect and lack of  visual representation in ILO stories told about Latinos and Latino history with parks. There needed  to be a building of trust, which required genuine emotional connections to be made between the  Latino community and parks/public lands and representation of Latinos in the narrative. I designed a  possible storyboard in collaboration with another Latina working at a park in Texas and developed  the concept of a Latino rangers speaking from their perspectives on why their park and their work  matters to them, offering a natural representation of the diversity within the community by  showcasing Latino staff members. These rangers would share their specific identities, cultural  background, childhood pictures of them at parks, pictures of them at work and in the field, and more,  to provide context and history to Latinos in parks. This historicizes Latinos in parks, provides depth  and complexity to the story and makes the emotional connection more personal to those watching. I  put in the storyboard for the rangers to speak to the camera as if they were speaking to a family  member, using Spanish and English in any way they were comfortable speaking naturally, giving tips  on visiting the park and park safety without sounding like a poorly translated brochure.

After pitching this concept with the storyboard and example script to several Latino staff

members at parks nationwide, San Francisco national parks picked the series up. I made the title  “Voces de los Parques” or “Voices of the Parks,” and Latino rangers from each of the San Francisco  national parks presented 2-5 minute videos introducing themselves and their parks, offering personal  context and tips for park visitation and safety in Spanish, English, and Spanglish. The storytelling  was poignant because it was authentic, it was rangers speaking to the camera as if they were  speaking to trusted community members, and it offered authentic representation of not only Latinos  visiting parks but also working for them in various types of leadership positions. This is the first  bilingual series, captioned bilingually as well, done by the SOCAMIRAL. San Francisco ILO  set the precedent nationwide, and I have pitched this concept to parks in Colorado and Texas,  hoping to start a domino effect, as Latino communities boom and the need for bilingual outreach  expands more than ever. I hope to have this type of representation expand for more communities

and in more languages. The storytelling component of this was intentional in its design: it promoted a  personal and emotional connection to the parks by having Latino staff speak to the camera as if they  were speaking to loved ones/family members, the idea that Latinos have always been using parks  but just haven’t been given the chance to tell their stories to a larger audience, and that the Latino  community is diverse and full of potential as visitors and of talent as staff at ILO. These videos  successfully formed emotional connections with staff recounting stories of them growing up going to  parks, and now working at parks, explaining themselves bilingually in a natural way. This storytelling  was Latino led and Latino presented, and it shows that ILO has made an investment in representing  Latino stories in an authentic way.

Insight & Approach

By applying storytelling into this Latino community outreach effort, we were able to form direct,  personal connections with viewers, speaking in English and Spanish and providing bilingual closed  captions to reach a greater audience and be American Disability Act (ADA) compliant. By directing  the staff to speak to the camera as if they were addressing family, we could introduce the park and  its features and safety information in a warm, welcoming manner that was authentically told, with  Latino staff members on-screen writing and reading their own scripts. This provides natural diversity  in representation of the Latino experience in different parts of the country by showcasing real Latino  staff members, and puts value on their personal perspectives, their cultural history, representation,  and visibility as park staff, working in the field.  This storytelling form is also environmentally  conscious, on an online platform that is free to access, easy to share intergenerationally and for  educational programming, and is COVID friendly. By thinking about the park brochure as a story to  tell differently for distinct audiences, rather than just words to run through a translation, we could  reach a wider net of potential visitors through genuine emotional connection and visibility and  representation of Latino ILO staff to welcome them.

This sets a precedent for the SOCAMIRAL as the first bilingual video series done for the  agency. This sets an important precedent and example for future video series done for other  languages and communities, as the agency continues its work of expanding its community outreach  and efforts. Latino staff taking control of the “narrative” of the virtual Park brochure in Spanish and  speaking in the Spanish they use with family, gives dignity, specificity of perspective to the often- generalized Latino community in the larger U.S. narrative. Each staff member will bring their own  cultural background, their own history, show childhood pictures of them at parks, explain why the  park is important to them. It provides personal connection to the viewer and a warm welcome to the  Latino community on a free, accessible platform. It sets the standard for other agencies in this type  of video outreach. Storytelling provided further humanity to be put on a virtual Spanish-language  outreach effort and expanded the possibilities for further bilingual projects based off this concept, to  reach other communities.

I would follow the storytelling strategy again for a similar effort – it was a useful structure for the  community outreach I intended with this Spanish-language communications project. It provided  authenticity and personal connection to what could have been a very basic bilingual communications  format, using only park B-roll, or using only generic translated information. By putting Latino staff in  charge of the telling of the story, and thus in charge of the outreach for their community, the  outreach is genuine, welcoming, and approachable. When often the narratives of marginalized  communities are told from a white American perspective, this type of narrative ownership is  refreshing. For this preliminary series for San Francisco parks, there have been introductory videos  made for each of the parks. These introductory videos, one each for each park, give only a glimpse  into the park’s information. This effort needs to be expanded across a series, divided by topic, about  recreation, safety tips, programs, events, etc. A longer term strategy needs to be planned for this  preliminary set of videos, to show an investment in uplifting Latino voices in ILO and in authentic

bilingual outreach for the Latino community by the agency. Perhaps a design thinking strategy of use  could be the mind mapping principle, to plan an arc for the series to follow for each park, a long-term  structure for the videos. This could provide greater detail to a manual I could put together for other  parks to follow to re-create these videos at their own parks, in other regions. This is all in an effort  streamline the process, so it is as clear as possible for other parks to replicate as possible.

Design Thinking for Innovation

by University of Virginia

Instructor:  Daniela Sangineto

Student:  Ruben Soria  matthew72@hotmail.com

Course Assignment - Mind Mapping – Integrating Solutions

Note:  The following is a true story with many of the details made generic in order to preserve privacy.

Challenge

Our firm recently acquired a technology company (TC) that built a suite of tools and services that serves  a niche market, opening up a new market for our firm.  Within that market, our firm has another  business unit (BU) that serves a segment of that niche market with a set of tools and services (some  similar and some exclusive), but within a smaller segmentation of that market.  I was selected to be part  of a team of 6 to evaluate the newly acquired TC to determine if there were tools and/or services that  could be integrated into the BU offering.  Goals include:

1. Keeping the various systems nimble.   2. Proving the efficacy of the front-end data reporting for existing business.  3. Exploring the feasibility of pursuing a larger segment of the market.

Selection

We conducted a dozen interviews with various stakeholders across both business units and other  technology experts.  We collected a large amount of data from those interviews, and chose as our  primary tool Mind Mapping to help aggregate and identify themes in the data.

Application

Each team member individually took notes from those interviews.  We then identified key terms and  themes from each interview and wrote them on sticky notes.  The team reconvened in a room with a  large white board and we drew a grid with 4 quadrants.  The top two quadrants were goals which were  separated by quotes/defining words and thoughts/beliefs.  The bottom two quadrants were pain points  separated by actions/behaviors and feelings/emotions.

Insight

Several themes and insights emerged:

  Data aggregation was a common pain point theme for the BU, but a strength for the TC.

  Reconciliation and entity accounting was a pain point for the BU, but a strength for the TC.

  Onboarding complexity, resources and time required was a pain point for the TC, but a strength  for the BU.

  Inflexibility of componentizing was a pain point for TC, but a strength for the BU.

  We also discovered there was very little overlap of market segments.

From these themes we were able to develop two primary hypotheses for testing:

  Work with the technology team to integrate both units into a shared platform to expand tools  and services available to the BU.  The BU could then pick the best of breed solutions.

  Develop an integrated sales team to cross sell offerings from both units.

Approach

The Mind Mapping process was extremely effective and helpful.  It allowed us to quickly narrow down  the ideas and develop hypotheses for testing.  Additionally, it would be helpful to explore the learning  launch method further to develop some prototypes.  Developing some quick and inexpensive prototype  ideas would help with evaluating our hypotheses without committing large resources.

2- Tool selection:

At that moment, I did not know the design thinking term, but now that I reflect, I think that we  use the Learning Launch tool. Student: Angelo Martello

Learning Launch project

Chapters:

Challenge

I’m a project manager, involved on new product development department within  a company which is a supplier of hi-tech equipment for the electronic business.  Our challenge is to develop new products hitting the roadmap established from  Top management especially for the budget, resources and technology  differentiation from competitors.  The project is limited within R&D Product  development department. In our first learning launch We will try to think out of  the box, trying to wear our customer’s shoes during the brainstorming activities.  There will be a further and parallel activities performed by sales dept. that will  collect man voice of the customers.

Selection

We already tried to use some Design thinking tools in the past but, at that time  just a part of the team was really engaged and even really conscious about the  potential of the instrument. Right now, more or less every resource within the  team has joined the Design thinking class, so the target is to adopt the tool for an  Alpha product all along the whole product development phases.

Application

On our First learning launch meeting we tried to wear the customer shoes  collecting a list of lacks that they have. It has been made thinking not only about  their supply chain, where we are currently involved, but also the current  technology gap they are facing due to the physical limits of the technology,

geopolitical scenarios. It has been done in this way in order to abandon our daily  way of thinking about the market. All the ideas had been written on a sticky note  and attached on a whiteboard. As a second step We came back in our mind  thinking which of those ideas could be fix by their supplier and ranking them  based on the value gained from customer if it could be solve in a way or another.  We choose to focus only on first 3 ideas with high position on ranking and where  their supply chain is involved. The first learning lunch session ends here after 3  hours meeting.

After one week We join the second session. We began trying to recap what’s  happened during the first one session and We start to think on which of the 3  idea We should invest resources. The analysis has been performed considering  the cost of resources, time to market, the customer’s interview collected by our  Sales dept. , the technology differentiation We could introduce in order to avoid  an easy adoption of the same idea from competitors. Based on data collected  from customers and the deep dive performed, the cost benefit analysis has been  terminated choosing only one Customer’s high value problem. We’ll invest in  order to fix only that point.

Insight

Applying the learning launch tool our team had identified the priorities of the  market thinking out of the box. The output of our analysis is essentially a forecast,  which is based on a deep analysis ran by a skilled team of engineers. We’ll  proceed with product development activities keep in mind what has been  highlighted during the first 2 sessions. The purpose is to  schedule at least another  session of brainstorming, this time with a very technical approach, and it will be  useful to address the hardware and software architecture of the new product that  will solve the problem we’ve identified. The insight I think is that moving in this  way the chance of release something that will be easily adopt from market has  been increased a lot.

Approach

Each member of the team has been fully engaged on this activity and now We’re  conscious of the potential of the tool. As I’ve previously mentioned We’ll keep

this approach during the next phases of the project. Till now We turned the  activities of learning launch as a marketing investigation but in the next phase of  the project We’ll face the technical side of the product development using Design  Thinking.

Challenge     I’m a member of sushi bar marketing department, and our challenge is to make some

changes on our menu due to increase the occupation of the restaurant during the

weekdays, more precisely at the lunch time. To help me with this mission I got all the

support from the owner to make any change which I believe that might put us back among

the best restaurants of the city as we were on our opening days last year. The results of

this project should be put on practice on the next month. So, we got around 30 days to

decide which changes we are going to do. On this context, it is important to mention that

the market of sushi restaurants has grown a lot on my city with the emergence of several

other similar restaurants. Because of that we must do something different to win back our

customers.

Selection

After all what was said and considering the short amount of time, we will have available,

we believe that the better tool to rebuild our menu and make the changes we are looking

for it will be learning launch, which can be define as an experiment meant to quickly test

an idea.

Application

For our learning launch, we focused on the rebranding of our lunch menu. First of all, we

did a little survey about the customers preferences. After that, we tried to figure out some

way to incorporate these preferences on our new model of menu. As a result of this

process, we discovered that the regular clients, those who frequent our restaurant on

weekdays when they are working, are not interested on the premium meals usually offered

by most part of the sushi bars around the city. Actually, this type of customer is looking

for something cheaper and quicker than these regular menus, which are based on “all you

can eat” model. That said, we worked on a special menu specifically for the lunch time

on weekdays. This new menu was simpler and was designed to combine our top seller

meals plus just one side dish on a smaller pocket. These changes accompanied by some

daily promotions made our menu cheaper and simpler, as well as making it easier for our

customer to not waste time.

Insight

What I have learned from this experience it was the important of a deep knowledge about

your customers before you try to put an idea into practice. And this is exactly your main

goal when you are applying the learning launch tool. For us to have the opportunity to

test a solution on the real world before we decide what to do was fundamental to our

organization measure the impacts of these changes and to reached good results too.

Additionally, we were very happy to have used some of the guidelines of design thinking

mentality, which is one of the most modern knowledge to develop ideas and apply

changes in organizations.

In the end, I would like to conclude saying that our actual results were very positive as

we’ve got an increase around thirty percent on your profits after the release of our new

lunch menu. Moving forward, our team will review this insight and incorporate it into

future launch designs.

Approach

Considering that our focus was on a quick implementation and that it would be important

to test the changes we provided, I think that the learning launch was the appropriate tool

for the situation we had faced. Despite that, I believe that there are other tools which could

be successfully applied, such as mind mapping and visualization. But in the end, I was

very satisfied with the results we got from the implementation of the learning launch tool

and all the modifications we put into practice. Future launch designs should reflect insight

gained, progress made, and acquired knowledge.

VISUALIZATION REFLECTION

Challenge & Selection  As an 8th grade student, I use visualization a lot in my life. In my classes, I strive to not only memorize the information presented but also understand it. In order for me to do this, I use visualization. Some of my peers who struggle constantly ask me for aid in their respective subjects which we share. I wanted to challenge myself to only use the tool of visualization to help them. I selected visualization as we are now studying geometry and it's very important to learn how to visualize things.

Application  The main problems that my peers have with math are fairly simple to solve with visualization. For example, some of them aren't comfortable with the relatively important concept of isometries. In geometry, an isometry is a rigid transformation between metric spaces. Most of my classmates simply try to figure out and isometry by using a formula. However while being sloppy, a formula can give you inaccurate results due to an unforced error. Geometry, however, is the perfect candidate for usage of visualization.    What you have to remember while doing simple isometries is that it is usually possible to do without any formula what so ever. One example a 180 rotation transforms from (x,y) to (-x,-y). For people who were just barely paying attention in class, this concept isn't one they are likely to remember. Challenge: Last year I had a rather important and responsible task: to make a new identity for the exhibition of  visual studies about Russian culture. The people who did these studies reflected on Russia from  different angles. The style uniting all these studies had to be recognizable and convey a sense of  Russianness. I decided to focus on my own cultural code of the Russian people. I set myself the  task of trying to make a style in isolation from stereotypes, to find something in Russian culture  that no one is looking at, to find different ways to talk about Russia. The identity of the festival  should not lose the feeling of Russianness, but at the same time it should be modern, so that com- munication with the target audience of teenagers and young people takes place in a language that  is understandable to them.

First of all, I sorted out the semantic and ideological aspects of Russianness, make a list of differ- ent meanings and meanings that can characterize Russia and the people living here. Then I re- duced it to a short list with individual words that were supposed to become ideological and visual  guidelines for my future style and business strategy.

Selection: The first tool I used was the visualization tool. Visualization is a method of design thinking when  we create a figurative prototype - a picture / diagram in the user’s head, and then proceed to its  implementation and sketches (this is a link to the lecture in which this tool was discussed https://www.williamson.net/wp-contentcategory.php)  I decided that the new Russian graphics should be created by people involved in this culture,  because only they will be able to visualize the necessary images and forms to form a new style,  based on old values, thanks to their innate immersion in the cultural context.

Application: I sent out sheets of different Russian words to different people and asked them to visualize each of  them by any methods they were interested in, whether it was a drawing, a photograph, a sculpture,  some kind of fake from any materials. And also write a few associations to my words. A few days  later, each of them sent me 5 visualizations of these words and a lot of new associations.

Insight : As a result, I received not only accurate images describing the feeling of Russianness that I need- ed for further work, but also words that helped me strengthen and clarify the ideological com- ponent of my future style. In addition, the little things in people’s works that they used, such as  colors, materials and the nature of graphics, line thicknesses have already formed the primary  constants of my future style. The biggest progress in the work happened thanks to a conversation  with different people about Russia and their everyday practices and feelings. I came to an import- ant insight that finally formed the ideology of the style. It turned out that Russian people are quite  hot-tempered, bright and daring, like to take on a challenge. It is important for them to show them- selves and feel their uniqueness. This prompted me to use red as the main color in the identity of  the festival. I used the information I received to finalize the characteristics of the style and business  strategy.

Approach : As a result, I decided that visualization is one of the strongest strategies of design thinking, allow- ing me to best convey the feeling and meaning of something to other people. The images give a  deeper understanding of how it is necessary to develop the idea further and turn it into a finished  product. In my further work, I would use the strategy of exchanging ideas and working with peo- ple immersed in the context at once at the visualization level at the first stages of the project, this  allows you to dive deeper into the context and more accurately formulate long-range methods of  work.

Reflection: Mobile Money for the Unbanked-Storytelling

Challenge & Selection

I’m working on a project that increases economic development in rural areas with little or null  access to banking services. The current solutions focus only on two things: the funds to be  intended to social programs and the way they are delivered.

What is this about? Well, they define the problem in a context that eliminates the opportunities  for innovation. They attack the problem in a general way, assuming total certainty and prediction  based on statistical data without exploring the details and characteristics of the persons In these  communities, for example, giving money cards in areas where there is not access to services  where they can be used, and providing food or money in areas far awy from these communities,  ignoring the transportation, time and security challenges faced by these people when receiving  support.

The person who helps one of my partners cleaning his house has shared with us the long and  complicated process that her mom faces triyng to receive these socials programs. With the history  of her mom plus histories shared by other persons that have knowledge of this situation we have  design a solution to develop an economic growth, and bring closer financial services into these  zones.

Application    The first time we presented the solution we were focusing presenting the problem, the proposed  solution and the impact of this in the lives of these people. Altought we did’t communicate a story,  we empathically connected the board members with the problem using an ethnographic  categorization and theorizing the results based on a similar solution applied in Africa where is a  success.

On the other hand, during the last presentation that we had with executives of another company  the results were different. We repeated the same formula that had previously given us success,  but we failed to communicate the problem and therefore the impact of the solution.

When we explained the scheme operation, they argued the use of electronic wallets that requires  a card to operate as a better solution. The presentation has turned into a debate looking for  defend their ideas rather than a business/solution presentation.

We tried to make them see the problem with a focus on the needs of the person and problems of  infrastructure and lack of banking services that they experienced in their communities, to which  they argued with statistical and market data, for example the extension of cellular LTE Coverage to  National level, among others. In this way all his answers and arguments to the problem were  based on "big ideas" and market research data of the current situation.

After all this, we have seen the need to create a story that communicates emphatic the situation  of the people and the problems they face.     Insight & Approach    Applying the storytelling tool, the team has managed to create a story based on the experience  shared by Paolina, the girl who helps my partner cleaning his home, to see the challenges that her  mom faces when using these social programs.    We have tried to build a StoryTelling based on the following points:

  Non-articulated needs of people.

  Using statistical information+results information from our investigation of the problem  (interviews, visualizing the problem) and then connect them with with the protagonist.

  Explain the current situation / problem based in  the emotional connection (empathy)

  Create moments of reflection through questions and suspense between them.

  The stresses that ignore the problem implies for the company.

  Communicate the strategy involved in the situation.

  The HardFact of the story is based on the challenges of the protagonist of the story and  not just in fixed data provides by reports/ market research.

“Design Thinking for Innovation”

I.  Challenge

I am in my second year in the MBA program at National University of Malaysia. I am currently

working on one of my elective classes, which is “Innovating through Design Thinking.” I

wanted to not only gain knowledge on the different processes that take part in design thinking,

but I also wanted to get my hands on a real project where I could see the results of such an

effective technique. I came up with the idea of developing a new solution for “poop scooping,”

since in the college town where I live, 6 out of 10 students own a dog.

The action of poop scooping can happen in different places such as home, sidewalks, parks,

friend’s house, or any place where a dog owner decides to take his or her dog for a walk. The

process of cleaning up the dog’s poop is, in my opinion, probably the least desirable stage

when walking a dog. Therefore, when I made the Journey Mapping of the poop scooping

experience, this was the stage with the strongest pain and with the lowest emotional point, thus

creating a space for innovation and opportunity to offer a better solution.

II.  Selection

I chose the tool of visualization, which according to the book “Designing for growth: A

Design Thinking Toolkit for Managers,” is “the transformation of information into images that

you see, either literally with your eyes or figuratively with your mind’s eye.” This tool is used

in the four “W’s” of the design thinking process: what is, what if, what wows, and what works.

I decided to use this tool in the process of “what is,” since it helped me make my ideas concrete

and situate the potential customer (students) on the same page when conducting ethnographic

interviews. Even though visualization does not eliminate the “vagueness” that is present in the

interviewer’s words (vagueness because I did not give students any clue about how my product

might look like, in fact, I did not know how it would), it de-risked my project by making the

students’ mental models more similar to mine.

III.  Application

I asked my university to send me a list of undergraduate and graduate students from

different colleges (business, applied science and technology, arts and sciences, education, and

nursing), and sent personal emails to a total of 300 students, asking if they owned a dog and

were willing to help me with a project. I filtered the list based off students’ replies and the

number came down to 50, to whom I contacted again for an interview.

Mauro Carella 2

The interviews took place in team rooms in the College of Business at Univesidad Nacional de Colombia Sede Manizales. When talking to students, the first thing I did was to show them pictures of puppies

having a fun time with their owners at a park, and asked them to tell me what thoughts and

emotions came to their mind. Soon after, I showed them pictures of un-scooped poops on

streets and at parks. Their reactions varied from gesturing and signaling disapproval, while

others even recognized that sometimes they do the same for different reasons.

IV.  Insight

Visualization provided me with many valuable insights that helped me untap into students’

way of thinking when it came to scooping their dogs’ poop. For example, I realized that the

main reasons students do not clean up their dogs’ poop is because current solutions in the

market are either too complex to use, too big to carry to parks, or too expensive for a students’

budget. Had I not used the visualization tool, it would have taken me a long time to explain

students my idea and the problem I was trying to solve. Showing pictures also switched the

emotional side of interviewees, making them more vulnerable to providing valuable

information. As for design thinking itself, I like to link visualization with prototyping (which

is also part of my project), or “thinking with your hands.” I realized how valuable this tool is

in every stage of the design thinking process because it speeds up meetings, problem solving,

and most importantly, feedback generation.

V.  Approach

Next time, I might do things a little differently. Instead of showing pictures to interviewees,

I might ask them to draw on a white board all the things associated with owning a dog (reverse

visualization). This might lead to clues about what owners like and do not like to do, such as

scooping their dogs’ poop.

Challenge

I work in an NGO as a Recruitment Lead. My organization’s key product is a Fellowship  program that is open for people who have at least completed their graduation. Though the  program is well established and around a decade old, recent times have seen a steep decrease  in the number of applications coming in from young college graduates. It has been  tremendously tough for the organization to solve this issue (i.e. increase the applications of  fresh college graduates). In my opinion, the only way to solve the issue is by identifying the  key reason which has led to the decline and then working on creating a solution. To identify  the reasons for the decline, we would have to employ historical application data, its analysis  and also look at some qualitative parameters which would include regional context, cultural  quotient, mind-set of the students, etc. Hence, design thinking would have to be adopted for  solving the problem statement: “What has led to a decline in the number of applications  received from fresh college graduates in the past two years?”

Tool selection

The tool I selected for this challenge is “Mind Mapping”. Mind mapping is the best tool to  identify the reasons/ patterns/ trends in the available current scenario. As my challenge is to  identify the root causes of the decrease in application numbers, mind mapping will help me to  flesh out the “What is” part of the bigger problem. Using mind mapping I hope to get a better  picture of all the quantitative and qualitative reasons which would have contributed to the  problem in the first place. Once I can identify and pinpoint the reasons, as Prof. Marian  Moore mentioned in the Week 3 Video 4, I will be able to Segway to “What if” and think  about creative solutions to the problem.

Application

Mind mapping in design thinking is to identify what goes on in the minds of our customer, in  this particular case, we were looking at the minds of the fresh college graduates. As the best  way to do it was to involve a team, I pursued 5 other colleagues of mine to join this process.  My colleagues were picked based on their background of having been college students who  had applied for the program and their experience of having worked on the ground with  college students in the past 4 years.

As the first step, I collated all the materials I had for this study. It included the following:

1.      Primary data from College students: it had details of their passion, short term and  long term goals, career aspirations, their knowledge about the program, knowledge  about the impact, the program will create in their lives, their interests, their source of  information about the program, along with some of their personal details. This was  collected by me during conversations with the students.  2.      Historical data about the number of applications we have received in the past  from these colleges.  3.      Information on demographics of the college students.  4.      The other opportunities which the students have opted for in the past 2 years  5.      The list of all the other social sector programs in the country

All this information was shared with my other colleagues to view. After spending about 45  mins of individual thinking time with the anchoring question “For the larger problem, which  parts of this data will add value?”, the members were asked to note down their observations.

Zakaria Hassan

The observations of the 6 of us were then grouped into 3 large buckets. We then sat down to  interpret the observations to come up with solid insights. With these insights, we came up  with the “Design Criteria” statement.

Insight

The following were the three large observations:

1.      Availability of other opportunities  2.      Incorrect/Lack of the details and impact of the program  3.      Parental pressure.

These three big buckets were then analyzed by the six of us and the root cause of the problem  were led to two main insights about why the application numbers have reduced amongst the  college students:

1.      The messaging about the program sends confusing ideas of what it entails  2.      Lack of strong brand image amongst the youth and their families

These insights have changed my perspective on the issue in general. Till before this activity, I  was convinced that the issue was with the customers and lack of inclination towards the  social sector. These insights have been able to direct my attention towards the change which  is under our control and action can be taken by us to solve the issue.

What should the action be like would be a part of “What if” which is yet to be analyzed.  However, as per our initial goal of identifying the root cause, we were able to come with a  strong answer.

Approach

I would prefer using the same tool as this is the best tool to identify the root causes and  answer to “What is”. Though the project gave really strong insights, I realize that some parts  of it can be improved to give a better result.  A major change I would bring to this approach  when I have to do it for the second time would be to involve a larger group of people in the  activity. With only 6 people (including me), the scope of innovation and thinking seems to be  narrow. In addition to this, the primary survey can be done in a written format with an  increased number of participants to get a better understanding.

Storytelling to improve government communication skills

Monica Torres

1. Challenge:

I work for the Colombian government since I was 23 years old. What I have seen during  that time is that: (i) State entities in Colombia have little credibility caused by high rates of  corruption and the popular belief that they are inefficient. (ii) people who work for the  government have difficulties to communicate what the government is doing because they  use a technical terminology that common people do not understand. (iii) Government  workers are used to do things in a certain way that allow them to keep their Jobs and get  things done accordingly to the law. Finally, (iv) government entities do not understand the  real problems of citizens.

In this context, we worked identifying a way to face those issues in our office. We decided  to start with the problem within our reach “improve my communication skills and my  colleague’s”. The main challenge was finding a way to change our mindset so we used a  tool that allow us to communicate better among us.

2. Selection:

Driven to improve our communication skills and connect with each other, we decided to  use storytelling as a tool to ease the presentations of our topics. Telling stories in our  presentations make them more interesting for the listener, helping to capture their  attention and empathize with the audience. The stories humanized our communication  and make our colleagues feel closer to topics different from their expertise. It makes them  the center of our presentations.

Taking in to account that our topics and the language we used was considered difficult to  keep up and boring, we decided to use examples and analogies in our personal stories to  connect with values, emotions and character. Like John Kaur, Global Leadership  Development Director from Mars Inc, says “(…) Every great brand has a story and that  story connects to the emotions, the characters, the values of the people (…)”. We wanted  to build the story behind our work, that’s our brand.

3. Application:

We started searching in to our personal repertoire of stories, looking for the key points that  could have a personal connection with our audience as well as with the topics we were  presenting. We chose the stories were there was a strong connection with the speaker but  also had a clear meaning to the listener. The criteria for determining the stories was that it  had to be funny as we realized that our audience was always leaning for this type of  content.

Once the stories were identified, the next step was to build the speech accordingly to what  we wanted to explain. The  purpose of this reflection was for students to pause a few weeks into their work and see what they had  learned and make any necessary adjustments for the rest of the course. The purpose of the final reflection was to  support students in looking back at their experience and thinking about what they had accomplished  and how it connected to their future. After each reflection assignment was submitted, the teaching  team read the individual reflections of each of the teams they were mentoring and provided feedback to  that team. The photographic project and visualization as a strategy of design thinking

CHALLENGE & SELECTION

My experience of applying design thinking comes from a area that is not linked to business

development,  but to the area of teaching in a Graphic Desigh School where my students require my

couching in the development of graphic design products and photographic images.

In one of the basic courses of photography students must develop a photographic series that must

have coherent unity in theme and in the use of the visual language. Participants in this workshop

have little or no experience in photography and can use any photography  device.

To achieve the objectives visualization is key through the whole process, we use the combination of

prototyping-visualization processes, development of concepts of design criteria and brainstorming-

ideation. We work in teams of 3 to 5 participants. All this is actually a combination of an iterative

process where divergent and convergent thinking is used in the project development.

In the present presentation, due to the limitations required, I will focus on three phases where we

select tools of Design Thinking which we denominate with other names, however, I will point out its

relation with the tools as they are denominated in the material of Designing for Growth.

APPLICATION

In the first stage which we have called "thematic-technical exploration process", the students try to

learn about the possibilities of the photographic medium for the development of an idea or theme

freely chosen by them  (What is?). The participants make several photographic shots approaching

the subject or object of study using directly the photography device they have available, allowing

them through the rapid photographic capture to learn in a visual way as much as possible about the

possibilities and technical difficulties of the chosen subject, which they have to show periodically to

his or her group allowing the visualization of the particular interests.

The previous phase leads them to the understanding of a series of key elements of the visual and

technical aspects of the project  which allows the participants of the group to understand the

aesthetic possibilities and thus organize that information in a way that should lead them to the

description of the possible visual criteria of the project. (Value analysis).

The group then carries out brainstorming to develop ideas that can help the accomplishment of

their partner's project. They do this by  searching  what we call "visual references" with their own

photographic works and especialy with visual examples developed by  various photographic authors

which allow them to shed light on to how to develop the project of their partners in a way that can

conform to the technical and aesthetic possibilities of the projects presented and discussed. This

process allows them to develop key aesthetic and design criteria (Concept Development).

INSIGHT AND APPROACH

One of the things I have learned is that at the beginning of the process it is necessary to overthrow

in the participants the expectations they may have of wanting to frame the possibilities of the

project without, beforehand, openly and without prejudice, to explore those possibilities.

Photographic  devices, whatever they are, are excellent tools for discovering things in the world that

one may not have seen before. The process, more than to look for,it is a process of discovery. Then,

sharing these visual findings in several cycles of conversation with colleagues and discussing the

possibilities, develops the understanding of the aesthetic-visual and technical problem of the

projects.

On the other hand, the fact that, in many cases, there is a good amount of common key elements

that arise in the various projects, it is possible to enrich the analysis of their aesthetic-visual values

as well as enrich, in the colaborative atmosphere, the search for "visual references"(visual

brainstorming) that can become possible solutions.

Firoz Khan Pandey Reflection – Learning Launch Challenge

I am a member of my organization’s supply chain project management department and my/our challenge  is to improve the workflow (activities and projects) within the department in order to reduce COGS in the  manufacturing processes and to cut lead times for active new project launches. The project scope included  the project management department composed of six employees, as well as the marketing department  and sales department, with whom we work closely. The project is limited to internal resources (i.e., budget  and employee time). The project should not exceed 90 business days and the solution should include an  even distribution of working hours amongst the team members. We will focus on trying to uncover what  our team members, as well as key stakeholders within the marketing department and sales department,  consider to be ineffective or problematic about the workflow.

Selection

Our team has already gone through several design thinking activities/tools, so we are ready to try the  learning launch tool. Broadly speaking, the learning launch is an experiment meant to quickly test an idea  and prototype.

Application

For our first learning launch, we focused on the structure/execution of our day to day project  management tasks. In particular, we wanted to see if we could structure our tasks, projects, and processes  to adapt the methods of Scrum project management for our work (e.g., time boxed, daily, specific  meetings, reviews, etc.) in an effort to become more agile. This tested our assumption that the structure  and execution were the main causes of our workflow challenge. Our team went through a two-day training  with a Scrum project management coach. Next, we went through five workshops to structure our tasks  and processes in a more agile way. These two sessions occurred within in a three-week timeframe. We  expected to produce a document with a clear description of our new, more agile processes/workflow. For  our second learning launch, we focused on gaining clarity about our tasks and priorities. This tested our  assumption that our prioritization of tasks was the main cause of our workflow challenge. Our team  completed an anonymous survey. Additionally, five key stakeholders from the marketing department and  sales department also completed an anonymous survey. The surveys included questions about our new,  proposed process, understanding the process and the prioritization of tasks, and feelings about the  change, and were conducted within a one-week timeframe.

Insight

By applying the learning launch tool, our team identified our assumptions and designed launches to test  these assumptions. Additionally, we thought through anticipated results, expecting to find that a more  agile approach would improve our workflow, and that both our team and the key stakeholders would be  fairly open to the new prioritization of tasks and process. Our actual results were slightly different from  what we anticipated: while our team was open to the prioritization of tasks and process, the key  stakeholders in the marketing department and sales department expressed some concerns around  meeting targeted cost goals and lead times on NPDs. Moving forward, our team will review this insight  and incorporate it into future launch designs. The ongoing incorporation of insight is particularly  important at this stage, as launches come before a full rollout in the design thinking timeline.

Approach

Given that our team has already gone through several design thinking activities/tools and are at this stage  in the timeline, the learning launch is the appropriate tool. As previously mentioned, our team needs to  review the insight gained from our first two launches and incorporate this insight into future launch  designs. Future launch designs should reflect insight gained, progress made, and come closer to a  compelling solution ready for full rollout.

Challenge   Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.    A significant part of my work as a corporate knowledge manager involves publishing books for different  internal audiences. We’re a small team and we manage everything from content development to  research and writing to editing and layout to pre-press production and distribution.     Because we cover a broad range of topics, this presents an opportunity to work with other teams,  sometimes from other affiliate companies as well as external resource persons.    And so the challenge posed by collaborating with others outside the team (especially those not familiar  with publishing) is how to engage them to be active contributors, perhaps with the same level of  enthusiasm that we ourselves have. There are many approaches we take, but I believe one of the most  critical and valuable methods is visualization.    Selection  In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected (e.g., what it is and why you selected it for your  challenge -- including any appropriate video lecture references).    If you’re an avid reader, you may appreciate that the visual aspects of books are as important as the  copy or narrative: the choice of fonts, the space the text takes up on a page, how data is presented in  charts and infographics, illustrations that pique your interest to read on.      From our production point of view, visualization happens at inception and is very valuable when it  comes to bringing other people to the table and to get them not only involved but also invested in and  excited to see a book project through.    And so the flowcharts in this course resonated with me, as they traced not only process but also  provided insights on the implications or cause-and-effect of how might one action and another and  another lead to the either the desired outcome or failure (not entirely a bad thing, i.e.., failure).     The table on design thinking vs. linear analytic methods provided a valuable insight that design thinking  fits our team’s philosophy when it comes to book development: human (reader)-centered, with a desire  to explore all possible aspects of a topic, the understanding that there are many uncertainties and  dependencies at the start of each project, and the fact that we sometimes only have basic reference  materials to begin with.    And finally, the waveform illustration of What is? What If? What Wows? and What Works? is the most  valuable visual guide that I take with me after this course. It’s both visionary and practical and should be  part of any professional function’s ethos, in my opinion.    Application  Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., what you did and how the tool  was applied effectively or ineffectively).

I’ve recently begun working on a new book project that required collaborating with another team in the  company as well as with an external resource person. It was important that we were all coming from the  same basic understanding of what we wanted to accomplish and how we can achieve it.    In the first meeting, the main visual that I presented were printouts of the covers and a few pages of the  books that we previously published. This proved to be a good start in getting my new project partners  interested as they can actually see what the final output could look like    Next, we made a freeform inventory of the materials that we have in our respective units, as well as the  gaps that we needed to fill. Taking turns while doing this, organizing the correlated items into a list, and  revisiting it at the start of each production meeting, allowed us to put in ideas from each other’s areas of  expertise, and got us even more engaged and invested in the project’s success.    As we gathered materials, using the framework of What Is? What If? What Wows? and What Works?  has been quite useful in further exploring the possibilities for the book’s content, while recognizing  necessary delimiters that would make the book a reality within the timeframe we set for ourselves.    Insight  Describe the insight you gained from applying the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., how an  insight affected your thinking about the challenge and about design thinking more broadly).    Visualization is certainly important in the work we do, because we cannot assume that our ideas will be  readily understood by other parties we work with. No matter how detailed or well written our  descriptions or explanations are, some things still get lost in translation. Presenting information or a  process in visual form can really make things simple and easy to understand.     I realized that putting ideas down in paper, in whatever visual form, and sharing it with other people  from disciplines other than my own, can also serve as a catalyst for generating not only more ideas, but  also more factors to consider. This part of the exercise certainly brings up the what ifs and wows, and  significantly, what works.     Approach  Describe what you might do differently next time -- applying the same tool you selected or a different  one -- and the reason(s) why.    In this case, we have had to adjust the production process to our greatest delimiter, which is working  remotely due to the pandemic. Visualization has certainly been doable; we’ve just had to make do with  shared screens and show-and-tell on video meetings.     But I think it is an even more powerful tool when we’re all in the same room, working on the same  whiteboard, bouncing off ideas on the fly, and putting up printouts of our works in progress. Add to this  mind mapping to recognize what else we need or how to present the content.     Is that a bit old fashioned now in the “New Normal”? I do value the energy and the potential that  collaborating in person can generate, and I certainly look forward to the day when we can go back to our  offices to do this. Enzo Richards, Design Thinking for Innovation

Example Reflection: Storytelling

Challenge

I work in Product Design & Development for a consumer electronics company.  Our products typically  perform very well, and receive great critical acclaim, but in general are primarily adopted by an older  demographic.  Our company had done both analytical and ethnographic research, both of which showed  that we had products that customers were aware of, but younger audiences were unable to move past  the consideration phase of the purchase process.  We had tried different advertising, with different copy  as well as more youthful images or scenes, and time and time again they had only managed to barely  move the needle, if at all.  We also saw that there were competitors with similar product sets that were  able to gain more interest (and later sales) with their offerings, which made us question what the  differences were and how we could improve.  My team was challenged to look at our product offering  as a whole and find a way to resonate better with the younger demo (Millennials).

Selection

The challenge was levied upon my team from an executive management council, who knew we were a  group that was very connected with the product, but also had a good deal of understanding of the  problem, given that many team members were millennials.  I preached that we needed to maintain a  sense of consumer empathy, and that while we were at work, it was easy to ‘drink the kool-aid’ and  have an inflated view of how we were perceived.  Given our heightened understanding as a team, and  the need to present a compelling argument to make some potentially radical changes to the products, I  knew we would have to use storytelling to provide a convincing argument.  With that in mind, we  worked together to sell the challenge that we had identified, of updating the image of our products to  enable them to resonate more with Millennials.

Application

Our company had always made really compelling products with fantastic technical prowess, which had  some of the best performance relative to the competitive set.  But what we needed to sell to our  leadership team was the challenge that the Millennial consumer was looking for more than just a  different color palette or video of younger people using older style products.  We used storytelling to  get this point across by referring to similar challenges faced by similar companies in other industries,  and how they were able to evolve.  Being a bit of a sneaker fan myself, I told our leadership about New  Balance, which is a very strong brand for high performance footwear, but hadn’t necessarily resonated  as well with younger audiences.  To combat that, they worked with some specialty designers to update  their products to feature precision, high value materials in updated colors, and made them somewhat  limited to help drive up interest.  I had shared photos of special edition releases that the New Balance  team had worked on successfully, which led to increased exposure in blogs and had kids camping out  overnight to make sure they could buy these limited sneakers.  I also showed that there were other  ways that the team needed to address the entire product selection holistically, and how that resonated

Enzo Richards, Design Thinking for Innovation

very well.  For example, Nike has their standard releases which are available broadly, but when they do  a really limited release, they update not only the footwear design, but also the shoebox as well, which  really helps the user validate their purchase (which is often at a premium over the standard offerings).

As I was sharing this with the leadership, I could see their eyes light up a bit.  Some were surprised, if not  initially confused, about how sneaker culture could relate to our consumer electronics business.  But  through the storytelling about sneakers, the blog posts and photos of the droves of fans that would wait  in line, and even some in person show-and-tell of how truly unique some of these materials and designs  could get, the leadership team grasped the story we were presenting so much so that I was asked to give  it to an extended team as well.  In summary, we were able to present the point that we needed to make  sure we were holistically approaching the entire product experience to enable Millennial consumers to  really want to purchase our products.

Insight

The team agreed with our conclusion, and that we could no longer expect to just throw a coat of trendy  paint on and think that would get the job done.  There was of course some tension here: how would  these changes impact our current offerings?  We had to be sure that we did not artificially move the  needle TOO far in one direction, potentially alienating our current core customer.  This led to us  updating our offerings to have unique, limited variations, complete with custom, refined carry cases and  packaging that was more considered and expressive.  The results were extremely positive: not only did  we move the average age down for the updated products, we also were able to get the gender split,  which had been skewing far more male than female, to be much closer to a 50-50 split, which was a  secondary goal of the program.  What I really appreciated was that this was able to impact our entire  design community, and put the focus that was deserved on making sure we spent as much time curating  our design as well as engineering our performance.

Approach

Being able to tell a compelling story to leadership to help them understand the challenges of appealing  to a millennial audience was definitely the right method to use for our team’s time and deliverable  constraints.  Given the scale of our company, and the intricacies with our sales and supply chains, a  learning launch may have seemed helpful, but in the end it wasn’t realistic enough for us to execute.  If  we had to go through a different Design Thinking tool or exercise, for future innovations I would  advocate doing some mind mapping exercises in order to get a better picture and answer the “What Is?”  question more thoroughly before transitioning into the actual product design and development.

Design Thinking Reflection: Storytelling

Challenge

In my organization, I am responsible for business development in the EMEA region, but apart from my  core role and responsibilities, I “wear many hats”, e.g. organize business conferences and events,  manage alliances and accounts, create collateral, etc. I work with clients, partners, internal teams,  external teams and various stakeholders, day in, day out and addressing diverse groups with different  goals, backgrounds, challenges, needs and wants has always been a known challenge, not only for me. I  needed to communicate more efficiently with different stakeholder groups, structure messages and key  takeaways better, create build up and align meeting participants, regardless if they are from Marketing  or IT, around a single vision of the problem we are trying to solve.

Selection

Unfortunately, I have limited opportunities under the circumstances of COVID-19 global pandemic and  lockdown to practice my new design thinking knowledge acquired during the course, however, luckily,  storytelling is a design tool I can practice every day on infinite Zoom meetings and it can be applied to  multiple contexts. Apart from the reason mentioned above, we learned from both Barry and  the Chief Learning Officer of Mars Inc. how storytelling is an important design tool and a tool that has  been increasingly leveraged in the business world as every product, service, solution and institution has a  story behind it. A good story in a nutshell is more than just conveying a message that has logic, it has a  larger emotional connection and purpose or i.e. it creates a cause that according to the CLO of Mars Inc.  “ignites people and unites people”. Hence, storytelling makes a difference between problem solving and  creating a cause; it is about taking listeners on a journey where human beings and their experience are  front and center. We as humans respond to stories, which can aid us in gaining deeper empathy of the  present and developing vivid images about the novel future that we are trying to create together. To  sum up, I agree that storytelling is a powerful tool to capture listeners’ attention and bring stakeholders  of different background together around a common definition of a problem, using clear structure,  empathy, problem statement and reflection.

Application

Although, storytelling is typically used in “What wows?” stage, where it is a powerful design tool to share  ideas generated during “What if?” stage, I applied storytelling in a different context, what might be  considered as “What is?” stage of the design thinking process. Furthermore, the example that I would  like to share was on a recent stakeholder call and my application of storytelling revolves around the  notion of aligning stakeholders around a common definition of the problem and the criteria of a solution,  which we heard numerous times from Barry, is a prerequisite for success.

We have been developing client-facing web and mobile apps for one of my clients for almost a year now  and it is time that the apps go live, which requires coordination of multiple stakeholders and a launch  plan. Therefore, I was invited by my client to the app launch kickoff stakeholder meeting with 15

Luka Stanic

johnsondavid@hotmail.com

stakeholders, most of which were from external marketing agencies; the meeting lasted for 1.5 hours  and of course, nothing actionable came out of the meeting. Most of the external stakeholders had  limited knowledge about the apps, but more importantly, they had no clue about the process, what  problems we were trying to solve and the vision behind our solution. The next stakeholder call we had  with a smaller group and I kicked us off with sharing a compelling story behind the app that had a clear  structure and build up, including context (what was the current state both related to the market and  client that motivated us to take action), vision (one sentence vision of the problem we are trying to  solve), internal and external project goals, overview of the app year-to-date (what have we developed,  tech stack, features, etc.) and lastly, the possibilities for the future, since the launch is just the beginning  of the journey. Having everyone aligned around a clear vision and criteria of building a launch solution,  enabled us we moved into the “What if” phase, where we are currently looking creatively at all the  possibilities and generating ideas on how we are going to launch the app.

Insight

Storytelling truly is a game changer for me with anything that has to with communication and content,  whether it is creating a presentation and presenting or communicating to different stakeholders. Overall,  I think the benefits of storytelling speak for themselves. We have all been on numerous boring  conference calls, uninteresting webinars and dull presentations that we leave exhausted, whereas  hearing a compelling story, on the other hand, is completely different, it moves us, intrigues us and  inspires us; we leave energized and ready to support its cause. As the CLO of Mars Inc. mentioned in the  lecture that most business leaders nowadays are bored with 90% of their everyday conversations, this is  especially where storytelling can make a pivotal difference. In my example above, having all the  stakeholders aligned around the same vision and definition of the problem we are trying to solve,  enabled us to move faster, make meetings actionable and above all, move into the “What if” phase and  generate some great “outside the box” ideas, which the marketing stakeholders would never had done  based on the limited information and insights they received from the client.

Approach

I am very much looking forward to trying out the new design thinking knowledge and tools learned  during this course and already have a couple of thoughts related to the existing project:

-  Storytelling – by leveraging storytelling on the first stakeholder call could have saved us some  time and effort

-  Ethnographic research – reflecting upon a project lifecycle of more than a year long, if I could  redo the ideation phase of our project, I would had applied ethnographic research on end-users  to capture their unarticulated needs, rather than relying only on project stakeholders

-  Journey mapping – plan to apply it on end-users once the apps will be live to have a better  understanding how they interact with the apps and what we can improve/streamline

Using Storytelling Tool for Student Counseling

 Challenge:

I am a faculty of a university and I have to deal with many types of psycho-social problems of the  students. Though my job is mostly academic, still being a mentor and adviser, I need to address  these issues. Students often do not open up at their first interaction. Their symptoms of disturbance  are usually expressed through their attitude in the classroom and other interactions. Some students  are irregular and remain unmindful in the class, others are ill mannered or rough in conduct. Some  students seems stressful and tired and even suffer from psychosomatic physical sickness. The  university has appointed a full time psychologist, with a separate office and facilities, who provides  Psycho-Social Counseling services for the students. But the students have some stigma regarding  communicating the psychologist as they think it will isolate them from others and they will be  considered mentally ill. Hence they sometimes share their problems with teachers and course  advisers. But the problem is teachers can listen to them with empathy and suggest some general  solutions, but they are not expert person for professional counseling. So, the challenge for the  teachers are to detect the students who need help and convince them to communicate the psycho  social counselor.

 Selection:

Just as this course resources mentioned, - through a good story, we could simply convey a message  that has logic. And also that a good story creates a cause and it ignites and unites people to solve  a bigger problem. Keeping the same spirit in mind, I have chosen storytelling as a tool to convince  the students to open up and address their need of counselling and eventually communicate the  Psycho-Social Counselor of the university for better solution of their mental anxiety.

 Application:

As a part of applying storytelling techniques, I have first tried to understand and gain some insights  of the audience, in my case, the students who seems disturbed. I built a good rapport by asking  his/her personal and academic aspects. Then I try to discuss whether the students have gone  through some kind of obstacles or any difficulties. When they share their problems that I feel  should be addressed by the professional psychologist, I suggest them to visit the psychologist of  the university. When the student feel shaky or uncomfortable, I start telling a story regarding how  some of my other students get benefitted from her counseling. I follow a clear sequence for the  purpose. I describe how one of my students could not express her willingness to her family,  regarding reading in a subject of her choice. Instead she has to carry her study in a subject, she  found difficult and not interesting at all just to keep her parent happy. She could not gather the  courage to confront her family in this matter and eventually become depressed and even physically  weak. At this point of time I try to build a suspense in the story and then ask some questions like  what would this girl do to overcome her fear and get her desired life. Then I answer that to gain  her confidence and fight back her trauma, she consult the counsellor working at the university.

And that, she eventually open up to her and found a way out to express her willingness to her father  through a written letter. At this point of time, most of the students become curious about the  outcome and this is the most powerful part of the story, where I explain how the students convinced  her father to shift her from one subject to other. And conclude with how splendid she is doing now.  Then I explain the disturbed student that his/her current status, where he/she is suffering from  problems are the worse situation ever happened. And that if he/she could cross the stigma and take  the necessary steps, this solution could be life changing and worth taking.

 Insight:

In most of the cases, I found this Storytelling Techniques effective. People tend to get influenced  by the story where they can connect themselves emotionally and spiritually. One good story can  lead them to think that if other people have gone through the same situation and could overcome  their problems why not he/she could do it. It helps them to think sequentially about what is, what  if, what wow and what works. The audience could chalk out where they stand right now, where  possibly they can go if they try, what benefit they will get and how they will reach there – all at  once. Thus, storytelling could be a good guild towards design thinking.

 Approach:

Besides the advisors, storytelling tool could be adopted by the organization as a part of their regular  communication options. The organization can develop promotional content using storytelling  techniques to influence the mindset and action of the students and other relevant audience.

APPROACH: Describe what you might do differently next time -- applying the same tool you  selected or a different one -- and the reason(s) why.
