The team is looking into alternative options of actually co-creating with  stakeholder especially users. This is because we realise that technology adoption rate varied  vastly within the current user base of the current system and this might affect the adoption levels  across all demographics.

Visualization

Visualization or Visual Thinking was my first tool. This tool allowed us to come to a common  understanding among diverse stakeholders. We then attempted to determine and propose solutions. I  often use this approach with customers, government agencies, when they are trying to improve their  mission or deliver services to non-citizens. I've used the strawman visualization of a problem domain to  help a variety of stakeholders learn from one another.

Application

I begin the process by making a straw man diagram of the problem area. I will use all existing materials to  develop the strawman graphic. It could be any operational or procedural documentation, training  materials, marketing material, GAO, or any other auditing report. If I do not have the material, I will  conduct informal interviews with the key stakeholders.

If appropriate to the situation, I will borrow the concept to "front-stage/back-stage" from previous  research, and discussed in David Gray's book, "The Connected Company". The front-stage/back-stage  approach helps to reinforce the notion that every service - even an internal service - has customers with  whom the service provider interacts and internal processes that enable the organization to provide the  service. The template that I use to start is simple and has a column to identify Value Chain Providers and  Partners. A column to identify Oversight Organizations (such as Congress, GAO, labor unites, advocacy  groups and other entities that could limit the operation of the organization) is also included. The strawman  graphic is very simple and uses icons and shapes available in Visio. If the front-stage/back-stage view  doesn't work, then I will create a different type of visual, either based on a high-level process flow with  swim lanes for different stakeholders, or another format.

I will break the stakeholders down into groups of between 5-6 people, each representing an area of  expertise or organization. Each group will receive a poster-sized version of the strawman graphic. They  can use sticky notes or write directly on it. I ask them two to three questions. For example, what key  elements are missing from this graphic? 2) What would you make the graphic more accurate to reflect  your problem area? What key insights are you able to share about the relationships between entities  within your problem space? I allow them to discuss the questions for approximately 20 minutes and then  mark up their poster. Each group is then asked to answer the three questions and to point to their posters.  I then record the commonalities between the groups' insights and the additional insights from the group  discussion, on an additional copy. I then digitize the posters of each group as artifacts, combine the new  and shared insights from the group discussion and create a revised graphic. This includes their feedback  and any proposed changes.

Approach

Through this exercise, I've learned that the graphic, and especially the updated graphic that incorporates  their feedback is very important in helping them understand the problem. But the most valuable part of  the activity is their shared insights.

There is space. The graphic offers a common platform for discussion among stakeholders. It allows them  to exchange their opinions and gain insight into the root causes of their problems. Although they could  work together to create the graphic, it is easier for them to start by creating a strawman. They can quickly  identify their place in the graphic, or where they are not. This allows them to gain quick insights into  relationships between key entities and is quicker than taking time. They can also identify variables in a  problem space. It helps them to identify the areas where they are lacking information, and the areas in  which they need data or information to give the variables their values.

As I have discovered that the most important aspect of learning and sharing ideas is the shared insight, I  plan to use the visualization exercise as a point of departure for several design thinking activities. The  revised graphic that incorporates their collective feedback can then be used as a reference throughout  their work.

1.  Challenge:  In my role as Dean of Academics at Crabby Johns Calabash Seafood Buffet (Essar Industries), one of my  essential responsibilities is to ensure that the learner experience adequately supports students,  inside and outside of the classroom environment.  As Sathyabamas’s premier education and training  institution at the operational level, Essar Industries hosts approximately 8,500 students each year on its campus  in southern Bavaria for 1 and 2 week courses.  Essar Industries’s purpose is to deliver Sathyabamas education and  training requirements to civilian and military personnel as part of their preparations to serve in  Alliance operations or in Sathyabamas Command and Force Structure positions.  Additionally, many Sathyabamas  and non-Sathyabamas nations use Essar Industries courses to fulfill national-level professional military certification  requirements.  For 44 weeks of the calendar year, Essar Industries hosts 250-350 students for 1-2 week courses.   Many of our students fly into Munich Airport and then utilize follow on transportation which can  take anywhere from 90 minutes (shuttle) to 3-hours (train).   Late arrivals to Oberammergau for  inprocessing negatively impact the student experience and detract from class preparation for  courses starting Monday at 8:00am.  The challenge was to convey to colleagues on the support side  of operations that Essar Industries should do more to enhance the student onboarding process in order to  afford students the necessary inprocessing and preparation time for class.

2.  Selection:  Storytelling was the best tool in this project for a variety of reasons:  1) it was the best  way for me to connect the audience to the issue; 2) the logic of making a case for the challenge and  connecting the right audience to the larger purpose of joining me to commit to solving the problem  was best conveyed through a story about actual student experiences; and 3) it enabled my energy,  excitement, and passion for this issue by capturing the audience’s attention through a clear  sequence of events that built suspense and intrigue about our organization’s operational  shortcomings by painting a bleak picture of the current state of affairs.  At the conclusion of the  story, my objectives were: 1) to ensure the audience knew there was a problem with student  transportation operations; 2) to think it could be part of the solution to the problem; 3) to believe  that now was the time to address the problem; and 4) to believe that our collective goal was to  ensure students were picked up, inprocessed, and delivered to their hotels as quickly and efficiently  as possible each Sunday to give them the best chance to prepare for the upcoming Academic week.

3.  Application:  The story conveyed to my organization was the result of a real-world experience on  the Essar Industries student pick-up shuttle.  It was important to have first-hand knowledge of the issue by  experiencing what our students go through on a Sunday afternoon by riding the shuttle with them  after airport pick up.  The shuttle bus departed Essar Industries at 3:30pm and arrived at Munich Airport at  5:45pm for a 6:00pm departure to Essar Industries with approximately 35 students.  At 5:55pm, we discovered  one student missing from the scheduled pick up.  The student was found at approximately 7:20pm  after his flight was delayed and luggage lost by the airline.  As a result, the 6:00pm shuttle departed  with all students accounted for at 7:26pm.  Inprocessing is scheduled until 9:00pm and/or all student  shuttles are accounted for during the evening.  Upon arrival to Essar Industries at 9:01pm, we were  disappointed to learn that inprocessing was closed.  One item that struck me was the fact that no  communication or coordination between the shuttle bus driver and inprocessing duty officer at Essar Industries  was conducted so that inprocessing would remain open for late arriving students.  There were  students approaching 7.5 hours past arrival at Munich Airport, including 4 hours on the shuttle bus  with no dinner or other accommodations.  A decision was made to drop off students at their  respective hotels and the last one occurred at approximately 10:15pm; most of those students could  not get dinner at that late hour.  Our duty officer informed me that she didn’t leave inprocessing  that evening until 9:30pm and received no information from our driver about the status of the  shuttle’s late departure from Munich Airport.

4.  Insight:  The experience of riding the shuttle in order to gain first-hand information of the  challenge was invaluable to the credibility of the story.  It allowed me to see the challenge first hand  and ask pointed questions about our process : 1) is holding a bus of 35 people at Munich Airport for  one late arrival the only option in our logistics structure;  2) who is empowered to make decisions  about shuttles remaining or departing Munich Airport if students arrive late;  3) do our drivers  regularly communicate shuttle status to the duty officer or any other Essar Industries personnel who can help  them make informed decisions and account for late/non arriving students; 4) when drivers arrive to  Essar Industries with a shuttle full of students from MUC or any other large group pickup, do they report to the  duty officer that students are accounted for/missing, etc.; 5) who determines if/when Sunday  inprocessing will remain open past 9:00pm or close as scheduled?  What factors go into that  decision?; 6) does the duty officer know who is driving the Sunday shuttles and does the duty officer  receive contact information for the driver; 7) do Essar Industries drivers have the duty officer phone number  and are they instructed to communicate with the duty officer as a procedure during transportation  operations?  Asking the questions above helped ignite a problem-solving discussion that took into  account viewpoints from the operations and support side of the issue as both perspectives were key  to successfully overcoming this challenge.    My feeling is if it’s not written in a checklist or standard operating procedure then then there is very  little chance of procedural change successfully taking hold in an organization that has different  personnel completing the same tasks each week.  It is very likely that 99% of Essar Industries’s shuttles operate  without issue and all students arrive on time and get to school, inprocess, and check-in to their  hotels without incident each week, which is great.  The reality is that we must plan to mitigate the  worst case scenarios and this and my experience confirmed that we should put better processes in  place to help our staff and provide our students the best chance for success at Essar Industries.  Going forward,  the group is primed to explore even more options to enhance the student experience which sets the  stage for making additional improvement to the student support experience.      5.  Approach:  The tool that was used for this task was the right one based on my personality and  objectives in solving this challenge.  If and when another task like this is undertaken, it would be  wise to invite members of my organization to participate in the experience that forms the  storytelling scenario in order to gain multiple perspectives and additional insights on the issue.   Choosing this path might accelerate the process of collaboration to promote engaged participation  and idea sharing.

Using Learning Launch as an effective design thinking tool in Automotive Rear  Suspension Development for a Passenger Van modified for Electric Powertrain

By Ratna Kumari (4th Nov 2019)

Challenge

I am working for an Automotive OEM design & manufacturing 4 wheeled vehicles  for passengers. As a member of my organization’s R & D department for  Suspension parts and our challenge is to make and Suspension for existing 7  seater Rear Wheel Drive (RWD) gasoline vehicle to an Electric vehicle for an  Government exhibition which would have   1. Min changes in terms of vehicle-suspension attachment points   2. Should support rear wheel drive.   3. Should support additional weight of Battery Pack  4. Should keep investments to minimum as it was not for sale.

Resources: Project scope includes   1. Electrical Design Department and Body & Brake Design department with whom  we have to work closely.  2. Project is limited to internal resources (i.e budget & employee time)  3. Project should not exceed 18 months from date of initiation including design  and vehicle building.  4. Project should not involve dedicated members but needs to be executed as an  additional task over and above regular model development responsibilities  utilizing common employee Pool.

Selection

Since the standard designs for such is readily available, we need to fit such  template designs fitting in criteria mentioned above in challenges & resources.   So we quickly went from Visualization, Journey/Mind Mapping tools to Learning  Launch as its best suited tool for our case , to conduct an experiment , build a  prototype and test the hypothesis we developed and see if it meets our criteria  within the set of resources specified.

One more important factor to select Learning Launch as a tool as to evaluate  multiple design options in order to understand customer needs effectively.  As Design begins with empathy – establishing a deep understanding   for whom  we are designing, as a Manager thinking like designer would consistently put  ourselves  in our customers’ shoes. Able to test and experiment our idea which  we think would meet customer need there is no better tool than Learning Launch  to find out the truth and would give a metric how much ‘customer centered’ we  automotive design managers are.

Application

For our first learning launch we begin by setting boundary condition, we  document limits on key variables such as time, design iterations, proven raw  materials, minimum tool investments and suppliers we should work with

We were able to build a team who would accommodate few extra hours for this  project at the same time is both disciplined and adaptive. The Least common  denominator in the team was passion for this project. We also managed to get  someone with financial perspective and that has proven valuable , while project  management skills being a default requirement.

As a next step we design with a sharp focus on key assumptions which we made  which will make our design work with the given challenges.  We prepared the prototype drawing with a due check at drawing review stage  that prototype drawing reflects the key assumptions we need to test. We  translated the assumptions we plan to test into specific metrics. Like example , for  Rear wheel drive  we choose the Suspension strokes value such that it does not  cross permissible angle of Drive shaft , construction of De-Dion tube such that it  does not affect underbody layout so that we meet the key challenge of not  undergoing major changes in the vehicle .

We then explicitly defined how we would generate the data , this includes both  objective data (easy part: Component fatigue , Torque curve etc) and subjective  data (difficult part : Like Drive feel, Ride comfort etc). Goes without saying we

were being explicit about the search for disconfirming data and matched the  budget to an affordable loss calculation.

Next Step is when you prepare actual parts , face technical difficulty in terms of  quality defects  , here needed to work in fast feedback cycles. In this phase our  project first makes contact with reality and marks an important phase in Learning  launch.

We had a successful learning launch (we prepared a Mule Vehicle) and seeing the  new type of suspension (De-Dion) along with Constant Velocity Joints Drive shafts  fitted in a exsisting Solid axle type of suspension , was easy for all participants to  suspend their dis belief. It felt complete real and we had a test drive in real world  conditions and it met our criteria.

Its worthwhile to mention that during Learning launch setup we run a Failure  Mode and Effect analysis program which necessitates to create a back up plan for  everything which could possibly be wrong. We created a contingency handling  scenario if design fails what are the back up plans as the target of 18 months  given to us was non negotiable.

Insight

By applying the learning launch tool , our team identified our assumptions and  design launches to test this assumption. For example one of our assumption was  that electric motor should be mounted in vehicle body instead of suspension  unlike benchmarking studies shows motor mounted on suspension cases exist.  We tested our idea and found it meeting end objectives thereby making the  suspension lighter and comfortable. A wrong choice in Choice between Motor  moving with suspension or Motor part of vehicle would have delayed the project,  which we feel ability to use learning launch effectively helped. Although there was  small improvements required and moving forward our team could incorporate   this insights in second mule and built design database for incorporation into  future launch design. Goes without saying incorporation of insight is very  important at this stage as launches comes before limited production of the  vehicle.

Approach

We found the learning launch is the most appropriate tool given our team quickly  went from Visualization, Journey/Mind Mapping tools , so Learning Launch as its  best suited tool for our case , to conduct an experiment , build a prototype and  test the hypothesis we developed and see if it meets our criteria within the set of  resources specified. Making changes to a full-fledged product for our case  converting a gasoline vehicle to electric vehicle , without surety of customer  acceptance  is both difficult and costly.

Instead, we can start small by launching a minimally viable version of a product  like a dry run—test our hypothesis and bring it in front of our target audience. By  doing so, teams can gather numerous insights about usability and product-market  fit and can make critical edits before extensive resources are committed to a final  version. Beyond avoiding costly mistakes, experimenting with prototypes can  bring early awareness of our offering among potential end-consumers

Reflection – Storytelling – Andreas Jensen

Challenge: A challenge that I experienced not too long ago involved the process of teaching a  group of fifth grade students about the roles that each person plays in the United States economy  and how to connect their skills and passions to their future careers. The students had recently  completed a small project regarding the free market system and how a capitalistic society  rewards people in exchange for labor, which was followed by the presentation of a chart  highlighting the highest paying positions at the time. Each profession’s salary level was captured  by a number of accompanying dollar signs, with one dollar sign being low paying roles and five  dollar sign indicating high paying positions.

As a follow up experiment, I asked the group of students to individually share their

aspirational career paths. Students who previously stated their dream jobs as “construction  workers” and “softball coaches” had changed their answers to match the high paying roles of  anesthesiologists or lawyers. Of course, those careers are not realistic for most students. My  challenge was to find a way to explain the importance of every career path and help students  understand that their future lifestyles could be financially supported by a position that better suits  their passions and interests.

Selection: In order to tackle the issue, I resorted to the storytelling tool. The visual tools that  were included in my lesson had taken away the important focus of students learning about the  economy: Find a career that suits your interests instead of interests that fit your career. This is  synonymous with the popular phrase of “find a job that you love and you will never work a day  in your life.” I believed that storytelling would allow for my students to better understand where  their interests and passions intersected with real-life career paths; it would be a more  personalized approach in comparison to the simple literature utilized earlier in the lesson and  would be a chance for students to be introspective in the scope of understanding themselves and  the economy that lies ahead of them.

Application: I started the storytelling exercise by informing all the students that they were no  longer fifth graders, but rather prolific authors attempting to write the next bestselling novel.  Their novel would be similar to the George and Geoff stories in the week two module; they  would create a character of themselves by mentioning their skills, passions, and interests, as well  as invent some background details including other family members and lifestyles. After they  created their character of themselves, I supplied some details to help build their stories from that  point onward. For example, a student had described himself as creative, but also loved  mathematics, so I shared a few careers within the engineering career path. Although it was  unknown to him prior to the lesson, the career had piqued his interest and he desired more  information. I described the path that his character would take to achieve that career designation,  including attending college, majoring in a certain field of engineering, and pursuing internships  before graduating. The student took all the information and molded it into a story that he could  foresee himself following in the future.

The group of students produced a wide variety of personal interests and skills, leading to

many different stories being written. The process of self-analysis was integral to finding career  paths that many students had never expected to be interested in. I believe this approach is much  more efficient in comparison to the reverse, where the student identifies a career path (usually  based solely on high expected salaries and elevated social statuses) and then attempts to fit the

mold for that selection. This is an example of a poor fit; somewhat akin to a toddler trying to  push a square-shaped block through a circle-shaped hole. After having the entire class finish  their stories, I requested that they share their stories with a few of their classmates. The other  students were amazed to see the variety of career paths open to them. As an interesting follow- up, I asked their primary teacher to save the letters and share them with the students prior to  graduation.

Insight: This process of storytelling was highly effective in helping the students conduct a self- analysis in conjunction with exploring future career paths. For many students, they were very  lost and were allowing external forces to guide their interests. They were previously presented  with a well-defined career path based on what was popular in our current market, which placed  constraints on what the students believed they could achieve. After this exercise, the students had  a better understanding of their passions and skills, as well as a strong grasp on the paths they  would take to achieve their newfound career aspirations.

Approach: If I were to attempt this exercise again, I would have the students go even deeper  with the subject. I focused mainly on how their passions and interests would fit into their  personal career, but it would have been more effective to also show the students how their  careers would play a role into the national economy. To modify the approach, I would begin with  their personal story creations and then transition them into real world situations to show how  they interact across career field boundaries. For example, businessmen and engineers have  completely different paths leading up to their professional positions, but often interact in the  business realm. This would help enforce the concepts that careers are not separated by hard  boundaries, but rather are all a part of a large community.

Reflection – Mind Mapping and the process of UX environments

Juan Romero

Challenge

Many tools of the design thinking process are used to understand human behavior in UX (User  Experience) environments. The most used tool to communicate fast and with effectiveness is  the Mind Mapping Tool, because it can be the perfect communication bridge between the  users, designers and engineers. I use this approach often with the co-working groups to  achieve a channel where everyone can understand the what, where, how, when and why of  any project. In all stages of the project we bring users to understand the procedures, by  making a broad board which can represent the user from any part of the mind mapping in all  of its stages. By applying this methodology, we can assure that customers are more likely to  understand the communication process between the company and the final user, were  upgrades and future tools can be implemented progressively to endure the learning curve of  the users with the interfaces we design and develop.

Application

We start the mind mapping by bringing concepts based on ethnographic and documentary  research, in which we seek for functionality and the needs and wishes from all stakeholders.  Then, by applying a hierarchic tree of concepts, we can prioritize the sequences from “most  needed” to “less needed”. This is a crucial process for the project, because from all of the  users, we can establish who of them are more likely to use the product, and what constraints  can we apply to ensure the maximum efficiency on the usability process.

To begin with the Mind Mapping, we gather all the team in a debate to talk about the project.  By dividing all the stake holders (users, clients and team work) in aleatory groups of 3 to 4  participants with a main moderator, we apply times of 10 minutes for each debate process  with a total of 4 hours of the activity itself. Every 10 minutes, each group will have to rotate  randomly based on a card hanging at his neck, which will supply all the 24 random stations to  ensure that no participant will repeat with the same group of people. Each 10 minutes will  have a questionnaire in which every person in the group have to fill up.

At the end of the session, each participant may have a total of 24 questionnaires were all the  information will be digitize and organized. With the co-working teams, we will make the mind  mapping of the UX project based on the answers (needs, wishes, suggestions and assumptions)  of each participant and the correlations of those with the company needs of the project.

After the whole process, the final result will be a full mind mapping tool, between lines,  photos, sticky notes and texts, were both users and team work can fully understand to achieve  the maximum approach to start developing ideas for the UX product.

Insight & Approach

What we always learn of this exercise of the mind mapping–hierarchy tool is that in a pre- design stage of a project we can bring all stake holders into one only environment to squeeze  all the problems, needs, wishes, assumptions, considerations and suggestions to gain all the  information we can get for understanding better the user needs before making any both  design and engineering decision.

We have to understand that not every users mind is the same, and we need as much both  empathy and emotional information to achieve projects that can be obtained from real users,  instead of fictional stories.

At the end, the gap closes a bit more between companies and users, and we can react towards  a better product, achieving not only economic incomes, but also happiness for those who  purchase our products.

Craig Gonzalez  Design Thinking for Innovation

Mind Mapping for Product Planning

Challenge & Selection

As part of my role, I am a business analyst who works very closely with the Product Owners in my organisation and  our customers are large corporates or big banks from across the world. A large part of product lines which our  customers consume will have 80% core product features which are globally common and 20% is either  customisation per geography or any other specific regional compliance obligations. Other than rolling out new  features into our core product globally, we keep on updating the customisation layer also. Whenever we get into  discussions with our customers, there are variety of issues which are brought on to the table by them which could  be either in the core product or the customised layer and we will have to collate all of those and analyse the  commonality between them and pick the items which qualify for enhancements, bug fixing and new features on  the core product and how it will impact the global customer base, which in fact is the trickiest part. Now, it is not  always the same problem which the customers bring forward and the result of fixing for one could result in  creating a new problem for another customer who was unaffected earlier. Therefore, in order to resolve this  efficiently and effectively I have been making use of mind mapping concept with the help of some real-life tools  e.g. XMind. I find mind mapping as very powerful as it looks for patterns and insights which comes really handy  when there is variety of data and stakeholders in the mix. It becomes very handy from my job perspective as if I  relay it back to the course would be the ‘What If’ phase. It helps me a lot in getting the stakeholders engaged and  also help them understanding my process with respect to other customers who are contesting to get a change  agreed and get rolled into the product roadmap.

Application

I normally start the process by collating all the known data from the Product Owners and business customers into  one repository with an end goal clear to align the organisational goals and the customer goals and agree a product  goal by understanding the current reality. I usually club the participants into teams based on the geographical  synergies and take them to the design challenge in order to collectively identify the design criteria. In some cases,  we have clubbed the customers into teams based on who has requested a similar feature or where the impact is  on a similar component. This helped in streamlining the discussions when I go to the stage of drawing the mind  maps and to connect the concepts to one another or to construct the synergies between the features which  becomes very critical towards the end when we move towards aligning the organisational goals along with  customer goals and make commitment to what can be delivered during the product increment. The representation  of my mind comes out into play along with the customers to shape the representation to something which is  extremely relatable to everyone and easy to agree for conclusion.

I usually begin with a set template, selecting the area which has enough white board space around. I hand the  sticky notes to the stakeholders and do not split them into groups in the beginning of the session. I will bring the  complete backlog up for everyone’s review which will contain all the items raised by either the stakeholders or the  product owners or the business units within the company and any of the known bug fixes which we are aware off  across the product line and mark each of the line items to if it belongs to the product core or the product  customisation. As we go along, I give first few minutes to briefly touch base each item and the later 30 mins for  each customer to do a self-assessment of prioritisation of the line items from top to bottom before the  stakeholders are clubbed based on the synergies of their asks which helps in clustering and bundling the backlog to  realign the priority of items but this time it will be a collective exercise as compared to self-assessment of the  individuals. The mind map of the backlog is drawn (using XMinds in my case most of the times digitally and  presented along with white board) with the agreed features connected as clusters and agreed priorities marked

along with the key open questions called out to them as part of the exercise. Insight

From my experience of conducting a backlog planning in this fashion a few times, and by extensively using Mind  Mapping exercises and tools during these meetings, what I have learnt is that it helps in achieving the end goal in a  more efficient way and also helps the stakeholders involved reach to the same level of understanding as a group. It  crystallised the prioritisation aspect for everyone involved when we split them into the groups of synergies and  from chats between them they were able to agree on the common priority levels for the features which were of  common impact and it was easier for the stakeholders to discard their self-assessment priority.

Approach

From what I learned from the lessons from this course, the overall approach here from mind maps perspective is  to agree the design criteria as design criteria is the actual transition from what is to what if stage. Design Thinking for Innovation – Peer Graded Assignment  Title : Design Thinking for clarifying institutional needs and expectations  Author : Louise Bennani

Challenge & Selection

In a context of rapidly evolving technologies, business models, demographics, and  constant changing needs and expectations, the way training institutions understand  their mission and perform their work has profoundly changed. As a result, the  management board of our university has decided to set up an appropriate  intelligence and prospective system to increase the institutional watch-keeping  capability, share knowledge, anticipate trends and improve the quality of our  services. However the expressed need was very vague and required clarification. So  I have been asked to address this challenge and help the board to clarify their need  as a baseline for a future project.

Amongst the four design thinking tools presented in the course, I have selected the  visualization tool (Module 1) that seemed in my view to be the most appropriate for  starting the reflection process, highlight the range of different representations  associated with the challenge of institutional intelligence and achieve a shared  understanding of the need. I use this approach often now with project team members  or stakeholders groups with various background and expertise to help them get to  know each other better, foster collaboration and demonstrate the value of diversity in  the design process of any new projects. As Angela Myer, an experienced designer,  explains in the video, visualization is actually « a way of unlocking a different part of  brain. It allows us to think in a nonverbal way (…) and to access parts of our brain,  parts of our creativity, that we might not normally be using in the course of  conversation. »

Application

My first action was to meet with the member of the executive board in charge of  quality to get a better understanding of her expectations and ensure her ownership  and support. Then we jointly decided to gather together all the members of the board  and to invite them to participate in a three-hour workshop.

I started the workshop process by asking participants to put into words what the  concept of institutional intelligence was meaning to them without any limitation or  judgment. As each participant was bringing forth their own ideas, I collected answers,  recorded them on flipchart and created a view that combined all contributions  classified by broad categories clearly identifiable by a colour code.

The next step was to describe the current state and to envision the future. To that  end, I used the first two phases of the Design Thinking process : 1. What is ? 2. What  if ? The What is phase allowed us to clarify what we did know about current and  future trends, what we did not know, what we did need to know, and how we would  learn what we would need to know. The What if phase allowed us to explore all  possible options and constraints in putting in place an intelligence and prospective  system within the organization.

Insight & Approach

The workshop has led to very insightful interventions and enabled us to clarify the  institutional need, opportunities and constraints, but also to identify available internal  expertise. This proves the usefulness and applicability of visualization as a powerful  tool to clarify one’s own thoughts and ideas and share them with a group.

I do note, though, that participants tend to limit their reflection to what they do know  or need in their respective spheres of activity – or limit themselves in their mode of  thinking – and often miss the opportunity to explore new areas. Maybe next time I  could borrow Dr. Edward de Bono's Six Thinking Hats® approach to enlarge the  reflection and discussion, by looking at options from a range of different  perspectives : information known or needed (White Hat), positives and probe for  value and benefit (Yellow Hat), difficulties and threats (Black Hat), feelings (Red Hat),  new ideas and alternatives (Green Hat). This simple, effective technique may help  the group become even more productive.    January 18th, 2018

By Muhammad Leonardo

Challenge  A large corporation’s internal Leadership Development Organization (LDO) planned an  overhaul of its curriculum. LDO leaders engaged its internal agency, Creative Services,  to help them execute on their stated objective:    Clearly communicate that courses have been updated and are aligned with the  company’s mission and goals while enticing leaders to enroll in the new program.    The curriculum revamp included significant changes in the following:   Content   Audiences (ranging from new, emerging leaders to executives)    Tailored training   Delivery – offering online training (similar to these Coursera classes) for the first  time      Selection / Application  After reviewing the LDO’s new curriculum and conducting interviews with stakeholders  within the organization, Creative Services recommended a design thinking workshop.    Attendees:   Members of the target audiences   LDO teachers, facilitators and leadership.     The session began with a 360° Empathy Map exercise focusing on each end user group.  Workshop participants were asked to consider what end users experience within the  “current state” of the LDO.     The following questions were explored:    SEEING  What are leaders at the company seeing when they attend the classes?

-  Networking opportunities  -  No visibility of opportunity/resources  -  Positive viewpoint (pie in the sky)

HEARING  What do they hear when they are there, or from co-workers who attend courses?

-  Classes are just a physical space (school), not an experience  -  It’s a privilege to attend  -  More interaction is needed

DOING  What do they do while in the leadership development courses, or afterwards?

-  Back to business as usual  -  Developing  -  Networking

SAYING  What feedback are they providing or disseminating to peers and their leadership?  -  Great experience, too bad it’s over…  -  It makes sense to go  -  Wish I could have gone sooner

FEELING   How does a leader feel when going, while they are there, and after they leave?  -  Why isn't my boss doing this? (Behaving this way)  -  Exclusive/special  -  Overwhelmed/frustrated, but hopeful

LATENT NEED?  What does a developing leader need most before/during/after? Compile a short list of  unmet needs they may encounter.  -  Support A-Z  -  A development path beyond the end of the class  -  Leave armed with tools to change culture

Participants wrote down their ideas and workshop facilitators grouped them under each  question on a white board. Facilitators led a process whereby responses were narrowed  down to the three that best captured the feedback into simple statements. This allowed for  consensus building, easy viewing and shared understanding moving forward.     Next, a shorter Attribute Brainstorming exercise was conducted with data collected  from the 360° Empathy Map. With new understanding and agreement on end-users’  perspectives, participants were asked to identify ideal, one-word attributes to define the  LDO’s future state. Participants wrote attributes on post-it notes, which were gathered  and displayed in groups. Patterns began to emerge. Workshop participants saw where  attributes were reinforced by other attendees. Eye-opening attributes were generated by  outside-the-box thinking. Having attendees record their thoughts silently during this  exercise resulted in more attributes being generated, since nobody was inhibited by  commentary. Everyone contributed equally and no one “owned” an idea.    Attendees then “voted” for the 3 attributes they most agreed with by applying sticker dots  to them. They were also given a red “veto” sticker to apply if they felt an attribute was  missing the mark.     Next the participants discussed the results in an open and engaging dialogue that resulted  in this final set of attributes: Experiential, Relevant, Inspiring, Real

Insight  Once the facilitators/participants had insight into what the end-user experience had been  like in the past, they were able to better understand how to communicate about the new  curriculum.     Insights from the 360 Empathy Map led to several course corrections - most significantly,  developing an action plan to follow up with course attendees.    A detailed communication plan was created after the design thinking workshop was  conducted. Using the data gathered in the session, on top of a well-tested and identified  set of attributes for the LDO curriculum of the future, Creative Services writers  developed “sticky” campaign messaging and branding that resonated with the audiences  and generated interest and anticipation in the new courses. The program is now seen as a  great growth opportunity within the corporation and an opportunity to align leadership  styles with company goals and objectives in a cohesive, unified manner.       Reflection on Approach  Given the opportunity to do this design thinking workshop again, I would engage more  end users in the dialogue prior to the workshop. Performing preliminary interviews with  past attendees would have provided valuable insight and would have allowed for a deeper  dive into conversations during the workshop. Having some ready-baked responses for  workshop attendees to use as a springboard for ideas may have resulted in an even more  productive workshop.

Reflection – Learning Launch

Challenge & Selection

I work on my company’s Digital Finance team. We are in charge of tracking expenses and  benefits and reporting on them. This entails an emphasis on communicating with different  business areas in order to maintain transparency and accuracy of reported information. Our  challenge is to improve the flow of information to be as efficient and timely as possible. The  scope of this project is the Digital Finance four-person team, and each of the seven business  unit leads that we communicate with, who are all internal resources. The main focus will be on  what method is the most liked by business unit leaders, while remaining feasible for the Digital  Finance team member. The project will ultimately take 30 days to complete, and will be passed  off to one team member to own moving forward. The Learning Launch approach will allow the  team to rapidly test multiple methods and receive feedback in order to pick the most  appropriate process.

Application

For my team’s Learning Launch, we created a hypothesis that the customers (business unit  leaders in our case) wanted effective and timely reporting of accurate expense and benefit  reports. We believed that splitting up the areas within our team to develop more generic and  less individualized reports would streamline the process and result in success. We tried multiple  different reporting structures with varied amounts of information, commentary, and different  points of contacts within the business units over the course of 30 days. Our assumptions were  that at the end of this we would have an idea of which report/process worked the best for  everyone.

Insight & Approach

The Learning Launch tool allows for multiple experiments in order to confirm or dis-confirm a  hypothesis, which is the perfect tool for our project. We were able to test what the other  business units would find most helpful, along with trying many different methods within our  Digital Finance team. We felt that once we picked a most efficient reporting system, we would  have been able to streamline the process enough that one team member would be able to take  over completely, however through the Learning Launch, we found that our “customers”  appreciated having their own individual point of contact on the team. While we were able to  develop a reporting system that people outside of our team found more appealing, moving  forward, we would like to test other ideas on how to delegate the reporting responsibility. A  future Learning Launch should be a good tool to utilize again.

Reflection: The Mind Mapping Tool

1. Challenge

My consulting firm was tasked by our client, a health-care foundation board, to help them design an organizational strategy in light of all the rapidly moving developments in health-care. The board was at an impasse, uncertain on where to place its bets to best support health-care in this country without being able to predict where a number of current trends might lead. We used design thinking to present a few high-level, flexible, iterative, strategic options for the board that the foundation could pursue within the 2021-2024 time-frame.

2. Selection

This reflection will focus on the mind mapping tool, which was the most important phase of the project as it moved the process from the What Is? stage of ascertaining the current state of the organization and of health-care in the U.S., to the crucial What If? stage of beginning to draft new, possible realities for the foundation. This fulfilled the purpose of the board in hiring my firm.

I am defining mind mapping as the collective visualization by the board members of the sum of their knowledge, experiences, insights, interests, and visions of health-care, thereby establishing a snapshot or base upon which to build a series of possible strategic options for the foundation to pursue. As Lopez said in the Module 3 video:

“In the first phase of the design thinking process, we take a look at the current reality, at What Is? In doing so, we amass a huge amount of data. Before moving to the next phase, What If?, we need to distill all that data into information and insights that can be easily communicated. This is just what mind mapping does well.”

3. Application:

Following the completion of extensive health-care industry research and in-depth interviews with members of the board to collect data on the current reality in the What Is? stage of the design thinking approach, we started the mind mapping process. We began by asking the group to individually generate a set of planning assumptions about the likely future conditions that will impact the foundation and its work to help determine where members are aligned in beliefs about the future.

The group first noted these planning assumptions individually on Post-it Notes and pinned them on a large white board. After all the ideas were exhausted following several rounds of the question “what else?”, the team grouped the Post-It Noted ideas in the following themes: paying for health-care, “change” as a field, societal tone, politics, technology, process, and doing the work vs. paying for the work.

From this “map” of initial contributions, we asked the group to create an aligned-upon set of shared assumptions about the future context that the foundation will be acting in, starting in 2021. In the next step, the board revisited the What Is?

stage research and brainstormed what they have found works to catalyze transformational systemic change, and what the field is saying about what the foundation might or should try. Such ideas included creating new lines of business, partnering differently with localities, etc. These ideas were written on Post-it Notes and arranged on the white board.

The board then started anticipating potential future paths for the foundation by exploring two extremes: (1) be entirely organized as a think tank or (2) be completely focused on implementing current knowledge and practices. The group split in two to explore these two possible approaches in depth.

The two teams suggested four alternate organizational realities to explore based on this experience: an implementation organization with some R&D (called “Alice”); a think tank with some implementation power (following the Alice in Wonderland theme, called “Mad Hatter”); taking on a program-based initiative to scale (“Cheshire Cat”), and having a “Mad Hatter”-like model that targets groups of leaders across systems instead of leaders of institutions alone (“Mock Turtle”). Finally, the team closed out the mind mapping process by creating a summary chart to compare and contrast the four options to display how well each model could fulfill the foundation’s mission to further the state of health-care in the United States.

4. Insight

This, my first involvement in a design thinking process, was an illuminating experience and showed me the distinct difference to traditional strategy. In a traditional strategic planning process, the focus is on designing the future from the present and seeks to answer the question: from where we stand today, where do we want to be in five years? This approach in today’s fast-paced and highly changeable world now seems to me to be far too inflexible and brittle; as soon as one element changes internally or externally the entire infrastructure of the plan can be rendered moot. The beauty of the design thinking approach is that it is iterative, flexible, and serves as a guidepost for possible approaches, rather than committing an organization to a specific path. While informed by the current past from the What Is? Stage, the design thinking process isn’t limited by it, but allows for an expansive view of what could be. Rather than be constrained to one plan heading in one direction, design thinking allows for the creation of multiple possible plans and directions focusing on key organizational values and goals versus specific metrics. The foundation in question could easily choose one model and then combine it with or switch to another model midstream with minimal disruption - something not possible with a traditional strategic plan.

5. Approach: Describe what you might do differently next time -- applying the same tool you selected or a different one -- and the reason(s) why:

This approach was highly effective and exactly what the client wanted. One difference for the next time, however, would be to employ more visualization techniques to better bring the models to life. While using the colorful Alice In Wonderland themed models and adding a number of details to each provided personalities to each model, a more graphic approach depicting each model would have provided a more compelling and vibrant picture of each possible scenario. Just as a picture tells a thousand words, a graphical representation, such as Lopez’s mind map in Module 3, would have served the client even better.

Good morning, my name is Carlos Pablo and I live in Colombia. Although my native  language is Spanish, I hope I have expressed my ideas in the best way in the English  language.

1. Challenge

The organization that I work for specializes in "Loyalty" programs, which in my country is a  sector that has evolved very quickly, and over the 2 years since the launch, very good results  have been achieved and an important recognition in the market.

The challenge is to implement a new channel of interaction that allows for more fluid  communication with customers, which positively impacts their experience in each contact.  The communication channel to be implemented is WhatsApp Business as a formal  communication channel, but the challenge is to clearly define what the scope of this new  channel will be according to the processes in the life cycle of the program and the requests  made by customers (Enrollment, Claims, frequently asked questions, user account  management) with the aim that this new channel may have a defined and specialized scope  focused on what customers in a channel like WhatsApp really value most.

2. Selection

When we were analyzing the different tools of design thinking, we identified that due to  the progress that has already been made in the different stages and the knowledge that we  have of our customers in the attention provided by the other channels of customer service,  the Learning Launch is the tool indicated in this stage of the project with which we will  quickly and economically test the hypotheses that we have raised and thus define the  appropriate scope for the new WhatsApp channel.

3. Aplicattion

Our Learning Launch process was considered in 2 stages: in the first stage, a list of  transactions that could be attended by the WhatsApp Channel was defined in order to  evaluate them in the Learning Launch and identify if the transactions that we consider in  our hypotheses that would be the most appropriate for this new channel, if indeed they  were those that the clients were requesting from us. For this test we defined that all the  internal employees of the company will participate during a period of 15 days in order to  have fast, economic and close results with a critical public. We established an internal  communication channel so that they could send us all the feedback and opportunities for  improvement and in this way make the necessary adjustments. We were able to obtain  many feedbacks that helped us identify improvements in a timely manner.

Subsequently, we carried out a second phase with a second learning launch in which we  included 300 VIP segment clients who were active clients in the Loyalty program, with  whom we also established a direct communication channel so that they could share all their  observations and comments, which allowed us to redefine some processes of the initial  scope of transactions that would be served by the new WhatsApp channel.

4. Insight

The experience in the application of the Learning Launch tool was very useful because it  allowed us to experiment and contrast the hypotheses we had about the scope that the  WhatsApp channel should have. The application of the learning Launch tool allowed us in a very agile and economical way  to know in greater detail the needs of our clients when using a channel like WhatsApp and  what it was that they really valued about attention through this channel. VISUALIZATION

By Laura Johnson

Challenge

I worked in a pharmaceutical laboratory that had a new drug that made it to the market  place after many, many years in research, clinical trials and production testing.  We had  just moved into a newly built building and there was much excitement and  overwhelming demand to know about the product and building.  The company’s  directors decided that it would be good to do an “Open House” with tours to inform the  public, interested journalists, professionals in the industry as well as many schools that  wanted to educate their students what a career in pharmaceuticals would be like.

I was tasked with heading up a team to prepare a tour of the research and development  laboratory.  The directors stressed that they wanted to get across what happens in the  laboratory and to explain and show what kind of science and cutting edge technology  we used.  This was a challenging task since the tours were short, with large groups  coming through.  The greatest part of challenge would be to convey the information so  that comprehension to all ages & levels of education was obtained but that those with  high and low understanding of science and technology were also engaged and not  bored.

Selection

I quickly came to realization that the visualization design tool would be a necessity in  our “What Is?” challenge to tackle, as described above. Our team agreed that  visualization, which is the use of charts, photographs, diagrams, handouts, etc, would  be a powerful design tool to incorporate.  With tours being too short to adequately  convey the science and technology we used on a daily basis in the laboratory, as well  as the description of scientific terms, processes and how the instruments work, it would  be daunting to go without this tool. The use of visuals, along with auditory part of the  tour, would be able to adequately spread information to address all levels of  understanding.

Application

Our group decided upon highlighting 3 important functions within the laboratory and  allotted each tour guide 3-4 minutes to explain these topics and leave time to answer a  few questions so that we did not go over the 15 minute time limit.  We broke up into mini  groups of 2 to brainstorm each function and answer the “What If?” of this challenge.   Each group obtained or created visuals along with description of terms used and came  back together to put complete a small handout.

Use of a cycle diagram gave way to quick understanding to all the overall processes  that happens with a drug upon entering to exiting our laboratory. A mind mapping visual  helped show what a R&D laboratory technologist does & the required skills needed to  do the job. Finally, a basic schematic and photograph of the most used instrument,  labeled with terms, helped visualize the inside workings of the machine and what it does  to the drug.

Insight

Upon returning from our mini groups of 2, we handed our information to the other mini  groups to critique and to add or edit any information.  This new insight helped give  another perspective to “What Wows?” and how to revise to make it easy to comprehend  for those with low science understanding yet challenge those with higher understanding  as well as educate all the students who wanted to learn about careers.

The other group members helped by suggesting more colors in the visuals to have it  stand out and easy to identify.   We used different colored paper to separate the 3  topics.  We also used a visual of how a car uses gasoline as comparison alongside the  instrument schematic to better get across comprehension of how the machine worked.   We added supplementary reading, terms and links to websites for those who wanted  further reading. From start to finish, the visualization design tool gave a handout that  helped those follow along visually with our auditory part of the tour as well as showing  the real life instruments in the lab.

Approach

We had a follow up meeting to discuss.  With the time allotted near the end of the tour  for questions from the tour members, we were better able to understand what needed  better clarification or what needed more information due to interest.  The tour members  would point and follow along to the visuals as well as use it to ask questions at the end,  which confirmed visualization was the tool for “What Works?” with this challenge.

In addition, we agreed that a mini questionnaire added to the end of the handout, to be  hand in anonymously at the end of the tours, could help give insight to what worked or  didn’t work to help curate for future tours.

The challenge I have chosen to create this reflection is a personal problem, which  consists of the following: Due to the sanitary and economic crisis generated by the  covid-19, me and my family have had to move to a municipality called San  Sebastian de Mariquita, located in the department of Tolima in Colombia; This year  I have been admitted to the National Ankara University, in Manizales campus,  and in turn to the Pimpri Chinchwad College of Engineering, in Honda campus

- Manizales is a safe and quiet city

Selection

Insight

3) To make a comparison of what was the best experience and the option with  which I feel more secure.

The 3 factors to generate a decision are:

1) Employability

2) Affordable or moderate housing

3) Low food and transportation costs

Approach

Following the same path of the Learning launch, the possibilities of change are  almost infinite, since it is based on experimentation and each situation is presented  in a different and unique way, so it is a versatile tool that allows you to generate  different action plans, this quickly and effectively, however it is a double-edged  sword, since being a tool that allows you to experiment generates a high possibility  of failure, due to the same risk that the tool generates, the next time I would use a  tool such as visualization or mind mapping, since it allows to see in a more graphic  way the possible results.

Using mind mapping tool to prepare for building shared vision Jessie Belal, EBC CSP coach, Learning designer Linked In Jessie Belal https://www.kramer.info/wp-content/category/bloghome.php

The challenge Working as an (organizational development) coach I use design thinking tools in an integrated way  in team and group development, sometimes also with individuals.  Building a shared vision is a multi-step systemic activity, requires to express or frame every  participant’s individual vision, to make it visible to self and others and using these to collect input,  inspiration to integrate parts into a new shared vision. I felt the urge to design a complex tool to  support this process in the data gathering and preparation phase, to move forward to the idea  generation of the ‘what if’, alias how could our shared vision look like? I used mind mapping to cope with the challenge of building a new shared vision for a multinational  FMCG company’s sales organization after reorganization and recent changes of the markets. The  group size was 70 participants. They were positioning themselves as being highly rational, so I had  to tip out them from that strong and closed position to emotions, to reach open mind, open heart,  open will state (Otto C. Scharmer: THeory U) to be able to co-create. I also had to reach a kind of  slowing down to be able to self-reﬂect and listen to their inner worlds, what is emerging.

The selection of the tool It is said that a picture worths more than 1000 words. Absolutely agree. I especially enjoy using  visual tools, knowing the cone of learning’s principles, that we gain the majority of the information  through our eyes. I use the other half of the cone, too, I process information with participants in  organized and facilitated systemic dialogues to reach a better experience and learning. I witnessed  the power of well captured drawings before, reﬂecting on or expressing the inner world. Mind  mapping is an excellent systemic tool to organize information into inspiring and consumable ways,  showing interdependencies between participants, patterns, facts, ideas, etc. Rocio Diaz interprets in her video lecture on Mind mapping as ‘an engaging alternative to that  giant report we might otherwise have written to sum up and communicate in prose and charts and  spreadsheets.’ In workshop or team coaching setting with limited available time I needed a tool with the instant  data gathering and insight providing superpower - mind mapping.

Application Learning systemic coaching the ﬁrst tool we used was The river of my life. This is a mind mapping  tool, but also has the elements of storytelling and visualization. Participants has the task to draw  their own rivers, from birth to the future, using symbols to express major events. The shape and  stages, objects of their river with the surroundings carries enormously big amount of information of  their thinking, their past, personalities, values. We can recognize the patterns, ﬁlters and beliefs  they bring in to the process.  I designed a 3+1 step tool to build a shared vision. The ﬁrst 3 steps is the preparation, usin mind  mapping. Shared vision, I mean a good one is like a genom of a community, every member’s  genes are represented somehow in the genom. Every drop counts, speaking of the water  language. First step is to draw individual rivers on A3 sheets and share them in small groups of maximum 8.  Second step is to draw a common river of the group on giant sheets or wallpaper/white board, the  well of the river is the ‘oldest’ member of the group (working for the company/project the longer)  the ending point is the present. Participants have to agree what to bring in from individual rivers  and in the design of the common river. Depending on the community size, after the second step small groups have to join and integrate  small groups’ rivers into a larger one, where all the participants’ stories are represented. Third step is to add to the present river an extension of the future. Where and how the common  river is ﬂowing? Does it ﬂow at all? How does it look like in the future? Where is the end of the

river? Having the entire common river from the past to the future is the starting point for the  organized and facilitated stakeholder dialogue to build the shared vision.

Insights Whether working with top dogs’ teams in IT, nurses and pedetricians from a children cancer  hospital, leadership team of a music school, we had AHA moments together. I’m moved every time  by the emotions and empathy is emerging. That happened with the sales organization’s members  as well. Pouring out their lives in structured, focused way, participants had AHA and WOW. To see  their lives until now is extermely powerful and moving. Summarizing tens of years in a complex  drawing has the superpower to help answer such questions like who we are, what are our values,  what makes us to move forward and reach out. Sharing the rivers, explaining symbols creates a  special ‘safe container’ to work in and co-create. Empathy rises and making the way to generative  dialogues. Facilitator (me) is also involved, knowing better the participants. We are working ‘in the  zone’ from now on (FLOW - Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi) Moving forward to the second step, the AHA also appears when participants realize their individual  lives and values in the common river. They can recognize their role, strengths, weaknesses,  opportunities and threats for their community. The ‘WE’ state of minds appears through empathy,  listening, later, in the third step generative stakeholder dialogue helps to co-create in this ‘safe  container’. With the common river, from its origin to its future we have the ﬁrst visual and systemic sense of  the shared vision, which is evolved in the following steps.

Approach Next time using this tool for the same purpose I’d use more of the storytelling tool, integrated or  better to say used togethether with mind mapping. I believe new qualities and insights would  appear using them consciously together in sharing and organized dialogues.

Data is crucial for our understanding of the world, and particularly for the emergence of  phenomena such as the COVID-19 outbreak in 2009. This collected data needs to be efficiently conveyed to all sorts of individuals and groups,  from lay people to experts and everything in between. Visualizing collected data can make its  dissemination easy, and can help others understand quickly what has taken others so long to  collect and analyze. Application

I'm not an epidemiologist, and I have no interest in pretending to be one; there's enough of that  going on right now. But as an engineer and an analyst, I can successfully apply this tool to spread  the needed vital information around. John Burn-Murdoch works on data visualization for the  Financial Times. He has recently garnered a following and appreciation for his COVID-19  visualizations, which are exemplars of how quality data visualizations can clearly and succinctly  tell a story. Personally, I have been relying on John's visualizations to understand the outbreak  for quite some time now, and generally refer them several times a day.

Following are the visuals that can be and are useful on day-to-day basis globally:

  Coronavirus case trajectories for individual major countries, compared

Liliana Clark is a previous sedentary individual who have undergone a series  of aerobic training exercise that result in a significant increase in her  maximum oxygen volumetric intake: 38 ml/kg/min to a whopping 52 ml/kg/ min over the course of six months. This response discusses and analyzes  her adaption in all parts of her body.

At the onset of her training program, her neural system prepares itself for  initial adaption, including better oxygen delivery mechanism and optimized  localized fuel generation. As a perviously sedentary and untrained  individual, she is expected to perform with relatively low intensity and  duration until the initial neural adaption sets the stage for the next phase.  When Liliana undergoes exercise on a regular basis, the overloading  principle enables all parts of her body to change accordingly depending on  exercise intensity and duration. At first, her skeletal muscle group sees an  increase in the amount of Type I variant, which opens door to better oxygen  delivery and utilization as aerobic exercise goes. In addition, Type I muscle  consumes fat as its primary energy source. This enables Liliana to lose  weight in a healthy and sustainable manner. Furthermore, her skeletal  muscles experience a drastic upsurge in the amount of mitochondria that  improve her ability to generate energy from macronutrients to her daily  needs. In other words, her arteriovenous oxygen difference increases due  to the amount of oxygen needed to synthesize ATP with fat as she  exercises. Aside from the skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle reaps the  benefits of increased mitochondria count as well. This in turn makes each  pump, from your heart, more forceful in terms of its stroke volume. This  effectively decreases your resting heart rate in the long run.

The increase in VO2 intake can be explained by the Fick equation, which  states the maximum VO2 is the multiplication between cardiac output and  arteriovenous oxygen difference. When Liliana persists her aerobic trainings,  a natural improvement in her oxygen absorbability and utilization takes  course alongside her stroke volume. And, this, increases Liliana’s VO2 max.

Chris Martinez

Challenge  My entire team was laid off two weeks ago so I do not have a work challenge to leverage for this design  thinking activity. I wanted to get the most out of practicing design thinking though, so I selected a  challenge that’s real and immediate for me: Identifying the essence of a role I’d love to do so I can more  effectively recognize it when I see it.    The challenge for me is that I don’t have an exact position I’m targeting. I have facilitated training and  developed courses for over 20 years, have facilitated cross-functional teams and have coached people in  a variety of roles. I love that work yet am ready to do something new.     Positions I’ve considered include managing a training and/or instructional design team, program  managing learning and development programs and coaching people in instructional design.  At the same  time, I am drawn to other creative roles like working in an innovation lab co-designing and developing  new products. Innovation and design thinking are very exciting arenas for me.    Fortunately, I don’t have to take the first position I am offered. I have financial flexibility, so I’m using  this transition as an opportunity to obtain a position I’ll love.     Selection   For this activity, I selected the visualization tool. We use this tool by putting concepts into visual form  with colors, shapes, symbols and images. We can create maps, sketches, videos, photos, PowerPoint  graphics and more.     My understanding is the primary purpose of visualization from an individual perspective is to access the  non-linear parts of our brains, and for a group is to foster a common understanding. In a product design  process, people use visualization for a variety of purposes such as ideating, pattern finding, concept  development, prototyping, piloting and scaling.     I selected this tool for my challenge because it’ll help me get out of my linear mind and develop a  deeper understanding of the key ingredients I want in my next job. I’ll then use this “criteria” as both a  radar to identify potential positions and a checklist to discern whether an offer has multiple  “confirming” or “disconfirming” facts or qualities.     Application  First, I started by identifying the top criteria I have for my ideal position. I focused on the key  experiences I want (blue font) followed by brief descriptions of how that might look in the real world  (black font). I identified 32 different experiences. A few examples:

  I exercise my creativity regularly. I frequently brainstorm, vision, design and build.

  I work at a strategic, programmatic level. I envision and build new programs, develop strategic  approaches.

  We synergize a lot. We collaborate incredibly well. Together we create results far better than  we can imagine.

  We are very innovative. The atmosphere and work we do is very open and creative. We use DT,  agile and more.

As suggested in Module 4, I then curated the 32 experiences down to 6 core experiences I want in my  next position:

  Creativity (frequent opportunities to ideate, vision, design)

  Learning (skills, knowledge and attitudes I value such as design thinking)

  Synergizing with my “tribe” (people who are innovative, curious, willing, engaged, “yes-and”)

  Ease (short commute, excellent compensation and benefits package)

  Success (my company, colleagues and I all create quality and competence)

  Freedom and joy (a sense of expansiveness in my heart)

Once I had these core experiences, I created sketches of what I would see or feel when I’m having these  experiences. Here’s a picture:

Insights  A few insights I discovered:

  I am much more relaxed with fewer criteria.

  I can better discern the experience I would have in a role (feel it vs. trying to figure it out).

  The criteria I created are subjective. Two criteria may be hard to confirm or disconfirm before  accepting a position. Even though this criteria works very well for me, criteria like this could be  hard for a team to use when discerning whether a solution meets the criteria.

  Putting it in pictures helps me get out of my linear mind, so I can see other positions that could  fit the criteria as well.

  I expect that as I talk with people and learn about various positions, I will discover numerous  tangible examples of the criteria. This could lead to my refining the criteria as well.

Regarding design thinking, this activity has increased my respect for the process. I have a better  understanding why people consider design thinking “messy” (it can be so creative and non-linear) and  also how it can help teams generate new, out-of-the-box ideas that have never been identified before.     Approach  If I were to use visualization on a different project, I expect I would want more concrete, less subjective  criteria. For example, “provides….information” or “arrives at answer in less than 3 clicks.” Objective  criteria won’t be the only useful criteria though. For example, descriptions of desired customer  experiences could be subjective.     I could also do this process with a group of people. If everyone were job hunting, we could interview  each other and gain insights we might not notice on our own. We could then create visuals that  represent these richer criteria. Another option would be to start with some images and use them to  elicit a more in-depth discussion of what we’re looking for in a role. This could help us define our criteria  even better.    I also would want to test using more and less detailed images to see what type of impact they’d have on  the depth and type of discussion elicited from participants.      I am very pleased with this activity as it’s been very helpful for me. I’m going to post the pictures in my  home for both inspiration and focus throughout my search.
