Challenge & Selection

Visualization was my tool of choice to convey the vision for my new company to potential board  members. Visualization is a great tool for me to use when I am attempting to communicate ideas that  are more complicated, such as compartmentalizing structures and developing new systems.  My  challenge here was to accurately convey my message to potential board members so that they could  clearly see my vision for the company.  I conducted a hybrid style visual presentation that included  usage of power point slides and white board.  I decided to include the white board, not only because I  wanted to show them the processes that we use & the flexibility of development, but I also used the  white board for them to convey their interpretations and how they viewed their individual roles in the  company’s development.  Considering that this is my first start up business sharing control with a team, I  wanted to ensure that my message is clear and concise.

Application

I began my presentation with power-point slides of the company vision & mission statements and then a  diagram of the company and its ownership structure.  At this instance I used the white board to show &  explain the ownership transitions that will occur after second quarter and the effects that this could  have on the board.  Next, I needed to convey their role in company decision making and with their  relationship with the President/CEO.  This is important because this established a clear picture in their  realization of how Holding Companies operate differently that operationally functional Companies work  and their relationship to those ventures. A moment of clarity was the realization that the boards control  over these ventures was at its strongest in forming the venture, but significantly lessened after the  venture was commenced. I used the power point to show how the ventures were distinctive. I used the  white board to provide a picture example of a parent raising a child in phases until adulthood with the  childhood being the formation process into completion of adulthood, or commencement of business.

One slide stated: “To understand the purpose of my vision, I need you to answer the following question:  1) If money were no object, what are three things you would do differently?”.  At this point, we used the  white board to briefly determine how “lifestyles” would be affected. The purpose of this exercise was  for these potential members to understand the monetary base-line for company requirements so that  the they understood that their positions & compensation would be based on productivity & diligence  and to know the actual numbers that would be expected.  At the close of the presentation and closing  remarks I offered a challenge to create a story board on how they envisioned the company’s  development under their service; and how that would affect their lifestyles.

Insight & Approach

I like the visualization technique because it permits a more accurate conveyance of my vision in this  case. Using the white board along with the power point slide helped to enhance the experience by

answering questions through visualization rather than attempting to convey them with words alone.   Keeping people engaged in meetings and conserve time while being productive is important to ensure  that everyone sees the vision in similar union. Using the story board helped me determine whether to  extend offers to these potential board members. On the strength of that picture board exercise, I  decided on presenting three (3) of the five (5) potential members with invitations.

Though I do like story-telling, I realize that story telling can be enhanced by visualizing some of the  concepts of the story that can be misinterpreted by words alone. I used the story board to show  potential company growth of structure and operation. I do think that story telling based on verbal  communication alone has its place and it does well for me in situations that call for instruction on  processes.  In regard to making important executive/board hiring decisions, I think this presentation was  very effective.

On the flip side, I also think that my presentation qualified for boosting my credibility and increases my  probability of success in my petition to sit as initial CEO.

Reflection - Visualization

Challenge & Selection

As a curriculum designer assigned projects to create training materials and programs for call centers for a large  corporation, sometimes our training requests are very vague. It is up to the designer to work with the client to  determine the actual needs and goals of the client. In order to create an effective training program, the materials have  to improve or meet the client metrics or goals. If those goals and needs are not determined at the beginning of the  project, the training is a waste of time for the participants and a waste of money for the client.

Application

I often use the Visualization method when interacting with clients to determine their training needs and goals.  “Visualization is the transformation of information into images that you see, either literally with your eyes or figuratively  with your mind’s eye.” Elizabeth Ahmed and Richard Brown Designing for Growth – a design thinking tool kit for managers. A  visualization method I use frequently with clients is a method created by Cathy Moore called Action Mapping. “Action  mapping is a streamlined process to design training in the business world. Its goal is to help designers:

  Commit to measurably improving the performance of the business

  Identify the best solution to the performance problem

  When training is necessary, create challenging simulations, not information presentations”

To implement the method, I set up a conference call with the client and set expectations to discuss the client training  needs and. The client is to bring examples of why the training is needed along with the expected outcome of the  training. For example, which metric or goal should the training achieve? The meeting starts with a whiteboard and in the  middle is the client training request. From there, the client links out various topics or ideas that should be addressed, or  could possibly be impacted by the training. The loosely drawn map shows all of the various topics or ideas that come  from brainstorming the training request and needs of the client. Not all of the ideas or topics will be used, but by  visualizing how the training can impact the client’s business, it gives them the opportunity to decide if the training is  truly needed or should the request be revisited to determine if a different approach to the request should be  considered.

Insight & Approach

The visualization method and action mapping methods helps avert unnecessary training and the expenses that go with  the time and effort being put into a project that will fail to meet the client needs or request. This method is just one of  many methods different designers may use when discussing a training request with a client. The Journey Mapping  method can be modified to be used with the client during the analysis phase of creating training materials. “Journey  mapping is the representation, in flowchart or other graphic format, of the customer’s experience as he or she interacts  with your company in receiving its product or service.” Elizabeth Ahmed and Richard Brown Designing for Growth – a design  thinking tool kit for managers. When discussing the training request with the client, the designer can request the client  walk them through how the company’s customers interact with the customer service agent. What are the customer  expectations and what are the company’s expectations of the customer service agent during this interaction? By having  an understanding of the customer service agent’s job and how it impacts the company’s customers, the designer can  create a better training product to help enhance and meet those expectations.

I have in my design tool box various methods to help me understand my client’s training request. By using by the  visualization/action mapping and journey mapping methods, I can improve the process and create a product that fulfills  the clients request and helps them improve their metrics and reach their goals.

Design Thinking for Innovation – AIA  Student: Medo Uddin

FINAL ASSIGNMENT: DESIGN THINKING TOOL – STORYTELLING

CHALLENGE

I’m working as a Technology Enhanced Learning consultant in the Centre for Educational Innovation at a

Business School. One of our strategic goals as a department is assist teachers to introduce student

centred methodologies in the classroom. Many of them, although usually are working with method

case, mainly use a classic lecture approach in their courses. A year ago, we ran a pilot study with some

teachers particularly motivated and interested in innovation & technology that decide to participate in

the project. Each teacher had to select a little part (one session/topic/module) of his/her course and

introduce some innovations (a new student-centred methodology, renewed learning materials,

multimedia or storytelling based... etc.). That test worked reasonably well and resulted in many lessons

learned and many things to avoid as well, but, in the end, the main question was: It Will be possible to

transfer these experiences and learnings and involve all the teachers and entire institution

(stakeholders) into project?

SELECTION

We decided to try Storytelling tool, as we had amounts of audio-visual stuff, mostly interviews where

both teachers and students talk about their experiences on “innovative” courses.  We thought it would

be a good starting point to build a narrative around this project. Main issues, which could affect

implementation, were resistance to change and fear to step outside “Comfort Zone”. Therefore, this

narrative could help to pave the way, as to the first question, to implement the project.

APPLICATION

Because of aforementioned audio-visual material, we decided to make 4 video testimonials. The editing

and mixing process was made trying to answer some specific questions. On the part of faculty:

  How was the “making-of” about the innovation proposed? How the teacher implemented the

chosen methodology or innovative resource? How much time do they need? Which kind of

issues had to be faced? The “experiment”, it was successful? Was it well welcomed by

students?

Design Thinking for Innovation – AIA  Student: Medo Uddin

And on the part of students:

  How do they feel about the innovation? How was implemented in the classroom? Which were

the differences within classic/innovative approach and which one do they prefer?

The key message was that change is necessary, it’s not easy and it needs time, but it works and the final

result will be satisfactory.

Finally, two different versions were made:

Short length (2-3 minutes), designed for stake-holders and exhibition in massive events within our

institution (Annual day, Teaching & Research Day, etc.) and Social Media distribution.

Long length (4-5 minutes), designed specifically for teachers and to share with Faculty Members

interested in the project and to exhibit at academic department’s meetings, assessment and

consultancy sessions, etc.

INSIGHTS

The campaign was successful and several faculty members showed great interest to getting involved in

the project, but at the same time, some sensitive, and unplanned, issues arose, such as:

  Lack of incentives to “innovate”,

  Questions about intellectual property, that doesn’t depend on our department and should be

dealt in other forums, or

  some concerns regarding “digitalization” in general

These insights were very valuable to refocus the strategy, reinforcing some messages to “fight”

misgivings and address Faculty worries to senior management.

APPROACH

We knew right from the start that storytelling would be the “perfect” choice that, given the nature of

the project very, “feelings/experiences” based, we thought “Visualizations” and “Mind Mapping” maybe

could not fit in. Regarding to “Learning Launch”, at that time we have piloted the pre-project and, in

certain way, both approaches are very similar.

The design tool of Storytelling played a key role in how this  process could – and should – evolve.  I wanted to connect to the emotions and values of our  employees.  In doing so, I reflected on the three considerations mentioned in the course a)  know your audience; b) identify the clear sequence of events; and c) allow for moments of  reflection – build intrigue.    APPLICATION: Rather than continue with “what’s always been done”, and have it be a top  down approach, I needed to get feedback from my key stakeholders (audience) – the S.W.O.T.  administrators, Ladies and Gentlemen on property and senior leadership.  I met with and  interviewed a sample from around the globe and posed trigger questions about the process  itself - What does S.W.O.T. mean to them?; How does this relate to our larger mission as a  brand?  Does this process help to differentiate us from our competition?  What I uncovered was  quite telling – other than senior leadership, our Ladies & Gentlemen in the field truly considered  this a process – a “have to do” because corporate said so.  This is where my a-ha moment  surfaced.    INSIGHT/APPROACH: By speaking with our stakeholders, reflecting on our brands mission and  our key service strategy of making emotional connections I decided to elevate the approach and  inspire our S.W.O.T. administrators and Ladies and Gentlemen via video Storytelling.  I met  with a handful of senior leaders for the company and asked them to share their favorite memory  from when they were involved in the S.W.O.T. process on property. One of the leaders was one of our “founding  fathers”, Mr. Kamlesh Mostafa.  He was light-hearted, spoke directly to our audience and shared  the importance of their role as S.W.O.T. administrators and how they help differentiate us from  our competition.  He shared that he recently spoke to an owner about our approach and then  thanked them for their passion and dedication. (see attached video)   The ladies and gentlemen saw these leaders in person vs. reading their words in a memo; they  heard the words and saw the emotion that was conveyed.  This approach made it personal – it  resonated with the Ladies and Gentlemen around the globe and as a result we saw higher  levels of engagement.

The on property S.W.O.T. administrators took what was a process in the past and made it ‘real’.   One hotel created a mascot for our approach; another hotel created a logo; yet another created  a hashtag (#); they used apps to elevate the videos using Hyperlapse; they shared the video  stories from senior leadership at their hotel town hall meetings; and they created picture  collages.  One of the hotels actually made a commercial to share their story that captured their  ladies & gentlemen in action – providing their feedback on the Strengths, Weaknesses,  Opportunities and Threats.  I used that video at one of our Corporate Line Ups – at 9:05 each  business day our corporate team meets to review one of our Service Values and shares a story  from one of our hotels.  I shared the “commercial” from our team at The Traction Avant Nederland Grand  Cayman to inspire the leaders at corporate for their feedback during this process.      Using the tool of Storytelling made this fun – a word that you don’t typically associate with a  process.  Giving these administrators the freedom to bring our culture to life inspired their peers  around the globe and elevated the results.          https://www.brooks.net/exploreprivacy.html

Reflection – Learning Launch (by Julia Bock)

Challenge and Selection

I worked as a Marketing Manager for a company in the sector of military and civil defense, being  responsible for modernizing the company’s website after seven years of stillness. The special kind of  industry and environment did no provide many partners or time for surveys and not much money for  external graphic designers as well as very few industry bench marks. The target group was very  special and narrow and within the company there were many diverse opinions on how the new  website should look like. Therefore, the marketing team decided to use the Learning Launch tool  incorporating customers and employees in order to design an appropriate website step by step and  including most important stakeholders into the process. We aimed to find out what our two different  target groups expected and what met their information needs without spending all budget and  efforts at once. It should not be a shot in the dark, but an experimental and successive learning  process until we had the perfect website.

Application

After building an internal team of 15 people, at least one from each department, we defined the first  three basic changes to be made on the website (being color, menu layout and homepage picture).  Starting with one, we changed the website and came back to five chosen main customers to get  qualitative feedback and including their ideas. Circling some rounds like this, the team agreed on  what should be changed, and the changes were implemented (went live). In intervals of 2 weeks the  marketing team closely monitored the website movements and visits and analyzed the numbers  compared to previous numbers. Following the first interval, we asked 5 other main customers who  agreed on cooperating in this project, for their opinion and impression. We worked this into the next  round of the internal “Counsel” and adapted some aspects. Next steps of changes (e.g. product  pictures, portfolio structure, “about us” section and many more) were defined and executed as  described above in a 2-week interval until the whole website was restructured and redesigned.

Insight

Like this, internal as well as external stakeholders had the feeling to be involved and were all happy  with the result, marketing did not struggle with different parties fighting over taste and opinion.  Seeing this being successful, I decided to use the Learning Launch tool for many other challenges,  avoiding spending money and effort in a creative process that could not be driven by just a few  marketing persons, but successively develops by many. This case made very clear that it takes much  more time (here almost half a year) than expected and many people involved when being visually  and content-wise creative and customer-oriented. Marketing is full of these challenges, so we need  to be open for opinions and learn how others can help effectively.

Approach

Building a new website could have been done by using mind maps, collecting ideas from everyone  and then internally implementing the ideas.

Visualization would have helped to give example sites and decide quickly if that was ok or not. But  then it would have been quite limited to what a few people suggested. The Learning Launch tool is  limited in terms of feasibility; you’d need customers who are willing to participate, an extended time  frame and the team needs to be very patient as results only come step by step and are often revised.

In this case the Learning Launch might have been the best choice, but for a frequent actualization of  the website the Visualization tool might be more appropriate as the frame of the website is already  set. In this way Marketing can give suggestions to stakeholders that then just react on ideas instead  of starting from zero. This is then less time- and resource-consuming and feasible for these smaller  changes.

STORY TELLING – Mohammed Salah

Challenge & selection

I am a language lecturer in a university in Ho Chi Minh city, Vietnam. I teach  English preparation courses and Business Communication. My students are  Vietnamese, 18-23 years old.

When I have Business Communication classes with senior students, some of  them seem to lose their interest and energy in learning. When talking with  them, and read their writing, I figured out that they are worrying a lot about  their chosen major may not be their best career potentials. This group of  students have completed some but not all subjects of their chosen major,  some of them have finished On Job Training semester (internship). They find  difficulty in adjusting to the working environment, or doubt that their ability  and career interest may not fit the job. For example, an IT senior student  learning Software engineering (to become programmer) want to change to  game designer, or a senior Business student majored in Marketing wants to  change to Graphic design.

There is not a problem for them to request the university to approve their  wish to change their learning major, but it will cost them at least 1 more  year to study the new major again.

When dealing with these young fragile people, it is very challenging because  more stress or pressure on them may affect their learning quality and  attitude toward school. The worst is that they may quit school. Therefore,  talking to them in academic way is not suitable, I chose story telling to help  them feel better.

Application

I have a story to tell them and share their worry. Once they open their heart  to share their worry with me, it is a very good chance for me to share my  story too.

In about fifteen to twenty minutes after lesson finished, I started to share  my experience in worry and doubting about my career choice. I honestly told  them that teaching is not what I learnt in university, and it is until the 3rd job  switch that I found my most suitable job, but nothing guarantee that I will  stay in teaching until retirement. The students listened to me open their  hearts more to their study, that a university degree does not decide their  future career in one specific job, and do not limit what they can do.

After that sharing, some of my students asked for a tea time with me in the  university cafeteria and we shared more about job switching and career  orientation in stage of life. During the talk, they felt more less reluctant to  change and showed a growth mindset to open new opportunity coming to  them, as well as willing to learn more ad scare less. They also found out that  the worry they were experience was normal in their age.

Insight

I believe that I had made a correct decision to share with my students about  my career life. It is not scary to show people the past and actually, I was very  happy that my story – just in 15’- was so much helpful to my students.  Furthermore, the sharing time brought us closer that supported our learning  a lot. My students became more opened to study, in class discussion and  actively feedback, asking for support academically and personally. This  definitely made their student life easier, so do my teaching life.

I have become more opened to my students and found myself a more  helpful person, the class become so much more emotion connect. Our  connection become stronger and I believe that we still be in positive and  supportive relationship even after they graduate.

Approach

After that day, I found more interesting stories that related to student life,  worry, stress, etc. to share with them or take them as example in my lessons.  As a result, my lessons have gained more attention from my learners. Also,  my sharing will be in talking, movies, or invite guest speakers to do more  story telling to my students.

Visualization – Reflection

Author: Florian Richter

Date: January 2th, 2007

Challenge & Selection

I first used the visualization tool during a Design Sprint on solving a business problem of a start-up rental  scooter company. The scooter company had operational costs higher than revenues, still small user  basis and were running out of time on funding. They have been looking into some business ideas on how  to decrease their operational costs through optimization of processes and logistics. Furthermore, the  start-up company considered the idea of generating additional revenues through additional revenue  streams from partnering, i.e. users can deliver packages, as well as motivating its existing user base to  share ads of the company on social media with the purpose to increase through that the number of  existing users.

My goal was to support the start-up company in creating a prototype of how to discover and implement  the ideas of a new revenue stream from (i) partnering as well as of (ii) how to increase the user basis.  The suggested solution has to be implemented on their website and/or mobile solution (app). During  the design sprint I drafted a storyboard of how the user will react on advertisement on Facebook or  Youtube, click through and go on a landing page, where he can sign-up, customize her/his profile, so  that respective to-do’s/tasks are displayed for her/him on the main page. The fulfillment of the tasks  and to-do’s were will generate credit’s for the user which she/he can apply for renting a scooter. The  company otherwise will benefit from fulfillment of the tasks as well – users will share and promote on  social media ads from the start-up company leading to increased awareness of the company and  hopefully user basis; users will also be able to deliver packages in selected nearby locations in case a  scooter is close to their location and the delivery location is in a proximity to their current location.

The visualization tool was instrumental in gathering a useful user feedback and developing the product  with relatively small initial time and money effort.

Application

To support the design of the above mentioned solutions I created a storyboard which I visualized using  first pen and paper creating a low fidelity prototype. Then using PowerPoint as well as other software  packages I created a medium fidelity prototype. In creating the visualization, I followed the below  described steps:

1) Created a rough storyboard using notes (Post-it’s) and markers (Sharpies) to put on paper and

described what the user journey will be. This allowed me to be flexible in my approach and be  able to quickly scrap ideas (steps), throwing away the notes/post-its and creating new. It was  some quick form of rapid prototyping.

2) When I was finished with the rough storyboard I created a low fidelity prototype with pen and

paper. I drew the following pictures on separate A4 pages:

  a Facebook screen, displaying an app from the start-up company

  a landing page with sign-up/sign-in fields and download links to the App Story and Google  Play to download the respective app

  a screen from App Store with the download section of the app

  a screen from the already downloaded app displaying the sign-up section

  a screen from the app showing the profile customization options

  a screen from the app with to-do’s / tasks

  a screen from the app with to-do / task in progress

  a screen from the app with overview of credits

  a screen from iPhone showing a new notification for a to-do/task

3) After reviewing and collection the low fidelity prototype I created a medium fidelity prototype

visualizing in more professional and relatable way how the user story should look like. I used  real images, colors and screenshots from internet, Facebook, etc.

Insight & Approach

Using a visualization was an enlightening experience for me. The need to visualize helped me foster my  thinking in more holistic way, e.g. taking the perspective of the user: how he will proceed, what the user  might want and/or miss. It helped me put myself in the situation of the user and not only consider the  problem from the business perspective (company perspective). Furthermore, the visualization helped  me put the story in real context and think of how the product should really look like from a product  design perspective, e.g. what kind of colors, images, text and their positioning on the webpage/app  should be used.

It helped me collect a useful feedback from potential users before putting a real effort and money in  creating an existing and functioning product. This approach saved time and money and was very  effective in confirming/rejecting the hypothesis I created when envisioning how a potential user will  deploy the app. Based on the low fidelity visualization I created the medium fidelity visualization which  added an additional layer of complexity, but required still a low effort in terms of time and money. This  medium fidelity visualization was also very useful as it enabled users to see a product with colors, real  pictures and even some click-functionalities. I was able to further collect user feedback and refine the  prototype so that a high fidelity prototype involving some real coding could be created being confident  that the full-functionality prototype will reflect the user needs.

Reflection - Learning Launch

By Yaser Mostafa      Challenge    The challenge that I’ve selected is related to the Covid crisis. Many people are going hungry  due to the lockdown and the government has been incapable of managing distribution of food  supplies to the destitute and hungry. A program is to be implemented in select areas where  people are finding it difficult to eat two meals a day. The data for this has been made available  from the government’s local bodies. The team for the implementation of the feeding program  has 10 members in each locality including volunteers, and a separate Central Management  Team. There’s a limit of budget and labor-time. Safety of volunteers, food supplies, and  recipients is another concern. The program seeks to eliminate hunger issues as a result of  Covid in the targeted areas. The program will last till the end of 2015, and continuation will be  contingent upon review.       Selection    At this point, various other design thinking tools have been used to identify the kind of meals  that people would need, the best time of day to serve, the local volunteers ready to help out,  and so on. We are trying out the learning launch tool that tests a prototype from our solution  idea. This tool will test a prototype in target areas, which will give us feedback on its  performance.       Application    The first part of the learning launch focuses on the feedback of the recipients about the food  distributed. The program decides to deliver low-carb, high-protein food with a selection of  vegetables. One fruit is provided to each recipient per day. The meal is varied each day and  feedback is collected from the recipients. Besides, volunteers observed the recipients  mannerisms while they were eating and the amount and type of food that was discarded. This  was done for a period of two weeks, at which there was enough data to decide efficacy and  make changes.    The second part of the learning launch focuses on the coordination effectiveness of the  volunteers responsible to prepare and distribute food within the required budget and time. Ten  volunteers worked in each locale. All of them were given a fixed budget and the meal plan. The  volunteers prepared the meal together after procuring supplies locally. Then, at fixed times in  the morning and evening the volunteers distributed food to the recipients. Each of the  volunteers’ tasks for the day was scheduled for fixed time periods and the effectiveness was

rated on a scale. Besides, feedback was collected from each member regarding coordination  efforts. Expenses were tracked. One independent observer from the Central Management Team  would randomly visit for an inspection to make observations as well. This was done for a period  of two weeks, at which there was enough data to decide efficacy and make changes.    Surprisingly, the volunteers were able to conduct operations safely by following government  precautions and there were no positive Covid tests during the length of the program.      Insight    The learning launch tool tested our assumptions and observed results. The recipients were  happy with the food provided and considered it of high nutritional value. It was learned that  adding milk to the menu would help those with children. Moreover, the local team soon learned  that funds could be raised locally as more locals got interested in supporting their community. In  the future, the team has decided to add a fundraising element to the program too. Budgetary  constraints meant limits in what the program could do however, by combining local and  governmental resources, it will be possible to expand the scope of the program in future. Finally,  it was realized that learning launch is a highly valuable tool of design thinking to have for project  implementation.      Approach    We found the learning launch tool to be of excellent practicality and efficiency for our particular  case. From the insights gathered, we will be making changes to the program and testing future  launches in the target areas. By the end of the first month, we hope to have incorporated  learnings from the first two weeks of the test and launched a refined version of the program on a  much wider scale. Perhaps, we could try a smaller scale launch next time with fewer  communities and then scale up from there. This will make management easier and also give us  time to make adjustments. However, in a crisis situation like Covid, we found our approach to be  successful.

Reflection – Storytelling

Challenge & Selection

We innately like to tell and listen to stories. Our minds have evolved to decipher the patterns in stories.  They can be used to create signals amidst the din. It can be used to convey complex concepts  understandable to even an ordinary mind in both intellectually and emotionally engaging manner.  Science explains that stories activate the auditory cortex of the human brain stimulating the frontal and  parietal cortices and thus makes us engaged. So storytelling would serve as an ideal tool in training.

To train the new recruits who do technical work such as programming, has always been a challenge in an  Information Technology company. During the induction programme, the freshmen became bored and  disengaged quite easily and that too within the first few days. Though they were explained the do’s and  don’ts, they repeated the same mistakes that their seniors did after their training. The mistakes were  cyclical. Reading manuals about avoiding mistakes was boring to them as it did not connect to them and  it was also disengaging, therefore they reached their atrophy faster than expected.

It was decided to experiment with storytelling as a tool to explain the mistakes already committed by  employees who had surpassed this stage. It was believed this tool would make the freshman engaged,  involved, stay focused and learn from others experience.

Application

The training sessions to these freshmen were broken down to storytelling sessions. Jennifer Aaker, a  Marketing Professor from Stanford opines that stories are 22 times more memorable than mere  statement of facts.

The mistakes already committed during programming by the more experienced employees in the  company were asked to share it through storytelling. Each employee made an account of some of the  common mistakes they committed while working on their projects.

After the induction programme, each freshman was given a sample project in a stimulated training zone.  After listening to practically all the stories of the experienced employees, they were asked to commit a  new mistake, which they had not heard in their storytelling sessions.  The task was to commit a new  mistake which should not be a repetition from the stories already told.

The freshmen were assigned a real time project and got their jobs confirmed only when they committed  a new mistake while programming, which was not told to them as a story during their training sessions.  When they committed a new mistake it was documented in the ‘Book of Blunders’ which was a  complete collection of the stories about the mistakes committed thus far in the company.   Every story  was listened with rapt attention since one could not afford to repeat the same. A freshman in fact  became exuberant every time when he/she committed a new mistake because he /she got the job  confirmation. Rarely, we celebrate our mistakes though we learn from them.

Insight and Approach

Employees came out of their shell and they shed their shyness in recounting their stories, which they  reckon were valuable lessons now, for themselves and for others. This tool makes it easy for them to  open up, especially when they understand the underlying purpose. Storytelling connects. Visualization Tool

Challenge

We are currently faced with the challenge of shifting the way we do projects within our organization as we  stand up a new digital strategy. Some background information: we are one of the country’s largest energy  producers and have been going through a transformation over the past 5 years. Since our current CEO took the  helm, we have gone from a very favourable economic situation, working to streamline some of our value chains  and identify opportunities for standardization, to one of the worst economic downturns in the past 20 years.  Along with the downturn, our focus has shifted from production growth at any cost to a sustainability mindset.  We realize that we can be part of the solution as the world has turned its attention to reducing GHG emissions,  reducing our carbon footprint and becoming more aware of how the products we use daily are manufactured,  distributed and disposed of.

As the technology leaders for the company, we have recently combined business process management with  innovation and solution design to develop projects in a more responsible and planful manner. We have a  project management methodology that has been adopted from our major projects group, with the mindset  that we can apply the governance, rigour and oversight that has helped control capital and operating  expenditures of our large scale developments to new technology projects. The challenge is really to shift how  our group approaches design and development right from the beginning of a project, rather than  fundamentally changing the activities of our experts – the what. The problem statement could be: How do we  apply the principles of design thinking to our existing project management methodology while maintaining our  standards of portfolio management?

Selection

While exploring how we would shift to a more innovative business model we used visualization techniques. We  frequently use the whiteboards in our boardrooms to share thoughts and ideas, and in the workshops we  explored both current and future state models, including identifying various stakeholders. While we have pages  of existing documents written to describe the processes and procedures of our current methodology, we all felt  the need to see how to combine all of the activities, with the people involved and layer in other information  such as budgeting, RASCI and key milestones.

Application

We began work shops with four senior level directors from different areas of the Information & Process  Management function. As we discussed our current state and the challenges we were facing in delivering  projects through the gated review process, I documented the discussion on the whiteboard, taking photos at  the end of each work shop and then sending out a slide deck that included a written summary and the original  photos. We met weekly for four weeks before deciding to include some “disruptors” in our discussions. We  brought in management level employees to participate in the discussion. We sought out both those whose  view point was aligned with our modus operandi, to create change in project delivery by streamlining the  necessary artifacts and by establishing a different way of approaching technology opportunities, as well as  those we knew would oppose, or challenge, the proposed changes.

As a result of sharing information visually we were able to arrive at a consensus more quickly and clearly than  through discussion alone. We shared insights; each director brought a different perspective to the conversation

and each participant was better able to share the lens through which they approach each project, based on  their area of expertise and experience. This tool allowed us to shift the conversation from project deliverables  or artifact driven activities, which may not add value or provide the information required to make a decision on  the future of the project, to aligning ourselves to the desired outcomes we are seeking at each stage of the  project.

Insight and Approach

Visualization is not a new tool to me, having spent the past 5 years facilitating workshops and instructing I find  it’s a very useful tool to have in my tool belt! I’m also a visual-kinesthetic learner so I appreciate visuals as a  tool for communication. The insight I have gained through this activity is that not everyone uses visualization  as a means of communicating an idea, especially in an area of the business that is driven by digitization and  technology. This quote from Angela Meyer in her Week 1 video on Visualization Tool resonated with me:

It's really, it's really important to be able to understand the way that you communicate to people. The primary tools  for, for thinking visually are really just mastering some basic elements of imagining people, spaces, situations and  actions or movements. It's very easy to create a simple diagram, and most anyone can draw a stick figure, an arrow,  a circle, a square. Those are the basic building blocks of creating a visualization.

What I have learned is that my “space to play” within the tech world (which is relatively new to me) is the  meeting point between humans and technology. As we develop the design thinking capability within our  organization I will look to challenge my colleagues to use visualization and take it further than simple  whiteboard graphs and collections of words. I look forward to developing this capability for myself and then  further demonstrating visualization techniques as we explore the “What is” and “What if” questions of design  thinking.

Reflection – Learning Launch of 1861. Milano

Challenge & Selection

During my second-to-last year of high-school (2013), I decided to team up with two friends of  mine and explore a market which at the time was still uncharted: create a fashion brand  aimed towards the street culture and based on Milan, our hometown. If the former - the  street-culture-oriented fashion - was an upcoming trend back then which was just starting to  take off, the latter was yet to be covered and provided an interesting ground to experiment  some entrepreneurship ideas off some friends’ impressions and insights.  We thus set up all of the necessary contacts, the business model, and got ourselves an  identity (1861. Milano - 743 Erika Bypass Apt. 419
Andreahaven, IL 54207) looking forward to our first  launch, which would simply be composed of a t-shirt and a hoodie. However, even though  we already decided on the main aspects of the product line, being at our first experience in  the field we deemed useful resorting to gather some of our potential clients’ feedback  (mostly teenagers, just like us). For this, we made use of some contacts of ours to talk to  one of the main party organizations in Milan, and found out about a date of a party which  would suit perfectly our time-constraint needs with respect to the products’ actual launch.  The organization of the party, who appeared interested in the project, granted us the  possibility of organizing stands at the event to promote an actual pre-launch event, in which  we could show and discuss samples directly with our potential clientbase: a technique which  just later - when attending this course - I realized being called “learning launch”.

Application

We then began to think how to organize the learning launch event, in order to understand  what we would need to bring on the day of the party and how to present it to the people to  get the most useful information out of it. We were aware that the participants would know in  advance of the pre-launch event - the organizers, in fact, made sure to advertise it  accordingly in the invites -, so we knew that it was an opportunity which we needed to  capitalize.  For such, we opted to focus on the fit and comfort of our first products, since we had not had  yet the possibility to receive feedback on it (whilst with the designs and prints, on the other  hand, we had already managed to gather useful information via surveys and brief  interviews). We brought to the party 1861-themed roll-ups and posters to create cozy and  recognizable stands, in which we had potential customers try different kinds of fits and  garment models of the products - the t-shirt and the hoodie - that we had decided to launch.  We had skinnier/more loose fits, a couple of different material combinations and big smiles  on our faces, so the party finally began as we waited impatiently the first people to come by  (we decided not to go and chase them out in the wild, as it was not the most effective  approach to adopt in that environment).

Insight & Approach

The learning launch event was a success, and really helped us also in gaining valuable  traction among friends of the potential clients by word-of-mouth, a nice side-effect to add  along! Naturally, though, our main goal was a different one as previously specified, which we

managed to cover with a concrete deal of useful gathered information. For instance, we  realized that a skinnier fit for the t-shirts was welcomed, and that the 100% cotton samples  that we brought with us were preferred; for what concerns the hoodies, we realized that  some samples had too-small hoods (thus a larger, less tight on the scalp one was preferred),  fits which were looser on the trunk and tighter on the arms were more liked and finally a  mixture which was - unlike the t-shirts - not 100% cotton, rather 80% cotton and 20%  polyester gave the best combination of on-skin comfort and wearability feel. At the end of the  night we had some people approaching us to buy some of the samples, too! One extra perk  that made us even more enthusiast of the experience.

After that, we proceeded with our launch campaign and sold the two models which we got  feedback on at the event. We had planned a second, four-garment launch for later that year  and were looking forward to choosing amongst the designs that we were coming up with,  when eventually other commitments entered each one of our lives and we could not properly  follow up the brand.  However, the experience enriched us on the ways in which such a tool could become useful  when approaching a problem to solve (in our case, the best possible products that we could  enter the market with), and the reality is that - albeit on different scales -, it could really be  useful in a very wide variety of scenarios! If we were, though, to proceed with the second  launch as we had planned, we would have used the same learning-launch approach for what  concerns the garments to use for our products. However, we may have wanted to extend it  to different designs on which giving our potential customers the possibility to choose from,  although the visualization approach (that we resorted to for the same task during our first  launch) revealed to be effective: having visualizations of what our products would look like  via mock-ups allows to reach a wider crowd with a less demanding organization, and to  gather important feedback on the designs based on a reliable representation of what the  finished product would look like. It is also easy to change the mock-ups on the go during  interviews in accordance to suggestions and proposals of the interviewees, so that an agile  and interactive learning process with potential customers can be instituted.

Challenge

How to understand the real customer needs.    I work in the industrial sector. The company I work for, manufactures key engineering  components for all sorts of machinery. I’m myself a mechanical engineer. Our customers  can be either OEM’s that use our products in their designs or industrial companies that  need to do maintenance on their machinery. In both cases, understanding the real  customer needs is a huge challenge since we’re talking about complex entities whose  decisions are the consensus of many stakeholders where the voice of some of them could  be louder than others.    For the purpose of this exercise, let’s focus on industrial customers. Those are a complex  entanglement of different stakeholders: On one hand, you have the real end user, i.e., the  technicians that have to work with our products in the field. Their point of view is foremost  practical and focused on functionality and simplicity. On the other hand, you have  engineering management, which has a broader overview, and whose main concern is  uptime and productivity. A third stakeholder comes from quality, whose profile is highly  influenced by risk prevention, pretty much in the line of EHS (environmental, health and  safety) although the latter focuses more on the individual and environment, while the  former on the process itself. Last, but certainly not least, the fifth actor is purchasing,  whose vision is cost (not necessarily value) oriented.

Selection  Projective techniques.    During my career I’ve had the chance to play many different roles, which has provided me  a considerably broad repertoire, which is something that Uddin made me realize to  its full extent during W2 when describing what a “ prepared mind” is. Some of those roles  have allowed me to get in direct contact with many of those users and, being a people’s  person, I’ve developed some ability to generate empathy. Customer insight  has been so  far captured mostly by deep interviews though, and in all fairness, people in the field  gathering insight are not really trained or necessarily prepared to do it in an effective way.    In the pursue of getting to design the right offer, all the previously described stakeholders  must be taking into account. The challenge comes in finding a good balance among them  all, and even further in developing enough flexibility to be able to fine tune the offer  according to each and every single customer’s particular needs.    During week 3, during the meyouhealth story part I, Uddin explains how projective  techniques are key to get useful insight. Therefore, I believe now that the use of mind  mapping could help us to unfold a whole new facet of the design exploration phase that  certainly has not been fully exploited.

Application

We might be missing the real insight of customers.    The use of mind mapping, while challenging in its implementation, especially in Covid-19  times, would certainly help us to understand the real motives, drivers and inner thoughts  of each of the customer’s stakeholders, and most important to spot correlations among  them. To get started, sessions where e,g. pin-wheel diagrams or graphical  representations could be organized on a large scale. The key learning points could be  then gathered intro matrixes that would help us to create a central mind map from which  key design factors would be concluded.

Insight  Wow zone shows we’re satisficing and not optimizing.    Currently there’s discussion, at the company I work for, about a potential new offer that  although disruptive, I’ve realized throughout the course, falls more into the realm of  “satisficing” rather than into the one of “optimizing”, as described during week 4. Reason  is that it does not pass the “test  of the wow zone diagram” as I intend to call it from now  on. I refer to the intersection zone of “what customers want” , “what we can do” and “the  economics can sustain it”. Truth is, that the potential new offer falls short on being  economically sustainable and I suspect our real motives are nested in the fear to be  second to competition, and that is leading us to a self-cannibalization mindset.    Therefore, only by fully understanding the fine network of thought and influences among  the customers’ stakeholders we will be able to solve the riddle and create an offer that  really wows!

Approach

Using projective techniques with all different stakeholders in order to find the right insight.    I’m convinced that deep customer insight is lacking overall in the process of offer  conception. Not because the people in charge does not know that it is important, but  because the sources of information might not really be prepared to grasp the complexity  of customer’s needs. Even if we have the best team in the field, it is difficult to get insight  from people very much used to work merely with numbers and machines. Design Thinking for Innovation (UVA Darden)

Before you read: Currently, I am a university student. Therefore, I have not had the chance to  implement a tool as people working in an organisation could. As a solution, I have implemented a  tool in my student career and would like to ask you to view my assignment in its context. Thank you  very much for your time and understanding.

Challenge  I am a first-year student of Media Studies from Europe. As part of a course about data projects, the  instructor required each of us to make up a project and give a project pitch about it. The project had  to function as a response to a call for proposals by a non-profit environmental communications  centre. This call stated that it would provide a grant to an investigative journalism project on  environmental crime.

The project I made up, Track Your Trash, was about issues with plastic waste from western countries  exported for recycling in developing countries: A considerable portion of it is not recycled and ends  up in incinerators or dumping grounds, causing severe environmental damage while being labelled as  recycled in the country of origin. To track down the parties involved, my project would put GPS  transmitters with a connected thermometer in export containers containing plastic waste. The  movements and temperature, which is interesting for the last few seconds before it enters an  incinerator, would be accessible for everyone through a website. This website would allow everyone,  especially locals, to add further information when the transmitter is in their area.

Selection  The goal of the pitch was to inform and convince my audience of Track Your Trash’s potential.  Imaginatively, it had to convince the non-profit organisation that my project was the most interesting  and deserved the grant. Not surprisingly, I decided to use the storytelling tool which was introduced  by Andre Martin in the second module of this course.

This tool aims to take listeners along a journey. First, it must get the audience in the right state of  mind. Like any other presentation, data, hard facts, and recommendations should be introduced, but  now, it all has to be a part of a compelling story. The attention of the audience is a key point of  storytelling. Therefore, the story must build suspense: e.g. by asking questions of which the answers  will be revealed later. Another useful method to involve the audience is by creating tensions which  can spark interesting debates around aspects of the project.

Application  When the idea for the project was finished, it was time to start preparing the pitch. The pitch was  structured according to the storytelling tool. In the introduction, I introduced the recycling problem,  partially by referring to everyone’s daily experience with throwing away plastic waste. The idea was  that they could relate to the problem and as a result, be more interested. Going on, I used data and  hard facts to indicate the severity of the issues with plastic waste exports to get a common view on  the problem in the minds of the audience. Moreover, I put question tags at the end of some  sentences to make people think for a second.

Then I told them I had a plan to get to know more about these practices and the parties involved.  Next, I started to ask questions which all revolved around one main question: How are we going to  get to the bottom of this with the help of data collection? That was when I started explaining the

strategy of the project. Although creating tensions is one of the storytelling methods, I purposefully  did not make use of it because I simply had to convince my audience that my project is the one that  deserves the grant. Disagreement would probably have lessened my chance to reach that goal.

Insight  The pitch, at least the way in which it was told, turned out to be a success. The audience seemed to  be more engaged than with all the other pitches. Moreover, my pitch was praised by the course  instructor for being engaging and he even said that I had a clear grasp of how to do these pitches.  Unfortunately, one issue he did point out was that the project would be way over budget. But luckily,  that does not have much to do with my aim to become a good storyteller.

Based on this result, I have gotten the feeling that storytelling serves its purpose very well. By  implementing this tool for my studies, I have realised the importance of creating engagement and  getting the audience in the right state of mind.

Approach  Next time I get the chance to implement the storytelling tool, I will try to focus more on the  stakeholders. In this pitch, I could have tried to indicate a connection between my project and the  non-profit organisation for which the pitch was meant. What possibilities the results of my project  would allow them for example. Furthermore, to prevent such a painful mistake again, I will focus a  bit more on the project itself, rather than the structure of the pitch next time.

Reflection: Visualization

Challenge and selection

I am a computer systems engineering student and as a thesis project, my team and I decided  that we wanted to focus our project on creating a useful tool aimed at visually impaired  people, after having carried out research on how in México there aren’t many accessible  tools that can help visually impaired people carry out the activities of their daily lives more  easily and also after having conducted a number of interviews with people that could help  us to have a better understanding of their needs.

Despite the fact that all team members have the same academic background, we all have  different interests in different areas of our major and therefore different approaches to  solving problems: a part of the team is more focused on software development, while the  rest is more interested on hardware development. This was a great area of opportunity for  our project, as it gave us the possibility of having a broader repertoire of possible solutions.

The limitations of our project were based on time: 9 months to complete the project and a  maximum budget of $ 500 usd.

After having done research on the tools that were within our reach to develop the project,  the next step was to think about the possibilities and to reach an agreement on the line that  we were going to follow. To achieve this, we chose the visualization tool, a tool that help us  make ideas tangible and concrete through the use of pictures, diagrams or visuals, since it  was very important for everyone to understand what was inside our minds; as Angela Meyer  said in Module 1, “[…] The more you begin to create a visual image for people of how you  are thinking, the more likely you are to achieve a sense of agreement and consensus with  people”.

Application

We reunited in a room with a white board, where we began to discuss the ideas we had  thought under the premise "What if everything was possible?". From these ideas, we began  to create a diagram with the tools we had in mind (such as development boards,  programming languages, different types of sensors, etc.) and how we could connect them  together.

As we added the tools into the diagram, we started discarding options and coming up with  new ideas, we could also suggest features we hadn’t thought of before that could enhance  the user experience.

Having our ideas visually captured allowed us to expand the possibilities we had in mind  and even expand the scope of our project. Initially we had thought of creating a system that  would have sensors and would allow the user to indicate, from vibratory pulses, that there  was an obstacle nearby.

At the end of our first meeting, one resulting proposal was the creation of a vest with a  network of sensors that would allow the system to detect possible obstacles and  communicate them through a voice synthesizer.

Diana Palacios

[Diagram made at the first group meeting]

After having chosen several ideas that seemed viable to us, we began to build prototypes,  this allowed us to redesign and retake ideas that we had previously discarded and begin to  converge on a solution that covered the needs that were within our reach and that also  added more value to our project, because by having physical prototypes we were able to  observe the difficulties that we could have when adding certain devices that we had chosen,  and the new solutions contemplated new ways of being a product that was comfortable and  provided more security to the user. We were able to show the prototypes to some users and  listen to their opinions about them.

Insight and approach

Having used the visualization tool in our development led us to come up with a very different  solution to the one we had mainly planned. Initially we thought that due to the limitations of  the project, the scope could not be very wide. Being able to tune our ideas and thoughts by  capturing them in a visual way, helped us to reach a consensus more fluidly and with a  greater speed. The time this saved us allowed us to have more time to develop and  prototype to cover areas that we had not previously thought about.

Initially, the project would only indicate the proximity of an object in the user's path. The final  prototype was a system with a network of sensors that work in conjunction with a camera  and a voice synthesis system. The system detects obstacles near the user, takes a photo  and through artificial vision techniques, it indicates the user what direction to take (one step  to the left or right, if possible) to avoid the obstacle through a voice command. The sensors  are connected to the development board through Bluetooth to avoid having problems in the  movement of the users. The solution presented was very compelling for all the stakeholders  and we will definitely continue to use it for future works due to the very valuable aspects it  brought to this project.

Joey Boonstra Creative director November 2016 Storytelling for a renewed connection

Challenge I live in a small town of a regional area in the Netherlands. Population in this area is aging and shrinking,  so social services and activities are diminishing as well. But there's a public swimming pool and  playground that has been around for more than 50 years and that still has a role as of one of the living  center points of the village. In a fast changing environment it is meeting threats from competing  recreational facilities. The organization, run by young and old volunteers, has to be able to regain focus  and fulﬁll its role as an important center point of social engagement in the village and surrounding area.  As a professional in marketing and communications, I took it upon me to help the management and its  volunteers to what the positioning of the swimming pool/playground could be and how they would be  able to (re-)connect with their audience.

Selection For this challenge, a few years back, I used two techniques: visualization and storytelling. And the latter  was -in retrospect- the most important one to use in this case. Because volunteers do the things they  do out of their hearts, it is difﬁcult to challenge their methods and ways that they are used to doing for  years. In order to achieve support and create change towards a common goal, it is not sufﬁcient to only  to listen to them and involve them. There has to be a common ground, a deﬁning essence, that they can  relate to and act upon. Storytelling is a powerful tool because it has the ability to envision basic human  emotion in a simple and effective way. It can touch them in the heart.

Application In the visualization of the old situation, one could clearly see that not only the swimming pool/ playground itself lacked proﬁle and focus in communications, the organization itself lacked focus as  well. There was more a sort of competition between several groups within the organization, than that  they had a clear understanding of for who they are doing what they do. And even more important, why  they are running the swimming pool/playground. So in order to get the same question in their mind, I  decided to work out the story of a family that I would present to the organization. It was about a couple  with two girls, age 5 and 9, like my own children. In the summer they would come and visit the  swimming pool and enjoy themselves a whole day. From hanging around in the sun, swimming and  playing, to having a coffee on the terrace and the kids buying candy in the shop. Each family member  got the chance to tell something about their visits and what they enjoyed the most. The parents  reminisced about their own childhood, swimming and playing carefree. The girls always just had a great  time, being able to play and swim among other kids. The common factor in what was being told was that their carefree day, their enjoyment of lazy time was  made possible by the swimming pool/playground. And more important, made possible by the  volunteers who are always ready to help or greet them with a smile. To show and tell the organization a  story, made as small as possible, was a great way to get them re-acquainted with their target group.  And that in a way that everyone could understand and relate to because it was a recognition of their  every day volunteers work and what they enjoyed about that.

Insight and approach In this case I didn't have the chance to talk to a large group of volunteers. Normally our agency would  organize a few workshops to get in depth. Now, the ﬁeldwork was limited to a few interviews with some   volunteers. Some of them I'm acquainted with on a private level. Therefore the organizational problem  was layed out pretty good. The facility itself I knew very well, as my family and myself are regular  visitors. To give the story more depth though, I'd like to have done some interviews with visitors as well.  On the other hand, it was somehow told from ﬁrst hand experience.

In my daily line of work as a creative director at an agency I am already using design tools. But more in  the creative ﬁeld, in the creative parts of projects. On incidental levels we use them in organizational  fashion: in workshops or change management projects. This course gave me more insight in how to  improve complete projects as I have now a more holistic view on the matter. Design thinking is not  strictly reserved for the creative ﬁeld. It broadened my view on how the design management tools can  be deployed within the same project to get a coherent result. A great improvement is the strengthened  link with my co-workers from the marketing department. As I form a link between marketing and  creative, I think I have a better understanding of the cross teamwork in eachothers ﬁelds.

And last but not least: I became a volunteer at the swimming pool/playground!

Reflection: Learning Launch

Challenge:

Educating initiatives for the Chronic Kidney disease patients on the Diet and Nutrition aspects of  Disease,  as the disease comes with lot of restriction in Dietary habits. The patient has lot of questions  regarding what is the right type of diet for him, but the most of the questions do not get answered at  the Clinics due to paucity of time. The challenge is to address it by creating credible patient awareness  content and providing one stop platform for the patients and care givers.

Selection:

The chronic kidney patients do not have many dedicated credible source available online on diet and  nutrition. Keeping in mind learning launch tool quick feedback/in sighting process we interviewed 5  Healthcare Professionals to understand the severity of this problem and also conducted the one on one  interview with 10-15 patients in a week’s time. We tried to understand the different platforms through  which patients try to get the information currently and how authentic that knowledge base is.

Application:

With the learning and feedback received from the market research we found that most of the patients  are not interested in reading and would like to view the informative content. The patients were  searching youtube for Videos on diet and nutrition. We decided to create a dedicated youtube channel  for educating the Chronic Kidney Patients on Diet and Nutrition. We generated credible content with  help of expert renal nutritionist and nephrologists. Also, the content was vernacular as lot of patients  requested for the same during our interaction with them. The channel is promoted organically and also  due to the quality of content being recommended by the peers and HCP to the patients.

Insights & Approach:

India is a vast country with lot of different languages and eating habits. We need to create the content  keeping in mind the regional eating habits and the preferred languages in those areas. Also, we need to  promote the platforms through other social media platforms available to maximize our increase to  Kidney disease patients.

We internally developed patient education content, content shared by the healthcare professionals, also  planning to add the Success stories of Patients who are coping well with the disease.

We saw a good traction in the channel with more than 2k subscribers. The learning that we got is that  we need to be regular in posting the content and try to make the videos more interesting with a short  duration of 5-7 minutes.

The learning Launch tool helped us in quick insights and enabled quick action within limited budget.

At the end we are happy that we are trying to address the need gap that currently Chronic Kidney  disease patients have and hopefully it would result in better outcome for the patients in longer run.

Regards,

Laxman Patil

STORYTELLING

Use case in a company - Selling to a ‘non-buyer’

By Felix Villagra – November 2017

This case of success begins like many others, with several successive failures that taught us  several lessons to be applied in future commercial actions. The purpose of the sale was a  medium-sized company, A.P. Moller Maersk, which was offered an expensive but effective software tool to  predict production defects and errors, CIBioFi.

A.P. Moller Maersk is dedicated to the manufacture of tools for printing sheet metal parts for automobile  bodies.

The first of the mistakes made by the commercial manager, Toni, was to offer CIBioFi to the  department that did not make the investment decisions, the technical manager worked with  remarkable efficiency and met the deadlines and quality levels required by their customers, so  that I saw the need to change nothing. The technical manager did not have an own budget for  investments, besides it was uncomfortable and expensive to try a tool, demonstrate its  effectiveness to the management and request a budget from the general management. In a way,  I saw that CIBioFi threatened its leading role in the department, a software cannot replace 20  years of experience according to their criteria.

Toni's second mistake was trying to sell CIBioFi with a trial period of only 6 months, when the  projects have a much longer duration to demonstrate the savings achieved. This, without  counting on the learning time that the solution requires and with a very tense planning to find  time available for training. Toni was under pressure because he would not reach his annual goals  without the sale of CIBioFi.

The sales cycles of these solutions were usually long, but this time there were two elements that  blocked success and had already been consumed two years. Toni was immersed in a loop that  did not work and his CEO made the decision to relieve him in the management of the account.  This account, represented 25% of the annual billing of the software company and the only  possibility of increasing the turnover with A.P. Moller Maersk was to sell a new solution, with the rest of the  solutions had already reached their ceiling and there was no prospect of growing with the  traditional products.    The new salesman, David, before presenting himself to the client, studied the case in great  detail. David travelled to the client's factory to see how they worked for two days, sharing their  points of view with them, making contact with many people from the management and staff. As  the commercial department of A.P. Moller Maersk was already a good customer of a solution to calculate  manufacturing costs, he asked them about their satisfaction with the use of the tool. He  discussed with them the possibility of introducing some improvement to reduce costs and  promised that he would come back with a proposal. Upon returning to the offices, David had a  clear picture of how the client worked and began to think of a strategy. Having an ally in the  A.P. Moller Maersk offers department was a plus that I could not miss.    The following week, David met with the CEO of CIBioFi. He asked for an extra time to implement  the solution in A.P. Moller Maersk. He reasoned the reasons that had led to the failure and why it was not  realistic to set a deadline of 6 months for A.P. Moller Maersk to buy.

Within a month of his stay at A.P. Moller Maersk, David met with the commercial management of this company  and got the CEO to be present to hear the proposal. David asked them if they would be willing  to test for a year a solution that would allow them to reduce manufacturing costs by 5%. He  gave them a presentation with a couple of success stories, a German client and a Canadian one.    After several phone calls, meetings and negotiations of economic conditions, the commercial  management and CEO of A.P. Moller Maersk agreed to test the solution and the technical director got the  commitment to test the solution. A.P. Moller Maersk brought in a brilliant engineering student proposed by  CIBioFi to take over the tests with the software, so they would not make the technical  department's workload worse.  After 10 months of testing, David got the signing of the CIBioFi sales contract. This case of  success of A.P. Moller Maersk is used for the formation of new commercial and also for the rest of  departments.    By using this tool, one of the best commercial strategies executed by CIBioFi is comprehensively  explained. It teaches how to change a bad initial approach for another of success, looking for  allies, analyse the points in favour to take advantage of them and how to fight with the weak  points.    Sometimes, this success story is used for presale, since the CIBioFi team has it well learned and  knows the benefits of this case. In addition, CIBioFi has since organized sessions to solve  problems, design sales strategies or even unlock internal conflicts.

Author's note: The names A.P. Moller Maersk and La Puerta Falsa are fictitious, although the case is based on a true  story.
