CHALLENGE; Market penetration

Power is a significant challenge in Nigeria. In about two decades this nation has expended  over twenty billion U.S. Dollars yet our total power output is about Five thousand  megawatts. This is a country with a population of about a hundred and seventy million  people occupying about a million square kilometres of land. Many people need power to  run their fridges, freezers, air conditioning etc but this lack of it created a challenge and an  opportunity. So we set up a factory to produce blocks of ice that we could provide the  people in our state to use in meeting some of their refrigeration needs. Because of the  burning nature of the need and huge population we believed this would be a no brainer  and would hit the market in a huge wave. This did not happen. As a matter of fact, we  struggled to make sales of 20 blocks a day from a 1000 block a day factory. This was not  sustainable and we had to take significant action and fast if were not going to shelve the  business.    This way we would get hard facts on why the market was reacting with such poor reception  to a product that was designed (as we thought) to meet an ardent refrigeration need.

TOOL SELECTED; Learning Launches

Lucky for us I had this challenge in mind while taking the course and it seemed sensible  to use the learning launches. This would keep is in the market experimenting to get to the  truth we required to take a decision on our current business and or, model. The whole idea  was that we would get the true market feel and information we would use. From the videos  Estela Perez on learning launches it seemed reasonable to get our product into specific  markets, get feedback and act on the feedback.    We could not continue to run the factory in perpetuity if were not utilizing the factory at  least at 80% and making 100% sales of whatever came out of it. We would not be able to  pay for equipment, diesel to run generators, maintenance, salaries and all would make us  bankrupt. So trying out well designed darts at the market and using the feedback to adjust  our offering cum operations would be our best bet and not just a set of brainstorming  sessions with the team.

APPLICATION and INSIGHTS

We first decided to call in for a meeting with all those we had tried to sell to who had made  claims of being re-sellers of ice-blocks for other producers. The meeting was a town hall  type set-up that would allow us hear from them what it was that made them purchase the  product from the competition despite what we believed were the attributes of our product;  high quality, hygienically produced ice, cost efficient since it lasted longer than their current  purchase (great value for money proposition), and we delivered to the client. We also  hoped to share with them our vision for the business and what benefits lay in store for re- sellers who worked with us.    The meeting held with us asking questions to participants like, how long they had been in  the business, what advice would they give to those who wished to start up such a business,  what were the pitfalls to look out for, what would a producer do for them that would make  them loyal, what sort of support would they wish they had, what kind of support where they  currently getting, had they tried out our product, what issues did they have with it, what  could we do to address these issues? Through this process we learnt about the seasonality

of the product demand which rhymed with the natural season. We also learned that pricing  was usually variegated from season to season and did not remain same especially for our  target market. That is not all, we also gained other insights as to what kind of support  would keep them loyal, their thoughts on our offers and other concerns.

APPROACH

What we did thereafter was to offer variegated pricing to those who would commit to certain  minimum volumes per week. We would also require their daily feedback so we could keep  tabs on our performance. In addition, we would attempt to support them further with storage  facilities such as coolers and freezers, not to mention ad campaigns that would now be  focused on them and not on us. This so far has increased sales volumes to about 30% of  installed capacity based on signing on 3 dedicated resellers out of our target of 10.    I think that going forward it would make sense to have stakeholders in a business give some  form of guided feedback that would allow for the launch of any product. Then launch out in  small areas based on that feedback continue to adjust where necessary.

Selection

Our team thought that using visualization  techniques would yield additional graphics to support developing an overarching strategy for the reform  plan.  Additionally, we felt that getting the stakeholders to visualize the various processes would ease  understanding and ease the path to consensus.

Application

As expected the meeting began with a heated discussion of various processes and procedures and  rapidly took on the air of complaint about problems within stakeholder’s mission areas. We started with having stakeholders develop a timeline incorporating a swim lane, similar  to those used with process flowcharts, and followed with markers to show major process points and  times. After the individual stakeholder “Maps” were created, we combined the individual roadmaps  into a single roadmap that visualized the current state of IT within the ISET Charguia. community town as a class, similar to the town they live in. They are in charge of  designing a variety of different buildings for our town proposal, to share with the  Town Board Zoning Director. They will work in teams of three to create their  building. But together as a class they must think of the logistics and sizing of the  buildings. As teams decide what type of building they are going to construct they  meet as a class to make sure they have the different buildings that are necessary  in a town. The students will then break off into their groups of three. The children  will learn that the only materials that are available for them to construct their  buildings are toothpicks and playdoh.

Each student will independently sketch their building. They will have

approximately fifteen minutes to sketch their building. While sketching, they will  also have to figure out the surface area, height, and width of their building.  Students will then have an opportunity to discuss their plans with their teammates  to determine how they would like to collaborate their designs to make the most  efficient building they can.

Once the team decides on the structure of their building and is within their

surface area parameters they can start building their building. They might have to  redraw a plan together that allows them to collaborate their ideas. During this  time, they might notice that their structure does not hold the weight they  anticipated. They then have to consider, what works? And possibly try again. At  the end of the assignment, students should be able to present a building  representation from our town to the Town Board Zoning Director. Their buildings  are sized down from feet to inches, but will be a presentation of how they feel the  town should be set up, while tying this into our math curriculum of learning about  surface area.     Insight and Approach    One thing that I learned from this experience was that, helping students

visually put something into perspective helped the majority of the students  understand the idea of measurement and area. Some children were confused that  many things start off as a scaled drawing and then evolve into something larger.  The students were able to use mathematical equations to determine how large  their building would turn out to be.     Many of the students worked very well together. I was happy to see the

collaboration that took place to combine the original drawings to do what was best  for their team. While the students were working, I began to hope that all of the  children were considering what is working at this time. I met with the teams  throughout this process and discussed different aspects of their building with  them. We found things that might not hold up the weight on the top of the  building, together we discussed our findings and were able to adapt from there,  considering what else could work. Some students also learned that with their new  team drawing, they exceeded the amount of area space they were provided.     Another approach that could help the students understand the idea of area

and think about their community would be to make this activity two dimensional  only. By providing the class with a large sheet of graph paper, the teams would  begin to plot their building on the map, together as a class they would have to  determine the logistics of where certain buildings should be placed. Each team  would take turns using the graph paper. But I enjoy the idea of having the children  think in an innovative way to physically construct their buildings using materials  such as toothpicks and playdoh, it allows them to connect with other learning  styles.

Challenge      My challenge was determining the reason for significant changes in demand in the first two

weeks of planning. I work in Supply Chain for a very large company. We recently implemented an  Advanced Planning and Optimization (APO) tool for planning inventory levels in the field (300 locations)  and at our Distribution Centers (3 locations). At its core, the APO system helps us plan the right  inventory, at the right place, at the right time, and in the right quantity. It does this by determining the  target inventory levels based upon pre-defined settings (parameters). These settings define how much  inventory we want to store as safety stock (inventory above exactly what is needed in case of  fluctuations in demand).

The field orders inventory each week. For the first time, we were letting a system make these

order quantity recommendations for us. Since correct inventory levels are critical, we built in a two-day  window where the field could review the system generated plans and adjust as needed. However, these  adjustments were happening significantly and in multiple directions. During the review process some  items were being increased while other were being decreased. To compound the issue, each of the  three different departments (Demand, Supply, Distribution) were making changes to try and correct.  These last-minute changes were causing us to send incorrect order quantities to the Manufacturers that  have long lead times. This means significant changes happening each week would take months to  correct.

Selection

The cause of the issue was not clear due to system complexity and multiple groups trying to

correct it so I ended up using most of the tools. Learning Launch was my last chance to find a solution. I  started with Data Analysis but could not pinpoint the issue. I then went to the customer (the field  making the changes) using Storytelling to understand what they were doing and why they felt like that  was the right decision. This resulted in a handful of possible causes. The only way to know for sure was  by making adjustments, understanding the impact, then iterating until something worked. Learning  Launch let me fail fast to get to the correct solution by testing my hypothesis’s.

Application      I selected 10 locations to use Learning Launch with. This left the other 290 locations as a

baseline to compare against. The 10 locations were chosen based upon how they were making their  adjustments. Some were making only a few changes while others were making the most. I initially met

with them as a group to introduce what I wanted to try. I reviewed what I was seeing, what the system  was trying to do for them, and walked them through why the system was making the recommendations  it was.

I then met with each location weekly during their adjustment window. Instead of them adjusting

their orders to what they wanted, I adjusted the settings to them. This accomplished two things. First it  confirmed that the settings were not correct for what the field wanted. Second, it built trust in the  system for the field. After several iterations, the system reached a steady-state of un-adjusted, system  generated orders. Absolute quantity adjustments went from over 70% each week to under 5% resulting  in fewer expedited orders and smoother signals to the Manufacturers. After a few weeks I convinced the  field that inventory levels could be reduced to normal levels without the risk of running out. This led to a  multi-million-dollar reduction of inventory levels in the field, especially important during times of  constraint.

Insight      Without Learning Launch I would not have been able to definitively settle on what was causing

the issue and implement the correct solution. By making the changes, reviewing the results, then  making additional changes each week I determined not only that the settings (not demand or other  factors) were causing the issue but which ones and how to resolve them long term.

Approach

I was using most of these tools before knowing about Design Thinking so some of my

approaches were not technically sound. In a similar situation I would use the full suite of tools to better  document the journey of discovery for future use. The use of Learning Launch in itself would not have  solved this issue but was absolutely key in its final resolution.

REFLECTION: MIND MAPPING

Challenge

I am managing a large, organizational transformation program for an international sporting  organization in Switzerland. The program portfolio includes over 15 internal projects and one of the  key projects for this year is working under a very strict timeline.

After an initial but short phase of well-intentioned discovery and data gathering, the project team  jumped into developing a new process, training a pilot population and implementing a new system to  support it. The team is making good progress according to their delivery plan while the significant  amount of data initially gathered has been left unanalyzed and unused.

However, early feedback and reporting emerging from pilot populations and senior management has  been very mixed and the team is growing frustrated. In addition, the project team’s laser focus on  delivery means that collaboration and alignment with colleagues and peers outside has suffered.  Finally, a program steering committee meeting is upcoming in the next two weeks and we are now at  pains to agree between the program and project teams on what to share with the senior  management.

Selection

To help the project team take a step back I decided to prepare the mind-mapping exercise. I initially  selected the exercise as a means of getting the team to take the time to immerse themselves in all  the available employee data they had amassed – but largely left aside –  since the beginning of the  project. I was tipped off to the idea from the Mind Mapping tool video in Week 3 with hbrown@yahoo.com  as a way we could “distill all that data into information and insights that can be easily  communicated.”

I also recognized the potential opportunity for the workshop to establish a “common mind”, i.e.  create alignment between the project team, the program management and some of the functional  colleagues. I proposed that we could use the workshop to produce learnings and insights that we  could share with the Steering Committee.

Application

Together with the project management officer we gathered elements from interviews, working  group summaries, surveys, governance minutes, training feedback forms etc., cleared a wall in our  project office and posted up all of the data we felt might be relevant. I invited the project team,  functional team members and the members of the program office to join the Gallery Walk and all  invited parties showed up. Everyone went through the gallery silently collecting ideas and notes on  post-its etc. Afterward, we worked in a group session to share each of our elements and  observations, identify themes and “map” them. Using the “So What?” prompt we were able to  identify a number of key insights.

Insights

Many insights emerged that were relevant for the project. One of the most important was that there  was a high level of agreement and alignment across the group on a limited number of important  themes. A common, clearer mind was emerging.

This led to a very open discussion on how these insights could not only be shared with the Steering  Committee but be integrated into the project scope, approach and delivery. Numerous new ideas  were born out of the session and all of us left energized by the shared clarity, which immediately  resulted in re-prioritization discussions, shared action plans and renewed overall commitment of the  entire group to the project.

Approach

Next time I would leave even more time for the discussion and formalization of common insights. I  would be more vigilant about keeping the team from jumping into solution-seeking and  brainstorming, which I found to be a strong temptation myself when confronted with such rich  conclusions.

Finally, I probably didn’t feel comfortable enough to trust the exercise as completely as I could have.  Having now seen the power of the exercise, I will feel more confident about the process and  wouldn’t hesitate to include even more people and breaking out into smaller discussion groups next  time.

Visualization Tool – Reflection on Beauty

Pattern

Problem Statement: The Challenge  In a daily basis, society is bombarded with media information that dictates beauty patterns. Constantly,  men and women of all ages are being told what is the accepted human pattern that they must belong,  suffering from the consequences of trying to fit into this beauty pattern. For example, the long-term  effects once a teenager girl starts to pursue the intangible beauty are widely known and reflect on  increased rates of eating disorders just to cite one consequence. In contrast, older women are being  heavily attracted to the pursue of the anti-aging era through more aggressive treatments (surgical and  non-surgical treatments). However, in this reflection, the hypothesis is that the pursue of beauty may be  endless and more than often, it does not bring happiness to those individuals. We all have seen  celebrities whose faces seem disfigured due to the high quantity of cosmetic procedures, but they keep  going on more. Such globally known examples are Michael Jackson, Jocelyn Wildenstein, and Rodrigo  Alves, the Human Ken doll.

In this reflection, it is also accepted the lasting benefits of skincare routines coupled with good lifestyle  choices. In another words, the usage of good quality cosmetics brands in a daily skincare routine by itself  does only half of the job of keeping a healthy look. It is extremely important that the lifestyle of choice  matches the common goal. However, most people expect that the cosmetic products generate not only  an amazing effect on their looks, but also a result that shows quickly.

The main challenge is to effectively encourage a lifestyle change that connects the individual to their  inner beauty and core values, but also provides information to feed into the self-care of their bodies and  deal with aging of their bodies and face, by using social media and/or online tools such as Facebook,  Instagram, Tik-Tok and other widely known networking platforms.

The Tool  For this challenge, I have chosen the Visualization Tool since it provides a blank canvas for the user to  dwell on many aspects they desire and at the same time, focusing on the current topic (the challenge).  The objective is to capture any information that flows naturally and with no direction from me – the  facilitator (no guidance will be provided, except by a few information) on how the user would expect to  connect the most important areas of facial beauty to their inner happiness, and how they expect to  achieve it. As Megan Cook stated in her video, Visualization is a way [that people] communicate in a  non-logical manner, and by using this tool, I expect to find categories of people and patterns of  problems, and finally, to be able to discover how people expect to deal with the body and facial aging. I  also expect to gain insight on the strategies that people may come up with in order to deal with the  aging process. Most importantly, as Myers highlights during her speech, the Visualization tool has a  major goal to understand the users in a passive manner, and this comes in direct alignment with the  Design Thinking practices.

Socorro Carlos – Final Assignment – design thinking @ coursera

Application   The user received two pages (on an A4 size paper) with a large face draw on it. The first face represents  their face now, and the second face represents their face at a future state (about 20 years into the  future). Both drawings of faces have no hair and are generalized simple faces with just the contour of  the head, lips, nose, eyes and eyebrows. The user was asked to draw/collage/paint/write the parts of  the face that brings happiness now. The second face the user was asked to draw/paint/collage/write  how they imagine their looks after all this time (20 years).

Once in possession of the results, I hold several 10-15 min interview with each user, individually, to ask  about their drawings. At this time of the interview, the question is “how are you planning to accept the  changes that you draw in your face?”. After collection of this information, all responses were  categorized in groups, patterns and insights were identified.

The categories of groups are divided by age, ethnicity, region (to capture the influence of weather  conditions) and social status. Additionally, I was able to analyze the results based on easily identifiable  concerns for example, if the lips are the most mentioned problem area in terms of happiness and which  groups consider that feature the most important. My major interest was to identify which strategies  users are planning to deal with the aging process.

Insights Gained & Approach  From this exercise, I learned that most people don’t have a defined strategy on how to deal with the  aging process and most of the responses indicate that this is an area of concern that we are not  prepared to deal with. While some responses mentioned that they consider performing plastic surgery  in the future, there was a consensus on how the surgeries are the last resort and users prefer a gradual  skincare routine to prevent major issues in the future.

Some answers included the healthcare aspect (for instance, skin cancer is a concern specially in the  Northern regions, in contrast with South American responses). But also, mental health was mentioned in  many answers stating that the aging process may cause depression in some, so definitely it is of public  interest to take preventative measures to prepare individuals for the future, in terms of skin and body  care.

The process in which the Visualization tool was applied seemed to be satisfactory not only because it  allowed each user to express themselves more freely, but it allows the user to not be tied to directions,  and therefore, the responses were of a varying degree of details and very different from each other. The  Visualization tool, as applied in this exercise, benefited on the post-interview. The rationale behind it is  that each user was able to express themselves in their unique way, and I needed some degree of  quantifiable information in order to categorize the responses. Therefore, when using this type of tool, I  recommend the interview or a table-format follow up in order to gather key points, otherwise the  exercise becomes very subjective.

Design Thinking Innovation – Reflection on Learning Launch

Mlungisi Msibi, 05.02.2021

Challenge

As a DIGITAL FACTORY, the training and the development of skills, especially technical, of employees  remains among the main concerns of our company, knowing that the Digital IT domain is undergoing a  very important evolution at this time.

However, the planning and selection of classic training courses is subject to many constraints linked  mainly to circumstances of the Covid-19 pandemic, the simultaneous unavailability of employees for a  specified period due of projects commitments, the uncertainty of quality of training and trainers and the  lack of visibility on the degree of learning per employee.

Selection

We decided to do a learning launch that allowed us to test very quickly & inexpensively whether we  were on the right track or whether we needed to pivot completely our thinking. Even if the outcome is  not as desired, the loss is minimal as the investment is low. A learning launch is in fact always beneficial:  you quickly know whether you are on the right track with something or whether you need to go back to  the drawing board and formulate based on the gathered insights a new or refined hypothesis.

Application

The online training seems to be the best solution that can meet our assumptions:

•  Respect for physical distancing (directive of the Minister of Health)

•  Flexibility in time, the employee can study in the evening, on the weekend

•  Multiple trainings in a short period of time

•  Monitoring progress and assessment of learning

The e-Learning platforms have become intuitive and interactive and offer a variety of confirmed courses  in partnership with internationally recognized universities as well as ways to monitor progress and  evaluate employees at the end of training.

We chose 2 online training platforms: Coursera and Pluralsight. In order to test the solution in action, we  created test accounts for 2 groups, the first composed of 2 project managers and the second of 4  developers. The trainings chosen are «Design Thinking» on Coursera for the 1st group and «DevOps» for  the other on Pluralsight and we started the training simultaneously with a period of one month to  finalize them.

Learning Launch

Solution to be

tested  e-Learning

Who  2 project managers and 4 developers

Where  online

How  Creating a test accounts on 2 e-learning platforms

Cost  NULL

Duration  1 month

As a member of the 1st group, the training of «design thinking» on Coursera was very satisfactory for  me in terms of content and quality, the learning path provides flexibility and content tracking of the  progress and the final exam allowed me to effectively evaluate the acquired knowledge.

Finally, all participants in this test confirm the reliability of the chosen platforms and the duration of one  month was enough to finalize the courses perfectly. We therefore decided to go to generalization by  creating accounts and collecting the training topics desired by the employees of the company in order to  develop a year training plan.

Insights

The learning launch has allowed us to reach the right solution with a total respect for the requirements  of our environment and in a rather limited period and with an almost negligible investment. In addition,  during the experiment, we discovered other opportunities and benefits offered by the chosen platforms  that can improve the sense of learning and sharing within our institution.

The learning launch has proven to be very reliable and it is a tool that can be particularly useful to us to  test all new concepts in a safe way in terms of time and money. It will also allow us to solidify our new  solutions in order to live a successful implementation both on the concrete side and on the satisfaction  of the various stakeholders!

Reflection – Mind Mapping

Michael Xu

Challenge

Nourishment is an essential function of survival and cooking can be one of life’s most simple  pleasures. Not only do many find it enjoyable, but it is also a very primary source of  independence. For someone with a physical disability however, preparing food can present many  barriers. Manipulating a kitchen knife to slice or chop can be difficult and unstable for someone  with limited fine motor function, grip strength, or finger dexterity.

This summer at my internship with the Studio 930 RIT Design Consultancy, my team and I spent  ten weeks implementing design and engineering skills to create an adaptive kitchen knife  solution to address such challenge. Our end user representatives were Robert, who has back and  hand arthritis, and Rob, who is affected by spinal cord injury and has the desire for more stability  and control while utilizing a kitchen knife for slicing or chopping.

Selection & Application

Mind mapping was a popular and trusted tool used in both research and ideation. This tool was  also well configured in Miro, the online whiteboard our team was using to collaborate and  communicate ideas during this pandemic.

To redefine the initially ambiguous problem statement, mind mapping was used in place of the  napkin pitch, branching out trigger words from the scope the problem, needs of the user, and  even early design criteria. This was our first attempt at what I call “controlled word vomiting”  and it was proven effective when, after interviewing our client, most of them matched his  preferences.

In benchmarking, we chose mind mapping to look for themes and patterns in the current assistive  kitchen tools market. The inputs of this mind map were up to ten specific products grouped in  categories and the outputs were neatly organized design conclusions about form, features, and  materials which were crucial for informed ideation.

And yes, divergent ideation is what mind mapping was also used for. Our team did a fun and  collaborative ideation exercise in which we brainstormed possibilities from eight frames. We  even included pictures to combine mind mapping and visualization for more clarity. For  example, in the frame named convertible, we explored different ways the handle can articulate to  adapt to different people’s ergonomics. Although this idea was eventually tabled, we were able  to stimulate creativity and think outside of the box with this tool.

Insight & Approach

Evidently, we found mind mapping to be one of the most intuitive and versatile design thinking  tools by far. Out of the ten sections of our virtual whiteboard, six of them involved some form of  mind mapping. Especially in research, mind mapping accomplished our goal of establishing  succinct yet specific design criteria for upcoming the idea generation phase and is the foundation

for our final concept with utility, safety, as well as user empathy in mind. Additionally, mind  mapping is very helpful for organizing thoughts and ideas. Instead of creating a chaotic cluster of  post it notes, our mind maps could tell us exactly where each idea is from so we can trace it back  to the fundamental concepts to understand why it is there and, better, offer suggestions on how  the current configuration can be improved for more clarity and efficiency. Design thinking is a  messy process, but only initially messy, and mind mapping does the work of cleaning and  converging.

Was there an overuse of mind mapping? Perhaps. Some phases of the design thinking process are  meant to be messy and patterns can’t be found everywhere. Next time, I’d like to specialize mind  mapping to an organization tool to wrap up the ideation phase while playing a more convergent  and conclusive role that makes coming up with new ideas much easier. For example, after a  brainstorming session, a mind map can be used to cluster the ideas into vague and sometimes  overlapping groups, subgroups and so on. And with connection lines, ideas can “talk to each  other” and form an internet of concepts from which we can start rearranging the mind map to  look for important patterns and generate trigger questions.

Journey Mapping - By Monika Wolf

The South African, State Owned, THE CYBER SPACE HUB (Triple Play) tasked me, as part of a two man  performance coaching team, with the following:  Increase participation and collaboration of engineers during *Production Meetings in order to

a. Establish plant stability and optimisation.  b. Increase productivity and Mega Watts produced

*Production Meeting: A daily morning meeting where all the relevant engineers (Boiler, Turbine,  Auxiliary, Chemical Services, Maintenance and Control & Instrumentation) and Management meet  to familiarise themselves with the plant condition and current production related challenges

Back Ground:

Power Generation in SA is in crisis. This has been true since 2003 when a moratorium was placed on  planned maintenance for the period 2009 until the conclusion of the Soccer World Cup event that  was hosted in SA during 2003.  Triple Play, to this day, has not recovered from the back log and  the subsequent increased damage and anomalies that has occurred right across power plants since  2009. Myself and another coach had been working on the Plant for about 6 months and had  established trust relationships with all stakeholders by then.    Selected Tool:  During the “What if?” phase, we decided to use Journey Mapping  as design tool to really  understand a day in life of an SA THE CYBER SPACE HUB engineer. In order to understand the lack of  participation and collaboration in the Production Meetings, we wanted to use a Customer Centric  approach to really dive deep and understand how these engineers experienced their working  conditions in an attempt to gain insights into their practical and emotional challenges being faced.  (As demonstrated in the lecture Video “The Good Kitchen”)    Application  During the course of 4 weeks we literally shadowed each engineer on the plant wearing hard hats  and safety boots, going into the belly of the power generating beast with them. There were nothing  off limits meetings for the coaches. We tracked and documented the following per engineer, on an  individualised journey map:

c. Name and Surname  d. Engineering Division and Job description.  e. Hourly activity log, including but not limited to:

i. Distance walked  ii. Plant Areas visited  iii. Conversations had with whom?  iv. Collaborated with whom?  v. Conflict experienced: with whom, why, where, was it personal or

professional?

vi. Communication: Clear?, Precise? Succinct?, Was the message received the same one

that was communicated?

vii. What did this engineer try to do? (Job to be done)  viii. What practical challenges were experienced?  ix. Engineer’s state of mind.  x. Reason for state of mind.

The gathering of this information naturally included a substantial amount of constant  interviewing.

Insights gained:  On completion of the Journey Mapping we consolidated the data gathered and started looking for  patterns, trends and commonalities. The insights gained were astonishing:

Emotions Experienced  Reason

Exhaustion  Average walking distance per day: 9km

Stress  Working under constant pressure due to unsustainability of work being done.

Frustration  Very poor communication between engineers and artisans. Lack of line of site  on work being logged - has it started and what the progress status is.

Disconnect  between  engineers and artisans

The incident log management platform was on their PCs and they did not  have constant line of sight on tasks logged and progress made.

Hopelessness and lack of  Pride

(** Note: Triple Play is a controversial brand and not loved by the public  due to being notoriously unreliable)  -  This led to a lack of Pride in the work  they were doing.  Hopelessness: The engineers felt invisible due to a lack of recognition by  Management.

Animosity  There was a lack of trust between Management, the Engineering

team and the artisans

Lack of Confidence  Due to the mistrust between Management and Engineering team, they did  not feel confident offering solutions nor that they had a voice.

Through the use of Journey Mapping I realised that the definition of the challenge as provided by the  SA Utility Management was extremely narrow and conservative. Production and plant stability could  not increase by solving the issue of collaboration and participation of people on a single level. The  level of dependency between engineers and artisan is so intertwined that applying Design Thinking  and a solution on one level only would have limited results.   Management did not realise that this challenge related to the culture of this organisation and  solutions had to be found for, and applied to every level of the organisation.    We invited all stake holders to share in the solution by co creating (inter alia) an app where  engineers and artisans and management can connect through offering a safe space to create a  personal profile containing “I am accountable for” and “what you do not know about me” space. On  this app we offered a life feed for participants vote anonymously during meetings on controversial  topics, rate the participation in the production meeting and reward people for making a  contribution, not only in the meeting but also through the work being done and the results thereof.  We added a life feed to the app from the Incident Management system to provide line of sight when  engineers was on the plant on not in their offices and provided scooters to relieve physical  exhaustion and just add a bit of fun.    Alternative Design Tools that could have been used:

Workshops and mind mapping were viable alternative Design tools, Yet, in retrospect, I realise that  the public nature of mind mapping and workshops, coupled with the lack of confidence and fear of  being judged, would not have yielded honest feedback and would have been detrimental to  understanding the true issues -  both practical and emotional .

Final Assignment – “Design Thinking for Innovation”

Matteo Cuda

2019, Oct 22

1. Challenge

In the Common Solutions Group of Applied Materials’ New Product Transition department,  troubleshooting and root cause analysis is where the rubber meets the road during the module  test and engineering validation phases of new mainframe and robot introduction.  The key here  is to quickly identify why a particular function or subsystem is not meeting expected  performance so that the system may be recovered.  A secondary goal – possibly more  important, in the grander scheme of things – is to treat each failure point as a seed for making  changes to prevent similar occurrences on future platforms.  Current methodologies and best  practices include fishbone analysis and a proprietary “8D” analysis.  Each of these methods can  be too slow to fit with the accelerated pace of product testing and aggressive shipment  schedules, and neither truly does a great job of finding and addressing the systemic root causes,  at best sharing a “lessons learned” slide with key stakeholders.

2. Selection

In my experience, mind-mapping has always been seen as a tool for organizing information and  tasks in a hierarchal, “tree” fashion.  This is undeniably very useful, but I had not attempted the  unique version of “mind mapping” as presented in this course.  That is, as a tool for finding the  “hidden” theme behind the more superficial symptoms.  I decided to use this method as part of  and an extension to our current root cause analysis culture, as I believed this would help avoid  time lost to chasing red herrings and would improve our post-mortem/lessons learned quality as  well.

3. Application

The particular problem selected was a random, chronic freezing of a front end wafer loading and  unloading fab interface for 200mm wafers into a dielectric application tool.  Specifically, the  front end robot would randomly freeze in between wafer transfer between loadports, forcing  the reliability cycling portion of the test to come to a halt, requiring the technician to manually  recover the system.  As a modification, I presented observed data (“gallery”) to a smaller group  of manufacturing engineers and technicians (stakeholders), and the process was conducted in a  more ad-hoc way, right in the test bay.

4. Insight

The method yielded several possible paths for us to follow, from errors in the code or failures of  the robot’s vacuum chuck to sags in the power supplies.  However, in fact, the key theme arose

from observation of an outlier!  Specifically, this was noticing a redundant feedback message –  an acknowledgement of the completion of the event onto which the system froze - seen upon  recovery of the system from the fault.  This lead us to ask the “so what?” questions which  brought us to realize that the message “pipeline” was being interrupted, and the robot could  not start it’s next task until receiving a message noting completion of the preceding task.   Ultimately, this turned out to be due to a random time syncing error between the serial  messaging processor on the indexer pod and the robot controller.  Incidentally, this was fixed  with a simple 10 millisecond delay - added to the control scripts – to “pause” the robot to wait  for the confirmation messages before proceeding.  This added 10-ms cycle time was  inconsequential to the productivity (throughput) of the overall system.

5. Approach

The biggest benefit from this exercise was seeing the bigger picture in that we need to be  reviewing the time synching of our related controls devices, especially for serial-controlled  (albeit legacy) systems.  Questions arise, however, such as “how will we know when to do this?”,  “what is the threshold?”, and “how would we have known to even look for this in the first  place?”.  Thus, the “takeaway” for the next application of this mode of mind-mapping shall be to  conduct a second round, after the acute root cause is found and addressed.  This second round  shall attempt to identify the design question for our business process as a whole, specifically  how to prevent a recurrence of the systemic gap that lead to the more specific failure mode.

I started using this tool to help me organize my own life in the beginning of  each year, as a way to help me visualize my new year’s resolutions.  I start by setting up  goals I want to achieve, action plans I would need to put in practice in order to achieve  those goals, stakeholders that would participate and contribute for those goals to happen,  and material and intellectual resources required to implement the actions.

When one of my goals is too complex or big, I usually dedicate a mind map exclusively  to tackle that specific matter.   A good and successful example of a mind map that helped  me to achieve a goal was couple of years ago, when I decided to pursue a master’s degree  in the United States. The mind mapping is a graphical tool that allows the user to mix words, images, color  and other elements, that at the end of the day, will make it easier for the user to  memorize, organize his thoughts, generate new ideas and explore different and creative  paths to solve a problem. The exercise can be done alone, but also can be used by a  group, making it possible for the participants to have a clear perspective of what other  members are thinking and creating an effective flow of ideas.

3. Application:

I start the mind mapping exercise by putting the problem in the center of a blank paper.   There are software and digital tools for mind mapping, but I am old school and usually,  when the ideas start to flow I do not have the computer or other digital devices with me.

Selection     Our team has already used another visualization tools for understanding the needs of our clients, we have  some ideas and we think that we are ready to try the learning launch tool. STORYTELLING AS A TOOL  Reflection – Fernanda Dourado, July 4, 2019

Background    In my profession, storytelling is one of the most important tools for shaping powerful and engaging  messages. I work as a copywriter at an advertising agency in Sweden.

One of our latest assignments was for a shoe retail company here in Scandinavia. The task was to re- position their brand so that it would better match an increasingly changing world and a younger  target group. At the same time, they wanted us to evaluate a new strategy they had formed - and if  we thought it was the right way to go - make this strategy more communicatively available.

Challenge

The new strategy was formulated "Everyday Shoe Fashion" – and although it was right in meaning - it  was not an expression that could engage and ignite its audience. Our challenge, therefore, was to  convince our client to use a more exciting message in order to achieve the goal.

Selection

To create a saying that could work as a cause and igniter we chose the story telling tool. This allowed  us to focus on the people in the process and their emotional experience. With a story driven  approach, we would bring employees together and make them work in the same direction. From a  consumer perspective it gave us the opportunity to stand out from competition and build loyalty as  well as “brand love”.

Insights

As a starting point we considered and investigated the company's target group – consisting of trendy  consumers who sought constant renewal. After some research and interviewing we realized that this  group of individuals most of all wanted new impressions, experiences and a sense of fast fashion to  feel attracted to our offer.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 It became clear to us that, in order to inspire and tickle the consumers desire, we needed to create  our own fashion arena and invite them there – regardless if it was our stores, the web site or a  temporary meeting place.     Application     We summarized our insights in one strong sentence – "Just walk in" - with the short supplement  "Welcome to our arena. Today it is yours.” By doing so we wanted to express the simple fact that an  arena is nothing without its audience. Our stores, web site and other appearances become truly alive  when customers come to visit. At the same time, we’re the ones providing the most interesting place  to be, by constantly presenting new fashion and exciting happenings. It’s easy, inspiring and fun to  visit us. There’s always a reason to stop by.

To bring the story to life and engage the employees, we proved how our message "Just walk in"  could be applied on several levels, with a similar story but a different angle.

1. With emotional and story driven commercials on an image-building level  2. With thematized fashion campaigns on a middle level  3. With sales-driven messages on a tactical level, without losing the passion in our story

Furthermore, we showed how the message “Just walk in” could be varied endlessly and how we  would talk about our arena in different contexts. What then happened was that the staff quickly took  the expression to their hearts and started using it in their daily work. By talking in terms of fashion  arena and being the one inviting to it, their work became consistent and successful. It also became  clearer to consumers what the company was standing for. But this is still an ongoing process.     Approach    Since our client had a clear vision of the target group and the strategy had already been decided, we  felt that mind mapping the customer journey was unnecessary. However, for describing how our  message could be applied on different levels we used the visualization tool by describing a marketing  pyramid with different levels (see Approach).     The assignment is still ongoing, and we plan to do a small-scale test by implementing one of our  ideas in real life – a kind of learning launch. Then we will be able to see how well the concept works  and what can be improved.

Reflection – Value Chain Analysis

Challenge & Selection

The first time I heard about Design Thinking was through my professional association, Norwegian Labor and Welfare Administration (Bachhpan). The article stated the numerous benefits of using this new tool or  approach in Recruiting.  As a recruiter, I was first curious to understand how this new method would be  beneficial and took on this course.

I recently accepted a new challenge: Talent Acquisition Manager in a growing firm specialized in the  Finance industry. The core business is to hire, train, develop and fill temporary positions for our main  customer in the banking business. This is a new role and therefore, I am a change agent within this small  firm.

Our goal is to grow the business and position ourselves against larger firms. We do this by hiring 50%  more resources (staff) to fill temp positions. We are currently unable to supply these roles as we don’t  have a pipeline of candidates ready to join or be hired. This business is sensitive for two major factors:  time and money.  With scares financial and internal staff resources, I quickly realized that a first  assessment was required to evaluate what we currently have available and design thinking would come  in handy to be creative in our approach in this context.

To name a few, here is our context : Meeting our customers need in a fast pace environment, competing  against larger firms, scarce financial and internal human resources, limited technology applications,  reduced available candidates to hire, cost of lost opportunity and growth issues.

In order to proceed with my assessment, I have selected the Value chain analysis tool.  I have decided to  use this tool in order to see the journey mapping through the eyes of the customer, of partnering  services and competitors. Before implementing changes, this tool will be valuable in the exploration  phase in the search for profitable growth opportunities and knowing what makes a new business model  attractive to our firm and which part is worth protecting.

Application

The first step is to draw the value chain of our core business. I decided to use the graph.1 (page 3)  working backwards from the end point to the value proposition delivered to customers.

Step 2, is the analysis of the competitive environment. The idea is to identify the key players and their  relative market share. By doing so, I quickly realized that our strength lies in the employee development  program. We do it well and we do it much faster than our main competitor.  However, our main  competitor is our client. Therefore, we are more or less partners in business.

Step 3, identifying the core strategic capabilities. This is the easy part! We need technical training  knowledge, technical finance knowledge, recruiting & hiring, negotiating and a strong customer service  team. The value chain allows me to pinpoint quickly in one direction. Our strength lies in the training

program and process. The program allows us to offer higher standards in terms of employability for our  candidates and quicker than our main competitor.

However, we need to hire more candidates to respond to our client’s demands. These demands are not  fulfilled in a timely manner and most of the time is not filled at all. In order to recruit, we require tools to  quickly identify potential candidates and a sufficient pipeline of resources to join the temporary  employees in various areas. Step 4, evaluate the bargaining power and influence of each player. This part brings valuable questions.  It allows me to evaluate each team member’s contribution. Everyone is replaceable however, there are  key roles that influences performance. The first key member is the recruiter. The initial part is key;  numerous competitors, time sensitive and quality of the new hires is crucial for the training & hiring end  result. The other key member is the trainer. This person is the last one of the value chain and drives  quality, retention and motivation for the final step in our control in the value chain.  Once the temp  employee is working at our customer’s location, we have little control of the outcome.

Step 5, determine the possibilities for improving the power and profitability in the chain.  As mentioned  earlier, strengthening and improving power in the initial hiring stage will generate more profit for the  firm.  The key areas are to ;

   Increase productivity in the initial phase 1 stage: increase the number of interviews and phone  calls.

  Add new resources : Implement an ATS system to sustain the needs and create an efficient  database of potential hires and hire an additional recruiter to the team;

  Review current sourcing & recruiting process to stream line the activities and respond quickly to  the growing demand.

Step 6, assess our vulnerabilities in order to play offense and not only defense. Where are we vulnerable  to others who might change their ways? Our competitors? This is quite easy as we only have one client  who we sustain with temporary employees.

Final step is to identify themes to bargaining powers, capabilities, partners and defensibility.  I see  potential for gaining new clients and reproducing the same value chain proposition for a different type of  business. As we recruit new hires, train them and develop these resources, we can repeat the same  winning formula and gain a new market share.

Maud Dias, Talent Acquisition Manager, Financial services

Insight & Approach

What I have learned from conducting this exercise is that while the graphic – value chain analysis  graphic– is important for reinforcing my understanding of the problem we are working to solve. The  more valuable aspect of the activity is that I have shared the graphic and my insights.

The graphic gives a focal point for discussion that allows them to share their perspectives and develop  insights into potential root causes of their problems.  While we could draw the value chain on a white  board, using this graphic and starting with a design starts the conversation with them. They can quickly  identify where they are in the graphic – or what is missing – and can more quickly gain new insights  about relationships between key entities instead of taking time to identify them.  They can also identify  variables in the problem space – that is, it helps them to identify what they don’t know, in what areas  they need to obtain information or data to provide the values for the variables.

Since I have discovered the value chain analysis, next time and come into a problem, I will review the  steps one step at a time and the questions associated with each step. It’s a helpful tool to review all  aspects, think strategically and align our priorities with the business goals.

It’s also a good reminder of what we do well and what we can do to improve ourselves. Opportunity  finder and weakness enlighten tool.

Maud Dias, Talent Acquisition Manager, Financial services

Visualization Reflection

Challenge and selection

For some years now I have used the visualization tool, or visual thinking, to understand the  present and future needs of customers with high domestic energy consumption, with limited  space on the roofs. The solutions that I offer to clients are rooftop photovoltaic systems, but  the variables of the solution (system size, module power, aesthetics, location, and wiring to the  main switch) completely depend on the client's vision of their future energy consumption,  expansion of bedrooms in the house, new heating or air conditioning systems, and many other  elements that could turn the established design, in an insufficient design according to their new  needs. I have used the technique of visualization to find out their plans for the future with a set  of questions or suggestions for discussion to allow the interested family to learn from each  other in the process of defining the scope, limits, key elements, and relationships between  elements to consider when identifying weak points and opportunities for improvements or  solutions.

Application

I start the process by creating a graph with their last 12 months of electricity consumption, with  this it is possible that they can understand the trends they have in recent months and the  energy environment in which they live. The next step is to locate the available space on the roof  of the house, considering the air conditioners, available pipes for laying cables, and possible  water tanks. A second graph is presented with the generation that can offer different sizes of  photovoltaic systems, depending on the space available on the roof, as well as the  representation of the space that the different solutions of photovoltaic systems would use. If  there is no way to get the models and available area to the roof, I make a model through the  satellite view of Google Maps. Once I have reviewed the models with the clients, it makes it  easier for me to know the habits they have on holidays and in summer. I even like to ask if they  would like to have more climates, a new refrigerator, a new microwave, a new heater, new  computers, or televisions. They serve me as my main points in the initiative for the future  growth of the photovoltaic system.

The knowledge of their future consumption habits helps me to present a linear growth of how  it is advisable to acquire those electrical products and the growth of the photovoltaic system(if  required) to continue paying the minimum amount to the energy supplier. The next step is to  show the variants of the default design and show the views of it from various points,  emphasizing not to damage the aesthetics of the house. This is achieved with a 3D model made  in SketchUp where it is easy to show the view from the street or the backyard of the house.  There are many customers where the rules of their neighborhood prevent them from displaying  the PV system, but there are also many who are proud to have a PV system and prefer to show  it in the neighborhood at all costs.

The next step is the stage of economic graphics, where the prices of the equipment are shown  according to the supplier, so it is easier for customers to understand the return on investment  of their installation, but always emphasizing that the price and quality of equipment they go  hand in hand at all times. Cheaper equipment most of the time does not have the same years of  warranty or high operating efficiency. I get clients to understand this by giving each supplier a  score of 1 to 5 so that they can identify how good the product is offered by the various  suppliers and thus make the best decision according to their needs together. Where 1 is the  supplier that offers the lowest quality products at a high price, 5 is a supplier that offers high- quality products at high prices, and 3 is a supplier that offers a product with average quality at  low prices.

Insight & Approach

I've learned to perform this exercise with many clients is that many are not well defined its  future consumption, which is why that questions how are your electronics today works to raise  awareness of how long to live them to these products and how long it is necessary to change it  or add more if you want an expansion of the house either in a new room or a pool with  integrated heating.

The modeling of the system according to the available space works as a starting point about the  maximum number of possible photovoltaic modules to install. I must clarify that this initial  model is never used as a final model since once seen by the client, comments that lead to a  new design always arise.

It is important to carry a power generation graph together with each design modification,  likewise, the client can see what repercussions each decision has with the energy that the  system can deliver. Personally, this is the simplest part of the process since normally the client  trusts the recommendations made by the engineers behind the model presented.

The most important part for clients is obviously the financial part. This decision is simplified by  having as visual support the rating of each supplier according to its price and product quality.  Over the years I have seen an average in terms of the rating chosen by customers, who usually  focus on providers of ratings 3 and 4, considering the price and quality of the products.

Reflection – Visualisation

Challenge & Selection

Of the tools presented in the lectures, visualisation is the one that I use most often. When  working with stakeholders of different backgrounds and abstract ideas, starting to visualise the  problem can help to create a common understanding. In these cases, conveying problems or  ideas via visualisation seem more effective than verbal discussion alone.

During the development of a search functionality in a client facing app, I faced the challenge  that technical stakeholders were discussing the search functionality’s capabilities in terms of  systems and data flows, while sales representatives (which were my internal clients) were  discussing the search functionality’s capabilities in terms of curated product offerings and lead  generation.

Application

As the two stakeholder groups were unable to communicate with each other, I started to draft  a paper-based visualisation of the search functionality within the client facing app. To achieve  this, I printed out snippets from the existing user interface of the app and overlaid part of it  with white paper, on which I sketched the search functionality. This rudimentary visualisation  helped to steer the discussion into a productive direction, as both parties were able to discuss  requirements for the search functionality based on something they knew (i.e. the interface of  the existing client facing app).

Insight

Using visualisation enabled the stakeholder to think outside of their siloed knowledge and focus  on creating something new. We were able to do several different iterations of the embedded  search functionality and found solutions for all the concern of the different stakeholders, before  testing the MVP with clients (in our client test lab).

Approach

A different approach, that could have been used to probably come to an equally good outcome,  would have been the mind mapping tool presented in week 4 of this course. We could have  printed out different existing search functionalities and use our client test lab to give the clients  a tour of the different functionalities and then let them pick out the “good stuff”. Then we could  have let them cluster the different functionalities. Finally, we would have been able to draw  insights and connections from the clusters and translate them into requirements.

Reflection Storytelling

(Nathan Kumar)

Context  I work for a government agency that promote a culture and holistic system of lifelong learning  through the pursuit of skills mastery, and strengthen the ecosystem of quality education and  training. The challenge is a lot of our initiatives and programmes are through an individual- targeted strategy (think B2C model) and we’re now developing a enterprise-targeted strategy  (think B2B model).    Challenge  I chose to use the tool storytelling to achieve a shared understanding of a problem space  among a diverse group of stakeholders who view the challenge of skills mastery from very  different starting points.     The first step I took was to define who are stakeholders are. Our stakeholders inside the  agency included the various departments such as the middle and back offices and critically  the policy owners who had to understand a new mode of engaging with enterprise. Whereas  our stakeholders outside the agency include the training providers, the educational institutes  and the individuals who now have to be viewed as employees instead of individuals.     The second step I took was to identify, articulate and define the ‘what is’ existing state of the  problem. I articulated 2 key points in my story: the emotional reason why we needed to have  employees pursue skills master and the larger purpose of workforce development. In the  context of a retail business owner, I painted a situation where we continued on our individual- targeted strategy (i.e. the individual learns e-commerce skills) but the employer is not in  support of training the staff as they believe in the traditional means of doing their work (i.e. via  a brick-and-mortar business model) and there’s conflict as the individual doesn’t feel motivated,  valued or supported to execute their job.     Selection  I chose to use the tool storytelling as it has the ability to connects the stakeholders to the  emotions, the characters, the values that we want all to feel. This can then be linked back to  the purpose of why each party works or partners the government agency and gives them a  sense of why they do what they do.     The third step I took was to storyboard and following the three rules raised in the lecture.  These three rules include:

1. identifying is who's your audience,  2. demonstrating a clear sequence of events, and   3. having moments of reflection.

Asking the stakeholders to rank who was responsible for the training of the staff, all  unanimously pointed to the employer. Understanding that the employer was the key audience  that we wanted action from, we then explore what was their customer journey in the thinking  through why they would or would not send their staff for training. I drew from existing materials  such as research publications, opinion survey, audit reports from other countries on why  employers are not sending their staff from training. I also conducted informal interview with  the employers I know who both did and did not commit their staff to any form of training  allowing them to have a moment of reflection.

Application   The fourth step I took was to expand further on the “moments of reflection”, I decided to raise  questions to all internal and external stakeholders that Paul VanDeCarr 1 asked around  audience motivation, these include:

•  What do we want to achieve?

•  How do we reach our target audiences?

•  Who can help us achieve our goals?

•  And what stories do I tell them, or ask them to tell?

I then curated representation from various stakeholders to represent different organization or  area of interest. Each group receives post-it notes that that they can write on directly or raise  more questions to delve deeper around motivations. As each stakeholder articulated their  perspective, I record commonalities in the insights of each group, and then additional  insights came from earlier secondary literature. I then developed a 400-word narrative with  sound bites and quotes that combines the shared and new insights from the group  discussion around motivation for sending staff for training and played that back to the same  group to get further insights.     Insights & Approach  The fifth step we took was to develop the stories further with visual support and  dramatization. I explored the idea further with our communication’s team who then roped in  film makers who managed to portray the everyday struggles of a local business in real and  relatable ways, which then drives conversation and engagement with audiences. I found that  with dramatization of the narrative, together with audio visual editing, it further pierced into  employers to embody the importance of lifelong learning and skills mastery.     The sixth and final step I took was to work with the team to publish the new employer video.  The final product of the video can be viewed here: https://www.viddsee.com/video/bak-gia- eyeglasses/ks31k where the 400-word narrative was picked up to drive the storyboard for this  video. Embracing the use of dialect which is commonly used by the local  enterprises, ‘Bak  Gia’ (Hokkien for ‘eyeglasses’) is the story of a senior optician who refuses to embrace social  media, until a younger shop assistant shows him how it can save his business.     Since publishing the video, I’ve noticed many employers who watch the video recognise the  importance of keeping up with times and how sending their staff for training can benefit their  business model. The story has lent itself to resonate with the audience’s emotions and I’ve  witness many tear-jerking momemnts. Since discovering the merits of storytelling, next time I  would incorporate an immediate call-to-action in the video by directing them to our website  to learn more or pledge their support for training.

Reflection – Storytelling

Link between research and commercial

products/services

Challenge

The main problem that I face in the research institution I work for as a Business Development  Manager is the lack of understanding of potential outcomes of research projects which can be  used to develop new products. Many of my team members have an academic background,  i.e. working as PhD or Post-docs with less industry experience. Therefore, their first priority is  to work on research projects and focus more on theoretical concepts rather than practical  concepts. However, in my case, I am responsible to derive potential products/services from  those research projects which is indeed a very difficult task and requires great imagination  power.     Selection  Based on the challenges described above, I chose the tool “Storytelling” since it will allow  me to create a story on particular outcome of research projects by putting them more into the  context of customer needs of industry clients (referring to lecture 4 of week 2, “Storytelling  tool” by Lorenzo Rosales). This would help to make my team members better understand the real  value behind the products/services which can help industry clients to reduce certain pain  points with less efforts.

Application  I applied the “Storytelling” tool in the following scenario:    Some of my colleagues work in the area of semantic data integration of big data. In the scope  of one specific research project the task was to create a semantic hybrid federated search  engine which would make it possible for the police to detect and trace potential criminals.     A short explanation on how the search engine works:  Following the input of a keyword, the search engine collects on demand data spread over  different data sources on the Web (social networks, e-commerce platforms, Open Data). The  data is integrated into a coherent knowledge graph, results can be filtered, visualized and  display summaries. Currently, it is possible to search for people, organizations, and products.     This research project is still going on and lot of modification and adjustment are made to the  search engine. In order to create a commercial product out of this research project I spend  some time in analyzing the potential of this search engine and tried to find an appropriate way  to “sell” it as a unique product to the sales team by packaging it into a nice and user-friendly  story. I brainstormed on potential application areas of this product in order to move away from

the already known use case, i.e. the criminal analysis. In this way, I would open up new  opportunities/ideas for the development team.     New application area: Why not use this search engine in the HR department of companies.  HR officers spend much time gathering information about the skills and qualification of a  candidate for a job (e.g. by searching on different platforms like LinkedIn). This problem can  be solved if those platforms are integrated to the search engine, allowing to search on just  ONE platform by browsing through many others.     I organized a workshop in which I invited the sales and development team and presented this  new application area by taking the role of a struggling HR manager searching for the right  people for his company and finally, getting to know about the semantic hybrid search engine  which allowed me to search on one platform and saved me a lot of time. I started with the  challenge or problem faced by HR managers, followed by a concrete use case, i.e. HR  manager is struggling and investing lot of time in searching for a suitable candidate for the  post of a Chief Innovation Officer. In the next step, the HR Manager discovers the great  semantic hybrid search engine enabling him to search on one platform and finding a good  match for the position. I concluded by highlighting the benefits of this product not only in the  crime domain but also in other domains like Human Resource Management.

Insight  I gained tremendous insights from applying the tool I selected for the challenge. Using this  approach, almost everyone in the workshop had a better understanding of the ideas and  participated with more interest on this particular use case. The development team  brainstormed on further enhancements with other platforms, i.e. LinkedIn. And, the sales team  took the role of the struggling HR Manager by elaborating on his/her pain in more depth. In  this way, the development team could easily respond to each of those pains by brainstorming  on technical adjustments/enhancement of the search engine. In conclusion, the development  team could focus on the technical modifications to create real value for potential customers  whereas the sales team successfully worked on a pitch for different customer groups.

Approach

Using the “storytelling” tool has been a great start. However, the next time I would organize a  follow-up workshop using the tool “mind mapping”. I would create one group consisting of  developers and the other one with the sales team. Both teams can use the stories and enrich  them with further insights by creating mind maps. They might explore more application areas  and opportunities for this product to reach a certain level of maturity. These maps can be  shared among the two different groups and also with others in our department to analyse the  different point of views and the further alignment to the departmental vision and goals.
