Reflection – Learning Launch

By Suliman Ansari

Challenge

During the COVID-19 crisis in the months of April- May 2021, me and my friends  currently in 12th grade, decided to help people in need due to the raging pandemic  in whatever way we could. We started very small with a team of 5-6 high school  students.  I am a founding member of a voluntary organisation,  Volunteers.Lionsgate Foundation (https://www.park-baker.com/tags/explore/blogpost.php) which along with my friends  came up specifically in the month of April 2017. Our challenge was to help as many  people as possible to find medical facilities, ICUs, oxygen cylinders, hospital beds,  medicines etc. who were distressed due to sufferings, either themselves or of their  family members. This exercise was specifically challenging as i) magnitude of the  crisis was huge, ii) we were confined to our homes due to the pandemic, iii) our  team needed to expand to reach out to more people, iv) gather real-time leads  about resources. Also, it was a time intensive requirement to be present round the  clock. Timely collection of information and its dissemination was of essence as the  cases were peaking at that time and it was distress situation.

Selection

My friends and I had been discussing about design thinking tools and how to use  them for our projects which we had been doing for our schoolwork.  With respect  to the challenges at hand, during our various brainstorming sessions, the learning  launch tool seemed to be the perfect fit because we were basically operating in  isolation from each other and the outside world and we needed to quickly ideate,  test and prototype it.  We decided to use the learning launch tool effectively for  our benefit and helping us out in the time critical challenge we were facing.

Application

Initially, the cases were being redirected to us by another voluntary organisation  who had more reach than us but very less manpower. As our first learning launch,  we decided to reach out to the patients/people in need ourselves but to succeed,  we had to focus on scaling up our operations and follow a streamlined workflow.

Our ideas were to cash-in on social media platforms like Facebook and Instagram  for maximum outreach and establish an effective workflow by dividing  responsibilities to avoid redundancy and wasted effort. We were able to gather  over a hundred volunteers through social media circles. The team’s outreach  touched 15,000 accounts in two days during the peak and at that time we were  handling over 20 critical cases per day. It was initially a challenge to handle more  than 200 individuals and follow a streamlined workflow. We put our idea to test by  dividing our volunteers into set of threes, with each shift having at least a  responder, a researcher, and a verifier.

The Responders talked to people in need through social media channels and asked  for important details regarding patients. This information was transferred to our  database which researchers and verifiers could access. Researchers would then  find leads using reliable websites and resources before sending the details to the  database.  The leads were then taken up by Verifiers and verification done in real  time as requests came in, so you could be sure that you have received latest  information.

It took some time to get used to the workflow and we had to orient the volunteers  when they decided to join our group, but the wheels were turning as expected.

However, we realised that not everyone was on Facebook or Instagram. Therefore,  during our second learning launch, we branched out by setting up WhatsApp  helpline, a website, and a database of resources which we verified in real time. The  idea of the workflow with respect to the responder, researcher and verifier was  working effectively and was tested successfully in the first learning launch itself,  therefore we decided to follow the same workflow. We were able to help over  1500+ people with reliable leads about hospital beds, medicines, oxygen etc.

Insight

By applying the learning launch tool, our team identified ideas, assumptions and  designed a workflow to test these assumptions. Additionally, we also learnt that  unlike our perception, as many people are not accessing social media platforms and  we needed to launch various other avenues for greater reach. Moving forward,  while attacking any more challenges, we shall utilize this insight and incorporate it  into any future launch designs. Also, other design tools such mind mapping or  storytelling could help us in our future endeavours of fund-raising for people under  financial distress for medical help.

Approach

Given that this was an unprecedented challenge, we think that out of all design  thinking activities/tools, the learning launch is the appropriate tool. As previously  mentioned, our team needs to review the insight gained from our first two  launches and incorporate this insight into future launch designs.

Example Reflection-Mind Mapping

By Karina Duque

Challenge and Selection

Mindmapping is a tool I used in my office; however, I was not aware that I was specifically  applying it although with a limited approach. It came to me first by instinct. I mean, I gathered  with my four-member team and we used to brainstorm ideas purposefully to solve an issue.  I  work in an International Organization in the Environment field. I am responsible for the  financial and administrative monitoring of environment projects according to the  organization’s and donor’s rules and regulations. These projects have their management units,  we call them PMU. Sometimes we forget that in those PMU, real people are working. We don’t  see these people we only see financial and administrative processes and requests coming from  them. The challenge we face is that these processes are not smooth and do not represent our  vision of “impeccable administration”. Therefore, project’s targets are delayed due to paper  work, bureaucracy, errors and long time processing.

Application

After learning what mind mapping really is, I decided to get close to my PMU colleagues. I’ve  been generally “judging” what they do from my supervision role rather than having a more  empathetic approach. First, I organized monthly meetings with my team to motivate them to  be more people centered when providing a course of action. Then, we started to interview, to  talk to people. This time, we made it with a different approach, using the invitation to “the  garage sale” event. We offered this time questions: ¿What makes your daily work difficult?  ¿What would you need to improve the processes you send to our Unit? ¿ From 1 to 10, how  empowered do you feel in your position to deliver a high-quality work? What do you want to  share? Well, we got surprised discovering that many of the challenges they have come from a  poor understanding of the reasons behind a regulation.  We understood there was a gap  between theory, the “must do” and the benefits of our policies.

Insight and Approach

Mind mapping facilitates to find patterns. With these questions, we got enough data to  analyze jointly and start to categorize the real needs and possible ways of dealing with them.  First, we discovered that no matter how big or small a project is, people face similar difficulties  such as: lack of a complete briefing when being hired, poor understanding of the processes  from beginning to the end and limitations to implement in the field due to covid restrictions.  Then, we realized that people felt somehow frightened because we are the ones correcting  and checking if their work was well done.

Our mind mapping led us to build on the “so what?” to move on to a different perspective. We  offered what people value the most in this digital era: being trained to grow professionally and  personally. Thus, we offered free nonobligatory training courses on different subjects to help  them strengthen their knowledge and skills and we started to ask a fundamental question:  What can I do for you?

Chris Hammond – Design Thinking for Innovation – Reflection Activity: Mind Mapping

Challenge

I work in consulting, and a major retailer asked us to help them understand how they could make  their in-store environments “more digital”. They have a long-term plan to move towards stores  which are almost fully automated and wanted to understand how they could design a store which  moved in this direction. Their brief to us was to assess ‘what is’ – that is, the current in-store  experience for customers and staff, and explore how staff and customers in different countries  would want to experience stores in the future. From this, we could then define ‘what if’ – the criteria  needed to develop a prototype store, and ideas about what the experience should be like.

Selection

We’ve worked with design thinking methodologies in the past, and given our objective was to help  define ‘what if’ we opted for a version of the mind-mapping tool. However, as the project was  international, had a limited budget and was fast-turnaround, we opted not to bring customers into  the room at the end of the project (co-creation, which is how this technique is explained in the video  lectures). Instead we would capture their views through qualitative research and play this back to  stakeholders in the mind-mapping session.

Application

We started off by conducting our qualitative research in different countries. This meant going to the  stores, interviewing staff and customers, capturing pictures and video of the store environments and  also recording how long customers spent in store, where they went, and so-on. From this we created  a detailed picture of ‘what is’, which includes current customer journey maps for the highest priority  customer missions our client was interested in (e.g. buying a new product, upgrading their existing  product, and more).

Subsequently we brought together all of the key stakeholders that had an interest in this problem in  a workshop, and started off by giving them an overview of ‘what is’. We put up pictures, video and  other research materials on the walls, and after our overview asked clients to immerse themselves in  these findings on their own. A few minutes later we put them into small groups to discuss what  they’d seen and come up with some common themes about the current experience and how it could  be improved.

Next, we facilitated a discussion amongst everyone in the room to draw out these themes, and then  together we wrote ‘what if’ customer journeys – that is, ideally how customers would want their  store experience to go. Once we’d created an overview of these journeys together, each individual  came up with ideas about how to deliver this and wrote them on post-it notes, before placing them  under the relevant part of the ‘what if’ customer journey. The final step was to review these ideas as  a group and decide which were the most promising, which we did via dot voting (giving everyone  stickers and asking them to place them on the ideas they thought best).

Insight

We learnt a lot from this approach. Three insights stood out for me:

•  We disconfirmed a hypothesis we had started the project with – that quick service was  important for all customers. In fact, we found this varied by a lot by mission (i.e. what the  customer was trying to achieve). People who had come to the store with a specific problem  to be solved wanted someone to come and talk to them straight away, but those thinking  about buying a new product appreciated a bit more time alone to browse, get comfortable  etc.

•  Therefore, we needed to target staff on people wanting to solve problems; those browsing  were often happier interacting with machines than people. This meant that the store would  need different zones, with a different atmosphere and different levels of technology.

•  One thing that emerged as a big problem for customers was waiting – once a customer had  decided what they want to do, they were only prepared to wait a few minutes to get it done.  This meant we needed to focus on using both technology and people to minimise waiting  times, and also make the store environment more pleasant and entertaining (to reduce the  pain of waiting).

Approach

We found conducting detailed research before the workshop and then giving an overview to  stakeholders was immensely helpful – this primed them on what we were trying to achieve and  helped focus their minds. However, not being able to have real customers in the workshop was a  downside – I think this would have really helped our clients understand the problems they were  trying to solve. Visualisation mixed with storytelling techniques

Challenge

While helping out a customer with their Agile Adoption we arrived at a team structure where it was  unclear ‘why’ certain things were on their todo list form a end-user perspective. There was no link  to their real customers and a true vision was missing for upcoming releases. The team was  building applications for internal customers (customer support, sales, infrastructure…) that would  reduce paper consumption as a whole but were unsure about the effects and effectiveness of their  deliverables. This uncertainty manifested itself in lack of motivation within the team and a lack of  adoption of the applications at the end-user side. A disconnect!

Selection

There was a long list of todo’s for the team to build available and an overall purpose was ‘assigned’  to reduce paper consumption. Facts we could not disregard as a whole as there were expectations  created within the organisation related to those facts. We could convince the team and their end- users to engage in a 1-day conversation on future releases with as purpose to align expectations  and generate a common purpose amongst them.

One part of the problem was known: paper consumption but there were lots of other, not yet  discovered, terrain that we chose to facilitate a collaborative session where diverse groups of  people would generate a visual representation of their expectations related to how new  applications should behave and affect the way they did their work. We were going to go for video  prototyping as a way to visualise the different perspectives.

Application

In order to guide the attendees we designed the 1-day in such a way that people would open up  their minds to other needs, wishes and insights. A true learning experience for all. We started the  day by decorating the workshop room with relevant posters related to persona’s (extisted before),  paper consumption trends and more; this way attendees would get into the subject just by entering  the room. As we had +/-30 attendees in the workshop we asked them to split into 3 different groups  looking at the applications from a different perspective.

Once the groups were formed and the perspective was clear, we guided them through an exercise  to shift their thinking from paper and application (or product) to customer and problem(s) using  some kind of Product Canvas*, guiding them step by step. First having 3-5minutes individually to  generate as many post-its as they could related to customer segments, from there on we guided  them through some Afﬁnity Mapping* exercise and consolidate the information on the canvas. We  repeated this (using the information already gathered) for the other canvas items: problems,  solutions and unique value proposition.

As soon as the situation was set forward we continued by generating characters that would be in  the end video using an adjusted persona template which we called a Persona Canvas*. The  canvas had as a purpose to create caricatures of real persona’s, to add some comic tough in them  as this would make the end results more effective. Having all this information at hand, knowing the  power of storytelling, we choose to create small video script using an adapted storytelling format  where they use +/-20% of the time to tell about the problem and a quick glance in the solution;  60% of the time to get us through the application of the product; ending with a summary & happy  feelings (20%). We provided them a Script Template* for that part of the thinking/discovery  exercise. We have learned from the Design Thinking course there is value in iterating on ideas and  thoughs in order to optimise (see week 4 strategy video in the course). As such the groups iterated

about 4-5 times on their ideas using a simple Success Test* template to challenge their ideas and  optimise the ﬂow. Ending with truly creating their persona’s and other movie attributes out of plain  paper, markers and scissors that were ﬁnally used in their own produced short-movie on the  product/application at hand. Even though the results are in Dutch I do want to show the end results  after they were collected and put in a single movie that is used for engaging others, explaining  the future needs and align product development towards. Check it out here: http://www.green.info/wp-content/wp-contentpost.html  Suddenly the application/product was not about paper consumption anymore, it became easy of  use, time saving and other more customer centric purposes!

Insight

I am a man of action and frequently fall into the trap of not being patient and explore the deep  needs, so at ﬁrst the workshop did feel a bit too much of exploring the context and a bit too less of  going into action. Man, was I wrong! I discovered that groups of people, who are generally action  driven, really need time to break through their general way of working and go deeper into the  context, problems and emotions. This sequence of exercises was a great way to do that, it  provided just enough guidance and was not too constrained so ideas could go nuts. Unexpected  ideas rises to the surface, product twists were amazing and the end results really affected the todo  list of the team thoroughly. This was for me the ultimate proof that visualisation and storytelling are  really powerful ways to discover unmet needs.

Approach

Next time I would design such a session I would not go for the posters on the wall as they were  distracting and adding imaginary constraints to the attendees, it took some time and facilitation  effort to get the attendees thinking beyond the visual facts on the posters. Maybe for a next time I  might invite attendees to bring treasures by themselves.

Challenge As a part of innovation & digital business unit, we tried to enhance the services catalog offered to our VIP customers. The main objective of this workshop was to collect and list all the pain points. To get a good result, we gave 5 post-it notes to each participant and asked them to write the most important pain point on each post-it according to their vision. Then we pasted these post-it notes on a board and we asked each participant to choose and mark 3 pain points from the whole list by indicate a star. The number of stars indicate the priority and the importance of the pain point. The next step was to classify the pain points according there category and indicated priority. Now, we are able to design a mind mapping diagram exposing the pain points. Through this diagram, it was simpler to identify appropriate solutions for the each pain point starting with the highest priority.

Insight Mind mapping is a powerful tool to get all the most important ideas and visualize them simply and bright them easy to remember. Applying this tool simplified team working on our subject, ideas was generated easily and the mind mapping diagram structure encouraged team to think efficiently.

Approach Mind mapping can give interesting results for ideas organizing and inciting stakeholders to share their comprehension and get solutions for issues and problems. Next time, it will be more efficient if we integrated a prototyping approach witch can improve results and let us know what will work without spending effort.

Learning Launch – Designing for Growth

1. Challenge: My great challenge would be to find out of many ideas the best working and

profitable idea with the highest IRR (internal rate of return.) You do not know the future and  the market developments or what other companies are planning for the future – so you have  to find out under un-security unique ideas that work which will be profitable in the future.

2. Selection: There will be many light bulbs with lots ideas. Making a business plan is not the

best way because you go to the unknown. Many guesses and assumptions are made and  everything is new to the innovation team and you (“the unknown”.)

Then you make financial projections based on the unknown. If the IRR is not met we “tweak the  assumptions”.

The better way would be – doing lots of experiments with customers and on the market, which  means the testing of a hypothesis (idea in a specific form). Experiments should be fast and cheap as  many companies do with computer simulations.

You have to do the learning process with customers quickly and also test your key customers  assumptions. To understand customers needs is one of the most important topic. Taking to  customers must be done very very quickly.

The process: Frist step will be a hypothesis – the idea relates to a specific target group / specific  persons – customers have a problem causing pain. With the idea the problem will be solved better  than the competition.

What must be true for a good idea? The purpose of a learning launch is to get the truth which can be  confirmed or disconfirmed.  The truth will save you money and surely time. The idea can be adapted  to a better working idea.

Customers have to be prioritized and the data must meet the key assumptions.

“You think – it is a great idea” but YOU are a problem – a risk to be managed because of confirmation  bias. You are looking for data that confirms your idea.

Solution to this:

  just the facts

  search for the big lie

  search for confirming / disconfirming facts

  small multi-functional teams – a skeptic person

Think about:

Under which circumstances will be the idea a bad idea (idea, service not sell) ? You make a list and  ask questions….and you search for these questions. Observation is a key way to learn!

We all are very biased. Everybody’s cognitive blindness is different. We have to share ideas also with  skeptic people. We always believe our ideas will work.

So ask many people about their biggest problems and then put the data together and identify the  biggest problem for the group.

Ideas are like sand on the beach – many…..

Design Thinking - Application of Storytelling

As quoted in the slides from Week 2 of the course, Slide 5, Storytelling is:

“Put the human beings and their experience front and center. Take the listener along on their

journey.”

That being said, I wish to apply it to a project we’re working on in Manufacturing Engineering to improve the use of Hanger 75 and make it a valuable space. It’s current use isn’t clearly defined, but is predominantly storage for equipment needed for various projects across site. There are multiple stakeholders involved who own certain areas of it, so the challenge is to bring these stakeholders together and help create a space that supports Manufacturing Engineering as a function.

The most recent brief on utilising the area is for it to incorporate the Industrial Strategy being implemented on site. Each department within Manufacturing Engineering as a whole have their own individual projects to focus on, but they all come back to key focuses for site such as digital and technology development.

In order to drive the team in the right direction, I wanted to use the Storytelling tool in order to effectively put our ideas across. We ‘storytell’ within a presentation taking the stakeholders round Hanger 75 location by location. As opposed to filling a presentation with numbers and facts, it’s taking the stakeholders through the use of the Hanger in a more descriptive view. In a way it also brings in visualisation as we’re helping the stakeholder picture Hanger 75 being used in a particular way. One example idea we’ve come up with is reconfigurable spaces that are adaptable to what is required, so we apply their use to projects currently being run on site. We provide a scenario to talk about. It helps picture teams working together and other important aspects to the stakeholders.

From using the storytelling method, it took us back to focusing on the end user to help generate out ideas. Our whole concept became more rounded as we think of the user interacting with Hanger 75 from start to finish. We started by thinking what would the user want to see when they first walked in, how would they interact on the way round, then finishing with what would round-up the users interaction with the area? The Storytelling tool helped generate our end presentation, so it helped focus our work to produce a well-polished presentation.

I think if I was to approach the same task again I’d utilise Design Thinking tools from the start to help establish ideas more fully. Reflection - Mind Mapping

Challenge & Selection:

As a board member of a non-profit student consultancy firm I was confronted with a strategic positioning  challenge. Historically, our organization linked students of the local University, who were eager to exhibit  their recently gained academic and theoretical knowledge into practice at local small and medium  enterprises (our clients) on a project base. The challenge was triggered since our key stakeholder/ partner,  the local University, decided to organize consultancy projects themselves instead of outsourcing this to a  semi-independent student entrepreneur organization. Since we were a spin-off of the local University our  very own existence was at stake unless we were able to reinvent our proposition. The only question was  ‘how’? We’ve always assumed that the main driver to do business with us for local small and medium  enterprises and the students themselves, was the fact that we were affiliated with the University. This  way the project scope included the strategic positioning of our non-profit student consultancy firm with  limited resources based on the added value to the several different stakeholders including a high urgency.  The goal was to unravel the intrinsic motivation of our current clients and students to do business with us  in order to reposition ourselves into the market and outsmart the new competition provided by the local  university (former key stakeholder). We expected to cluster the different stakeholders based upon their  motivation to do business with us.

Our challenge was to understand the current reality/ ‘as is’ of our organization by collecting high

amounts of data from several stakeholders and to look for patterns, insights etc. in order to develop  design criteria for the ‘what if’ of our organization. Therefore the mind mapping tool proved to be the  ideal tool to come up with creative solution since it would enable us to make a smooth transition from  the current situation to the future/ desired state of our organization.

Application:

After finishing a projects with our clients we invited both the students (who executed the project) and the  client, to participate in projective techniques to uncover their reason to work with our organization and  to share their experiences. In this way we were able to align our own organization on the current reality  since some of us stated that students were (since we were non-for profit) more important than our clients  and vice versa. In order to solve this puzzle we asked clients and students to post their experiences on the  sticky notes. After a break of 30 min we asked them to cluster their own experiences. Then the insights  were identified related to each cluster and connections between clusters where highlighted. This proved  to be one of the toughest parts of the exercise. After asking ‘so what?’ related to several clusters the true  meaning of the experience emerged. For example, the amount of freedom during the project indicated  by the students became: the amount independency compared to normal university assignments or usual  student jobs (e.g. call centers).

By this it became clear that the main driver for both the students and our clients was that our

organization existed of young student entrepreneurs who didn’t follow the University rules but were  willing to take risk and experience things outside the box. After having this insight the pivot between ‘what  is’ and ‘what if’ started focusing on the creation of the criteria which was in our case the fact that it should  be entrepreneurial. By thinking: ‘if anything was possible’ how would our organization look like, we  entered the next stage.

Insight & Approach:

By designing the new positioning of our organizations based upon the new design criteria (e.g.  entrepreneurial)  we were ultimately able to position our organization as the platform for ambitious and  entrepreneurial students, who want to organize consultancy projects for themselves. The mind mapping  tool showed how our different stakeholders were interlinked. Since our clients were looking for this exact  entrepreneurial spirit our organization ensured its long-term survival as a springboard for students  allowing them to put their theoretical knowledge into practice and triple the turnover in the first year.

This course made me understand the importance of mind mapping in creating design criteria

when being in the transition from the as is to what if. Especially, the ability to process high amounts of  data and cluster them struck me. Therefore I would definitely perform a min mapping exercise when being  in a similar situation. When I’ve done it before it would be aimed at looking for immediate solutions  instead. I would not have discover the specific application of mind mapping without the course and by  that misusing this very valuable tool.

the ‘game’ of plastics recycling

by Alexandra Serafini – 17 Feb, 2021

Index

1.  Challenge .................................................................................................................................. 3

2.  Selection.................................................................................................................................... 3

3.  Application................................................................................................................................. 3

4.  Insight ........................................................................................................................................ 4

1. Challenge

In recent years, doing something for our planet has become an essential condition for  each of us. Everyone can help the safeguard the natural environment, changing small  gestures and incorrect habits.

In the city where I live, in Italy, there are many green initiatives that are put into practice,  but they are never enough.

My challenge is to put into practice a method for making the younger age groups learn  and practice virtuous and correct behaviors, in a fun and stimulating way. Doing so, they  can contribute to protect and preserve the well-being of the planet and have a better  future.

The project will initially have these features:

 limited to a maximum of 10 kindergartens, where it is possible to place a corner

dedicated to plastic collection;

 supply of small plastic-eating machines made from recycled material, with an

appearance that recalls colored cartoon characters: this is possible thanks to the  collaboration with AMIU, the local authority that manages the collection and  recycling of waste;

 duration of the experiment: two months.

2. Selection

In design thinking, there is no secret recipe to achieve innovation, but there is an  iteration of design processes that enable innovation to happen.

The learning launch principle is one of the most important tools of design thinking for  innovation. This principle consists in doing small experiments to test a prototype in the  real world. It is a relatively fast, and represent a low-cost way to validate the innovator’s  ideas.

Using the learning launch principle for this challenge ensures to verify that solution is  oriented toward the target people. This process does not necessarily prove that the  initial idea is the best, but it enables an innovator to identify how the idea can be  improved or if it should be discarded.

3. Application

For every child, everything can become a game, even plastics recycling.

The herein proposed learning launch consists in teaching kindergarten children,  supported by the teachers, to collect plastic material in the plastic-eating machine.

This practice can be interpreted as:

 a behavior that helps children become more responsible;   a challenge that allows to earn rewards: a plastic coin will be issued every time a

suitable object is introduced into the machine.

Every child, with parents help, can convert the coins collected into tangible good at  affiliate businesses for example:

 toy store;   ice cream shop;   amusement park;   etc.

4. Insight

This idea is born to involve both children and adults in the goal of plastics recycling:

 plastic waste collection thought to children, makes it to become a spontaneous

gesture when they will be adults;

 adults, helping children, will lead by example.

Monitoring children's progress for a period of one or two months will allow to appreciate  this kind of initiative.

If children will consider this activity enough stimulating, will try to earn as many coins as  possible, maybe even bringing some empty plastic bottles from home.

5. Approach

The idea herein exposed can lead to several other practical implementation:

 the plastic eating machines can also be installed in public areas, for example near

playgrounds;

 in addition to plastic materials, the machines can be designed to collect other

types of waste, for example paper: doing so, children have the opportunity to  develop their own material perception;

  the project could be extended to adults: by means of a smartphone app, it is  possible to track waste collection in order to obtain coupons or some discounts.

Linda Moore REFLECTION – VISUALIZATION

CHALLENGE

While working for my previous employer, a large defense contractor offering products and services from undersea  to outer space, I managed all tradeshow and sponsorship activity for a sector headquartered in Herndon, Virginia.  Before I arrived, each business unit was managing their own pool of funds, deciding which shows and sponsorships  in which to participate/contribute and there was no overall structure as to the total sector spend. Decisions were  being made with no regard to sector priorities, large contract bids or future bid considerations. Additionally, there  was no alignment on any of the branding and marketing material, and more than once different business units  from the same sector were appearing at trade shows, without knowledge the other was participating. There was  an immediate need to align the funds under one umbrella and to develop a unified approach to spend, messaging  and participation at tradeshows and with sponsorships.

SELECTION

For this exercise, I opted to apply the design thinking tool of visualization to first uncover the issue at hand. To help  with our fight to align the budget under one umbrella (managed by me), I first needed to shine a light on just how  many unnecessary (from a business perspective) trade shows the business units were attending, how much in  sponsorship money was being dispersed, as well as the total sector spend in these areas. As we know, visualization  as a design tool (as per slide five in the week one slides) means to “make it tangible and concrete; to draw a  picture, tell a story, take a photo, make a map…” By pulling together historical data about these spends, compiling  it into one location, making it colored-coded and easy-to-read/filter, I was able to get senior leadership to  understand what I was trying to accomplish and persuade them into what I was trying to do for the organization as  a whole by taking the budget ownership and participation management.

While the new tradeshow and sponsorship process would be an evolution beyond just shining the light on the  need (identifying which to participate in and why, aligning objectives to meet customer and business needs, etc.),  this first step was important in being able to secure buy-in.

APPLICATION

This was a larger undertaking than one might initially believe. After having initial conversations with each of the  business units, it was clear that not everyone was on the same page; why would they be? After all, it did appear as  if we were taking away their autonomy in this area. That was when it was apparent that visualization needed to be  used, in order for the larger picture to be seen. I started first by trying to wrap my head around just how many  tradeshows and sponsorships our business units were participating in and contributing to. Since this function was  never “managed” appropriately, there was little documentation and I had to rely on speaking directly to those  within each business unit (three, in total), and digging into past financial history. They were a bit reluctant at first,  but eventually, I was able to garner the insight I needed to begin pulling together all the data into one place.

I used Microsoft Excel to house the data, using different colors to identify the three business units. In doing this, I  was able to provide an all-up look at what tradeshows the sector was paying for exhibits and sending attendees,  primary business objective for exhibiting/attending, what sponsorships were being purchased, dates/locations of  all activities and total spend for the sector. By using different colors for each business unit, it was easier for  leadership to sort and better understand if the selected events/activities aligned with the larger strategy for each  business unit. It also allowed me to keep everything in one place while having the ability to sort and filter to tailor  different conversations based on the audience. It may seem like a simple approach, but after uncovering that there  was participation in over 60 tradeshows, and contributions to more than 200 sponsorships, it was clear that to  start, all information needed to live in one place and leadership needed to see this visually. Since the budgets for  tradeshows was separate from that of sponsorships, I separated those entries on different tabs.

Below is a screen shot of the tradeshow list, with colors and some columns not shown, as to avoid potentially  sharing any proprietary information. The light green highlights shown reflect international tradeshows.

Linda Moore REFLECTION – VISUALIZATION

Linda Moore REFLECTION – VISUALIZATION

INSIGHT

This exercise turned out to be extremely valuable and was eye-opening for sector leadership. By being able to see  and sort all the data in one place, leadership was able to just how much money was being spent, and where each  business unit was deciding to focus their budget. In creating a common understanding, through the use of  visualization, eyes were open not only to the challenge the sector was facing, but that there were options and  opportunities to be better aligned and consistent with messaging and approach. Leadership was able to better  understand the problem itself and use data that was already available (just now in one, organized place) to begin  considering a more reasonable approach to managing this process.

APPROACH

This exercise taught me the value in keeping data such as this in a central, organized repository from the  beginning. If there had been better management of tradeshows and sponsorships prior to my starting with the  organization, this would be one step that could have been avoided in the process of identifying a new approach. I  have since taken this more detailed, structured approach, to a new organization with great success. With this  specific example, I would not choose a different design thinking tool based on what was uncovered by going  through this exercise. Visualization was the missing component to connect the dots for those further removed  from the process, and set the stage to use other design thinking tools further along the process to find a new,  unified approach to managing these efforts.

Reflection – Visualization

Course: Design Thinking for Innovation

Student: Randy Sanz

I.  Challenge

I was part of the A.T. Kearney account team for a Consumer Packaged Goods (CPG) customer in Lima, Perú. The  customer needed to implement a process to accelerate the time to market for new products. In order to do so  they needed to include all the steps required, from idea generation, through launch.

The customer had already selected the software they wanted to use which handled the core Product Lifecycle  Management (PLM) and engineering functions.  They wanted us to implement it for them.

As A.T. Kearney, we wanted to provide the customer additional value by proposing a more complete solution and  while doing so, include additional A.T. Kearney products. We needed to include these products in order get internal  approval since we were not allowed to sell and implement a non-A.T. Kearney product in isolation.

Our challenge was to design a solution that brought value to the customer by integrating a specific, third party  software with A.T. Kearney products. This software had never been integrated with the A.T. Kearney platform before.

II.  Selection

In Module 1 we reviewed a video by Angela Myer. In her video she tells us that visualization is applicable in  situations where we need to apply the right side of our brain, when we’re dealing with a creative process and  when we’re trying to figure out how to do something that has never done before.  We also learned that  visualization is an excellent tool for team collaboration.

In retrospect it made sense to apply visualization at this stage of our proposal development. We needed to gather  a diverse group: consulting, marketing, sales, technical specialists, and the software vendor (Afterscool) to build the  solution and we were trying to design something that had never been done before.  However, the reality was that  the choice was made as a matter of course, it seemed clear to all that we needed to whiteboard some ideas in  order to figure out the solution.

III.  Application

As the A.T. Kearney Consulting Services consultant on the team, it was my responsibility to lead the design. I basically  began with what we knew: the customer had already selected a specific product that needed to be included in the  solution. Based on this I drew a box in the middle of a blank whiteboard and we began to discuss different  possibilities. We started by trying to get an understanding of what the customer wanted to do with the software,  how this fit within their overall processes related with product launches and who all the corresponding  stakeholders were within the company.

After many meetings lasting several hours, all of which began with either a version of the solution or a completely  blank whiteboard, we came up with a model that visually described the components of the solution and their  interactions. This is a simplified version of the solution we designed:

IV.  Insight

An interesting insight from having done this exercise was that in addition to our stated goal of coming up with a  design, we learned a lot about the customer’s processes, its stakeholders, their interactions and ultimately about  the overall problem they wanted to solve. As a matter of fact, when we finally presented the solution to the  customer we realized that we not only added value by bringing a solution to the original customer problem but  that we helped the customer have an expanded view of the problem itself and the value they could gain.  The  customer did in the end decide to go ahead with the project which took 18 months to implement. Through these  18 months, the project followed almost completely, the design that we had come up with in those original  visualization meetings.

Having now gone through this course, this experience is a very personal proof point of how the design thinking  tools and processes can be applied in real world scenarios.  It also helps be feel more confident that with  additional research and practice, I can personally apply a design thinking approach in the future.

V.  Approach

The project was in the end successful by most measures; however, I believe it would have been very valuable to  conduct a mind mapping exercise with the customer, prior to designing the solution. This exercise would have  allowed us to do an even better job at understanding what the customer wanted to accomplish, what core  business value they could’ve attained.  With this improved understanding we might have been able to gain  additional insights and in turn proposed a better solution. We could have even been able to expand our  involvement to include additional critical areas of the business. By collaborating with the customer from the  beginning we would’ve deepened our relationship and improved our positioning as a strategic vendor.

Bruno Milani    Challenge – How might we cultivate creativity in the workplace?    I chose the challenge of increasing employee engagement in the Federal Government by cultivating  cultures and leaders who inspire and unleash everyone’s creativity.  Studies show that only 65% of  Government employees are engaged at work.  It’s lower in the private sector.  But, as managers, we should  ask whether we are contributing to their disengagement.  Are we allowing them to share their ideas? To  discover their talents?  Are we bringing them along on the journey?  To meet this challenge, I reached out  to a group of leaders in the Government in charge of training and talent development and management.   This like-minded group faces this challenge too, but may not see it in the same way.     Selection - Storytelling    To reach my audience, I turned to storytelling. I find that telling stories is a powerful way to connect with  others and persuade them to listen to my ideas.  We all grew up hearing stories.  Of far away lands.   Princesses and dragons.  Magical spells.  These stories fueled our imaginations and captured our attention.   But what exactly is storytelling, especially in the design thinking context?  As we learned in Week 2,  storytelling is a design tool we can use to put human beings and their experience front and center.   Storytelling is not only educational and compelling, it is informative and inspiring.  The stories we tell can  raise questions and offer our audience opportunities to contemplate the status quo and how we might  redesign it.     To address my challenge of driving more innovation in the Federal Government by creating cultures that  support everyone’s creativity in the workplace, I told the story of the current environment.  As one of my  teachers, Deek Mela of the design firm, IDEO, says, “every innovation begins with a story.”  I explained  how employees may become disengaged because they don’t feel comfortable sharing their ideas.  Maybe  this is because managers rejected their ideas before or didn’t allow them to speak up.  I combined appealing  to the rational and emotional concerns of both the employees and the managers, and explained how my  audience might have the ability to use learning and development to reframe and reshape culture to alleviate  these concerns.     Application     To tell my story, I designed a webinar presentation.  Specifically, I wanted to take my audience along on a  journey.  I wanted them to know what it felt like for employees who feel like their voice is NOT heard, but  who have a lot of ideas to share. But, as the lesson in Week 2 explained, I thought about my audience and  their needs and concerns.  To start, I researched recent articles about employee engagement that my  audience often referred to, including from Chief Learning Officer magazine and Deloitte.  I even asked  friends who have this role what their interests, concerns, and needs were.  I actually reshaped my  presentation then after colleting this data.     I then developed a Powerpoint presentation for my webinar.  Because my audience would not be in person,  I created simple slides with one image and a few words on each that helped me guide the audience on a  visual journey through my story.  For example, when talking about how we develop a “creativity scar”  when people reject our ideas, I just wrote the words “creativity scar” and had an image of a broken heart  with a bandaid on that slide.  Other slides were similar.     My story reminded my audience that we are all creative.  We play and use our imagination as children, but  we grow out of it, or it’s taught out of us, as Sir Ken Robinson says.  I then described how instead, we  could cultivate cultures and leaders who support everyone’s ideas.  I even took them through some creative  exercises to give then a feel for it themselves.     I told the story of a disengaged employee and how we might collaborate to change the culture to allow her  to share her ideas.  I even explained how we could use design thinking as a collaborative tool to achieve  this goal and how we could cultivate leaders to lead for creativity by using design thinking tools.

I ended my story by asking them to think about how they might reframe their jobs or experience, thinking  about it from their users’ perspectives – how the employees they lead might feel or think, and to question  what they really want and need. As a result, my audience was energized and felt passionate about my ideas.     Insight     After my presentation, some told me they found my approach and strategy easy to implement and started  using “how might we” questions to collaborate together, as I suggested.  They told me they really  connected with the feeling these rejected employees had based on the story I told.  My story helped put  them in their employees’ shoes.  Some examples I gave, like my first boss telling me “we don’t pay you to  think” really resonated with my audience.  Looking back, I would stress those personal examples some  more and early on.    Approach     Alternatively, I could have created and presented mindmaps that highlighted specific insights from  interviews with employees who felt their ideas were not heard.  I could have created personas that  summarized the themes and patterns from multiple employees, developing examples of those.  In a way  similar to storytelling, this would have allowed me to focus on the questions to be answered, but based on  the empathy and insights gained from specific employees.

WHY PEOPLE ARE NOT COMMITTED TO RECYCLING IN LIMA (PERU)?

by Miguel Caceres

Challenge

I am a member of a start-up focused on solving the challenge of recycling in Lima (Peru), with the

aim of achieving greater awareness in the citizens about the importance of recycling. We found

that in Peru more than 18 tons of garbage are generated daily, half of which is generated only in

Lima (capital of my country) and 2.4% is only recycled1. The reason: The lack of culture by the

recycling of the Peruvian. Therefore the scope of this project is to understand this situation.

Selection

The tool I used was visualization, for have a broader, deeper and clearer understanding of the

problem, so we share the problem with citizens in Lima.  To do so, I selected some techniques as

ethnographic interviews, “5 Why´s” 2  and Empathy Map with a set of questions or guidelines to

know stories and discuss about the problem of the recycling culture, with the objective to delimit

the scope of the project and key elements to discover opportunities, and then, define possible

solutions and prototypes.

Application

I started the process with ethnographic interviews (25 citizens), I prepared a set of questions that

included from general overview, like as: “Could you show me/tell me how you usually throw the

garbage?”, “What like/dislike from this process?” with the aim of discussing patterns of events. I

used too, the technique ´5 Why’s´ for seeking the evocation of stories, in order to explore in depth

the emotions of citizens and recyclers concerning the problem. After that, I unpacked all

information collected on the first step, with ´Empathy Map´3 graphic to synthesize, I wrote the

answers in 04 categories: What say, do, think and feel, organized with sticky notes on poster. Later

1 Available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NuacmGHLDqw  2 Available at: http://designresearchtechniques.com/casestudies/5-whys/  3 Available at: https://dschool.stanford.edu/wp-content/themes/dschool/method-cards/empathy-map.pdf

I continue the process with satured & grouped technique, for uncover insights through abductive

thinking.

Insight & Aproach

What I have learned from conducting this exercise with different points of view from citizens and

recyclers was to demystify the initial assumptions about the lack of recycling culture over

ignorance about how to separate the garbage, lack of time to do it or want to receive some type

of profit or economic reward for doing so, however we found that citizens in Lima would be more

committed with recycling activities if they would know how their individual actions generate

concrete social and environmental impacts and in the short term, they also do not consider

important to receive economic benefits for their recycling actions.

The Empathy Map- gave me the diverse points of view, started in ethnographic interviews, a focal

point for the project that allowed me to understand their perspectives and uncover insights into

potential root causes of the problem.

Reflection -  Learning Launch

By Joe Ferrara

Challenge

As a member of a team who manage a large portfolio of critical IT projects for a big national company, I’m  invited regularly to collect the needs from my clients, launch and manage new projects, and especially to  meet the deadlines, the budget and requirements. It’s such as successive challenges I faced in my business  life, especially when client’s requirements and needs changes continuously. This is the reason why I was  always wondering the following: When I have a challenge, how do I approach it? In reality, even in our  personal life, we face many problems and we go through different challenges every day. We solve most  of them every day too.  The most important thing I learned from this “Design Thinking” course is that we  should resist the temptation to jump directly to a solution and that the value is in realizing that we can  create something that can help people make their lives easier.

Selection

There are several tools and techniques of understanding the needs of a user, client or a customer, but in  my point of view, Learning Launch is the most effective way. To rephrase “Learning Launch”, it is a manner  of creating a minimum viable product that let customers or users test their key assumptions and get an  answer to the big question “What if?”. The point is to start creating a minimum and test it, then we quickly  get more feedbacks and clearer ideas that led us to a prototype. We could also iterate this operation as  much as we need until we get sufficient prototypes, and finally choose the appropriate prototype for our  project or product.

Application

In one of our first learning launch application, I focused on providing an online platform to our users. This  platform was technically complex as it exchanges many encrypted informations with a couple of high  secured systems, using different communication protocols. We were facing another major constraint  when client changes some of their needs every time. We didn’t have any other choice, but adapting our  work and processes to be more agile. After organizing an agile workshop and training to all staff members,  we started being more flexible and soft after receiving any change request from the client. After testing  every milestone of the deliverable, we conducted interviews with users to understand their experiences  and to find out if this new prototype meets their expectations with a priority to ensure that users could  use the platform easily.

Insight

By applying this learning tool, we designed and tested our solutions / product following the agile  methodology. Through the learning process we got to improve our online platform to meet client’s  expectation even if it was changed a lot of times all along the project phase. It’s through this process we  realized which version of platform that users were more comfortable with. We also realized how agile  approach can improve our processes. From now on, all team members and stakeholders welcomed any  new requirement’s change and accepted to review the task’s priorities according to the new change of  needs.

Approach

Therefore, I’m convinced that the Learning Launch is the ideal and appropriate tool four our kind of IT  businesses. Since I already experienced this experience in my professional path, I would recommend this  approach in the future in case of similar activities and/or circumstances.

Reflection - Storytelling    Challenge     We are a group of school friends who have got together ‘virtually’ almost twenty-five years  after leaving school. -  We had to be able to communicate with the target audience in a language that they  would find interesting and appealing

-  The people who would contribute were busy folks and I had only a few seconds to  grab their attention

-  Because it was a medical emergency, there were medical terms associated with the  illness and the remedial processes – they were not understood by the audience.

-  There are many skeptics around crowd-funding appeals of this nature. So our appeal  had to stand out in terms of authenticity.

-  The process of remittance also had to be very simple and convenient

Selection     We decided to use the tool of Storytelling to make my case. We wanted to create an  impression in the shortest possible time to allow the donor to make up his mind and  contribute to my cause.     I remembered the lecture by Ricky George from Mars and how a human being needed to be  at the centre of the conversation and used a real story in my appeal.    Application     My story centred around the young boy’s love for cricket – a game that is very popular in my  country. Design Thinking Challenge - Learning Launch

By Asia Lemus, 4/2/19

Challenge

I am a project manager in field operations and recently inherited a project to change behavior of our  field technicians.  The “ask” is for our field technician’s to start leaving descriptive notes as to what they  did to resolve a customer’s issue.  The importance and value of this effort is tremendous.  The intention  is to leverage the data we collect from the notes and other relevant data (such as call reason and  technician resolution) to influence how our call center team is trained and to improve their tools to  eliminate sending technicians for issues that can be fixed by us remotely or by guiding the customer  through the fix.  It is extremely important for the technicians to embrace and adopt this new procedure  by not only entering these notes, but entering the right information to support data analysis to uncover  the root cause.

Selection

While myself and many other identified subject matter experts could have easily pulled together several  solid solutions and approaches to this project, I opted to leverage the Learning Launch to ensure we  identified and deployed the best solution to not only be successful but to ensure we sustain our success.   Due to the fact that I am very much aware that changing behavior is no easy feat and by already having  a keen sense of who my customers are and what is important to them, I did anticipate they would feel  uneasy about the request as it will add time to their job and they may even be fearful to enter honest  and accurate information in the note the learning launch felt like the right tool to ensure we were  creating a simple and intuitive solution to help create their buy in and adoption.   The learning launch  process allowed me to focus more time on generating out of the box ideas and surfacing even more  assumptions than we have today.  But most importantly, the process of conducting a small test with  those that actually have to use it, adopt to it and embrace it is where the most value came from.

Application

I gathered subject matter experts, those that had previously been field technicians and others that did  not, as well as, included a few with technical solutions expertise.  We reviewed past training and  messaging published to get a sense of what the current ask was.   We reviewed data around how many  technicians leave notes, on what type of jobs, what type of information does the note include, are there  some technicians that do this every time, some that never do it and what is the difference between  those technicians?  We evaluated how the system presented the note field today, where it was in the  workflow, what was the verbiage and graphics around it, etc.  We then generated ideas to get  technicians to be committed to leave a note every time that included the specifics of what was done to  solve the problem they were sent there to solve.  However, we did limit ourselves to ensuring we  focused on making this simple and not adding time to the technicians job.

We came up with several good ideas and then picked the one we knew we couldn’t do without.  We  tested our solution with a small group of technicians and found our assumptions were correct. Our  technicians embraced the new flow and tools and it was very apparent that giving them options of how  they will enter the note was very important (ie, voice to text, text entry, picking from a defined list or a  combination of all options).  However, we discovered we didn’t spend enough time ensuring our testers  understood why the change was so important.  This was a huge discovery that we should have prepared  for as we readied the team for the test and is now something we are incorporating into the launch  package, but will be testing that through a Learning Launch first to confirm we have it just right.

Insight

The benefits to being able to perform a quick hands on experiment or test is a win for all involved.  Not  only were we able to confirm our assumption of what was needed, we also found that our oversight  around explaining the Why was a big miss.  In addition, the test allowed us to get our technicians  involved early and they quickly felt a sense of ownership and pride in helping to make this the best  solution it could be.  The learning lesson concept is truly a quick way to confirm if ideas make sense in  application not just on paper or in theory and if they will ultimately support the goal.

Approach

We are incorporating a bit of a different approach to our next learning launch for this same challenge by  incorporating Story Telling into the launch.  We will focus more on benefits for the technician (what’s in  it for them) and to tell that story in many different ways to support different learning types such as  visual, aural and verbal.  While we can easily modify our systems to support technicians entering notes  in many different ways and can make the note a mandatory field the bottom line is we still need the  technician to feel compelled to leave a note that accurately describes what was done to fix an issue.  In  order to drive this behavior we will tell a story to reach people emotionally in a way that ensures  genuine commitment to the cause, engaging their hearts as well as their minds in our call to action,  making them feel as if they are part of a game changing program.

Storytelling provokes emotions, tells the stories we want to know, is able to entertain and transmits  the experiences that each of us needs to share, is a fantastic tool that I always use. Application

For the meetings with the kids, the agency had proposed a format to be followed in a more or less  rigid way, that was inclusive and allowed to dedicate the same time to each of the boys. So I decided to do a variation of  the format and asked the guys to visualize and draw, instead of discussing it all together, objects  related to their greatest passion,  and in the meantime I sat next to the silent guy, And I talked to  him gently. The boy and I focused on the fact that each of us has a talent and that there is no "I can’t, I can’t do  it, I can’t" but with hard work, commitment and perseverance you can get everything.  This theme was very much felt and the boy began to open up and talk about his fears and fears, the  conviction not to believe in himself, not to be able to do or accomplish some things. Visualization Challenge

The Challenge

You work for one of the world’s largest media and communications companies. Currently your company  has five apps the customer can use to pay bills, troubleshoot service issues, chat with a customer  representative, customize internet features, and stream video and music. The problem is your  customers feel this is way too many apps, and it is confusing on what app does what. You notice that  because of this fact customers have elected to use none of them, but instead simply use your company  for service access, and use competing companies such as Netflix, Hulu, and Spotify for the other  services. This is a serious problem because it is through your apps that you can collect data about your  customer’s entertainment habits that you can use to sell advertisement space on your service. Your  challenge is to come up with an app that is an all in one app. Customers can do everything your apps do  and more without the hassle of bloating their smart device with groups of tedious apps from your  company.

Selection

I would start off with the flow chart technique of drawing what our individual apps do and ask the “5  Ws”. Why do we need FIVE apps? What does each app do? When do I think we can launch the new all in  one app? How do the five apps currently flow? Who is the target audience for these apps (business  customers or residential customers?). Where can we make some cuts to our current digital footprint?  Having a hand drawn layout of how each of the five apps work would make it easier to see what needs  to stay and what can be cut for the new all in one app.

Application

Using the “Key Principles of Mobile UX Design” by Nick Babich (Editior in Chief of UXplanet.com) which  states that consumers want simple, quick, and easy to understand apps, I would assemble the best  designers, software engineering, programmers, and stakeholders to discuss the current problem, the  solution, the benefits of going the one app route, the execution of design, release timeline, the costs  involved, and any possible hurdles we may face during this process. Using a blank wall we will use a  series of colored post-it notes in different categories to come up with how the new app will function.

Insight and Approach

What I learned from this challenge is that for designing something as complex as this it does take an  incredibly talented and dedicated team to accomplish the task. Getting everyone to share the same

vision was not the hard part, but it was actually having too many GOOD ideas that made it hard on  knowing what to cut and what to keep. Once we took those ideas and trimmed them down to what a  real life customer would want we felt we had something to present to higher ups.

What I learned from this is visualization is truly a valuable tool in design thinking. I feel it’s the one tool  that everyone can get behind because you are actually displaying the ideas versus just blindly discussing  them. I know not every situation is going to call for a visualization tool, but in the future I hope to take  what I learned and apply it even better for the next great idea.

Peer-graded Assignment Reflection: Learning Launch

Elena Chernov

Challenge & Selection

I have a customer in the consumer goods industry that needed to solve a communication gap with their  manufacturing workforce.  They explored an opportunity to leverage mobile app technology to send  work related content such as plant closures, overtime commitment reminders and plant events to their  3000+ non-technical employees.  They determined that they would build a Minimum Viable Product  (MVP) application for both Android and IOS mobile devices.  It was determined through ethnographic  research that the workforce had a mix of personal device types, devices varied in age and operating  system versions, and simple applications were preferred over applications with too many layers.   Additionally, the staff is non-technical and would need assistance with loading the app on their devices.   My team selected a Learning Launch which is a small experimental test to determine if the idea was  viable in the marketplace or an internal user base, in this challenge.  This tool was a good fit for an  experimental mobile app that was 70% complete with an unknown potential adoption rate.  What my  customer assumed to be true was that the workforce would be interested in receiving work related  content quickly and conveniently through their personal mobile devices.  As indicated by Walton in his  video, my customer had the need to confirm or disconfirm their assumptions which would save them  money and time spent on developing a full mobile app.  Similar to the trade show Learning Launch for  IBM, our team gathered information on additional key factors that would inform the application  content, preferred deployment process and understand any risk or challenges that had not been  discovered to date during the project.

Application

It was agreed upon to roll out the mobile application to one selected manufacturing plant for a (90) day  period.  The application would be deployed in the first two weeks of the learning launch using a mix of  trained contract employees and app team members. A communication plan started 30 days in advance  to notify the employees of the application pilot and invited them to try the test application.   The team  equipped with launch materials set up tables at multiple “high traffic” locations in the plant for visibility.  On day one of the pilot, all team members deployed the application while other team members  watched how the employees reacted, documented any challenges in the deployment process and  questions that were asked by the employees.  Observations were collected after each of the three shifts  for a brief discussion the next morning.  Pivots in deployment processes or explanations of how the  application would be used were done regularly throughout the first two weeks. For instance, the use of  company Wi-Fi was not in scope but the use of personal data became a concern to many pilot users.   After a review with leadership, company Wi-Fi access was opened up to the pilot users which drove  more adopters, but started the discussion on new governance usage policies, and the need to review  possible expansion of the Wi-Fi system to include new wireless access points to improve coverage.  A  technical concern that became a barrier to adoption was the employees concern over “Big Brother” on  their personal devices.  Several questions arose over the concern of tracking and use of location services

at the plant and home which were not part of the application but required explanation.  All of these  concerns would have to be addressed prior to a roll out to the entire manufacturing team nationwide.

The launch was so effective at collecting issues surrounding the use of personal devices, that a second  Learning Launch was added at the half-way point.  The team needed to limit the operating system  versions and size of the phones that they could deploy the application on in order to provide the best  customer experience when using the application during the pilot.  The new launch deployed strategically  placed company shared iPads that had the mobile application already loaded on the device. Employee  sign-ins and content utilization rates for both device types were collected to determine if one, both or  none would be in the final solution at the end of the Learning Launch events.

Insight

What was gained from both Learning Launch events greatly impacted the client considering the  application as a means to provide corporate driven communications to the plant employees.  All the  data collected through the mobile app usage, in-person engagement and deployment challenges the  team faced was aggregated and reviewed to see what worked. Key implementation and support factors  were uncovered during the launch deployment process that would relegate the Apple or Android  minimum device specifications. It was also determined that acceptable use polices for Wi-Fi and shared  devices would need to be drafted and approved through senior leadership and legal.   Adding more  coverage to the plants existing Wi-Fi infrastructure was a hidden cost that would require a new project  and a new budget to ensure high workforce adoption rate and alleviate the employees concern of  depleting their own data packages.   The Design Thinking Framework provided an understanding of ways  that could have been used to uncover some of the basic concerns over how the mobile application  would be used by the company from a user perspective, a design tool such as Journey Mapping during  the ‘What is’ stage could have driven out better interaction points to include the concern for data usage  and company Wi-Fi constraints in the plant.  Many assumptions by the company were confirmed, but  the newly uncovered challenges at this stage provided invaluable insight that could be reviewed to pivot  at a savings to a full deployment of a mobile application that would require re-work and a poor  customer experience with their employees.

Approach

If faced with a similar challenge, I would use a Learning Launch again with the Journey Mapping design  tool.  With Journey Mapping I would hope to gain insights on how they would use it during their day in  the plant and what is/could be of concern while using the application. As a non-technical person, would I  understand that it would not track my location if the services were not turned on in my settings?  I  believe there were several opportunities that could have aided in the preparation of the app team and  educated the pilot base prior to the Learning Launch event.  The Learning Launch is still the right choice  in this scenario.  The employee/app team touch points were both enlightening and provided additional  feedback for alternative tools that the employees were looking for in the future – new ideas/new  opportunity to ‘WoW’.

Reflection – Learning Launch

By: Rafaela Nasser

Challenge: A professional development organization had been hearing anecdotal feedback that  it wasn’t communicating or sharing resources with its members effectively. The word on the  street was that they were sending way too many communications, often not even relevant to  the individual and that it was hard to find any useful resources on the existing platforms. Many  members were also younger generations and communications had not been optimized for  mobile devices (where the majority of younger generations spend their time). A solution was  proposed to resolve this issue which consisted of implementing a new platform that was highly  personalized to the individual and optimized for mobile devices. This way members could  receive personalized information at their fingertips on their terms.

The project was viewed positively by internal staff, however minimal data existed to drive  decisions in designing the new platform. As the Project Manager, I was tasked with leading the  project team to test if these assumptions were accurate and design a platform that would add  value to members. But where should the project team start if minimal data existed to guide  decisions on design? Also, some members of internal staff expected a big launch of the new  platform with only one chance to get it “right”.

Selection: As the project began, we realized the need to experiment and test key assumptions  given the lack of data and understanding of the membership base. I decided that a learning  launch was crucial to the success of the project. A learning launch is “a small experiment that  tests your new idea in the real marketplace” (University of Darden). The project team had to  start somewhere and given the current environment (lack of data, need to launch ASAP), the  team did not have time to gather additional data needed to drive the project. A learning launch  would allow the team to experiment with and test small ideas with actual members to gain the  insight they needed to add value for its members. In addition to engineering success on the  project, the learning launch would minimize the risk associated with a big bang launch and  allow the project team to “fail fast” instead of betting everything on getting it “right” the first  time.

Application: I lead the team through an effort to give some definition as to the goals of the  platform and the tactics we could use to accomplish those the goals. We then prioritized the  tactics by the value we thought they would deliver to our members. We used our best  judgement based on the data we did have. We then developed our idea in small incremental  stages of testable functionality. We rallied up a small group of members that represented

various age groups, backgrounds, specialty areas, genders, and demographics to conduct a  learning launch. The group of members was tasked with using the new platform. We observed  how they used the platform, analyzed data on usage, and surveyed the members after they  spent some time with the new platform. This allowed us to test our assumptions before putting  the new platform into the broader marketplace.

Insight: In conducting the learning launch, we realized that while we had provided value to a  specific segment of our membership base, we had not added value for a different segment of  our membership base. We realized we needed to hone in on the needs of these different  segments of members so that we could provide real value for all our members. We needed to  run additional experiments for these groups were neglected. Conducting the learning launch  made us realize that design needs may not always be universal and to really add value to our  members, we need to look at the needs of individuals and not just the group as whole. The  learning launch helped us see our members as people and allowed us to more deeply  understand their needs as humans.

Approach: While the learning launch was successful and allowed us to understand the needs of  various members more deeply, we realized that next time mind mapping at the beginning  would be useful. Mind mapping would help us organize ideas and needs of various segments so  that we could design with the segments of members in mind.
