Design Thinking - Assignment - Design Tool ‘VISUALIZATION’

1. Challenge

I work within the technology consulting domain focussed on banking and capital markets. We  serve a large European bank with an in-house solution. After working with the client successfully  for 3 years, the client expressed cost pressure and the need to bring down cost of operation. Client  gave a specific mandate that the additional cost savings would have to come from (a) building  scale in the solution (b) mutualize cost with other banks in the market by proposing a common  Utility model. This posed huge challenges -   (A) LOT OF REDTAPE - The business that we operate in 'Banking' is fraught with Compliance, Risk  and Licensing laws & regulations which made it almost impossible for us to realize this solution  requirement.  (B) SELF INTEREST GROUPS - Key vendors that provide data to our current solution do not want a  mutualized solution which would lead to consolidation and reduce their own revenue generation.  (C) UNCHARTERED TERRITORY - As we found out, there was only 'one' other company in this world  which is 'trying' to build a similar solution with another bank. We were stepping into an unknown  territory.

2. Selection

As any product/solutions designing company will tell you that it is a highly competitive business  and hence information is highly secretive. There are non-disclosure agreements signed annually to  ensure employees do not divulge key information to competitors. There was no comparative  data/knowledge available for reference. This led us to using VISUALIZATION as the core design  tool. The rationale behind using VISUALIZATION was precisely because 'imagination' would play a  key role in this solution design challenge. We knew key challenge areas would need  VISUALIZATION techniques applied to generate ideas and WHAT IF scenarios/Use Cases. Key teams  had to unlock their creative side and VISUALIZE a solution as described in Module-1 of this course,  VISUALIZATION.

3. Application

VISUALIZATION Workshops with 4 different groups were organized. We identified (a) Business  Development/ Legal Team, (b) Technology, (c) Operations Staff & (d) Business Analyst as the core  groups we need to visualize with.  (a) Business Development/Legal Department (2 members) - We asked them to visualize all possible  worst case scenarios linked to contract we had signed with client bank or vendors companies. We  asked they divide the whiteboard vertically (two halves). One side would capture breach of  contract scenarios with client, the other would focus on vendor.  (b) Technology Department (2 members) - We asked them to VISUALIZE using a high level  architecture diagram. We gave them a scenario where 50 banks would like to use the existing  solution under a common platform. This question was sufficiently broad enough to help us get the  right scalable technical design visualized.  (c) Operations Staff (3 members) - As an experiment we asked them to list down all the areas of  improvement and challenges they face on day-to-day basis. This was intended to stimulate their  thought process to foresee challenges in managing a platform used by more than one bank.  Something they are not used to handling. The initial white boarding process focussed on current  Bank's staff challenges. Once these where captured, we ask them to visualize the same problems  under a multi-bank design, so they could validate if the problem/challenge would further  deteriorate or remain same.  (d) Business Analyst (4 member team) - were given the same challenge as the Technology team.  They had to image the current platform being shared among 50 Banks. They had to VISUALIZE how

each module within the solution would cater to 50 different banking clients. How the different  business requirement and timing differences in markets location would impact us and which  functional components would fail or deteriorate in functionality. They would visualize using MS- VISIO based Flow Diagrams.

4. Insight

VISUALIZATION helped us unearth some very interesting risks and opportunities. Having 4 groups  visualize in isolation helped reduce the chances of each group getting influenced by the other. This  ensured that we got a large set of diverse data points for further brainstorming and WHAT-IF/  WHAT-WOWS analysis.  (a) Legal departments visualization - made it clear that there was bad news - the scalability of this  solution was tied down to convincing vendors to a different contract terms and those terms were  not something vendors would agree to. This had the highest level of impact in our final solution  design. Good that we had these session with them  (b) Technology Team - made it look like cake walk. They backed their architecture requirement  visualized in the diagram with clear reference to Retail/Healthcare domains where similar  technology was already in use. This provided us a lot of relief and confidence that this is doable  (regardless of legal issues)  (c) Operations Staff - Though the insights visualized through this team were not adding to our  overall solution design decision process. The data points visualized helped capture some long- existing pain areas in current solution. We added them to a to-do list as they had the potential to  be our 'WHAT-WOWS' feature enhancements.  (d) Business Analyst - This visualization exercise was taken up for several weeks due to the sheer  size of the scope. These Visualization sessions brought out a clear functional design and pointed  out components that would regress and those that would need to be newly built. In subsequent  sessions with BA Team, we added new constraints to the visualization criteria that were based on  Legal department's contract related constraint. This lead to significant changes to our functional  design

5. Approach

Though VISUALIZATION worked wonders for us, we might have also used Learning Launch in this  case. The key argument against using learning launch was the requirement of dedicated people  and resources for several weeks which would need significant funding and approval.  VISUALIZATION is more cost effective and easy to implement. Learning Launch might have added  advantage of providing us additional insight into risk areas that may have been overlooked in the  VISUALIZATION exercise, however, that was not a significant concern for the stakeholders.    VISUALIZING with Legal, Technology, Business and Operations staff provided us not only the  required data for solution designing, but also helped build a second layer of network group that  could be utilized for more consulting, prototyping & testing opportunities down the line. The  solution design was not addressing all the constraints we would have loved to address, however,  with VISUALIZATION data on our side, we were able appropriately call out the constraints as out of  scope areas.

Reflection Agim Krieger – Mind Mapping

1. Challenge & Selection     I used mind mapping, as one of the key tools of the design thinking process, in my research process of my  master thesis. The thesis was about the business model implications of the autonomous driving technology on a  leading German automotive company. In this context, I applied a qualitative, inductive research method with  the help of semi-structured expert interviews. The challenge was to gain information and, finally, knowledge  from the raw data. Therefore, I needed a tool that can set qualitative data in a context and relation to each  other. Since mind mapping can be used for looking for patterns and insights in a large quantity of data that a  design thinker gathered from the exploration stage “what is”, I applied mind mapping as the initial tool.     2. Application of Mind Mapping     In my explorative mind mapping process, I used an online whiteboard application called “Miro” to map the key  insights from the experts. Firstly, all relevant insights were written on digital sticky notes and got initially  mapped with other statements of experts. This represented the initial data set for the mind mapping process.  The first layer of the mind mapping process was to map the data to the three research questions of my thesis:   •  Does the BMW Group face the typical Innovator’s Dilemma in regard of autonomous driving technology?

•  How could Business Model Innovation help BMW to solve the Innovator’s Dilemma in the future?

•  Which organisational conditions need to be established today to enable this kind of Business Model  Innovation and the development of the autonomous driving technology?

Based on the three categories, the statements in each category were set in context and overall categories were  derived. To support this mind mapping process, theory-based frameworks like the value proposition canvas or  the fishbone diagram were applied. Hence, a multi-layer and iterative mind mapping was applied. The Miro  whiteboard enabled a flexible and shareable approach of mind mapping. Hence, I was able to integrate my  colleague in the iterative mind mapping process. She reviewed my mapping and presented her opinion and  perspective on the raw data.     3. Insights from applying Mind Mapping     Mind mapping clearly helped me to structure my thoughts on the raw data and enabled me to create relevant  categories and insights into the impact of autonomous driving on the company’s business model. If I look on the  design thinking processes, mind mapping helped me to find enough answers to the questions “what is” and  “what if”. Although it is recommendable to do mind mapping in a diverse group, for me, it also worked in a  setting where I was the only design thinker. It is highly valuable for qualitative insights like expert interviews. It  helps to curate and merge the collective knowledge of the heterogeneous expert panel. From my perspective,  mind mapping still needs a framework to derive information and, finally, knowledge from the data. A fishbone  diagram or other theory-based frameworks help to guide the mapping.

4. Lessons Learned    As a result, mind mapping was the perfect tool for my challenge. It helped me to understand, structure and  analyze the data derived from the expert interviews. The choice of the medium for mind mapping is critical from  my perspective. The digital whiteboard was appropriate, since I was able to quickly change categories and  statements. This was important since the character of the research was very explorative and, hence, one new  insight can change the whole knowledge outcome of the mind mapping. I can really recommend the digital  whiteboard as a medium, especially in times of the COVID-19 crisis. However, my mind mapping approach  lacked the multi-perspective aspect of design thinking. It would be recommendable to build up a mind mapping  process that includes third parties like colleagues or other business students to ensure multiple perspectives on  the same case. For ideation processes regarding the questions “what is” and “what if”, mind mapping is a strong  and suitable tool. Also in the context of business model innovation, mind mapping is a critical task to develop  suitable ideas for further development.

Design Thinking for Innovation – Assignment Two

By Byron Morton

Challenge

As a language travel agency, we knew that our product offering was too wide.  We offered multiple  partners in numerous locations. This caused inefficiencies in three main areas; administration,  commission and sales education. Administration was made difficult as each partner has its own  accounting and booking processes, our power to negotiate commissions was weakened as bookings  were widely distributed and our education of the sales staff was lengthy and complicated as they  were required to visit and learn about so many schools. We proposed too that customers were also  overwhelmed with so many choices.

The obvious solution was to slim down the portfolio, but where and how? So we challenged our  stakeholder group to define who we should work with.

Selection

Collective mind mapping presented many benefits for this exercise.  It allowed us to bring together,  improve relationships and gain ideas from sales people, product managers, administrative staff and  key clients. Partners were not invited as they had the potential to lose out from this process and  were therefore unlikely to prove objective.

Application

Twelve carefully selected stakeholders were invited for a two-hour afternoon session. We spread  relevant information around our largest meeting room. This included sales volumes and sales  revenues by city, country, school, course level and language. We included an overview of our  company vision, mission and objectives and also included our product brochures, but also those of  our competitors and summaries of analysis we had undertaken on their market positioning,  marketing and sales. We included information on our partner schools, including locations,  differentiating features, fees and commissions. Finally, we also included information provided by the  industry governing body on current and future booking trends.

Participants were invited to pick out the important elements from all this information in a 45 minute  session, noting down interesting points on sticky notes. They then had ten minutes to organise their  sticky notes and thoughts before sharing their inputs in two groups of six. Inputs from all  participants were grouped during this process and then once again reviewed by the group to gain  insights.

Insight

Our identified insights included:

•  A few strong partner recommendations displays knowledge, clarity and confidence to the  consumer

•  Perceived value is more important than cost

•  Partners of low financial value can be important in rounding out a portfolio and offering  solutions to customers in unique and sought-after locations

•  Value can also be created by offering unique solutions rather than obvious ones

•  Sales staff sell the products that excite them, we need to really excite them about our core  products if we are to limit what they can sell.

Approach

In future, I would mix the groups at the point where they were asked to review their whole groups  inputs.  My hope is, that this would create more ideas as this element was did not work so well in  our practice as participants had already felt like they had done this when explaining their own  insights to the group.  Refreshing of the groups would have required members of the original group  to better explain the input overview they had created and may have lead to more ideas.

Design of digital sales process

Ivica Marija

The challenge I had was designing a new, “digitalized” sales process for lending products for  large corporate clients. In my Bank, “Large Corporates” refer to companies that have more  than €500 million yearly turnaround and require multi-million financing deals for their needs.  Negotiations and contracts are commonly very complex and can last for weeks or months.  Despite having many systems available, the whole process was still mostly manual: data  required for a credit application was manually copy-pasted from source systems to  predefined forms in Word; calculations of exposures and limits were calculated in variety of  Excel sheets and also copy pasted to these forms, and these forms were sent by e-mail to  different approvers who would review them, print them, sign them and send it back in pdf  format. Finally, data from contracts was manually entered to booking systems. Only this task,  due to complexity of contracts (>100 pages) was usually taking 4-8 hours(!).    The initial set of requirements we got could be summarized with famous quote from Henry  Ford: “give me faster horses”. Despite having very modern digital workflow systems and  Customer Relationship Management (CRM) system, everyone expected “easier way of  handling documents”. “Problems” that were identified were mostly around >20 systems being  used, primarily to extract data needed for the application, but nobody thought about big  picture. We could do that, of course, but that wouldn’t be digitalized and automated process.    In order to give participants the sense of complexity, I decided to use visualization – a tool  well described in video of Angela Myer in Week 1. I often use Visualization, primarily for my  own better understanding of a problem, but also to ensure that there is a shared  understanding of the problem and possible solutions among groups of stakeholders. The  approach is very useful when stakeholders are diverse, in my case businesspeople from a  bank, and IT people from IT division.    In this particular case, I painted the entire process on the wall in a way that I:

1) highlighted the number of different tools they actually use to extract data they need

for an application – indicating that the problem is not in these tools, but in the fact that  they need to manually copy-paste data from different tools into application forms.

2) Listed different forms that are used for different approval bodies in several steps of

the process – indicating number of data items that are in common to these forms (i.e.  client data) – that are repeatedly copy-pasted into these forms.

3) Listed documents client needs to provide for the approval, which we now store for

compliance reasons, whereas we don’t need documents, but information from these  documents (i.e. confirmation from Commercial Register that company is registered) in  order to proceed with the application.

4) Visualized document flow and number of e-mails, printing, physical signing of a

document and again scanning and forwarding – in order to “collect all signatures” for  the approval – whereas “approval” in form of confirmation in a tool would be sufficient.

Needless to say – no PowerPoint slides could describe the volume of waste we created in  every single step of credit approval process. Picture hardly fit on 10x2m wall (I had to repaint  it several times to fit it properly). But, I managed to made my point: problem is not in  systems, but in the way we approach the process. By integrating data sources to the  workflow and using built-in capabilities of CRM tool, administrative overhead could be  decreased by more than 90%! Moreover, the most of information we require from a client in  the form of a document – we can get by ourselves from public registries – automatically. This  would dramatically reduce the amount of work for our clients too and reduce waiting time  from days or weeks to minutes or even seconds.

The second phase was, however, more complex and more important. Now we knew the  problem – but what is the solution? This took several weeks of discussions in smaller groups  and common meetings among groups to figure out:

1) Which data we really need? In some cases, account managers collected a lot of

information about the deal, hoping this will help the case and get the approval from  the investment committee – whereas committee members admitted they don’t need  these data to make their decision at all.

2) Which controls we need? The whole process is rather collaborative, especially for

more complex deals, and there is no classical “flow” (handover). Squeezing this into a  workflow would actually make it worse. So, we needed to be careful with defining  process steps and decided to minimize them to data collection and approval only –  despite the fact there are several formal approvals needed.

3) How to organize the data in a screen – especially on different screen sizes

(smartphones/laptops/monitors) to make the overview possible. Since we talk about  250 different data fields, among which there are “free text” fields containing several  sentences, images and graphs – this was the most challenging one.

Although I used visualization before, only now I got the true power of it. It was also very  interesting to observe how it also helped clients to involve themselves more. Previously,  “specifications” were written in words. And, it takes thousands of words to describe – and  later, read a requirement. And nobody has time for that. Requirements were written  superficially and understood accordingly – wrong. Once when clients actually saw the vast  number of systems they use and the number of interactions they made – with picture – only  then they realized the problem they had.    On the other hand, something that would previously be written as “simple” requirement (i.e. “I  want all the data on one screen”), brought them to the understanding that it is them who  need to make priority which datasets they want where, based on the importance. Because:  all the data couldn’t fit into a screen (especially smartphone screen); scrolling was needed,  so the data that is more important – you should put to the top.    Despite the fact that we did a lot of painting, the whole process proved to be very light in the  documentation – and yet, more descriptive. Additionally, it brought people together and made  the approach collaborative. Businesspeople understood limitations a system has, but also  benefits it can bring if we use it properly. IT people got better understanding of client needs –  and come with very valuable ideas that helped clients make better choices. And on the top: it  wasn’t boring at all – it was actually fun!     Finally: there was no (bad) surprises about the final outcome. Clients knew exactly how the  new system will look like and how will they use it. There was no need for user manuals nor  training either – they know how to use the system, because they designed it together.    The only thing I would do differently in the future is: jumping immediately to visualization,  without spending time on interviews and data gathering. A high-level overview is important at  the beginning, but that’s all. Once when painting starts – there is no need for further “data  gathering” because clients can do quite a lot by themselves too.     Of course, some data gathering is still needed (i.e. in this case we needed to list all data  source systems, and data we need to collect), but visualization helped us determine what we  really need – and what we thought we need. This made data gathering rather slim.  Nevertheless, the common opinion once we finished with design was: none of us could  imagined the new process the way it turned out – if we didn’t use the visualization. What we  understood as a problem, and what we envisioned as a solution before we turned to  visualization was completely different from the final outcome. Visualisation helped us

understand the big picture, understand the impact different teams have on each other and  design much better solution.

Business lead on the design and launch of the company’s first mobile app. The company was an  insurance company specializing in Property & Casualty Insurance. Development of this app would be considered a phase one  approach, based on customer feedback and suggestions to improve; these can be build out in  subsequent phases/upgrades of the mobile app.

During the app development, the team notices that a large majority of the claim officer’s time is spent  on documenting claims rather than processing them quickly. Another factor also influenced the decision  to develop the app; the rise of smart phones in the country and mobile web technologies. The company  decided to merge these two major factors to develop a solution that would meet the needs of its  younger emerging customer who are tech savvy and rather conduct business transactions online with  convenience at their fingertips. This was would coincide with the overall insurance group’s strategic  objective of embracing technology to improve efficiencies with which the company treats with  customers and as a mechanism to continue to differentiate itself from the others to maintain the  company’s leadership role within the local/regional insurance industry.

The major challenge of this project would be to drive app acceptance and move the customer base to  conducting business online; reporting claims, queries and general information about company products.  I would like to mention here that in my country, we have a population that’s skewed to the older  generation so changing that culture of in person claim submissions would be a challenge.

Selection

The launch tool would be the most effective method to gain buy-in from customers and to received  direct feedback from our target audience on the app’s design, user ability, functionality and aesthetics  just to name a few. The launch tool would also serve as a final test before the app is submitted for  acceptance by the Google & Apple Stores.

Application

Before submitting the app to the respective store, the aesthetics was tested by our sample audience for  menu option and priority listing, elements, titles, fonts, colors etc for acceptance. Apple’s iOS and  Google’s Android design principles describe the basic requirements for designing a user-friendly  interface. We built the app using a cross-platform development tool, therefore the app’s conformity and  consistency had to be tested using a wide range of mobile handsets that uses both IOS and Android.  By  previewing the app in the launch test for both operating systems, we were able to make adjustments to  the apps to ensure that we met the design requirements of the operating systems.

We also tested the app’s usability for ease of navigation and user experience. All the menus, drop down  for sub menus and navigation through these menus and functions were tested and customer feedback  was given on areas of improvement.

The workflow for the app was also tested; the user access was set up to pull information from the  company’s ERP so as to display as much information on the customer we had on the system. This was  essential to the app’s functionality as well.

Insight

Applying the launch tool was somewhat logical, it would have been irresponsible of me as the business  lead to launch a mobile app geared towards customers of various backgrounds and tech savvy levels  without it first being tested by a sample audience. The test would help us iron out any navigation issues  that the team may have over looked because of our involvement in the development of the app, it  would be wise to get feedback from the faintness of mobile users to ensure a smooth and user friendly  approach that would ensure that we meet the customers’ needs and expectations.

There were some major changes needed; during the testing phase we realized that an added feature of  the app was to locate gas/service stations but testing revealed that some of the service stations and gas  stations were no longer operational and these where not updated on Google Maps.

All other functions of the app were tested and updated for optimal use.

Approach

Launch testing is hard wired into the design process, the design must be tested to ensure that it met all  of the customer’s expectations. To test the app, we selected a wide cross section of our customer base  to ensure we covered all segments of customers; from first time mobile user to the very young  professional who’s always on the go. Each function of the app was tested and we asked that the users  rate the effectiveness of each function and application. We asked customers to give suggestions as to  improvements to the app and what they would like to see for future upgrades to the app. This approach  is vital to the survival of the app because the app was developed for the customer therefore it should  meet the desires and expectations of the customer.

Nowhere in the world it is allowed to throw a car “wherever I want” - across the  sidewalk or the road. It is impossible to solve this problem in such chaos“, Sobyanin  said in his interview for the newspaper “Vedomosti”. The pilot project for the  introduction of paid parking started on November 1, 2012 from the Karetny Ryad.  An hour of parking cost 50 rubles. Parkons examined the payment; they were cars  with video clips. In the absence of payment, a fine was given automatically. Its size  was 2500 rubles. For parking in the wrong place the fine was 3000 rubles. Such  fines are valid even now.

Within a few months, paid parking began to spread around the city gradually,

and in 2015 they went beyond the Third Transport Ring (TTK), and their maximum  cost in the center and on the embankments of the Moscow River reached 200  rubles per hour. Today the city has 80,000 paid parking. Most of them are located  in 85 districts of the city, in 36 districts parking remains free of charge.

According to Viktor Osipkov, the project manager at “Probkovorot”, it was

the draconian fines that influenced the fact that people stopped throwing cars  anywhere, and the average speed in the city began to grow.

“If it were not for the Moscow Parking Space project, a transport collapse

would have occurred in the capital of Russia”, says a representative of the transport  department. “Every day, the number of cars on the roads would be about 10%  more than the current traffic (3.9–4 million), and Moscow would be in 9-10-point  traffic jams”, he adds.

“Today, Moscow is no longer the world champion in traffic jams,” Sobyanin

said recently. “Motorists are increasingly refusing to travel to the city center by  their personal cars”, a spokesman for the transportation department said.  According to him, today in Moscow 70% of the population uses public transport.  This is one of the highest rates, in European cities it is about 60%.

But paid parking is believed not to affect the traffic situation in any way -

traffic jams still remain. Kirill Yankov, a member of the public council at the Ministry  of Transport of Russia, believes that in the center, on the contrary, they have  increased. “The number of parking spaces has been drastically reduced, but there  are categories of citizens who do not refuse to travel by personal transport, now  they come to the center and travel in circles in search of parking,” the expert  indicates. In his opinion, Moscow needs a large-scale program for the construction  of underground parking in the center like in European capitals. “But if the real goal  of the authorities is not to unload the roads, but to remove business life from the  city center completely, then their strategy is correct”, Yankov summarizes.

But it is possible to convince people to change their own cars to public

transport. Squeezing people out of personal vehicles, it is necessary to create  alternatives for them. The rejection from personal transport should be stimulated  by introducing the MAAS (mobility as a service) service, which will allow planning a  trip by public transport in real time. And it is necessary to provide a convenient  opportunity to compare the duration and cost of various combinations of transport  means through “one window”, configure the integration of public transport with  taxis, car sharing and other services.

Under Sobyanin, the city built more than 650 km of new roads, reconstructed

departure highways and interchanges, accelerated the construction of new lines  and metro stations, and commissioned passenger rail services along the Moscow  Central Ring.

Ground transportation has become more comfortable, but not enough, as

Yankov believes. “People have to walk for 15–20 minutes to the nearest metro  station. The metro is built mainly on the periphery, but it is not being developed in  the center of Moscow. In the center of Paris, for example, metro stations are very  densely located, while in Moscow the lines are much longer.

2. Selection: In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected (e.g., what it is

and why you selected it for your challenge -- including any appropriate video lecture  references).

Since the information was available but only as a caution, with no reasoning or logic  given. I had very limited choice of tools to work on other than trying to understand  through visualization as to what really could be the cause, which is if the causes or  causes could be defined. Once defined, then one could think of a solution to the  problem which definitely was serious. Hence, I went about inspecting the vehicles  and moving around them, getting light vehicles in different positions, etc.

3. Application: Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g.,

what you did and how the tool was applied effectively or ineffectively).

It was a rather difficult task I had assigned myself. It took me a few days of sleepless  nights to make sure that I must complete the convoy movement without any  accidents. Not only that I need to accomplish the task to get away, but may be provide  a solution to insuring that this dangerous way of moving becomes history. A detailed  visualization study involving making of rough diagrams (mood boards as they are  now called) and putting myself in the drivers seat of all possible vehicles at all  possible situations – left  right turns / curves, uphill / downhill, slow / fast moving  lanes, by day / night, etc.

Slowly, a picture started to emerge. The heavy vehicles had a single rear view mirror  which was giving the driver a view of what traffic was coming up from behind the  vehicle or associated trailer. But he did not have a picture of what happened to the  vehicle which had crossed the line of “behind” but had not yet overtaken. This parallel  vehicle was no longer a part of the situational analysis being in the unknown zone.

I tried an experiment of getting a additional rear view mirror fitted in 3-4 vehicles which  would provide a view of alongside the heavy trailers. Both the mirrors were fitted right  next to each other, and with a little experiment, I finalised the location of this mirror  as just below the existing mirror. Thus, it gave a complete picture of the situation the  way it was happening and did not require a shift of glance (precious focus time of the  human brain).

you selected or a different one -- and the reason(s) why.

I feel that getting into the situation and living it is what  helps in getting answers.

Design Thinking for Innovation (Jan – Feb 2018)  Final Assignment - Learning Launch     Submitted by Jyoti Ward – 2 February 2018    1. Challenge: Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.

My company has in invested in Microsoft Office 365 – a suite of software services and apps to aid  collaboration, document access and productivity. Whilst adoption is gradually increasing, our staff  are not yet taking full advantage of these tools (and so not harnessing savings and benefits to the  company). Some people are relying on ways of creating and sharing documents that they have  become familiar with over many years, but which don’t have the benefits new functionality offers –  e.g. they will email a document to colleagues rather than collaborate online through the enterprise  social network, Yammer.

We want to foster a mindset and skills base across our workforce where the digital tools offered  by O365 are routinely used, providing demonstrable benefits to the way people work.

Using a ‘design thinking’ approach, we carried out some ‘skills insight interviews’ in November.  Assisted by a group of around 15 Office365 (O365) champions (individuals who have taken on a  role to support colleagues in the use of the Microsoft Office 365 suite) we sought to understand  what’s holding people back. We have used these insights to formulate hypotheses that we can  test. This covers the ‘What is?’ and ‘What if?’ steps described in the Design Thinking for  Innovation course.

The next step is to test some of the ideas we generated using experimentation. The ‘Learning  Launch’ tool provides the means to do this in a practical setting with real end-users. This will allow  us to test whether the action taken meets our requirements: namely to increase the skills and  capability of end users in using O365.

2. Selection: In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected (e.g., what it is and

why you selected it for your challenge -- including any appropriate video lecture  references).    A learning launch is a way of getting real-life feedback on an idea without the need to invest  significant amounts of time and money. The module refers to ‘placing small and affordable bets’  so that you can take stock of what you’ve learned then either refine the idea (iterate) or pivot  (change direction). The purpose of a learning launch is to improve and learn. If assumptions are  true you can scale it up. If assumptions are untrue – you can ‘table it’ go back to others ideas that  have been generated to test these.

In the interviews people had said that if they were unsure how to do something in O365 they said  they would seek support from someone who was more ‘tech-savvy’.     So our ‘fast and cheap’ experiment using the learning launch tool was to test whether end users  would take up an offer of a 30 minute 1:1 personalised support session on using O365. We  anticipated this would prove popular, being bespoke to the needs of the individual and not taking  up too much of their time.

3. Application: Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., what

you did and how the tool was applied effectively or ineffectively).

To apply the ‘learning launch’ tool we asked each O365 champion to send out a standard email to  3 individuals offering a personalised 1:1 support session lasting 30 minutes. A screenshot of this  email is shown below:

To quantify what ‘good’ would look like our expectation at the outset was in excess of 50% of  people would take up the offer.    To gain further insights into how people are using O365 and the difficulties experienced we  created a data capture sheets for the champions to complete after running the 1:1 support  session.

4. Insight: Describe the insight you gained from applying the tool you selected to your

challenge (e.g., how an insight affected your thinking about the challenge and about  design thinking more broadly).

We were surprised that less than 30% of people receiving the email offering a 1:1 support session  took this up. We had thought this would be an attractive way for people to ask ‘burning questions’  or develop their skills in using the new software. This is a good example of us ‘failing fast’ – we  didn’t invest inordinate time in implementing something that was not going to work.    When we explored this further with the O365 champions they told us that reasons people gave for  not taking up the offer included:

•  No specific questions to ask about O365

•  Lack of time / other priorities

•  People thought they were already competent in using O365 (but the champions refuted  this – they could see the individuals were not using the functionality of the software to the  full extent)

We also noted that whilst some champions had had 3 positive responses (people who took up the  offer), others had no positive responses to the offer – so there may be something about the  relationship between the champion/end user that is worthy of exploration.

5. Approach: Describe what you might do differently next time -- applying the same tool you

selected or a different one -- and the reason(s) why.

The findings from the learning launch has led us ‘pivot’ from our initial hypothesis that having a  1:1 support session would be beneficial. The reason for doing this is the take-up being less than  30% – below the threshold we had identified at the outset. This hypothesis been discarded for  now – but we will keep this idea ‘on the shelf’ in case elements of it have merit at a later stage in  our discovery process.    Instead we have turned our attention to another of our ‘portfolio of ideas’ that we wanted to test  that was uncovered in the ‘What is?’ and ‘What if?’ stages – namely that people don’t understand  the benefits O365 can offer. This builds on the finding from our first experiment people did not  have specific questions to ask (perhaps because they don’t understand the benefits?) We have  now designed a second experiment or ‘learning launch’ that will help us explore this.    So we are on a journey. The design thinking methodology has already helped us avoid investing  in something that seems to make intuitive sense, but in practice was shown not to work.

Improving distribution penetration and awareness of branded medicines in rural India

Learning Launch:

Challenge: I work in a pharmaceutical company which sells branded medicines across different  therapeutic areas cross India and many more countries. Healthcare facilities in most countries,  including India, are better in cities and Tier I towns compared to smaller towns and villages. This is  applicable right from infrastructure of hospitals, diagnostics centres, and availability of branded  medicines at pharmacies. The intent was to provide access to good quality medicines to the patients  in smaller towns and thereby increasing sale of our branded medicines. However, it was believed that  patients in smaller towns prefer to use generic unbranded medicines which are cheaper than branded  medicines. Hence, most of the distribution points and sales force of pharmaceutical companies are  based in cities and tier I towns.

Selection: I had some data and a hypothesis which said that people in Tier II and below towns want  good quality medicines for their near and dear ones but branded medicines are not available easily in  these towns. I visited smaller towns in different states and interviewed patients, pharmacists, doctors  in these towns. Since I only had a hypothesis, a plan and an intent, I was not sure about the success of  the plan. The project will require a large field force when operations will be in full scale. That’s when  I selected learning launch tool to quickly experiment in the market place.

Application: I deployed a team of 9 members to start a pilot project in one of the states in India. Each  member had to visit doctors and pharmacists in 24 smaller towns, twice a month. The purpose was to  increase awareness and educate doctors about well-known branded medicines and to make our  branded medicines available at 3 to 4 pharmacies in these towns. The team had to also connect these  pharmacies to large distributors in the tier I towns who would supply medicines to these pharmacies.  Members from various functions like finance, distribution, strategy, human resources also visited  these towns along with the 9 members for insights. Data during the pilot was captured by the 9  member team in specific formats through a mobile application.

Insight:  Insights from the data captured in the mobile application and from the conversations with  doctors, patients and pharmacies were very encouraging. I found that there were a set of patients  that had prescription of a doctor that he/she visited in a city and purchased branded medicines which  were available in a pharmacy in the small town. There were also a few doctors in these towns who  prescribed branded medicines to a few patients when they wanted a quick recovery. These doctors  also preferred branded medicines in certain therapies. Such insights helped in selecting well-known  brands in specific therapeutic areas to be promoted in these markets.

Approach: The tool that I selected, “Learning Launch”, helped me in proving my hypothesis and  making necessary changes in the go to market strategy. In this case, selection of brands in specific  therapeutic areas was very important and selecting specific states, where health care was not well  penetrated in Tier II and below towns, was important. The insights from the pilot also helped in  creating mechanism to connect the pharmacies in these towns to distributors in the larger towns.  There were also changes done in the mobile application to capture sale and process metrics data and  in designing dashboards. The approach helped in scaling up the project to 8 different states within 6  months which helped in additional growth of 5% in sale for these branded medicines. There was a  greater satisfaction that good quality and affordable medicines were made available to patients across  the length and breadth of these states.

VISUALIZATION TO TRANSFORM LIVES

Diana Alfonso – Engineer/Researcher

Colombia

Challenge

I work in a huge research program in my country, Colombia, regarding the development of  renewable energy to be used in the country by 2030. The program is divided in ten different  projects, I collaborate as a researcher in one of the projects that is related to the costumer  challenges within the adoption of these new technologies we are researching. We as  researchers, tend to be very quantitative so we first started with a marketplace research and  used only tools that were entirely related to the data we had and, because our team is mostly  compounded with engineers, they were oddly satisfied with the results of this first outlook of  the market. Yet, here is the challenge: The technologies that are being developed are (because  many scientific reasons) being designed to be used in country’s poorest zones, tending also to  transform lives and environments, so in the first marketplace research we did, we found that the  new technologies were indeed going to help this poor regions (quantitatively). But, there’s a  deeper challenge we didn’t notice: we didn’t really know our costumer, we didn’t gave a deep  thought about the fact that we were going to disrupt many communities way of living that have  had almost none contact with technology at all, and that they weren’t going be able to use it or  even understand it once they were installing it. So, we needed to study our market and costumer  in a deeper way, but this time using a different approach.

Selection

This time, the objective was to get to know our customers and help them get an insight on what  is coming in their communities. We chose to use visualization, not as a tool to represent what we  wanted the community to do with the technology but rather to explain to them and see how  they imagined and reflected in the things we wanted to do. Since I learnt about it, I have always  thought that visualization is a very powerful tool mostly in a co-creation processes because both  the company and the client must have the same visualization of the product so they can both  achieve their goals and satisfy their needs. But I think in this case, co-creation is not about a  product but instead about building an image together. We get to know our customer, how they  see themselves in these coming changes and everything that comes along, and they get to  understand the technologies and the way they are going to change their lives.

Application

We set up an interdisciplinary team to decide which communities we were going to visit and how  we were going to do it. We decided to make a social workshop. At first, there was interaction  between social workers and the community and then the engineers prepared an intervention  when they explained very easily the concept of energy and all the changes the government was  going to start bringing to these zones. At this point, we proceeded with the greater part of the  workshop with was direct work with the community, we gave material so they could express

creatively how they see themselves and how they thought this was going to change their lives.  The participation varied from children to older people and the acceptation was very positive.  Visualization was very helpful in both sides, we as engineers learned a lot about all the  communities we visited and researched our marketplace in a way we were not used. This stage  took us about three months to visit and work with communities and then other months getting  deeper into the results and constructing something very positive about our new market  research.

Insight

We gained a lot of insights. Most importantly, we discovered that people in the communities see  this project very positively, first because they feel back up from the government and also  because through renewable energies we are going to be able to give them some dignity, starting  by something as basic as drinkable water. Also, we learned a lot about the things we needed to  help them adapt into this new life.

I cannot really write about our research results because they are in a publication process. Yet, I  really want to say that Design Thinking tools and approach in general is the most valuable thing  I have learned in the last few years, because our mindset is always about data and as engineers  changing our fixed mindset to a learning mindset brings so much new information and so many  ways to understand the context of our work.

Approach

I would not really change anything from our approach and if we were to repeat this activity, I  would use the same tools because the findings were amazing. You could say that qualitative and  mixed research has always existed, and it is true, however you can access to a much deeper and  innovative insights by using design thinking tools.

Ana Perez  Challenge & Selection:    The first tool I used was the tool of Visualization, or Visual Thinking, to achieve a shared understanding  of a problem space among a diverse group of stakeholders before attempting to identify and define  possible solutions to the problem. I use this approach often with our customers, who are government  agencies working to apply technology innovations to modernize their mission or the delivery of their  services to their customer, which may be U.S. citizens, businesses, and non-citizens. I have used the  technique of using a straw man visualization of a problem domain with a set of questions or prompts for  discussion to allow a diverse group of stakeholders to learn from each other in the process of defining  the scope, boundaries, key elements, and relationships between elements to consider when identifying  pain points and opportunities for improvements or solutions.    Application:    I start the process by creating a straw man graphic of the problem domain. To develop the straw man  graphic, I will draw from any existing material available to understand the environment. The existing  material may be operational or procedural documents, training materials, marketing materials, GAO or  other auditing reports. If materials are not available, then I conduct informal interviews with one-three  of the stakeholders who serve as my main points of contact on the initiative.    If appropriate to the situation, I will borrow the concept to “front-stage/back-stage” from previous  research, and discussed in David Gray’s book, “The Connected Company”. The front-stage/back-stage  approach helps to reinforce the notion that every service – even an internal service – has customers  with whom the service provider interacts and internal processes that enable the organization to provide  the service. The template I often start with also has a column on the left to identify Partners and Value  Chain Providers and a column on the right to identify Oversight Organizations, such as Congress, GAO,  labor unions, advocacy groups, and other entities that may add constraints to how the organization  operates. The straw man graphic is simple, using simple shapes and icons available in Visio or on the  Internet. If the front-stage/back-stage view doesn’t work, then I will create a different type of visual,  either based on a high-level process flow with swim lanes for different stakeholders, or another format.    For the activity, I will divide the stakeholders into groups of 5-6 participants each representing a  different organization or area of interest. Each group receives a poster-size copy of the straw man  graphic that they can write on directly, or use sticky notes to make comments. I give them two-three  questions to answer, such as: 1) What key elements are missing from the graphic? 2) What would you  change about the graphic to make it more accurately reflect your problem space? 3) What key insights  do you have about the relationships between the entities in your problem space? I give them  approximately 20 minutes to discuss the questions and mark up the graphic. Then I have each group  report out on their answers to those three questions while pointing to the mark-ups on their poster. As  each group reports out, I record commonalities in the insights of each group, and then additional  insights that come from the group discussion on an additional copy of the graphic. After the session, I  digitize each group’s poster as an artifact, create a view that combines the shared and new insights from  the group discussion, and then create a revised graphic that incorporates their feedback and proposed  changes that they agreed to as a group.

Insight & Approach:    What I have learned from conducting this exercise with several groups is that while the graphic –  especially the revised graphic that incorporates their feedback – is important for reinforcing their  understanding of the problem they are working to solve, the more valuable aspect of the activity is the  shared insights and shared learning that occurs while they are working to define their problem  space. The graphic gives the diverse group of stakeholders a focal point for discussion that allows them  to share their perspectives and develop insights into potential root causes of their problems. While they  could create the graphic from a blank slate in a collaborative manner, starting with a straw man jump  starts the conversation for them. They can quickly identify where they are in the graphic – or if they are  missing – and can more quickly gain new insights about relationships between key entities instead of  taking time to identify them. They can also identify variables in the problem space – that is, it helps  them to identify what they don’t know, in what areas they need to obtain information or data to provide  the values for the variables.    Since I discovered that the most valuable aspect is the shared insights and learning, next time I would  use the visualization activity as a starting point for a series of design thinking activities. Then the revised  graphic that incorporates their combined feedback can serve as a reference tool throughout the  remainder of their work.

I am Oscar Santos, a Lawyer Student in the Kenyon College and I have to use the online marketing department and

increase sales in the online channel and to spend marketing budgets on the right

campaigns. The project scope includes the online marketing department composed of ten

employees, as well as the larger marketing department and IT department, with whom we

work closely. The project is limited to internal resources (i.e., budget and employee time).

The project should not excees business days and the solution should include an even

distribution of working hours amongst the team members. We will focus on trying to

uncover what our team members, as well as key stakeholders within the larger marketing

department and IT department, consider to be ineffective or problematic with regard to

the workflow.

When we Selection Our team has already gone through several design thinking

activities/tools, so we are ready to try the learning launch tool. Broadly speaking, the

learning launch is an experiment meant to quickly test an idea and prototype. Application

For our first learning launch, we focused on the structure/execution of our online

marketing tasks. In particular, we wanted to see if we could structure our tasks, projects,

and processes to adapt the methods of Scrum project management for our work (e.g., time

boxed, daily, specific meetings, reviews, etc.) in an effort to become more agile. This

tested our assumption that the structure and execution were the main causes of our

workflow challenge. Our team went through a two-day training with a Scrum project

management coach. Next, we went through five workshops to structure our tasks and

processes in a more agile way. These two sessions occurred within in a three-week

timeframe. We expected to produce a document with a clear description of our new, more

agile processes/workflow. For our second learning launch, we focused on gaining clarity

about our tasks and priorities.

This tested our assumption that our prioritization of tasks was the main cause of

our workflow challenge and the principal carateristics of the law in Guatemala. Our team

completed an anonymous survey. Additionally, five key stakeholders from the larger

marketing department and IT department also completed an anonymous survey. The

surveys included questions about our new, proposed process, understanding the process

and the prioritization of tasks, and feelings about the change, and were conducted within

a one-week timeframe. Insight By applying the learning launch tool, our team identified

our assumptions and designed launches to test these assumptions. Additionally, we

thought through anticipated results, expecting to find that a more agile approach would

improve our workflow, and that both our team and the key stakeholders would be fairly

incorporate it into future launch designs.

stage, as launches come before a full rollout in the design thinking timeline. Approach

Given that our team has already gone through several design thinking activities/tools and

mentioned, our team needs to review the insight gained from our first two launches and

incorporate this insight into future launch designs. Future launch designs should reflect

insight gained, progress made, and come closer to a compelling solution ready for full

rollout.

Challenge:  Working at a media agency, there is nothing more important than understanding targets. As a part  of the Knowledge and Research department, it was important to supply employees/planners with  relevant information. The company always relied on quantitative data to propose media plans for  big brands. But employees were usually afraid of data or they got lost in the inﬁnite pdfs and excel  tables, not knowing how to read vertical and horizontal percentages or how to link one information  to the other, losing the greater meaning of the data itself. The company had already designed a  study to cover most of the information need of clients, but this data was really hard to work with, as  it came in a non-friendly format for employees, resulting in a wasting of time and efforts of our  employees/planners. Employees received raw data on a monthly basis, having to search for their  own insights in order to complete their work every month.

Application: To understand the ﬂow of data, our team got together with two planners to understand the process  of media planning and how the information ﬂowed inside the company and got to the clients. We  identiﬁed all the touch-points and drew a map + timeline which clearly showed how much time was  being spent on each task, and what were the ﬁnal results for the clients. We then brainstormed a  whole new process, which took into consideration all of the details that came in touch with our main  challenge. One important fact was time, as in the original process every employee had to go  through the data too look for the same. As we visualized this, it was easier to understand that we  could centralize this process into an automatic report. Seeing every step and touchpoint versus  times was really eye-opening. So for the solution we created automatic reports customized to what  planners were expecting to see from the data. By having them involved in the process, we were  able to come up with a solution that included their vision and their real needs, instead of only  supplying the information that we thought they needed (which is what we as a Research  department used to do before). We visualized again how this new report could look, what  information it could have and how we could create value from data through it. We then used  storytelling to present the new proposals and prototype to the head of the company, who approved  immediately the new changes.

Insight:  Thanks to the visualization process, we were able to see beyond the main challenge, and add  more value to the same solution. For example, we created a report template that connected data  that the planners thought it was important, to data that we as a research department also saw  important from the market. For example, to see only how your brand and category are doing is not  as useful as to see how the market is ﬂowing in that same time, because you get a better overview  of any change your brand has had. This could also help to see these reports as part of a  timeframe, and notice season ﬂows. Another thing we came up with was a user friendly report. Of  course, reports should always be in pdf to assure no manipulation of the data outside of the  department/company, but to make data understandable was a huge step-up. The new report came  in an infographic manner, speciﬁcally designed so that the planners could use them in their own  presentations. This helped with data visualization and also saving time for the planners, while  improving the image of the company in front of the clients.

Approach:  The results were really impressive for both our internal clients (employees) and our external  clients. As part of an evaluation process, I think it would’ve been great to have integrated the IT  department, because we struggled a bit trying to come up with the prototype of the report. We  could have saved a couple of months if we could have visualized our new tool as an  interdisciplinary project, were experts within the company could also have helped with their  expertise. Of course, our project needs to be continuously revised, so we have set a revision  meeting for every year. It is impressive as a research department to be able to bring value to  employees through a good design.

Reflection on Mind Mapping | Jan Peters      Challenge  My Client is a European governmental institution embarking on a new way of working.  One where different Service Providers work in an ecosystem to collaboratively provide  end-to-end services to their IT users, bringing value to the Client. Being the Service  Integrator, my organisation takes over the operational responsibilities of the Service  Management processes, on behalf of the Client. For that to be possible the project  needed the to implement the Service Management framework and processes.     To be successful I realised that, more importantly, we also needed the engagement and  contribution of the Service Providers to collaborate and support each-other, playing as  one team. To reinforce that idea, we needed to introduce “Ecosystem Commitment” into  the contracts between the Client and the Service Providers.     The challenge was to establish common grounds with a diverse group of stakeholders  with the intention to emphasise how we would like to see all of us working, with respect  and consideration of the impact on each member, and where everyone is clear on  expected behaviours and outcomes.    Selection  This tangible result to achieve, the “Ecosystem Commitment” document, is empty at the  start with the intention to jointly discuss and agree during the first stage in the project.  Because it is not adding new metrics or services but rather taking a different perspective  and thinking on how we can achieve this commitment, we proposed to leverage the Mind  Mapping tools. As Mind Mapping is intuitive, creative, and engaging, we used Mind  Mapping to boil it down into a jointly agreed charter for how everyone will behave and  operate. Facilitated workshops, Mind Mapping and visualisation helped us to distil the  common grounds for the collaboration principles.    Application  Prior to the facilitated workshop we instilled the idea with the stakeholders that no-one  can pull off a delightful collaboration experience on their own and invited 35 participants,  in different roles, representing the ecosystem partners, to discover what it would look  like. At the start we have made a lot of inputs available to the participants such as:  Strategic Objectives, Statement of Works, Service Level Agreement, Governance  Exhibits, RASCI Matrices, Key personnel and the different views and understanding on  ecosystem collaboration from the Service providers.

Powerful live-cartooning facilitated from ComicHouse  (https://comichouse.nl/category/live-cartooning/)  helped us clarify and it immediately led us to new   discussions and to new insights. All of which were  collated and then grouped.     The participants were grouped into mixed teams across  the Service Providers and assigned to have a discussion  related to collaboration rules and principles. We used  the Mural canvas,  online whiteboard

(https://mural.com), to collaborate with the teams,  to collate and combine virtual post-its.  In the plenary  session, teams reported-out and the workshop was  successfully concluded with a set of 10 collaboration  principles (rules) we could all jointly agree upon.

ComicHouse Cartoon

Mural Canvas

Insights & Approach  Due to Covid-19 restrictions we needed to convene fully remote workshops, we used MS  Teams (with separate breakouts) and collaboration tools. Most of the participants did not  know each other beforehand and yet we decided not to waste time on introduction  rounds. We expected such introductions to occur organically during the workshops and  we have learned that it did.     We also learned it is a good idea to share the objectives (i.e. establishing collaboration  rules and principles) prior to the workshop with all participants. It turned out most of  them came with a prepared mindset, were able to browse the input materials, and  quickly further develop their views into the principles that we were aiming for.     The Mural canvas provided the diverse group of participants a central point, it enabled  their discussions and the sharing and exchanging of (virtual) Post-it memos. The  powerful visualisation tools (ComicHouse) helped us exchanging ideas, sharing insights  and, as an extra benefit, it provided us with a lot of graphics. The Service Providers can  now use the graphics even beyond the workshop to evangelize the behaviour principles  we had established in their respective organisations.     I have learned Mind Mapping provides for a structured approach for establishing common  grounds (with great contribution from powerful visualisation) and in future I would  structure the flow of the workshops even more to get the most out of it. I believe an  even better output quality can be achieved when leveraging more Mind Mapping  resources than we have done in this case.      Although we were restricted in many ways (working remotely), the results were no less  than we have previously experienced in pre-Covid on-site workshops, thanks to Mind  Mapping.

Anas Naser

1. Challenge:

I work in a special sales unit inside a big multi-national manufacturing business.  Our Sales unit is specialized in Travel Retail channel (Airports, cruise ships, boarder  stores, etc). The unit is semi-autonomous in terms of structure, strategy, internal  processes and business objectives than the rest of the company.  The unit structure consists of three departments: Sales, Marketing, and Finance.  The other resources (example: HR) are leveraged from the total group.  The challenge that the unit is facing is in internal communication between the three  departments.   The current communication is intense, casual, and repetitive in many cases. This is  causing considerable time to be wasted in answering communications and providing  information.

2. Selection:

An ambassador was selected from each department (Sales, marketing, and finance)  to tackle this issue.  It was agreed to use Visualization as a tool to highlight the current What Is?  Situation.  According to Fatma Ivanova and Sandeep Jones’s book “Designing for Growth”, this tool  transforms information into images and is used to make sense of our observation of  customers and their journey, in our case the customers are actually personnel in  each dept.

3. Application:

The ambassadors agreed to be included in cc in any info or feedback request sent by  someone in their department to another department.  For example, if a marketing personnel sends a request for retail prices overview to a   sales personel, he or she needs to put the marketing ambassador in cc in this email.  Then all ambassadors will collect data over a certain period of time and all  information will be demonstrated in one visual.  A geometric symbol was assigned to each unit (Rectangular: sales, triangle:  Marketing, square: Finance).  Arrows were used to indicate the direction of info request or communications from  one department to another.  The font thickness and colour of the arrows indicated the number of times an info  was requested (for example: blue Thin arrow/1 to 2 requests – red thick arrow/3 or  more).  Since there are many types of requests which could not be demonstrated on the  visualization tool, this type of information was left to the ambassadors to highlight in  a summary below the visual.

4. Insight:

After compiling and translating all data into the visualization tool, the following  observations were clear:

a. Thick and red arrows heading from finance and marketing towards sales

department.

b. Thick and red arrows heading from sales to marketing (thus two-way heavy

communications between both departments).

c. Black thin arrows heading from marketing and sales departments towards

finance.

Additionally, the ambassadors indicated below the Visualization tool that some  requests were actually repetitive.  From this overview it was clear that sales and marketing departments lacked a  coherent-single data base to share with the other units.  Since the red thick arrows pointed out mostly to sales from the other departments,  this indicated that this department was a major source of information from the field  of business while it didn’t have a common and regular source for this information.  Each sales region had a different form of the same data and each kept it in isolation  of the rest of the regions and departments.  Marketing had the same issue to a lesser degree.  The best practice was finance department, which managed to keep a meaningful and  updated source which they used to systematically share information with the other  departments.  By using this design thinking tool, we were able to demonstrate dull data in an  interesting way to all stakeholders in one snap shot.   We were able to indicate the magnitude of the communication problem per  department and where mostly the problem lays.   Also we were able to indicate a department that might have a best-practise  approach that we might be able to build on (finance).

5. Approach:

The Visualization tool was a great indicator but it had limitations too.   As can be seen above, ambassadors from each department had to quote impressions  or feedbacks from remembers of their departments.   Perhaps in next round of finding out What is, we could use Journey mapping to add  another layer of info.  This layer would simultaneously present the highs and lows of each dept in  connection to the others on the same journey or process of work. In this case we  could capture stages of struggle between the departments, where a high point of  one department is a low point for another on the same stage, and try to make all the  journey of all departments a journey of high points.      Thank you.

DESIGN THINKING APPLICATION  This paper aims to show how I applied a Design Thinking tool to a current challenge I am working on in  my professional work.

I.  CHALLENGE

I am currently doing projects for the ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY (WWF) in the Philippines that  advocates a new concept of Corporate Social Responsibility, but brought down to the level of an  individual, and in particular for the youth. We call this Personal Social Responsibility or Personal CSR  (CSR 3.0) which is anchored on 3 values:

a. Citizenship – where the individual is aware of his or her responsibility in the community, and

society

b. Sustainability – Where each person tries to live in a sustainable way that respects the

environment.

c. Responsiveness—Where each person responds to those in need, and uses his or her talents to

contribute to social good.

The reason why our Foundation believes in this concept of Personal CSR for the youth is because of the  following reasons:

1. The youth in our region (Asia) comprise majority of our population. Therefore they are a force

who can contribute a lot of positive impact for socio-economic development (UNFPA, 2014).

2. Young people are always asking themselves – “How do I create meaning in my life?” “How do I

make a difference?” Hence they are constantly looking for avenues to discover what they want  to do in life, while finding that sweet spot where they use their talents and passions to serve a  specific need in the world (Wong, 2012).

3. Because corporations are always looking for innovative ways to contribute to society, it is

recommended that they engage more young people in their CSR efforts because the youth have  these innovative ideas, and have the passion and ability to execute them (Klein, 2012).

Obviously , Personal CSR is a big concept that can be a challenge for young people to understand. Hence  the project I am working on is a Digital Lifestyle Magazine for the Youth in Asia (starting with those in  college). It aims to showcase inspiring stories of young people and organizations who are creating  positive social and environmental impact, and who embody the values above. It hopes to show role  models that young people in Asia can emulate, and later on realize that doing good for society need not  be hard. They can start with themselves and in their own community. We also want it to be digital in  order to reach as many youth as possible, in this age of social media and connectivity.    My team and I are currently in the brainstorming stage for the pilot issue. The challenge however was to  figure out the right “voice”, “personality” and “content” that we must use in our digital magazine, in a  way that will be relevant to our target market. There are many lifestyle content platforms available  already. So we need to develop content that is distinct, innovative and compelling for the youth of

today. We even had several arguments because they were struggling to understand how the CSR  concept (which normally is discussed among the corporate and academic world) can be brought down  to level of young people.     Hence our team focused on answering the following questions?

 Who exactly is the young person that we are targeting?   What kind of content will resonate with this young person so he/she can be inspired to act and

do good for society?

 How do we reach this young person, and all the other youth who fit this profile?

II. SELECTION  We used the “Storytelling” tool as a starting point to answer the questions above. I agree with Kazi Regan of Mars Inc. who said in the video compiled in Claire Parodi’s course, that storytelling is a great  way to connect with the “emotions, characters and values of the people” we want to serve (Ale,  2016). It is also relevant for the Digital Magazine, because what we are essentially trying to do is to  empower young people by telling stories.    I think the reasons Regan articulated regarding storytelling is most appropriate for the challenge we  face in creating the Digital Magazine:

a. Storytelling can allow us to create energy, excitement and passion around a cause and advocacy.

This is exactly what we are trying to do – we are advocating a way of life: to live a  lifestyle of contributing to the common good in our own way.

b. Storytelling allows us to make strategy accessible.

The concept of this Personal CSR philosophy is actually result of more than a decade of  research on the evolution of Corporate Social Responsibility in Asia, particularly in the  Philippines. Our founder believes that in order for the social responsibility initiatives to  be effective, youth engagement is key. Hence this Digital Magazine is indeed an attempt  in the strategy to connect young people to these organizations who need them to  amplify their social impact.

III. APPLICATION  For more than a year, our Foundation has actually collected real interviews with young people to talk  about how they are volunteering to help society (https://www.youtube.com/user/vdrake). I also got to  share stories from youth awardees that our Foundation recognized who are exemplars of this Personal  CSR advocacy: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y1ZQmZmkaDD,  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HePCiQaZo2X, ).

During the brainstorming we had a week ago, I showed these interviews to our Digital Magazine team.  As I mentioned, prior to that, we had several discussions and even arguments about CSR, and what  exactly we are trying to achieve. But when I showed them these videos, which are real stories of young  people, they started understanding the objective.

Some of us in the team are also teachers in a local college, where we teach the subject Social  Responsibility and Good Governance. Our experience was that although there are many inspiring stories

of young people doing amazing work that tries to address social problems in developing country, many  of our students are not aware about these stories. They either lack awareness, or are apathetic to this  notion of contributing to society. Most of the time, they just care about getting a good job to help their  families (most of them come from middle to lower income brackets).

But exposure is the key to get these young people to be engaged.

The showcasing of real stories to the Digital Magazine team was effective in contextualizing the kind of  direction we can take when creating our content. It also helped us put a “face” to the target market.

We also identified cases of social media content from pop culture that trended in our region, which gave  us an insight as to the digital strategy to reach the target youth. This strategy involves creating content  that is as “sticky” as the current pop culture trends, but has the messaging that we want to get across.  We need to use hashtags to maximize the multimedia platforms, particularly mobile social media, so we  can reach more audience.

The main point was that we must focus on these personal stories. We eventually decided to adopt the  title of the video blog, and launch “CSR Stories” as a pilot to test this content to our target market.

IV. INSIGHT  This storytelling tool gave me the insight that stories are indeed more relevant and more resonating for  people. To deconstruct a business and academic concept like CSR, into shareable content in a Digital  Lifestyle magazine, seemed pretty daunting for our team. But when I showed the videos, that was when  they understood more what we are trying to achieve.

This makes me realize that stories must be indeed the center of our content. We can show short video  clips (like an Instagram or Vine video) of young people sharing their “CSR Stories”. We also realized that  there are existing content platforms like “Humans of New York” that have executed this strategy of  storytelling well, in a way that became a viral movement across the world. Therefore, this became one  of our benchmarks for the Digital Magazine.

V. APPROACH  These insights eventually allowed our team to construct this model which represents (for now), the goal  that our Digital Magazine must create:
