Using the social media hashtag #LiveYourCSR, we want to create a movement for young people to go  through these stages of being involved (attending events, engaging with our magazine content)  then  deciding to volunteer with a purpose (volunteering in an organization of their choice)  then  committing to this concept of Personal CSR with Citizenship, Sustainability and Social Responsibility,   then deciding to Make CSR a Lifestyle by signing some sort of Personal Social Responsibility Pledge  which we will put in our site.

It may still be a little vague and general at this point, but at least for our team, it was a good step  towards concretizing the direction we want to invite our readers to, when they engage with our Digital  Magazine.

Moving forward, we are planning to apply the other design thinking tools like Visualization, Mind- mapping and creating a Learning Launch.

Visualization will be helpful to brainstorm the look / branding / color scheme of our Magazine. We can  also collect real photos of young people and create a customer profile which best represents our target  market.

Mind-mapping will also help us plot and organize the theme and the content for our first issue.

A learning launch is also something we want to do to test the reception of the magazine to our desired  audience. We will establish success measures and articulate the assumptions that we want to validate.

It would be interesting to discover how this impacts our target market. Hopefully, by imbibing the design  thinking philosophy we can create a Digital avenue where the youth of Asia can be inspired and  empowered to do something that helps society.

With the problem already in hand, I selected the Mind-Mapping tool at this stage of my design. Design Thinking for Innovation Assignment - Reflection

By Abdiel Rios

Challenge    I work as a General Manager for one of my country’s most prominent law firms.  As an engineer,  project management professional and MBA, I have a strong orientation towards process  improvement, efficiency and innovation through the use of digital technologies.  Most of the  partners, lawyers and paralegals have common backgrounds on legal studies that do not include  business related courses, therefore, it becomes difficult for them to understand how business  processes work and the impact that their individual decisions have on the end customer’s  experience with our services, as well as, the company’s functionality as a whole.  One of my main  objectives as a business leader is to modernize the law firm and minimize the use of manual and  paper-based processes to which the personnel is very accustomed and attached to.  One of my  greatest challenges is to be able to transmit to them not only the benefits of creating efficient  digital processes, but also to help them visualize how things would work once they are  implemented so that they assist me in the process instead of resisting it.  On occasions, some key  personnel resists new ideas simply because they are afraid of change or because they cannot  visualize the complete current process or the new idea.    Selection    To help solve this challenge, I chose the Visualization tool.  Visualization is a tool that can help  different individuals from various backgrounds get involved in the innovation process, as well as  assisting them to reach a common ground and understanding on the topic at hand such that a  more productive discussion can take place.  Specially in a situation like the one I described  previously, for innovation to take place and be accepted by the stakeholders, we all have to be on  the same page with regards to what is the problem we are trying to solve, what does the proposed  solution look like, how it can be implemented and what each stakeholder’s contribution or role  will be once it is up and running.  Visualization can also help the participants become more  engaged in generating ideas or recommendations, as well as provide their buy-in to the solution.    Application    The way that I apply the tool, is by getting a group of around 6 of the key stakeholders in the same  room at the same time, in front of a whiteboard.  I usually like to start by getting everybody on the  same page as to what the current situation or process looks like.  I ask the group to take about 10  minutes so that each of them individually draws on a piece of paper what they think the current  process is like from their perspectives.  Then, each of them takes 5 minutes explaining their  drawing to the rest of the team and tapes the drawing to the wall next to the whiteboard.  After all  of them have completed their explanation, then I moderate a discussion and integrate the  drawings of the current process on the whiteboard, while making sure there is consensus and  agreement from all the members of the team.  The process is drawn using elements such as  arrows, squares, circles, writing, drawings or even taping elements to the whiteboard, depending  on what best describes what needs to be communicated.    Once the current process is fully recorded and consented, we proceed to discuss and brainstorm  about “how may we…” achieve a series of objectives.  For example, how might we make this easier

for the end customer, how might we make this paperless, how might we shorten the amount of  time it takes to complete this, how might we eliminate waste, how might we enrich the  experience, how might we achieve more than what we achieved with the standalone process, etc.      As some of the key stories become apparent, then we proceed to draw a how we would like the  new process to be.  Once again, we allow for some individual drawing and visualization, followed  by explanation by each member of the team, and then compiling the new process while reaching  consensus.  Finally, once we know where we stand right now (A) and where we want to go (B), we  develop an implementation plan to get from A to B.    Insight    It is evident that visualization as a tool is a key element in not only reaching consensus, but also  getting all the key stakeholders involved in innovating a solution.  By allowing each person to first  draw their point of view of the process individually (current and new), it provides an opportunity  for the team as a whole to understand that each one of the stakeholders has a different point of  view and sees certain aspects of the process that may be completely invisible to others.  By  unifying the drawing and creating consensus of the process (current and new), we make sure that  everybody understands verbally and graphically what is being discussed, and therefore minimize  the risk of people thinking they are talking about the same thing, while imagining or visualizing  completely different things inside their minds.  By literally “putting it out there” on the wall, it  allows the team to identify things that become apparent when drawn, but that were not apparent  when written or imagined.  And finally, by drawing out the current and proposed solutions,  visualization provided increased engagement from the team and better idea generation.    Approach    With regards to visualization, one thing that could be done differently is to allow individuals to  work on their respective drawings prior to the meeting, such that we may do a more efficient use  of time.  Another key point that I noticed during the meetings, is that it may be helpful to have two  whiteboards or large format post it notes taped to the wall.  This way, it is not necessary to erase  what was drawn about the current process before starting to draw the new one.  It is of great  value for the team to be able to visualize both the current and new solutions simultaneously,  specially when we are developing the implementation plan to get from A to B.

Use of Design Thinking Tools for Behavioural Change towards

Sanitation

Reflection: Storytelling

Md Rashid

Challenge

As part of my role as a Consultant to the Govt. on the ‘Sanitation for all’ project, we faced a  challenge where we found that the mere availability of the physical infrastructure, i.e. toilets,  was not leading to higher usage of toilets for safer sanitation, by our target audience in rural  areas. This was more of a behavioural issue than anything else. It was hence essential to  understand the target audience’s behaviour, not restricted to the sanitation habits, but also about  the overall way of life. Earlier solutions were neither human-centered (Week 1-Video 1 and  Week 1-Video 5), nor based on customer empathy (Week 2-Video 3). The core challenge was  to bring about a behavioural change in the target audience w.r.t. sanitation habits, which would  lead to higher usage of toilets and adoption of safer sanitation practice.

Selection

The task at hand required engaging with people and making them interested to collaborate and  co-create a solution which is sustainable (Week 4-Video 5). Human beings love stories, and  more so when stories are relatable to them, or about them. While we chose more than one tool  since the task was multi-fold – to understand the behaviour (Journey Mapping, Week 1-Video  3), and then be able to involve and co-create a sustainable solution (Mind-Mapping, Week 3- Video 2; it was Storytelling as a tool (Week 2-Video 4), that i am explaining for this  assignment. Storytelling as Design Thinking tool was picked up to build a connection with our  audience. Storytelling not only helps the audience build interest in, relate with and visualise  the context, but also creates a space for feedback and comments, which was valuable in our  case since sanitation is not a subject that people wanted to openly talk about anyway. It was  also the easiest medium to convey a message for the kind of target group that we wanted to  address.

Application

We wanted to make our storytelling exercise a coherent, relatable and interesting one, which  will not only encourage the target group to get involved in it, but also have an emotional  connection, which is critical. The stories were built around the specific community and village  or hamlet, and characters were named same as some of the people there. The ill-effects of poor  sanitation practice were conveyed in form of a story which had characters in it, who had a  similar lifestyle as that of the target audience who was listening to story. However, endings of  the stories were not disclosed. This was to build suspense (Week 2-Video 4), and more  importantly to keep space open for discussion and feedback. Essentially, this was a space that  was left for others to contribute (Week 4-Video 7).

We also left the story at a point that various solutions to tackle the challenge of behavioural  change can come from audience themselves, hence increasing the participation from the group.  Since the solutions came from the target group themselves, there was a sense of ownership and  co-creation in the target group that led to higher compliance and engagement with the solutions  implemented on ground. The tool was then implemented at multiple places with a bit of  tweaking depending upon various extraneous factors, but led to a positive result in terms of  engagement, collaboration, co-creation and sustenance of solutions.

Insight

Storytelling tool generated a host of insights for us. Some which confirmed our assumptions  and others which disconfirmed our assumptions. While we assumed that using Storytelling as  a tool will help us convey message in a more succinct and interesting manner, we were  pleasantly surprised to see the engagement that it created.  In the first few exercises the endings  were disclosed and audience was then encouraged to participate in discussion. But we found  out that an undisclosed ending creates more interest, engagement and also encourages people  to come up with their own endings. This helped us mapping behavioural aspects of the specific  individual or hamlet where the exercise was being done. This was an additional bit of  information over and above ethnographic research that helped us in tweaking our tools for  better performance. Finally, between the groups where the solutions are co-created with the  help of storytelling, versus places where solutions are offered and explained to groups, the  former had a stronger sustenance and compliance for solutions.

Approach

There are various design thinking tools and each one can be used for a different purpose, or  can complement each other. In the case discussed, Storytelling came out as an efficient tool,  however, there can be other tools too that may be adopted for the same objective. Since in the  given case, it was paramount to understand the stakeholder mind-set to before co-creation can  happen, especially since the challenge was on bringing about behavioural change, Mind  Mapping can be a potent tool. Mind Mapping would have allowed us to engage with all  stakeholders and bring out personas of each stakeholder. Depending upon the personas,  solutions specific to a persona could have been looked at (Week 3-Video2). Closed group or  personal interviews with relevant stakeholder where open ended questions are asked which not  only reflect their persona, but also express their own views about the challenge, can be  conducted. Finally, based upon the themes and patterns that lead to mapping stakeholders to  specific persona, solutions could be looked by using further tools for idea generation and  piloting like learning launch.

Incorporating Mind Mapping – As a Last Resort

Final Assignment for Becky Shepherd

Challenge    One of my clients was a major Federal agency whose bureaucratic foundational  heartbeat, so to speak, is what they call the Task Management teams.  The term ‘task’  is used in this system as a blanket term for any and all documentation that goes up the  chain of command or external to the organization.  These documents range from brief  internal communications to official memorandum, program handbooks, and even  Congressional correspondence.  The current Task Management teams were  underutilized.  Given that they have the best seats in the house – visibility on all  proposed documents, signed documents, and upcoming issues – it was to the client’s  best interest to leverage their insights.  These Task Management teams saw  themselves as paper-pushers, and it was our job to help them reevaluate their  responsibilities, purpose, and their overarching mission to help them go from reactive  analysts to proactive strategists.    Selection    We began with our research phase, digging up old Task Management policies,  guidance documents, and even interviewing current and past Task Management  personnel.  Then we held numerous facilitated discussions where we put all current  Task Management personnel (stakeholders) in one conference room to learn about their  basic job tasks and prioritization.  After many meetings with no resolution or consensus  amongst the different teams, we decided that in order to branch out of the current “What  Is” or as we often heard in these sessions as “the way we’ve always done it” – to a new  realm of “What If” we would need to conduct a mind mapping exercise.    Application    In our mind mapping exercise, we included all Task Management team members from  the organization spanning three hierarchical tiers.  The stakeholders’ experience ranged  from approximately five years in their current task management role to merely three  months.  Our thought process was to incorporate the current personnel as much as  possible, in hopes that if they had a hand in the process, they would buy-in to our efforts  and feel compelled to change their behavior.    We pulled the research from our initial steps and asked all members to read the longer  documents prior to arrival.  We clarified that the intent of this session was to determine  all job competencies and responsibilities to then reach an ultimate job description or  ‘motto’ that everyone would agree on.  When participants arrived, we provided sticky  notes and markers to each stakeholder to jot down all ideas on the sticky notes, one  idea per note.  Then, the facilitator clustered the sticky notes on the white board based  on similarity.  The facilitator then posed the question to the group to label and

characterize each cluster.  We left the session with a handful of competencies that the  group agreed upon and we felt confident about the progression of our project.    Insight    Our mind mapping exercise was a very telling activity.  Notably, we learned that even  amongst teams of the same level in the organization, there were great differences in  expectations, responsibilities, and even employee morale.  We learned that there were  already some teams who held a mindset of being strategic influencers, and we then  leveraged their support throughout the project.  The mind mapping exercise provided us  with common job competencies and an overarching job description.  As we entered the  “What If” phase we were armed and ready to begin brainstorming the new job  responsibilities.    Approach    Admittedly, this project was conducted prior to learning this Design Thinking  methodology and exercises.  In hindsight, this mind mapping exercise would have been  stronger if a wider net of stakeholders was cast.  The agency has a strong culture of  respect for authority.  If we had incorporated some of the leadership of the organization  in this exercise alongside the Task Management team members, there likely would  have been greater buy-in and a wider range of “What If’ statements in the brainstorming  phase.    We viewed mind mapping as a last resort when it should have been included in our  project plan all along.  Now that I am well-versed in the Design Thinking practices, I look  forward to applying this innovative approach when tackling new challenges in ‘the  unknown.’

Michael Kl Reflection: Visualization

Challenge

Competitive organizations continuously face evolving market conditions, customer preferences,  and changing laws and regulations within their respective industry. Therefore, it is essential to  lean on, as well as advocate for, continuous improvement and innovative practices. The  challenge that I have recently faced is at an assembly manufacturing organization that is  comprised of a large warehousing space and two large production rooms. Within these  production rooms, various components enter and are either prepped for production (e.g., cutting  tubing, counting gauze, stacking towels, etc.) or go straight into the assembly process, but both  occur at the production line in its current state. Where the challenge begins within this process is  figuring how to effectively separate prepped components from production to maintain teammate  headcount, but increase productivity. Being tasked with this project along with a team of various  professional backgrounds, miscommunication, misalignment, and misinterpretation occurred.

Selection

When implementing improvement initiatives, various change models are utilized to ensure that  the improvement project is on time, covering all aspects of the respective process, and  sustainable for the long-term. Additionally, consistent, professional, and creative forms of  communication are taken advantage of to ensure that all active teammates fully understand the  progress, barriers, and actions of the project. In this particular instance, the team and I resorted to  utilizing the visualization design tool to ensure that each teammate, as well as stakeholders, had a  solid understanding on the new process flow, material flow, and work cell layout of the  preparation area. When using the visualization tool, teams communicate with imagery to make  ideas more visible. In other words, visualization is about visual thinking and assists a team with  communicating more effectively. Further, the visualization tool was ultimately vital in  successfully communicating the future state of the preparation process to stakeholders, both  vertically and horizontally.

Application

At first, the team communicated ideas, suggestions, and concerns verbally to one another in an  attempt to make progress on the improvement initiative. After some time, and getting more in- depth into the project, teammates experienced confusion about the future state process flow,  material flow, and physical layout of the preparation area. At this point as the project lead, I  decided to create visual representations of the process flow, material flow, and layout of the  work cells to assist the team in identifying areas of interest, misunderstanding, and barriers to a  successful implementation. Having each functional area now represented by a layout map, the  team was able to effectively identify what their concerns were, as well as ideas to make the  project more of a success. Applying the visualization tool assisted the team in gaining a clear  understanding of one another’s concerns, ideas, and suggestions.

Insight

When applying the visualization tool, I found that teammates were more engaged when  comparing it to situations when I was essentially attempting to verbally communicate the future

state of the improvement initiative. Additionally, having the visual component of the initiative  allowed the team to generate questions and develop answers in real time, all while referencing  the visualization tool, or the various process flows and physical layout of the preparation process.  However, when looking back at the initiative, a design tool that I would have used in parallel  with the visualization tool is that of mind mapping, which is utilized to identify how ideas from  the team correlate with the main purpose of the project, as well as the ideas of their respective  teammates. In all, the visualization tool enhanced the thought process and effectiveness of the  team in ensuring that all barriers, ideas, and possibilities were appropriately addressed to ensure  a successful improvement initiative.

Approach

As previously mentioned, applying the visualization tool during this improvement initiative was  an effective decision that paid of tremendously in the form of increased participation and clearer  communication. However, incorporating the mind mapping tool would have offered me the  ability to capture the thought process of the team during these sessions and identify how each  teammates ideas and concerns correlated with the purpose of the improvement initiative.  Although, I have found that the visualization tool made a positive impact of the outcome of the  project, has been added to the organization’s arsenal of project tools, and has paved a lasting path  for other design tools to make their respective mark on future improvement projects to come.

Hussain Mohammed (ITALY)

January 5rd 2019

Design Thinking for Process review

Challenge

I work in an aerospace company, in particular inside customer support and training department and my  responsibility is the exploration and development of new service solutions to generate new business as full  service provider. In the last two years the company has focused its attention on the digital services for  which me and my colleagues has started a dedicated project. After reinforcing the digital foundations and  current available digital tools (to deliver new digital services), we have focused on the change management  and training stream in order to create the correct mindset in the company and proceed with an extensive  review of the internal processes. The population of the training has involved six hundred colleagues, on top  of which we have selected twenty-five change agents, so called evangelists, to create a community that,  leveraging on the sponsorship of senior executives, can disseminate a digital transformation. In 2014, we  did six sessions for our evangelists starting from a preliminary understanding of the major digital streams  that our top management is investing on (digital roadmap), and then the creation of subgroups, whose  focus is the change of a subprocess, related to the digital roadmap, that can benefit from digital solutions.  We tried to expand what our evangelists feel important, as well as top management consider to be  inefficient or problematic and be improved adopting digital solutions. The project included the possibility to  interview customers of different product segments and different geographies and have dedicated  workshop with other companies from similar businesses and close markets. The tool we applied is learning  launch in workshop five in December 2020.

Selection

In the first workshop we provided the overall digital roadmap and framework on which company wants to  commit on; a brief illustration of the major achievements of the last year have been provided. Between the  two workshops, evangelists had the possibility to discuss through a sharing web platform the pain points,  opportunities, potential constraints and enablers (available or not) to identify the sub-processes to attack.  They reviewed outcomes with their own managers in order to start disseminating a new digital mindset and  concepts (and to understand if there were blocking points inside the organization). We followed a kind of  approach similar to the four questions to select the projects: what-is, what-if, what-wows, what-works.  Every single step was done to reach the learning launch: evangelists had the possibility to test the ideas  with stakeholders: few customers and senior managers.

Application

During the second workshop we focused on brain storming in sub groups. Questionnaire and post-it had  been the main tools required for the session. We were able to structure the tasks, grouping the projects  into five of them, and sub-processes in an effort to become feasible for part-time resources, which on top  of their company role spent effort for their evangelist journey. This tested both the current situation in  terms of preparation of the evangelists, and their managers to support such change mindset required,  which we consider to be the main cause of our workflow inefficiencies, rather than lack of digital  technologies (already available inside the company). The first two sessions were held in July and  September, while the total journey is expected to last 6 months timeframe. After the first two workshops,  we had preliminary subgroups defined, project cards drafted, including benefits, KPIs to monitor the  success rate of the single project and a draft schedule.

The third workshop has been dedicated to understand much more from other markets (data quantity and  quality), and similar businesses, in order to motivate the evangelists and to challenge them in following  different approaches taken by other companies which could inspire their own project. The sessions were  the opportunity to illustrate progress and achievements of the projects, issues and priorities for which an  internal escalation was required (top management delegated digital champions to lead the digital  roadmap). Third workshop was dedicated to review the approach, discuss with other colleagues the pain  points and submit questionnaires, complemented by an anonymous survey to be conducted inside their  own department. The surveys included questions about as-is process, new proposed process, prioritization  of tasks, and feelings about the change mindset, to be conducted within a two-week timeframe. Between  the workshops the evangelists had to define private sessions in group, work on the projects, supported by  the external consultancy for the mapping of the as-is and to-be process.

Workshop four has been dedicated to learning launch. Evangelists had the possibility to interview external  customers (invited in video call) for those projects involving digital services for external customers, while  for internal processes internal stakeholders (executives and top managers) has been invited to test the as-is  process and to-be process. Cheap mock-ups were more than welcome in order to test if the project  benefits were the ones expected, if the major burning need of the customers were satisfied. The purpose  was not to prove to the community who were the best evangelists, but to get the truth about idea and  assumptions, at the cost of cancelling the project if not feasible or in scope. Therefore, confirmation bias, as  well as group-think and self-serving bias, were limited leaving short time to review the projects if required.

Workshop five and six will be dedicated in 2017 to refine the project and to have a mock-up ready, with the  support of the consultancy. In workshop six the evangelists will illustrate their own project to top  management (managing director included) to get the right and final sponsorship to enter into the execution  and deployment phase. After the final presentation our HR department will have a comprehensive view of  the single evangelists in order to improve their own career development plan and reorganize some  departments depending on the results of the projects, leveraging on the skills of the evangelists.

Insight & conclusion

Our hope was that the evangelists identified pain points (identify the need with a lot of questions),  brainstorm on potential ideas and solutions (search for truth and not for winning), discover obstacles and  blocking points inside the organization and test these assumptions (put not in scope ideas on the shelf).  Our major concern was related to the capability of the management to sustain these projects and embody  the real digital transformation: while evangelists are currently open to the process review, the key  stakeholders in the larger departments could raise some concerns or further constraints. Digital roadmap  therefore will have to take into account theses insights and incorporate it into future initiatives.

Evangelists had not attended any design thinking activities/tools relevant to the digital transformation yet,  so preliminary results are not astonishing. However we are confident that after the first sessions, a new  learning launch tool before end of the training journey will be a useful and effective this time (considering  also a new perception for all the managers about the digital transformation). Evangelists will need to  review the insight gained from the first session and be responsible to collaborate with management in  order to remove obstacles and deploy solutions/new processes, ready for full rollout.

Best Regards,

Hussain Mohammed

Name:

Carolina Finetti

Date:

February 15th, 2021

Challenge

My name is Carolina Gomez, I am currently studying Engineering in Development and

Innovation, where the application of design thinking is crucial for my career to know

how to create a new product idea or even optimizing one that already exists. The

reason why I started this course is because one of our final projects on the subject of

“Innovation and experimentation of creative processes” is to design furniture made

out of cardboard. This sustainable furniture must help the elderly to carry out

different activities, such as putting on shoes, cutting their toenails, moving around,

doing flexibility exercises, and other simple activities that may be difficult for them

due to their age. Thanks to the different steps of the design thinking process, I will be

able to successfully create these innovative cardboard furniture and empathize with

the user in the best possible way.

Selection

I believe that using the visualization tool allowed me to get to the main purpose of

the project, to empathize with the user through innovation. As Angela Weyes said in

her video explaining the visualization tool, this leads us to extrapolation, which is

inductive reasoning and thinking about possibilities that we have not yet seen. Finally

the way we did it was by doing sketches of our ideas, in order for the whole team to

understand what we can not explain in simple words. Fortunately, each member of

the team were from different careers, so having different points of view on how to

make this sustainable furniture allowed us to consider all possibilities and led us to

having one big idea. Later on, each member of the team did their own sketch on the

cardboard furniture, and by the end we created one single final sketch that

complemented each of the other sketches.

Application

Since the objective of the project was the design of the product itself, the team and I

decided that brainstorming would be the best way to get there. This however, was no

easy task, since everyone had different ideas on how the product should be, but at

the same time, it allowed us to share ideas and merge them into one single idea.

Therefore, I think that visualization would have been the most helpful innovation tool

as we wanted to create an idea with a team from a diverse background that offered

expertise and insight in various different subjects.

Furthermore, using the visualization tool allowed us to have a very clear idea on how

the furniture would be and how it can be innovative. As a team, we decided that

making a table that could elevate only by pulling a cardboard bar up and down would

be sufficient enough to cover the necessities of the elderly mentioned above. In this

way, they could use the mini table for any purpose they wanted. Also, the cardboard

table could lift up over 35 kg, which we considered is enough since the whole thing

was made out of cardboard.

Insight

After finishing the course, I learned that in order to generate an innovative product, it

is not enough to have a new idea, you got to know how to implement it in your

day-to-day life. Just like the visualization tool, it takes several steps to even generate

a simple drawing. What I noticed about the team is how we focused on making the

cardboard furniture simpler rather than innovative. To achieve this, we must have a

broad repertoire and think outside the box. Continuously, know how to change the

mindset of people so that they can see what we want to convey, which is how a

simple piece of cardboard can help the elderly in a way that they did not know it

could be done.

Approach

Another tool that I consider important throughout the course was the learning launch

tool. Personally, I think it goes hand in hand with the visualization tool because you

can not use one without using the other. For example, when experimenting with your

final prototype, you should have first generated it by making sketches of it. On the

other hand, when generating these sketches, you should think about whether it really

is a market need, rather than just a design that looks aesthetically good. That is why

it is important to know how to communicate with people and be able to be

empathetic with users in order to generate data that will help the user to use your

product. You must capture your design and make it a reality, because if people start

to believe in your product, you are already creating innovation.

Simona Blasi, Peer-graded assignment, Design Thinking for Innovation    Challenge:    The health care experience is typically straight forward; we expect it to have an outcome that  provides us with a course of action (i.e., an intelligent, honest provider who tells us what’s wrong  and sets us on a course of action). But, what about all the other pieces of the journey along the  way?    We define our patient journey as of discovering, engaging, caring, getting better, managing  costs and living life. Every patient has a story; a place they’re trying to go. Along this journey, it’s  important for us to remember that and offer ourselves to help them get there.     With that, each piece of the journey has potential to add small, but significant, experiences that  build personal, meaningful elements.    We feel virtual reality could be one of those experiences during the caring part of the journey.  But, I didn’t want to offer it and not know what patients thought (e.g., content, feelings, physical  reaction). We don’t really know how patients will react to it so we need to learn more.     Selection:    A learning launch is just what’s needed to help guide this decision and learn more about how  patients feel about a virtual reality experience added to care. As I learned in this course, the  times of the standard business plan are gone. It’s time to experiment and not just base our  actions on guessing and projection.    As defined, a learning launch i​s a carefully designed experiment or prototype designed to test  the key underlying value-generating assumptions of a potential new-growth initiative. A  “business-world application of the scientific method.”    As Sebastian Garcia said in the lecture, “​at learning launch you are launching out there into the unknown.”  And, that’s exactly what we need to do to learn more about patients’ feelings on virtual reality.    “New-growth” for this launch is adding a meaningful experience to patient care through virtual  reality. It’s not based on ROI, it’s based on adding value patient experience. We need to learn  how value is defined in this case.    For this we will go through the key stages:

1. Immerse yourself in the data that already exists.

2. Generate a new business idea - an educated guess about the opportunity.

3. Articulate the assumptions on which the new business idea’s success is based.

4. Design and conduct a learning launch to test assumptions.

5. Revise or kill the idea based on your findings.

6. Scale the business idea when appropriate.

I have found that in health care, learning launches can be a bit tricky as it can be hard to stay  quick and nimble along that way. That is the biggest challenge as there are additional variables  at play (consent forms, ensuring confidentiality and total privacy, scheduling and help from staff,  cleaning of the equipment - building a protocol).    Application​:    I researched the existing virtual reality research and testing that has been done in other health  care settings. There is a decent amount of information, but focused on inpatient settings.  Overall, the experience is positive in many different applications (pain, experience, distraction).    Based on that, we wanted to focus on the outpatient setting and make it transferrable across our  regions.     Our hypothesis is that virtual reality will help patients’ immerse themselves in content and be a  positive distraction away from treatment in an outpatient setting. Our goal: to talk to 60 patients  and 25 care providers across the three regions.    What don’t we know is the value of virtual reality as an experience. Does it have a long term  effect on patient experience or just a short-lived feeling? How nimble can we be in making  changes after we implement the program? If we create a virtual reality program for outpatient  treatments and it means short-lived freedom for one patient, isn’t it worth the effort?     We created a simple testing protocol and discussion guide to test our hypothesis. First, we ask  patients to tell us a little about themselves and their experience at the clinic. Second, we find out  what they know about virtual reality. Then, we give them a choice between two different pieces  of content and they experience it. Finally, we ask about their emotional and physical feelings  after watching, what they liked, didn’t like and if they’d want virtual reality as an option when  they come in for treatment.    Each interview takes 15-45 minutes depending on the patient. We estimate it will take about  three weeks to interview patients. This is a fast moving test in our world. As of this assignment, I  have interviewed 26 patients and 25 care providers. We have also talked to three caregivers  who were also interested in trying it out.     Insight​:    At this time, we have run into overwhelming positive results. Nearly all patients feel a sense of  transportation and joy with the content. They have been immersed enough that it has served as

a distraction from treatment and many have used the words “relaxing,” “transported,” “calming,”  and “awesome” to describe their experience. All but one person would want to use it during  future treatments. Most rated the experience as a 4 out of 5 with many 5 ratings.    If we were to stop here (and, it would be plenty of interviews to do so) we’d be able to make a  strong case to get a program in place to enhance experience at the care stop in our overall  patient journey.    We’ll continue our interviews so we can have a good sample across our regions, but the  learning launch has been very eye-opening to helping understand more about the  implementation of virtual reality and helps go beyond typical “guessing” approach of business  plan and moves us to learning more about real value and definitely builds a stronger case for  why this could be a valuable addition to care.    Approach​:    Quite honestly, as I’ve stated above, I will continue to apply the learning launch technique to this  specific challenge. It allows me to be nimble and test new hypotheses quickly and cheaply. As  virtual reality technology and content changes, we’ll need to be agile and keep doing small tests  over time to enhance the experience, but also make sure it is still making a difference along the  patient journey.     Before this class, I was going to write a lengthy business plan built from secondary research  and a lot of guessing. Now, I have an agile testing process that allows to learn from real patient  experiences and the ability to learn and grow after implementation.

USING MIND MAPPING TO UNCOVER CLIENT INSIGHTS

CHALLENGE The big challenge in my project is extracting the most signiﬁcant insights from the important quantity of information gathered from  quantitative research and qualitative consumer interviews. These insights will be used both to structure our offers to clients and prioritize mass  communication messaging in a new market.

SELECTION I chose to use mind mapping to help us develop a common understanding of the challenge and agree on the most signiﬁcant insights.

APPLICATION We invited 20 stakeholders in the project to a full-day session. In the ﬁrst part of the session, participants were invited to visit our  « gallery ». All the information, quotes, statistics, pictures from consumer homes, were put up on the walls. The room was covered in information  (picture 1).

Participants captured on post-it notes the information that felt most signiﬁcant to them as they wandered throughout the room.

We then divided participants in teams of 4 and asked them to share the information they had found signiﬁcant to ﬁnd overarching themes (picture  2). We asked them to look for patterns in the information they had collected but also to be mindful of anything that stood out as being particularly  different. Their overarching themes were noted and developed on large ﬂip charts (picture 3).

In the second part of the session, each team presented its themes to all the participants for discussion and comparison. We were then able to ﬁnd a  common understanding of the « So whats? » and start working together on the design conditions as the project moves forward.

Regina Parker — November 2016

INSIGHT Most participants in the Mind Mapping exercise never truly experience our destination as our clients do. Their visits are carefully orchestrated and mapped-out.  Mind Mapping was truly enlightening for them as an occasion to understand the client experience without the ﬁlter of a report or analysis.  Mind Mapping opened many  eyes.

Using direct quotes gave us access to the words our consumers use to express their feelings which in turn informed us on how to address speciﬁc barriers and activate  certain triggers. It removed many ﬁlters.

Regrouping the information also helped better command of it. Participants deﬁned together the full meaning of the different themes, giving each one the depth and  richness required. This comprehension helped move the project forward in a direction everyone felt comfortable with.

Finally going beyond the simple deﬁnition of each theme and asking « so what? » contributed to our understanding of each theme in the speciﬁc context of our organization  and project. This last question truly brought the project to life in a very relevant and applicable way.

APPROACH Mind Mapping is a great tool for extracting insights from large quantities of information. It is also very useful to establish common understanding of a  challenge to allow a project to move forward as it takes away from opinion and into our consumers’ minds and hearts. I would use the same tool again.

What went well Participants were very good at spotting the information they felt was important and discussions were backed with solid quotes from real-life consumer  interviews or quantitative data that made discussions very authentic and inspiring. Using the quotes helped the group be more empathic and keep clients at the center of  our discussions.

What I would do differently I would plan for more time for the « wandering & information gathering » part of the session. Half a day was perhaps too short. Participants  need time for the information to sink in and overarching themes to emerge. In the time we allotted, participants could not process all the information leading them to feel  they might be missing one key information.

Reading all the information is a very tiring exercise. I would made sure the information is on different colored paper to help with short attention.

Regina Parker — November 2016

Fazal Ahmed for Darden-U “Design Thinking for Innovation” - Learning Launch

I advise research students in my work as a senior high school science teacher. Empathizing with  the COVID-19 situation, a group recently proposed a smartphone-based app to augment the  traditional contact tracing methods used in the Philippines. The research panel is a learning  launch where the students draw insights from the assembled academicians, whose opinion is  collegial yet not fully aligned with the field situation.

One issue that arised from the discussion, is that a large portion of the Philippine population is  unsupportive to, dismissive of the purpose, or misrepresenting information to commissioned  contact tracers. Among these outliers are: (a) 72% prepaid segment of the total mobile phone  users whose identity is not registered with the authorities; (b) indigent sectors of the  community whose mobile communication is based on hand-me-down devices; (c) rural areas  yet to be covered by mobile Internet or if any, is not stable enough to support app bandwidth  requirements; and (d) people who strongly guard their privacy or are untrusting of their data- handling authorities.

To better address the needs of these sectors, the students were instructed to host a focus  group, another learning launch session, where attendees representative of these marginalized  group will evaluate (a) visual process diagrams of the communication protocols; (b) paper- prototypes of the app user interfaces and server software; and (c) role-play of the human  actors in the system.

The focus group, having earlier advised of the purpose of the meeting, was informed of the  minimum requirements said app based on the updated US-CDC guidelines for the  implementation and use of digital tools to augment traditional contact tracing  (https://cdc.gov/coronavirus). A community contact tracer – a panel member – noted that their  paper-based contact tracing method is aligned with that guidelines and that their app-based  system recommends a decision of whether the contact need to isolate or quarantine. According  to her, the official contact-tracing app issued by the Department of Health, StaySafe.ph, (a) is  not yet widely used by the masses being voluntary/opt-in; (b) need data access for upload of  data to the servers; and (c) is prone to misrepresentation of user-entered travel history and  symptoms. At best, the app is usable in generating QR codes for entering establishments.

That significant prepaid segment of the populace is the biggest player because, even though  they might have decent access to mobile Internet, we cannot fully trust their information  because according to a prepaid user attending the session, he preferred it because of the  numbers nature being disposable and anonymous. The privacy pundit avers. The skeptic  millennial in the group cited that the Philippines being dubbed the social media capital of the

world does not jive with this data that privacy is a concern among Filipinos. Based on my  expertise, I remarked, that the Filipino needs educating on this matter.

The student researchers then presented their plan of having a web-based system for primary  use in browsers, which can then be deployed by Apache Cordova (or similar HTML5 wrapper) as  smartphone app. Access requires two-factor authentication and a JSON-based serialization  handles client-server communication. Client retains history and symptom daily data in SQLite  while the server retains 14-day historical contact data for each user. Data is secured through  AES256 public key security.

At this point, privacy concerns prevailed because the users are afraid of the stigma and  restrictions when even if the contact is yet a suspected case. The contact tracer attendee noted  that, indeed, some contacts are hesitant to disclose their travel history, symptoms, and  contacts. At one time, she mentioned that she received threats not to track in a certain  establishment because of it effect to their business. Having reached an impasse, the student- researchers hazarded: “WHAT IF there is a system that assures near complete anonymity to  participants?” The privacy proponent liked this so much but the contact tracer emphasized that  it is still our social obligation to assist in the containment of the pandemic.

Participants concede that they are very much willing to inform their contacts if they themselves  are infected BUT, and this they say is non-negotiable, they identity – or even a hint of who they  are – should not be disclosed in any way. I opined that a server will be redundant in this setup,  and then the technical consultant, who happens to be the very same skeptic, had an idea that  this might work if the server is just an ad-hoc message forwarder, and the apps are Java- based clients.

This became a WOW moment because for the first time the group came to an agreement. The  students’ study objectives will be revised such that, the research: (a) will be a crowd-sourced  system of people informing the community that they are infected; (b) has a client will send to  the server list of mobile numbers of contacts in the last 14 days, via SMS; (c) has an ad-hoc  server that will send messages to a list of mobile numbers passed to it by the Java-clients via  SMS; and (d) that retains no user-data in the server after all messages has been forwarded.

In the end, participants learned that data privacy is a huge consideration in this data-sharing  systems, and that most are willing to eke a portion of their personal space, physical or digital,  if assured security from stigma or social isolation and if the purpose is for the common good.  As this is an on-going project, there are resultant issues such as (a) misuse of the system (data  flooding, misrepresentation), (b) usability and efficiency of the transmissions, and (c) its  interoperability with official contact tracing protocols that, given time and expertise, will be  improved by iterative prototyping and learning launches.

EMPOWERING ICT CONSUMERS DURING THE COVID-19

PANDEMIC:

REFLECTION LEARNING LAUNCH

Challenge    The consumers of communication services have rights and responsibilities when purchasing  and using regulated communication products and services in a market. The manager in charge  of consumer protection at the ICT regulator with a team of six staff are responsible for  safeguarding consumer rights and developing mechanisms to protect consumers in this sector.     The regulator has in place an effective consumer education and outreach program that seeks to  empower consumers with information that will enable them make informed purchase decisions  in the market. In addition, consumer protection mechanisms and regulatory interventions are  developed based on data and information from annual consumer behavior and trends surveys,  customer satisfaction surveys and quarterly customer complaints reports.    Following the Covid-19 pandemic and a sharp reduction in operation costs at the regulatory  office, the division has no funds to continue executing it’s mandate and furthermore, the  Government measures to mitigate the pandemic has also affected ability of the division to  execute consumer education and outreach activities. In addition, during this period, there has  been an exponential increase in the number of consumers leveraging technology as they work  from home or access e-learning for their children.     During this period it is noted that there has been an increase in consumer complaints that have  been escalated to the regulatory office seeing that the licensed communication service  providers have not been able address consumers concerns.    It is therefore crucial that the regulatory office develop a new initiative that will provide  consumers with information that they require to exercise their rights in the market.     Selection    Following a brainstorming session with the team, and in view of the need to develop a platform  that will enable consumers engagement at a low/minimal costs and will allow for great  improvements going forward, the manager leveraged the learning launch tool to progress the

implementation of a new idea. The learning launch tool being an experiment based tool will  enable the manger establish the truth about the assumption made on increased consumer  complaints viz consumer information (The University of Virginia, 2020a). The manager, while  using this tool, will further execute quick engagement with consumers and facilitate testing  the  assumption that increase consumer complaints is as a result of lack of consumer information  (The University of Virginia, 2020).    The learning launch tool was selected seeing that it shall involve quick engagement with  consumers and testing of assumptions (The University of Virginia, 2020a).     The teams idea to host a live interactive podcast session with consumers will enable the  regulator interact with consumers and disseminate consumer information. This tool has never  been used before by the regulator and neither has the regulator held podcasts to engage  consumers.     Application    The consumer protection team hypothesized that increased escalation of consumer complaints   to the regulator was occasioned by the lack of consumer information who are consequently not  able to exercise their rights.    The consumer protection team  prioritized the consumer concerns that were to be addressed  and further develop a methodology and mechanisms to engage consumers and establish the  extent to which free podcast application can be exploited in order to achieve this. The team  also undertook research on how to set up a live podcast.    The team shall further determine and plan the implementation of online publicity by leveraging  inhouse social media management team so as to maintain costs at minimum. The team shall  also facilitate the participation of consumers whose complaints were escalated to the regulator.  All staff members of the regulator shall also be in attendance so as to participate and give  insights after the end of the podcast session.    For the execution of a live podcast with consumers to be deemed to be great idea/true, it is  anticipated that the main reason why consumers of ICT must have been having trouble making  purchase decisions in the ICT market is due to lack of information.    Insight    Following the execution of the interactive live podcast with consumers, the consumer  protection department analyzed the data on the number of consumers who attended, actively  participated, and positive feedback indicating that the podcast is insightful. This data enabled  us conclude that the idea to have a live podcast with consumers was valid. Data on the rate of  decrease in the number of consumer complaints escalated to the regulator will further validated  the hypothesis that information gaps are the main source of pain point for consumers.

Analysis of data on attendance and feedback information from consumer who declined the  invitation to attend the podcast session provided insights on areas that require improvements  in the dissemination of information via the podcast sessions. The analyzed data further  endorsed the idea to hold a live podcast was not a good idea.    Further still the positive feedback from the executive management and staff members at the  regulatory office went a long way in securing funds to execute programmes and further  endorse  the podcast idea.     Approach    An alternative approach would seek to leverage the mind mapping tool. The tool will enable  the consumer protection team highlight the patterns and insights from large quantities of data  drawn from annual consumer behavior and trends surveys, customer satisfaction surveys,  quarterly customer complaints reports and reports of previous consumer education outreach  activities (The University of Virginia, 2020).    The consumer  protection teams hall gather all the relevant data and information and avail it a  large hall to show case it to relevant stakeholders (consumers, licensees, staff et.c.). Due to the  government measures on social distancing, they shall schedule the various stakeholder groups  and request them to note all the important staff and notable information. The team shall then  engage the stakeholder through an online collaboration board so as enable stakeholders share  there insights and collaborate to identify trends and linkages.    Through the use of this tool, the relationship between the regulator and stakeholders will be  strengthened as it shall also serve as a platform to collaborate and resolve a common problem  The University of Virginia (2020).

Reflection – Visualization

By Bilal Khan

Challenge & Selection:    Visualization is one of the widely used design thinking tools which is easy to prepare  and comprehensible by different stakeholders. If there is a gap in understanding  among different stakeholders of the same thing, then the presentation is not correct.  In order to ensure clear intelligible communication of the problem we can use  visualization. This design thinking tool brings all the stakeholders on to the same  platform of understanding and eradicates any communication gap or any kind of  misunderstanding. Through the visualization processes everyone sees through the  same glass. I have used this process in process map visualization in my previous work  where we were stuck on a problem.

Application:

During my engagement with a real estate company I was assigned a project which  involved construction of a residential housing complex and selling the apartments to  customers. The process included a couple of steps - First, the project team would  complete the work. Second, the project team would hand over the apartments to the  Customer Relationship Management (CRM) team. The CRM team would then inspect  the completed apartments and provide feedback to the project team. The  implementation of the feedback would be done by the project team. After the changes  suggested by the CRM team had been done, the Customers would inspect the  completed apartments. Post inspection by the customers and final changes, if any  requested by customers, the apartments would be handed over to the customers. The  CRM team was primarily responsible for the handover, which should have happened  within seven days after the CRM team had taken the handover from the project team.  However, this process would take much longer sometimes up to 30 days instead of 7  days. To understand the problem, delay in the final handover to the customer, we  created  a  process  map  for  visualization  of  the  problem.

After perusing this visualization map, we understood that the feedback  implementation process was being done twice, and the inspection by the CRM team  and the customers was being done separately. After discussions with the project and  the CRM teams, I suggested to merge the inspection by the CRM team with that by the  customers. This would help the project team work on the rectification at one go.

Page 2 of 2

When the inspection by the CRM team and the Customers were done in parallel, the  time interval between the first and final handover decreased. The final handover to the  customers was indeed achieved in seven days after the initial handover by the project  team to the CRM team.

Insight & Approach:

After using the visualization tool for process mapping, we understood that different  stakeholders (Project team, CRM team, and customers) view the problem with the  same lens, and understand with the same reasoning. This tool helped all to understand  the root cause problem very easily without much explanation. The creation of the  process map for visualization was easy. For me this visualization tool was really helpful  to understand the problem very easily and could be used in any type of problem  identification. Albert Einstein said, “If I had an hour to solve a problem, I'd spend 55  minutes thinking about the problem and 5 minutes thinking about solutions.” I think  this visualization tool in design thinking perfectly justifies the saying of Einstein.

Challenges & Selection

It all started years back when a colleague of mine shared with me his dilemma about  choosing between two fundamentally different career opportunities. The classic “Marwa,  would you have a minute for me?” in the office right after the first coffee in the morning.  What initially sprang to my mind to ask him was: “What is it that you’d expect from what’s  left of your business life?”

He replied that he had never thought about that in detail. I continued: “What do you think  you’re really good at?” This is a question that is on the no-go list in today’s formal job  interviews as much as “What do you think you’re really bad at?” because there can’t be an  honest answer. I got trained on that 16 years ago already in my hiring certification classes at  November. However, it is totally OK between two friends in a secluded setting. His answer  struck me as I had a totally different picture of him. At this point it became clear to me that  his situation and decision process would require some formalization and visualization. And  this is how I started to use mind mapping.

Application

I start with general ideas and get more and more specific as my idea develops. Structure  does not develop in my head. Information does. That means that I must put down my  information somewhere and structure it there. Linear representation is difficult to structure.  Hence, a mind map comes in handy: I can see things at a glance and add topics where I see a  gap.

While developing the method, I used a mind map to dump my thoughts and experiences in.  After a while, these topics could be organized into clusters, which then mercilessly pointed  out to me what was missing. I literally saw it! In short: Information creates clusters, shows  missing information and promotes further clustering. A very creative flow. Putting things in  a meaningful order requires a lot of shuffling around of information and re-clustering. Try to  do that in a flowing text and you know why I always choose to use a mind map.

When the mind map was finally as complete as I wanted it to be, the question was: How to  present it to the target audience? How can a story unfold in the eyes of the beholder? Going  through this map is not a linear process. While you answer one question in the map,  another answer to an unrelated question on the other side of the map might just pop up in  your mind. Because you always see the open spots, you can easily jump left and right, top  and bottom and still stick to a structure.

Collaboration is the key element of my method. Collaboration works perfectly fine when  face to face over a glass of wine. But this is a process that will never conclude, as previously  noted. Thus, remote collaboration is a smart way to interact. Set the preferences for the  map to notify when changes are applied and trigger off a constant flow of remote  interaction, which will continuously fine tune the map.

Finally: Seeing and listening closely are important while working on such an intimate topic,  but you need to go one step further and truly capture the meaning. A mind map will help  you to see things in context and see how they develop and relate to each other. This is key  for being able to open and challenge, respectively. When providing feedback, adding visuals  to indicate feelings about a certain topic, emphasizing certain elements through formatting  and showing consent or dissent by voting, commenting and, most of all, asking (Carl Rogers)  are strong tools to drill deeper into the matter and look behind the statements being made.  You are able to actually “describe” digital information (text, content) with analog elements  (icons, formatting, position, relation) to create a picture in the mind of the collaborators  that they can even talk about without the map in sight.

Insight & Approach

A mind map is a means to visually represent ideas and their relationship to one another. It’s  a brainstorming tool frequently used in education, the business world, and the  entertainment industry – often in collaborative projects.

There are times in your life when you need to make significant decisions about how to  continue in your business and/or personal life. At these points, it’s necessary that you  establish a clear vision about certain life facts. This process must be honest and complete.

In my experience, mind map and the method behind it helped me a lot during my journey of  self-evaluation by compiling relevant information and presenting these facts in a  comprehensive format to a friend for input.

Essay

Design thinking: visualization

Challenge and selection     Due to my specialty of studying, I resort to visualization very often. In most cases my  aim as a future designer to solve the task and create a unique style for some object,  organization or idea. In this case, when I mention «resort to visualization» I mean a  formation of mood boards, portraits of the target audience, finding associations, drawing  schemes as a result and so on. In this essay I would like to describe a part of my  working process, visualization, on the example of creating a book.    Visualisation — it is a method of thinking, during which you use your ability to draw,  write and sketch. In another words, it is a process of thinking in pictures. However, it is  necessary to mention that there is no need to be a real painter, as your aim is not, to  make an object of art, but to understand an issue and to find a suitable visual move to  solve the task. Challenge & Selection:

Our government customer was used to relying on proprietary data collection and analysis tools  specifically tailored for the government operating environment.  Over time, the government customer  realized that commercial solutions offerings existed that could provide highly accurate data analysis to  enhance their knowledge and awareness of their operating environment at a very affordable cost.   When compared to designing and acquiring their own proprietary system, the government customer  realized that our commercial solution could have the potential to enhance their capabilities, but were  interested in understanding how our data analysis system could be integrated into their normal daily  operations.

Selection:

I chose the “Learning Launch” tool for this customer, because it allowed our team to work very closely  and collaboratively with the customer in an environment that closely mimicked how the system would  be deployed if the project proved to be a viable prototype that should be scaled.

Application:   Since the customer was already a receiver of raw data from my company, we were able to  generate a high number of data sets over a 6-week period to include disconfirming data in our test  batches.  The cost of the “Learning Launch” was largely limited to labor costs associated with two of our  analysts and software engineers that supported the active contract with the customer for data  collection.  The individuals chosen to support the “Learning Launch” were very disciplined in their  approach, but also had a history of listening very well to customer and tailoring the response to best  meet the customer’s needs.  Since the nature of the project was leveraging real world data that  generated potentially hundreds of datasets daily, we were able to both develop fast feedback cycles and  present real world examples to our customer to garner their feedback.

We built the test around several key assumptions developed in consultation with the customer: (1)  Accuracy of data analysis was the most important attribute of the data collected and analyzed; (2) Speed  of data delivery was the second most important attributed; (3) Number of samples daily was the third  most important attribute.

Insight:  The “Learning Launch” provided to be successful in both walking towards a scalable prototype  to meet the customer’s needs, but also to aide our team in testing assumptions.  Both the customer and  our team were surprise that the order of priority for “Learning Launch” assumptions changed to: (1)  Speed became the most important attribute for the customer; (2) The customer identified the “number  of samples daily” as the second most important attribute; (3) Accuracy, which was the attribute we  assumed was most important, actually became the least important attribute.  The customer realized  that if the data collection and analysis process could happen at the speed they desire with a higher  number of samples daily, they would get a higher level of accuracy in their data over time.  In the end,  their most import outcome was to know very early that the system detected something.  If perceived as  a significant issue, the customer could choose to deploy additional resources to help resolve.

Approach:  The “Learning Launch” tool proved to be an excellent method to test assumptions with real  data in an environment that provided customer collaboration and controlled cost over the 6-week test.   In the end, the scalable prototype met the needs of the customer who has significant “buy in” given they  helped shape the final product.

Peer-graded Assignment: Reflection | Tool: Learning Launch

Challenge and Selection

As a sport and technology lover, I started a few months ago a company in Brazil. The idea is to  give everything the professionals have to the amateur soccer players, from scores and graphs  from the matches to automatic generated videos making the experience of playing soccer  digital and social we would charge the players to deliver this to them. It is not a secret that  soccer is one of the most popular sport around the world, and our goal was to build something  scalable and worldwide applicable. Since the money was short, we guided ourselves by Lean  Startups and fail fast concepts, in order to learn about customers’ needs to address it quickly.  The selection of Learning Launch for this reflection is because we use some of its concepts and  that helped us to shape the solution, mainly because we started doing experiments instead of  a Business Plan, this saved us time and money.

Application

It is almost impossible to talk about Learning Launch without mentioning the previews phases.  We went from the observation and data collection (what is) from our friends and started  generating some hypothesis (what if), we did it structured and non-structured way and then  we started making some experiments based on them, using correlation with other things for a  better visualization (another tool from Design Thinking) of what we said. Anyway, it was  helping us to construct, and co-create with the people that would be one day our customers.  At that time, they did not know that yet. Once we learned a lot of what would make sense  (what wows) we decided to build a prototype (what works) and go sell it – Learning Launch.  We build a structure with security cameras and it automatically recorded the matches and the  players could use it was a social network; they could cut their moves and goals scored sharing  it with friends and so on. Good features! We started offering, different prices, different ways  of approaching them, because by definition Learning Launch is the time where the output is  not a GO-NOGO decision, the output is learning and improving it. Of course, it was un- structured, we did it naturally, and somehow things led us to it. Then we started discovering  some stuffs we did not see on the observation phases.

Insights

Most of our customers were playing regularly (once a week), for stress relief, with couple of  friends from work or college. Yes, we knew that already. But what the Learning Launch showed  us were some hidden traps on the way. We had competitors, the first one the beer and  barbecue after the matches; they rather spend money there than paying for a video from their  matches as memory. The second one was the timing. After every match, we uploaded about  one hour of video, that’s depressing, they wanted to see only the best scenes, the highlights,  they didn’t want to see the whole match. Yes, we thought about it, using machine learning to  try to extract goals and highlights automatically to make the experience better, but for that,  we needed to spend hours of development, research, and money of course, which was out of  question at that time. But we kept going, we made small changes in the platform meanwhile.  We offered for different aged people, different gender, then we discovered a segment that

saw other benefits of our solution. By the end of 6 months, we had only 5 recurrent customers  paying 40 dollars a month to have their matches recorded, team and personal profiles. That  was much lower of what we expected. Nevertheless, one day, a person we offered the solution  came to us asking if we could help him with a championship, he was organizing. His pains were  a little bit different from the players, but he saw that we would help him in several aspects.  With some minimal changes on the platform (when I say minimal change, I am saying not more  than one day programing – that was our fail fast and cheap way of thinking), we created new  features to attend this new persona; suddenly we became a championship platform! Now our  customer were the championship organizer, he paid us, the players of a championship have  other pains and expected something very different from the regular weekly player (despite we  know most of the championship players are also regular weekly players). The emotional was  different when they were playing a championship; they wanted to feel like a professional  player. That was the biggest lesson we learned.

Nowadays we are still learning, we are going to our 10th cup and we have something around  10.000 players registered.

Approach

We had done two things wrong. First one were installing the security cameras for the MVP.  That was not scalable, that was difficult with a high cost of implementation. We tested with a  GoPro previously, but the time we spend using it was not enough to notice the “competitors”,  and the second one, when we switch from a GoPro to a security cam, you lose a lot of quality.  That is a big change. From customer perspective, once you introduced something good, you  cannot go back; their expectations are up high, if you do so, you will have trouble as we had.   We should have invested a little more time in the Visualization of this change, this certainly led  us to failure of the real test, but what is funny to mention is because of this failure we found  what we think is the right path. Of course we didn’t give up on this idea, we just put it on the  shelf, we are now trying to develop the machine learning to collect the highlights, seeing  possibilities to use players own smartphones to record the videos, an easier and scalable way.

Life is a journey; learn fast and cheap, if failure is the way to learn you should pursue it!
