Insight & Approach (What Is)

As a starting point we picked all the lessons learnt documentation where the team faced quite number of

challenges in completing the milestone within last one year. Rather than looking at specific incidents

pinpointing to certain flaws, the next objective was understanding common trends common unidentified pain

areas can be nailed down especially during the tight patch of critical delivery timelines.

A series of calls were scheduled with project stakeholders. The team divided into groups consisting of 2-3

members was given task to come up pain areas within themselves and project community.

After series on call, floating several sticky notes, few critical observations were made after series of calls  

1. The frequency of adhoc communication (emails & Teleconferencing) with project stakeholders

increased drastically as the project deviated further from the original plan. The majority of  communication was involving asking similar same set of status metrics – how much we have  completed, how many more to complete, key blockers and their action owners etc.

2. Triggering the automaton regression testing and sharing the respective result involved someone

to be at desk. By regression testing, I mean testing existing functionality just to ensure developer  has not broken something else while fixing a specific bug. This activity is required to iterated  large number of times at different inconvenient time zones especially for projects where large  number of bugs or critical bugs are discovered.

3. Many Business Analysts and Designers while reviewing specific testing details  needs to logon

to Defect ( code bug) management tool manually or need to dig up lots of emails if they needs  to find specific result of bug,

Insight & Approach - Continued (What If & What Wows)

The team has as such good experience of skills on automation of testing functionalities on software  applications they were working on. While learning through the pain areas, the idea emerged to  automate the communication areas so that 

1. They are less involved in adhoc communication and focus more on pain areas   2. The stakeholders gets the details instantly rather being dependent on the team  3. The productivity of team will be less impacted when Senior Management is looking for adhoc

details.

The team then thought of building the framework where they could automate 

1. Providing details of progress (right from High Level to Micro Level)   2. Trigger automation testing by development team   3. Provide adhoc specific details of testing.

After series to several brainstorming sessions, the approach was taken to use “email” as source of  automation. This idea was picked to ensure 

1. Automating this task should not involve any human interaction apart from triggering email   2. Stakeholders of various kinds (technical/non-technical )  could use this framework rather than

thinking of training on any automation tool

An example of what above means is, whenever required to run regression testing after bug fix, any  person within project just needs to do is send email to testing team and he/she  should get response  back with details. The received email on any of the testing team desktop should trigger automation  work in required work. The technical feasibility was studied and checked carefully across other teams  and we also got a framework to build what we were thinking of.

Prototype (What Wows)  

Rather than jumping directly making ‘cool stuff’ we decided to test our idea with Business Project  Manager, Designer and Development Lead.  We initially gave a walk through about the framework we  want to build and its advantages.

Later they were asked trigger email with certain keywords in the subject to one of my team member  who had a sample response already prepared and responded with 2 minutes delay.  The overall  approach really worked out well with feedback of what details they were seeking in automated way  and review system.

As a team we got a brilliant feedback to come up with this initiative and approach.  One of the few  compliments from Senior Management came up for the team as “This team is one of the most pro-active  and highly committed team seeking continuous improvement“.

My team has completed built of first frame work now which is covering regression testing and final  stage of internal testing before rolling out to project.

Conclusion

On several projects of various kinds, human pain areas may mostly not get documented. It is only the

systematic implementation of Design Thinking Methodology can improve business substantially or

even bring in disruptive innovation that remains key challenge for large organizations.

APPLICATION  We brainstormed the main topics and items that we should contemplate, from pricing to  type of students and their goals, using a black Sharpie and a white paper. Reflection – Learning Launch

Linda Mthethwa               19 November 2018

1. Challenge

I was contemplating starting my own business. I own some quality optic instruments like binoculars,

rangefinders and spotting scopes. My friends were always borrowing my equipment and it got me

thinking that maybe there is a market for renting out this kind of equipment. I live in Windhoek, the

capital city of Namibia. Namibia is a very popular tourist destination because of the beautiful and

unspoilt nature and wildlife. I made the assumption that tourists that visit Namibia do not necessarily

want to buy and travel with equipment like binoculars, spotting scopes, satellite navigation devices,

e.g. the kind of equipment and gear a tourist will require for a trip to Namibia, and that there would

be a business opportunity for providing a service for renting out this kind of gear.

2. Selection

My “what is” was a desk study on the number and type of tourists that generally visited Namibia. My

“what if” was the idea that there will be a market for renting out certain gear to tourists to Namibia.

Thus, for my “what wows and what works” I needed to test my assumption that tourists will be willing

to rent gear when travelling to Namibia, as opposed to buying and travelling with their own gear.

I did not want to invest too much capital into buying a lot of equipment that I could rent out to tourists

before I knew that my assumptions were actually valid. Thus, I had to do an experiment that was fast

and cheap and I therefore opted for the learning launch – which is in essence the prescribed design

thinking method to test the key underlying value-generating assumptions of a potential new-growth

initiative quickly and inexpensively before going into a detailed investigation with the commitment of

further time, people and resources.

3. Application

My hypotheses was that tourists could make good use of binoculars to get the most value on a trip to

Namibia (i.e. a view of the beautiful fauna and flora) and that tourists would rather rent binoculars

than buy and travel with their own binoculars. The learning launch involves the series of small moves

that will allow you to gather data to test whether or not your assumption/s turn out to be true as you

launch the product or service. Critical here is getting a prototype in the market with prospective

customers as quickly as possible.

Hence, I bought a number of binoculars and I hired a website developer to build a simple website

(http://www.chapman-robinson.com/explorelogin.htm) where tourists could rent and pay for binoculars for a specific time period.

The process was simple, the prospective client could specify the number of binoculars required, the

start and end dates the equipment was required and locations for receiving and dropping of the

binoculars after use. The website also made provision for secure online payment for renting the

equipment.

To promote the business I designed and printed a small brochure to advertise the service and explain

how it works, and I distributed these brochures to a number of travel agents in Windhoek. The

assumption was that travel agents were usually the first and a key points of contact for tourists, and

would therefore be the perfect channel for promoting the business. I also recruited a few temporary

resources to hand out brochures to tourists at key tourist attractions in Windhoek.

4. Insight

Based on the tourist data in the “what is” stage and the feedback from travel agents (most of them

thought it was a great idea) my expectation was that the binoculars would be rented out continuously

and that the business would be highly successful. My actual results were very different from what was

anticipated: very few binoculars were in fact rented by tourists. In my view, the learning launch

provided exactly what was expected, i.e. a fast and cheap way to test my assumptions for this business

idea. I got my answers without investing a lot of capital, I did not buy a lot of binoculars and the

website and brochures also did not cost a lot of money.

5. Approach

Looking back I realized what I could have done differently was to first spend time actually talking to

tourists and getting their opinions on if they would make use of such a service in the first place and

what kind of equipment they would rather rent than buy. Although my experiment (learning launch)

was fast and cheap, by thinking through it and by specifically focusing on how it could be done even

faster and cheaper, I could have validated my assumptions much more efficiently.  Thus, for the

learning launch, I learned that always consider getting prospective customer’s feedback first by talking

to them.

Challenge

A few months ago while attending a design seminar, a

challenge was given to all the present attendees: “Try to

define a new service or product about the already

saturated coffee industry, that could generate new value

to the customers or the producers”. Then the attendees

were organized into diverse multidisciplinary teams and

the discussions began.

Design Tool Selection & Application

After a brief discussion that took place to organize the

creative process, we decided to initiate with a simple

exercise. Each team member wrote down in sticky “Post

It” papers, any idea that landed in our heads when we

think about coffee, the post its were sticked to the wall.

After only 10 minutes, we had a wall full of different

thoughts, ideas and keywords related to coffee. With all

that information, we decided to generate a ​“Mind Map”​,

and the team began to arrange the notes that naturally fit

together in categories. A very nice mind map was

created, with around 4 different categories covering

insights that ranged from coffee crops and production

process to the consumption practices and even cultural

behaviors around coffee preparation.

Insights

The team reviewed, analyzed and discussed the

resulting mind map. After a few minutes, there was

consensus in one insight: “Little to no recognition is

given to the real hands that gather the coffee from the

plants and that actually enable the rest of the world to

have access to this amazing drink”, then we immediately

decided to work around this idea, and generate a

proposal that returns something back to these people

that have an important role within the coffee industry.

Approach

A new coffee brand was proposed to be released to the

market; this coffee brand will work around an

“ecosystem” concept, considering the fact that those

hands working at the crops are as important as the

coffee itself. The brand will represent an extension of

those hands, serving coffee straight to your homes.

Pictures of real coffee pickers will be displayed at the

packages with positive messages underneath. Also, all

the organic waste generated during the coffee bean

processing will be handled to a “coffee pickers

association” which will be organized to manage it and

process it to generate paper made of organic fibers. This

paper will be used to make the coffee packaging bags.

The association will be paid for this bag supplies and the

profit distributed between all the collaborators,

generating additional profit and more diverse working

opportunities to these people working in the crops.

Additionally a stamp in the coffee bag will make the

consumers aware of this sustainable and social-friendly

practice, which will result in the final acknowledgment of

the coffee pickers as important contributors of the coffee

supply process.

Final Reflection

The ​“mind mapping” tool, quickly enabled the team to

think about new ideas derived from already available

and common knowledge about the coffee industry. What

could be a chaotic brainstorming process where hardly

people converge into the same agreements and

disconnected ideas are thrown, was naturally handled

and organized into categories by the “mind map”; once

there all topics were ready for discussion and analysis in

a better, organized and constructive way. I personally

found this approach extremely enlightening and

constructive, and in order to enhance the experience, a

little bit of research previous the idea generation process

will definitely enable the teams to construct even better

ideas full of innovation.

Example Reflection - Learning Launch

Challenge

My name is Caterina Mauro. I am a mechanical engineer and my profession is heating and cooling system  designs. Moreover, I am a member of garment care department at my company. My challenge was  increasing ironing performance for handheld irons. It was my first iron project and I had not got  adequate information about this issue.

According to user experiment studies, every Turkish people want to wear ironed clothes. Wrinkled  textiles are not acceptable for them. For this reason, my department kicked off improve the ironing  performance of our irons.

There are two main parameters for improving ironing performance. First factor is steam rate and  second one is temperature of iron sole plate. If you increase steam rate and temperature of sole plate,  you can improve your ironing score.

Selection

I checked design thinking tools and decided to use learning launch tool. In my point of view, this tool  is more useful for our challenge because I had lack of information about irons and the factor of ironing  performance. In addition, I had limited time for solving this problem. The learning launch given chance  for quick prototyping and test.

Application

At our first learning launch, we discussed above steam rate and sole plate temperature in order to  improve ironing performance. In consequence of first learning launch, we decided to modify sole plate  steam channels. At that point, we designed 3 alternative sole plate channels and asked ourselves “How  do we decide which design is best?” In order to answering this question, we sent these 3 designs for  quick and cheap prototyping.

As a result of first tests with these three prototypes, we arranged second learning launch. We  evaluated test results and sole plates during this learning launch. Moreover, we choose best sole plate  channel alternative and improved the design of this alternative. We tested again with improved sole  plate. According to test results, our steam rate and sole plate temperature increased.

Sensitivity: Public

Insights

By applying the learning launch tool, we enhanced our knowledges about irons and produced some  prototypes and applied steam rate and sole plate temperature tests with these prototypes. After that,  at second learning launch, we improved steam rate and sole plate temperature thanks to final steam  channel design.

Thanks to improve these parameters, our ironing performance dramatically increased. Our final ironing  performance test results were slightly different from our existing irons.

Approach

In brief, learning launch tool was best tool for solving problems, if you have insufficient problems. We  discussed with my team above this tool that will use at new research and development projects. What  is more, I discussed with other departments and explained learning launch tool to them. They may try  this tool for their projects.

Reflection for Design Thinking    Frederic Singh

“Visualization”                                                                                                                                           10-18-2018

Challenge & Selection  "You know those linear actuators we need in 4 months? They just went to 12 month lead time. I think  we have an alternate." The Project Manager hadn't been at my desk for more than 30 seconds and my  stomach already felt like I'd checked a text as the driver took our car over an unexpected hill. In the  semiconductor manufacturing equipment company where I work as an engineer, supplier part delays  (and substitutions) in the recent booming economy are a common occurrence. Typically, it's for a minor  component with several alternates of similar shape or "form factor" and handled by a single designer.  Think "all-weather" instead of "snow" tread for your car tires. This one, however, was more involved.  The linear actuator is a central part, a sliding component used as the backbone of a lifting robot, and the  one thing that everything else (motor, brackets, sensors, base stand, etc...) attaches to. No, this was not  choosing a tire, this might be swapping wheels from 14 inch to 16 inch rims or maybe 6 lug to 5 lug nut  hole pattern! This was going to require the "What is?" and "What if?" of Design Thinking, a design  review relying heavily on Visualization.      Application  Not surprisingly, in manufacturing engineering you use a wide variety of visual tools and resources. The  "back of the napkin" doodle is alive and well in industry. One also comes across technical diagrams on  supplier "datasheets", color pictures in parts catalogs and designs 3D models and creates 2D  documentation 'prints' using computer aided design (CAD) software. For this design review, we used all  of these and more.     A meeting was scheduled for the following week to review the details of the current design and  determine the feasibility of the alternate supplier's replacement linear actuator. Design reviews in  manufacturing often include technical and semi-technical people. This design review was no exception.  Invited to the meeting were a couple of attendees from Purchasing, a mechanical engineer (me), an  engineering technician, a couple of manufacturing technicians and the Project Manager.     I had booked a room with a digital projector and plenty of dry erase white boards for doodling. To be  sure we all got our hands dirty, both literally and figuratively, I brought an old (greasy) linear actuator  from the lab for "show and tell" around the table. Each seat received a printout of the old and new  datasheets/catalogs showing dimensions and technical information. I find it's helpful to have printouts  in front of everyone for note taking, for reference and again for doodling.     At my company, many of us have to work remotely, so I had set up a WebEx emeeting and started off by  screen sharing a PowerPoint slide show with the Project Manager (now traveling out of state on  business) and with the people in the room via projector. After a short discussion of the slides and  challenge at hand, we went free form and handed off the presentation to the engineering technician  manning a CAD program called CREO. The following hour plus was spent determining the "What Is?" and  some of our "What If?" challenges and advantages of using the alternative actuator and its impact on  our current design and parts.            Insight & Approach  The design review was very productive due to Visualization used: WebEx and PowerPoint slides, video  projectors, CREO CAD models, samples, whiteboards and datasheet/catalog handouts. Visualization was  key here, since it communicates more than just language, where the technical terms may not be familiar  to all and the discussion revolves around shapes and fit between parts. The saying, "A picture speaks a  thousand words", was very, very, true.

"Linear actuator??", say the Purchasing buyers. "Oh, it's a 'SLIDE'. Got it." Seeing and understanding the  technical terms in use would help them know what to look for and communicate with the alternate  supplier(s).  The introduction PowerPoint slide show explained the situation to all the participants and  primed the discussion. The Project Manager was able to see and participate from offsite. Looking at the  CAD and catalog diagrams of the alternate linear actuator, the technicians and I identified its different  shaped features and drew on the white boards some basic design concepts to accommodate those  features.    The visual aids, especially the linear actuator sitting on the desk, spurred a lot of discussion of the "What  Is?" and "What If?" of the current designs. "The screws are larger…" and "That flange feature really isn't  needed on the original design and can actually go away…" and "What if we used their industry standard  motor mount and not our custom one?" Participants often pointed to a feature on the physical part,  then pointed out the significance of that feature in the "where-used" example CAD models on the  projector screen.  The engineering technician was able to rotate or explode the views in CAD projection  to show how parts connected and to better make the point.     The time constraints and scope for this first design review meeting did not allow it, but follow-up  meetings would continue the "What If?" redesign with new concept parts modeled in CAD. Seeing the  engagement of having an actual, physical object on the table to see and touch, I want to use that as a  Visualization tool going forward. Carla Yadav  Learning Launch Reflection  Design Thinking for Innovation    Challenge

While completing my doctorate degree in France, I was a representative for my team

on the Doctorand Council which was charged with facilitating the integration of doctoral  candidates into the environment of the laboratory, as well as aiding them for all university  administrative processes. The principal challenge for our group was that there were multiple  Doctoral Schools within the same laboratory, and each school has its own registration  process and general organization for the doctorate degree. Additionally, the lab welcomes  students from all over the world, where the language barrier for interactions with university  and doctoral school personnel as well as all the written resources for students can be  difficult to overcome.     During my time on the council, we decided to affront this problem and develop a

new website that would provide comprehensive information for each doctorate school  process in multiple languages. Furthermore, we decided to pair each incoming foreign  student with another doctoral candidate further along in their process. This became the  cornerstone project for the Doctorand Council during my time.     Selection

After a full year of intensive research into the experiences of different foreign

students using many design thinking techniques, such as storytelling and developing  personas based on ethnography, our team had amassed a large number of common  patterns of difficulty for their integration into the program, in addition to access to previous  years’ feedback from earlier councils. We also had held a meeting with the directors (full- time personnel) of each doctoral school within the laboratory to see what was possible  within the constraints of the requirements of the schools. Given the large scale of the  project to address all of the different schools’ processes and intricacies, we decided to  employ a learning launch for our website and mentorship program for one doctoral school,  which was the majority school for many on the council who had personal insight into that  particular process.     In general, a learning launch is a small-scale experiment for a larger solution directly

in the actual marketplace, where the major interest is to learn and iterate on the idea,  rather than decide to go through with it or not. This was perfectly suited to the next step in  our challenge, as the immediately received feedback from the focus on this one school  would help point out important changes needed for the future full version of the program.     Application    For our learning launch, we first developed our basic website with all general

information that can be helpful to any newly arrived students to the city and within the  laboratory. We developed specific pages, such as detailing what extracurricular activities  through the university were available to doctoral students, based on the original student  feedback through surveys and personal interviews.      We further established a fully detailed check-list like website on the registration for

students from the specific doctoral school that we chose and we paired each new doctoral  candidate enrolled in that school with a more seasoned doctoral candidate who intimately

knew the inscription process. In total, we had twenty mentorship pairs, and decided to put  five new students with mentors who shared the same native language to see if that could  help integrate new students more. Finally, we implemented multiple feedback options to  observe the learning launch including a dedicated feedback page on the website, a survey  sent out to all doctoral candidates, and one meeting with each mentorship pair together, as  well as one meeting with each individually paired person to ask for direct feedback on the  mentorship program. This first launch was set to run for one period of “new students”  meaning six months, so that the feedback could be understood and integrated into a better  product for the next semester of new doctoral candidates.    Insight    Over the entire process, design thinking tools were absolutely necessary to approach

this project. The insights that we received from student feedback allowed quick, executable  changes that augmented the experience for all users. Immediately, the feedback webpage  provided easy, important changes ranging from spelling errors, offers from students to  translate the page to help, and ideas to interactive ways for the website to help students  further. The best part of considering this a learning launch meant that we could quickly  implement the feedback on a regularly basis, continually improving our product.    However, the biggest insights came from the mentorship program and the meetings

in person for the “users” to provide their own feedback by telling their own stories. First, we  found that providing same native language mentors was not the best solution, as their  shared biases could actually lead to problems in the same step of the integration process.  This led us to decide to try the exact opposite on the next iteration, pairing foreign students  with French students who could then help the new doctoral candidate to better integrate  into the international community at the lab, and also. assist in the language barrier for more  administrative concerns. Additionally, we recognized many important human factors that  should be taken into account when looking for mentors, such as availability, languages  spoken, and even trying to pull from different friend groups/teams within the lab. The  design thinking principles were perfectly suited to this very human-centric problem.    Approach

The design thinking principles were perfectly suited to this very human-centric

problem, which required and continues to require actual personal feedback on what each  person has had trouble with. The learning launch was the perfect step at that time for the  project, as we had years of ethnographic research from past years as well as current, and  the council in our time had already brainstormed the website and mentorship solution. The  learning launch during my time on the council was cited as a major aid to new students and  has continued to be iterated and improved throughout the past four years as new ideas  come to the table.

Storytelling to Show Gaps in Our Customer Application Journey.

Challenge   I am a Process Improvement Manager in a company that provides fuel credit cards.   Our team's mission is to digitally transform our customers' journey; specifically, the current  online path that our prospects experience to apply for our cards. Our leader asked us to improve the customer’s usage, to increase the number of transactions by  10%, and consequently, revenue. Also, our leader gave us 2 weeks to present a problem  statement with solutions and recommendations.     Selection  (Why) Our team has already gone through several different tools to try to explain to our leaders  our complex customer journey. (What is it) So, since Storytelling is a tool that takes the listener along on the human being journey  and creates empathy, we decided to implement this tool in this project so we can create a vivid  experience. After doing our own research, analyzing the data, reaching out to the customers who don’t use  the cards and asking their feedback; we found out that these customers were very frustrated  with the entire customer application process. After hearing all their stories, we could synthesize  every single journey into a single fictional one, recreating this experience using one of the  personas we have identified. Hector Momentos – Final Reflection

Challenge

I work as Head of Operations for a consulting firm that has over three decades of  experience implementing training programs for micro, small and medium-sized  enterprises (SMEs). Given this trajectory, the organization’s execution process -including  consultant manuals and training toolkits- revolves around traditional on-site training  programs. However, over the past year most of our projects have begun to include new  digital solutions like mobile apps and e-learning platforms for SMEs. My challenge is that  the current execution process does not consider digital projects, therefore it has been  very difficult to standardize activities and to guarantee the quality of the implementation.

Selection

My team and I have decided to try the learning launch tool because we have already  drafted a new execution process with a clear understanding of our pain points. However,  we made the mistake of waiting for this new process to be more robust and almost  perfect on paper before testing it out. Therefore, we figured using the learning launch tool  would help us to quickly figure out what works best during the implementation process  for digital training programs.

Application

We used an ongoing program with an e-learning platform designed for small businesses  and entrepreneurs to receive training in topics such as sales, finance and accounting,  inventory control, etc. Up until this point the program has failed to meet its goals on two  key metrics: # of registered users and # of lessons completed by registered users.

We did a brainstorming session to decide on possible actions we could take to improve  these metrics and we decided on two key assumptions that we shall validate in our  learning launch:

1) The registration form it too long and complicated, therefore users begin but fail to

complete registration.

2) Users lack incentives to complete the lessons within the platforms

To validate our assumptions, we created a new registration form that reduced the  mandatory fields from 20 to only 4 questions. In addition, we incorporated introduced  loyalty points that could be earned for every completed lesson and then the loyalty points  could be exchanged for different awards (i.e. Netflix gift certificate, grocery store coupons,  etc.).

Insight and Approach

We tested both changes on the platform for a full week and the results were evident:  registration was up by 60% and the average number of completed lessons per user went  up by 35%. We decided to establish design principles for any new project involving e- learning platforms for SMEs and the first two principles are: simplify the registration  process and provide rewards to incentivize the completion of lessons/training modules.

From a broader perspective, thinking about the overall challenge of the organization’s  execution process, I understood the importance of running small experiments for each  part of the process instead of simply drafting every piece of it on paper without validating  any assumptions. Moving forward I will make sure to continue testing our new solutions  with small learning launches that allow us to quickly determine the optimal  implementation process for digital training programs.

Challenge and Selection

The tool that I have found consistently useful throughout my career thus far is visual thinking or  visualization. Whether it is in a group or just me, as an individual, trying to demystify a problem space, the  act of putting abstract ideas a figures or diagrams, opens the minds for a more constructive and productive  interaction. Putting words into graphics like straw man, geometrics shapes enhances the quality of output making.

Application

Using Visualization in Root cause analysis.

When researching a problem reported by a user, I being my investigation gathering the facts around the  event. These could be logs, audit traces, print outs, anything. Then I try to piece the flow of events one  after another in chronological event of say time. When I feel I have a hunch of where the root cause is or  whenever I am completely stuck in my analytical track, I resort to visualizing the journey of events. As a  process, I always deliberately, set the key statement aside, temporarily. Then I start drawing the facts  ‘what I know’ say in boxes. Engaging in this process, has multiple benefits, almost immediately I can see if  I have made false assumptions, or reveals that I need to look for more data, or it simply solidifies the  inferences drawn.

Another benefit of this visualization practical is that almost immediately I can see if the processes /events  are indeed working as designed (not a defect) else these actions serve are valuable aids to recreate the  issue. These pictures many a times have been attached to problem-statements which are sent for defect  fixing. Visualizing issues and documenting them also helps the testing teams down line who can now  inspect these visuals and prepare their test cases accordingly.

Customer Interactions

I have found visualization is a great tool in breaking down communication barriers. When meeting clients,  using props like post-it notes, charts etc., serve as great aids in understanding the requirements, both  expressed and unexpressed. Many a times, I have used these visual tools to map solutions to  requirements, thus saving a lot of time and effort. Functional diagrams, flow charts, Visio mind maps, are  all tools I have used both understand and explain complex concepts. On many instances, the group or  individual can see errors or missing pieces and quickly correct course when explaining requirements to  us. Another benefit of using a multi nodal visual approach, is that the core verbal discussions become  healthier and productive.

Technical Discussions

On many an occasion, I have used the post it notes, flip chart diagrams mentioned above, to serve as  supporting documentation in technical discussions with the development team. These visual aids then  spur the process of demystifying the requirements. Many a times, these aids help me recollect vital points  and fill the gaps in our recollection. Visualization takes on a different flavor when we discuss technical  challenges. Using white boards, flow charts to represent process flows, design diagrams allow me to  understand the technical challenges in a much better form. Taking a photo of these visual artefacts, and

using them as aids to the documentation, helps me when we are composing the training and information  material later in the project.

Insight and Approach

What I have learned in the course and the experiences from my professional life lead me to conclude that

1. Graphically representing abstract ideas, greatly hastens the process of unbundling complexities.

Be it an attempt to understand what is, or when exploring different options under what if, creating  a low fidelity what wows or trying to find out what works, a visual artefact becomes  polymorphous.

2. A visual artefact is also a great attention grabber. Being the focal point of the conversation, it

enables collaboration and collective thought and action.

3. It helps in overcoming obstacles like analysis paralysis, when one is stumbling around abstract

ideas.

4. By allowing the mind to work freely, it unshackles ideas at many levels. Morphing ideas and

thoughts into graphics, helps us convey our ideas more effectively

Example reflection-Visualisation

Challenge and Selection-

One challenge within an organization is to develop new innovative products and services and

present them to the market. These products must be developed in an economical and

sustainable way. They must also answer a desire or need on the market, be technologically

and organizationally feasible and financially viable (Brown, 2009). Design competency in

organizations can help to improve the processes of creating innovative, sustainable products

and services. A typical design process includes generic steps such as the identification of

needs, idea generation and conceptual design, detailed product design, the preparation of

production and design of production system, production, marketing and delivery. Defined

generic design phases include Idea and Concept Design, Product Design and System Design.

These phases often differ from each other in objectives and approaches but have the design

concept in common. Another aspect these phases share is the use and need of visual

communication.

Application-

Visualisation is a core component of the way that we communicate, whether we're aware of it

or not. When we're dealing with very complex problems, we're enacting a different kind of

problem solving that has to bring in more than just logic. Visualisation is really important for

the process of Design Thinking because it's actually a way of unlocking a different part of our

brain. It allows us to think in a non-verbal way and access parts of our brain, our creativity.

Most design thinkers call visualisation as “the mother of all design tools”, because they are

used in every stage of the design thinking process.

Visualisation is equal parts listening, thinking and drawing. Listening is the input, thinking is

the processing and drawing is the output. These three skills work together equally in

understanding complexity, visualising outcomes to create new possibilities.

Do not let drawing eclipse the importance of listening and thinking skills just because it is

more visible and tangible. In my own experience, we can cultivate this skill set. Visualisation

takes us beyond just using words or language alone. The beauty of using Visualisation is that

we can tap into a single picture. The more you begin to use pictures, the more that you begin

to diagram while you talk and create a visual image for people of how you are thinking.

The world will always need people who can see the bigger picture - those who listen, who

find patterns, and make connections. The world around us is complex and needs us to

strengthen our ability capture and organise ideas. We need more clarity. We need more

shared understanding. We need more simplicity. The more likely you are to achieve a sense

of agreement and consensus with people, the more you are likely to draw out conversation. In

an environment where your ability to get things done and to solve problems is dependent on

other people being able to understand you and align their ideas with yours.

Insight and approach-

It's really really important to be able to understand the way that you communicate with

people. The primary tools for thinking visually are really just mastering some basic elements

of imagining people, spaces, situations and actions or movements. It's very easy to create a

simple diagram –  and most anyone can draw a stick figure, a circle, a square, or an arrow.

Those are the basic building blocks of creating a Visualisation. We can unlock the power to

think differently by doodling. Alicia Diane Durand’s Discovery Doodles - The complete

series is a good starting point if you are in search of confidence and want to learn basic visual

elements. I try to practice with and learn from my three little girls Princess (7), Princess (4)

and Princess (2). The kids doodle naturally not afraid of judgement. I am not a Picasso. I

might not pass the high-school ‘arts’ exam even if return to it once again.

Visualisation has a role to play throughout the Design Thinking. It's an incredible tool, in that

sense, in that we're using those tools and that part of our brain at each phase in the design

process. It's not just something that has an application in one part of the Design Thinking. It

has many ways of being useful at different parts of the Design Thinking process.

When you get to concept development, Visualisation becomes incredibly useful. Your brain

is creating pictures of something that doesn't yet exist. It's creating pictures of something that

will soon be. As we move forward into prototyping, we get much more detailed in the way

that we start to visualise. Then we create very complex diagrams or maps of how we think the

customer experience is going to work ideally. Pictures and images enable us to not only help

people understand what it is we're trying to do but to help persuade them in the worthiness of

that particular idea or the strength of that concept.

This can be a little intimidating at first for some. I think that people will find that once they

start getting in the habit of doing that, you quickly see how the rest of the room responds to

you when you get up and you start drawing.

Design Thinking Reflection

Mind Mapping

Challenge:  Creating a comprehensive multi-year strategic plan that captures new value- driven company goals and objectives that allow for business growth and  innovation is a difficult task. The level of complexity increases when prioritizing  which objectives offer the most value while minimizing risk; based on stakeholder  input, market data, employee feedback, and past lessons learned.

Selection:  To better understand the individual business components (gaps, past targets, key  performance indicators, etc) and align them with the collective stakeholder input  (data, key lessons etc) I selected mind mapping as my preferred tool.

Application:  Mind mapping was instrumental in my ideation sessions held over several days  with stakeholders across my company. Each session was 2 hrs long (3 sessions  total) with key stakeholders participating in all 3 sessions. The goal of my  ideation exercises was to:   1. Level 0: Start with the organization’s mission, vision, value at the center circle

2. Level 1: Itemize the various departments/business units that are parts of the  organization as a whole

3. Level 2: Create the following groups for each department: 1. Staff 2.  Technology 3. Process

4. Level 3: Create the following categories: 1. Challenges 2. Successes 3.  Future Goals then place stakeholder input, data, insight within each bucket

5. Draw connector lines for all dependencies and/or similarities between  departments

Insight:  Having the ability to visualize the various components of my organization and  showing how each department and their challenges, successes, and goals were  directly connected gave all stakeholders that participated in the exercise much  more clarity on the current-state as well as where they needed to be for the  future-state. The mind map made prioritizing the future roadmap less complicated  since all stakeholders were onboard. We all knew we were on the same bus and  finally had a map with a pin for our destination.

Approach:  I would not change my approach. Humans are visual creatures that identify  patterns naturally, that makes mind mapping an outstanding tool that can both  capture input from lots of stakeholders in real-time and connect all components  of a challenge at a 50k ft view down to a 1k ft view.

Reflection - Storytelling

Context:  I am a content marketer and often take on freelance consulting projects to learn more about  different industries. Recently, as a part of one such project, I was asked to review and potentially  rewrite a case study for a tech company that creates business management software for activity- based organizations such as gyms, ballet studios and parks & recreation centers.     Challenge:  The case study was about how the company’s software had helped improve the day-to-day  operations of a local cheerleading gym thereby improving overall efficiencies, customer service and  coaching. The purpose of the case study was to help the tech company generate leads from the  market segment of gym owners and administrators. When I read the case study for the first time, I  was left with a vague sense of accomplishment and many unanswered questions. The way it was  written was all over the place as it tried to address too many concerns in a hurried fashion without  communicating the impact the tech company’s software solution had on the gym business.    Selection:  To tackle the rewriting challenge, I chose to use the storytelling tool. As we learned from Raymond Baird of Mars Inc. in week 2, “Storytelling is the difference between solving a problem and creating  a cause.” Stories are based on empathy and therefore are powerful tools to make any problem,  challenge or situation seem more relatable. The consumer is therefore more inclined to react to a  story than a presentation full of graphs and numbers.     Application:  Simon Sinek urges us to “start with the why” to inspire action. What this means is to get people to  do anything, we must get them to understand our purpose. When I began deconstructing the case I  was given, my first step was empathy mapping to answer the question, “who is reading this case and  why?” to put myself in the shoes of the consumer the case was trying to target. To better  understand the plight of gym owners and administrators, I asked myself questions such as “What are  the top issues faced by cheer gym owners?” and “What do the right tools look like to tackle these  issues?” among many others.  Once I had a clear understanding of the gym owners/administrators’ pain points, I was able to create  a flow for the story I was writing. This included identifying the key problem we wanted to tackle and  explicitly stating it in 1-2 lines to establish the purpose of this particular case study. Doing so also  helped me to choose which aspects of the software solution I would highlight in this case study.  Ultimately, I asked the client to identify the quantitative impact the solution had had on the gym  business in the form of time savings and return on investment.     Insight:  Any story is incomplete if it fails to answer the “so what” question. The stories that we find most  frustrating/dissatisfying are the ones that raise questions and fail to resolve them. I chose to address  the “so what” with a combination of qualitative and quantitative impact. To communicate  qualitative improvements, I leveraged testimonials from the gym owners, coaches and customers to  cover the different perspectives of various stakeholders. To communicate quantitative impact, I  created a simple, easy-to-understand infographic highlighting the top 3 metrics that gym owners  most cared about (return on investment, reduction in financial reporting errors and time savings).  The final step to get people to do something is to give them several opportunities to do it. I did this  by adding multiple calls-to-action in the case study that would allow the consumer to act on a desire  by either requesting a demo or scheduling a meeting or simply learning more about the tech  company and its solutions.

Approach:  The transformation of the case study was very evident through the results it generated once it was  published. Not only did the case study surpass the company’s monthly lead generation average but  also helped the tech company improve visitors’ time spent on the website and reduced bounce  rates. Considering the success of the case study compared to others, the storytelling approach has  now been adopted by the company to create all of its case studies.

Using the design thinking methodology to adopt a more consumer focused approach meant  addressing the consumer’s concerns instead of trying to sell a solution. Incidentally, we were able to  sell the solution as a happy by-product of this approach!

Storytelling—Bringing the Human Back Into Healthcare

Carolina Nieto, LCSW

Challenge & Selection

There are few things, if any, in life that can shake us to the core more than a threat to our health or the  health of our loved ones.  For those of us in healthcare, we are entrusted with the awesome  responsibility to care for and comfort people who may be experiencing the worst day or scariest  moment of their life.  Most of us who entered healthcare did it because of a passion for helping and  connecting with people. However, in a the current landscape of large health systems working under  insurance driven models, healthcare providers can get easily trapped in the vicious cycle of chasing  productivity driven goals with the patient as the widget to help achieve said goals and for healthcare  administrators to become so far removed from the actual patient care that a human life becomes but a

number on a report. In my opinion, storytelling is one of the most powerful tools that can bring the  human back to the center of focus and remind those of us in the healthcare industry why we are here  and why we get up and go to work every day.

In the video lecture, “storytelling Tool”, Carlos Hermosillo describes storytelling as a tool we can use  to connect to the emotions of the people when giving them the information we would like to share. It  allows us to share information and messages that have logic, but to present that information in an  interesting and interactional way that evokes an engagement in a purpose or cause, not just a  transactional dynamic of one person providing information and another person receiving information  that information.  I cannot think of a situation where it is more important to remember and emotionally  connect with the cause and purpose than it is in healthcare. There has not been a time in my healthcare  career when there has been so much focus on numbers, reports, ratings, and finances and so little focus

on the human recipient on the other end of our workflows. I believe we can use storytelling as a tool  in which to reconnect and refocus on the human beings we care for.

Application

I had the opportunity to create a new service line that included a team of providers that are charged  with providing a holistic and wrap-around approach to a group of Medicaid recipients with significant  struggles with co-morbid mental health disorders and chronic diseases, with the goal of lessening the  group’s overall healthcare spend. The care approach was fluid and flexible allowing the providers to  provide care in the way that most makes sense. Sometimes this meant the providers would work with  the clients in the community, in their homes, in healthcare offices, or via an electronic media. The  requirement for reimbursement for the model included providing at least one episode of care to each  client no less than once a month.  I created a tracking system to ensure that every client was served  each month and our budget was built on the assumption that we would serve at least 90% of our clients

each month, leaving room for the possibility of 10% of our clients not being available or having lost  contact with them.

I realized, that while the business model appeared solid, it was failing because of the lack of human  connection. I had allowed the human connection and our purpose for the work to get lost among our  team when I started to see a pattern of providers serving all of their clients only one time per month and  their efforts to serve any more clients stop as soon as they reached 90% of their client list.  I had allowed  the business and financial requirements to take priority of focus over the client care.  Through the use of  storytelling, I brought real-life examples of our clients to the team. I shared emotional stories of  successes of clients who received excellent care when providers went above and beyond one encounter

a month because that is what the client needed at the time.  I shared stories of struggles of some of  our isolated clients who felt abandoned and forgotten when they had higher needs, but their provider

stopped meeting those needs after one encounter. And I shared stories of those with the most acute  emotional and physical needs who have essentially been given up on by much of the healthcare care  providers because of their “lack of compliance” with treatment and missed appointments and shared  our team’s opportunity to be the only people in their world who will not give up regardless of missed

appointments or environmental barriers.  It was these stories that provided the reminder and  connection as to why the providers entered the field to begin with. The result was the team  conversations  and focus shifted from making the financial productivity goal to meeting the service  excellence goal.  Ultimately, it was this shift that allowed for a better financial outcome and in a more  sustainable way as the team was emotionally connecting to the reason for service—helping fellow  humans, not just to the work-place expectation of checking the box so a bill could be dropped.

Insight & Approach

If I were to summarize the insights I made in the application above in one sentence, it would be:  As a  leader, your team will follow the story you tell, make sure you are telling the right story.  In  retrospect, I recognize that early in the program development, my philosophical goal was always to  create a great service with an excellent experience for our clients, but my daily focus was that of  creating a financially viable and sustainable service line for my hospital. I expected my team to do what I

said, not what I did and hold a different primary focus than I.  I now realize that stories are not just  pre-meditated presentations to business leaders or consumers in efforts to sway their opinions, but  stories often come out in the every day actions with our peers and clients. I need to remain more

cognizant of the story that I am telling and make sure it is the story I intended to tell.

Ultimately, I am pleased with the storytelling approach used in the application above and I believe it

was successful. However, next time, I think that the stories can be shared and portrayed in more ways

than an oral presentation at a staff meeting. I need to immerse my team in the story I want to tell.  I

might supplement the oral stories with visualizations.  I could include pictures around the office  depicting the struggles and success of our clients and the healing power of the relationship between a

provider and client. I could also use journey mapping to remind the team of the complicated and  frustrating social and health system their clients have to navigate each day, thus reminding the  providers of a tangible purpose of their job. I would create more space/airtime for team members to be

active participants in sharing their clients’ stories, struggles, and successes.  The first use of  storytelling outlined in the application was a very important component to setting the stage for the

program. The constant use of storytelling is an absolute necessity in keeping the human and  emotional connection alive.

Mind Mapping

Challenge & Selection  The first tool I used was the Mind Mapping tool when I initially joined my current company where  I was brought on to chart the current onboarding process for new customers and identify areas  of opportunity for process improvements.  I decided to use this approach because I could begin  by mapping out my own onboarding experience as a customer (because I had my own data  points) which could easily be described as dreadful and I had tons of feedback. I then extended  the invitation for other associates to map out their experiences as well, giving us a broad sense  of what was happening across the process since no documentation for this existed at the time.     Application  I started the process by designating a huge whiteboard (conveniently located to senior  leadership) as the space where myself and other associates could place visuals of their  onboarding process – application information, messaging screenshots, printouts of emails  received during the onboarding time-frame, copies of welcome materials, call recordings with  service agents and relevant information about product usage/ease, etc. I also asked everyone  to write sound bites of their experience – what went well, what did not, what was devastatingly  awful, would they recommend to friends and family.  I then added actual customer complaint  verbatims to this board that we received through website surveys, social media, call listening  sessions and regulatory organizations. This whiteboard turned into a very powerful visual of an  undocumented process that was ripe with opportunity to make it better for our customers.      As more and more associates contributed their information on the board themes started to  emerge.  We grouped together pieces of the experience into groups, sorted by channel and  interaction type, which began to tell the story of the current customer onboarding process - lack  of relevant information about what was going to happen next once the product was purchased,  over communication via email regarding cross sell or simply providing useless information and  clogging inboxes, untimely delivery of product via snail mail, poor lengthy service calls with  agents that oversold additional products when customers clearly were not interested.  Senior  leadership was able to have sequenced visuals to react to and get a sense of what was  happening to our customers during this valuable first interaction with new customers.  They  were then able to prioritize projects to improve the experience for the customers and inform  impacted business lines about the current process failures and keys to best practices for future  sales.     Insight & Approach  This was the perfect tool to use to map out an undocumented process that was considered a  “black hole” within the organization. Through the use of visuals and plotting, we were able to pull  together data points compiled by actual associate experiences married with hundreds of  customer complaints to provide fact-based insight into what was actually occurring and where  things were broken, demystifying what we were assuming was happening during this vital  portion of a customer lifecycle.  We were able to pinpoint root causes of customer pain points  and make big process improvements to create a better customer experience. Associates shared  their insights and learnings with their individual teams to influence the creation of better  business processes to ensure a positive customer experience. Since the overall customer  experience told such a valuable story, next time I would like to dig deeper, using storytelling, to  show case individual customer experiences to gain even more insight into customer  needs/expectations/dislikes, etc. to implement additional process improvements.

Author: Javier Castellanos

Visualization Tool

Challenge

Earlier this year, as part of a course of Problem-Solving Methodologies that we take in college, we  were required to develop a project aimed at solving a soft problem in any kind of business or  company. A soft problem is not related to problems like productivity of a manufacturing process o  reducing costs from certain department, but it is a problem that aims to solve issues related to  interpersonal relations among workers, or even with customers. We found a local clinical analysis  laboratory that let us help them to deal with the increasing customer complaints that they were  receiving, so the laboratory’s director told us to aim our project in improving the experience of the  customer through the process that they have to go through to receive their service, since they make  the appointment until they receive their results.

Selection

When started analyzing the information that the laboratory gave us about their processes, how they  measured satisfaction and even how the organization was structured, we realized that we had a lot  of information to analyze and many stakeholders whose opinion was important and had to be taken  into account, such as the customers, the customer service department, the chemical analysis  department, and also the middle and top management. So, to understand their perspective of the  problem, we interviewed many people from all the different areas involved, and after we gathered  all the information about the interests and concerns of each of the stakeholders, we developed a  visual representation of the process using a tool called Rich Picture, which is basically using drawings  to graphically identify how a process flow, considering the physical route that the people follows  and also how the information moves through the different steps of the process and across the  departments

Application

First, we drew the first sketch of the rich picture to have a better perspective of the information that  we got from the historical data and the interviews to understand how the departments were  interconnected, which were their activities that were actually adding value to the customer and how  the information flowed through each area. Them we had a meeting with the stakeholders to show  them the sketch and explain the main issues that we found in it, so that they could give us some  feedback about it, to effectively correct mistakes and create a final sketch that we could use to  identify opportunities in the process. I think that applying this tool was great to start the project and  for the stakeholders, because in a visual way we communicated our perspective of the process more  effectively than just giving them an oral explanation of our findings, and that inspired them to give  ideas of how the process could be improved to increase the customer satisfaction with the process.

Insights

Applying this visualization tool (rich picture), we were able to have a broader perspective of the  problem and suddenly the scope of the project increased because many other problems arose that  were not directly related with how the customer was treated during the process, but also on how  the information flowed across the different departments, having a lot of delays that caused a large  lead time for the results to be sent to the customer, which at the end caused customer’s  dissatisfaction. Also, as the drawings also facilitated the stakeholders understanding of the problem,  the meeting was so productive because it became a brainstorming session in which they provided  very useful ideas and potential solutions to the problem, and we were able to use that information  for further analysis, using other useful tools, such as affinity diagrams and prioritization matrix.

Approach

In my opinion, applying visualization tools is very useful for mapping processes and to identify  opportunities to improve, and as we perceived during the project, it helped other people to  understand our perspective of the situation and inspired them to share their thoughts. But, if I an  opportunity in the future to do a project with similar characteristics, I would use the journey  mapping tool to follow the process from the client’s perspective, to better understand their reality  and the problems that they may have while passing through the different steps of the process,  because this could lead to better insights about the pain points and needs of the customers and to  the generation of better ideas to solve them.

Storytelling – A computer science course  Ana Gonzalez

Challenge & Selection

Mind mapping is a design tool that captures the mind of the customer. As Maritza Morales  explains (from video lecture week 3) the tool is used to look for patterns and insight that can  lead to a better and more creative solution. I use mind mapping to create a better  understanding of the customers mind and be able the design a holistic solution for the  customer’s needs.  By conducting mind mapping several “what if” ideas are created by the  team from the “what is”. Mind mapping was used to explore the development of a computer  science course.

One challenge with mind mapping is that team members at first can be shy and don’t want to  share their ideas. The selection of the team should be diversified since this reduce the risk of  bias and makes the creativity better. I usually use team members with different educational  backgrounds e.g. business, technology and social science otherwise the generated ideas might  be too single minded.

Application

At the first mind mapping meeting I usually start by telling the team that no idea during the  mind mapping is too stupid. For our team we usually start the mind mapping by having a  theme (product or service) that we look at from the customers viewpoint. As the mind  mapping goes on, we also use other stakeholder e.g. competitors and suppliers to find more  insight about possibilities and limitations. It is important to look at the need and solution from  different stakeholders’ point of view, by doing so the complexity of a need is better  understood.

During Covid the mind mapping sessions are done online and some limitations have been  experienced it is more difficult for team members to collaborate e.g. draw on a white board  or use sticky notes, although, there are digital tools like Canva (ww.canva.com) it is not the  same. Perhaps this will become better and more effective as the team gets better at using  digital tools for mind mapping (and also the tools/software becomes better)

Insight & Approach

The mind mapping result in the development of a few key personas that are also used in other  design step e.g. prototyping and testing. Some services can be done using different  approaches such as over phone, online or person-to-person and the prototyping and testing  could be done by using first using personas and later real customers.

Often the personas are not only key customer groups that could be found by doing customer  segmentation i.e. who are our largest and most profitable customer groups, the 20/80 rule  (20 percent of our customers generate 80 percent of our profit). The personas can be  important for example influencer or early adopters that are important if our product and  service will become successful. Competition is fierce and to get a competitive advantage is  difficult.

Diversity is important I made the mistake of creating a team of members with the same  education and the discussions and ideation was limited to look at possibilities and limitations  from one certain point of view and no one challenged the assumptions behind this point of  view. One insight for the computer science course was to not change the programming  language at this time, since other courses also would need to change, also the paying student  preferred to keep Java as programming language.

By doing mind mapping we also understood the importance of all stakeholders, the suppliers  are very important and can be crucial in the development of a service or product. We now  think more about creating strong business networks together with our partners. Mind  mapping is a great tool to generate a lot of ideas in a short amount of time. The team  continuously learns from each mind mapping session and improves the teamwork.

This is due to the extreme  amount of paperwork, financial history & requirements that are unrealistic for SME’s.  We (a bank in the UAE) had the opportunity to collaborate with the UAE government,  regulators & the team responsible for a “digital shift” federal initiative.       Selection (WHY)  Visualization, as described by Denise Gomez, is a method or tool of thinking visually  which allows a multitude of people, or their brains, to be on “the same page”. A way  for everybody to be able to relate to & understand the problem, idea or solution the  same way. Visualization removes the ambiguity & imagination our brains do naturally  when in discussion or when reading words by replacing it with pictures, diagrams or  drawings.     For this reason, visualization was used throughout this project and throughout the  design thinking process. With a number of different stakeholders, expertise & a  range of understanding of the problem, visualization was seen as the best way to  achieve mutual understanding and also a way of expediting meetings, explanations  and ideating.       Application (HOW)  As mentioned, visualization was used throughout the project from discovery or the  “What is” phase of Liedtka’s process (whiteboarding, stakeholder mapping & process  mapping) to final concept (wireframing, storyboarding etc.). For the purpose of this  document, I have selected an example where visualization was extremely beneficial  - “digitising paper forms into a web application”.    I was tasked with evaluating the current process of account creation, with multiple  forms and documents to be submitted by the applicant. After a full evaluation I  presented my findings to all stakeholders by showing them a complete application,  around 5cm thick worth of documents and a simple user journey between the sales  rep & customer. Not only did this  highlight the number of times duplicate information was asked from the customer but  also the amount of “non mandatory” information. Having a full view of the stack of  documents, customer journey & the diagram made the project team realise how  tedious and unfriendly the customer experience was.

THE CHALLENGE1

I am a systems thinker, learning to think-design. In the last six months I have been involved  in a multidisciplinary design project led by design teachers and students from Alliance University. The project has to do with Concord, an amusement park under construction in  Costa Rica.  Concorde is going to be a park able to offer its Costa Rican’s (CR) visitors a  space-time shell for both a ludic reunion with their culture and with ancestral mother earth.  And for non-Costa Ricans an opportunity to know more about this rich culture-nature.  As a  matter of fact, the originators and financial supporters of this undertaking aim at building a  thematic park able to offer visitors a variety of ludic interactive experiences to recover both  the meanings that historically have shaped CR’s cultural identity and the respect for their  natural legacies.

In preliminary meetings with management to define the design challenge, they pointed out  that they had paid much attention to the “reunion with the culture” aspect of the project but  that they needed to think more thoroughly the “reconnecting with mother earth” aspect.   Accordingly, management posed the following challenge: design experiences that could  open the senses of the visitors to the surrounding nature and to the particular disruptive ways  we relate to her.

We began our design-thinking process with the what is stage. Accordingly, we launched a  series of activities such as interviews to management, gathering of relevant written and video  materials and visits to the park under construction. Using tools like mind mapping, several  issues began to emerge from the data thus collected. One issue was related to management  preoccupation with appropriate waste disposal in the park and how to relate this to the need  to contribute to raise consciousness on the harm done to nature and to the future viability of  the planet, shall our intensive-waste economies continue to rule the world. In this direction  they felt an amusement park could be a powerful educational tool. As a matter of fact, they  said   the park should be a living example to their visitors of respect and care for nature. They  wanted to make transparent to the visitors the innumerable provisions management has taken  during the construction of the park (35% so far) to protect the surrounding flora and fauna,  the natural sources of water, and to ensure a clean energy supply. Another “proof” of their  concern with environmental issues was their adoption of circular economy practices in the  operation of Concord. An interesting insight arose from one interview in which one of the  managers explained why the park’s name was Concord: We want visitors learn to weave a  new covenant with mother nature. Some design criteria also began to emerge. The

educational activities of the park should make ample use of ludic and experiential learning.  Visitors should be invited to experiment and play to become aware of their connection with  nature (or the lack of it).
