Another idea related to the  previous one was the use of banners throughout the park with pictures representing flora and  fauna of the region and a QR code to obtain 3D eco-information on the spot.

After a couple of months, we programmed the first meeting with management to elicit their  feedback on some of these ideas to tackle the challenge. Their reaction was: we like them but  they are quite unarticulated both between themselves and in relation to some attractions of  Concord like the Butterfly Nursery or the mythological malokas (like huts where mother  nature plays a central role). At this point comes into play the Storytelling Tool whose  application I would like to present in this written assignment.

SELECTION OF THE TOOL

We felt our power point presentations were far from inspirational. Furthermore, as  management has pointed out, our business ideas were quite unarticulated.  A story, we  thought, could help us to string them together in a coherent meaningful whole. Which in turn  will help us to inspire our clients, in relation to the challenge. Storytelling is a powerful tool  used by design thinkers to communicate business concepts in a way that is inspirational for  business leaders and stake holders involved in a design-challenge situation. (Week 2. Video:  Storytelling tool). Its power lies in that we are, as many have said, storytelling beings. That  is why we all resonate with a good story. There is an emotional connection with it that allows  design thinkers to more easily communicate with business managers.

APPLICATION OF THE SELECTED TOOL

Voyage to the center of mother earth. This was the Vernian-like title of the story we created.  Visitors would undertake a reunion journey with mother earth to ask her forgiveness and  listen to her breezy words of wisdom to help humanity draw a new covenant to save Pacha- Gaia-Us. In this new covenant the earth will recover its sacred condition and humans will  become again her sacred children, committed both to mend the harm made, and care and  honor their mother ever after.

The journey starts in a Maloka (American Indian hut) with an introduction to the visitors to  the local Pachamama mythologies of ancestral cultures of Central and South America. The  universality of this archetypal figure is shown to the visitor by introducing Gaia, the ancestral  mother of all life in Greek mythology. These mythologies were powerful “stories” which  inspired and organized human action for centuries in complete harmony with nature. How  have we become to the present condition on the verge of the total destruction of the earth?

Perhaps we need a new powerful mythology, within which a new covenant with mother  nature can be embedded. These reflections will set the tone for the journey to the center of  mother earth (Pacha-Gaia).

The trip will unfold through a trail which has five stations related to the five senses. In each  station the initial message will be revisited. In effect, visitors will receive a gift from mother  earth followed by a short video showing how that gift has been destroyed by us, consciously  or unconsciously. In the first station visitors will come across Dancing Colors. It is a butterfly  nursery. Butterflies of the region are well known for the beautiful colors of their wings.  In  this setting, one will be able to appreciate their magnificent colors flying and drawing all  kinds of color patterns in the air. In the same place visitors will see a video showing how  intensive agriculture based on agrochemicals has poisoned this beautiful gift. Before heading  to the next station, visitors will be asked to reflect on how are they responsible of this tragedy.  In the next four stations, Healing Fragrances (a flower garden), Golden Nuggets (Maize, a  sacred plant, a gift from the Sun God), Garden of  Sounds (nature-made sounds),  and  Caress  (barefooting walking on grass, or a path of stones and water, or simply plain earth), the gift  followed by the gift destruction and the self-reflection pattern will be repeated, the only  difference being that  the reflection at each station will be compounded with the previous  reflections  to finally reach  a climax: the encounter with Pacha-Gaia at the end of the trail.

The storytelling approach to communicate to management our business concept was  remarkably much better than our previous ppt. presentation. In addition, the voyage story    allowed management to see how this whole narrative could help to define more clearly the  identity of the Concord park. In fact, some of the settings required in each stage of this  Journey were already in place in the park (particularly the butterfly’s nursery and the  mythological hut), and others could be integrated into the narrative to provide visitors with a  holistic experience.

INSIGHT AND APPROACH

An eye opener was to see how difficult was to communicate a complex business concept  using traditional ppt. presentations (even when taking care of choosing very carefully the  images in such presentations). The story telling tool improved communication with  management 100%. An alternative approach came to mind during the application of the ST  tool. It was the use of Visualization in the form of a storyboard.  The linear direction of the  cells in a storyboard is quite suitable for storytelling.

Reflection – Learning Launch

Submitted by: Steven Richards

Date: November 25 2018

Challenge and Selection:  My first experience of using tools related to Design Thinking was the  Learning Launch – or Experimentation.  I’ve been working with a number of global consultants from  all over the world in seeking hypothetical, disruptive innovations that World Wild Foundation might  potentially consider commercializing and scaling as part of their existing Consumer Health portfolio.   This was an entirely hypothetical example for them to consider – and may never see the light of day  – but we need to show them how the innovation process works and what it might produce.  As part  of that innovation phase – a critical part of it involved collecting external data from pharma  executives, technologists and actual consumers to validate if any of the rather zany products or  services we were creating might actually have merit in considering.  Thus a Learning Launch was  undertaken to develop a hypothesis for each of the proposed products (10 in all), and we quickly  realized that, as many of our ideas utilized the same technologies (block chain, VR, big data, nano- technology, wearables, etc.) we might be able to consolidate 10 product Learning Launches and  reduce that number to about 4, as we had very limited time and needed to move fast.  Learning  Launch provided us the critical platform to take our rather wild ideas and see if there were any  issues, worries, challenges or out-right fails associated with chasing these further down the  innovation path.

Application:  We started by looking at the core or ‘crux’ hypotheses we needed to test with external  sources – and identified 4 key hypotheses to address.  In each of these, we need then to determine  what were the most effective means of gathering the most illustrative data that would either  validate our concepts – or prove them to be ineffective, too expansive, technologically impossible or  otherwise of little concern to the consumer and/or problematic with our client company.  We  ultimately landed on using on-line surveys using Survey Monkey, where we sought demographic  data to address ethnographics, then dug into the challenges/problems the respondents experienced,  and further drilled down (based on answers to key questions), as to what their experience was with  each of these elements in terms of available relief or cure.  This was used to qualify respondents to  be able to participate in the next phase of questioning.   We then introduced a prototype concept to  them, simply explaining the basics and what use cases we planned to implement. This then framed  up the follow on questions that queried whether or not they would feel comfortable engaging with  the technologies we proposed, the techniques and methods involved, and whether or not they  would consider using these concepts were they readily available tomorrow.  We were seeking, as Heiko Meier described in week 4’s Learning Launch presentation, the truth about whether or not our ideas  were even worth considering – or would the fall at the first hurdle.  We further sought open-ended  responses as to why they might use or not use our disruptive innovations – and then poured through  the results in earnest.  We launched these extensive surveys via various social media tools to gain  access to as large a sample size as we could – to maintain a level of statistical significance.

We then divided the responses into appropriate groups covering each of the disruptive innovations  we were seeking insight about – then into ethnographic categories, to see if patterns would emerge  on that demographic breakout.

In some cases – where responses appeared to lead towards deeper, more insightful learning – we  reached out to individuals for one-to-one interviews (with their permission, of course), and dug  further into the details of why they responded the way they did, and why they would either choose  to engage or pass on the concepts we created.  We were deeply aware of confirmation bias, and  seeking to really understand why the sceptics were feeling the way in which they did.

We then met as a team with a specific focus – which was only to validate or invalidate the concepts  – based solely on the data we received back, and sought to ignore any personal attachment to the  concepts we’d created initially.

Insight and Approach:  The insights we gained by reviewing the data from the surveys and interviews  was rather insightful – and challenged all of us to reconsider several aspects of our disruptive  innovations.  We found the people had very specific notions and pre-conceptions about the pharma  industry, misuse of personal data, the use of wearable data gathering devices and multiple  perspectives (POVs) represented from each of the constituent groups (internal pharma execs,  consumers, technologists).  What we quickly realized was that all parties felt that the innovation  activity that led to our particular concepts were laudable and worth exploring ultimately as ideas for  the future.  But in most cases – only the least invasive concepts were ultimately rewarded with an  appropriate level of validation – mostly in the realm of using wearable devices such as smart  watches or using VR tools (but not implants, smart tattoos or nanotech ingestible technology).   Other ideas that involved genomics, open source data-base queries using their personal data (even  anonymously using block chain management) and creating a highly personalized ‘Health Cockpit’  were met with high levels of scepticism – based on the multitude of data breaches, misuse by profit  driven insurance companies, and poor data management in previous efforts to create data oceans  by the likes of Google working with the National Health Service in the UK – as well as the typical  commercial selling of personal data to marketing companies.  Invasive technologies were also met  with a level of concern – mostly around the unknown effects these devices might have on the  human body – not to mention what is done with the data they create and who owns it ultimately.

This was massively mind-expanding and brought to bear many aspects and knock-on effects of  intense media coverage, negative perceptions of capitalistic organizations, misuse of personal  information, the seemingly tone-deaf and uncaring approach that major technology companies have  architected their early experiments – as well as how they’ve dealt with security breaches –  ultimately leading to an overall mistrust of new technologies potentially producing the same  negative outcomes for our respondents.  Had we simply went along with our own biases, where we  felt new technologies offered powerful diagnostic insights, leading to new treatment regimes, new  drug creation or use of alternative means to reduce anxiety, ease pain and suffering and reduce  dependence on drugs – we might have imagined humanity would receive us with open arms and  consume what we created with great enthusiasm.  We would have used traditional business  modelling, creating presumptive market penetration and use acceptance data – likely using  previously existing research that was confirming of our innovative use of technology – and never  would have seen the brick wall sitting in front of us as we sped along that the road ahead was wide

open.  This exercise in seeking ‘the truth’ and removing confirmation bias challenges, while then  focusing only on whether or not the raw data received either validated or invalidated our original  hypotheses save us time, money, and wasted innovation and manufacturing cycles, not to mention  failed marketing and sales activity and reputational damage we could have imposed on an unwitting  client who otherwise might have been completely sold on our ideas.

Teresa’s Reflection- Mind Mapping  Challenge  I work as an intern in the human resources department of a startup company. Our  team plans to implement a project that would improve employer branding strategies.  Employer branding is how the company is viewed by employees, in other words, it is  about how to market the company to desired job seekers. A positive employer brand  is very critical in the increasingly competitive job market nowadays because hiring  and retaining the best employees could be challenging and costly. Our team wants to  attract senior talents in specific fields through this project to improve the  recruitment difficulties in these specific departments, and we decided to mind  mapping for clarifying the design criteria before brainstorming the “how-to” ideas.  The challenge of mind mapping is that we do not have much budget to invite lots of  stakeholders. Moreover, this is also our team’s first time trying mind mapping and  none of us has experience of it, so we might encounter some problems due to  unfamiliarity.     Selection  Our team has gained much information including company values and culture,  location and facilities, overall compensation, management style, and so on.  Therefore, we need to organize the data properly and find out the crucial design  criteria before brainstorming, that is why I chose mind mapping tool. At this point,  my team decided to invite 15 senior talents of specific fields from inside or outside  the company to a meeting, and all of them are our target audience for recruitment.  Our team decided to mind mapping with post-it notes. We explained the data we  have first, and gave each participant a stack of sticky posts, and ask everyone to note  on separate sticky posts any item they believe could inform ideas. The reason why I  chose post-it notes for mind mapping is that participants are able to classify ideas by  different colors notes, moreover, everyone can see each other’s posts easily and  stimulate more ideas. I will explain more about how we apply it in the next part.    Application  Our team conducted mind mapping step by step. As mentioned above, we first  illustrated our data and then asked the participants to write down their thoughts on  sticky posts. In particular, this activity was limited in time for promoting senses of  urgency in order to encourage sharing every thought rather than carefully measure  each idea. After that, participants started with only one theme at a time, presenting  related sticky posts on a board while others who had thoughts related to the theme  could stick the posts nearby. Then moved on to another theme, and so forth, until

everyone stuck their posts on the board. Next, we led the participants to identify the  meaningful insights behind their observations by discussing and asking questions.  They were also asked to note the connections between each theme or insight to find  the core insights. Last, it is our team's work to grasp the design criteria, and we did  understand some important conditions that our method for improving employer  branding must satisfy. For instance, our method will have to be shown on websites  that most of our target talents constantly review rather than popular social media.    Insight & Approach  What I learned from mind mapping with my team is that this really allows us to stay  on the “what is” and clarify before generating innovative ideas, and we could listen  to different perspectives of participants from diverse backgrounds. Mind mapping  also avoids us from starting the solution-generating process and judging others' ideas  at the beginning, which often clutters the entire discussion.   Although it is an effective tool to use on looking for design criteria for startup  companies, we do come across some messy situations while mind mapping, perhaps  teams who try to mind map have the same problems at first. Since the participants  are senior talents, some of them are managements, I found that they usually rush to  draw conclusions and possible solutions. Another relative situation I found was that  some interesting thoughts were not expressed at first because participants thought  they were not 100% related to the theme, and they were afraid that people might  question their abilities. These conditions might be due to the negative experience of  traditional meetings, people just jump to conclusions and start looking for direct  solutions, which makes it hard to see other possibilities.   To solve the problems, I tried to encourage everyone to stay on mind mapping, and  don’t rush to generate solutions and draw conclusions. This also made me realize  that mind mapping is easier said than done, and it needs lots of practice to subvert  the traditional thinking mode.

Employees need to understand the need of  observing certain procedures and to be able to see how that affects their day-to-day work. Visualization  tools like drawings, images, sketches, flowcharts help to connect and develop step-by-step understanding  and build a visual aspect to it. ASSIGNMENT REFLECTION  Busi Tarek  2019-12      Challenge

Last year, as part of my master’s degree in Digital Marketing, I wrote a professional thesis

about the “what’s for dinner tonight” question. I wanted to understand why, even today with

all the digital tools available, it is still complicated for families to decide easily what to eat at

home on weekday evenings. I learned a lot during my thesis research. But, when I decided

to turn it in a product or service, I felt that my school research was good, but too light to

reflect the true reality of my primary user group. I had plenty pain points on my whiteboard,

but finally no really idea what the real problem was.       Selection

I decided to conduct further individual interviews with a group of ten users, mothers between

25 and 45 years old. I began created an interview guide with a dozen open-ended questions

focusing on my user's behaviors in the kitchen and it was in its first version, the perfect

boring survey. I realized that just asking a question would not bring me the genuine answer.

Especially since in France, it is almost disturbing to say loud and clear that we don't care

about what we eat... this is becoming less and less socially acceptable.   I needed a way to encourage my users to express themselves freely and fully. And that's

when a friend of mine suggested I use images. According to him, images are very useful to

capture non verbal thoughts or emotions. I chose to try this tool called visualization, hoping

that it would unlock any discomfort by placing the user in their daily situations and actions.       Application

This was my first time using this method. I chose to try it on two potentially sensitive

questions : “what does it mean to you to cook?” and “how's mealtime with your kids?”. With

these two questions I wanted to know how important it is for my interviewee to respect and

pass on the principles of good nutrition.   For the first question, I searched on Google and chose 15 images I felt relevant to me ; a

smiling family eating pizzas in front of the TV, a plate of pasta with ham, industrial products

already prepared, a mother and her daughter cooking with joy, a pot overflowing …   For the second question, it’s was more difficult to find a diversity of situations. When you

Google “cook with your kid” or “what children eat?” you just find a lot of cliché pictures. So I

selected 10 ; child sulking in front of vegetables, child smiling in front of an orange juice,

child happy to eat a hamburger…    Each batch of images was put in an envelope and when the question arrived in the interview

I took them out and laid on the table in front of my user. Then, I asked to select the ones that

were meaningful to her. Once the images were separated into two packs, I asked to explain

each choice freely.

Insights

Thanks to this exercise with images, I learned more specific aspects on my targets -

especially with the first question. Their approach to food was much more complex than two

opposing camps, fresh produce versus industrial products. For the majority, food was an

important subject, but the choice of whether or not to cook was subject to multiple

influencing factors such as the weather and the products available, the family's desires and

the mood of the day. However, the visualization tool appeared not relevant for the second

question. The choice of life situations was too limited and didn't really seem to touch the

hearts of my targets. Even if I progressed in my discovering, the insights I collected lacked

something to fully embrace my primary question.      Approach

This experiment convinced me about images on a discovery process. But next time, I’ll do a

little bit differently to gain more precise insights. I’ll select 10 images maximum, because with

more, I had the feeling that users were lost. I will spend more time on the pictures selection

to be sure to express various and relevant situations.   I’ll also try a new approach with dot voting. As I read a post on the MOOC forum about it, I

found this approach very interesting. I am thinking about trying it with images to identify

emotions linked to situations. I plan to choose three colors ; green for feeling at ease, orange

for a neutral emotion, and red for upsetting circumstances.     In any case, I am going to continue exploring design thinking because I really enjoyed this

first experience.

Using Visualization in Business Coaching

(Design Thinking Assignment – by Vipan Rashmi)

Challenge

I have recently started practicing business coaching for young entrepreneurs as a full-time  career after almost 27 years of corporate software professional experience. During my  coaching sessions with young entrepreneurs, it has always been challenging to understand  their vision, product roadmap and business plan as nothing is ever documented. All the  ideas and plans are in their head and every time I meet them, I used to get a different  version of it.

Selection

After the Design Thinking lecture of Module 1, I decided to implement visualization technique  in my coaching sessions to make it more effective. I started using “In-Time Timeline”, “cross- road” and “future visual” to pen down their ideas and plan. I picked the “In-Time Timeline”  tool so that I could visually make them traverse time to get better understanding of their  business plan and product roadmap. I used “cross-road” to put their various options before  taking a decision. I also use “future visual” way of visualization for them to imagine a live  event happening after a year that gives them maximum happiness and satisfaction (like  giving a speech after winning a trophy/award, spending time with family at a hill top resort,  opening a new office, etc.). These tools were selected so that I could go back to these  visuals to arrive at a common meeting point.

Application

Let me share three examples where I applied these tools. In first case, I asked the 2 co- founders in a coaching session, to draw their business plan for a year. I used “future visual”  and asked them to visualize where they would be, how they would be feeling, what would be  their customer saying about them, what would be market talking about them, how much  revenue they would be having after a year. As they started talking, I kept on documenting  the points on the timeline. I asked them to keep that visual picture in their head that will  always inspire them.

In second case, I asked my coachee to visualize a meeting with his client – I asked him to  visualize the room, the chair, table, clothes, smell, temperature, etc during the meeting –  then visualize the discussion. I kept on documenting and drawing on paper as he spoke.

In third instance, there were 2 founders and were not clear of the direction to move the  company – they had to choose from designing new product feature, go for angel funding,  develop skills in team, or a mix of any two. I used “cross road” picture and drew a road, drew  2 people walking on it and reaching a “cross-road” that had 4 possible directions to take.  Using that picture, we discussed about the path to choose that would finally lead them to the  final destination.

Needless to say, at the end of these sessions, the founders, in all 3 cases, were very  pleased with the outcome as they could visually recollect the discussion!!

Insight

I realized that visualization is a great tool to be used in coaching as coaching is also about  energizing your right brain. As a coach also, we need to ask powerful questions, we need to

be patient and empathetic, should be able to connect the dots, etc. just like it’s mentioned in  this course. I have bought Professor Daniel H. Pink’s book “A Whole New Mind” and will use  insights from it as well as visualization tool more in my coaching sessions.

Also, I see visualization can be applied more broadly in any situation where I have to explain  my point of view or understand others viewpoint. I plan to use it with my children soon!!

Approach

As an extension of using visualization in coaching, I would be adding story telling in my  coaching session. I plan to use visualization and storytelling together – so for example, after  using the timeline tool for visualizing, then, in the next session I plan to narrate the whole  thing as a movie story - starting with the last scene first and then saying “12 months before”  and just unfold all the events. I think that will bring logic, emotional connection and meaning  in the coaching sessions along with the visual impact. I have not been a good story teller in  my life and it would be good for me learn this skill as well!!

Challenge and Selection

Coming from a family who were Joseph Campbell gurus, members of AA and  writers, Storytelling is a revealing tool of connection, information, and shared  insight.

This was the first time I was on the other side of the deal. Instead of asking for  investments for operating Vessels, I was now on the financer investor side. The  president had called for an off site conference to work on our deal closing  process and ask all of us to contribute new ideas that could improve closing  portfolio deals. Application

As a new employee, I decided that for me to contribute anything of value, I  needed to have more information about the company’s deal procedures. Like  any small busy office, free time to explore is rare, except lunchtime. Most days  we have a choice to eat at our desk, go out or eat in the conference room. The  off- site conference was 3 weeks away, and I needed to get as much  background information as possible, so I started asking anyone to come have  lunch with me in the conference room, that I didn’t want to mess up the  paperwork on my desk. Slowly within the first week, most of the 15 employees  were having lunch together from 30 minutes to an hour in the conference  room.  I put together several prompt questions in my head to encourage  employees to tell their experiences on past deals. Whenever there was a lull in  the conversation, I would use one of my prompts, i.e. “What was the best or  worst deal you ever had, and followed up with what made it so great or  horrible?”.  Eventually the funny, euphoric, and disaster stories came pouring  out. My favorite one was an 11th hour hold on wire transfers because an Owner  purchasing a vessel did not want to pay for 50 pounds of ghee butter in the  stores onboard the ship. One lunch lasted 2 hours as we heard the stories of 3  past costly deals. The natural sharing of experiences became a midday stress  relief. After lunch I would quickly write on post-it notes the highlights of each

story. Days before the conference, I put together common themes of the story  telling including my perspective from my past history of being on the other side  of the deal table. I combined the paraphrased story quotes to present to the  conference, highlighting the common areas where the specific procedures were  key to the success or common roadblocks that kept repeating themselves.

As a new employee I was essentially an outsider, and I wasn’t able to provide  answers, but I was able to contribute a non threatening spot light on common  key components from both sides of the deal process.

The story sharing was a wealth of information, that revealed several times  international funds were delayed during investment closings, late information  that rendered a deal dead with much expense to tales of Ship owner’s  disagreements on last minute inventories while partaking in several shots of  vodka. I do not come from a design thinking background, but have realized that  design thinking tools can be used even for the smallest projects. Anyone  regardless of position or experience can apply design thinking tools to find  improvement.  I found people love to share their own history, with humor and  to this day most of us still have lunch together in the conference room. I plan  to continue to incorporate and explore the tools I have learned as I pursue my  midlife career, and volunteer work.

I am currently working in the Human Resources Department.  One of the most  important pillars of management consists in carrying out actions that promote and  maintain a healthy work environment in which employees can feel comfortable with  their workplace, with their leaders, with their colleagues and with the responsibilities  assigned  to their job position.    Several times, the efforts made to achieve this ideal work climate are not easily  perceived by the staff. Application

In my previous job, we held an activity called Semiannual Congress every six months  in which each area manager had to share the efforts and results of their management  during the semester that was ending.    In one occasion, we were about to conduct the survey that allowed us to measure  the level of satisfaction of the staff in relation to the work environment in the  company. It was going to  be conducted a few weeks after the Bi-Annual Congress,  in which 100% of the staff was present.  It was considered an excellent opportunity  to communicate the actions that was needed for the employees to recognize and  value the excellent place to work that was this company. For that purpose I made  my presentation supported by the History Telling tool.    For this presentation I created a character named “Pedro”.  The story begins since  Pedro first day at his new job in the company.  The presentation includes striking  images, background music, animation and my voice as the narrator of Pedro's story.    I was developing in history each of the stages that Pedro had gone through since  the induction process. It was accompanied by the benefits that each of these stages  represented for Pedro and the emotions that he felt passing through each stage.    I included information like when the photo was taken for the identification badge,  adding phrases such as “he gave his best smile to look very professional in the  photo”, “he felt joyful and excited at that moment that he was confirmed part of a  great company”. Wearing that badge would allow him to tell his family and friends  about the great job he had gotten.     After that, it was mentioned how he got to know his work team and other personnel,  how they supported him to get to know the company. How he was learning and  growing through the training plan that the company offered him and how he could  share with the other team members in the activities in which he was invited to  participate. Also, it was shared about  the celebrations that were held and how he

Valeri Barco  History Telling Tool      was also part of them.  How he had the opportunity to participate in the creation of  new initiatives and committees, and also how the benefits that the company offered  helped him to be well organized, take care of his health, etc.    Insight

The idea of this story was to offer Pedro some guidance and companion during the  time that he had been working in the company, how he lived the company culture. Design Thinking for Innovation                                                                                 Nandan Velasco

1. Challenge

During my Master Thesis in Marketing, one of my course mate (let’s call him Nandan) asked  me and 5 other students to develop an idea. The idea itself was quite broad and not  well defined, and since Nandan didn’t explain this idea to all of us simultaneously, we all  have different opinions and impressions about that. Briefly, the idea was to build a  website where students like us, or just young people, could visit and check which are  the nicest spots in the city, events and so on. Of course, we wanted to make it different  from other similar websites, and this was the main challenge. No one of us had any  particular skill but we were all diverse in our personality and mindset, so we all had  different points of view, which can help in terms of creativity but can make it slow when  it comes in taking decisions.

2. Selection

The tool we selected was Mind Mapping (of course, without knowing it). This tool looks  for patterns and insights in the data collected, and it’s especially used when it comes  to establish some criteria and assumptions for the next steps. Since our team was  formed by 7 people with different “personas”, we thought that mapping would be  better to pull together what we had in our minds in a way that we could all add some  value... some smaller idea into this project.

3. Application

Basically, everything we did was meet and brainstorm, by trying to understand how to  develop this idea in something that was different, more creative... and maybe  innovative?! We had meeting once per week and the week before we always had some  assignment like “write down from 3 to 5 column you’d like to have in the website” with  no restrictions. Then, once we met we were looking at all the different proposals.  However, the main purpose of Mind Mapping is to clarify what is not clear and to  converge all the smaller ideas into a main one. Unfortunately, we didn’t manage to do  it. What we had in our mind was somehow different from each other. We didn’t find a  starting point as well as an ending one. For instance, someone believed it was better to  make it more social-based, while someone else though it would be better to make it  more informational. As I learnt from Design Thinking course, when reflection and  disagreement are involved in the process, it becomes inefficient.

4. Insight

What I understood from this experience and from what I studied in Design Thinking is  that an idea cannot simply be developed. The process from idea generation to its  development is intricate. In that team, we all had good ideas but they just didn’t fit with  each other’s. The reason why we just stopped meet after a while was that we were not  even sure what we were trying to develop anymore. When the idea is too broad and  vague, insights are way too harsh to find.

5. Approach

Now I understood that our mistake was that we didn’t start in a proper way. Before  applying any tool, we also should have clear in our mind what we and our customers  were looking for. What is the opportunity? What is the purpose of our project? What is  our plan? These basic questions didn’t have answers for us, so it’s easily understandable

that this project didn’t go in the right way. Next time instead of rushing with  brainstorms and Mind Mapping I would rather consider other ways to make the idea  more concrete. Nandan should have shown us the idea using another Design Thinking  tool, like Visualization which comes in an earlier stage and helps in making an abstract  idea more real.

Maybe we were just nobodies… or perhaps we just needed a different approach.

The first and most obvious fact is that the overall temperature is getting

hotter. The statistic shows that the global annual temperature has increased at an  average rate of 0.07°C per decade since 1880 and over twice that rate (+0.18°C)  since 1981. People need to somehow cool down  their flats or houses and the request for air conditioners and cooling systems has  risen in the past years.

Not only does our society know about the climate change problem, but it also

is looking for a solution to it. Some actions have already been taken and some are  just about to be so. Climate change has proved the weakness of the modern economic  model. For more than 60 years the economy of consumption was thought to be the  most effective and dominant model, however, its time has to end very soon in order  to slow down global warming. Here’s why: first of all, the more natural resources  people consume, the more damage it brings to our planet because of the greenhouse  gases’ emission. have already started using alternative sources of energy such as solar batteries, wind  farms, wave power plants, etc. These energy sources do no harm to the atmosphere  and help slow down climate change and global warming.

income”. This idea has been supported by many scientists across the world. This is  how it works: a tax will be imposed on fossil fuel companies and the revenue will  be handed out to people. economy is positive or negative. On one hand, it “kills” some niches of the economy  and makes people lose money. Even though there are might be some difficulties now,  I tend to think that the impact of climate change on the economy is rather positive.  Sooner or later, people would learn how to earn money without terrorizing the  natural resources so that we can keep our planet clean and safe.

Challenge      Storytelling as one of the strategies for design thinking requires more personal interaction

considering that it is an ‘essential human activity’.  It allows one to share experiences reflective of  his/her values and comes up with possible solutions through verbal and visual accounts.         It is in this context that the use of this as a strategy for design thinking in a formal

organization becomes a challenge.  The methodology for solving problems focuses more on asking  questions and requires more listening with empathy to the needs of the members of the  organization including its stakeholders. Apart from it, not all group members find it easy to share  their personal accounts.  The sharing of the narrative of the members can only be done once trust,  motivation and confidence are built between and among those who are within the organization.       Selection      Storytelling can be a powerful strategy for design thinking considering that it is provides

the “big picture” of the organization.  The organization’s including the members’ narrative are  presented in a manner that the story of each one completes the entire picture.  It will move the  organization in coming with the appropriate plan as demanded by the ‘stories’ of the group  members.        It is in this context that storytelling becomes a lead way in setting up goals and objectives

for the organization.  The consideration for these process is anchored on the personal accounts  and narratives of the group members who are providing the context for brainstorming and for  developing new insights which can utilized in coming up with organization’s plan.     Application      Storytelling as a strategy for design thinking have been utilized in my workplace.  As one

who is into the provision of capacity development activities which come in the form of training  and facilitation activities, this strategy has been applied.  Specifically, it is used to get insights from  the participants and members of the organization, to build empathy in reaching them emotionally  when they have to share personal ‘stories’ and in coming-up with possible conflict resolution  measures on some narratives of the group members or whenever it is required by the situation.      This strategy requires more personal interaction with the ones involved.  The ‘designer’

has to give due consideration on the personal ‘stories’ and narratives which are very personal in  nature to come up with possible solutions on the issues or concerns.  There should be more  ‘balancing’ of what the mind and heart takes to get a solution(s) which are appropriate on the  situation.

Insight      Storytelling is very powerful and at the same time an inspiring way to come up with

solutions.  The solutions are framed based on the stories and or narratives of the group members  and the stakeholder(s) involved.  The accounts of events including their reflections and insights of  a given condition or situation are real and experiential which make it very significant in the  organization. The stories which provide concrete details can easily move ‘designers’ in coming up  with solutions which are based on the experiences.  Further, it strategy which will allow designers  to get narrations can inspire to have more opportunities, ideas and solutions.     Approach      Storytelling as a strategy aids in explaining the interconnectedness between and among

the members of the organizations including the stakeholders, situations and settings or the  situations.  Further, it generates relevant lessons as it engages the ‘human’ side of the  organization, specifically the people.  To quote Tim O’Brien, writer, Storytelling is the essential  human activity. The harder the situation, the more essential it is. Thus, to come up with a design  that is giving due emphasis on the human side and at the same time getting better understanding  on the behavior and attitude of the people in the organization, storytelling as an approach in  getting solutions on the issues and concerns in the organization can be adopted and or  appropriated.

Ahmed Elnemr // Reflection – Learning Launch

Challenge

I am founder and president of an art and culture association in Milan, Italy. Since its foundation, this association has  had the goal to engage foreign students and expats living in Milan and the Italian society in a dialogue through cultural  events. For this purpose, we design and produce numerous cultural events (mostly concerts) during a year and this  requires a comprehensive knowledge of the audience. Initially, to understand better our market, we relied on  traditional market research methods. Thus, we sent out surveys to define our target audience’s taste and preferences.  However, the results were not satisfying. Non-Italian respondents were interested in cultural events that would not  attract the Italian audience, therefore, they could not result in the desired interaction between these two  communities.

Moreover, we wanted our cultural events to be of high quality and have a positive impact on the cultural taste  of our  foreign community. Cultural events which precisely matched this community’s taste could not result in their cultural  growth, and thus did not satisfy us as cultural activists. Our confusion and lack of experience resulted in a dramatic  failure of our first project. We organized a high-quality jazz event in one of the best music halls in the city. This event  cost us a lot of money and energy, but, unfortunately, our ticket sales were not even close to satisfying and the  expected interaction between foreigners and Italians, of course did not happen. Following this defeat, we decided to  take a different path and try a new approach.

Selection

After an extensive discussion in the association, we decided to try the Learning Launch or the experimentation  approach. We decided to follow the suggestion of Dennis Lehmann that he made in his lecture: “The key is to do experiments  that are fast and cheap”.

Application

After convincing other members of the association, we decided to design a higher number of smaller and more  affordable projects which could be implemented more frequently. This allowed our learning-by-doing and to helped  us to improve our cultural events in process considering feedback from the audience and other stakeholders. Since  then, our cultural events were prototypes, designed and planned in collaboration with our audience, which was  enabled to express its opinions and discuss the event’s content, schedule, timing, etc. on our social media platforms.

After each event, we conducted surveys in which we asked the audience’s opinion on the event and their expectations  regarding our future activities. We also made in-depth interviews with those who had more to say. Moreover, we  tried to understand to which extent our events influenced our audience’s taste and how much they facilitated their  interaction with the local society. This new approach proved to be highly efficient. In few months, we started to make  profits and were able to invest more in new projects. An organization has to have a set of prototypes which are designed based on research and tested early in  the process, so that if not successful, they can fail fast and cheap. This model allows the organization to test, improve,  and review the product on the iterative basis. Continuous experimentation allows not only to find the product that

Design Thinking for Innovation

Author: Paolo Rossi

Reflection

Tool: Mind Mapping (Module 3)

1. Challenge and Selection

I work in an engineering company and it often happens that my team has to  create new concepts of new products that will have to be placed on the market.  Often these products have to be innovative and have to solve problems in an  ingenious way so that the customer is positively involved in using these  products. I chose the mind maps tool because it is based on creative abilities,  they can be created with colors and images, on processes that spontaneously  restructure information and that each time leave more than one interpretative  key open. For these reasons, mind maps are particularly effective for processing  thought and creativity, and this thought process can be very useful when  technical solutions to real problems need to be found.

2. Application

Concept development begins with brainstorming sessions, and mind mapping is  used to work out the relationship between topic information and new ideas. In  this brainstorming, each participant is encouraged to think out loud and  spontaneously come up with as many ideas as possible, no matter how wacky or  crazy it may seem. The problem or question is written in the center of a large  sheet of paper and the solutions are spread over the entire surface of the sheet.

The focus is on the topic; it is written in the center of the sheet and enclosed by a  circle. Branches branch off from this circle that divide and fan out the topic in  its individual areas. The keywords are written on the branches. The topics  represent the main branches. Details are written in the branches.

After creating a mind map, branches can be combined again or branches that  were not previously connected can be linked together. In addition, you can  search for missing branches to identify gaps for troubleshooting /  brainstorming. Mind mapping can also be understood as a continuous process in  which you start with a mind map on a more abstract level and become more and  more detailed over time through additions but also deletions.

Color and pictures or symbols can make a mind map even more meaningful,  often the result is so pleasant that I take a photo to have memory of the work  done, but unfortunately, these "works of art" cannot be printed because they  contain confidential information.

3. Insight & Approch

Mind mapping is able to present ideas in an intuitive and non-linear graphical  way and encourage a brainstorming approach to generate new ideas and make  connections. I've seen during these sessions that this approach encourages  enumerating and linking concepts without starting with a specific conceptual  framework. It often happens that the idea is divided into more related ideas  with additional lines in the map.

During these sessions, I usually take notes of ideas and creative thinking, while  critique and judgment of ideas are only allowed when the brainstorming session  is over. This rule allows people to think outside the box and freely suggest any  ideas that may seem remotely possible. The purpose of these sessions is to get as  many ideas as possible for later analysis. Therefore, people should build on the  ideas suggested by other participants.

The next step for my team will be to perform brainstorming sessions with the  creation of online mind maps by using dedicated software that allows to share  information in real time between teams located in different places such as  America and India. This tool could make people with different cultures and  problem solving approaches work together in the same time and I hope that this  methodology could give life to truly innovative ideas and products.

Reflection on Learning Launch

Jorge Bernardo, 18.05.2021

Challenge

As a head of remote entry agency for clients using wallets for a popular Moroccan bank, my main  goal is to ensure that the services ordered by a client are successfully activated. However, successful  integration is only guaranteed if the customer carries out certain steps himself.

These steps are emailed to the customer after placing the order. Although these emails are very  personal and detailed, we noticed that customers often did not complete the steps and as a result  the onboarding did not always go as smoothly which also resulted in a drop in the customer  satisfaction.

Selection

Due to several possibilities to solve this problem, we decided to launch a learning launch. The  learning launch tool allowed us to test very quickly and at minimal cost if we were on the right track  or if we needed to completely change our thinking. Even if the result is not what you want, the loss is  minimal because the investment is low. A learning launch is indeed always beneficial: you quickly  know if you are on the right track with something or if you need to go back to the drawing board and  formulate a new or refined hypothesis based on the information gathered.

Application

Our guess was that the text of the mail might have been too long and people hadn't bothered to read  it. Based on this hypothesis, we decided to create a digital milestone plan. We were very excited  about the launch as we were hoping to see a lot of people click on the stage map. We did notice,  however, that the click-through rate was very low.

So we had to rephrase our hypothesis and realized that maybe the format was not the biggest  obstacle but maybe the channel! Our assumption was that customers viewed these emails as spam.  We decided to send our customers an SMS including a link to the stage plan. The results have been  phenomenal! Customers were actively viewing the road map on their cell phones.

Now that we've noticed that customers are hitting the milestone plan, we've decided to improve it  even more in a future sprint release. The plan was to make it interactive so that customers could  have an instant view of what steps have already been completed and what remains to be done.  Customer feedback was excellent! They considered this to be their personal to-do list and actively  wanted everything checked out.

Insights

With the first prototype, we quickly realized that we were not on the right track and not solving our  problem. But this idea itself was already so valuable to us that it outweighed the investment limits  we made in this prototype. Because it forced us to go back to the drawing board, change our  assumption which ultimately led to an even better result in the end.

Approach

I cannot stress enough the importance of data. It is very important with such a learning launch to put  in place the necessary metrics to measure its success. Always go back to the original problem and  watch closely whether the prototype fixes it or not. For example, we initially focused primarily on  click-through rate, but actually just opening the stage map wouldn't solve the problem. Equally  important in determining whether a customer is actively completing the milestone plan was to  include the number of visits as a metric. Data is essential!

Innovation Today

In my short life, there are many experiences that could qualify as life-changing. Every  new experience was, at one time or another, the first experience. For good or bad, each  instance changed the course that my life has taken. But, the most transformative  experience was the birth of my youngest brother.

Juan is someone my parents often call a happy accident. At the time that my mother  became pregnant, I was 13, and my other brother, Juan, was 10. We were what you  would call a well-rounded, perfect family of four. We neatly fit into the perfect  classification in nearly every way. We didn't realize what we were missing until the  moment that my youngest brother first opened his striking blue eyes.

In truth, I resented the fact that I would be having another sibling. Nothing needed to  be added to our family, and my mother, already 38 at the time, was considered high risk  because of her age. The pregnancy itself was full of complications that sent the straight  course of my life into rollercoaster-like loops that my 13-year-old mind had a hard time  comprehending. But now, I can see how forging through those loops helped me to roll  with the punches that life inevitably brings

The day Juan was born, my mother took me with her to the hospital rather than my  father. It wasn't a planned move, but Juan and my father were both feverish; I was the  next best alternative. Sitting with her through every contraction, I gained a new respect  for just how powerful and strong a woman could be in what might be considered their  weakest moment. Holding her hand and feeding her ice chips, I gained a connection  with my mother that I didn't realize we were lacking.

The moment my new baby brother came into this world, I realized two things nearly  simultaneously. First, you don't realize how much you need something until it's sitting in  your lap. Second, my life after this moment would never be the same. The moment he  curled his chubby little finger around mine, I understood the words "happy accident"  completely.

There are many different experiences in life that have changed a part of me as a person.  But, nothing so profoundly changed my views and outlook on life like the birth of my  youngest brother. Juan's arrival was a life-altering event that caused me to see the world  through new eyes.

Design Thinking for Innovation: Final Assignment

CHALLENGE

Last month, a friend of mine  a software developer at a local tech startup  asked if I would be  interested in designing the UI for a mobile app that he and a colleague had begun developing in their  free time. Before committing to anything, and interested to learn more, I asked If we could all get on a  call. I wanted to know what inspired the project, who its stakeholders were, and why they would care  about our solution. They agreed, and we set up a time the following day.

The next day, as we walked through these questions, I noticed that something  or rather someone   was missing.  Yes, there were prototypes and a growing list of features, but where was the user? What  did they think? How would this fit in their day?

Listening, I felt that decisions were being made without an adequate understanding of what is. In other  words, an app was being developed without a story to support it. Surely there were things we didn’t  know that were worth knowing?

After raising this perspective to the group, I was  understandably, met with some resistance.  What I  suggested wasn’t part of the plan; it wasn’t within scope. And with that, I had my challenge.

In order to create alignment, I needed to demonstrate that our understanding was insufficient. Our  product’s story lacked depth; and without it, it’s value would be significantly reduced. Moreover, I  needed to demonstrate that this knowledge gap was worth exploring.

SELECTION

To address my challenge, I used the storytelling technique. Storytelling encourages designers to create a  narrative centering on the user’s lived experience. Beginning with the current state, a journey is  envisioned and articulated; revealing the actors, emotions and motivations which propel the user and  connects them to an offering.

I selected storytelling because I felt that in our discussions and decisions, the contexts, goals and  constraints of the people who stood to benefit from our solution had taken a back seat to speculation.

Through storytelling, we would have to come to terms with the bigger picture. We would have to  articulate a logical series of events that would connect our audience to our proposed solution (see Week  2: Storytelling Tool). If we were unable to do this, the necessity of further research would become  apparent.

APPLICATION

In applying the tool, I first reviewed the notes from our discussion and highlighted anything that spoke  to our understanding of the user or how the proposed solution created value for them. Then, I

converted this information into a set of statements. These in turn represented the current state of our  knowledge.

Second, using a modified version of a story template 1 as a guide, my colleagues and I attempted to map  each statement to one of the questions. If a statement was a sensible fit, we filled the blank. Otherwise,  it was left empty.

Once complete, we walked through a series of questions I had prepared to encourage reflection on the  quality of our story. I asked, as the story evolves, do its outcomes follow from its events? Are its  characters and their world realistic? Are there compelling reasons to act?

With the answers from these questions we considered the implications for our approach to the project,  making note of what could be changed, and preparing a list of research questions to be answered before  future design decisions were made.

INSIGHT AND APPROACH

The insight I gained from applying this technique is that alignment is best established when individuals  are allowed to arrive at a conclusion organically, rather than through someone else’s point of view.  Further, that it is the outcome of collaboration, and not debate.

Initially, I believe we each saw the project through a different lens. We each had our own criteria for  what success looked like and the steps required to achieve it. Through utilizing the storytelling  technique, however, we saw through the same frame. In this case, the product became part of the story  and not the story.

In a broader sense, I believe this reflects one of design thinking’s core value propositions: building  understanding. Here, it’s primary role was to help create it between members of a project team, but I  believe that it was also a step in the right direction for helping us better understand our users.

Looking forward, if I was to run this exercise again I would have each participant complete the story  individually using the same set of statements. Then, they would communicate their stories to the team  in order to create an agreed upon story.

I would take this approach because I believe the current approach is susceptible to groupthink. In  mapping the statements as a group, initial suggestions unduly influence the pairings. If each participant  was allowed to build out the story individually, it could create alternate narratives. In trying to reconcile  those alternates for the agreed story, I believe that at the least, participants would be forced to further  empathize with the user, and at best, new insights would be revealed.

Visualization

Challenge & Selection

Recently I happened to be at a ‘formal’ meeting seated around a table trying to  verbalize a problem and develop a concept. 30 minutes into the meeting  someone had the courage to break the formality and started to draw on a  piece of paper. What happened next didn’t surprise me. It’s not the art that  mattered, but the surfacing of the problem, conceptualizing ideas and gaining  the engagement to shape it better .Visualization is a core component of the  way that we communicate, whether we're aware of it or not. When we’re  dealing with very complex problems, we’re enacting a different kind of  problem solving that has to bring in more than just logic. Visualization is  really important for the process of Design Thinking because it's actually a way  of unlocking a different part of our brain. It allows me to think in a non-verbal  way and access parts of our brain, our creativity. Most design thinkers call  visualization as “the mother of all design tools”, because they are used in  every stage of the design thinking process.

Application

Visualization is equal parts listening, thinking and drawing. Listening is the input,  thinking is the processing and drawing is the output. These three skills work  together equally in understanding complexity, visualizing outcomes to create new  possibilities.

It's really  important to be able to understand the way that you communicate  with people. The primary tools for thinking visually are really just mastering  some basic elements of imagining people, spaces, situations and actions or  movements. It's very easy to create a simple diagram and most anyone can  draw a stick figure, a circle, a square, or an arrow. Those are the basic building  blocks of creating a  Visualization. We can unlock the power to think  differently by doodling. Alicia Diane Durand’s Discovery Doodles - The  complete series is a good starting point if you are in search of confidence and

want to learn basic visual elements. I try to practice with and learn from my  three little girls Khairah  (7), Safiyah  (4) and Hannah (2). The kids doodle  naturally not afraid of judgement. I am not a Picasso. I might not pass the high- school ‘arts’ exam even if return to it once again.

The world will always need people who can see the bigger picture - those who  listen, who find patterns, and make connections. The world around us is  complex and needs us to strengthen our ability capture and organize ideas.  We need more clarity. We need more shared understanding. We need more  simplicity. The more likely you are to achieve a sense of agreement and  consensus with people, the more you are likely to draw out conversation. In  an  environment where your ability to get things done and to solve problems  is dependent on other people being able to understand you and align their  ideas with yours.

Insight & Approach

I think that people will find that once they start getting in the habit of doing  that, you quickly see how the rest of the room responds to you when you get  up and you start drawing. This can be a little intimidating at first for some.

When you get to concept development, Visualization becomes incredibly  useful. Your brain is creating pictures of something that doesn't yet exist. It's  creating pictures of something that will soon be. As we move forward into  prototyping, we get much more detailed in the way that we start to visualize.  Then we create very complex diagrams or maps of how we think the customer  experience is going to work ideally. Pictures and images enable us to not only  help people understand what it is we're trying to do but to help persuade  them in the worthiness of that particular idea or the strength of that concept.

CHALLENGE & SELECTION:

Reflection – ​Visualization

Challenge and selection  I am a project leader in a software company. We work with clients that bring us some

needs, and we create a solution for them. We created what our clients tell us to do

without questioning whether the solution will really fit their needs. This approach

impacts the clients’ satisfaction at the end of the project. We had several dissatisfied

customers, even if we deliver the software as they asked. So, I realized that the

problem is not in the production, but it is in the idea conception.     We received a new project to design a website to help mothers buy baby and kids

clothes. In the first meeting, we proposed our client apply an ethnographic to help

understand the real problem. We aim to create a visualization of the process of the

clothes purchase of the mothers. The client is a little skeptical, but after we explained

the possible benefits, he accepted. So, we started our project by doing a Journey

Mapping with mothers. The main idea was to discover which are the primary needs

of these mothers in this process. Besides just analyze the process, we tried to

understand their fears and the emotions in the process.    Application  We selected 20 mothers from 22 years old up to 33 years old with newborn children

up to 3 years old. We follow these mothers in the entire process of searching and

buying clothes. We go along with each mother individually, from the shopping mall

entrance, choosing the right store, looking at the entire cloth catalog, finding the

clothes that fit in their kids, and, finally, finalizing the buy. We also accompanied how

they organized the clothes and what they did with the clothes that no longer fit.

Finally, we also asked these mothers to maintain a photo diary with each clothes the

kids used. They take pictures and created an album of them.     With these data, we created flows of each mother’s process to describe how they did

her process. We also used the album to see if the kids used the clothes recently

bought.     Insight  We discover a whole new world! The first thing is that the mothers have two types of

purchases that we classified as an emotional purchase and a daily purchase. The

emotional purchase is that clothes that generate a good feeling in it. The mothers

loved to search for a lovely piece of cloth for their kids and feel the material. This is a

moment of the mother with her kid. We do not think to change that. But the daily

purchase is fastly, and there is not an emotion in it. We found out that the daily

purchase is the purchase which fills the bigger part of the clothes necessity. Also,

this daily purchase is very stressful for the mothers.

We also discover that the process of deal with clothes that do not fit anymore is

complicated. Some mothers passed these clothes to other mothers, but most do not

have someone to transfer them. Therefore, the mothers maintain these clothes,

creating messy and difficult management. Another insight was that the clothes of

daily purchase are the clothes with more utilizations! We saw that in the pictures

from the album.     Approach  I think that the first experiment was excellent and deliver to our client a lot of

important insights. The next time, we need to found how to do this in a less invasive

way. We take a lot of time for these mothers, and this was stressful for both sides.

The album is a good idea for maintaining a diary easily. The mothers prefer that then

write which clothes are used.     Our client saw the visualizations created in this process and changed the entire

application to meet these needs better.

By: Savita Narayn

Challenge & Selection

The tool that I chose is “Storytelling”. I work with vulnerable populations, women and young girls who  have been sexually abused, raped and  molested. Many of them suffer from mental trauma and  couldn’t get over a certain situation for a long time, which leads to depression, suicidal thoughts and  sometimes even suicide. . I spend a lot of time “opening them up” and finding ways to inspire them to  improve their circumstances, by giving them courage and motivation. When I work with women, we  share stories for different situations and reasons. Most of the time because they are scared of society  being biased against them and will declare the victim as criminal. Sometimes because they lack family  support and ultimately everyone just blames them for their clothing and personality.  When I talk to them, it makes them really happy and relief to share stories of their lives and connect  with me. It overwhelms them as they never found anyone who would understand them and support  then rather than blaming them. With my survivor clients, I share stories of my life as well to make  them realise that they are not alone, standing in that situation and we all support and understand  them. To make the realise that they are not “victims” but “fighters”.  I use this information to develop  different strategies to try and find  ways that works for them to gain more independence, self  confidence in the areas they find lacking in their lives.    Application

I have a story about using storytelling. In a counselling session in a school, I was trying to explain people  the importance of them and self confidence in life and how each person is unique and  beautiful and  addressing their individual needs first and foremost. The speech also focused on anti-bullying and self- protection. I was also explaining how sometimes addressing the needs of one individual can impact  everyone for the better, even if it seems extreme or out of the ordinary. I also shared stories of me  motivating and inspiring women who had suffered from rape and abuse.  . Everyone was doing really  well except for one girl whose stress was making her very emotionally volatile. I could tell she needed  attention. In my mind I decided I needed to talk to her and she would be my Princess for an hour. I  poured her a cup of chai and sat down with her and let her talk. It turned out that she has been sexually  abused by her uncle, and she recently came out to her mother about it. She was terrified and at first  because her mother blamed her and didn’t understand her, but gradually her mother understood her  point and supported her. Me mentioning about sexual abuse and rape just brought back all the bad  memories to her which was overwhelming and emotional for her.    Insight & Approach

Well, that was an eye opener. The girl was terrified and was in trauma at first, but now she is calm and  doing very well. Clearly it was time for me to open up with my story. I told her how traumatized I was  when my private tutor started touching me inappropriately and how it affected my studies because I  never talked or opened up about it to anyone. By noting that how she and I both have faced similar  situations and that she was not alone. I later inspired her and gave her motivation for being a fighter.  This worked really well. She really needed individual attention for that brief time, and she ended up  with that and a true support. She calmed down. Peace reigned again in our little heart to heart  conversation room. So I told this story to the other women facing similar situation, and I think it had  a big impact on people there. Sometimes a little story can do a lot of good. This course made me see  this as a tool in a new way. Now I can prepare ahead and think of stories that will assist me in  presenting my ideas and best illuminate them.

Mind mapping.     Selection   Mind mapping is one of the most powerful tools in the design thinker's toolbox. It's used to  look for patterns, for insights, that lead to more creative solutions to your design challenge.    Formal definition:   Mind mapping looks for patterns and insights in a large quantity of data you have collected  during exploration of what is the current reality. The goal is to establish criteria for the what-if  idea generation phase.  This phase is pivotal in the design thinking process. Mind mapping  provides a segway from what is to what if.  In design thinking we use the mind mapping process to capture and represent the minds of our  customers. We involve our colleagues in order to develop a common mind among them  regarding the current reality of a design challenge.  Through mind mapping, we extract meaning from data in a way that lets patterns and insights  emerge.   Mind Mapping is a great way to align the organization around a common understanding of the  current reality.    Challenge   I use this approach often with my clients to understand the mind of their´s  customers. I am an  independent consultant, so Iam used to  work  applying new methodologies or developing  culture transformation process in different companies.    In this case, I used mind mapping in a bus transport company that wants to  develop  a new  management model, with news  KPIs  to monitor and simplify the management of the area.  Also the company was in the grip of a “compliance culture” and its workplace was failing in this  non-empathetic, rigid structure.    Application   First, we began with laying out the data we have collected of the different issues, for example,  repetitive maintenance failures, communication problems, staffing issues, technological needs,  etc.  Then  the team and some outsider  colleagues,  met in a conference room, it was  a  wonderfully confortable,  where all the collected data was shown.     After the participants viewed the information, they arranged themselves at tables of four  participants. Before they started to share their good stuff,  they had ten minutes to review  their own sticky notes and group them into themed clusters on their clipboard.  Then the sharing started.  Each member of the team shared her/his discovery.   Finally comes the big payoff,  identifying the insights that each cluster reveals.  This was also one of the toughest parts of the process.  Then we wrote the inside statements on large sticky notes and place them on top of the  appropriate sticky note clusters. The team notes the connections between and among the  clusters for even better representation of “what is”.  Finally, we needed to translate the insight in the design criteria.  The design criteria are the  conditions your design solution must satisfy in order to solve your customer's problem.      Insight & approach   By applying mind mapping, our team capture and represent the minds of our customers.  Additionally, we easily identify  patterns and insight  in the large quantity of data. Finding a  more agile approach to establishing criteria for the “what if” phase.   However, It was very  difficult to  keep our focus, and sometime the team wants to do everything. So, it is very   important to reinforce the understanding of the key problem we are working to solve.

1 - Challenge

I work as a trainer and coach with teams of customer consultants and their leaders in the  German cooperative banking Sector. We had the following situation: The aim for the team is  providing excellent consultation and achieving good returns.   With digitalization they have to use a technical process with their customers, which is relatively  inﬂexible and in some points difﬁcult to handle. Primarily it was necessary to describe a precise heading or goal, that stands in the middle. The  stakeholders searched a long time for a real short description: ‚Consultation that is fun for the  customer and for the consultant‘.   To get activity in the team, I let them work in little groups of 2 or 3 people. They can take a short walk outside to discuss or have a cup of coffee together. Finally they  have to reach an agreement all together in the big group to describe their goal.In the next step  they found two way-points that need to be solved.  ‚Getting close to the customers need‘ and ‚Get the computer-based process out of the focus‘

Challenge    For some time I frequented a public gym and showered there before my work day.  Although the  showers may have been cleaned daily, they were not cleaned between each use - sometimes  the floor was, well “icky” and traditional flip-flops just didn’t cut it.  I searched and searched, for  an existing product that would provide the protection I needed, without any success.  I then  realized a need for a solution for increased sanitation when using any facility that has communal  showers - gyms, dorms, camps, athletic training facilities, etc.  I came up with an idea that would  provide antimicrobial protection for the feet while using these facilities’ showers.  The challenge  was how best to explain my idea, prove that there was a need, offer a solution, and propose it to  potential sponsors for development.    I spoke with fellow gym rats, college students, moms of summer campers, professional athletes,  etc. to see if they agreed that a product like mine could be helpful. Once I received excited  interest in my solution, I set about trying to find a way to make it a reality. My next step was to  submit a formal request for a design patent. Then, equipped with a list of businesses from my  target market, I would need to find the best way to get my idea out to the potential backers.
