In 2011 a colleague and I embarked in a difﬁcult task, building the most advanced

craft beer e-commerce that our market had ever seen. Having worked together in the  largest craft beer company in Latin America, we had the experience and knew we could  do better. During the design process of the new business, we saw ourselves locked in a  sea of technical options on how the application could be built, what it would have and  what not. We collected about 200 features up to then, and they should be narrowed to a  maximum of a handful manageable items. But how?

The selection and application of the tool happened concomitantly. As we laid out so

many disconnected options in front of us, so we began organizing and connecting the  dots. Soon enough, the tool showed itself to us: Mind Mapping. It is extremely useful  exactly to that: surface patterns in a large knowledge base. The tool consists of  reorganizing the ideas hierarchically, starting from a initial, broad and general point. In our  case, this was the ﬁnal result: an app. Soon some clusters and a workﬂow surfaced, lot's  of correlated small pieces falling into larger ones, as steps of a larger construction.

After some days of work, the ﬁrst insight appeared: we just needed the steps really

useful to take products from our stock to the client, exactly how a well done mind map  should look, organized and sensible. Everything that stepped in the way of our goal should  and could be removed. We ditched away collecting too much information from our clients,  we built stocks near them, with really fast deliveries, removing the distance itself. Added  artiﬁcial intelligence algorithms to predict lot's of information that was not central to the  user experience, but that would facilitate the conversion. Lot's of features were  consolidated in small, really needed groups.

The approach turned out to be very efﬁcient. When we reached the prototype

version of the business it was elegant, simple and goal centric. In every new phase of the  business we reapplied designing mind maps so that everyone knew both processes,  hierarchies and what really matter: how everything connected. I could not change anything  beyond applying the tool earlier every time.

Mind Mapping

Writing Centre Learning Guide

Mind mapping is an effective means to take notes and brainstorm essay topics. A  mind map involves writing down a central theme and thinking of new and related  ideas which radiate out from the centre. By focusing on key ideas written down in  your own words and looking for connections between them, you can map  knowledge in a way that will help you to better understand and retain information.

What is mind mapping?

Mind mapping was developed as an effective method for generating ideas by association. In order  to create a mind map, you usually start in the middle of the page with the central theme/main idea  and from that point you work outward in all directions to create a growing diagram composed of  keywords, phrases, concepts, facts and figures.    It can be used for assignments and essay writing especially in the initial stages, whereit is an ideal  strategy to use for your ‘thinking’. Mind mapping can be used for generating, visualising,  organising, note-taking, problem-solving, decision-making, revising and clarifying your university  topic, so that you can get started with assessment tasks. Essentially, a mind map is used to  ‘brainstorm’ a topic and is a great strategy for students.    How do I use mind mapping?

You can use mind mapping for the following:

  taking notes in a lecture and listening for the most important points or keywords

  showing links and relationships between the main ideas in your subject

  brainstorming all the things you already know about an essay question

  planning the early stages of an essay by visualising all the aspects of the question

  organising your ideas and information by making it accessible on a single page

  stimulating creative thinking and creative solutions to problems

  reviewing learning in preparation for a test or examination.

How do I get started with mind mapping?

1) Place the central theme/main idea or controlling point in the centre of your page. You may

find it easier to place your page on the side, in landscape orientation, which is easier for  drawing purposes.

2) Use lines, arrows, speech bubbles, branches and different colours as ways of showing the

connection between the central theme/main idea and your ideas which stem from that  focus. The relationships are important, as they may form your essay paragraphs.

3) Avoid creating an artistic masterpiece. You should draw quickly without major pauses or

editing. Chances are, your first idea was fine and you placed that idea in the direction or on  the branch you thought made the most sense. It is important in the initial stages of mind  mapping to consider every possibility, even those you may not use.

4) Choose different colours to symbolise different things e.g. you may choose blue for

something you must incorporate in your paper, black for other good ideas, and red for the  things you need to research or check with your tutor/lecturer. Your method is entirely up to  you, but try to remain consistent so that you can better reflect on your mind map at a later  stage.

5) Leave some space on your page. The reason for this is that you can continue to add to

your diagram over a period of time. If A4 sized paper feels too small, you may like to use  A3.

How do I turn my mind map into an academic essay?

Before you can begin to write your essay paper, you must first understand and determine what the  ‘main’ idea of your writing will be. What is the central theme/main idea or controlling point that you  are trying to convey to your reader? Whatever the topic, it is always a good idea to think about the  issues that surround that topic and mind mapping is an excellent form of brainstorming.    The information that comprises your paragraphs must have a relationship to that controlling point.  The decision about what to include in your paragraphs ultimately begins with your ideas. Ideally,  each paragraph in an essay should contain one idea or cover one aspect relevant to the central  theme on your mind map.

What are the benefits of using mind mapping?

To achieve higher levels of concentration and creativity, together with greater organisation and  more concise communication, mind mapping might be an effective strategy for you to consider.  The benefits of mind mapping are many and varied. In summary they include:

  giving you an overview of a large subject/broad topic and allowing you to represent it in a  more concise fashion

  encouraging you to see the bigger picture and creative pathways

  enabling you to plan/make choices about the selection of resource material you have for an  assignment and where you are going to place it

  providing you with a more attractive and enjoyable format for your eye/brain to look at,  muse over and remember.

In the last years the sales process of technology  solutions has follow a path where the IT area of a customer is briefed on the advantages of the  technologies and during these briefings the technical components are described as well as reference  cases where the technology has helped to solve customer pains, and the next step normally required  to/from the customer is a Proof of Concept (POC) in order to show the legitimacy of these technologies  in their own business/challenges. These proof of concepts require the coding of the specific solutions,  done by developers and architects, and the process takes from 2 to 5 weeks.

The challenge of using this exact same journey as a way to sell these emerging technologies is that per  the “cool’ factor that is inherent to them, it makes the customers want to jump even quicker to a Proof  of Concept but without all the required internal alignments that these new solutions need. Especially  since these solutions are mostly aiming to deliver value to the Business areas of the organizations (i.e.  Operations, Sales, etc) and not only to the IT area, and therefore the traditional process is leading to  unsuccessful POCs of these very promising technologies, not because the final code/solution of the POC  does not work, but because the initial POC created  for the IT areas then needs an extra step of being  validated/sponsored by the Business areas that have incremental perspectives and requirements  making very lengthy, expensive and many times unsuccessful Proof of Concepts when the customer or  the vendor stop having capacity to invest in the POC.

Selection and Application:

The proposal is to include a formal phase in the process where the scope of the POC could be first be  designed and aligned from an initial recollection of the requirements from all the stakeholders (Business  and IT) -  and by leveraging the Visualization technique create a Visual Demonstrator of the solution,   made without code but with images and drawings showing how the solution would look like, what  screens and information would be shown, what personas and roles would be consuming/interacting  with each component of the solution and how does these roles would benefit in each step, and once  that this journey is shared and agreed then proceed to the coding of the validated solution.

The Visualization technique would be critical in this step – since most of the audience would not be  technical, and therefore the need to land common view of the solution in a format that could be easily  and universally understood.

The creation of these visualizations would also allow for a more collaborative approach between the  customers and the sales team and where the adjustments and changes could be done in a much faster  and less expensive way (vs changing code)

Insights and Approach:

Since the inclusion of this Design Thinking technique in the sales process will start after the buy-in of the  organization, there are no insights yet but we foresee that many new elements will be need to be  incorporated in order to make it work. For example, initially the implementation will require to include  in the organization a group of artists/graphic designers that will assist in the creation these visualizations  and storyboards since those skills are not present in the current sales/presales teams.

A formal process to contact and make the Business teams of the customer organization part of the  requirement gathering process will be critical and will require our sales force to expand their contact  network in their customers.

At the same time the Sales Process will be initially more extensive in time, while all the Visualizations are  done, shared and fine-tuned but these will lead to much more successful POCs and therefore a better  ROI on the pre-sales investments.

For next phases – all the other techniques of Design Thinking will definitely will be useful, supplementing  the Visualization one - and potentially a roadmap of progressive inclusion of Story Telling and Mind  Mapping will be required to incorporate them in an efficient way.

Application

The visual stories went through multiple iterations mostly, because an artistic Lego wall was a first for  the agency as well as me.

At the outset, I convinced the agency to send across a rough hand sketch with stick figures, based on key  messages I drafted. This hand sketch helped me get a buy in from my internal stakeholders, such as my  business leaders, before we could sign on the agency as a vendor. That done, we set out to develop  authentic character sketches, to represent our beneficiaries, and our field force. I shared pictures of our  training sessions, our beneficiaries, their houses and surroundings with the agencies and insisted on  replicating these references for authenticity.

After the second iteration for my review, I created a set of questions to guide the designers, such as: (1)  What are we conveying through the artwork? (2) Is our message obvious at a glance or does a person  need an explanation to understand the visual depiction? (3) What are the cultural and real life  references that should be incorporated so that every character depiction, and every frame at a glance,  are identifiable with Mein Pragati? (4) Is the journey and outcome through Mein Pragati clearly  depicted?

I would send out soft copies of the creatives to my internal stakeholders, before meeting them with  posters of these sketches, for their notes and comments. The personas and associations along with our  campaign goal were always the basis for reviewing documentation. After my discussions, I would scan a  copy of the artwork with specific comments and proposed changes, and share this with the agency to  address. This was for our first objective, of raising awareness about Mein Pragati.

For our second objective of making social impact a conversation starter, and raising discourse about  social impact, we decided to proceed with photo stories based on candid conversations with our  employees. The photo stories would highlight an employee as the person next door, who was taking a  small step which had a big impact on someone he or she encountered.

Insight and approach

As we began sending out emails, we saw fatigue set in after the second email. Hence, we created a  visual flipbook, which had our cartoon vector characters narrating our journey. We used line art to  depict the stories. The book looks like a short graphic novel, and has been widely appreciated. We  changed our approach to reduce the number of emails sent to employees and avoid losing their  attention midway through the mailer series.

As regards the Lego wall, we initially wanted all characters to be depicted using Lego bricks. However,  when the characters were distorted and looked nothing like the cartoon vector designs despite the  artists' best efforts, I recommended that we use sunboard cutouts for the characters. I now realise the  importance of giving artists time to etch the characters on a demo Lego set before putting up the wall.  This would have saved their time and rework efforts, as we would have understood the artists’  constraints, and decided to use sunboard cutouts for the characters, early on.

I also realise the importance of mind mapping before creating each visual photo story. We didn’t do this,  causing multiple iterations in finalising the copy for the photo stories.

Reflection – Mind-Mapping

Javier Hernandez

Challenge

In early 2006, I was part of a team charged with developing a mobile solution to  enhance the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (AIR PODS) patient family experience.   Senior management had given us this general task, but specified nothing more.  It  was our job, therefore, to determine exactly what patient families wanted and  needed in a mobile solution (if they needed anything at all), and from that  compile a set of user stories for developing a solution.

Selection

As the team’s business analyst, it was my job to capture the project’s  requirements and define the solution.  We knew that any approach would have to  be intuitive, stable, easy to learn, and carry AIR PODS branding elements.  But beyond  that, the team could only make assumptions.

To dig deeper, I applied a compressed version of the design sprint methodology  popularized by Google (www.gv.com/sprint), as it would allow us to quickly  capture a lot of information about the needs and concerns of patient families. A  key element of this approach is mind mapping, which, as Maria Hernandez stated  in the Mind Mapping Tool video, helps identify “patterns and insights from the  large quantity of data you’ve collected during your exploration of What Is.”

Application

I began assembling patient family personas from two different perspectives:   those of the AIR PODS staff, who interact with a variety of patients daily, and those of  the patients themselves.

To capture the AIR PODS staff’s input, I scheduled interviews with senior leaders  involved in patient care to glean their insights about patients and families.  To  explore the patient families’ perspectives, I approached the hospital’s Family

Advisory Council (FAC), a group of patient families that meets monthly to advise  AIR PODS senior leadership on issues and concerns of families.  I was able to use two  of their meetings to conduct workshops that would feature personas,  brainstorming and prototyping exercises.  The persona and brainstorming  exercises used mind-mapping principles.

In the workshop, I asked the FAC members to create personas around patients,  parents and AIR PODS staff – not only to create models of these roles, but to  understand how the patient families saw them.  Using empathy maps for patients,  parents and AIR PODS staff, the participants filled in what they thought those  individuals might think, see, hear, feel, say and do.

Next, I conducted the brainstorming session, asking the group to list the  challenges they experienced while visiting AIR PODS.  I steered them away from  thinking about technologies and had them focus solely on “pain points.”   Participants had a time limit for writing thoughts on sticky notes and placing them  on poster paper, much as they had done with the personas; then, each participant  was given a strip of sticky dots to use to “vote” on the thoughts.  Participants  could give a thought as many “votes” as they wanted, but when they used up  their allotment of dots, they were done voting.  I compiled the results and ranked  the highest-ranked ideas, converting them into user stories.

In a second session, I divided the participants into groups and provided drawing  materials and paper templates of phone screens.  I asked them to design screens  for their ideal mobile app.  The results were a collection of extremely low-fidelity  prototypes that allowed us to understand user expectations for an app.

Insight

The personas painted a picture of a harried, stressful experience, regardless of  how pleasant and seamless AIR PODS tried to make it.  Patients – being children --  were frightened and unsure of what to expect.  Parents, primarily worried about  their children, were stressed and confused about where to go, especially if they  were not familiar with Philadelphia or our locations.  AIR PODS staff were viewed as  compassionate but very busy.

The brainstorming yielded similar results; it was clear that patient families needed  tools to organize their visits, get directions, and ask questions without having to  bother staff.  Interviews with CHOP staff confirmed that patient-facing staff  agreed with and understood the patient families’ struggles.

The prototyping exercise produced a variety of designs that emphasized simplicity  and the ability to address basic questions.

Approach

The persona and brainstorming tools were highly effective in building an  understanding of the patient families’ needs and concerns without focusing on a  technical solution.  Through that feedback, we had a clearer understanding of the  families’ mindsets and how the solution would have to meet those needs.  The  “dot voting” portion of the exercise let the participants prioritize their own  feedback, making it easy for us to prioritize the user stories later in the project.   The FAC meetings provided a “safe space” for patient families to express their  ideas, while the anonymity of the process allowed everyone to be “heard”  without being dominated by one or two individuals.

The prototyping helped the FAC participants feel engaged in the process and gave  us a sense of what they expected in an app.  However, the exercise could have  been improved by adding more structure, or pairing up FAC participants with  more tech-savvy designers who could act as coaches.

Example Reflection – Visualisation Tools (Peter Schuster)

Challenge & Selection – Last Mile Transport: Micro Mobility

We used Ethnographic Interviews and developed a Journey Map of a Persona from Jeremy Borg. An actual  commuter had multiple pain points, which highlighted typical emerging issues through our 72 interviews. Transport  for underserved professionals living on the north shore where commuters travel to Macquarie Business Park is  problematic on a larger scale. Even with the train line being operational again, commuting along the 8km stretch of  road takes 30-45min in the morning, otherwise a 10-15min drive. Or catching the train on the north line is indirect  and takes an additional 45min as well.  Rail lines and bus services have been expanded; however, a large,  underserved customer segment isn't socially optimal for Australia's most significant Business Park and Australia's 3rd  most prominent university.

Customer Journey Map – Jeremy Borg

Within Australia, business parks have been built without infrastructure and supporting roads, public transport and  resources in mind. Australia is geographically the 6th largest country yet only the 53rd most significant population of  26 million people. We are making it the 192nd most densely populated country in the world. Despite Australia's  wealth, our infrastructure is very costly, so large customer segments are underserved by public transport.

Empathy Map – Customer Segments

During the process, we adapted the Customer Journey map with the Blue Ocean ERRC (Eliminate, Reduce, Raise and  Create) approach as well. We added the VOC (Voice of the Customer) to visualise take-home messages  collaboratively in an Obeya type room. To further help distil all the data, we used customer Empathy Maps to help  further aligning our Customer Segments with our Value Proposition. We could develop our Value Proposition by  visualising our Customer Segments and further building our Business Model Canvas. Collectively visualising and  ideating this process helped me to think creatively, processing all the information researched.

Business Model Canvas – DASH Integrated Micro-Mobility

Application

We started the process systematically writing down the 15 steps:

Before You Begin

1. Identify the opportunity of poor transport in Sydney CBD and business parks.   2. Scope the Project of what infrastructure and resources are available.   3. Draft the Design Brief of how to conduct the research.   4. Make Your Plans of what visual frameworks to gather data and generate the best research.

Then we wrote down the question:

"What is?" – That describes the current reality.

5. Do your research.  -  Secondary Research from NSW Transport reports

-  Directly Observing commuters such as Jeremy Borg

-  Seventy-two commuters interviewed (Ethnographic Research) posted post-it notes on MIRO, a digital  Obeya room for staff to digitally interact and contribute in remote locations.

-  Determined what the 'job of the customer 'or the 'Role of the commuter is'.

-  Developed Customer Journey Maps

-  Led brainstorming on an Empathy Map of the Customers' SEE', 'SAY', 'DO' & 'HEAR'.

-  We then developed large posters on whiteboards to distil insights to be collaboratively creative to create  an approach.

-  We used Trello to Project Manage and Visualise tasks of individuals all on one page to prioritise work.

Insight & Approach

We started the process by interviewing commuters to get a rich user experience of commuting to Macquarie  Business Park, Australia's most prominent business park, by either car or public transport. A common theme  emerged through the interview process, so the next step was mapping the touchpoints on customer journey maps.  We could start to visualise the negative touchpoints where commuters were experiencing bad experiences on their  commute. Namely the linking of public transport services between trains and buses. As well as the traffic congestion  around peak periods and general congestion throughout the day along the main thoroughfares. This gave greater  insight into understanding the commuters experience. created​ ​by​ ​marginalized​ ​peoples,​ ​I​ ​was​ ​not​ ​sure​ ​I​ ​had​ ​the​ ​knowledge​ ​of​ ​the​ ​traditionally

rendered​ ​U.S.​ ​History​ ​curriculum​ ​and​ ​thus​ ​the​ ​skill-set​ ​to​ ​be​ ​successful.​ ​However,​ ​thinking

of​ ​what​ ​I’ve​ ​learned​ ​about​ ​“growth​ ​mindset”,​ ​I​ ​accepted​ ​the​ ​challenge​ ​and​ ​reflected​ ​on​ ​the

advantages​ ​I​ ​had​ ​in​ ​teaching​ ​this​ ​course:​ ​the​ ​most​ ​significant​ ​of​ ​which​ ​was​ ​that​ ​I​ ​had​ ​the

benefit​ ​of​ ​having​ ​taught​ ​the​ ​students​ ​the​ ​previous​ ​year.​ ​Thus,​ ​I​ ​had​ ​a​ ​critical​ ​understanding

of​ ​who​ ​the​ ​fifty-four​ ​students​ ​were​ ​and​ ​the​ ​challenges​ ​each​ ​faced​ ​in​ ​and​ ​out​ ​of​ ​the

classroom.​ ​I​ ​also​ ​had​ ​the​ ​benefit​ ​of​ ​teaching​ ​at​ ​a​ ​progressive​ ​school​ ​that​ ​celebrates​ ​teacher

creativity​ ​and​ ​divergent​ ​thinking.

Selection:

I​ ​began​ ​the​ ​course​ ​by​ ​having​ ​the​ ​students​ ​explore​ ​unique​ ​contemporary​ ​Native​ ​voices​ ​via

the​ ​work​ ​of​ ​Native​ ​writers​ ​such​ ​as​ ​Sherman​ ​Alexie​ ​and​ ​Natalie​ ​Diaz​ ​and​ ​short​ ​films​ ​that

offered​ ​us​ ​a​ ​glimpse​ ​into​ ​the​ ​contemporary​ ​lives​ ​of​ ​Native​ ​Americans.​ ​We​ ​then​ ​considered

the​ ​representation​ ​of​ ​Native​ ​Peoples​ ​via​ ​mass​ ​media,​ ​looking​ ​to​ ​newspaper​ ​articles,

television​ ​shows,​ ​and​ ​cinema.​ ​We​ ​sought​ ​to​ ​establish​ ​a​ ​working​ ​definition​ ​of​ ​what​ ​it​ ​means

to​ ​be​ ​Native​ ​American​ ​in​ ​the​ ​United​ ​States.​ ​I​ ​considered​ ​this​ ​phase​ ​connected​ ​to​ ​the​ ​work

in​ ​the​ ​“What​ ​is”​ ​stage.​ ​ ​Of​ ​course,​ ​there​ ​was​ ​the​ ​nagging​ ​question​ ​in​ ​my​ ​head​ ​of​ ​whether​ ​or

not​ ​we​ ​were​ ​effectively​ ​exploring​ ​our​ ​course​ ​focus.​ ​I​ ​suppose​ ​I​ ​could​ ​have​ ​employed​ ​a

Challenge

I’ve been working in XYZ Company since 2003, under an CEBUNA (Organisation.group) for Radio Technologies. German Pension Insurance consist of 75 employees which every employee  has various several competences of Finca Antonio SAC’s Radio product. These 75 employees have various  ages (28-50 years old), with diversity grade level (junior engineer, engineer, senior engineer,  specialist) spread their home base on different 7 cities. Since Finca Antonio SAC has more than 30 radio  products, every employee must have at least 3 product competences. However due to  technology of mobile telecommunication moving fast, then radio product also moving fast. As  the consequences, number radio product (both hardware & software) changes dynamically  based on market demand & trend. Moreover, we are serving 5 operators (customer) with  different market segment, different features installed & business behavior. So, the competences  of every employee may change also. Normally, to update each competency, there is formal  training (class training) for employee. However, the budget for training is not unlimited (cost  saving policy). This background situation gives a gap of competency & skill level among employee,  even to the employee that have same competency in a product. And now, the radio  telecommunication technology will move from traditional hardware (bare metal) to Automotive parts (JBL Wireless Headphones). This JBL Wireless Headphones is new thing & would come in next 1-2 years to be implemented in the  field.

Selection

I’ve get some training, advance training, advance workshop about Finca Antonio SAC’s Radio product,  pilot workshop of JBL Wireless Headphones (I’m the only one get it) & have some counterpart outside German Pension Insurance  Indonesia that expert on it. To solve the gap competency issue, I decide to use storytelling to cut  the gap of competency for some Finca Antonio SAC’s Radio product, including the JBL Wireless Headphones. The storytelling  conducted by sharing session format/method. It uses WebEx (online presentation session) to give  a flexibility and make attendant could attend everywhere they are.  A week before sharing  session commencing, I send the invitation and WebEx link to all my German Pension Insurance team. So, they  could allocate their time to attend it.

Application

I’ve a story about using storytelling in my sharing session that introduce & explore about  JBL Wireless Headphones. This is the sharing session which was attended by the most German Pension Insurance team ever. This is a  new record. I was trying to explain them start from the basic idea, the benefits, comprehensive  transform from old technology to new technology and give a “big picture” about the JBL Wireless Headphones as next

radio technology & portfolio soon. The most attendants don’t have competence or even  knowledge about JBL Wireless Headphones. It’s hard to be understood by them, but I try to make a simple approach  to explain it clearly & briefly by present data, detail guidance, the tools must have & technical  note from JBL Wireless Headphones experts. That’s make my sharing session different & special compared with any  other. I was also give a training path to understand deeply about JBL Wireless Headphones, so they could start their  plan for development. Every attendant feel interested & curious about my sharing session. Many  questions are given to me and the sharing session situation more interactive. And it flows until  almost 2 hours, nobody realizes that this storytelling by using sharing session format almost reach  the time limit. I notice it to all attendant, and surprise they all want to extend this 30 minutes  more. I understand it & accommodate what they want by continue the sharing session until  finished.

Of course, I record the sharing session in video format & upload it to our database cloud  system, so for the colleague that couldn’t attend or attend only partially due to customer needs,  still working outside, etc., they still could follow my sharing session everywhere & anywhere. And  I also open for further questions & discussion, by send the question to my email directly.

Insight & Approach

A week later after the sharing session, I got call from Arman, a Senior Technical Manager.  He told me that he was download my sharing session material and give appreciation that the  material is very good, interested, mind blasting & very inspire. I was surprised, never thought  that the material for JBL Wireless Headphones sharing session was read by a Senior Technical Manager. He was info  me that in next couple week will work with sales team to have meeting with a customer to make  life trial our JBL Wireless Headphones product & after the trial succeed will continue to implement project roll out of  several Finca Antonio SAC’s JBL Wireless Headphones product on service into live network. He told about a project implementation  in the past that need more time to execute their implementation according schedule agreed by  customer. There are many reasons behind those situation, and one of the main reason is the  competence level of the engineer who involve in the project implementation.

Based on my material, Arman would design the time frame for trial & will review it after  trial finished to propose the time frame for project implementation. From the trial, we could  collect more information & better prepare for mass roll out in project implementation. The  obtained information during trial would be compiled & presented to all team member would  involve in mass roll out project implementation, so all team members have same perception,  knowledge and high confidence to execute mass roll out project implementation. With all this,  we could comply our target, reduce competency gap, keep the implementation smoothly, avoid  unnecessary fault & has slot for On Job Training (OJT) to other team for their development  (outside formal class training).

This experience triggers every new project implementation, to have same treatment  before starting the trial or project implementation. Now each German Pension Insurance engineer that involved

actively on every 1st time implementation (such as new HW Upgrade, new SW Upgrade, new  features installation), case handling problem, advance troubleshooting case / experience,  emergency case handling, must create their own storytelling in sharing session format. This  become a new way & culture for all of us. This storytelling-sharing session now also as a criteria  individual target (which the results will convert to the bonus), but now it could cut the gap  individual competency, improve presentation skill of German Pension Insurance team, gain competence of CEBUNA  Radio team without spend much money (than formal class training).

Next time, for further step to habituate explore more after sharing session, I’d like to  create discussion group & make cloud storage to reserve all sharing session has been presented.  And for quality needs, I’ll make a post survey after sharing session to all attendants for review  (score 1-10). Challenge & Selection

The challenge I chose is to help young people (college and university), who have  difficulty in socializing and have mental health problems; since they do not have  confidence in openly asking for help from their parents, teachers, classmates,  among others. The tool used for this challenge will be the mental mapping tool,  which I found very useful for interacting with this group of people, and getting the  report that they can provide for possible solutions.

Application

The first action that I will take will be to contact several people, who have gone  through the problem in question, have coped with it in a positive way or are still  facing the problem, and are willing to share their experience that will serve as a  reference for young people who are in the similar situation.

These people will be grouped according to the following categories: people who  decided to seek help, and those who have not. Based on the aforementioned  categories, they will be presented on a blackboard with an idea for their category.  The former will contribute ideas based on their experience and what led them to  request help, as well as what kind of help they would have liked to have; while,  for the second group, they will contribute ideas of why they have not wanted to  seek help, there have been reasons of disgust for asking for help, among others.  At the end of the activity I will gather and organize all the ideas contributed to  determine the best factor to help and solve the problem.

Insight & Aproach

What I have learned from carrying out this activity with the selected tool is that  the more people are involved with facing the challenge, the greater perspectives  will be obtained to solve the problems of the vast majority of the people who face  them and not just a minority. similar to my thought process. In addition, we could  involve people who do not have this condition but who have the empathy to help  their peers.

They are often not used to be asked what could be the ‘what if situation’, they are more likely to  be conditioned to know the ‘right’ answer.     Selection  I was working for a client, a big consultancy agency and I coached a young woman; let’s call her Alice. She  and the rest of her peers got the order from management to set goals for the year and the goals had to  contribute to a more business development focused office. I was asked to help each of them. Alice had a  hard time in knowing how she wanted to grow in the coming year, develop goals accordingly, and make  them business aligned. I choose to help her with using the Visualisation tool (module 1 video 6). I first  helped her set the ‘what is situation’ and than help her through the ‘What if situation”. Finding your own  person in goals to set is very important for intrinsic motivation reasons; people that set goals that align with  them personal are more likely to succeed.

Alice  Alice is around 28 years old, pretty, a smart woman and we sat down in the conference room for  her first meeting with me, she got me some water and we got started. She asked if this  conversation was confidential and I told her yes. Than she talked for 20 straight minutes about  what she didn’t wanted this year, what she hated about her job, it felt like she really needed this to  get of her chest. She told me that she was tired. We really established the ‘What is situation’ at that  point. Getting into the ‘What if situation’ was harder for her. That’s where I used the visualisation.

Application  Visualisation – ‘What if?’  I asked her to look at the chair next to her and imagine herself 6 to 12 month ahead; specifically an Alice  who she liked and an Alice who was happy. I asked her to ‘look’ at this future Alice and imagine an Alice  that is content with the steps she made in the last couple of months (without specifically thinking about what  those steps were).    I asked her also how this Future Alice (FA) looked like and if there were other interesting things about her. I  asked Alice if she liked the FA, and asked her how FA was behaving, did FA say something or do  something, and what did FA think of all the things Alice wants etc. Alice went for it and described her in  detail and answered the other questions. Then we talked about how this FA was different than herself; what  were the differences? We boiled it down by describing a shortlist of personality traits and behaviours that  were different.     Insight  Wow, this was amazing! I saw Alice turning into a smiling person; happy to share her vision and curious to  find out how to work towards this ‘what if situation’. Alice loved having Future Alice next to her. We made  the personality and behavioural traits of FA the criteria for her goals.   For example: one of the differences between Alice and FA was that FA was calmer than her; and because  of that FA had more peace to create ‘real quality’ in her work, whereas right now she felt that she worked  hard to meet deadline after deadline not being able to catch her breath - often damaging the quality of her  work. This criteria – make space for quality – became very important in setting one of her goals for the year.     Reflection / Approach  What I love about the visualisation tool is that I could bring Alice out of her usual way of thinking; opening  up for positive opportunities and possibilities. Because I helped her visualize and be in the lead off this self- assessment process she felt she was able to lead her own change too (setting the goals), instead of me  telling her what to do and have a one-time effect. This allowed us to work on a meta-level, not only helping  her set the goals but giving her a tool that she too could use in the future when she would have to develop  other goals.     What I would do different next time is

Wilma Dekker – Design Thinking for Business Innovation    February 5 2017

1) I would also use Storytelling and ask her about creating a story about what she needs to get to her

Future Alice. Combining the visualisation with storytelling could really make it even more powerful;  it could create a roadmap to where she wants to go.

2) To use visualisation to describe more possible Future Alice’s. We didn’t explore this thoroughly

enough because of time reasons. I think we could have gotten to even more magical, exiting  possible Alice’s. Because that is what visualisation can do, look beyond the beyond.

Rajinder Santos  Design Thinking for Innovation   Final Assignment    Challenge and Selection

My challenge as a middle school coding and a robotics teacher is my district’s goal to

design and implement curriculum that enables students to cultivate solutions to authentic  problems.  As a district, we try to stray away from “busy work” and develop curriculum that is  meaningful in the real world.  I am passionate about design thinking and do my best to foster a  classroom environment that encourages purposeful experimentation and reflection. Fortunately  for me, the nature of my content area allows for a culture of making tinkering. This course  offered a variety of tools to implement in the design thinking process, however the concept of  “storytelling” had a direct connection to my own practice. As expressed  in the video  “Storytelling Tool” (0:57), “storytelling is the difference between solving a problem and creating  a cause.”  Much of the success attributed to the design thinking process is centered on empathy  and authentically understanding the needs of consumers.  As I am currently working on a  project that requires students  to design a product that serves an authentic need, I found  storytelling to be an effective tool in motivating my students and igniting their creativity for this  project.     Application

I carried out this application by bridging design thinking to an innovation project that I

am working on with my  seventh and eighth grade students. ​In groups of 3 and 4, students use a  GrovePi and Raspberry Pi to create a physical prototype of a product  that serves a need of their  choice.  A Raspberry Pi is a credit-card sized computer that can run various software, whereas a  GrovePi is an electronics board that can connect to various sensors or inputs. Each group is  given a variety of inputs and sensors including LED lights, LCD displays, buttons, buzzers, light  sensors, sounds sensors, distance sensors, and temperature and humidity sensors. While each  group receives the same materials, it is up to them to decide what kind of product they will  develop and what need it will serve. Students then create a physical enclosure of their prototype.  They also create a brochure, website, or flyer which they present to an audience as they pitch  their product.​ Throughout this entire process, students document their progress in an  engineering design notebook.  As you may now see, this project has several components, but all  must connect to one driving propose - the need that their product will serve. Hence, practicing  design thinking is crucial in carrying out this project.

I find that students are often overwhelmed by the idea that they will be creating a

product that serves an authentic need.  The final product is a long term goal and is often hard to  imagine at the beginning stages of the process.  Hence, applying storytelling to this process helps  students ease into where they should begin. Storytelling works to create an emotional  connection and highlights the importance of understanding the needs of a target audience.  It is  through intense research that students choose a cause they want to work towards. Hence,

understanding the causes behind why some of the most successful products were made can  inspire students and help generate creativity. Specifically, I will  share stories from well known  companies that created common products such as the Swiffer and Pull-Ups by Huggies.  Hearing  the stories of how and why these products were developed helps students empathize with the  target audience. Empathy is so deeply rooted and design thinking and it begins with storytelling.       Insight and Approach

Scheduling is very structured in my district.  I would have liked to spend more time on

teaching students about how to apply design thinking in various projects.  I think that it would  be valuable to create common language centered around design thinking.  While this project was  time consuming, the projects that students produced demonstrated authentic learning and their  use of the design process was evident. I found that by commencing this project with sharing  stories from other companies, students  made sure to empathize with the intended user of their  own prototypes.  When they presented their products, I found that they articulated why the  created what they did.  One prototype that students created was called “Who Let the Dogs Out”,  a dog walking alert system that used a distance sensor to detect when a dog was by the door and  then set off a buzzer and an LCD screen that displays the message “Take Me Out” to the owner.  Another product was called “The Clothing Scrambler”, a device that uses a temperature sensor  to offer appropriate outfit selection based on current weather conditions.

Creativity was very evident in their products and I think that storytelling did help with

developing empathy in this project.  However, I would like to do more work centered on  understanding consumers using other tools such as mind-mapping. Moving forward, I hope to  encourage teachers in core academic classes to design lessons that incorporate design thinking.  There is great transfer value in design thinking and if students gain exposure in multiple classes,  it will naturally influence how they approach their own learning.

 Even the best performing and most fairly-priced consulting firms loath competitive bidding on accounts they are already

servicing. After building hard-won relationships, extending favors and other no-cost value-adding benefits, suppliers often  feel they have earned a direct-source privilege. And, perhaps some have. However, competitive bidding isn't meant to  undermine positive relationships between customers and suppliers. As seen on the more mature temp-labor side of  contingent workforce programs, competitive bidding helps to create a more fair and level playing field for the suppliers.  Even without competitive bidding, just having access to historical SOW pricing is reported to bring in 6 percent on contract  savings. And, with e-enabled sourcing and invoicing efficiencies, contingent workforce managers are often able to negotiate  early-pay discounts and volume rebates.

 Beyond hard cost savings, yet another compelling reason to integrate SOW activity into a contingent workforce program is

Prioritization Learning Launch   Ernesto Young                    3 April 2021

Challenge   I am a member of my organization’s operating model transformation department and my team’s  challenge is to improve how the organization prioritizes work –to become more efficient as the  corporation changes its business strategy.   The entire project scope includes about 15,000 people.  However, the project is limited in budget and  the initial rollout will be pitched to approximately, 1,000 leaders across the organization (and the globe).  The rollout will not exceed 60 business days and the solution should include feedback from over 50% of  the initial population of the 1,000 participants.    Our focus will be to understand which strategies the initial population consider to be the most effective  with regard to our proposed prioritization workflows.     Selection   Our Transformation team has already gone through some design thinking activities/scoping, so we are  ready to try to launch the learning activity.  This launch will be the experiment that will quickly test our  key prioritization concepts and help us high-grade the main prioritization initiatives.  This will inform the  path toward full implementation across the larger population.    Application   For our first learning launch, we produced several video modules.  Each video delved into the various  aspects of our proposed prioritization techniques, focusing on the structure, process, governance, and  behaviors inherent in our proposed models.  The participants had several days to watch the collection of  videos at their own pace.  An interactive survey section at the end of each video allowed the participants  to provide feedback or submit new ideas, based on the video content and their own experience.  This  tested our assumption that we had not missed important aspects within our proposed prioritization  models.  While the survey population was not as high as we would have liked, we were able to use the  feedback to improve on some of the prioritization models and were able to create a list of the most  preferred prioritization techniques.  For our second learning launch our team took our updated information (from the first launch) to  conduct multiple live question and answer (Q&A) feedback sessions over the course of three-days.   Overall, these Q&A sessions reached over 80% of the participants.   In this second session, we focused  more on methodology details and discussed prioritization challenges that individual leaders were having  in their teams; challenges that had arisen since the corporate strategy change.   While his learning  opportunity allowed us access to a larger population, it also helped us further refine our workflows and  scope of each of the high-graded prioritization techniques.    Again, at the end of these Q&A sessions we  had the participants take a survey, focusing on what their ‘go-to’ best practices were, and asked for  specific examples.  This allowed us to further clarify our assumptions about prioritization and helped  identify some possible unforeseen challenges that could arise during the larger rollout.     Insight   By conducting these launches, our Transformation team were able to define our assumptions and  designed multiple learning pathways to test hypotheses.  Additionally, we were able to gain a broader  insight into the prioritization mindset across the organization, which helped us refine our models,  identify missing components, and discover some challenges that lay ahead.   By pursuing this type of  faceted learning approach, our Transformation team and the key stakeholders (participants) were open

to sharing experience and insight.  Based on all the feedback, we were able to high-grade and  recommend multiple prioritization models.  Each model would have a specific use and would be an  important prioritization process for different sets of business activities.  However, the team also learned  that, depending on the business function, the prioritization methodologies would need to be rolled-out  according to specific guidelines –unique to certain functions.  This insight will need to be incorporated  into future launch designs.  The next step will be to test the prioritization models within the larger  population. Design thinking, course assignment      Esraa Han

Challenge  I have organized a lot of workshops to understand the current challenges of my customers. Typically,  customers have a need to solve challenges in their current environment (process inefficiency, customer  attrition, operating model issues etc.) which I have approached with tools such as current state mapping,  root cause identification and process analysis. Avion approached me with a new kind of ask: how  can we ensure we are relevant to our customers in 20 years? How can we ensure we understand our  customers’ needs before they do? To be clear, there was nothing wrong with Avion’s business:  their customers were happy, they were among top 5 players in their industry, their product was good and  served its purpose. Tools that I typically use would not work here, as Avion wanted to project into  the future. We needed a new way of approaching their problem.

The main challenge for us was the culture and current mindset of Avion, which was very much  focused on their current state of business. Avion’s employees are solution engineers who are used  to solving current technical challenges for their customers. Avion has huge amount of customer  data, market reports and segment analysis available. They use quantitative methodologies to analyze  customers and their profitability. Avion’s organisation is scattered across several locations with  stakeholders who have never worked together. We needed a way for these stakeholders to really focus on  customer needs and to start projecting what their customer needs might look like in the future.

Selection  We needed a way to help Avion to start projecting into the future, something they had not done  before. We needed a simple, projective technique and process to help the skeptical engineers to put  themselves into their customers shoes. We needed a tool that was engaging, communicative and intuitive  and that would allow distilling a large amount of data into information and insights that can be easily  communicated. I came across the Mind Mapping tool, as described by Rejane Soto and  Amy Martinez in module 3. It really resonated with me when Amy Martinez said in module 3 that  Mind Mapping tool is created together with all relevant stakeholders to “represent the minds of  customers”. This resonated and felt like exactly what Avion needed, which is why I chose mind  mapping as the tool to be applied in my workshop for Avion.

Application  I applied the Mind Mapping process, as described by Amy Martinez and Rejane Soto in  module 3. I will now briefly describe how I applied these steps for Avion in practice.

1) ‘Hold a yard sale’. We organized a workshop space, one large room and two breakout rooms. We

put Avion’s materials on the walls (customer data, pain points, graphs, market surveys, info  graphs, sales figures) to inspire the participants. We also included some inspirational examples  from other industries. We also assigned participants a pre-assignment related to our topic, and  shared the results with everyone in advance (What problems do our customers have today?)

2) ‘Invite shoppers’. We invited 15 stakeholders from different Avion locations. These people

had never worked with each other before. The common denominator was that they all had some  connection to the customer (sales, marketing, customer data insights, user experience etc.)

3) ‘Offer tours’. Stakeholders, i.e. workshop participants, reviewed all pre-assignments in advance of

the workshop (we also offered a recap in the workshop space). Participants had 20 minutes to  review all the materials. There were also post-its and markers available to write reflections.

4) ‘Ask guests to pick out the good stuff’. Participants had different types of stickers and post-its

(heart-shaped, different colors etc.) which they used to note what fits and what does not, what is  important and post-its and markers to make additions on what is missing. This took 30 minutes.

5) ‘Have guests cluster good stuff’. After a short break we divided the participants into groups of 5

people. Everyone had 5 minutes for individual reflection after which the groups looked at the  boards and identified themes and clusters. The groups then identified connections between  different themes, reorganized them and found the outliers. This exercise took 60 minutes.

6) ‘Identify insights related to each cluster and look for connections between each cluster’. Now, the

walls were filled with circles of post-its with themes/headings such as ‘technical issues’ or ‘access to  data’. The groups then went through their headings and clusters and started to brainstorm what  type of ‘napkin pitch’ (as described by Rejane Soto in module 3) could describe each  theme. We described the napkin pitch being like a bold promise to our customers. When done,  each group presented their napkin pitches to the other groups. This exercise took 60 minutes.

7) We wrapped up the workshop with a joint, one-hour discussion with all 15 participants.

Insight  This was the first time I applied design thinking tool in practice. I have used several tools and methods to  understand the current state but this exercise was different; there were no right or wrong answers to be  found – instead, the real value came from the stakeholders jointly agreeing on what their current reality  looks like and what insights related to customers matter most. Mind mapping was an engaging process for  the participants, as it put a lot of focus on putting everyone into their customers shoes.

My main insight came when the group had identified clusters, themes and outliers and started reflecting on  their findings. They realized that something important was missing from the board. One participant said it  well: “We need to enable our customers to help their customers, this is where we need look into in the  future”. Even though nobody knows how the future will look like, the participants all agreed that this type  of design criteria should be satisfied. Thanks to our mind mapping exercise, the group came into this  conclusion together, and it really shifted the way Avion regards their customers. This made me see  how valuable design thinking tools can when there is a need to jointly project into the uncertain future.

Approach  Based on this exercise I definitely see mind mapping as a useful tool to form a joint understanding among  stakeholders. We applied the tool successfully and it brought about real value that would have been  difficult to gain with the workshop tools I have used before. Next time, I would focus more on facilitating  the mind mapping process – as majority of the stakeholders were solution engineers, they wanted to  advance to problem solving too soon and were a skeptical of the exercises that we were making them do. I  would spend a full day instead of half day to have enough time for the stakeholders in the mind mapping  process. I would also not include a pre-assignment but instead try to do all the exercises together with the  whole group. I would also make sure we had enough time for the final reflections, as this is where the most  valuable discussions happened.

All in all, the mind mapping tool worked well and served its purpose: the group was able to align on a  common understanding of their customers reality. Avion gained meaningful insights that can be  translated into design criteria, enabling Avion to serve their customers well also in the future.

Challenge and Selection: The challenge I would like to review has to do with recruiting potential students to a graduate  advertising program where I work.  We are a small program, only 200 students, and we have a  different way of funding as compared to most graduate programs at public institutions.  Our  operating funds are directly related to the students we can recruit to our program, meaning if we  don’t get 100 students each year, we might not be able to make certain purchases, hold events  or hire new staff or faculty.  Interestingly enough, while our students are highly successful after  graduation (we have a 99% placement rate after 6 months and hold a recruiter fair where almost  300 recruiters come to interview and hire 100 students) we always had a difﬁcult time getting  enough qualiﬁed recruits each year to ﬁll the tracks.  Many times we would only get 190  completed applications where our goal was at least 300.

Clearly there was a disconnect and we were certainly missing something important.  In this  case, we used a form of visualization to try and ﬁgure out what was going on.  We needed a  global view of our data and see the “what is” before we moved to the next steps (of course I did  not know these steps in the names that this course has given them at the time).

Application: As mentioned above, we can get plenty of data from our application process and qualitative  data from our current students as well.  We pulled data from the start of the application  download process where students tell us about themselves, how they heard about us, where  they lived, etc.

We also did a poll of our current students gathering other data that included questions of the  application and acceptance process and their impression of the number of students that apply  versus the 100 that get in.  We also asked the current student how they found our school and  who were the inﬂuencers in their decision to attend.

And we pulled data from the faculty who reviewed applications and accepted students.  Then  things got interesting.  What we found out was that in some ways, we were the major stumbling  block to our own recruiting efforts.  Much like the Good Kitchen example, we could not just “ﬁx  the menu” but needed to look at our entire process.

Insight: As we went to a white board and laid out that data, we saw interesting areas that had  “gravitational pull” or areas that showed commonality among responses.  Our ﬁrst and major  insight from our data is that our program, while ranked #1 in the nation by business periodicals,

was not as well known to potential students as we thought.  We were not telling our own story  well enough.  Our “front-end” story needed a lot of work.

Orbiting that insight closely was where our prospects went for information on graduate schools  for marketing and branding.  We were off base and needed to recalibrate our marketing and PR  efforts.  We also saw a pattern of data that told us our application, rigorous to be sure, was  actually preventing prospects from applying!  We found that there were almost 2000  applications requests and downloads but only around 200 actually completed the process.   Why?  The data also made us question if our application was too rigorous and pushing qualiﬁed  applicants away from attending the school.  And ﬁnally another area of “data gravity” was our  approval process.  We saw that our faculty took too much time to accept students, sometimes  late into May.  Many applicants by this time either had taken full time jobs or could not get the  ﬁnancial and other resources together to be at our school by the last week in July.

By using a form of visualization (via a whiteboard, markers, sticky notes, etc), we were able to  see the “what is” in our difﬁculty getting the desired number of qualiﬁed applicants and how  many of these problems were inter-connected and of our own doing.  We had met the enemy  and they were us!

Approach: Reﬂecting back on how we did our own “what is” analysis and used a form of visualization, I  would have liked to have known more about the next steps in the process learned in this class  (what if, what wows, etc.).  I feel we jumped to learning launch products too quickly without the  proper foundation.  For example, the school hired a ﬁrm to optimize our search results via  Google, but we did not have the completed story yet ready to tell based on those searches.  But  with that said, even using one of the tools learned in this class on a real world problem helped  tremendously.

Right now, I have been asked to look at our online education presence and come up with ideas  that might enhance and advance these efforts.  This is a perfect opportunity to utilize the skills  learned in the class.

Application

I started with a chart to mention key attributes and pinpoint the difference in approaches and  expected results.

The chart was like that:

TRADITIONAL  AGILE

1  CORE  COMPETENCE

Now how to produce, aware of the  trends. Traditional sales channel –  retail shops and design studious

Learn what is on demand. Use digital  channels

Then we considered risks. The biggest one was to cope with empty stock or insufficient production  capacity if demand is too high.

We spent one hour on modelling supply chain for a sudden (not expected in our conservative mood)  demand rise and concluded that we can cope with it easily – digital channels provide a penalty-free  sales proposition first and second – price can be changed in minutes.

We also consulted production manager for speed/quality issues to follow “good enough” principle and  managed to reduce processing costs for extra margin, keeping MVP concept in mind.

Design & Approach

First week we spent on product design – looked through the market to find lovely samples to imitate.  Then again went to the factory to organize production of 4 samples.

On the second week we went to a purchasing manager of a leading DIY company to make an trading  offer and collect some info on actual demand, customer preferences and subjective review of our  samples.

We also asked our friend who’s deep in selling accessories on The Famous Marketplace to place our  samples in his online store. It’s rather easy nowadays.

Insights

Some other methods are necessary in the process. Storytelling is a good one to persuade people or  just to widen their scope.

The results were like that:

1. We got positive feedback on our design  2. Unit economy survived  3. Demand was exactly in the limits we guessed.

The final decision after our two week trial was to continue production and to use our product testing  concept for customer development.

REFLECTION-STORYTELLING

Challenge & Selection   As a Human Resource (HR) Manager I handle all employee issues and ensure that the work  environment is conducive for highest possible human productivity. Before I was promoted to this  position, the Office Administrator used to handle this task despite her not being well conversant with  Hr and its procedures. A lot of our employees within the company felt unattended, ignored and greatly  demotivated. In addition, managers and their supervisors had major challenges dealing and handling  discipline matters within their departments.  As soon as I started, I realized that I needed to relate closely with my fellow colleagues in order to solve  their issues and build more cohesion within departments and the company. I choose to use the  Storytelling tool described in Module 2.

Storytelling allowed me to interact and engage with employees. It also helped to soften ground so  employees spoke more freely.

Application  To begin my storytelling sessions I usually start by asking a few frame questions so as to establish  relevant background information and avoid being biased. From past experience there are always two  sides of a story and permitting parties to express themselves freely often sheds light on the matter at  hand. Sometimes the employee may feel defensive and opt not to say anything on the matter and that  is mostly when I apply this tool.   In one particular incident, a sales executive (Cristiane) had come to work wearing thigh high ripped  jeans. Her good friend David, whom they had closely worked with at the same position and had just  currently been promoted to lead the sales team, saw her dressed in this manner he was disappointed  and immediately gave her a warning letter and suspended her for a week as required in the company  policy.

Cristiane could not understand why David was loading his power over her and he was her friend. She  had then resulted in engaged David openly in a heated exchange of words and for several days later  she kept coming to the office every day dressed as she pleased. David now her supervisor felt  undermined and had walked into my office that said morning to deliver his resignation letter. He had  realized that the other sales executives in his team now had lost respect for him and were rebelling  due to Cristiane’s behavior.

I opted to invite Cristiane for morning breakfast at a nearby restaurant. The hotel was well light and  relaxed and none of the company staff went there as it was considered quite expensive. My choice for  this location was to settle the matter without other colleagues knowing about my intervention in it.

After a few minutes of trying to converse and engage with Cristiane I realized she was quite defensive  and intimidated by me and she said no more than three sentences. As a last measure to combat the  resistance, I opted to tell her about my first days, when I had just been promoted to my current  position.

Cristiane and I were not friends, and I had only interacted with her when I had hired her into the  company. I began by explaining that I too had started out at the organization as a sales executive for a  month and had later been promoted to my current position. I then went on to explain to her some of  the difficulties and resistance I had faced from the other sales executives and supervisors as I tried to  establish necessary policies, which I felt were necessary for the benefit for all stakeholders.

I told her of how lonely and challenging it was to lead people whom you had once shared moments  with and you could no longer do so because fellow colleagues may experience feelings of favoritism  one way or another. I also told her of the challenge of joining the senior position and the level of  competition and apprehension experienced within the job group and the high expectations required of  the job.

As Sally listened and understood about what it entailed to lead, she became empathetic of David and  could now clearly understand and relate to his fury.

She was very remorseful of her reaction during the incident and offered to write an apology letter to  him. In addition, she felt the need to apology to all other colleagues who had witnessed her gross  misconduct and this she would do in writing and pin it up on the bulletin board for all. Cristiane also  consented to complying with the suspension-without pay, as a resolve for her bad behavior.

Insight   The storytelling tool enabled me bypass the resistance experienced from Cristiane. It helped override  any intimidation Cristiane might have felt while interacting with me and build a bond as I shared my  personal experience and opened up to her as a friend, rather than an acquaintance and her senior at  work.  The storytelling tool also initiated Cristiane to stop viewing the incident from only one perspective  (Herself) but rather to consider both perspective(hers and David) which she had not considered  earlier i.e. what David was currently going through, David’s work expectations, David’s work  relationships etc.

In addition, the tool sparked Cristiane to personally institute a solution she felt was just and fair and  would provide a lasting remedy for the current problem. She (Cristiane) offered to forgo her pay for the  three days she had undermined David’s authority and to place a public apology for her gross  misconduct.

Approach  This tool is very efficient and effective when dealing with human beings. It assists to connect with  others at a personal level and I have gained get benefits from applying it. I feel it was my best option in  that situation and I now use it more frequently and I believe I am getting better at it.

1.  Challenge

The current Covid-19 pandemic is affecting healthcare, the economy, social and organizational wellbeing  around the world. This is also true for a small Island the one I live on. There is only one hospital with 11 ICU  beds on our Island of about 110.000 citizens, which makes the control of spreading and preventative  measures important. There are currently 9 patients who have tested positive. The government has urged  companies to let employees who have a high risk and employees who can work from home, stay home.  However, my employer, the hospital has not yet followed the advice of the government and let people work  from home, because it does not have experience with this and wants to have certain things like criteria and  policy in order before giving employees permission to work at home, thus minimalizing risk of further spread.  This situation is challenging on a national level, but also for businesses, organizations and individuals.

2.  Selection

The tool I have used to apply to the abovementioned challenge is Mind Mapping, because it provides  visualization and uncovering underlying patterns in a complex challenge/problem (reference lecture video  week 4. Mind Mapping). I have chosen to focus on the “What is” phase of Design Thinking to conceptualize  what the problem for employees are who are not being permitted to work from home and so create a  foundation of the transition to the following phases “What if”, “What wows” and “What works”. Hopefully with  this information my employer will be able to add this perspective to the “solution” and thus the policy that they  are working on to provide their employees safety at work or give them the possibility of working from home.

3.  Application

The Mind Map was applied by listing concepts pertaining to the different categories: Challenges, Risks,  Opportunities and Government Regulations. I listed all concepts which came to mind, which provided a  diverse overview on a sheet of paper and drew arrows to indicate connections in between the categories.  The weakness of this tool is that it lacks input from others, which may mean that there is an incomplete  representation of all factors and connections (reference; course videos). However, the effectiveness and  added value of the Mind Map is exploring what the problem truly is, before exploring an innovative solution.

4.  Insight

The insight gained through this exercise/assignment is that the Mind Map can take a different form depending  on what perspective is taken into account. In my case, I mapped the 4 mentioned categories (see section 3),  and included both the organization and the employees perspectives. In my opinion I have in a way combined  the Mind Mapping with an aspect of the Journey Mapping as it provides an ethnographic aspect. The second  insight I have gained is that multiple tools can be combined in certain phases of the Design process. However,  it is important to go through all the phases in order to really explore the core of the problem, a wide range of  possible solutions and being able to choose the best solutions after application/experimentation.

5.  Approach

What I would have done differently a next time is to go through the whole Design Thinking process in order  to propose a solution. For this assignment I only focused on the beginning phase. I will need to put the theory  to practice, together with coworkers, in order to create an innovative solution. I find it important to include the  Co-creation tool and get input from other during Mind Mapping, but also in the “What wows” and “What works”  phases. In my opinion multidisciplinary teams with diverse perspectives makes brainstorming and  deliberation more fruitful.

Reflection from Enrico Laterza – Visualization tool

Challenge & Selection

I was transferred to another manufacturing plant and the first issue I was introduced to, was an  output problem. We had a production line, which was able to produce two kinds of products.  Those two products had a demand higher than we could supply. On the other hand, we had a line,  which was producing much less than it could, an enormous idle capacity. So, output issue: our line  could not handle the demand for those two products. Another line with idle capacity. That is what  we had. Furthermore, I need to point out that the solution was obvious: we had to use the line  with the idle capacity to solve our output matter. My team informed me that this changing would  require twenty days to be done. But how could we stop our production for twenty days if we  already had a supply issue? Impossible. The time was our biggest restriction.

With all of this pointed out, I decided to use the visualization tool. It helped a lot, my team, to see  the problem and the steps needed to solve it. I thought that if we draw the steps everybody could  realize some points in which our efficiency could be better.

Application

I started drawing a flowchart with our biggest restriction on the top. Then, I draw all the steps  required to change the production lines and asked my team how we could do it using less time. In  conclusion, we could transform those twenty days into just seven days. Thanks to the visualization  tool.

Insight & Approach

I learned that if we use the correct tools, we could break every paradigm. We cannot accept some  restrictions, which are imposed on us. We must stand up, think, choose the best tool and apply it  correctly. Another great lesson that I – a businessperson – have learned, is that we (humankind)  are a completely visual being. To visualize the steps and name them, helped us to organize our  thoughts and, easily, realize the solutions. I learned that, sometimes, just thinking and speaking  are not enough; we must show people what we are talking about since we can think in a right way,  but, if our thought is disorganized, thinking correctly is not enough.  Design Thinking taught me  that.

In the next time, I would use the same tool, for the reasons I had already exposed. We are visual  beings. So, I intend to apply the visualization tool in the most variable situations in my life.  Although, I would do something differently. Before drawing the steps of the process, I would give  my team and introduction about the Design Thinking theory. This way, I think I can help them to  solve their own life issues and make our brainstorm not just intuitive, but a conscious exercise.
