Reflection – Learning Launch – Creative agency challenge

Challenge & Selection

I work in an advertising agency and I often have to do an activation for a brand that wants to create awareness and  retention on the market towards consumers.

In my specific case, we had to create, for a famous brand of sparkling drinks, an installation to show to the public  during the design week in Milan. The brand wanted to launch a light product on the market and the goal was to  connect this lightness to the world of design. The project was very complex, since we had no way to make  attempts and tests during the weeks before the event.  This installation was, in a nutshell, the creation of a new  place where consumers could discuss design issues while drinking this new drink. All in a "lightness" environment.

The project had to be created in four days and the installation had to be ready to be installed in an urban context  for a week. In the agency we were a lot of creative people focused on the project and there were a lot of ideas.  The client, on the other hand, had already had the opportunity to try a similar idea created, the year before, by  another agency, but this idea was very generic and had little impact on customer.

Our team had never used design thinking tools, so I decided to propose the use of the learning launch, even  though we had to create the new lightweight design concept and we had to create a prototype of the installation  in a different place from the final event.

It was seen as a very challenging idea but everyone accepted. As is well known, the learning launch allows to test  key customer, execution and defensibility assumptions, following a simple process: finding an idea that can solve a  specific need of a defined person, that causes pain and must be solved. This approach allows to verify if the idea  meets the need in the best way compared to competitors.

The challenge, in this case, concerned two aspects: to make the concept of "design in lightness" without making  the concept simplistic, and how to graphically develop the installation.

Application

For our first learning launch, we focused on the concept of lightness applied to design. Starting from our  target group, people of a certain age worried about not always feeling up to it and wanting a simpler  life, we hypothesized that the basic idea could be: don't take yourself too seriously. Surely this allowed  these people to feel less guilty, living life more lightly. To avoid the classic phenomenon of confirmation  bias, we found everything that could refute this idea, but from the data collected we had confirmation  that this would have been the right choice. The target in fact was not young and energetic, able to be  flexible and not inclined to obey social laws, but a mature target who feels very strong the weight of  responsibility.

We decided to set up our working group with people from different backgrounds, with two people  (Kate and Daniel) sceptical and not very optimistic about the project. This allowed us to refine the idea  more and more. We took a very large pool of consumers (women, 40-50 years old, Italy) and this  allowed us to be accurate both qualitatively and quantitatively.

Given our main assumption we had the confirmation that our people do not want to take themselves  too seriously, and want to live life not up to expectations but up to their own desires. This idea was  scalable and declinable in many aspects, such as design. The idea that would have led to this connection  between these two distant worlds would have been the “mix and match”. So we tested this idea by

taking a pool of consumers (50 people) as a target and, in a one-day workshop, we had them apply the  idea of mix and match to the table, to home furnishings, to clothing. At the end of the test we asked:  how much lighter do you think design is if you don't take yourself too seriously? The feedback and  ratings were all very high.

So we decided to make the second learning launch, proposing an installation for the design week: two  designers who in real time are inside a glass box creating a mix and match place (like a mise en place or  a home environment). We asked the same question at the end of the experiment. And we realized we  were on the right track.

Insight & Approach

By applying the learning launch tool, our team was able to test creative assumptions that would  otherwise only remain generic. We managed not to focus on an individual idea through collaboration.  We avoided giving much value to our idea just because it was our idea. We clearly had the costs and  time frame in mind, and we could have made a mistake without wasting so much time and money. We  understood the value of anticipating the results, without expecting failure in the creation of the work. A  more agile process led to a more agile, dynamic result.

This approach will certainly be used for other projects conducted by our agency. I am curious how this  tool can also be used to solve problems within the agency. Linked to system architectures or HR system  innovation in general. Since the goal is not to show that you have had a good idea but that you have to  find the truth and it will be the one to confirm or not the assumption, we will have a much more  collaborative environment and focused more on the "journey" than on the "destination-result".

Story telling

Fatin Tam goes on to tell us about how stories can be used as a great

motivating factor with your kids.

If your child’s low on confidence in certain areas, instead of just asking

How to tell stories to your child:

Challenge:   The Covid-19 pandemic hit the world hard globally. Countries and organizations struggled to  keep going and each one invented their own ways to cope up. As per a recent survey by Ehsaas, people living below poverty  line in Pakistan increased from 21% to 36% (~40% as per IMF) due to COVID. Hence, I was  given the responsibility of bringing everyone on one page and devising a strategy to  generate sustained livelihood opportunities by utilizing ~ PKR 160 million.    Selection & Application:   I used the mind mapping tool to generate ideas as to how to attack the problem and devise  a workable strategy that is mutually beneficial for all. There were many questions that  needed to be addressed which included what to do, how to do it, with whom to do it, what  is the value proposition for all stakeholders involved.     Hence, the first thing I did was to reach out to Engro Foundation who was leading the  Leanpro. We then mutually decided to reach out to Ehsaas Foundation in  Pakistan, which is responsible for alleviating the masses out of poverty and enable more  women entrepreneurs, because of our shared goal. We then sat with them to assess their  different programs in order to choose which works best for achieving our goals and  generates value for all of us. There, we discovered an additional objective which was of impact  investing. Challenge and selection

My main field of employment is within mechanical engineering, which I’ve only been working

in for a short period of time as a fresh graduate mechanical engineer. My technical field is mostly

centred around automated construction methods, most of which are (completely) new. One of my

functions in my organisation is to continue where I left off after my graduation thesis, where I

researched a conceptual design for a new type of construction machine. This meant already working

some steps of the processes described throughout this course, mostly focussing on the “what is” and

the “what if”. After being rehired at this company to continue my thesis project, I’ll now be further

developing my conceptualised machine and it’s further phases.

My challenge for this project is to continue a strong development curve along the timeline of

my employment at this company and perhaps even continue after the completed project.

Already (somewhat unknowingly) using some methods of visualisation, I feel like I barely

skimmed the surface of what this design method has to offer. Therefore I’ll be attempting to broaden

my use of this technique and its implementations across the different phases of the creation of this

new machine I’ve been developing.

Application

As a more literal application of the title of this course, I’ll be using the techniques as ways to

improve the physical designs I create. I previously explored sketched visualisations of interpretations

of a variety of design concepts that could be implemented into the machine. However, I kept these

explorations, experiments and developments mostly to myself. This course showed me the possible

depth these visualisations can provide if I share my thoughts and processes with others.

My first application is to sketch out the ideas that I have into collages, segmented into various

design philosophies. I’ll incorporate various types if imagery (non-sketched) into the collage to provide

the source of inspiration. Another thing I’ll add for clarity is the use of various colours to highlight

certain sections for importance. These collages should function as a broad overview of the ideas that I

have regarding a specific feature. I’ll repeat this step for a multitude of features (about 2 or 3 to start

off).

Now comes the part where I involve my colleagues. I’ll present the collages to a couple of

colleagues after equipping them with post-its. Followingly, I give them 15 minutes to provide my

collages with feedback through the post-its. After these 15 minutes I gather all involved people and

will ask them to explain or give further comments regarding my designs and ideas.

The last step is to ask my colleagues to provide their own sketch (on A4 paper) of their

interpretation of the ideas I came up with.

Insight

One of the main things I learned from this shared experience with my co-workers is the

amazing value of their perspectives on my ideas. I found that their comments provided insight

regarding gaps in my knowledge and oversights in my designs. While not always comfortable, I was

able to process their commentary in a collaborative effort to create a better common understanding

of the project as a whole. We worked together to further make a better design for these

subcomponents.

Another great benefit of using this technique of collaboration was the strengthening of the

bond between myself and my co-workers. Even though we already (somewhat) worked together

before, we now have a better understanding of each other’s views on the project and designing as a

whole.

Approach

I can conclude from the previous section that (a more thorough than before) visualisation of a

certain concept can greatly help with creating a better concept, while also improving other aspects of

a project. Further design should definitely make use of more of this collaborative visual process to gain

more and more common insight and improvements.

A slight alteration for future reference is the increase of the amount of detail within a given

design. I noticed that some ideas weren’t sketched with enough detail, leaving too much room for

personal interpretation where it wasn’t necessarily needed. More detail should give a clearer picture

of the idea I’m trying to convey towards my co-workers.

Leading the Learning with Design Thinking  Design Thinking for Innovation – Peer Graded Assessment  Antonio Ledezma  March 15, 2018    Challenge  I work for a Pharmaceutical Company, and we follow our parent organization’s  business planning process of developing “Mid-Term Plans (MTP)” that are 3-year  road maps that help us map our departmental goals to the overall corporate  goals.  We are nearing the end of the MTP that covered 2009-2015 for the  Training Department, and will be preparing to refresh our goals for 2019-2021.  In  the past, the Leadership team has completed this exercise on our own, and then  cascaded our plan down to the rest of the department.  I believe that we have an  opportunity to improve upon our plans by including the individual trainers and  support staff in this process.  Applying the principles learned in this course,  specifically the idea generation insights from Week 3, could really provide us with  a robust plan for the next three years.    Selection  My rationale behind choosing to leverage idea generation stems from the  thinking around the questions “What is” and “What if”.  As a Training Department,  our Vision is to Lead the Learning for our customers.  You will note that we do  not say “training” and that is by design.  We strive to make our classroom events  more than traditional lecture sessions with interactive workshops, the inclusion of  technology, and leveraging different room layouts for a more immersive feel.  In  the spirit of keeping things fresh – using “What is” could be a perfect start for  taking a look at our learners, how they learn today compared to how our classes  function, and to really dig into their needs.  Then we can leverage “What if”  sessions to build out a host of ideas that can reinvigorate what we do.  The goal  would be to end up with a practical plan that focuses on both near- and long-term  opportunities to enhance our learning platform.    Application/Approach  I will outline my application and approach through a description of a series of  planned workshops.  Unfortunately, as we are on a Fiscal Year, this course has  coincided with year-end business, and I will not have the opportunity to run the  sessions and report outcomes.  I will provide context around expected outcomes  that will be hypothetical in nature, and hope that they will help illustrate the vision  for how I will apply my learning.      As is standard practice for our planning sessions, each team will be required to  bring research to help shape the discussion.  Our team spends 2-3 days per  month engaging directly with our customers in the field.  They have already been  given direction to spend time discussing how our representatives learn in their  day-to-day business.  What is their method for learning during the day - do they  take time during sales calls to review marketing materials?  What is their

preferred method for learning - are they listening to developmental podcasts or  reading books/blogs?  What is their favorite tool to use for learning - are there  any apps they use on a personal basis to develop themselves, maybe learning a  new language?  The most important question to ask – what is their biggest  challenge in continuing their development with our organization.      Our first session will focus on this research and we will develop our Napkin  Patches based on common areas across each team.  Following our team read  outs, the group will be divided into mixed teams (to maximize different views &  thoughts) to determine the needs and benefits of our customers, and leveraging  our white boards in the Learning Lab we’ll identify our baseline plan for the  current year, as well as those ideas that will take a few more years to develop.    The next session will be our “What If” session where teams will begin to gather  their ideas for how our plans can meet the identified needs, and to do so in a  fashion that really evolves our ability to Lead the Learning.  We will again use  mixed groups to maximize our ideas, and will spend time discussing ideas and  building out our Napkins.  Since we have two primary types of learning –  classroom and virtual – we will use different colored post-it notes to identify  where ideas fit for delivery methods.  In addition, we have a Learning Technology  team that focuses on novel methods for training delivery – virtual, eLearning,  apps, etc. – so they will have a different color to identify any new technologies  that we would need to invest in or pilot.      Ideas from this session will further be grouped into “Now” sections to help build  out near-term initiatives, and “Future” sections to identify those that will need  more time to develop and implement.  These will finalize our Napkins as the team  can group them further into Big Ideas that we can align to the business needs of  the organization, and map out our MTP for 2019-2021.    Insight  As I stated earlier, our Leadership Team traditionally sets the direction for our  Department as it pertains to aligning with corporate goals.  These plans tie to  business need and our delivery methods fall within a typical learning and  development framework for supporting the training needs of our organization.  In  essence, we build what the business asks for to meet their goal, and run  workshops to help communicate them.      This method will enable us to bring more innovative ideas to the table, but more  importantly, ideas built for our customers based on their preferences.  We have  the ability to design learning programs that are atypical in nature, and go beyond  our standard workshops or virtual classrooms.  By gaining feedback from our  customers, they can feel like they are a part of their own development.  In  addition, bringing the full department into the discussion and development of our  plans should provide a connected team, which can ultimately lead us to success  through a sense of ownership and shared direction.

innovation which are the strong points to help customer understand the true value I bring to

them. However, what the most important for me is time management, I need to show the

improve my ability to understand ideas and collaborate during meetings. In a research by

Chuck Frey, mind mapping expert, employees who use a mind mapping method believe

that their productivity increased by 25 percent. Therefore, in the project two week ago, I

try to apply what I have learned from the mind mapping course to manage my time and as

the result, I had achieved the following:

management planning

•  Improve communication and collaboration inside and between teams

What is more, Mind mapping is not only bring the effects to my career but also my study

since I still attend the extra classes for soft skills. Unlike traditional teaching in classes,

visualizing ideas through mind mapping help me to think better and separate complex

problems into simpler topics. Furthermore, I also support me to understand and analyze

ideas through visual elements and colors. When I face problems to organize my thinking

flow, tools such as mind mapping help me to a better thinking experience through the

coherent process to analyze problems and situations. For instances:

•  Brainstorming and creative thinking sessions

•  Analyze research and projects

•  Find innovative solutions for projects

•  Training in decision making and understanding problems

Insight & Approach

What I have learned from conducting this exercise with several groups, I found that When we

are thinking of an idea, taste a specific food or visit a place, our mind starts to link this

action with our memories and previous experience using a relevant model. Our brain starts

with one center action, color, taste or image and builds branches of thoughts that are used

as a base for other multiplied ideas. How we think works very similar to tree branches.

This concept is used as the basis for all mind mapping systems and approaches. And for

what I known from the past - the usage for visual recording of ideas was first used in the

3rd century by Porphyry of Tyros to visualize concepts and theories from Aristotle and

Ramon Llull. However, it is introduced again as one of the thinking methods by British

psychologist, Tony Buzan – Mind mapping from this course add the powerful weapon to

guidelines:

•  It starts with a single idea that is represented with text, color or image. Each idea should

be presented with one single word and use visual elements to categorize it such as,

upper an lower words, colors, codes and images.

•  More subsidiary ideas are added around the main idea and connect with it by lines. All

the branches should have connection lines that link it with the center idea.

•  Unified hierarchy styles should be implemented through the mind map. This style uses

different visual elements to organize ideas.

would use the visualization activity as a starting point for a series of design thinking activities.

tool throughout the remainder of their work.

MIND MAPPING

Mind Mapping application for smartphone app project

Challenge and Selection

As part of an ongoing innovation project, I decided to apply the Mind Mapping tool in the sequence

‘what is?’ of the design thinking process. The project concerns office space equipment; the company

in which I work specializes in Internet of Things (IOT) control applications for the residential market

where we have some significant success. With this experience we want to develop applications in the

business or tertiary sector, however it turns out that the needs are different from the residential

sector and that we do not have a client but several who are involved in the value chain.

So, we analyzed the stakeholder’s experiences to ascertain the opportunities. The marketing

department initiated the traditional approach of researching needs with our customers and I decided

to extract the ethnological part discussed in the interviews, in order to reframe it in the approach

‘what is?’. The reason for this activity was to provide the opportunity to apply a design thinking tool,

Mind Mapping, and thus highlighting the needs of customers, create clusters, find links, and define

design criteria. The interviews and graphics from the marketing study allowed me to define typical

user profiles and to create a virtual panel of 5 persona. This type of document does not fit with the

notions of visualization necessary for our exercise, according to the precepts of Design Thinking.

Therefore, I called upon a professional illustrator to visualize the life scenarios of the users (the 5

persona), he drew on a large board for each persona, the different actions, habits, and routines…

which usually takes place in a typical day.

The circumstances of the COVID19 health crisis greatly disrupted the organization of the exercise. I

had to adapt because I managed the exchange remotely as the people were all working from home.

So, I put together a team of different profiles (sellers, designer, marketing manager) and a few loyal

partners (facility manager and office manager). I invited them to a 4-hour session to establish the

Mind Mapping. This constitutes the preparatory work for the Mind Mapping session which, as

Professor Ludovic has shown us, will allow us to establish a representation of our clients’ minds and to

identify the relevant criteria in a more visually engaging way. This will facilitate everyone's creativity

in the idea generation phase.

Application

First, I chose the central theme of Mind Mapping while targeting our research on improving working

life. The interviews were quite broad, we took up the needs of 5 key persona: the Space Planner who

must create environments adapted to workers; the Furniture Manufacturer who must face new

electrification needs integrated into the furniture; the Facility Manager who manages the building

functioning and its maintenance; the Office Manager who manages the allocation of office spaces

and, of course, the end user. Based on the central subject of Mind Mapping and the deployment of

the 5 persona needs, we started to create links between them. With the help of the illustrated

boards, sent beforehand, the participants quickly grasped the Mind Mapping tool and the

progressive and synthetic construction of our reflections gradually unfolded before our eyes. The

Xmind tool that I used for the exercise was quite practical because it allows you to add annotations

as you comment. Certain needs on the secondary crown triggered debates between the participants,

I simply chose to develop the ideas on a third level to keep track of the exchange so that I could

return to it later. For example, End Users wanted to have feedback from the company restaurant to

organize their departure for lunch based on attendance, being able to cancel their meal based on the

menu, having access to the daily menu, and so forth.  As a result, I created a "restaurant needs"

family. Once all work life improvement needs were listed, I suggested that the participants attempt

to link the needs of each persona. Continuing the example of restaurant needs, we were able to link

those of End User, Facility Manager and Office manager, who wanted him to know more precisely

the volume and frequency of attendance in the company restaurant: Same cluster for different

reasons! We created a third crown to detail these the reason of needs.

Mapping Visualization:

The map is voluntarily simplified to maintain the project’s confidentiality, a part of the needs

examples remains to illustrate the links between clusters.

We were thus able to link a dozen needs between the persona, which could be identical,

complementary, or interconnected. At this stage, the team was actively engaged at the same level

and ideas began to surface, such as creating a smartphone application which could connect persona

and meet their different needs in a complementary way. I proposed to define the design criteria for

each need, knowing that for the same need the design criteria will be different from one persona to

another. This would facilitate the evaluation of ideas in the next ‘what if’ phase as described by

Professor J. Liedtka. Having completed the Mind Mapping phase, I was then able to start the next

phase of the design think process which is the brainstorming session (Not detailed here).

Insight and approach

First and foremost, I really enjoyed managing this Mind Mapping process and I think the participants

also appreciated this working session. I was very apprehensive about the videoconference

organization (apart from the course recommendations). In the end, people were very relaxed and

willing. Everyone contributed and the exchanges have been quite numerous. I limited the exercise to

4 hours and the participants to 7. I think it would have been difficult to have more participants in the

videoconference. There is another gap with the course recommendations: the participants were not

the interviewed users due to the fact the marketing study had already been carried out. In this case

the mind mapping was more a reading and an in-depth analysis of the expressions of the interviewed

people.

The construction of the Mind Mapping developed is quite easy, it is undoubtedly the simplified

visualization of the Mind Mapping and the summary descriptions of the clusters (sometimes

comprising just a single word to illustrate the need) which allows everyone to move forward at the

same time , without getting lost in overly detailed lists. As a result, the relationships between the

different clusters literally jumped out at us during the exercise. This would have required more

memory if we had listed needs (as they were initially in the marketing study). The hardest part was to

define the design criteria. I think I found the limit of the form I had chosen because they would have

been easier to determine with real customers. Besides, one of the participants was a Facility

manager, and I could observe that the definition of the criteria concerning this persona was

developed faster.

I think I will reuse this tool in my future work. However, I note that the design thinking approach

does not correspond to an addition of creativity tools and that to be effective it is necessary to

scrupulously follow the different stages. At this stage of my reflection, I see that I have a better grasp

of my subject and that certain ideas are already taking shape in my mind; I hope in the following

phases they will prove to be a source of innovation.

Name:   Arnaldo Campos

Forgive me in advance if you, fellow student, get stuck while reading my paragraphs. I’m a Spanish  native speaker, but I’ll do my best to get understood in the assignment.

Challenge:

I haven’t worked in any organization yet, I’m an industrial engineering student from Peru,  in South America. But I found a way to utilize the Visualization Tool. Due to the quarantine  imposed in my country, I’m currently taking virtual classes at my university, which didn’t  have enough experience imparting online courses before. So, I’ve struggled while learning,  and also while trying to do group work with my classmates. We were used to study  together in the study lounges of the campus. There was some kind of cubicles with tables  and whiteboards that help us study together and sketch any idea that we may have. But  dealing with online education is so different and the communication between peers has  been reduced to virtual meetings via Zoom or Google Meets. Hence, the challenge for me  is to implement a kind of visualization using our laptops or another way to communicate  graphical ideas to understand situations.

Selection:

I figured out an application for this Visualization Tool while I was using Microsoft  WhiteBoard to simulate, forgive the redundancy, a whiteboard to solve some math  problems for an assignment. As it was said in the screencast related to this tool,  visualization is about visual thinking, and that’s an ability that my partners and I, as  engineering students, were used to putting in practice in presential classes. One of the  main reasons why I chose this tool is that it lets us portray ideas that don’t even exist yet  actually. Similar to what the lecturer said, university students usually generate new ideas  and possibilities for improvement (while doing some academic research, for instance) that  haven’t been seen before. And sometimes is easier to get a common understanding of an  idea using visualization rather than verbalizing that notion. Based on those ideas, I realized  the importance of a virtual whiteboard (or slides, a Prezi presentation, etc.) to enhance  online education for engineers. Ideas are commonly misunderstood if a peer or a professor  just talks in a videoconference since is difficult to understand even what is the topic  they’re trying to communicate. So, I decided to implement the Visualization Tool.

Application:

The first time I implemented the Visualization Tool was while my classmates and I were  trying to figure out how to design an improvement plan for a company in an Introduction  to Management course that we’re taking. I realized that we were exposing our ideas at the  Zoom meeting, but none of us could fully understand other ideas. It was difficult to fully  imagine a situation just by verbalizing it. At that point, I suggested that we could use  Microsoft Whiteboard and the share screen function of Zoom to simulate the whiteboards  that we used to have at the campus and portray there our ideas.

So, all of us started to diagram and capture our thoughts on our screens. I have a multi- touch notebook, so it was easy for me. However, I realized some of my friends struggled  while sketching with the mouse, but their sketches were still understandable. At the  moment we started sharing our screens via Zoom, we were able to better understand the

ideas of the others. For instance, a friend of mine sketched a situation in which a company  is reintroducing itself to the market after the quarantine, with the safety protocols  required, and I think that’s something each person can imagine differently without having  a base drawing. I think the Visualization Tool was applied satisfactorily overall, as it helps  us to use our visual thinking related to the right part of our brain, but I think that the  inability to draw at the same time, as in a physical whiteboard, was a constraint.

Insight:

What I discovered is that, indeed, is much better to understand others’ ideas if they draw  something or use a picture to describe their thoughts. I gained the insight that is important  to completely understand the “what is” part of the problem, that is to say, the complete  scope of the problem and prevent to make it too narrow. Talking about online education,  many students claim that there’s a problem that involves the teaching quality, but some of  them don’t broaden the issue to the absence of a whiteboard or a plenty life interaction  between peers.

Another insight I gained is the relevance of acquiring a uniform understanding of the  issue/problem/situation between your peers of you. What I mean is that everyone in the  group has to have the same concept of the problem and manage the same design criteria  to reach an innovative solution. That idea of Design Thinking applied to my described case,  I think, it’s represented in the fact that my peers and I had to “speak in the same terms” in  order to come to a solution for the business case of our assignment. If we couldn´t plenty  comprehend the situation, we’d have problems while developing a solution. That’s the  situation in which Visualization Tool helped us a lot.

Approach:

Finally, the next time I utilize the Visualization Tool, I’ll tell my peers that if they don’t have  to use the screen to draw, they can diagram a picture in a paper and then take a photo and  present it during the virtual conference. Also, I think the application of this tool could be  improved a lot if there’s software that lets people draw simultaneously on their screens.

As I wrote in the start of my assignment, I haven’t worked at any place yet, but I become  amazed by the possibilities and tools that Design Thinking offers us, it even helped me  adopt a more growth mindset, and I hope I could use its tools in my future working life.

Challenge:   In 2019, I was trying to find out how to promote online tutoring to tutors, parents and students in Singapore.  Online tutoring in Singapore had not really taken off yet at that time. In fact, everybody had different ideas of  what online tutoring was. Parents were generally skeptical about its usefulness, students mostly did not have a  clear idea of what online tutoring looked like, and most tutors were adopting a “wait-and-see” approach  towards this emerging technology.    There were also multiple factors that affected the adoption rate of online tutoring. Among these are: maturity of  online tutoring software, availability of on-boarding training, cost of subscription of online tutoring software,  effectiveness of learning through online tutoring, cyber security concerns, etc.    My team conducted training for approximately 150 freelance tutors who showed interest in online tutoring but  only a handful of them really adopted online tutoring as part of their offer. We tried to engage parents in a few  parents workshops; they produced only a few customers.    Due to our limited resources, a multi-pronged approach like that was very hard and slow work. The challenge  was really to identify a few critical factors that had maximum impact on the adoption rate of online tutoring in  Singapore, and to act upon them.    Tool selection:  It was mentioned in the Mind Mapping Tool video in this course, “Mind mapping is looking for patterns and  insights in a large quantity of data you collected during your exploration of what is the current reality. The goal  is to establish criteria for the what-if idea generation phase.”    Since my challenge was to make sense of the current situation (“What Is”), I had chosen to use a modified  version of Mind Mapping, called “Systems Mapping”. I learnt this tool from Cobus Mpanza, who also attended  Alexandr Ospina’s Design Thinking course.    Application of the selected tool:  Step 1:​ I started off by writing down all the possible factors that affect adoption of online tutoring, one factor on  a piece of post-it note.     Step 2:​ Then I got a large A1-size paper, and divided it into two sections - “Reinforce” and “Hinder”.     Step 3​: Next, I assess the current state of each factor; if the current state of a factor reinforces the adoption of  online tutoring, I will stick it under the “Reinforce” part of the A1-size paper. The same went to factors which  were currently hindering the adoption of online tutoring. For example, “subscription of online tutoring software”  is a factor. Now the cost was currently considered affordable to most tutors, so I placed the post-in note of this  factor under the “Reinforce” section.    Step 4​: Once we have all the factors categorized in either “Reinforce” or “Hinder” section, I started to draw  lines to link up factors that either drove another factor, or was driven by another factor.    Step 5​: The final step in System Mapping is to do a tally. The factors that had the most number of lines going  into and going out of them, are the key driving factors to adoption of online tutoring.    This is a somewhat tidied up version of my Systems Map.

Insight gained:    What I concluded from this exercise confirmed my suspicion, that the key driving factor to online tutoring is  really how tutors perceive it. In 2019, most tutors clearly were not taking online tutoring seriously. The exercise  suggested that by focusing our resources to change tutors’ perception of online tutoring, it would have the  greatest impact on the adoption rate of online tutoring.    Approach:    I found that it was very important that I was able to stand in the position of stakeholders, to come up with as  many factors as possible. It was important to state factors as neutral rather than to add my assessment of it  prematurely, for example, a factor should be “possibilities to access tutors on demand” and not “should be able  to access tutors on demand”. This is something I will pay more attention to in the future.    It was also challenging to hold my bias and assess the current state of things impartially, so that I can place  the factors in the right sections. The tendency was to think that most factors were doing well, and they were  reinforcing the adoption of online tutoring. The truth was that they were not, which was exactly why I was doing  this System Mapping exercise in the first place. This is also something to pay attention to in the future.

Pong Ng – Reflection – Visualization

Challenge    I am a Product Manager in the digital space. My current project is to implement a complete  redesign of a government agency’s website. The goal is to drive up interest and therefore  increase the number of quality candidates applying to work at this agency. My team tackles  design challenges using a human-centered approach. We started our project off with a  Discovery period where we employed ethnographic research and affinity mapping to draw out  users’ deepest pain points and effectively synthesize those findings.     The challenge was figuring out a way to quickly translate those insights into designs, to validate  those designs with users, to update those designs, and to revalidate before pushing to  Engineers. We wanted to get the designs right as to avoid the additional cost of excessive  rework down the road.    Selection    I felt the best way to handle this challenge was with rapid prototyping using the Visualization  tool. Visualization is the act of translating thoughts into a visual format so it can be easily  shared and discussed among teammates and users. As opposed to written notes or just verbal  explanations, Visualization enables people provide an easier and more effective way of  communicating information. It provides context and helps jog peoples’ creative juices.    I selected Visualization based off Angela Myer’s discussion in Week 1. I learned that helping  folks visualize something may improve the chances of achieving a sense of agreement and  consensus. Visualization would help draw out conversation and solicit feedback in a way that a  verbal overview would not. In the end, it was the best tool to help align our designs to users’  mental models.    Application    I suggested that we begin the design phase by using low-fidelity prototypes. I wanted designers  to start sketching out solutions in a quick, iterative manner. Although the prototypes were not  in color or finely tuned, it allowed designers to flex the right side of their brains in a creative  way. As a Product Manager, I was also involved with sketching out various solutions.    These wireframes were no more than basic layouts with squares and circles. These were built  out for various pages throughout the website and allowed designers to rapidly create and test  different designs with users. Users would provide feedback on page structure and hierarchy,  not focusing too much on visual design. I would log that feedback and the designers would get  to work integrating the user’s feedback into their designs. We would repeat this process until  designs matched the user’s expectations. These simple sketches captured so much user  feedback and in context, too!

Once wireframes were finalized, we moved onto high-fidelity compositions. Here designers  applied color theory, visual hierarchy, and iconography to the designs that were validated by  users. These visual compositions were also clickable. This allowed users to be fully immersed in  the designs and yielded valuable feedback.     Once we gained consensus from users on the high-fidelity compositions, we were ready to hanf  off to our Engineers to bring these designs to life. Overall, I’d say the tool was incredibly  effective in helping solicit feedback, explaining abstract concepts, and gaining consensus on  various designs.    Insight    By applying the principles of Visualization to my team’s work, we were able to acquire key  feedback from our users. It also helped facilitate internal conversations between designers and  engineers.    It resolved the primary challenge I faced – that I needed to translate research insights into  design. But it did so much more than that. It fast-tracked the design validation process as  described above.    Throughout the process, I learned that it was so much easier to test something when there was  a visual aspect to it. I learned that users were happy to test using low-fidelity prototypes – they  even found it fun and didn’t require high-fidelity designs. It didn’t take colors and pixel-perfect  designs to solicit important feedback.    More broadly, utilizing the Visualization tool helped validate Design Thinking as a process to  use on future projects. I saw a lot of success using visualization and am excited to try the other  design tools taught throughout the course.     Approach    Although we experienced a successful implementation of Visualization. Next time I would want  to have other team members involved with wireframing – not just Product Managers and  Designers. I think it’s especially important for Engineers to get in on the fun. It helps build  empathy between Designers and Engineers and also helps them communicate their unique  perspectives for design.

Reflection – Mind Mapping

Challenge & Selection    The design thinking tool that I choose as a final reflection is mind mapping. Design  thinking is applied for a group final project in one of the courses that I teach in higher  education. Undergrad students with a mayor in Tourism studies that are close to  completing their credits for graduation take an Information Systems course with the  purpose of achieving better practices on administration. The final project that they work  on is a work-in-progress website that they feel is needed in their field of study. Before  they even start with the website design, they narrow the project idea to an area of  interest within tourism in one of the following fields: gastronomy, health, museums and  exhibitions, and event logistics. After that, they think of a problem that may be solved  by a website or app and begin working on an idea that ends in a user ready prototype.  During this whole process they receive feedback until they are ready to present their  final product and hand in their documentation. The idea to use design thinking with the  mind mapping tool, is for the students to better understand the needs of their future  customers as a human-centered solution, by generating an idea that will be transformed  into a real world creative and useful solution with a user-friendly interface design.    Mind mapping as a tool for this project starts as a mind map, once the area of interest  is chosen, and in a process with the proper design criteria. Design criteria brings a  meaning to all the data by transforming it into information, with the required conditions  met to satisfy the customer’s problem. As said before, the areas to explore are  gastronomy tourism, health tourism, museum and exhibitions tourism, and finally  tourism for event logistics. Once the group chooses an area, they follow the design  thinking steps in the process of: what is, what if, what wows, and what works. By using  this tool, groups prevent countless attempts that end up in no-good solutions, while  creating a visual and engaging design challenge proposal. All of the concepts  encountered by using the mind mapping tool, start connecting within each other in a  visual way, by representing the minds of customers, in order to deliver an intuitive and  creative website or app.    Application    Mind mapping and gathering data starts after choosing the specific tourism area  proposed for the project, as mentioned in the Challenge & Selection section. Afterwards,  the group starts writing ideas in sticky notes that they think customers have trouble  with, while thinking in chosen the tourism field. This step defines the “what is” in design  thinking. The group consists of 3 to 4 students, so each of them is required to start  conversations with potential customers and write the brainstorming ideas in the same  sticky notes. Afterwards, the group reads them all and makes clusters of related data  that may channel the project orientation in the designated area. Sticky notes should  contain short descriptions of ideas of problems that customers have, same as  interactions that may improve in the area of tourism to explore in a website or app.

The process of identifying the clusters starts defining the representation for the design  criteria. The next step is for the group of students to sort out the sticky notes into the  cluster in which it belongs; all of them are included. Later on, each cluster delivers insight  for the “what if” part of the design thinking mapping process and traces the design  solution to satisfy the customer’s problem. The process of mapping or relating the ideas  starts, defining the mind map and keeping in mind the customer’s needs. In this step,  data is being transformed into information that has a meaning. By this design thinking  step, the group has resolved the idea about what to develop (either website or app), the  product name, a brief description of the system, as well as the product justification and  objective. Other aspects of the preliminary project evolve as well, such as target market,  list of customer needs, system functions to integrate, and a brief and simple project  management plan.    Once the project idea is defined, the user interface design starts based on the ideas from  the “what if” step. Next, students start to develop a prototype of the website or app  pretending to deliver the “what wows”. Through iteration steps, constant feedback from  the instructor and from several potential customers that participated in the idea  brainstorming, the product is transformed to a final version of the “what works” step in  design thinking.    Other few project requisites apart from the website or app prototype, regarding system  documentation are delivered as well, including the product financing proposal, a  reflection of the project process and how it relates to the concepts learned in the course,  and a final reflection in terms of product feasibility, system maintenance, etc. The mind  mapping tool is of great use to find the right problem to solve with all of the implications,  by thinking about the user, and by creating a functional prototype that works in a  creative and fun way.      Insight & Approach    Students often have trouble finding the right problem to solve that represents a creative  solution for tourism customers. They often lack originality or depth in the functionality  of the system, being an app or website. By using the design thinking mind mapping tool,  students get engaged into innovative solutions and get to understand the problem much  better. The focus in using the mind mapping tool since the beginning is human centered  based on the user’s needs. This involves analyzing the project and getting a much better  understanding of the latter, in order to deliver a prototype that is being tested  throughout the rest of the design thinking process. Students get to stand in the customer  shoes while finding or identifying a new problem, or one problem that already has a  solution but gets to be fixed into an even better solution. By practicing design thinking  through mind mapping, students get to practice important values such as empathy while  defining and idealizing the solution. The following steps in the process involve constant  prototyping and testing, that end up in a real world challenge that delivers a successful  product.

Finally, for user design projects proposed by students based on potential customer  needs, I strongly agree in using the mind mapping design thinking tool. Mind mapping  in this type of project ensures that a creative solution will be delivered, that the project  will be engaging for the students, and that the solution will help the final users and  customer needs because in the end the idea has been born in a human centered way.

As we’ve seen, the Design Thinking has a wide range of resources depending of the  type of need we have, problem we would like to solve or simply, to share an idea. Reflections of Marcelo Caroline related to Visualization

Challenge

As responsible for the IT department in the company, I have constant challenges related to the  interpretation of needs and technical requirements of the business for the development of  solutions that create value and are easy to maintain. This challenge has increased as new process  automation needs arise, new needs for analysis of large volumes of data, new digitization needs  sometimes brought by business areas and sometimes fostered by the IT team.

Specifically in this case, my team and I were asked to develop an App that facilitated the recording  of mechanical, electrical, civil problems, etc. found in our hydroelectric and wind power plants, with  the objective of allowing the analysis, comparison and centralized prioritization of the solutions to  be applied in the power plants using the Root Cause Analysis (RCA) method.

Departments interested in this solution were: Local Maintenance, Health Security, Safe end  Environment, the centralized area of Projects Engineering and IT.

Selection

To facilitate the understanding of the various departments involved, I chose to use visualization  tools to translate the document of requirements, spreadsheets and other documents collected with  the requesting areas.

Because meetings are remote, using the Microsoft White board in combination with scanned paper  drawings seemed like a good choice because of the ability to make changes and even new drawings  in real time as solutions were discussed. Later we were able to prove that the use of the White  board was a good choice.

Application

Even before the app's development, the customer areas were already doing problems management  in a precarious way using forms and a giant Excel spreadsheet. In the spreadsheet were all the rules  of analysis and prioritization of solutions by project and maintenance engineers.

The first meeting was organized to allow everyone to come forward and report their role in the use  and development of the solution.  Then, the maintenance area demonstrated the form (in Word)  and the worksheet where they recorded the problems. They also demonstrated the current process  of problem analysis, application of the Ishikawa method (Root Cause), search for similar problems  in the knowledge base (in Excel) and finally prioritizing the application of the solution. In this way,  my team was able to clearly understand the need of the business and thus prepare a document  with the primary requirements of the new App.

We then made some paper drawings demonstrating the normal activities of maintenance  professionals and the suggestions of screens of the App with the various stages of the process. We  also designed the phase of analysis of problems with research to the knowledge base, division of  the problem into several probable causes, access to other important bases for validation of  previous equipment conditions and finally the screen of prioritization of the resolution action in the

backend of the system. We present the various drawings and screen suggestions of the system to  the requesting areas that confirmed the understanding. We then set out to develop front-end  prototypes of the App according to the specifications and validated designs.

Insight / Approach

The use of visualization to demonstrate the understanding of the entire process has promoted  greater collaboration of the requesting areas. Once a visualization of the problem is clearly  understood, we start to discuss deeper aspects of the problem and how the App should be  developed to cover the needs. The use of drawings has also helped to increase the contribution of  engineers on the necessary actions of mitigation and resolution of problems since it also allows  them to present drawings of the solution in the App itself. Additionally, we develop graphical  reports with the results of root cause analyses, resolutions applied and gains obtained with the use  of the method. This has further fostered the imagination of user areas in search of digital solutions  that facilitate their work.

The challenge is to transition  from an approach of strict compliance to a customer service approach where our staff are looked to as  partners instead of police officers. MIND MAPPING

1. CHALLENGE

I was asked to co-facilitate a design thinking workshop within the Digital &  Technology Sector of our organisation a few months ago, during the second wave of  the pandemic in my country. Our organisation recommended all staff to work  remotely, thus our workshop had to adapt to a virtual environment which was new  to not only the facilitators but participants. The intention of the design thinking  workshop was to solicit user stories from all project managers and business analysts  in the sector on the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning in all  areas of the organization. Our Chief Information Officer suggested that a horizontal  approach would allow efficiency gains in the in-house development or procurement  of a solution that caters for the organisation’s needs. Our team of two facilitators  alongside the lead project team managers regrouped virtually to decide on the best  approach to conduct the virtual design thinking workshop and discussed various  tools, methods and platform to collaboratively gather user stories for a group of 30  participants.

2. SELECTION

After much discussion on the agenda and main objectives of the design thinking  workshop, our team of facilitators felt comfortable with selecting the mind map  method as the method to gather user stories. According to Wikipedia, a mind map is  a  diagram used to visually organize information. It is hierarchical and shows  relationships among pieces of the whole, created around a single concept, drawn as an  image in the center of a blank page. Major ideas are connected directly to the central  concept, and other ideas branch out from those major ideas.

Having participated in a global design thinking workshop, I proposed Miro as the mind  map platform as it catered to multi-user collaboration in conjunction with Microsoft  Teams as the meeting platform.

3. APPLICATION

I volunteered to design the mind map to fit to the objective of collecting user stories  from participants. Centrally, I overlaid the mind map with an image of a neutral network  representing the human brain symbolic to artificial intelligence. At the top of the canvas,  I placed visuals to remind participants what user stories are, which are personas that we  want to gather with use cases for each department across the organization.

Each branch connected to the central concept referenced a sector in our organisation  and its branches referenced specific types of staff in those sectors. For example, within

the administration department, there were three sub-branches representing a staff filing  for claims, the claims processing officer, and the finance officer disbursing the funds. We  then got each participant to pen down how artificial intelligence and machine learning  could improve each user story, essentially a wishlist. A staff would want their claims to  be automated through a mobile app by taking snapshots of the parking receipts, a claims  processing officer would want the web app to assist with approving whitelisted claims  and only highlighting exception cases, and the finance officer would want to only  perform an audit only on accounts that breached authorised limits.

4. INSIGHT

Mind map was applied effectively in the 1 hour workshop whereby participants were  split according to their assigned portfolios and collaborated to mind map each user  story. At the end of the workshop, us facilitators recapped and debriefed each user story  to all participants.

Feedback given to us facilitators was positive whereby participants did not feel fatigued  as they could take their time to pen down ideas. This workshop managed to gather close  to 70 unique user stories and these were all big ideas that had not been filtered to see  ‘What Works’ because our CIO wanted us to think big! Because participants were asked  to empathize with the personas rather than themselves, as a staff in the IT sector, user  experiences were captured well in the mind map. Miro’s interactivity of the canvas  whereby we could all see every participants cursor on the browser helped with keeping  energy levels high as it was a fun and de-stressing activity for all.

5. APPROACH

Next time, I would spend more effort in designing the layout of the mind map that allows  for greater intuition from a participants perspective on what is required from them. For  instance, I would display an example user story that has been mind-mapped at the start  of the exercise. Additionally, I would recommend all participants to have their videos  turned on to keep to the collaborative spirit in a virtual design thinking process even if it  means using a secondary mobile device as the video camera. I would also have a debrief  among facilitators to get their views on the effectiveness of the mind map tool in meeting  the objective of gathering user stories because Miro had difficulties exporting data into  CSV from mind maps.

Mustafa Majid  Design Thinking - Assignment  Learning Launch       Challenge and Selection     I am a graphic designer at my work and also do some industrial design and conduct  experiments often to help bring new products to market. My team and I were challenged to  develop a Construction toy to sell along with our existing starter kit. The toy is geared for kids  ages 5 and up and consists of flat base pieces or blocks that can interconnect and gears that  can be pegged into the multiple holes in the base pieces. It has holes on top and bottom of the  base piece and they're like puzzle pieces that fit together and make a larger base. The gears  can mesh together so they can be turned by a battery operated motor.  My team and I were  challenged to create an advanced kit to sell along with our existing starter kit. The advanced kit  will include more pieces to build bigger models and also include instructions booklets to build  special theme characters to develop lateral thinking and planning skills. We went through  market research, competitor analysis and idea generation to develop some themes for the  advanced kit. We wanted to test the different themes and see which ones are marketable, fun  and challenging.     Application     Out team built models/themes: a car, dinosaur, train and many others that my company  researched and created instructions booklets on how to make the models. We set up  experiments with groups of five kids. I gave them basic instructions. I handed them printed  instruction booklets of different themes. It has a visual of the themes toy on the cover to identify  the instructions booklet.  We asked towards the end which toy they liked best, the least, which  ones were easy or too hard.     Insight     We learned that building sets were a bit more challenging, the problem is that the base pieces  has multiple peg holes and can be confusing when building one of the character/themes for the  MoGee Advanced Kit sets. A few kids placed the gear peg in the wrong hole and gave up and  did their own modification. Also, the younger kids couldn't identify the top of the base from the  bottom since they look similar so they get confused on following directions on placing the base  piece in the right orientation and connecting two base pieces with the right sides. The younger  kids were not as persistent when following through with directions and overcoming challenges  so they become more creative and designed it their own way. The older kids were more  persistent and see it as a challenge to overcome.

For the second learning launch we made two different instructions. One booklet includes  beginners instructions for ages 5 and up were the gears didn't have to be in the right peg hole  and the base pieces didn’t have to be in place in a certain orientation.  It has step by step  instructions with 3d views of the model, highlighting the current part that needs to be connected,  a blown up view of the base piece with the highlighted peg hole and instructing to count from the  top left hole to find the correct position. This builds their skills for following directions and  attention to detail, so these instructions are geared for advanced builder. We also made the  instructions more engaging, more colorful and used readable typefaces for the beginners  instructions. Our assumptions were correct for the improvement on the instructions, kids were  more engaged and excited in building the different sets. We chose the favorite themes kids  enjoyed and made the set a 5 in 1 with instructions.     Approach     Our company learned a lot from the learning launches. There are few things we do differently for  a third learning launch. We would differentiate the top and bottom base piece by naming it "T"  for top and "B" for bottom or giving the peg holes a different color. Also, invest some time in  creating a video with step by step instructions that would be placed on the website or a phone  app that can somehow track the children's creations and have a reward system. Also they can  interact with other kids and challenge each other.

Example Reflection –Learning Launch

1.  Challenge

Our company decided to invest in an online education platform on financial education issues with  the intention of marketing these courses in the cooperative sector, in higher education colleges  and the general public in Colombia.

The technology on which the platform was assembled was revised and modernized and  additionally a pedagogical and instructional review was made to allow meeting the pedagogical  requirements of the schools.

Additionally, a digital marketing process was started, generating paid campaigns on Google and  Facebook in order to attract attention to the courses to potential customers and users. Contacts  were also made with some public and private schools and officials from the Bogotá and Chía  mayors.

However, after a year of starting the project, the commercialization had not generated the  expected results in either of the two selected market segments despite having a very good quality  product, faced with the decision to continue with the project or not.

2.  Selection

As Stephan Naumann indicated in his lesson on Test Launches in Module 4 of the Design Thinking Course at  the University of Darden, we in the company made a business plan and analyzed it theoretically  and with the knowledge available on our part (limited because the line was new) and the business  partner (whose main strength was to be the pedagogical expert) and we launched ourselves to  execute it without previous tests.

However, given that the results were not occurring after more than a year of having started and  taking into account that the company was not in a position to make major investments in the  project, it was decided before aborting the project to seek a less traditional approach to refine the  business model and we found in the test launch methodology an interesting and appropriate  alternative to “learn quickly and cheaply”.

3.  Application

Before deciding to use the chosen model, we had been operating the Financial Education  Courses for free in four public schools in the Municipality of Chía (Colombia) with a view  to publicizing the product and achieving that in 2020 it could be switched to a paid

modality achieving that an item was included in the budget of these schools to be able to  pay for the service.

Additionally, the aim was to generate referrals to other schools, thus seeking to link a  greater number of schools. However, seeing that the inclusion in the budget of this item  was not easy because the subject of financial entrepreneurship in which this course was  being included was not part of the formal curriculum and that investment decisions were  not the exclusive power of the rectors the aforementioned revision stop was made to  rethink the continuity of the model.

Following the methodology defined by the model, the following elements were  established:

• Hypothesis: There is a significant number of people and entities that need training in

financial education and are willing to pay for an excellent product and we have such a  product which surpasses the products available in the market to meet this need.

• People: Among the potential clients, the following types of people were identified:

 Individuals interested in acquiring financial education to achieve proper and

responsible management of their finances and to be able to generate financial  stability and / or successfully advance in their ventures.

 Cooperatives that within their social mission and support their associates want to

offer them training in financial education.

 Higher Education Colleges that as part of their training programs must include

Financial Education topics to comply with the national government guidelines  aimed at increasing financial inclusion (which in Colombia is well below developed  countries) and improving PISA-type exam results that include such content.

• The need: To have a high quality financial education program which is not geared

towards selling you a financial product as is the case with most available programs.

• The idea that meets the need: The financial education program which consists of

three courses that cover the basic concepts required to make efficient use of financial  resources and products:   Finance from home   Finances for entrepreneurs   Technical analysis

• Better than current alternatives: In our review of the products offered, most are

shallow courses developed by financial institutions to meet a Financial Education  requirement of the Financial Superintendence and to promote the consumption of  their products . On the other hand, there is an offer of seminars that promise to  change the mentality regarding money and remain on motivational aspects and few  practical recommendations.

Therefore, it was decided to set up a pilot course with students from various schools,  including public and private, some cooperatives and a representative sample of individual  users with which to test our hypothesis and the basic assumptions of the business model  described above.

4.  Insight

As a result of applying the Learning Release Tool, our team identified our hypotheses and  assumptions and designed releases to test these assumptions. In addition, we thought  about the possible results and how they would confirm or distort our assumptions  through sprints similar to those we use in the company for software development.

To date, we have not yet finished redefining the product's business model, nor are we  fully certain that we will achieve that the business idea is the successful undertaking we  want with a presence not only nationally but also internationally, but we are sure that the

path we are traveling is the best approach to achieve it and that if we are wrong in our  assumptions along this way we will know it as quickly and cheaply as possible.

5.  Approach

What we have learned as a team from carrying out this exercise is that the design of new  products, especially technology, requires a less traditional approach and that Design  Thinking tools such as Launch Design allow us to mature the business idea and gaining  knowledge iteratively without incurring large capital investments that ultimately do not  generate any results after a considerable time.

We have decided to implement this methodology for the development of new products in  the line of innovative solutions and we are seeking to apply it also for other types of  internal change initiatives in which the level of certainty and available information is not  the most adequate to handle it with traditional tools.

CHALLENGE

Being a part of an international organization aimed at addressing real world concerns on health, literacy,  poverty, and sustainable development proved to be challenging at times, despite the fulfillment that  one gets as a catalyst of change. As a member of Manuela Beltran University, I often deal with people from different walks of  life where we share moments that would be mutually beneficial and where we could learn from each  other’s experiences. A big challenge in this is the reality that we do not all share the same privileges and  sometimes, it is hard for us to conceptualize one’s story simply because we weren’t given the chance to  experience what another person has experienced. This explains how storytelling can be so powerful in  this line of work. It enables both parties to somehow allow the other to live the moment through  creative narration.

SELECTION

In carrying out the organization’s mission of serving humanity, one must get out of his comfort zone  literally and figuratively and visit places wherein the said person can make a difference. At first, the  receiving community wouldn’t open that much to you. This is understandable since we all undergo a  process of familiarization when encountering new faces. Story telling will allow you to creatively and  confidently introduce yourself and your advocacies so that you may encourage them to cooperate with  you.

APPLICATION

In one of our humanitarian trips to an island down south, we were briefed by our local government  partners that we should expect that the local community doesn’t get to experience interactions like  these too often, and that we should find a way to soften them up if we want to interact with them.  Fortunately, we share the same language and they understand our casual dialect, which gave us ample  opportunity to get close to them. We told stories of our group’s purpose and what we’ve been able to  accomplish in different communities around the globe for the past few years, and what we intend or  aim to achieve moving forward. You can tell their interest and excitement in our narratives as they  continuously asked questions and inject insights on their perception about groups similar to us. An elder  even shared past experiences wherein they felt as if they were being exploited, and later apologized if  they didn’t warm up too quickly. The exchange of stories led to the bonding of the two groups and  establish a relationship which led to celebrations and a feast later that night.

INSIGHT & APPROACH

Younger members of their community then proceeded to share their experiences on their daily living,  what type of problems they experience in their community, and how they deal with problems. They also  even acted out scenes on some part of their stories just to give us a clear depiction. One person also  expressed her desire to someday, experience living the urban life, just so she could have a glance at both  worlds.

Storytelling has brought immense satisfaction for both parties and this proved to be an efficient tool in  carrying out what both groups meant to convey. The exchange was meaningful and the means of  narration was effective enough to lead to understanding and fruitful collaboration.

Reflection: Mind Mapping

Challenge

I am a student of Computer Engineering department and our

challenge is to develop an android application. Our project is developing  an application to learning with Augmented Reality. We are the team of 4  of my classmates. I face various difficulties in choosing the way to  approach a new problem which is because the varied ways of developing  the solution which has to be cost-effective and a time-saving approach  simultaneously.     Selection      We go through various design thinking activities/tools, and we

started using Mind Mapping at the work place. Mind Mapping is more  intuitive, more creative, more visual and its more engaging. We go  through to few frequent classes and also schools and collect information  about learning in AR.     Application      We asked the teacher to write down few things that they would

love to have in an app while they are using one. We also gave them the  freedom to install other competitive e-commerce app so that they can  figure out some loopholes if there are any. This is Stage 1 and this is an  individual task. In Stage 2, we then formed 5 groups each of 5 members  and asked them to do a group discussion and asked them to come to a  common approach of what they already have in their individual sheets.  Meanwhile, our developers were analysed each team’s common  approach.  At the end of Stage 2, each of the 5 teams had 1 common list  of features that they want in an app. In Stage 3, our own team of  programmers were involved in the discussions of the 5 list we have got.

Insight      What we as team learned in this process is that, there are different

ways of visualizing your needs. Every individual we called in has a  different way of approaching to learning with AR. Some would don’t  want an AR headset. There are numerous approaches and that being  said, not every approach a demand can be actually implemented in the  actual development because the currently obtained data may or may not  match the analytical data that we already had from past also the  difficulty of actual programming can’t also be ignored     Approach

The only way out of it is to try and see if the student actually love

the new features in the app and asking them for the feedback. They  can quickly give new insights about the new problems that are  occurring in the app or the new features they want in the next update.
