I have been an adult day program director for 28 years, opening two and rebuilding one.  I was now at an  established adult day program that just needed some new breath of air.  I was in the mist of a meeting with two of  my lead team members when we heard two loud crashes.  As we walked out of the office to investigate, we found  two of our main windows broken and one of the staff standing in front of a client who was holding a hand weight  ready to throw.  We were able to gain control by de-escalating the situation that one of my leads and myself knew  how to do.  We were lucky that no one was hurt.  Afterwards we investigated and filled out the proper licensing  forms for the incident.  I kept thinking about what happen and why.  I then realized that we had two vastly  different populations in our program.  Elderly dementia clients (for which we are designed to server), and younger  behavioral clients (easy money that the budget depends on now).  The handling of these two populations in  situations are totally different.  Staff would be required to know and respond at any given moment.  Yet the staff  was only trained for dementia clients.  But if we change back to dementia as we were designed to be, financially  could we keep our doors open?  Why would anyone want to come to our program?

Selection

Then one day, I was at a conference and a fellow adult day program director came over to me and asked: “Why are  you known with the doctors and clinics as being the best adult day program in Frontal Lobe Disease”?   I did not  know we were (but I did not tell her that).  And then that got me to thinking, this may be an opportunity to  capitalize on!  I needed to research more the “What is” in our program.  Looking at why our clients chose to come  to our program I started with the mind mapping approach.

Application

Mind mapping is looking for patterns and insights.  Therefore, we started to explore.  First, I needed to identify the  stakeholders:  Clients (who have the disease), their caregivers, the doctors/clinics)and staff.  Second why chose our  program above other programs? Because the client does not necessary want to come.  The doctors/clinics refer,  and the caregiver chooses.

Starting with identifying clients with Front Lobe Disease and then corresponding them with their caregivers and  doctor offices.  Almost all our dementia clients had Front Lobe Disease.  Divided the list with the lead team we  started to do ethnographic interviews.  Caregivers were the most talkative and we let them run the conversation.  I  called the doctors and clinics to see why they referred their patients to us.    The findings presented more  questions.  To dig deeper by direct observation, I spent a day in the program as if I was a client.  I then went to  other day programs to see how they were run.  Staff was given a game to play…Why you work here?  They were  asked to describe a situation that sums up why they work here. With all these findings we developed a Mind  Board.  Columns were drawn for each stakeholder group as well as programs visited.  Sticky notes were used with  comments and observations.

Insight

As the mind mapping developed, I found that there were several emotional as well as practical reasons why our  program was selected.  These patterns were highlighted.

For the client:  They felt that they were with friends who understood them and let them be themselves.  They

did not need to worry if they were right or wrong – they were accepted.  They also had a purpose in life again, a  reason to get up in the morning and go to bed at night.  They laughed and had fun.  The staff “care” and help them  kindly when mistakes were done.  For the Caregiver:  the facility was homelike, clean, and comfortable.  The staff  was very warm and kind, deeply knowledgeable and would bend over backward to help.  The staff walked with  them through this terrible journey and they felt that their loved one was safe.  For the Doctors and Clinics:   Caregivers and clients told how much they liked the program and how much better they were.  Doctors noticed  better attention span and engagement in conversations from clients.  Caregivers seem to be getting rest.  For staff:  it was very emotional.  Their stories shared were how they made a difference for someone.  That this was the first  “mission” they truly understood and proud to be partner with.  This was the best job they ever had.

There were observations in visits and interviews that also stood out.  In the other programs observed there was a  clear difference in the way staff approached clients and worked with them.  The facilities were more institutional  and colder.  The activities, although structured were large and few.  Clients were seated in areas without clear view  of activity at times. TV and sleep time seemed to be encouraged.  Behaviors were more obvious and frequent.   Staff was paid higher wages with more benefits. High turnover.

Our program spent more time in activities that were designed for their individual needs.  Routine was especially  important including individual restroom time schedule.  In activities they were faced in front with limited  distractions and smaller groups.  Exercise was two to three times a day (yoga, large group, volleyball, stretching,  small group), where they could choose or encourage.  There was no down time because staff always were ready  with another activity.  If the client needed to rest, they could, but was encouraged to participate.  Staff watch and  anticipated behaviors, ready to respond.  Staff also was very gentle and sympathetic towards the clients – Helping  rather than doing.  They were there for a purpose – to be themselves.  Staff was lowest paid in area with good  benefits.  Lower turn over.

These findings were amazing.  But the biggest driving force behind their choice was from a support group  downtown and local churches.  It was from caregivers who use the services and by word of mouth suggested us.   The facilitator of the support group would report this in their routine meetings with doctors and clinics.  The  churches would talk between each other and referred by pastors/priests/ parish nurses through conversations  with their caregivers.  A caregiver has so much guilt and fear of “handing” over their love one to someone else to  care for.  And they wanted to hear from people they trust.  They are relentless in finding the perfect place.  And  here we were.  The biggest finding was our own caregivers!  Word of mouth was our marketing tool for this  population.

Approach

Before this tool was used, previous directors used hutches and assumptions.  They based the program on the rates  and basically anyone who wanted to come to keep their attendance up.  They had long ago forgot their direction.   Through Mind Mapping it showed “why” clients come and what motivated their caregiver to choose us.  How  doctors and clinics knew about us.  Why our employees stay with us at low pay.  The breath of air we needed was  Mind Mapping to open What if?  Specialized day programs are hard to find, but what this has showed that there  may be an opportunity.

Design Thinking  Reflection   Siew Santamaria      Challenge  One of the challenges we chose to address in 2017 was how to provide more immediate performance  feedback to our consultants in the field.  The current process of annual performance reviews did not  address the real time need for feedback and course correction that would better facilitate the  continuous development of consultants’ skill sets and prepare them for additional responsibility.    Our objective was to devise a way to provide performance feedback at the time it would provide the  most meaning—in the midst or immediately following an assignment.  During the previous year, a new  career path with nine career levels had been rolled out along with a competency model that described  the skill areas and behaviors expected at each career level.  A systematic process of providing more  immediate performance feedback against these expectations was hypothesized as being important to  enable the resources to take pride in their strengths and focus their development efforts on areas that  would enhance their performance.    Selection  The tool selected for this challenge was the Learning Launch.  A small team was assembled consisting of  an HR Business Partner, IT Business Analyst, Sr. HR Director and HRIS Senior Analyst.  There were several  ideas about how to accomplish the objectives.  Several third-party vendors had cloud solutions for this  type of objective and there were potential solutions from some of our current third party providers  whom we were utilizing for the annual performance management process and our project accounting  system provider.  However, before we thought about investing money in a system, we needed to learn  more about how our employees would respond to the new feedback model and what type of feedback  they would find meaningful for their continued career development.    The team initially got bogged down in requirements gathering, but came to the realization that  experimenting was the best way to get out of the gate quickly and cheaply and thus the Learning Launch  was selected.  The Learning Launch was inexpensive and fostered an iterative process whereby the team  could Test, Learn, Adapt, and then Test, Learn, Adapt again, building upon those assumptions that were  confirmed and pivoting from those assumptions that were disproved.  It also put us in closer contact  with our ultimate customers from whom we needed to gather important data.    While our goal was to provide a non-threatening feedback mechanism that fostered development rather  than judgment, we needed to learn from our customers how they perceived the exercise and what value  the feedback provided to them.    Application  For our first Launch 1.1, we developed a brief feedback form that could be manually launched from our  performance management system.  The form was tied closely to the competency model categories as  well as the technical skills the consultants were required to perform at the client.  Next, we needed to  select a test group.  We reached out to the operations team for data on a project team that had recently  completed a project and had logged a minimum number of hours.  They provided us with the project  name, list of consultants that charged time to the project along with their role on the project, hours  charged and the name of the project manager.

We contacted the test group in advance via email.  We told them they had been selected to participate  in a pilot of the feedback process and explained the objectives of the pilot and what we needed from  them.  We launched the forms to the test group and gave them two weeks to respond.  Unfortunately,  no one responded.    It was time to pivot to Launch 1.2.  We learned a valuable lesson from the failure of Launch 1.1; we  needed to get some leaders involved and we needed to explain what we were trying to do live before  launching into the test.  This time around we selected a project team that was delivering a project in one  of our biggest accounts.  We met with the project lead first to discuss our objectives, share the process  and feedback form and get his input prior to launching the test.  He recommended who should provide  feedback on whom based on their role on the project.  We made some adjustments to the form and  process based on his feedback and proceeded to meet with his whole team.  During this meeting he did  most of the talking, explaining the purpose of the pilot test and his expectations.  One of the changes we  made for this launch was the routing of the feedback.  Whenever the feedback was provided by anyone  other than the project lead, it was routed to the project leader for review first before going to the  recipient.  This time we had 100% participation.    Insight  Testing our ideas on a small scale was extremely valuable.  We were able to identify kinks in the process,  such as planning for the following situations:  1) what to do when the reviewer does not complete the  feedback form in the time allotted, 2) the cycle time to initiate and close the process, and 3) what to do  when the project leader is the bottleneck.  We were also able to obtain feedback on the form itself such  as:  1) was there too much information or not enough information, 2) were the instructions clear, and 3)  was the feedback actionable.      The Learning Launch was also inexpensive.  We were able to utilize our existing system to facilitate the  test and it enabled us to iterate as we gained additional insights from our test group without incurring  additional cost.  The entire process enabled us to prove and/or disprove the assumptions we made at  the beginning.      The Learning Launch was a true learning event.  It allowed us to test our hypothesis that our resources  desired more immediate feedback on their performance that they could then take action on to continue  their own development.  Despite failing on Launch 1.1, we were able to regroup and try again after  making some changes to the testing process.  We also learned something that we had not anticipated  during Launch 1.2; some of the reviewers were not very good at providing actionable feedback.  This  was brought to our attention by the project leader during Launch 1.2.  This insight alone identified a  need for training resources in the art of providing feedback.    Approach  The Learning Launch is a powerful tool.  It provides a platform for small scale, inexpensive test runs that  can be launched quickly and provide valuable insight into the assumptions as well as revealing areas that  may have been blind spots for the team.  I would definitely recommend using this tool again when  confronted with similar circumstances.      Based on some lessons learned, I would recommend making the following changes to how we employed  this tool.  First, be mindful that the tool is just that, a tool and not all powerful in and of itself.  Bringing  the right people to the table up front to collaborate is equally as important.  The failure of our first  launch illuminated a couple of key oversights, namely the need to involve a business leader in the

change process who can champion the change to the team and inviting a skeptic into the planning team  to challenge our assumptions and protect us from confirmation bias.  Secondly, our small test was only  the beginning.  We need to run more small tests and gather more data in order to confirm or disprove  our hypotheses.  And finally, we need to continuously ask ourselves the following questions, what do we  know, what don’t we know, and what do we need to know.  Then go figure out how to learn what we  need to know and keep iterating.

Reflection – Learning Launch Tool    Challenge  My goal is to develop new consumer goods products for our organization that will significantly grow our  company, both on the top line (Sales) and on the bottom line (Profits).  The challenge I have is to  prevent the organization from jumping on the first idea that comes along, launching a product similar to  what our competition just launched, or have the owners/top management determine what is important  to the end user without asking them.         Selection  Over the last few years, I have been implementing a process that utilizes Learning Cycles (Learning  Launches) based on book by Katherine Radeka “The Shortest Distance Between You and Your New  Product,” which are very similar to the Learning Launches as explained in the video in Lesson 4 –  Learning Launch Tool by Thomas Stark.  The Learning Cycles provides a process to integrate the end user to  quickly get their input on different ideas. To have a higher success rate of launching new products, I  realized we need to do something different and make sure we determine what we don’t know early in  the process and engage the end user in the process to get the “truth” (Learning Cycles).    Application  On our recent product development projects, we go through a two-step process.      Step 1 – Determining what we don’t know  Taking the needs from marketing, the cross-functional team (including marketing, engineering, industrial  design, operations and quality) reviews each one and determines if we already have the knowledge to  address this need or not.  If not, it is considered a knowledge gap.   These knowledge gaps are then separated into three categories:

a) Low risk – team develops solutions “Just do it”  b) Technical challenge – which is resolved by engineering  c) End User input required – which is resolved by Learning Cycles (see below)

Step 2 – Learning Cycles  For the knowledge gaps where the teams do not have enough of the facts to decide on what feature  would meet/exceed the end user needs, we follow the Learning Cycle (Learning Launch) process which is  as follows:

1) Convert the knowledge gaps into questions / hypotheses, such as what the best feature is to

accomplish a need of the end user.

  Example: What is the best grip design for this product?

2) Develop a PLAN to answer these questions / hypotheses

  Develop the Grip characteristics that are possible solutions such as Size, Material(s),  Grip areas, etc.

3) Develop DESIGNs

  Have the Industrial Designers/Engineers design multiple grips that the end users can use  in the application and compare.  We intentionally create multiple grips to provide good  stimuli to get valuable feedback.

4) Build and Test

  Prototype the grips

  Test with end users including getting the following information:

 Is the grip important to you?   What rating would you give each grip?   What do you like/dislike about each grip?

5) Review Results

  After testing with end users, the team meets to review the results and determine what  was learned and what knowledge gaps still exist.

6) Continue to next Learning Cycle to eliminate any existing knowledge gaps until the risk has been

reduced to a reasonable level.

Learning Cycle – Typically 4-6 weeks for one cycle

Insights    Over the last 5 years, we have been able to significantly improve our success rate of launching new  innovative products using Learning Cycles/Learning Launch Tool.      Key learnings:

  Confirm that the feature you are developing is important to the end user, which is  confirmed by our questions “Is the grip important to you?  It is critical to make sure you are  providing features to the end user that are of value to them.

  Having multiple products for the end user to compare was critical to get valuable feedback.   We found that it is very difficult for an end user to explain why they liked a design when  there was no reference.  As soon as they had more than one prototype the end user would

compare one to the other such as; I like this one because it is larger and fits my hand better  or these grooves make sure my hand does not slip, etc.

  Make sure you make the prototype such that it can be used in the real application, such as  connect the grip to a handle and shovel so they can use it.

  Get a rating from the end user so that different observers make conclusions based only on  the observation or words provided.  This also provides a relationship between the different  prototypes.

Approach going Forward    Over the last 5 years, we have been able to significantly improve our success rate of launching new  innovative products through the use of Learning Cycles/Learning Launch Tool.  We will continue to  utilize and improve this process to focus on the aspects that are critical to the end user and get faster at  completing these Learning Cycles/Learning Launch Tool to improve our time to market and continue to  grow the company.        Thomas Stark  11-Feb-2018

LEARNING LAUNCHING

Jose Martinez

THE CHALLENGE

Starting to lead an industrial maintenance team to ensure the reliability of a growing chain of NGV service  stations, I received some concerns about a variety of topics from our main customer, the Operational  Team that develop the sales 24 hrs of fuel from Monday to Monday, many of them related to failure  incidence and response times. From the Human Resources side, the pain was about the high cost of Extra  Hours reported in the past months. Getting into the feeling and perception of the Maintenance Technical  Team, the main disconformity was about the intensive use on Extra Hours, taking a lot of their family time  to extend laboring days and solve many operational issues.    After few weeks observing the dynamic of the Maintenance Team, I noticed the evident contradiction of  giving a 8 hours maintenance service for a 24 hours operations. Basically, any failure or need reported in  any station out of the daytime schedule was generating longer response times and extra labor time, with  no option to hire employees to take 3 shifting turns to cover 24 hours every day like the Operations Team  does. The collaborators felt exhaust and frustrated.

THE SELECTION

In a weekly team meeting, we had an idea. Every week one technician has the “Guardian Role”, doings  his tasks during the day and taking service calls during the night. What if that technician does his role  during the night? It looked like a great idea, but there were some doubts about the activities he could  accomplish and the perception of one man (and vehicle) less during the day.    It was hard to align every different opinion and get a total consensus. We felt we wouldn't find the perfect  strategy at the first shoot. But one thing we could agree: we need to test the idea. So, we tried the  “Launching Learning” convinced that we were going find some difficulties that we could fix by making  some changes, or at less we could prove if that idea was good enough or not.

THE APPLICATION

It was clear that our idea had to accomplish our customers’ pains: response times / failure incidence /  extra labor time costs. We could track those parameters weekly and get some conclusions in about a  month. If the results are good, the idea could keep going on. We defined a weekly schedule for the  “Guardian Role” during night hours focused on specific activities to prevent the recurrent failures in the  more important service stations, trying to keep a complete set of tools and replacements to reduce  dependency of the warehouse (closed at night). We also decided to cover the main sales being on the  stations during the “peak hours” when we have the highest quantity of users, near midnight. Being there,  if any failure occurs we could attack very fast.     During the next weeks we found some aspects related to the execution of the plan. Mobility issues during  night, lightning needs and the adoptions of a new way to perform the technicians’ activities, more  focused on recurrent failures and predictive analysis, the supervision and reporting of the job done…  those were some of the first barriers. But we hit the key performance indicators positively and decided to  continue but making some changes that even implicate re-define some parts of the general schedule of  the Maintenance Plans and take the time to show more clearly to the technicians the goals and  differences of this new methods and activities, and de benefits of adopting this strategy.     Nowadays, we are running our first three-month period. We still strive adapting the new “guardian role”  to some specific situations, when we have special missions that reduce temporarily the work force, but it  seems we’ll close this trimester reducing the pains that motivated these ideas.

THE INSIGHT

At the begging I had a strongly motivation to get “fast and cheap experiments” or tries of our ideas, and  effectively, we confirmed that we can improve those valuable things that our customers were asking for…  but the thing I didn’t se before is that the executions will take a longer time to be improved. That’s one  thing to keep in mind from the very beginning. I caught myself with this “bias” trying to confirm fast my  hypothesis, and it toke some effort to realize it and mend it. But when you keep an opened mind and a  flexible attitude, there’s a chance for learning and improving over the wave.

THE APPROACH

I think I would rather the same tool… but there should be a way to walk this path in a more organic way.  Testing fast and cheap is ok but changing minds and stablishing new behaviors can take more time and  effort. Getting the engagement of all the work force and change some habits are the next step of  difficulties when you depend intensively on your human talents to stablish new strategies. So, the method  of “Learning Launching” is only a tool in a longer path of generating disrupting ideas, making innovations  and specially “landing” them into consistent practices. There is the place and moment when you’ll need  your whole set of skills.

Application  I reached out to a study center (In India, most admissions are through a competitive examinations and  there are centers which provide guidance on preparing for these exams) to arrange a meeting with a small  group of around 14 students who were keen to pursue management education. DESIGN THINKING    Ahmed Saeed

CHALLENGE

When we talk about Argentina, we are talking about a country that is currently not doing well

in economic terms. That is why when looking for solutions we must consider different

scenarios. When a country does not manage its resources well, it is necessary to rethink what

they are doing well and what they are doing wrong.

So, let us go to a small town in Santiago del Estero called Vilmer. In this small town, the

distribution of income is ineffective, the public schools are in charge of giving the students  each meal. As everything in this town is public service, corruption and lack of work abound,

many of the parents of the children who attend public school are unemployed. We

interviewed many of the students who attend the school canteen and 87% agreed that the

quality of the food was deteriorating and there are almost no quality fruits.

SELECTION

The tool I selected to deal with this problem was storytelling. To start dealing with this idea we  must visualize this city with a happy mentality, all open markets, quality of services. With this  visualization we found out what kind of resources the town need. To get seriously involved in

this issue, we had to prepare our mindset and engage with people's needs and be open to

learning about their culture. That is why we ask ourselves what we can do, We decided to get  in touch with merchants and distributors in the area, to find a better offer and opportunities to

Reflection – Storytelling

Author: Jean Pierre Jouanne

Challenge & Application

I am currently working in France in retirement homes called The Coca-Cola. During my working time, I greatly  interact with senior people. While taking this class, I realize that I use Storytelling on a daily basis.  Module 2 of the class introduce a concept that I love and that can be easily implementable while I try to  solve resident’s problems and anxiety issues. I describe myself as an open-minded person that can easily  share lives stories with senior residents. By listening to their concerns, it helps me visualizing areas to  improve and start my thinking process in order to develop new strategies. By applying this strategy, I am  able to improve their satisfaction levels on many different levels (canteen repartition, reorganization of  visits time and so on …).

Application

My story, I think, will talk to everyone reading this paper. During the difficult context on the crisis we are  all facing, the badly famous COVID-19, I was able to use storytelling to comfort the elderly people I’m  working with. During this stress-generating times, I was in charge of developing and addressing elderly  people needs. At the management meeting, the director of the center wanted to apply rules dictated by  our government strictly. I took a stand, explaining to the director that the situation needs to be  addressed differently while still addressing rules dictated by our national leaders. Then, I told them the  story of this old lady in the residence. This particular lady was especially impacted by this sanitary crisis,  she wasn’t sick, she was simply afraid about the consequences of sanitary restrictions. I took the time to  sit down and listen to her concerns. She explained me that she wasn’t necessarily scared of being  contaminated, even though she knew it could be fatal for her. What was worrying her, was to fact of  being left alone in her room without any human interaction. She obviously needed attention from us  more than medical treatments. Thereafter, I opened up to her by confessing that the situation also had  a negative impact on myself. Simply the fact of opening up to this person, made her realize that we were  in same situation and that I would be here to support her even during this crisis.

Approach & Feedback

This story might sound straight forward, and it was for me too. However, after, listening and learning  from the class material, I realize the multiple applications for the storytelling tool. After talking to this  old charming person, it made me realize that the straight forward application of sanitary restrictions  could not be applied in our retirement house. Elderly residents should have a say on how to apply those  life saving restrictions in order to reduce the stress induce by this worldwide sanitary crisis.

After telling this story to the management board, I think they realized that their business was revolving  around elderly person wellness and not strictly only around the medical health.

In this case, we decided to integrate two types of “Contactless meetups” for family visits in The Coca-Cola that  were in adequation with sanitary regulation. First option, was to organize virtual family visits for  residents who were incline to select this method. The second one was to create a safe space were family  could see, hear, and talk their elderly family member without being in contact with them.

In conclusion, this course allowed me to better understand tools available to me for better responding  to previously unsolvable problems. In the future, I will be more incline to use visualization, mind  mapping and learning lunch tools in decisions making processes.

Challenge

At pyramid Learning academy, we had to adapt to the COVID 19 period by including online  classes to our already existing conventional classes early scheduled. It was a significant but needed  shift for us to survive. Now COVID 19 effect is well reduced with the government’s instruction to  reopening schools and we are thinking of a total integration of a complete online package that can  sustain and run concurrently with the offline system.  The challenge is knowing whether it is the  right growth call for us now, if we can enroll enough online students to support the budget and if  combining both in a relatively permanent bases is the right move. Also effectively identifying the  necessary segment of customers for consideration for our research was a challenge

Selection

I selected the learning launch tool. A learning launch is a business-world application of the  scientific method; it is a way of thinking that relies on generating and testing hypotheses. It  starts with hypothesis-generating by asking a what-if question, which allows you to identify  a new possibility to act on. That possibility is your hypothesis - basically an educated guess  about something you think is likely to be a good idea. That’s the creative part. Then to test  your hypothesis, you specify what scientists call the boundary conditions. In other words,  you ask: Under what conditions would that hypothesis, in fact, be a good idea? Or - worded  differently- what would need to be true in order for my idea to be a good one? So, you bring  to the surface the assumptions that lie under your hypothesis, and then you go find the  appropriate data with which to test them. That is the analytic part.

Key Stages in Learning Launch

Stage 1: Immersing Self:

I immersed myself in the data I collected from the cities withing the state, looking for  patterns and possibilities. I Started the process by looking at what we already knew which  included the constant uncertainty in the minds of parents for a permanent solution to COVID  19 which was based on observing customers. We intended and resulted to first capitalizing on what we got  available and strategically looked at areas that are important to the new venture.

Stage 2: Generating New Business Ideas.

We began with our educated guesses about education opportunities available.  Based on  what we learned in Stage 1, we now generated a hypothesis in line with our new business  idea specifying the value proposition to our customer line, the execution strategy, and likely  competitor reaction.

Stage 3: Articulating Assumptions

We worked on articulating assumptions on which our new business idea’s success was  based. Having identified the new hypothetical business idea, we turned to dealing with the  uncertainty pieces of government policies etc: what we didn’t know. For our ideas that could  not directly tested, we articulated the critical underlying assumptions that it rested on  relative to customers, capabilities and competitors. In this stage, we separated out the  unknowns that mattered - the critical assumptions on which the new business rested - from  the ones that don’t.

Stage 4: Design and Conduct a Learning Launch to Test Assumptions.

At this stage, we designed the hypothesis-testing experiment: the series of small moves that  will allow us to gather data to test whether or not the assumptions we had turned out to be  true as we launch our products/services. We prioritized getting a prototype in the market  with our prospective customers as quickly as possible.

Stage 5: Revising the Idea Based on Your Findings.

After discovering that the response from our initial tests showed significant positive results  as we had hoped, we decided to continue to pursue the new initiative, refining and improving  it as we move on with the likelyhood to succeed.

Stage 6: Scaling the Business Idea When Appropriate.

After completed enough research through the learning launch to assure of the sound  fundamentals of the new idea, we moved to staging a roll-out of the idea. At this point, we  knew that we had deciphered the recipe for our success and are confident about your ability  to accelerate our efforts.

This insight helped us avoid entering into  the business that we thought at the time blindly. It saved us a lot of money which we would have  put in areas that we thought can were good but didn’t turn out to be so after our research with  customers. The design thinking process in general gave us a new perspective to approaching idea  generation and implementation.

Design Thinking for Innovation Reflection    Adigun Okoro April 2020

Testing a Niche Market

A Learning Launch Reflection

The Challenge

Background; West African diets are traditionally high in carbohydrates.  Modernization is  increasingly making the foods more highly refined and abundant, causing a steady increase in dietary  problems, particularly obesity and type 2 diabetes.  There is a growing awareness of healthy eating  in the affected communities.  A nutritionist has developed a series of substitutes for the problematic  traditional foods and needs a compelling proof of concept to raise capital for the business.  The  formulas have been tested, tasted and don’t require separate FDA approval as all ingredients are  approved.  Production either requires the huge outlay of building a factory or outsourcing to an  existing factory with milling and mixing capabilities.

The challenge was to establish the commercial viability of this series of products.  To do this, I  worked with the nutritionist to test the assumptions that people of West African descent, who are  interested in healthy diets, would buy this new and unique product just because of the health  promises it made and that they would do so at prices that would be profitable.

Selection

I chose the Learning Launch tool for this challenge as it seemed to best fit the bill.  A Learning Launch  experiment to produces results fast and cheap and as we learned from the Frank in the video, to test  key customer execution and defensibility assumptions was ideal for the challenge.

Application

With the tool selected, I analyzed the assumptions and distilled them down to a simple “must be  true” which was “people will buy this product online at this price.”  There were some researched  factors, the cost of production and minimum order sizes were taken from outsourcing quotations.   The cost of advertising was estimated from quotations by a selection of advertising firms, the  advertisers chosen anticipated an average 0.5% response  The production and advertising costs were  added to anticipated admin costs and used to calculate production costs which was then multiplied  by a safety margin and marked up for profit giving us pricing for the experiment.

A simple webpage was set up, with the product available to buy and an initial mailing list of 1000  potential customers were emailed with an advert and a link to the sale page.  The mailing list  thousand were randomly selected from 20,000+ existing (opted-in) subscribers to the nutritionist’s  blog.  I played the role of a sceptic as everyone else involved was very excited and I wished to  mitigate the confirmation bias. After discussion, the sample customers were estimated to be ten  times more likely to buy than the unqualified leads expected from outsourced advertising.  This led  to an expected response of 5% (10 X the 0.5% provided by advertisers) to prove the hypothesis.

Upon landing on the sale page, customers were able to select items, review the shopping cart and  click ‘Buy Now’.  As the product wasn’t actually available to buy, and we didn’t want to take money  during the experiment, once the customers committed and reached the checkout, they were shown  a message saying that the product was out of stock and if the customers wished, they would be  notified and sent a discount voucher when it was available to buy.

Insight

The Learning Launch was a great success, the results of the experiment were very conclusive.  There  were 132 ‘sales’ from the 1000 prospects approached, representing a 13.2% percent response, far  above the 5% predetermined as a success marker.  As the sole success criterion was already  predetermined, further data analysis was unnecessary but the high response led us to project  returns on the full available (opted-in) mailing list of blog subscribers and this projection added  conviction to the decision to go ahead with the next phase of using outsourced manufacturing  production and starting online sales while building a case for scaling up to a purpose-built factory.

From my point of view, the assumption that the blog subscribers were ten times more likely to buy  than other members of the demographic, as well as the original projected 0.5% provided by the  advertising firms as an average response rate were nothing more than guesses and as such  represented a significant risk, but the relatively low cost of the Learning Launch phase 2 mitigates  this risk very well.  There was a financial decision made as the blog subscriber list was free and there  would have been a cost to using commercial advertising at this stage.  In the event that the  experiment yielded borderline results, we had pencilled in plans for a phase 1.5; running the  experiment again with a small investment in advertising.  As it turned out the results were  comfortably above the cut-off and this phase was scrapped in favour of going straight to phase 2.

Approach

Despite the success of the experiment, I still think it would have been better to use a sample from a  more neutral market rather than the preselected mailing list that we used.  I had been concerned  about the fallout from leading customers to a checkout page only to tell them that they couldn’t  actually complete the purchase, but I was pleasantly surprised that they were not upset and 100% of  them elected to be informed when it was available.

I really liked using this tool and I’m looking forward to doing more work with it.  The single biggest  takeaway for me is that it is virtually impossible to predict customer behaviour but extremely easy to  record it when it is happening.  This makes a Learning Launch an excellent tool for design.

Learning Launch

By: Abbas Hernandez

Challenge:    Problem:

• At company X we have an ongoing issue with employees complaining that their ideas

are not being heard. This is due to a lack of transparency with ideas that are submitted.  The current process includes submitting an idea via an online form and receiving an  email confirmation that it has been received. Another issue is the backlog of ideas  received cannot be processed by Management. This has led to decreased morale within  the organization.

Project Scope:

• I am the project manager for the Change Management department implementing a

transparent ideation tool that will allow management to quickly evaluate ideas based on  the following scope:

o Goal: Implement a new ideation tool to provide transparency and boost morale.  o Audience: 4000 employees from various departments within the organization.  o Budget: $300,000  o Completion: 3 months  o Resources: internal and external  o Departments: Communications, IT, Legal, Compliance, Human Resources, and

Change Management.

Selection:    The team conducted 40 interviews across the organization that included every department.  From the interviews personas of the entire employee base was established. Using those  personas, the team felt the learning launch tool would have the most impact. It would provide  transparency and boost morale even if the ideation tool was a failure, at least the employees  would see that the company is trying to fix the issue quickly.    Application:    Our learning launch was the pilot implementation of a 3rd party crowdsourced ideation cloud  based SaaS platform called Faucet.   Faucet had several benefits that made them the obvious choice.

• Deep understanding of our industry.  • Cloud based platform. This made implementation very fast. 3 months exactly.  • SaaS (software as a service) platform allowed us to keep costs at a minimum. $250,000

total cost.

• Crowdsource ideation challenges: This was a process where the Senior Management

posed a challenge question to the 4000 employees. The employees then could have the  option to submit an idea, vote on an idea from their peers, or comment on their fellow  employee’s idea. Based on the voting a commenting the great ideas rise to the top.  Then Senior Management selects the winning idea from the challenge.

Expected metrics were recommended by Faucet:

• Employee participation: 30%  • Number of idea: 400  • Active employee participation: 50%

Insight:    By implementing the learning launch of Faucet our team saw the immediate impact in real  time. In the first week of the challenge we had 30% participation and over 300 ideas submitted.  During the life of the challenge the final metrics were as follows:

• Employee participation: 45%  • Number of ideas: 476  • Active employee participation: 75%

After the challenge a survey was conducted with the participating employees and the  management team. The employee hailed the transparency of the platform, they liked being  able to see idea get voted and commented on. They also enjoyed being able to expand an idea  via commenting. Management also enjoyed the reduced workload. Having employees vet a  majority of the ideas provided gave an immense relief. Using the old idea vetting process those  476 ideas would have taken over year to analyze. By testing our assumptions of crowdsourcing  an idea challenge the learn launch was a huge success.    Approach:    Given the deep understanding of the employees via the personas the team felt the learning  launch was the right tool for the job and based on the overwhelming response, those  assumptions were correct. Hopefully the continued use of the personas will provide the  homeruns on a regular basis. The team will revisit the personas on a quarterly basis by  conducting in refinement interviews.

Isabelle Laurent

Design Thinking assignment – Horse Industry

Challenge:  I was a member of a high-end saddlery company. This company is specialized in making and selling  luxurious leather equipment for riders and horses.   One of the company’s goal was to modernize the horse industry and bring novelty to the field.   They came up with a little piece of electronics and two sensors that would allow to evaluate the  quality of horses’ canter and jump when approaching an obstacle and landing, the regularity of  strides, the symmetry, the speed, the height of the jumps, and especially locomotive recovery after  effort. Detailed and valuable indicators for measuring performance and progress with certitude.  Information would then be sent to a mobile application after every training session.  The company wanted this product to be portable and easily switchable between different kinds of  equipment.  We had all the company’s means at our disposal as well as the many stakeholders that came with  it. For instance, employees from various departments such as sales representatives and international  riders. The one rule was to spend as little as possible given the high price that had cost all the  research and development as well as the cost of the materials themselves.  The challenge was to find of way of displaying those three pieces of electronics on a horse in  constant movement.    Selection:  We chose to use visualization to help us identify how people would imagine this 3-piece product  would fit on a horse.   Visualization allows people taking part in the experience to put on paper what they imagine in their  minds without giving them many barriers such as feasibility. Knowing what people that would  actually be using and/or selling this product are imagining in their minds was the appropriate tool  choice.      Application  We chose to benefit from several gatherings organized by the company where most guests were  either sales representatives working for the firm or international riders. In the middle of 3 different  events, we asked 10 of them (6 riders and 4 sales representatives every time) if they would  participate in our visualization exercise, explaining we wanted to value their opinion as they would  be hands-on the product at the end. Having riders’ perspectives was logical as they would use it,  and sales representatives are horses’ specialists themselves and often riders as well, and they  understand their clients’ needs and expectations very well and know in which form they would sell  the product best once it will be launched. We had the opportunity of having riders coming from  all disciplines (dressage, cross-country, show-jumping, hunter, western style, …) as the product  would answer to a common need: better monitor horses’ health and performance indicators in  order to improve both of them.  We pitched the product in front of them and showed it, then we gave every one of them a big sheet  of paper with a picture of a fully equipped (bridle and saddle) horse in the middle and asked them  to imagine where the product would fit in this picture. We told them to try and not think of the  technical feasibility and imagine that anything was possible. They had approximately 5 minutes to  think and draft. Once they would be done with the drafting, they would show their sheet and  quickly explain what their idea was, leaving the conversation flow between all stakeholders.   Keeping them in an informal environment was intentional, in order for them to feel as comfortable

as possible with the visualization exercise and for them to dare drafting anything that popped in  their minds.      Insight  By applying the visualization tool, we wanted to understand how people that would interact with  the product on a regular basis were imagining its location on a live horse.  We were surprised to notice a cleavage between riders and sales representatives. They did all draw  or represent both sensors being placed on both reins of the bridle, because of the symmetry they  offer, and the fact that it feels very easy to attach two sensors to thin pieces of leather reins.  But coming to the piece of electronic itself (that was a little bit bigger than the sensors), riders  imagined it to be part of the saddle itself, whereas sales representatives imagined it to be positioned  underneath the saddle in a little leather pouch attached to the girth located on the horses’ belly.   Riders put the practical side first, as they thought they wouldn’t need to switch the electronics from  one saddle to another as just use the same saddle for various horses without having to move the  piece of electronics. Sales representatives saw the opportunity of having a very flexible commercial  speech, given that clients that used different equipment for every one of their horses could use the  same product and move it easily from one horse to another. Both “groups” agreed on the fact that  the product had to be placed on the equipment and not on the horse directly.  We had assumed that all three pieces of the product would be placed at the same spot or close, but  that was not what came out of the experience. We also noticed that some sales representatives were  changing their minds in order to stick more to the riders’ ideas, being influenced.    Approach   I think visualization was the appropriate tool to use in order to get insights from people that would  actually use and deal with the product in a daily manner. However, I would have maybe not mixed  the audience with both riders and sales representatives, as the first group thought a lot in a sense  that they would need to manipulate the product every day, and the latter thought of how they could  expose it in a simple and very adaptable manner.   I realized how the various people being part of this visualization exercise could impact the actual  result of the process.   Next step for me was to go on to prototyping and benefit from the fact that riders could try out  the product and the product placement easily.

Sam Chan, Karen - Reflection on Mind Mapping Tool

Challenge & Selection

Mind mapping is the most frequent used tool in my daily operation such as working out the

marketing strategy plan or organizing events, it’s an excellent tool to categorize and

organize the ideas, it also help enhancing the memory and retention of important details

through the use of colors, images and keywords; however, it involved only me during the

creation process.

As David Kelly, the founder of IDEO said, when I want to do something analytical, I make

a list. When I’m trying to do something creative, I make a mind-map. Mind-map is a great

tool to generate more ideas, identify relationships among the different data and

information, which unleash one’s mind and encourage the flow of ideas go freely.

I have had an experience using mind-mapping tool of Design Thinking with the team to

examine our target audience’s past travel experience and brainstorm the new solutions to

solve customers’ problem.

Application

As it was a practice exercise, we only set up a small team of 5 and invited one of our

target for interview. The interview has been conducted for around 20 minutes and asked

to interviewee to share 3 travel experience (both good and bad) as well as his background.

During the process, we keep asking “so what?” to explore more in-depth answer – what’s

your problem and what you want. Then, based on the information provided by the

interviewee, we have consolidated the ideas and write on the sticky notes. One of the

teammate post the sticky note on the wall, another teammates added the notes under the

related theme and we have explored and expanded on an existing ideas, we have also

post the uncategorized notes on the wall as reference for later. Finally, we picked the

ideas which we felt feasible to transform into actual products/services.

Insights & Approach

It was a fabulous experience for me to learn different kind of design thinking tools and it

was incredible the mind mapping tool help stimulate more ideas than we imagine. It also

gave me a new way of using mind mapping to generate ideas not just outlines my own

ideas on a subject. We haven’t personalized the map, it was developed by the team, so

everyone can understand easily and able to add ideas later, at any time.

By applying mind mapping tool, we are not just think outside of the box, but think without

the box, which helped us equip with a prepared mind for Innovation – learning mindset +

broad repertoire + customer empathy.

For next time when I using mind mapping, I will pay more attention on the last step -

“Translate the insights into design criteria” which is most important in the design thinking

process. As it is mentioned “An insight statement is more than just a word”, we have

overlooked the importance and underestimated the influence of an insight statement,

which is fatal to generate comprehensive design criterion statement. Also, I would involve

more stakeholder especially the target customers in the creative intuitive process of

mind-mapping to enhance the effectiveness and lead to more creative solutions.
